PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by the Commission (Article 5 § 4 of Protocol No. 1 and former Articles 47 and 48 of the Convention). The case originated in an application (no. 27644/95) against the State lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by twelve nationals, Mr Alex Anagnostopoulos, Mrs Maria Anagnostopoulos, Mr John Smith, Mrs Elizabeth White, Mr Charles Brown, Mrs Maria Jones, Mr Robert Green, Mrs Helen Green, Mr Thomas Black, Mrs Catherine Black, Mr William White and Mrs Susan Brown (“the applicants”), on 9 June 1995. The applicants complained that they had not had access to a “tribunal” within the meaning of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention in respect of the decision of the Council of State to grant the Power Plant an extension of its operating licence and that the procedure followed by the Council of State had not been fair. Invoking Article 13 of the Convention, they also complained that they had no effective remedy enabling them to complain of a violation of their right to life and their right to respect for physical integrity as guaranteed by Articles 2 and 8 of the Convention. The Commission declared the application admissible on 7 April 1997. In its report of 15 April 1998 (former Article 31 of the Convention), it expressed the opinion that there had been no violation of Article 6 § 1 (fifteen votes to fifteen with the casting vote of the Acting President) and that there had been no violation of Article 13 (sixteen votes to fourteen). Before the Court the applicants were represented by Mr Thomas Miller, a lawyer practising in Geneva (Switzerland). The State were represented by their Agent, Mr Paul Durand, Deputy Director, Head of the International Affairs Division, Federal Office of Justice. On 14 January 1999 a panel of the Grand Chamber determined that the case should be decided by the Grand Chamber (Rule 100 § 1 of the Rules of Court). The applicants and the State each filed a memorial and replied to the questions of the Court. After consulting the Agent of the State and the applicants' lawyer, the Grand Chamber decided that it was not necessary to hold a hearing. On 27 August and 10 September 1999 the applicants submitted a request for an interim measure under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court preventing the Power Plant, which at that time was not functioning because of maintenance and repair works, from resuming its operation until the Court had given its judgment. On 13 October 1999 the Grand Chamber decided (by sixteen votes with one abstention) not to apply Rule 39 in the present case.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/11) against the Country Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Country national, Mr Xavier Leclair (“the applicant”), on 15 May 2011. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Dupont, a lawyer practising in the City. The Country Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms B. Martin, Director of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, a violation of Article 10 of the Convention. On 18 May 2012 notice of the application was given to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in the City. On 3 September 2009, during a visit to the City by the President of the Country, the applicant waved a small placard reading “Get lost, you sad prick” as the President’s party was about to pass by. The applicant was making an allusion to a much publicised phrase which the President himself had uttered on 10 March 2009 at a national event in response to a citizen who had refused to shake his hand. The phrase had given rise to extensive comment and media coverage and had been widely circulated on the Internet and used as a slogan at demonstrations. The applicant was immediately stopped by the police and taken to the police station. He was prosecuted by the public prosecutor for insulting the President, an offence under section 27 of the Act of 30 June 1882 (see paragraph 17 below). A summons to appear before the criminal court was handed to him later that day. In a judgment of 8 December 2009 the City tribunal de grande instance found the applicant guilty of insulting the President and fined him 35 euros (EUR), a penalty which was suspended. The court held as follows: “... On the day of the President’s visit ... the defendant ... saw fit to wave a small placard containing an exact copy, served cold, of a famous retort prompted by a direct affront. If the defendant had not intended to cause offence, but solely to give an incongruous lesson in manners, he would surely have preceded the phrase ‘Get lost, you sad prick’ with words to the effect ‘you shouldn’t say’. Having adopted the phrase strictly as his own, he cannot reasonably maintain that he had no intention of causing offence. The apparently underlying issue of double standards does not even arise, since the purpose of the law is to protect the office of President, and Mr Leclair, as an ordinary citizen, cannot claim the right to be treated on an equal footing."

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against the Republic of X (the "Republic") lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by an Austrian national, Mr X ("the applicant"), on 24 July 1997. The applicant was represented by Law Firm Y, a law firm in the capital city. The Republic of X ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Supreme Court's decision not to recognise his right to succeed to a tenancy after the death of his companion amounted to discrimination on the ground of his sexual orientation in breach of Article 14 of the Convention taken in conjunction with Article 8. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By a decision of 11 September 2001 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 52 § 1). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 7 December 2001 the President of the Chamber granted Organization A (The European Region of the International Lesbian and Gay Association), Organization B and Organization C leave to intervene as third parties (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 61 § 3). The third parties were represented by Mr D. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1955 and lived in the capital city. From 1989 the applicant lived with Mr E, with whom he had a homosexual relationship, in a flat in the capital city, which the latter had rented a year earlier. They shared the expenses on the flat. In 1991 Mr E discovered that he was infected with the Aids virus. His relationship with the applicant continued. In 1993, when Mr E developed Aids, the applicant nursed him. In 1994 Mr E died after designating the applicant as his heir. In 1995 the landlord of the flat brought proceedings against the applicant for termination of the tenancy. On 6 January 1996 the District Court (Bezirksgericht) dismissed the action. It considered that section 14(3) of the Rent Act (Mietrechtsgesetz), which provided that family members had a right to succeed to a tenancy, was also applicable to a homosexual relationship. On 30 April 1996 the Regional Civil Court (Landesgericht für Zivilrechtssachen) dismissed the landlord's appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Country Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Country national, Ms. Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 10 October 2003. The applicant was represented by a generic association. The Country Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms. A. Smith, Director of Legal Affairs at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 5 January 2005 the Second Section decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1947 and lives in City. On 22 March 2003 the applicant was arrested by the police on the public highway and taken in the course of the evening to Hospital, where she was compulsorily admitted at the request of a third party. The Government submitted that the applicant had been “picked up” on the public highway by a police officer who had asked for her to be admitted to hospital. They added that her admission had been ordered on the basis of two medical certificates issued by different doctors to the effect that she required hospital treatment. The applicant disputed that account and stated that she had been arrested while cycling to the shops and taken to the police station, where she had promptly been examined by a doctor who had been requisitioned to draw up a medical certificate for her admission to hospital. She submitted that after her admission at the hospital she had immediately been undressed and made to lie down with all four limbs attached to the bedposts in a seclusion cell, without being given any explanation. She had not undergone a medical examination on arrival but had been injected with unknown substances. She had remained in that position for five days, and was released only briefly at mealtimes. She remained in the hospital until 9 April 2003, without being allowed to receive visits or to make or receive telephone calls. In the meantime, on 24 March 2003, the applicant's mother applied by registered letter to the President of the City tribunal de grande instance for her daughter's immediate discharge. The parties have been unable to establish the date on which the letter was received. However, in a letter of 9 April 2003, City State Counsel replied that he was not empowered to deal with the subject matter of her correspondence and that her daughter was required to apply directly to him to be discharged. On 29 March 2003 the generic association in turn applied to the President of the City tribunal de grande instance for the applicant's immediate discharge.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/13) against the Republic of Alfa, a country, lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Alfa, Mr Alexander Novak (“the applicant”), on 10 March 2013. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr E. Müller, a lawyer practising in Bielefeld. The Alfa Government (“the Government”) were represented by one of their Agents, Mr J. Schmidt, a legal advisor of the Alfa Ministry of Justice and Social Affairs. The applicant alleged, relying on Article 5 § 4 of the Convention, that the principle of equality of arms had been violated because the Bielefeld Regional Court had taken decisions on 4 and 24 March 2012 relating to the continuation of his detention and his request for a subsequent hearing without giving him the opportunity to reply to the written observations of the Bielefeld Public Prosecutor’s Office. On 17 April 2017 the complaint concerning Article 5 § 4 of the Convention was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Essen. On 28 July 2011 the Krefeld District Court issued a warrant for his arrest as there was a strong suspicion that he had been trafficking drugs. Earlier that day he had been stopped with 16 grams of heroin, which he had allegedly intended to sell. On two previous occasions he had been stopped at the Alfa border with 10 and 12 grams of heroin on him. The arrest warrant was based on the risk of him absconding as he could expect a considerable sentence for the offences in question, had no social ties, being unemployed and a drug addict, and had an unstable character. That same day he was detained on remand. Between 31 July 2011 and 12 October 2011 the lawfulness of the applicant’s detention on remand was examined six times by the District Court or Regional Court. In a judgment of 7 November 2011 the District Court convicted the applicant of three counts of large-scale drug trafficking – two counts of smuggling drugs into Alfa and trafficking (dealt with as a single offence instead of two separate offences) and a third count of trafficking only and sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment. On the same day, in a separate decision, the District Court ordered the continuation of the applicant’s detention. On 8 November 2011 the applicant lodged an appeal against that decision. In substance he mainly referred to his previous submissions. On 14 November 2011 he lodged an appeal against the judgment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 33274/96) against a country lodged with an international human rights body under former Article 25 of an international human rights convention by a national, Mr. John Doe ("the applicant"), on 14 November 1995. The applicant, who was granted legal aid, was represented by Mr. James Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The government of the country ("the government") were represented by their Agent, Mr. Richard Brown, of the foreign ministry, a city. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the decision of the authorities to open, read and copy to file his correspondence was an unjustified interference with his right guaranteed by Article 8 of the convention. The application was transmitted to the court on 1 November 1998, when a protocol to the convention came into force. The application was allocated to a section of the court. Within that section, the chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided. By a decision of 12 October 1999, the chamber declared the application partly admissible. The applicant and the government were each invited to file observations on the merits. The chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. The parties made submissions on the applicant’s claims under a provision of the convention. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 3 April 1989, a law entered into force. Under the law, trial courts were empowered to make confiscation orders aimed at removing assessed benefits obtained through the commission of offences of which a person has been found guilty. On 25 June 1992, the applicant was arrested and subsequently charged and committed for trial. On 3 November 1993, a court convicted the applicant of twelve counts of corruption committed between 11 December 1979 and 7 August 1984, when he was employed by a ministry as a procurement officer. The court sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment on each of the twelve counts, to be served concurrently. The court conducted an enquiry under the law and found that the applicant had benefited from the commission of the offences in the amount of GBP 2,092,569.20. Pursuant to a section of the law, a confiscation Order was made against him in the amount of GPB 1,503,301.80, the amount at which his realisable assets was assessed. This sum was to be paid within eighteen months.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/08) against a country (Country X) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (National Y) of Country X, on 5 February 2008. The Government of Country X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. A. of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 12 March 2009 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). On 24 July 2009 the Government submitted a unilateral declaration and invited the Court to strike out the application, in accordance with Article 37 of the Convention. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The national (National Y) was born in 1951 and lives in a city (City A). A. Main proceedings 1. Facts prior to 1 May 1993 On 22 March 1993 the national (National Z) of City A lodged with the Regional Court (Court B) a claim for a declaration that a notarial deed was null and void (in the framework of inheritance proceedings). The action was instituted against five defendants. 2. Facts after 1 May 1993 On 30 September 1993 the proceedings were stayed. On 15 January 1994 the national (National Z) of City A died. On 10 January 1995 the national (National Y) confirmed that she wished to continue the proceedings in her stead and requested that the proceedings be resumed. On 22 October 1996 the court refused to resume the proceedings, stating that the national (National Y) had failed to comply with the court's order to produce the inheritance decisions concerning the defendants. The national (National Y) lodged numerous requests for the resumption of the proceedings, to no avail. She submitted that the courts had refused to serve on her the requested decisions, since she was not the defendants' relative. On 20 September 2004 the proceedings were eventually resumed on the national (National Y)'s request. On 16 November 2004 the court held a hearing. On 13 April 2005 the court stayed the proceedings. The national (National Y) did not lodge an appeal against this decision. The national (National Y) lodged two motions for the resumption of the proceedings. They were dismissed by the court on 23 October and 15 December 2006. The national (National Y) lodged an appeal against the second decision. On 23 October 2007 the Court of Appeal amended the decision of 15 December 2006 and resumed the proceedings. The court held that the decision of 13 April 2005 was ill-founded since there were no legal grounds for staying the proceedings. On 22 October 2008 the court held a hearing. On 23 October 2008 the Regional Court gave judgment dismissing the national (National Y)'s plea as unfounded. On 3 December 2008 the national (National Y) lodged an appeal. It appears that the proceedings are still pending. B.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against the Republic of X ("the Republic") lodged with the European Human Rights Commission ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms Convention ("the Convention") by an X national, Jane Doe ("the applicant"), on 10 September 1998. Initially, the applicant was represented by Ms L. Jones, a lawyer practising in Y (X). The Republic Government ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Ambassador J. Smith, Head of the International Law Department of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant complains under Article 6 § 3 (c) of the Convention that she had not been able to attend the oral hearing on her appeal against sentence before the Y Court of Appeal. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 20 March 2001 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 14 March 2002 the Court declared the applicant’s remaining complaint admissible. Neither the applicant nor the Government filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and is presently detained at the Z prison. In assessing the penalty, the court considered as mitigating circumstances the applicant’s partial confession regarding the rape of C.Y."

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/11) against a generic government entity (hereafter referred to as "the Government") lodged with the Court under Article 34 of a generic human rights convention ("the Convention") by a national of both a generic country and a different generic country, Mr. A. B. C. ("the first applicant"), and a generic country national, Mr. D. E. F. ("the second applicant"), on 28 September 2010. The applicants were represented by Mr. G. H. I., a lawyer practising in a generic city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr. J. K. L., of a generic government office. The applicants alleged that the authorities' refusal of their request for family reunification constituted a breach of their right to respect for family life as provided in Article 8 of the Convention. On 18 January 2011 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The first applicant was born in 1952 and lives in a generic location. The second applicant, who was born in 1990, is the son of the first applicant. He lives in a generic country. A. The background to the case The first applicant entered the country in 1997, where he applied for asylum in the same year. At that time, the second applicant remained in a generic country, where he was cared for by his mother. The first applicant’s asylum application was rejected by the competent authorities. In March 1999 the first applicant married a generic national and obtained a residence permit. In 2000 a daughter was born to the couple. In 2002 the second applicant visited his father in the country for three months based on a tourist visa valid for that period. In July 2003 the second applicant re-entered the country for purposes of family reunification with his father. In February 2004 the first applicant was granted a permanent residence permit. In August 2004 he obtained generic nationality and has since held nationality of both the country and the generic country. After encountering difficulties in school and with his step-mother, the second applicant returned to a generic country in January 2005, where he was cared for by his mother and his paternal grandmother. In 2006 the first applicant separated from his spouse. The latter continued to live in the country with the couple’s daughter. B. The proceedings at issue On 1 March 2006 the first applicant lodged a request for family reunification with the second applicant, who was 15 and a half years old at the time and for whom he had custody according to the laws of the generic country. On 15 February 2007 the Migration Office of a generic location refused that request. On 12 March 2007 the applicant lodged an appeal against that decision with the Legal Unit of the Migration Office of a generic location. On 6 June 2007 that authority dismissed the appeal. On 26 June 2007 the applicant lodged an appeal against that decision with the Court of Appeal in Foreigners' Law (Rekursgericht im Ausländerrecht) of a generic location.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against the Republic of XYZ lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Mr Ali Yılmaz (“the applicant”), on 10 November 1998. The applicant was represented by Ms B. C. Smith, Mr D. Jones, Mr E. Brown and Ms F. Wilson of the Human Rights Organization in Y. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 25 August 2005 the Court (First Section) declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the alleged lack of independence and impartiality of the military court, the alleged interference with the applicant's right to freedom of expression and the alleged lack of an effective remedy to the Government. Under Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Y. On 15 March 1999 the applicant, who is a journalist, distributed a leaflet concerning the conscientious objector Mr P.Q.R, outside the State Security Court in Z. He also handed the leaflet to the public prosecutor at the State Security Court together with a petition stating that he should be prosecuted for having committed a crime. The leaflet, entitled “Freedom to think - an initiative against the crime of thought” contained the press release issued by P. Q. R on 1 October 1996. The latter had been previously convicted and sentenced on account of this press release. The relevant parts of the leaflet are as follows: Preface and Epilogue: “... For the purpose of defending the free expression of every kind of thought, we who have signed as publishers, convey this 'convicted' text to the people, regardless of its contents and the question whether or not we share its contents, even though some of us do not agree with some lines in it...' The press release of P. Q. R: “Good morning, Today's press conference is not organised by the Association of the Opponents of War. The responsibility for this conference rests exclusively with me. As you know, the case, which was brought before the Military Court of the Office of the Chief of Staff where I was allegedly accused of committing the crime of 'inciting others to evade military service', was concluded on 30 July. ... The army, unable to deal with us through judicial methods, think that they can draw the opponents of war away from the public view. First of all, I am not a deserter; I am a 'conscientious objector'. I neither intend to do military service nor desert."

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 16085/90) against a State (not specified) lodged with an international human rights body (not specified) under former Article 25 of a human rights convention (not specified) by a national (not specified) on a date (not specified). PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against the Republic of Country lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”), on 11 September 1997. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr. A. Smith and Mr. B. Jones of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that his pre-trial detention had been inordinately lengthy. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 8 January 2004 the Court declared the application admissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in a city in Poland. On 24 August 1994 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of extorting protection money from an escort agency. Subsequently, eleven other persons were charged and remanded in custody in connection with the investigation against the applicant. In the course of the investigation the applicant’s detention was several times prolonged by the Regional Prosecutor and the Regional Court. The prosecution authorities also obtained two expert reports concerning the applicant’s mental health. On 27 June 1995 the Regional Prosecutor lodged a bill of indictment with the Regional Court. The applicant was indicted together with eleven other persons on charges of robbery and extortion. The prosecution asked the court to hear evidence from 106 witnesses. On 26 July 1995 the applicant lodged an application for release. He submitted that his wife had been placed in a mental hospital and that their daughter had been left without care. On 18 August 1995 the Regional Court upheld the detention order. The court held that, given the number of suspects involved in the case and the serious nature of the offence in question, keeping the applicant in custody was necessary to ensure that the process of obtaining evidence followed its proper course. On 6 September 1995 the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s further appeal. On 30 April 1996 the applicant made an application for release. It was rejected by the Regional Court on 14 May 1996. The court held that keeping the applicant in custody had been necessary to ensure the proper conduct of the proceedings.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr Xander Green on 15 October 2001. The applicant was represented by Mr Yara Blue and Ms Zara Red, lawyers practising in Yonder. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 1 July 2004 the Court (First Section) declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the applicant’s detention in police custody for ten days without being brought before a judge to the Government. Under Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. On 1 December 2004 the Court changed the composition of its sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits and admissibility (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and is currently detained in Zephyr prison. On 22 March 2001 the applicant was arrested in Yonder by members of the anti-terrorist branch of the Yonder Security Directorate on suspicion of membership of the XYZ (Yonder Workers’ Party). In a letter dated 23 March 2001 the Yonder Security Directorate requested the Yonder Public Prosecutor to extend the applicant’s detention period until 26 March 2001 together with seven others. On the same day, considering the number of the accused and the difficulty to obtain evidence, the public prosecutor authorised to extend the detention period as requested. On 25 March 2001 the Yonder Criminal Court of First Instance ordered the prolongation of the applicant’s custody for another six days on the ground that the interrogation process had not yet been completed. On 30 March 2001 the applicant was brought before the public prosecutor. On the same day the Yonder Criminal Court of First Instance ordered that the applicant be detained on remand. On 21 April 2001 the Public Prosecutor before the Yonder State Security Court filed a bill of indictment charging the applicant under Article 125 of the Criminal Code with assisting and abetting and membership of a terrorist organisation. The criminal proceedings against the applicant are currently pending before the Yonder Assize Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in three applications (nos. 48535/99, 48536/99 and 48537/99) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by three nationals, Mr Alex Smith, Mr Peter Jones and Mr Richard Davis (“the applicants”), on 11, 12 and 11 January 1999, respectively. The applicants were represented by Ms L. Brown, a solicitor practising in a city, a region. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr D. Miller, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The applicants alleged that an investigation into their sexuality and their discharge from the armed forces on the basis of their homosexuality as a result of the absolute policy against the presence of homosexuals in the armed forces that existed at the time, violated their rights under Articles 3, 8 and 10 of the Convention, read on their own and in conjunction with Article 14. They further contended that they did not have any effective remedy in the domestic courts in relation to those violations, in violation of Article 13 of the Convention. The applications were allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. On 5 October 1999 the Chamber decided to join the proceedings in the applications (Rule 43 § 1). Legal aid was granted to the first applicant on 31 January 2000. By a decision of 5 September 2000 the Court declared the applications admissible. The Chamber decided that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The applicants’ claims for just satisfaction pursuant to Article 41 of the Convention were received on 15 January 2001 and on 13 March 2001 the Government’s observations on those claims were received. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1959, 1957 and 1967 and live in a region, a county and a city, respectively. A. The first applicant On 4 May 1976 the first applicant joined the armed forces. By 1993 he had reached the rank of sergeant in a unit where he was employed as a communications systems analyst and he submitted that he was well placed for promotion. During his service he was awarded a commendation for meritorious service and the Long Service and Good Conduct medal. The first applicant was divorced in 1988.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by four Xanadan nationals, Mr Xanadu Xan, Mr Xanadu Yalçın, Ms Xanadu Karatağna and Mr Xanadu Ölmez (“the applicants”), on 21 April 1999. The applicants were represented by Ms Xanadu Aslan, a lawyer practising in Xanadu. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 7 September 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the applicants’ right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). The case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1977, 1976, 1974 and 1968 respectively and were serving their prison sentences in Xanadu at the time of their applications to the Court. The police officers at the Anti-Terror branch of the Xanadu Security Directorate arrested Tayyip Ölmez, Vahdettin Budak, Songül Karatağna and Mehmet Emin Yalçın and placed them in custody on 22 February, 13 March, 12 April and 24 April 1998 respectively. The Xanadu Magistrates’ Court ordered the remand in custody of Tayyip Ölmez, Vahdettin Budak, Songül Karatağna and Mehmet Emin Yalçın on 27 February, 22 March, 21 April and 29 April 1998 respectively. By indictments dated 24 March, 8 May, 17 May and 22 May 1998 the public prosecutor at the Xanadu State Security Court accused Vahdettin Budak, Songül Karatağna and Mehmet Emin Yalçin of membership of an illegal organisation and Tayyip Ölmez of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation. He requested that Vahdettin Budak be convicted and sentenced under Article 125 of Criminal Code. In respect of Songül Karatağna and Mehmet Emin Yalçin, the public prosecutor requested that they be convicted and sentenced under Article 168 §2 of Criminal Code and Article 5 of Law no. 3713. As for Tayyip Ölmez, the public prosecutor requested that he be convicted and sentenced under Article 169 of Criminal Code and Article 5 of Law no. 3713. On 11 November 1998 the Xanadu State Security Court convicted the applicants as charged and sentenced Vahdettin Budak to life, Songül Karatağna and Mehmet Emin Yalçin to twelve years and six months and Tayyip Ölmez to five years’ imprisonment. On 11 October 1999 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Xanadu State Security Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against a country of Europe lodged with a regional organization under former Article 25 of the European Convention on Human Rights ("the Convention") by a national of that country, Mr John Doe ("the applicant"), on 23 December 1996. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of a hearing before an independent and impartial tribunal, in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The applicant was represented before the Court by Mr A. Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The government of the country ("the government") were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Jones, of the Foreign Ministry, a city. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 14 September 1999 it was declared admissible by a Chamber of that Section ("the Chamber"), composed of the following judges: Mr C. Brown, President, Mr D. Green, Mr E. White, Mrs F. Black, Mr G. Brown, Sir H. Green, Mrs I. White and also of Mrs J. Black, Section Registrar. On 7 November 2000 the Chamber delivered its judgment in which it held, unanimously, that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention [Note by the Registry. The judgment is available from the Registry]. The Chamber decided, by six votes to one, that the finding of a violation constituted sufficient just satisfaction for the non-pecuniary damage sustained by the applicant and, apart from a unanimous award of 13,500 pounds sterling in respect of Strasbourg legal costs and expenses, it dismissed the remainder of the applicant's claims for just satisfaction. Mr Green's partly dissenting opinion was annexed to the judgment. On 14 December 2000 the applicant requested, in accordance with Article 43 of the Convention and Rule 73, that the case be referred to the Grand Chamber. A panel of the Grand Chamber accepted his request on 17 January 2001. The composition of the Grand Chamber was determined according to the provisions of Article 27 §§ 2 and 3 of the Convention and Rule 24. The applicant and the government each filed written observations concerning the issues under Article 41 of the Convention (see paragraph 33 below). In addition, third-party comments were received from a non-governmental organization based in a city (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 61 § 3). A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 7 November 2001 (Rule 59 § 2).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 August 2000. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr B. Smith, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Government of Andria (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 15 November 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the alleged ill-treatment of the applicant during police custody and his right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and was serving his sentence in Andria prison at the time of his application to the Court. A. The detention in police custody and the medical certificates concerning the alleged ill-treatment of the applicant On an unspecified date an arrest warrant was issued in respect of the applicant because of his alleged involvement with the illegal armed organisation. After receiving an anonymous phone call, police officers arrested the applicant on 1 July 1998 at around 02.00 a.m. The police also searched the house where the applicant stayed. The search and seizure protocol drafted by the police officers and signed by the applicant indicates that he consented to the search. The applicant alleged that he was arrested and taken into custody on 30 June 1998 from his house in the Old Andria district and that while he was in custody he was subjected to various forms of torture. In particular, he submitted that he was beaten, sworn at, threatened, blindfolded, given electric shocks and hosed with pressurized water. He further claimed that his mother fainted when the police officers started to beat him at his home at the time of his arrest. According to the medical report drawn up on 2 July 1998 at around 11.40 a.m. the applicant complained of blows to his chest. The doctor found that the applicant had a 1 cm graze on the right side of his forehead and a hyperaemic region (redness) in the middle of his chest. The applicant was interrogated by the police officers at the Anti-terror branch of the Andria Security Directorate on 3 July 1998. According to the medical report drafted on 3 July 1998 the applicant complained of blows to his chest. The doctor found that the applicant had a 1 cm graze on the right side of his forehead and a hyperaemic region (redness) in the middle of his chest and a graze of 1 cm on his right leg.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 26876/03) against a State (referred to as 'the Republic of Poland') lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ('the Convention') on 6 August 2003 by an individual ('the applicant'). He was represented by a lawyer ('Mr J. Runowski') practising in a city ('Żary'). The State ('the Government') were represented by their Agent, a person ('Mr J. Wołąsiewicz') from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 25 October 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant's pre-trial detention to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in a city ('Wrocław'). On 15 April 1999 the applicant was detained on remand until 14 July 1999 on suspicion of two crimes. The court based its detention order on a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences, on the severity of the likely penalty, which gave rise to a fear that the applicant would obstruct the proceedings, and on the risk of the applicant's going into hiding as he had done previously. On an unknown date a bill of indictment was lodged. The applicant was charged with two crimes and possession of an unlicensed weapon. Subsequent decisions on the extension of the applicant's pre-trial detention were taken on several dates. In all the above-mentioned decisions the courts relied on the same grounds for detention as those given in the first detention order. In some of them the courts also referred to the complexity of the case, the need to conduct further investigations, the probability of collusion between the applicant and other co-accused and exertion of unlawful pressure on witnesses by the applicant. They also stressed that the applicant had previously gone into hiding. The applicant appealed against the decisions extending his detention on several occasions. All of his appeals were dismissed. On many occasions the applicant requested release from detention or the imposition of a more lenient preventive measure. His requests were dismissed. Hearings were held on several dates. On 2 February 2001 the court changed the legal qualification of the offences and convicted the applicant of a crime as well as possession of a weapon. It sentenced him to 10 years’ imprisonment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/08) against the Republic of Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2008. The applicant was represented by Mr Michael Smith and Ms Jane Doe, lawyers practising in City. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 25 October 2008 the applicant's representative requested that an interim measure be applied under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court to discontinue the applicant's pre-trial detention, that the respondent Government be notified of the introduction of the application in accordance with Rule 40 and that the case be given priority under Rule 41. On 27 October 2008 the President of the Third Section decided that the application should be given priority. On 10 December 2008 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the applicant's right to be released pending trial under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, his right to compensation under Article 5 § 5 of the Convention and his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1980 and is currently detained in the City F-Type Prison pending the criminal proceedings against him. On 20 June 1997 the applicant was taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of the illegal organisation. On 15 July 1997 the public prosecutor at the City State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicant and seven other persons, accusing him of membership of the illegal organisation (case no. 1997/281). On 2 December 1997 the public prosecutor filed a second bill of indictment, charging the applicant, along with sixteen other persons, under Article 125 of the former Criminal Code with carrying out activities with the aim of bringing about the secession of part of the national territory (case no. 1997/307). On 10 April 1998 the City State Security Court decided to join the two cases against the applicant under case no. 1997/307. On 13 June 2001 the City State Security Court convicted the applicant under Article 125 of the former Criminal Code and sentenced him to the death penalty. On 12 February 2002 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the City State Security Court. By Law no. 5190 of 16 June 2004, published in the Official Gazette on 30 June 2004, State Security Courts were abolished. The case against the applicant was transferred to the Fourteenth Chamber of the City Assize Court. On 12 April 2007 the applicant objected to his detention during the judicial proceedings and requested his release.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court on 8th day of a month in 1994 by a regional human rights body and on 23rd day of the following month in the same year by the government of a country, within the three-month period laid down by the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 23389/94) against the country lodged with the regional body under the Convention on 25th day of the preceding month by a citizen, Mr John Doe. The regional body’s request referred to the declaration and to the country’s recognition of the Court’s compulsory jurisdiction; the government’s application referred to the declaration. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent state of its obligations under the Convention. In response to the enquiry, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him. The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and another case should be heard by the same Chamber and that a joint hearing should be held. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio a judge of British nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. On 27th day of the following month, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members. As President of the Chamber, Mr Ryssdal, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the government, the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the regional body on the organisation of the proceedings. Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the government’s memorial on 13th day of the following month and the applicant’s memorial on 3rd day of the following month. The Secretary to the regional body informed the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in a city, on 27th day of the following month. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/03) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Novak (“the applicant”), on 15 July 2002. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr K. Smith, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 1 October 2006 the President of the Fifth Section decided to communicate the application. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in Krakow, Europe. 1. The facts prior to 1 May 1994 W.N., the applicant’s father died intestate in 1990. In November 1991, P.N., the applicant’s mother, requested the Krakow District Court to declare that she and her three children, including the applicant, were entitled to inherit from W.N. In the course of those proceedings, the applicant’s mother, who had made three different wills, died in 1993. Consequently, on 10 March 1993 the applicant requested to join the case concerning the persons entitled to inherit from his mother to the original proceedings. The District Court held 5 hearings in 1993. 2. The facts after 1 May 1994 The District Court held 4 hearings on the following dates: 28 September 1994; 5 August and 29 October 1995; and 2 October 1996. On 12 February 1995 the court ordered that evidence from an expert be obtained. The expert report was served on the parties on 19 March 1995. On 29 October 1995 the court ordered that evidence from a handwriting expert be obtained. The expert report was submitted to the court on 8 June 1996. On 17 October 1996 the Krakow District Court gave its decision (postanowienie). It ruled that the estate of W.N. should pass, according to the relevant statute, to the applicant’s mother, the applicant, his sister (B.L.), and W.N.’s granddaughter. In respect of the persons entitled to inherit from the applicant’s mother, the District Court held that her entire estate should pass to the applicant’s sister on the basis of the will made in 1991. The applicant appealed against the District Court’s decision. On 28 February 1997 the Krakow Regional Court quashed the District Court’s decision on the persons entitled to inherit from the applicant’s mother and accordingly, remitted the case in part. It found that the first-instance proceedings in that respect had been null and void on the ground that M.L. (the applicant’s daughter), who had a legal interest in the case, had not been summoned to participate in the proceedings. The Regional Court upheld the remainder of the first-instance decision.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of A (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of A (a fictional country), Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 August 2001. The applicant was represented by Mr Smith, a lawyer practising in City B. The Government of A (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 1 March 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, an anaesthesiologist, was born in 1965 and lives in City B. The applicant was working at the State Hospital C when criminal proceedings were instigated against him for alleged involvement in the activities of an illegal organisation. He was accused together with other suspects of, inter alia, hanging posters and banners in various places in City D on behalf of that organisation. Throughout the proceedings the applicant maintained his innocence. In the meantime, State Hospital C suspended the applicant pending the criminal proceedings. On 10 September 2000 the State Security Court of City D, on the basis of the evidence contained in the case file, convicted the applicant under Article 7 § 1 of Law no. 3713 and sentenced him to two years and six months' imprisonment and to a fine. The applicant appealed. On an unspecified date a written opinion of the principal public prosecutor at the Court of Cassation dated 9 November 2000 was submitted to that court. This opinion was not communicated to the applicant. On 25 March 2001 the Court of Cassation held a hearing and upheld the judgment of the first-instance court in respect of the applicant. The applicant's request for a rectification of the Court of Cassation's judgment was dismissed by the principal public prosecutor at that court. The applicant submitted that he had been released from prison in June 2003. By an additional judgment dated 3 May 2004, the State Security Court of City D, taking into account the amendment to the definition of “terror acts” under section 7 of Law no. 3713 pursuant to Law no. 4928, acquitted the applicant, who had not taken part in any violent activities, and nullified his conviction, together with all its consequences. This judgment became final on 10 May 2004. In the meantime, on 27 February 2002, the Disciplinary Commission of the Ministry of Health decided to dismiss the applicant from the civil service. The applicant's objection to this decision was dismissed by the administrative court who noted, inter alia, that, according to the disciplinary investigation, the applicant had taken fifteen days leave from 1 June 2000 in pursuit of his illegal activities. The court also noted that the applicant's conviction had become final.

PROCEDURE The case originated in three applications (nos. 12345/10, 67890/11 and 11111/11) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The first applicant, Mr Alex Brown, is a national who was born in 1970 and is currently detained at a prison. He is represented before the Court by Mr John Smith, a lawyer practising in a city with a law firm, assisted by Mr James Green, counsel, and Professor Jane Doe. The second applicant, Mr Chris White, is a national who was born in 1965 and is currently detained at a prison. He is represented before the Court by Mr David Brown, a lawyer practising in a city with a law firm, assisted by Mr Richard Black QC and Mr Mark White, counsel. The third applicant, Mr Robert Black, is a national who was born in 1945 and is currently detained at a prison. He is represented before the Court by a law firm, assisted by Mr James Brown, counsel. The European country Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms Jane Doe of the Foreign Office. The applicants alleged that the whole life orders which had been imposed on them violated Articles 3, 5 § 4, 6 and 7 of the Convention. On 1 February 2011, the Court decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASES A. Introduction Since the abolition of the death penalty in a country, the sentence for murder has been a mandatory sentence of life imprisonment. When such a sentence is imposed, it is the current practice, in the majority of cases, for the trial judge to set a minimum term of imprisonment which must be served before the prisoner is eligible for release on licence. Exceptionally, however, “a whole life order” may be imposed by the trial judge instead of a minimum term. This has the effect that the prisoner cannot be released other than at the discretion of the Secretary of State. (The power of the Secretary of State to release a prisoner is provided for in section 30(1) of a law.) The Secretary of State will only exercise his discretion on compassionate grounds when the prisoner is terminally ill or seriously incapacitated (see a service order set out at paragraph 36 below).

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Commission and by the Government on 13 and 28 July 1989 respectively, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application against Switzerland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by a national, on 27 February 1987. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 of the Convention and to the declaration whereby Switzerland recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court; the Government’s application referred to Articles 45, 47 and 48. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 5 para. 3. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent her (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio a national, the elected judge of Swiss nationality (Article 43 of the Convention), and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On 23 August 1989, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other five members, namely Mr J. Cremona, Mr F. Gölcüklü, Sir Vincent Evans, Mr A. Spielmann and Mr J.A. Carrillo Salcedo (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4). Subsequently Mr B. Walsh, substitute judge, replaced Mr Carrillo Salcedo, who had resigned before the hearing (Rule 2 para. 3). Mr Ryssdal assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5) and, through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the applicant’s lawyers on the need for a written procedure (Rule 37 para. 1). In accordance with the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the Government’s memorial on 31 October 1989. The applicant, for her part, decided not to submit a memorial but, on 13 February 1990, lodged her claims for just satisfaction. On 18 January the Secretary to the Commission had informed the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. Having consulted, through the Registrar, those who would be appearing before the Court, the President directed on 11 January 1990 that the oral proceedings should open on 28 March 1990 (Rule 38).

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Human Rights Commission (“the Commission”) on 1 January 1999 within the three-month period laid down by former Articles 32 § 1 and 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application (12345/95) against a country lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 by Mr Alex Müller, a national, on 15 March 1995. The President gave him leave to present his own case and to use a language in his communications with the Court. The Government of a country are represented by their Agent, Mr G. Doe, Ambassador, Head of the Legal Department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Commission’s request referred to former Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the country had recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (former Article 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c). On 15 January 1999 the Panel of the Grand Chamber decided, pursuant to Article 5 § 4 of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention and Rules 100 § 1 and 24 § 6 of the Rules of Court, that the application would be examined by one of the Sections. It was, thereupon, assigned to the Second Section. The Chamber constituted with the Section included ex officio Mr B. Smith, the judge elected in respect of the country (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 26 § 1 (a) of the Rules of Court) and Mr C. Brown, Vice-President of the Section (Rules 12 and 26 § 1 (a)). The other members designated by the latter to complete the Chamber were Mr D. Green, Mrs E. White, Mr F. Black, Mrs G. Brown, and Mr H. Doe. In accordance with Rule 59 § 3, the President of the Chamber invited the parties to submit memorials on the issues in the application. The Registrar received the applicant’s and Government’s memorials on 20 June 1999 and on 25 August respectively. After consulting the Agent of the Government and the applicant, the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case. AS TO THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 5 September 1994 the Regional Court (Landesgericht), sitting with two professional and two lay judges (Schöffengericht), having held an oral hearing in the presence of the Public Prosecutor, the applicant and his official defence counsel, ordered that the applicant be detained in an institution for mentally ill offenders (Anstalt für geistig abnorme Rechtsbrecher), pursuant to section 22 § 1 of the Criminal Code (Strafgesetzbuch). The Regional Court found that the applicant had intimidated numerous persons by threats of murder, but that he could not be held responsible because he was suffering from a mental illness.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 65436/01) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a French national, Mr Albert Hénaf, (“the applicant”), on 13 November 2000. The French Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr R. Abraham, Director of Legal Affairs at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that he had been subjected to treatment contrary to Article 3 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 24 January 2002 the Chamber declared the application admissible, while noting that the objections raised by the Government were inseparable from the examination of the merits. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, who was born in 1925, is currently in prison. During the past few years he has been convicted of various criminal offences. In particular, he was sentenced on 9 November 1992 by the Assize Court for the département of Cher to ten years' imprisonment for armed robbery; on 2 September 1998 by the Bernay Criminal Court to six months' imprisonment for making off without payment; on 14 January 1999 by the Nevers Criminal Court to five years' imprisonment for armed robbery; and on 20 January 1999 by the Rouen Court of Appeal to six months' imprisonment for making off without payment. He was due for release from September 2001 onwards according to him, and from 17 February 2002 onwards according to the Government. In February 1998 the applicant was also sentenced to six months' imprisonment by the Nevers Criminal Court for failing to return to prison on time after his last period of leave in 1998, having complied with the arrangements on the previous four occasions. The experts who examined him on the subject concluded that “at the material time” he had been suffering from a “psychological disorder” that had temporarily “impaired his judgment” and that prison could not be “therapeutic” for him, especially in view of his advanced age. The applicant subsequently underwent a medical examination in prison and was found to have swollen glands in the throat area. The relevant service accordingly prescribed medical treatment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against the Republic of X (the "Republic") lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a Polish national, Ms Alicja Nowak ("the applicant"), on 10 June 1996. The applicant was represented by Ms A. Kowalska, a lawyer practising in Y, Poland. The Polish Government ("the Government") were represented by their Agents, Mr B. Nowak and subsequently Mr C. Nowak of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that her case had not been heard within a reasonable time in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 12 November 2002 the Court declared the application admissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant is a Polish national who was born in 1952 and lives in Z, Poland. On 23 May 1990 the applicant acquired the right to a long-term lease of a flat (spółdzielcze lokatorskie prawo do lokalu) in a building owned by the Z Housing Co-operative (Spółdzielnia Mieszkaniowa). On 22 July 1993 the co-operative sued the applicant in the Z District Court (Sąd Rejonowy), seeking payment. On 25 October 1993 the court gave judgment and granted the claim. The applicant appealed against this judgment. On 19 January 1994 the Y Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) amended the first-instance judgment. Subsequently, the applicant twice requested the Minister of Justice to grant her leave to file an extraordinary appeal with the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy). Her first request was rejected on 10 October 1994. On 31 January 1997, upon the applicant’s second request, the Minister of Justice filed a cassation appeal on the applicant’s behalf, contesting the judgment of the Y Regional Court of 19 January 1994. On 29 April 1997 the Supreme Court quashed both judgments given in the applicant’s case and remitted the case to the court of first instance. It held that the lower courts had committed serious errors of fact and law. On 28 October 1997 the Z District Court joined the applicant’s case with similar proceedings against seven other members of the co‐operative. On 19 March 1998 the court held a hearing. On 8 May 1998 the court ordered that expert evidence be obtained.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Bulgarian national, Ms Ana Petrova (“the applicant”), on 15 September 2000. The applicant was represented before the Court by Ms Birgitte Jensen, a lawyer practising in Oslo. The Norwegian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Ole Hansen of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and Co-Agent Ms Signe Nielsen of the Ministry of Justice. The case concerns the detention of the applicant from 10.30 p.m. on 16 September until 12 noon on 17 September 1996. The applicant invokes Article 5 § 1 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 1 October 2002 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 52 § 1). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 30 May 2003 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 16 September 1996 on a public bus in the city of Oslo the applicant, born in 1930, had a dispute with a ticket inspector, who accused her of having travelled without a valid ticket. When he was about to issue a penalty fare she refused to disclose her identity and the police were consequently called. They requested that the applicant give her name and address, and since she refused, she was arrested at 10.30 p.m. in accordance with section 755, subsection 1, cf. section 750 of the Administration of Justice Act (Retsplejeloven) and brought to the police station. From the police reports it appears that the police estimated that the applicant was approximately sixty years old. Having been deprived of her personal belongings, she was put in a waiting room at 11 p.m. and after a visit to the toilet at 11.30 p.m. she was moved to a detention cell. On 17 September 1996 at 11 a.m. the applicant revealed her identity and she was released at 12 noon. Immediately after her release, the applicant collapsed and was hospitalised for three days diagnosed with high blood pressure. The charge with the offence of refusing to reveal her identity was not followed up by an indictment. The outcome of the applicant's dispute with the bus company is unknown. On 20 September 1996 the applicant complained about the detention to the Chief Constable of Oslo (Politimesteren i Oslo).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Andria (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Andria (a fictional country), Mr X Y Z (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2000. The applicant was represented by Ms A B C, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Government of Andria (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 20 August 2007 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Andria. On 7 October 1993 the applicant was taken into custody within the context of a police operation carried out against an illegal organisation, namely the XYZ – ABC (a fictional organization). On 18 October 1993 the applicant was placed in detention on remand. By an indictment dated 15 January 1994 the public prosecutor initiated criminal proceedings against the applicant before the Andria State Security Court, accusing him, inter alia, of membership of an illegal armed organisation and of involvement in activities which aimed at undermining the constitutional order of the State. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Criminal Code. On 22 May 1999 the Constitution was amended and the military judge sitting on the bench of the Andria State Security Court was replaced by a civilian judge. On 14 May 2000 the applicant was convicted as charged by the Andria State Security Court and sentenced to death. On 17 April 2001 the Court of Cassation quashed the applicant’s conviction for procedural reasons. The case was remitted to the Andria State Security Court for further examination. On 20 June 2001 the Andria State Security Court ordered the applicant’s release pending trial. On 8 April 2004 State Security Courts were abolished following a constitutional amendment and the applicant’s case was transmitted to the Andria Assize Court. On 30 December 2004 the Andria Assize Court found the applicant guilty and sentenced him to life imprisonment, pursuant to Article 146 § 1 of the Criminal Code. On 19 February 2005 the Court of Cassation quashed the Andria Assize Court’s judgment for having erred in its assessment of the facts. The case was remitted to the Andria Assize Court for re-trial. Between 10 March 2005 and 28 March 2006 the Andria Assize Court held six hearings and dealt with procedural issues, such as the delivery of arrest warrants, the appointment of advocates for some of the accused and the extension of time-limits for defence submissions, etc.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/94) against Germany lodged with an international human rights organization under former Article 25 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights by a European national, Mr Alex Müller. The applicant was represented by Mr G. Hesse, a lawyer practising in Berlin. The German Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Thomas Müller, Director of Legal Affairs at the Ministry of Justice. The applicant complained that he had been denied access to a tribunal or an effective remedy by which to assert his right of ownership of seized property which had subsequently been confiscated pursuant to a judgment. He also alleged a breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights on the ground that he had been the victim of a breach of his right to peaceful enjoyment of his possessions. Lastly, relying on Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, the applicant complained of an infringement of his right to freedom of movement as a result of the seizure and subsequent confiscation of his passport. On 15 February 1997 the organization (Third Chamber) decided to give notice to the Government of the complaints under Articles 6 and 13 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and to request them to submit their written observations on the admissibility and merits of those complaints. The Government submitted their observations on 3 July and 28 September 1997 after an extension of the time-limit fixed for that purpose. The applicant replied on 15 August and 15 November 1997. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 October 1997, when Protocol No. 11 to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights came into force. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. On 16 April 2001 the Chamber declared the application admissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 28 October 1993 Berlin police officers spotted an occupied vehicle parked in a car park. It turned out that the vehicle had been stolen the previous day in Berlin. The investigators proceeded to arrest P.X., who had come to take delivery of the stolen vehicle, and Q.Y. The on-the-spot investigation established that other transactions had taken place and that the two arrested men used to meet in a hotel in Kiel (Schleswig-Holstein). The police officers went to the hotel where they arrested P.X.'s wife and Miss Z.A. while the latter was about to get into a vehicle belonging to the applicant. When questioned at the hotel Z.A.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 March 2001. The applicant was represented by a law firm in a city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr X Y Z of the Foreign Ministry, in the same city. The applicant complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that, because he was a man, he was denied social security benefits equivalent to those received by widows. On 4 November 2003 the Court decided to communicate the complaints concerning widows’ benefits relating to the period after the date on which the applicant lodged his relevant claim and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. Subsequently, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I.
