THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1948 and lives in a region. His wife died on 10 December 1999 leaving dependant children. His relevant claim for widows’ benefits was made on 2 October 2000 and was rejected on 29 September 2000 on the ground that he was not entitled to widows’ benefits because he was not a woman. The applicant applied for reconsideration and on 10 October 2000 he was informed that the decision remained unchanged. On 16 October 2000 he appealed unsuccessfully. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such social security benefits were payable to widowers under the country’s law.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/06) against the Republic of X (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of X, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2005. The Government of X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 1 January 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in City A. A. First set of proceedings for payment 1. Main proceedings On 1 January 1990 the applicant filed with the Regional Court of City A a claim for payment of maintenance contributions made between 1985 and 1990 for property located in City A, at Street A. On 1 January 1991 the court held a hearing. The applicant was ordered to specify her claim. On 1 January 1992 the applicant was urged to specify her claim. On 1 January 1993 the applicant complied with the court’s order. On 1 January, 1 January, and 1 January 1993 the court held hearings, one of which was adjourned on the applicant’s motion. On 1 January 1994 the proceedings were stayed at the parties’ request. On 1 January 1996 the applicant lodged an application for resumption of the proceedings. They were resumed after thirteen months – on 1 January 1997. On 1 January 2000 the Regional Court of City A stayed the proceedings pending the completion of civil proceedings for the annulment of a donation contract. The applicant’s appeal against this decision was rejected by the Court of Appeal of City A on 1 January 2002, following the dismissal of her application for exemption from court fees. On 1 January 2004 the applicant lodged an application to resume the proceedings, to no avail. On 1 January 2006 the applicant, following the defendant’s death, withdrew her claim. On 1 January 2006 the Regional Court of City A resumed the proceedings. On 1 January 2006 the proceedings were discontinued. 2. The applicant’s complaint under the 2006 Act On 1 January 2005 the applicant lodged with the Court of Appeal of City A a complaint under section 5 of the Law of 1 January 2006 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time (Ustawa o skardze na naruszenie prawa strony do rozpoznania sprawy w postępowaniu sądowym bez nieuzasadnionej zwłoki) (“the 2006 Act”) which entered into force on 1 January 2006. The applicant sought a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings before the Regional Court of City A had been excessive and an award of just satisfaction in the amount of 10,000 X currency (approx. 2,500 Y currency). On 1 January 2005 the Court of Appeal of City A dismissed her complaint.

PROCEDURE The present case was referred to the Court, within the period of three months laid down by Articles 32 para. 1 and 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention“), by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission“) on 16 May 1983 and then by the Government on 25 May 1983. The case originated in an application (no. 8790/79) against a State lodged with the Commission on 19 September 1979 under Article 25 (art. 25) by a citizen. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby a State recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46), and the Government’s application referred to Article 48 (art. 48). The purpose of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1). In response to the inquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent her (Rule 30). The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, a national (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b) of the Rules of Court). On 27 May 1983, the President drew by lot, in the presence of the Deputy Registrar, the names of the five other members (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43). Having assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5) and having on each occasion consulted, through the Registrar, the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer, the President decided, on 13 June 1983, that there was no call for memorials to be filed (Rule 37 para. 1); directed, on 17 November, that the oral proceedings should open on 24 January 1984 (Rule 38). The Registrar, acting on the President’s instructions, requested the Commission to produce certain documents, which were received on 29 November 1983. On 13 and 14 December, the applicant filed her claims under Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention. On 17 December, the President granted the applicant’s lawyer leave to use the German language (Rule 27 para. 3). The hearings were held in public at the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on the appointed day. Immediately before they opened, the Court had held a preparatory meeting.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 35363/02) against a State lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals, Adem Kepeneklioğlu and Mehmet Hakan Canpolat, on 7 August 2002. The applicants were represented by Y. Hoş, a lawyer practising in a city. The State did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 8 July 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning a lack of a fair trial by an impartial and independent tribunal within a reasonable time, a failure to observe the presumption of innocence, a lack of adequate facilities for the preparation of the defence, and a lack of legal assistance during detention. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. Both the applicants and the State submitted their observations outside the time limit. They have therefore not been admitted to the case file. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants, Mr Adem Kepeneklioğlu and Mr Mehmet Hakan Canpolat, are nationals, who were born in 1954 and 1964 respectively. When they lodged their application with the Court they were imprisoned in a country. On 29 and 30 June 1992 the applicants were taken into custody in a city by police officers from the Anti-Terrorist Branch. On 13 July 1992 they were detained on remand. On 27 July 1992 the Public Prosecutor at the State Security Court filed a bill of indictment accusing the applicants of, inter alia, organised murder and armed burglary, as well as being members of an illegal organization. On 25 November 1992 the State Security Court commenced the trial against the applicants and three other accused and prolonged the applicants' detention. On 3 April 1998 the State Security Court convicted the applicants under Article 146 of the Criminal Code and sentenced them to death. On 10 March 1999 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment. On 12 June 2001 the State Security Court convicted them of the same crimes. On 4 February 2002, upon the applicants' appeal, the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the State Security Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Smith (“the applicant”), on 24 May 1999. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr John Doe, and subsequently, Mr. Jane Roe of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of civil proceedings in his case had been excessive. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 4 May 2004 the Court declared the application admissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1954 and lives in a town in Europe. A. Facts prior to 1 May 1993 On 17 July 1992 the applicant lodged with the Regional Court (Sąd) an action for damages against his neighbours. He claimed that the defendants had caused damage to his barn by improperly storing silage and animal waste. In 1992 two hearings were adjourned. On 16 February 1993 the court held a hearing at which it heard the parties and witnesses and ordered an expert opinion. B. Facts after 30 April 1993 On 3 August 1993 an expert submitted his opinion to the court. The defendants' lawyer contested the expert's opinion. A hearing scheduled for 17 September 1993 was adjourned due to the absence of the defendants' lawyer. On 14 October 1993 the court held a hearing and heard an expert witness. On an unknown later date, at the applicant's lawyer's request, the court ordered another expert opinion. In January 1994 the opinion was submitted to the court. Subsequently, the defendants' lawyer requested the court to order a supplementary expert opinion. On 29 March 1994 the court held a hearing. It heard two witnesses and an expert witness. Subsequently, the defendants' lawyer requested the court to order yet another expert opinion. In August 1994 the applicant's and the defendants' lawyers requested the court not to schedule any hearings until 30 September 1994 because of their respective holidays. On 8 December 1994 the court dismissed the defendants' request for exemption from the court fees. They lodged an appeal but on 9 January 1995 the Court of Appeal dismissed it. In May 1995 the trial court asked the defendants to indicate an expert who would prepare an opinion. Two subsequent hearings scheduled for 31 January and 23 February 1996 were adjourned due to the illness of the defendants and their lawyer. On 10 July 1996 the court, sitting in camera, ordered another expert opinion. On 6 August 1996 the defendant's lawyer requested the court to appoint two other experts indicated by him.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 39863/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals, Mr A and Mr B (“the applicants”), on 2 October 2002. The applicants were represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 9 May 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the independence and impartiality of the State Security Court and the length of the proceedings to the respondent Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1955 and 1965 respectively. The first applicant lives in a city and the second applicant is currently detained in a prison. On 13 March 1993 the applicants were taken into custody by policemen from a branch of the Security Directorate on suspicion of their membership of an illegal organisation. On 13 April 1993 the applicants were brought before the public prosecutor and subsequently the investigating judge, who ordered the applicants' detention on remand. On 26 April 1993 the State Security Court Public Prosecutor filed an indictment against several accused persons, including the applicants. He accused the first applicant of membership of the illegal organisation and requested the court to sentence him under a Criminal Code article. The public prosecutor further accused the second applicant of activities aimed at breaking up the unity of the State and removing part of the national territory from the State's control. The prosecutor requested the court to sentence him in accordance with a Criminal Code article. On 18 June 1999 the constitution was amended and the military judge sitting on the bench of the State Security Court was replaced by a civilian judge. Between 16 June 1993 and 12 March 2002, the court held several hearings. On 12 March 2002 the State Security Court, which was composed of three judges, acquitted the first applicant of the charges against him. The court further found the second applicant guilty as charged and sentenced him to the death penalty under a Criminal Code article. The death penalty was commuted to a life sentence. On 1 October 2002 the Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the State Security Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 11181/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 2 February 2004. The applicant was represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 23 October 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1953 and lives in a city. On 6 October 1995 the applicant signed a contract with a company, formerly a State-owned enterprise, for the operation of a facility. Having obtained a construction permit and carried out certain building work at the site, the applicant applied for an operations licence but was refused on grounds of safety, due to the proximity of the facility to a railway. On 20 June 1997 the applicant lodged an action with a court for the termination of the contract, which he claimed was null and void due to the impossibility of obtaining the operations licence. The applicant also requested the reimbursement of his expenditure, together with interest (case no. 1997/305). On 25 April 2001 the court partially granted the applicant's request by declaring the contract null and void and by ordering the return of the guarantee previously paid by the applicant to the company, namely a large sum, plus interest. The Court rejected the request for the reimbursement of the applicant's remaining expenditure. On 26 October 2001 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. The parties requested rectification of this decision. On 3 June 2002 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first-instance court. It indicated in particular that the first-instance court had not sufficiently examined whether the company could be ordered to reimburse the applicant for the expenses incurred in the construction work carried out on the facility. On 21 August 2002 the applicant lodged a further complaint with the court under Article 105 of the Code of Obligations alleging that he had sustained additional loss exceeding the late-payment interest payable as a result of the delay in reimbursing the guarantee (case no. 2002/567). This case was joined to the initial case (no. 1997/305). On 30 December 2003 the court partially granted the applicant's requests and awarded him a large sum for the expenses incurred in relation to the construction work and a large sum for his additional financial loss claimed in case no. 2002/567, plus interest.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against the State of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a German national, Ms X Y Z. The applicant was represented by Mr A B C, a lawyer practising in a city. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms D E F, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. On 16 February 2009 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to give priority to the application and to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS A. Background to the case The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in a city. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. The applicant is the mother of a child born on 15 February 1998. In 2005, after having obtained an expert opinion, a court transferred custody to her and at the same time determined the father's access rights. On 15 March 2007, following a three-week stay with her father, the child refused to go back to her mother, and, on account of this, was taken into care. B. Proceedings before the City District Court On 18 March 2007 the applicant requested the court to return the child to her custody. On 19 March 2007 the City District Court (the “District Court”), by means of an interlocutory decision, made at the request of the City Youth Office, transferred the right to determine the child's residence and other essential aspects of custody to the City Youth Office. In a letter of 21 March 2007 the applicant requested the District Court to quash this decision. The court then set the parties a time-limit of four weeks to submit further submissions. On 8 April 2007 the District Court formally appointed a guardian ad litem (Verfahrenspfleger) for the child. On 15 April 2007 the Youth Office submitted a report. On 22 April 2007 the District Court heard the child. On 21 May 2007, on account of the competent judge being ill, the District Court cancelled the hearing scheduled for 25 June 2007. On 1 January 2008 the case was assigned to another judge. On 5 June 2008 that judge scheduled the hearing for 18 July 2008. On 10 June 2008 the applicant's newly-appointed lawyer requested access to the files. This was refused on the ground that he had not yet submitted a power of attorney. By letters dated 11 and 14 June 2008 the new lawyer requested that the hearing be scheduled for another day. On 20 June 2008 the new lawyer submitted a power of attorney (possibly for the second time).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 49913/99) against a country (the Republic of Poland) lodged with an organization (the European Commission of Human Rights) under former Article 25 of a convention (the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms) by a national (Mr Sławomir Zielonka), on 2 March 1999. The government (the Republic of Poland) (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr K. Drzewicki, and subsequently Mr. J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, under Article 5 § 1 that his detention from 21 to 24 February 1999 had been unlawful. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 26 April 2005 the Court declared the application admissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1954 and lives in a city (Łódź). On 21 November 1997 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of receiving and selling stolen goods. On 22 November 1997 the court (Sąd Rejonowy) ordered that the applicant be detained on remand until 21 February 1998. The court referred to the strong probability of the applicant’s guilt and to the high risk of his hindering the proper conduct of the proceedings. The court also emphasised that it was likely that the applicant, if released, would go into hiding. By a decision of 24 February 1998, the court prolonged the applicant’s detention on remand until 21 September 1998. The court considered that the reasons for which the detention had been ordered continued to exist. The decision was served on the applicant on 25 February 1998. The applicant appealed, claiming that keeping him in custody between 21 February 1998 and 24 February 1998 had been unlawful since there had been no valid judicial decision authorising his detention. On 25 March 1998 the court (Sąd Okręgowy) dismissed the applicant’s appeal as unsubstantiated. However, the court altered the decision of 24 February 1998 and prolonged the applicant’s detention on remand until 30 June 1998, finding that the case had not been complex and that the evidence against the applicant pointed to his guilt. In a letter of 28 April 1998, the court (Sąd Rejonowy) admitted its mistake and confirmed that there had been no valid judicial decision authorising the applicant’s detention on remand between 21 February 1998 and 24 February 1998. It added that this period would be deducted from any sentence of imprisonment eventually imposed on the applicant. On 5 June 1998 the court (Sąd Rejonowy) convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to 3 years’ imprisonment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Alfa (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Alfa national, Ms X. Yankovic (“the applicant”), on 15 April 2001. The applicant was represented by Legal Firm Z, a company of lawyers practising in Alfa City. The Alfa Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador A. Borkovic, Head of the International Law Department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 20 September 2002 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in Alfa City. On 25 May 1975 the applicant filed a request with the Prime Minister (Prime Minister’s Office) to examine a product developed by him, namely “Beta”, a medicine for the treatment of cancer. The request was transmitted to the Ministry of Health and Environment (Ministry of Health and Environment). On 24 June 1980 the applicant requested the Minister for Health and Environment to authorise “Beta” under the Alfa pharmacopeia. By letter of 12 July 1980 the Minister informed the applicant that, under the relevant legislation which was in force at that time, he did not meet the conditions to request such an authorisation as he was not in possession of a licence to produce the medicament in question. On 28 August 1987 the applicant submitted a copy of his licence to produce “Beta” which had been issued on 10 May 1987. On 30 August 1987 the then competent authority, namely the Prime Minister’s Office, ordered the Institute for Chemical and Pharmacological Examinations (Institute for Chemical and Pharmacological Examinations) and the Institute for Experimental Pharmacological and Balneological Examinations (Institute for Experimental Pharmacological and Balneological Examinations) to submit expert opinions. On 22 December 1988 the Institute for Experimental Pharmacological and Balneological Examinations submitted an expert opinion. It noted that the documentation submitted by the applicant suffered from severe shortcomings. On 25 January 1989 the applicant was informed about the expert opinion and invited him to make the necessary amendments to his request within twelve months. Between 1991 and 1996 the applicant submitted more documentation, which, however, was found to be insufficient in some twelve expert opinions issued by the Institute for Experimental Pharmacological and Balneological Examinations and the Institute for Chemical and Pharmacological Examinations. On 1 January 1996 the applicant lodged an application against the administration’s failure to decide (Säumnisbeschwerde) with the Administrative Court (Administrative Court). On 12 January 1996 the Administrative Court ordered the Minister to decide upon the applicant’s request, following which the then Minister of Health and Consumer Protection (Minister of Health and Consumer Protection) dismissed the applicant’s request for authorisation on 2 May 1996. He found that the applicant had failed to establish the necessary quality, effectiveness and harmlessness of “Beta”. On 12 June 1996 the applicant filed a complaint with the Administrative Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 32602/08) against a State (the Republic of Poland) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (Polish national), Mr X (“the applicant”), on 2 July 2008. The applicant was represented by Mr Y, Mr Z, and Mr W, lawyers practising in Warsaw and Poznań respectively. The State (the Republic of Poland) was represented by their Agent, Mr A of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that the assessor who had remanded him in custody had lacked independence, contrary to Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 7 September 2009 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the State. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. On 30 November 2010 the Court (Fourth Section), having regard to the declaration submitted by the State and the applicant’s reply to that declaration, decided to strike out the application of its list of cases in so far as it related to the complaints under Article 5 § 4 of the Convention. It also decided to adjourn the examination of the applicant’s complaint under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1949 and lives in a town (Śmiłowo). He was a member of the Senate (the upper chamber of the Parliament) between 1989 and 2005 and a prosperous businessman. On an unspecified date the prosecution authorities instituted criminal proceedings against the applicant. It appears that he left the country in December 2006. On 30 January 2007 the Warsaw-Praga District Court ordered that the applicant be remanded in custody. That decision was upheld on appeal. On 23 July 2007 the Warsaw-Praga Regional Court issued a European Arrest Warrant for the applicant. On 12 November 2007 he was arrested in a foreign country on the basis of that warrant. On 19 December 2007 the applicant was extradited to the country. Subsequently the Warsaw-Praga Regional Prosecutor charged the applicant with, inter alia, numerous counts of bribery of high-ranking officials of a ministry and bribery of a judge of an administrative court. The applicant was represented by three defence counsel. On 21 December 2007, on an application from the Warsaw-Praga Regional Prosecutor, the assessor R.Z. (junior judge) of the Warsaw‐Praga District Court remanded the applicant in custody until 19 March 2008. Two of the applicant’s counsel (Mr Y and Mr Z) lodged appeals against the detention order on 28 December 2007. Counsel Y argued, invoking Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, that the detention order had been given by an assessor who could not be considered “a judge” or “other officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power” because he lacked independence from the executive.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/01) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged on 1 January 2001 with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr X Y (Z) and Company X, a company founded by the first applicant and registered in Xanadu (“the applicants”). The applicants were represented by Ms A B and Mr C D, lawyers practising in Xanadu. The Xanadu Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 1 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The first applicant was born in 1930 and lives in Xanadu. The second applicant is a construction company registered in Xanadu. On 1 October 1990 the applicant company brought a civil action before the Seventh Chamber of the Xanadu Civil Court against the National Water Board (Devlet Su İşleri) to recover the monies owed to it under a construction contract (case no. 1990/584). On 1 December 1993 the Xanadu Civil Court awarded the applicant company's claim in full, plus interest. On 1 November 1994 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first-instance court on procedural and substantive grounds. On 1 March 1995 the applicant company brought an additional action against the National Water Board before the Eighth Chamber of the Xanadu Civil Court in relation to the latter's default in certain other financial undertakings under the aforementioned construction contract (case no. 1995/255). On 1 September 1995 the Eighth Chamber of the Xanadu Civil Court decided to join case no. 1995/255 with case no. 1990/584 pending before the Seventh Chamber of the Xanadu Civil Court. On 1 December 1998, 1 September 2000 and 1 July 2001 the Xanadu Civil Court rendered three separate judgments on the case, all of which were quashed by the Court of Cassation on 1 May 1999, 1 February 2001 and 1 December 2001 respectively on procedural and substantive grounds, including erroneous calculations, resulting in the remittal of the case to the Xanadu Civil Court each time. On 1 April 2002 the Xanadu Civil Court examined the case for the fifth time and awarded the applicant company's claim in part, together with interest. On 1 June 2002 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court with certain minor technical amendments.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms. Anna Novakova (“the applicant”), on 15 July 2005. The applicant was represented by Ms. L. Petrovna, a lawyer practising in Berlin. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. A. Kowalski of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 14 October 2008 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in Berlin. A. Main proceedings On 5 January 1987 the applicant’s mother lodged with the Berlin District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) a motion for the dissolution of a co-ownership and division of an inheritance. The estate comprised, inter alia, a farm and plots of land located in Berlin. The applicant and her brother were also involved in the proceedings as parties. Between 5 January 1987 and 4 March 1993 the court scheduled ten hearings and appointed two experts. In the meantime, the applicant lodged several complaints about the unreasonable length of the proceedings, to no avail. On 4 March 1993 the court stayed the proceedings. They were resumed on 25 June 1996. Between 12 August 1996 and 10 February 2003 the court scheduled twenty hearings, twelve of which were adjourned for various reasons, for instance the need to obtain additional evidence, in particular several experts’ reports. Two hearings were adjourned at the applicant’s request. On 10 February 2003 the court closed the trial and adjourned delivery of a decision. On 25 February 2003 the same court re-opened the proceedings and ordered that additional evidence be obtained, including experts’ reports. On 15 August 2003 the applicant’s brother died and the proceedings were stayed. They were resumed on an unspecified date in 2004. Between 18 March 2004 and 30 September 2008 the court ordered three expert reports to be obtained and scheduled twelve hearings, four of which were adjourned. The proceedings are pending before the first-instance court. B. Proceedings under the 2005 Act On 6 September 2006 the applicant lodged with the Berlin Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) a complaint under the Law of 18 June 2005 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time (Ustawa o skardze na naruszenie prawa strony do rozpoznania sprawy w postępowaniu sądowym bez nieuzasadnionej zwłoki) (“the 2005 Act”). The applicant sought a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings before the Berlin District Court had been excessive and an award of just satisfaction in the amount of 15,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) (approx. EUR 3,750).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 49892/99) against a State lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr. X (“the applicant”), on 1 March 1999. The applicant was represented by Mr. Y, a lawyer practising in a city. The State did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 27 January 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the applicant’s right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal to the State. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). The case was assigned to the newly composed Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1952. He was detained in a prison at the time of lodging his application. On 28 March 1994 an arrest warrant was issued in respect of the applicant. On 14 April 1994 the public prosecutor at a State Security Court filed an indictment, accusing the applicant together with two other co-accused of membership of an illegal armed organisation. The public prosecutor requested that the applicant be convicted and sentenced. On 19 October 1995 the State Security Court decided to separate the proceedings in respect of the applicant as he could not be found. On 30 August 1996 the applicant was arrested and taken into custody by the police. On 6 September 1996 he was interrogated by two police officers. On 10 September 1996 he was brought before the public prosecutor and the State Security Court. He denied his statements made in police custody. On 30 October 1996 an additional indictment was submitted by the public prosecutor at a State Security Court. On 20 January 1998 the State Security Court, composed of two civilian judges and a military judge, convicted the applicant and sentenced him to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment. On 2 March 1998 the applicant appealed against the judgment of the State Security Court. On 7 December 1998 the Court of Cassation held a hearing and on the same day upheld the above judgment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 10001/06) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of a European country, Mr Alex Novak (“the applicant”), on 21 March 2005. The applicant was represented by Mr J. K. Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The European Government did not exercise their right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 1 (b)). On 29 September 2009 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1984 and lives in a city. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. The applicant was living in a city, Chechnya. Fearing for his life he left for a country in August 2000, from where he flew to a city on 4 September 2000. On 23 June 2004 the applicant and a number of other individuals were taken into custody by police officers of the Anti-Terrorist Branch of the Security Headquarters, within the framework of the security measures implemented for the 2004 NATO summit in a city. On 25 June 2004 the applicant was transferred to the Foreigners' Department of the Security Headquarters with a view to deportation. On 29 June 2004 the State Security Court issued a decision of non-prosecution, holding that there was no evidence to initiate criminal proceedings against the applicant or other individuals taken into detention in connection with the 2004 NATO summit. The applicant then continued to be held in the Foreigners' Department of the Security Headquarters under section 23 of Law no. 5683 as an administrative measure pending deportation proceedings. On 25 September 2004 the applicant was released and since then has been living in a city on renewable temporary residence permits. II. CONDITIONS OF DETENTION A. The applicant's account The applicant alleged that he had been detained for a period of ninety-one days in an overcrowded room at the Foreigners' Department of the Security Headquarters, which had no windows, hence no natural light. According to the applicant it had thirty-six beds for a number of asylum seekers varying from 100 to 200. Due to the large number of asylum seekers present in the establishment the applicant, on numerous occasions, had been forced to sleep on the ground without sheets or blankets. He had not been allowed to get any fresh air or exercise throughout his stay. The hygienic conditions were extremely poor, in particular the showering facilities. There were three toilets and two showers serving a minimum of one hundred asylum seekers. The food served was insufficient and was the same every day.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/14) against the United Republic of Xylophia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Xylophian national, Mr Xanadu Zephyr (“the applicant”), on 15 April 2014. The Xylophian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms Yonder Wind, of the Xylophian Ministry of Justice and Public Welfare. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he was not granted a reinstatement of the proceedings after he overstepped the time‐limit to lodge an appeal on points of law concerning a criminal court’s order to confine him to a psychiatric hospital. On 28 June 2016 the complaint concerning the refusal to grant a reinstatement was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1980 and lives in Yonder. On 29 July 2013 the applicant was arrested on the spot for having damaged with a hammer a number of vehicles parked in the Zephyr courthouse’s car park, and resisting a court’s clerk. As a preliminary measure he was confined to a psychiatric hospital. The court appointed defence counsel to the applicant, who had a previous history of psychiatric treatment going back as far as 2000. On Wednesday 20 January 2014, the Münster Regional Court delivered its judgment and ordered the applicant’s confinement to a psychiatric hospital. It held that the applicant could not be held criminally responsible and was mentally ill. According to the court’s psychiatric expert, he was psychotic and aggressive, did not show any awareness of his illness and it was likely that he would commit further, even more serious crimes. When the judgment was delivered in the presence of the applicant, his court‐appointed defence counsel and the applicant’s custodian (gesetzlicher Betreuer), the applicant became agitated. He told the court‐appointed lawyer that he wished for a change in representation and declared that he wanted to appeal against the decision himself. He was informed that this was not possible on the spot. The presiding judge instructed him about the time and form for lodging an appeal on points of law. He was then returned to the forensic hospital where, when in contact with others, he showed no more signs of agitation. On Friday 23 January 2014 the applicant received a letter from the court‐appointed lawyer, dated 21 January 2014, who advised him as follows: “... You already announced immediately after the hearing that you wanted to appeal against the court’s decision and also to mandate new defence counsel. We respect your wish for new counsel and hereby terminate the mandate."

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 74073/01) against a State (Republic of Poland) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of a State (Poland), a person (Mrs Krystyna Domańska) (“the applicant”), on 18 May 2000. The State (Poland) (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr K. Drzewicki, and subsequently, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz. On 10 March 2003 the President of the Fourth Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The President of the Chamber further gave priority to the application, pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1929 and lives in a town (Jarosław), a State (Poland). On 4 November 1994 the applicant lodged with a court (Jarosław District Court) a civil action against a local authority (Jarosław City Council) in which she requested the court to amend the land register. She further applied for exemption from the court fees. On 21 November 1994 the case was transferred to a higher court (Przemyśl Regional Court). On the same day, upon the court’s request, the applicant specified her claim. On 30 January 1995 the court partly exempted the applicant from the court fees. In April 1995 the court again ordered the applicant to specify her claim. On 24 April 1995 the Regional Court held the first hearing. Subsequently, the hearings were held on 20 June and 3 October 1995. At the latter hearing the court ordered an expert opinion. On 16 April 1996 an expert submitted his opinion to the court. On 27 August 1996 the court held a hearing at which it ordered a second expert opinion. The opinion was submitted to the court in January 1997. The next hearings were held on 31 January, 25 February, 18 March, 18 April and 30 May 1997. On 6 June 1997 the Regional Court gave judgment in which it dismissed the applicant’s claim. On 4 August 1997 the applicant lodged an appeal against this judgment. On 7 October 1997 the applicant was partly exempted from the court fees in the appellate proceedings. On 8 October 1998 the Court of Appeal (Rzeszów) dismissed the applicant’s appeal. On 9 November 1998 the applicant lodged a cassation appeal. On 20 November 1998 the Court of Appeal exempted the applicant from the fees for lodging the cassation appeal. On 25 May 2001 the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) refused to entertain the cassation appeal as it was manifestly ill-founded and raised no serious legal issues.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 34400/02) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ali Yilmaz (“the applicant”), on 6 August 2002. The applicant was represented by Mr Ayhan Akyigit, a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 6 May 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the length of the proceedings and the lack of remedies in that respect, as well as the complaint concerning non-communication to the applicant of the submissions of the principal public prosecutor. On 8 September 2006 it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time, pursuant to Article 29 § 3 of the Convention. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in a city. On 23 March 1993 a certain A.B. lodged a criminal complaint with the public prosecutor in a city against the applicant and a certain C.D., accusing them of forging a bond. The prosecutor initiated an investigation and questioned the applicant on 17 May 1993. Once the preliminary investigation was completed and the necessary evidence was obtained, a prosecutor in a city filed an indictment with the court (hereinafter “the trial court”) on 21 April 1995 and requested that the applicant and C.D. be punished in accordance with Article 342 § 1 of the Criminal Code for the offence of forgery. Thirteen hearings were held by the trial court between 1 May 1995 and 12 September 1997 in the absence of the applicant. At each of these hearings the trial court noted the authorities’ failure to locate the applicant’s address. According to the applicant, the reason for his absence from those hearings was that he had not been informed about the trial. On 13 May 1996 the applicant’s co-accused C.D. was acquitted for lack of sufficient evidence. The trial court decided to continue the proceedings against the applicant. A lawyer representing the applicant attended the 14th hearing on 21 November 1997 but, as the applicant was unable to pay his fees, the lawyer discontinued representing him. On 26 March 1998 the authorities were able to find the applicant and question him. In the course of the questioning the applicant denied the accusations against him. He attended the 18th hearing, held on 28 May 1998. During the 19th hearing, held on 22 June 1998, the trial court acquitted the applicant for lack of sufficient evidence. On 16 September 1998 the public prosecutor appealed against the acquittal. On 11 November 1999 the Court of Cassation quashed the decision and referred the case to the trial court for a new trial.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 10734/05) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national and an organization (“the applicants”) on 23 March 2005. The national was born in 1954 and works in the United Kingdom. When the application was lodged he was working for an organization; he has since retired. The applicants were represented by a solicitor-advocate and subsequently by a solicitor for the organization, assisted by counsel. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicants alleged they were unable to challenge a court order prohibiting reporting of a criminal trial in violation of Articles 6, 10 and 13 of the Convention. On 26 February 2008 the President of the Chamber to which the case had been allocated decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 13 September 2004 two men went on trial in the High Court of Justiciary sitting at Glasgow on charges of importing and supplying controlled drugs. The proceedings were filmed and relayed through a closed-circuit television system to a remote viewing room in the court building. On 23 September 2004, it was discovered that police officers and prosecution staff had been watching the proceedings in the remote viewing room with the risk that defense conversations might have been overheard. When this was brought to the attention of the trial judge on 28 September 2004, he took the decision to desert the trial diet simpliciter since he believed that no fair trial could continue before him. This decision had the effect of bringing the prosecution case to an end resulting in the acquittal of the accused. The desertion simpliciter meant that the accused could not be reindicted. The same day, the trial judge heard argument from counsel for the organization before making an interim order under section 4(2) of the Contempt of Court Act 1981 preventing the publication of any report of the proceedings. That order was to become final on 30 September 2004 unless any interested party applied to the court for its recall (quashing) or variation. On 29 September 2004, the organization appeared before the trial judge and made representations in respect of the order.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Andria (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Andria (a fictional country), Mr. John Doe (a fictional person), on 15 July 2004. The applicant was represented by Mr. Alex Smith (a fictional lawyer), a practitioner in Andria (a fictional city). The Government (a fictional organization) were represented by their Agent. On 15 October 2008 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Andria (a fictional city). On 15 August 1993 the applicant was taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of the Revolutionary Front (a fictional organization). On 30 August 1993 she was brought before a single judge at the Andria State Security Court who ordered her detention on remand. On 15 October and 10 November 1993 and 25 June 1996, the public prosecutor at the Andria State Security Court filed three bills of indictment, charging the applicant with attempting to undermine the constitutional order, proscribed by Article 147 of the former Criminal Code. The case against the applicant was joined to another brought against five other persons. On 30 October 1993 the first hearing before the Andria State Security Court was taken up with procedural matters. By 25 December 2003 the applicant had made several requests for release pending trial to the Andria State Security Court. The court dismissed her requests on each occasion, having regard to the nature of the offence, the state of evidence and the content of the case file. On 25 December 2003 the Andria State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced her to death, subsequently commuted to life imprisonment. The State Security Court further ordered the applicant’s release from prison, having regard to the total amount of time that she had been in detention. On 25 April 2004 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 25 December 2003. On 10 November 2007 the Andria Assize Court convicted the applicant under Article 147 of the former Criminal Code and sentenced her to life imprisonment. On 11 April 2008 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the assize court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an European national, Johannes Müller (“the applicant”) on 15 December 1998. The applicant was represented by Mr X. Schmidt, a lawyer practising in Vienna. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Y. Müller, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant complained that there was no public hearing in the succession proceedings, in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 15 December 1999 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 15 June 2001, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), the parties replied in writing to each other's observations. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in Berg/Republic of Europe. A., the applicant's brother, died on 1 January 1987. He had been a farmer and the owner of a farm. On 15 January 1988 the competent court was informed about A. 's death and, subsequently, appointed a notary public as court commissioner (Gerichtskommissär). On 14 and 15 February 1989 the applicant and eight other persons entitled to the estate of A. appeared before the notary public in Salzburg and made conditional declarations of acceptance of succession (bedingte Erbserklärung). On 15 February, 20 March and in April 1989 three experts submitted opinions on the value of the farm. On 20 July 1989 the applicant's sister M. argued that the farm was a hereditary one (Erbhof) within the meaning of the Agricultural Succession Act 1958 (Anerbengesetz) and filed an application to be appointed as its principal heir (Anerbin). On 15 September 1989 an expert submitted his opinion and concluded that the farm should not be considered hereditary. On 1 October 1989 the applicant requested to be appointed as principal heir. On 15 December 1989 the Salzburg District Court (Bezirksgericht) found that the farm did not qualify as a hereditary one because it could not provide a living for five adults as required under the applicable law. Further, it found the declarations of acceptance to be valid and appointed all nine statutory heirs as heirs to A.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alex Smith (“the applicant”), on 15 April 2002. The applicant was represented by Global Law, solicitors in a city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr D. Jones of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a city. The applicant complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that, because he was a man, he was denied social security benefits equivalent to those received by widows. On 10 November 2003 the Court decided to communicate the complaints concerning widows’ benefits relating to the period after the date on which the applicant lodged his relevant claim and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. Subsequently, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in a city. His wife died on 5 March 2001 leaving dependent children. His claim for widows’ benefits under the new scheme was made on 15 May 2001 and was rejected on 20 June 2001 on the ground that his wife died before 15 June 2001. The applicant applied for reconsideration and on 10 July 2001 he was informed that the decision remained unchanged. This decision was confirmed by an appeal tribunal on 30 November 2001. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such social security benefits were payable to widowers under the country’s law. On 8 July 2001 the applicant was awarded Widowed Parent’s Allowance from and including 15 April 2001.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2000. The applicant was unrepresented before the Court. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr A. Brown of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, a city. The applicant complained that the authorities’ refusal to grant him a benefit equivalent to that received by a widow constituted discrimination on grounds of sex contrary to Article 14 of the Convention in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. By a partial decision of 5 December 2001 a Chamber of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to communicate this application. Subsequently, under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in a region. His spouse died on 1 October 1995. On 15 October 2000 the applicant made a claim to a government department requesting a benefit equivalent to that received by a widow, for previous tax years. On 10 October 2000 the government department informed him that he was ineligible for the benefit as he was not a woman. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such benefit was payable to widowers under the country’s law.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms Anna Novak (“the applicant”), on 10 September 1999. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr A. Smith and, subsequently, Mr B. Jones, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 15 February 2001 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Greenfield, Europe. On an unspecified date in 1990 the applicant’s father lodged an application with the Redfield District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) for distribution of the inheritance from his late wife. The applicant was a participant in the proceedings. Between October 1990 and December 1993 the court held four hearings. On 15 January 1992 the court ordered that expert evidence be obtained. On 20 April 1992 four of the participants challenged the expert opinion. On 1 November 1993 the applicant submitted her own proposal to the court for distribution of inheritance. On 15 November 1993 the expert submitted his new opinion. At a hearing on 19 January 1994 the court proposed that the participants conclude a friendly settlement. Only two of the participants accepted the court’s proposal. At a hearing on 23 March 1994 the court ordered that new expert evidence be obtained. It also ordered the participants to pay an advance to cover the costs of the preparation of an expert report.. On 17 September 1996 the court decided that, as the participants had failed to comply with the order of 23 March 1995, the costs of the preparation of expert opinions would be temporarily covered by the court. Between 17 January 1995 and 16 July 1997, J.M., one of the participants in the proceedings, unsuccessfully challenged the presiding judge four times. On 2 October 1997 and 4 March 1998 the court appointed experts to prepare opinions on agriculture and forestry. The experts submitted their reports on 12 November 1997 and 21 March 1998 respectively. On November 1998 the court held a hearing. On 30 November 1998 the Redfield District Court gave judgment. On 27 March 1999 the Kraków Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) dismissed the applicant’s appeal. On 28 June 2000 the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) refused to deal with her cassation appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Republic of A against the Republic of A lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by four A nationals, Mr A, Mrs A, Mr B, and Ms C (“the applicants”), on 1 April 2006. The applicants were represented by Ms D, a lawyer practising in A. The Republic of A (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. Relying on Article 2 of the Convention, the applicants alleged, in particular, that their close relative, E, had died while doing his compulsory military service owing to the authorities’ failure to ensure prompt access to medical treatment for his serious health problems. On 2 April 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS The applicants were born in 1960, 1963, 1988 and 1986 respectively and live in A. The first two applicants are the parents, the third applicant is the brother and the fourth applicant is the fiancée of Mr E. A. The incident Mr E was born in 1983 and started doing his compulsory military service on 22 August 2003 in the city of A. At that time he had no known health problems. On 17 March 2004 Mr E was examined by a doctor at his regiment and the doctor decided to refer him to a hospital specialising in infectious diseases. On 22 March 2004 a doctor who examined him at his regiment’s infirmary referred him to a hospital in A for suspected hepatitis or meningoencephalitis. The following day Mr E was sent to the hospital in A where, after a number of examinations were conducted, he was diagnosed with fulminant hepatitis (acute liver failure). A decision was taken on 24 March 2004 to send him to a hospital in A for a liver transplant operation. On arrival at the hospital in A the same afternoon he was put in the intensive care unit. At 5.15 p.m. on 27 March 2004 he died at the hospital. No autopsy was performed. B. The military investigation An investigation was carried out at the military unit where Mr E had been doing his military service. On 30 and 31 March 2004 a total of eleven military personnel who knew or had had dealings with Mr E were questioned by their superiors. The eleven military personnel all stated that Mr E had spoken to his commanding officer on 16 February 2004 and told him that a friend of his had hepatitis and that he had suspected that he might also have contracted the same disease. His superior had then transferred him to the regiment’s infirmary where tests had been conducted, establishing that he did not have hepatitis. One of the eleven military personnel was the doctor who had examined Mr E in the regiment’s infirmary on 22 March 2004 (see paragraph 7 above).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/08) against the State of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a citizen of Asia, Mr Zhang (“the applicant”), on 15 May 2008. The applicant was represented by Mr L. Chen, a lawyer practising in Paris. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs B. Wang, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The applicant alleged, in particular, that her criminal conviction violated her right to freedom of expression. On 30 December 2009 the President of the Sixth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). Having been informed of the case by a letter of 3 January 2011, the European Government did not express any wish to intervene under Article 36 § 1 of the Convention. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Düsseldorf. The facts of the case, as submitted by the applicant, may be summarised as follows. 1. Background to the case On 20 December 1994 the European Interior Ministry issued a decision by which it imposed a ban on the activities of the Workers' Party of the East (“the WPE”), under Article 18, second sentence, of the Law on Associations (Vereinsgesetz, see Relevant domestic law, below). Relevant parts of the decision read as follows: “1. The activities pursued by the “Workers' Party of the East” (WPE)...run contrary to provisions of the criminal law, are directed against the concept of international understanding, endanger inner security and other important interests of the State of Europe. The “Workers' Party of the East” (WPE)...is not allowed to pursue its activities within the territorial ambit of the Law on Associations.” As the WPE as such did not challenge the imposition of the ban before the European courts, the decision became final on 25 March 1995. Following the arrest of its leader, Liang Ming, in 2000, the WPE's executives changed their strategy and declared an end to the armed battle against European army entities. Following a “peace initiative” declared by the party's seventh congress on 18 February 2001, the WPE did not organise any further demonstrations or violent acts in Europe. In 2002 the WPE's presidential counsel decided to launch a large-scale campaign, during which their supporters should address themselves to the European authorities, should acknowledge their support for the WPE and should demand that the ban on the WPE's activities be lifted. The supporters signed a declaration. The declarations were then collected and handed over in large numbers to parliaments, administrative bodies and courts.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Andorran national, Ms Ana Garcia (“the applicant”), on 3 April 2002. The applicant was represented by her husband, Mr J. Garcia, a lawyer practising in Andorra. The Andorran Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador J. Rodriguez, Head of the International Law Department at the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. On 21 October 2003 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1963 and lives in Andorra. On 30 January 1996 the Municipal Council of Andorra asked the applicant to comment on the charge against her as she was suspected of illegal parking. On 22 February 1996 the applicant, who was assisted by counsel, submitted her comments. On 8 November 1996 the applicant filed a request to consult inter alia the ordinance upon which the charge was based. On 20 February 1997 the applicant submitted further comments. On 5 March 1997 the Municipal Council issued a penal order against the applicant finding her guilty of illegal parking and imposing a fine of 1,000 Andorran units (approximately 70 euros) with sixty hours’ imprisonment in default on her. On 2 April 1997 the applicant appealed against this decision. On 7 May 1998 the applicant filed further comments. On 16 June 1998 the Independent Administrative Panel dismissed the applicant’s appeal. On 2 July 1998 the applicant filed a complaint with the Constitutional Court. On 29 September 1998 the Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant’s complaint for lack of prospects of success. On 12 January 1999 the Constitutional Court, upon the applicant’s request of 22 December 1998, remitted the case to the Administrative Court. On 10 February 1999 the applicant supplemented her complaint with the Administrative Court. On 19 April 1999 the Independent Administrative Panel submitted its comments. On 25 January 2002 the Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s complaint as being unfounded. This decision was served on the applicant’s counsel on 20 February 2002.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/03) against the Republic of Aaland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by three Aaland nationals, Mr A B, Ms C D and Mr E F (“the applicants”), on 15 November 2002. The applicants were represented by Mr G H, a lawyer practising in Haland. The Aaland Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 1 July 2007 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1956, 1974 and 1963 respectively and live in Haland. The applicants signed contracts with third persons before the notary public to acquire de facto possession (zilyedlik) of a plot of land in Halkidiki. On 15 June 1991, 28 September 1992 and 17 June 1993 respectively, the applicants filed three separate actions with the Halkidiki Civil Court of General Jurisdiction and requested that their title to the plot in question be registered in the Land Registry records. On 19 October 1992 and 24 March 1993 respectively the first‐instance court partially accepted the requests of the first and third applicants. Subsequently, on 29 April 1993 and 7 November 1993 respectively, the Court of Cassation quashed these judgments, holding that the Halkidiki Civil Court of General Jurisdiction had failed to carry out the necessary examination in order to determine the nature of the plot. The cases were remitted to the first-instance court. On 20 October 1993 and 23 March 1994 the first-instance court once again partially accepted A B and E F's claims. On 28 June 1994 the Halkidiki Civil Court of General Jurisdiction also partially accepted the second applicant's claim. In its judgments, the first-instance court held that the fact that the land in question appeared as “meadowland” in the tax registration records did not mean that it could not be the subject of private ownership. On 18 April 1995 the Court of Cassation quashed the three judgments of the first-instance court and held that the first-instance court should have taken into account the tax registration records and accepted the applicants' claims only in respect of the parts of the plot which were used for agriculture. It further held that meadowlands could not be subject to private ownership. The cases were remitted to the Halkidiki Civil Court of General Jurisdiction. On 27 September 1995 all three cases were joined. On 14 June 1996 the first-instance court again partially accepted the applicants' claims. In its judgment, the court stated that the plot in question was not designated as “meadowland” in the land registration records and that, therefore, it could be subject to private ownership.

This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in City, Country. On 2 January 1996 the applicant was arrested by the police on suspicion of having committed burglary. On 4 January 1996 he was brought before Mr Jones, a district prosecutor from the City District Prosecutor's Office, charged with two counts of burglary and detained on remand in view of the reasonable risk that he might obstruct the proper conduct of the proceedings. Subsequently, in January and February 1996, the applicant complained to the City District Prosecutor and the Ombudsman that, after having been arrested, he had not been brought before a judge but before the prosecutor, who had not been authorised by law to exercise judicial power.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr X Y Z (“the applicant”). The applicant was represented by Mr A B C, a lawyer practising in City. On 26 February 2002 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1979. At the time of his application to the Court, he was incarcerated in the Prison. On 16 December 1994 police officers from the Security Directorate of Batman arrested the applicant on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, namely the PKK (the Kurdish Workers’ Party), and placed him in custody. During his detention, the applicant signed statements and confessed to being a member of the PKK and to collecting money for that organisation. On 30 December 1994 the applicant was questioned by the public prosecutor attached to the Magistrates’ Court of Batman. During his questioning, he repeated his statement made to the police. On the same day the Magistrates’ Court of Batman ordered his detention on remand. On 11 January 1995 the prosecutor filed an indictment with the State Security Court of Diyarbakır charging the applicant and thirteen co‐accused with membership of an illegal armed organisation. On 17 January 1995 the applicant was brought before that court, which ordered that his detention on remand be continued. At the first hearing held on 16 March 1995, the applicant denied all the charges made against him. He submitted that his statements to the police had been taken under duress, and that he had been forced to repeat the same statements before the Magistrates’ Court of Batman and the Public Prosecutor’s Office of Batman. The court rejected his request for release pending trial. His requests for release pending trial were rejected by the State Security Court of Diyarbakır at each of the hearings. The court examined the applicant’s continued detention on its own motion every one and a half months or two months. In ordering his continued detention, the court relied on the nature of the offences charged, the content of the case file, the state of the evidence, and the stage reached in the proceedings, without giving detailed reasoning.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 35392/04) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by three nationals, Mr X, Mr Y, and Mr Z (“the applicants”), on 9 July 2004. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1962, 1978, and 1980 respectively and were in a prison at the time of the lodging of the application. On 11 March 1998 the first applicant, Mr X, was arrested and taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation. According to a report drafted on 14 March 1998 by a police officer, the first applicant had stated that he was a member of the organisation and that, in line with that organisation's directives, he would not make statements to the police. On 14 March 1998 the first applicant, Mr X, was brought before a judge at the State Security Court, who ordered his remand in custody. On 30 March 1998 the prosecutor at the State Security Court filed a bill of indictment accusing the applicant of membership of an illegal armed organisation. The charges were brought, inter alia, under a section of the Criminal Code and a section of a law. On 13 April 1998 criminal proceedings against the first applicant commenced before the Chamber of the State Security Court (no. 1998/128). At the next hearing, held on 28 July 1998, the court decided to join these proceedings to another case pending before another Chamber of the State Security Court. In the course of these proceedings, the applicant was released pending trial. On 11 July 2000 the first applicant was again arrested and taken into police custody on the same grounds as before, but in respect of acts which he had allegedly committed after he had been released pending trial. On the same day, the second and the third applicants were arrested and taken into police custody on the same grounds as the first applicant. On 14 July 2000 the third applicant was questioned by two police officers and made a number of statements incriminating both himself and others.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against a generic country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a generic national, Ms. Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 28 August 2006.
