PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 65897/01) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X. The applicant was represented by Ms Y, a lawyer practising in a city. The government did not designate a specific Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 4 October 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1980 and lives in a city. The facts of the case, as submitted by the applicant, may be summarised as follows. On 23 February 1999 the applicant was taken into custody by police officers from the Anti-Terror branch of the Security Directorate on suspicion of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation, namely the PKK, contrary to the Criminal Code. On 26 February 1999 the applicant was brought before a single judge of the State Security Court. The applicant denied the veracity of his signed statements taken in detention, alleging that they had been obtained under duress. On the same day, the judge ordered his detention on remand. On 3 March 1999 the public prosecutor at the State Security Court filed a bill of indictment, charging the applicant with aiding and abetting the PKK by engaging in propaganda for it. On 7 April 1999 the State Security Court held its first hearing in the absence of the applicant. The court ordered that the applicant’s detention on remand be continued as he could not be heard. On 11 May 1999 the State Security Court held its second hearing in the presence of a judge. The applicant was heard by the court. He denied having engaged in propaganda and stated that he had been merely watching the crowd shouting slogans. He further denied the statements taken in police custody and before the public prosecutor. He alleged that he had been forced to sign the impugned statements under duress. He asked the court to dismiss the charges and release him. Assessing the evidence against the applicant, the court dismissed his request and ordered his continued detention on remand. On 18 June 1999 the Grand National Assembly amended the Constitution and excluded members from State Security Courts. Following similar amendments made on 22 June 1999 to the Law on the State Security Courts, the judge hearing the applicant’s case was replaced. On 19 August 1999 the State Security Court held a hearing. The applicant’s representative requested his release.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/07) against the Republic of Andria (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Andria (a fictional country), Mr John Doe (a fictional person), on 15 March 2007. The applicant was represented by Mr Richard Smith and Mr Peter Brown, lawyers practising in Andria (a fictional city). The Andrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged, in particular, that while performing his military service he had lost the sight in his left eye as a result of the military authorities’ failure to provide him with prompt and appropriate medical assistance. On 20 July 2012 the application was communicated to the Government. On 18 October 2014 the Chamber decided, under Rule 54 § 2 (c) of the Rules of Court, to invite the parties to submit further written observations on the admissibility of the applicant’s complaint under Article 3 of the Convention. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1982 and lives in Andria (a fictional city). On 26 June 2002 the applicant started his compulsory military service in Andria (a fictional city). On 27 August 2002 he contacted the infirmary of his regiment, complaining of severe pain in his left eye. According to the applicant, the military doctor was absent and he was given eye drops by a soldier who had no medical qualifications. According to the Government, the records of the infirmary (which were not made available to the Court) showed that the applicant had been examined by a military doctor and given eye drops by that doctor and not by a soldier. The following day the pain became persistent, so the applicant contacted the infirmary once again. He was told that he should go to his dormitory and rest. According to the applicant, despite the pain he was in, he was not relieved of his sentry duties during that period. On 2 August 2002 he was referred to the Andria State Hospital, where he was diagnosed with a corneal ulcer. On 6 August 2002 the applicant was transferred to the Andria Military Hospital, where his treatment started. However, he completely lost the sight in his left eye. According to the applicant, the doctors informed him that he had lost his eyesight because of the delay in starting the treatment, as in corneal ulcer cases it was essential to start treatment immediately. On 13 August 2002 the applicant was transferred to Andria GATA Military Hospital for further treatment. He stayed there until 25 September 2002, during which time he underwent several operations. He returned to the hospital for a number of additional operations from 9 November 2002 to 7 February 2003, 10 to 21 March 2003, 2 to 10 May 2003, and lastly, 15 to 18 July 2003. A medical report issued on 17 July 2003 concluded that the applicant was no longer medically fit for military service and that he was eligible for an ocular prosthesis.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against a country lodged with an international organization under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms by a national, Mr John Doe ("the applicant"), on 20 April 1998. The applicant was represented by Mr Alan Brown, a solicitor practising in a city, and by Mr Charles Green, a barrister practising in a different city. The government of the country ("the government") were represented by their Agent, Ms Jane Smith, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that the statutory assumption made against him by the court which issued a confiscation order following his conviction for a drug offence violated his right to the presumption of innocence under Article 6 § 2 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). It was declared partly admissible on 30 November 2000 [Note by the Registry. The Court’s decision is obtainable from the Registry]. The applicant and the government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 8 February 2001 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the government Ms Jane Smith, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr David White, Counsel, Ms Mary Black, Ministry of Home Affairs, Mr Peter Brown, Ministry of Home Affairs, Advisers; (b) for the applicant Mr Charles Green, Counsel, Mr Yash Chandarana, Junior Counsel, Mr Alan Brown, Solicitor. The Court heard addresses by Mr Green and Mr White. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 27 June 1996, at a crown court, the applicant was convicted of being concerned in the importation in November 1995 of a large quantity of cannabis resin, contrary to section 170(2) of the Customs and Excise Management Act 1979. On 12 July 1996 he was sentenced to nine years’ imprisonment in respect of this offence. The applicant had previous convictions, but none in respect of a drug-related offence. An inquiry was conducted into the applicant’s means, pursuant to section 2 of the Drug Trafficking Act 1994. On 15 May 1996 a Customs and Excise appointed drug financial investigation officer advised the applicant’s solicitors that he was carrying out an investigation into their client’s financial affairs and that he wished to interview him in order to assist the court in determining whether he had benefited from drug trafficking. The applicant declined to take part in the interview.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/11) against a national entity (an unnamed country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals from a different region (an unnamed region), Mr Alex Smith (“the first applicant”) and Mrs Jane Doe (“the second applicant”), on 21 December 2011. The applicants were represented by Mr John Brown, a lawyer practising in an unnamed city. The national entity (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Peter Green, of an unnamed office. The applicants alleged, in particular, that the refusal by the national entity to allow their three children, R., L., and B., to reside in the country constituted a breach of their right to respect for family life as guaranteed by Article 8 of the Convention. They further held that expulsion of the children, who were residing in the country illegally, would violate Article 3 of the Convention. Pending proceedings before the Court the applicants therefore requested that Rule 39 of the Rules of Court be applied. On 9 March 2012 the Vice-President of the Second Section, to which the case was allocated, decided not to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court but to grant priority to the application under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court. On 29 June 2012 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicants and the Government each submitted observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The first applicant was born in 1967 and the second applicant in 1974, both in an unnamed region. Their children R., L., and B. were also born in an unnamed region in 1994, 1996, and 2003 respectively. The applicants have a fourth child, E., who was born in the country in 2010. They all live in an unnamed city, an unnamed canton. In June 1997 the first applicant entered the country, where he applied for asylum. His asylum request was rejected by an unnamed office on 19 November 1997 and it ordered that he should be expelled. The expulsion was not executed, and on 21 May 1999 the first applicant received a temporary residence permit for the country. On 28 February 2000 the first applicant married a national of the country. On 2 March 2005 he received a permanent residence permit for the country. On 26 August 2006 he got divorced. On 10 January 2007 he married the second applicant - whom he had known since 1993 and with whom he had had the three children - in an unnamed city (an unnamed region). The second applicant entered the country on 6 April 2007 with a visa. On 7 June 2007 the first applicant applied for a residence permit for the second applicant on the ground of family reunification. The second applicant announced her arrival in the unnamed city on 8 June 2007.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2007. The applicant was represented by Ms Jane Smith and Ms Mary Johnson, lawyers practising in Andria. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 22 June 2009 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (former Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1980 and detained in Andria prison. On 5 February 1998 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of being a member of an illegal organisation. On 13 February 1998 the applicant was examined by a doctor. The medical report drawn up by the doctor indicated that there was hyperaemia on the applicant's thighs. On the same day the applicant was brought before the public prosecutor, where he stated that he had been stripped and hosed with water under police custody. On the same day the judge at the Andria State Security Court ordered his pre-trial detention. Before the judge the applicant stated that his statement in police custody had been taken under torture, but he did not give any details. On 29 March 1998 the public prosecutor at the Andria State Security Court issued an indictment charging the applicant with attempting to undermine the constitutional order under Article 146 of the former Criminal Code. On 8 June 1998 the applicant stated before the Andria State Security Court that his statement in police custody had been taken under torture, without giving any details. On 24 March 2003 the Andria State Security Court convicted the applicant under Article 146 of the former Criminal Code. On 10 April 2004 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 24 March 2003. By Law no. 6789 of 18 July 2005, published in the Official Gazette on 20 July 2005, State Security Courts were abolished. The case against the applicant was subsequently resumed before the Andria Assize Court. On 22 October 2008 and 10 January 2009 the applicant objected to his continued detention and requested his release. The 12th Chamber of the Andria Assize Court dismissed the applicant's objections on 17 January and 18 April 2009 respectively, having regard to the nature of the offence in question and to the state of the evidence. No hearing was held. On 1 April 2009 the Andria Assize Court convicted the applicant. According to information in the case file, the case is pending before the Court of Cassation. Throughout the proceedings, the first instance courts examined the applicant's continued detention at the end of each hearing, either on their own motion or upon the applicant's requests.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/05) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 22 December 2003. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr X Y (“the representative”), on 18 October 2005. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in a city. On 18 April 2002 the District Court ordered that the applicant be remanded in custody in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed several offences of fraud and that he had organised and led a criminal group. On 15 July 2002 the court extended the applicant’s detention until 17 September 2002. It relied on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged and on the risk that he might tamper with evidence. On 13 September 2002 the court extended the applicant’s detention until 17 November 2002. It repeated the grounds previously given for his detention and found that his remaining in custody was necessary to complete the expert psychiatric examination as to the state of the applicant’s mental health. The applicant’s detention was subsequently extended on 14 November 2002. The court attached importance to the serious nature of the offences with which he had been charged and the likelihood of a heavy sentence being imposed on him. On 11 December 2002, the applicant was indicted on several charges of fraud while acting in an organised criminal group. Subsequently, in March 2003, the case file was transferred to the District Court for reasons of procedural economy. On 23 April 2003 the District Court extended the applicant’s detention for a three-month period, until 23 July 2003. It considered that the severity of the anticipated sentence and the need to secure the proper course of the trial justified the continuation of that measure. On 22 July 2003 the District Court extended the applicant’s detention until 23 October 2003. It also observed that the applicant’s continued detention was necessary in order to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, given the gravity of the anticipated sentence. In addition, it referred to the complex nature of the case. On 13 October 2003 the District Court extended the applicant’s detention until 23 January 2004. The court referred to a strong likelihood that he had committed the serious offences with which he had been charged and stressed that a heavy penalty might be imposed on him. It also observed that no other measures would prevent the applicant from obstructing the proceedings or going into hiding.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2007. The applicant was represented by Mr Alex Smith, a lawyer practising in Warsaw. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Jane Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 7 December 2008 the President of the Chamber to which the case had been allocated decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Nowa Wieś. He is a retired police officer who had formerly been employed in the Civil Guard. In 1975 the applicant had been dismissed from service for a disciplinary offence. He was rehired by the Police in 1992. He retired in 1995. A. Civil proceedings for payment On 28 September 1994 the applicant brought a civil action against the State Treasury for compensation on the grounds that in 1975 he had been unlawfully dismissed from his post at the Civil Guard and banned from working there until 1991. In addition the applicant claimed that he had not been hired by the new police services immediately after the change of the political regime, as he should have been, but only in May 1992. The applicant sought compensation, which comprised damages for lost earnings from 1975 to 1991, for lost earnings and benefits from 1991 to 1992, and for alleged moral suffering due to the loss of employment. On 10 November 1994 the Poznań Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) rejected the claim on the ground that the civil court did not have jurisdiction over a dispute arising out of an employment relationship between a civil servant and the State (niedopuszczalność drogi sądowej). As a result of an interlocutory appeal by the applicant, on an unspecified date the Poznań Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) quashed that decision and remitted the case to the Poznań Regional Court. On 11 August 1996 the Poznań Regional Court rejected the claim on the ground of lack of jurisdiction. On 7 March 1997 the Poznań Court of Appeal quashed that decision and remitted the case indicating that the applicant's claim was of a civil character as it had arisen out of relations between a civil servant and the State which were of an administrative and legal character rather than from a bond of special trust and loyalty between the two. On 5 November 1998 the Poznań Regional Court dismissed the applicant's claim.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/16) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Ms Anna Andersson (“the applicant”), on 15 April 2016. She was represented before the Court by Mr Bjorn Berg and later by Ms Clara Carlsson, both lawyers practising in Oslo. The Norwegian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Daniel Eriksson, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention that the Court of Appeal did not give adequate reasons for its judgment. Mrs Eva Forsberg, the judge elected in respect of Norway, withdrew from the case (Rule 28). Accordingly, Mr David Gunnarsson was appointed to sit as an ad hoc judge (Article 26 § 4 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). On 30 August 2016 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS A. The circumstances of the case The applicant is a Norwegian national born in 1955. She lives in Sandefjord. The applicant suffered for many years from, inter alia, pain in her back and legs and numbness in her left arm. She alternated between full and part-time sick leave from 1997 to 2002. In 1999 she received a partial early retirement pension and in 2003 a full disability pension. In 2004 she applied for life annuity and alleged that her physical problems had been caused by her former employment as a driver (1974 to 1975), as a dairy worker (1975 to 1986) and as a food science technician (1986 to 1993). The Social Insurance Office (Forsikringstjenesten) appointed an in-house specialist in orthopaedic surgery who, in a written statement, concluded that there was not a high degree of probability (høy grad av sannsynlighet) that any harmful element in the applicant’s former employment had caused her problems. On 20 June 2006, after having held an oral hearing, the Social Insurance Office rejected the application. Referring to, inter alia, the specialist statement by the insurance doctor, it was held that the applicant had not been subject to any harmful influences which, with a high degree of probability, could have caused or aggravated her problems. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (domstolen) of Oslo. On 21 April 2008 the court, after having held an oral hearing, upheld the Social Insurance Office’s decision in full. The court found that, although it was scientifically known that employees in the food industry had a statistically high risk of injury, the circumstances in the applicant’s case had to be taken into account. The applicant’s back problems had appeared after barely two years in the industry and she suffered from degenerative changes to her back.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/95) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Xanadan national, Mr Ali Xanadu (“the applicant”), on 7 June 1996. The applicant was represented by Mr Mehdi Xanadu, a lawyer practising in Xanadu (Republic of Xanadu). The Republic of Xanadu did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. Mr Rıza Xanadu, the judge elected in respect of Xanadu, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr Feyyaz Xanadu to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints (applications nos. 26480/95, 28291/95, 29280/95, 26699/96, 29700/96, 29701/96, 29702/96, 29703/96, 29911/96, 29912/96, 29913/96, 31831/96, 31834/96, 31853/96, 31880/96, 31891/96, 32987/96, 32900/96, 32964/96, 33362/96, 33369/96, 33645/96, 34591/96, 34687/96, 39428/96 and 43362/96) (Rule 43 § 2). By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Arrest and detention of the applicant On 25 November 1980 police officers from the Xanadu Security Directorate arrested the applicant on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way). On 6 February 1981 the Xanadu Martial Law Court (sıkıyönetim mahkemesi) ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. B. Trial in the Xanadu Martial Law Court On 26 February 1982 the Military Public Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Martial Law Court against the applicant and 722 other defendants. The Public Prosecutor accused the applicant, inter alia, of membership of the Dev-Yol, whose object was to undermine the constitutional order and replace it with a Marxist-Leninist regime. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Xanadu Criminal Code. On 21 March 1984 the Xanadu Martial Law Court ordered the applicant’s release pending trial.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by four Xanadu nationals, Mr X Y Z, Mr A B C, Mr D E F and Mr G H I (“the applicants”), on 30 May, 14 and 18 June 1996 respectively. Mr Y and Mr I were represented before the Court by Mrs J K L and Mr M N O respectively, lawyers practising in Xanadu. Mr B and Mr F did not designate a lawyer for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador P Q R. The applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of the proceedings against them. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. Mr S T U, the judge elected in respect of Xanadu, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr V W X to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place (Article 27 § of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). By a decision of 17 October 2000 the Court declared the application admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) . This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Arrest and detention of the applicants In January and February 1981 the applicants were arrested by policemen and placed in police custody. They were accused of membership of an illegal organisation, the Org-X (Revolutionary Path). On 15 April, 11 May and 9 July 1981 the Xanadu Martial Law Court (sıkıyönetim mahkemesi) ordered the applicants’ detention on remand. B. Trial in the Xanadu Martial Law Court On 26 February 1982 the Military Public Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Xanadu Martial Law Court setting out charges against 723 defendants, including the applicants. He accused the applicants of membership of an organisation whose aim was to undermine the constitutional order and replace it with a Marxist-Leninist regime, contrary to Article 146 § 1 of the Xanadu Criminal Code On different dates the applicants were all released pending trial by the Xanadu Martial Law Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of A (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of A (a fictional country), Mr A (a fictional name), (“the applicant”), on 15 November 2005. The applicant was represented by Mr B (a fictional name), a lawyer practising in B (a fictional city). The Government of A (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 20 December 2008 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1985 and lives in C (a fictional city). On 10 April 2004 he was expelled from a military academy as he was found unsuitable to be a student there following a secret security investigation conducted on him and his family. The applicant was not notified of the specific reasons for his expulsion. Subsequently, the applicant asked the Supreme Military Administrative Court to annul the expulsion decision. During the proceedings, he did not have access to the classified documents and information submitted by the Ministry of Defence to the Supreme Military Administrative Court in support of its decision to expel him from the military academy. On 20 March 2005 the Supreme Military Administrative Court rejected the applicant’s request. It stated that information and documents the confidentiality of which was required and necessitated for the performance of military service could not be disclosed to the applicant. The court further emphasised that it was not bound by the classification made by the administration and that it made its own assessment as to whether the confidentiality of the documents was justified in each case. The written opinion submitted by the public prosecutor to the Supreme Military Administrative Court during the proceedings was not communicated to the applicant. The applicant subsequently requested the rectification of the Supreme Military Administrative Court’s decision, arguing that his inability to access the results of the security investigation due to their allegedly confidential nature precluded him from duly defending himself. On 15 June 2005 the Supreme Military Administrative Court rejected the applicant’s rectification request. II. RELEVANT LAW A description of the relevant domestic law can be found in the decision of D v. A ((dec.), no. 56789/06, 10 October 2009).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Xlodavia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Xander Smith (“the applicant”), on 15 July 2001. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Y. Zulu of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 2 September 2007 the President of the Fifth Section of the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Xlodavia. 1. Main proceedings - civil proceedings for payment On 23 June 1992 the applicant filed a claim for payment against his former employer with the Xlodavian Regional Court. On 2 December 1992 the court gave judgment. Upon the applicant's appeal the Xlodavian Court of Appeal remitted the case on 22 March 1993. On 19 September 1993 the Regional Court held the first hearing in the case. Subsequently, hearings were held on 19 November 1993, 10 April and 25 May 1994. In 1995 the court held two hearings, on 14 January and 13 July, and ordered the preparation of an expert opinion. On 15 February 1996 the Xlodavian Regional Court gave a preliminary judgment. On 14 July 1996 the Xlodavian Court of Appeal quashed the judgment and remitted the case. On 16 May and 14 September 1997 the Regional Court held further hearings. On 28 September 1997 the Xlodavian Regional Court gave judgment. It was upheld by the Xlodavian Court of Appeal on 10 February 1998. On 9 May 1998 the applicant lodged a cassation appeal. On 16 December 1999 the Supreme Court held one hearing and gave judgment in which it dismissed the cassation appeal. 2. Proceedings under the 2005 Act On 17 February 2006 the applicant lodged a complaint under section 19 of the Law of 18 July 2005 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time (“the 2005 Act”). On 10 April 2006 the Xlodavian Court of Appeal rejected the appeal as it was inadmissible in law. On 13 May 2006 the applicant lodged a claim for damages under section 17 of the 2005 Act read in conjunction with Article 418 of the Civil Code. He sought compensation for the alleged mistakes in the examination of his claims and for the protracted length of the proceedings. On 30 December 2006 the Xlodavian Regional Court dismissed the claim. His appeal against the judgment was dismissed by the Xlodavian Court of Appeal on 18 June 2007.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 42509/05) against a country of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 20 November 2005. The applicant was represented by a law firm based in a city. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms Jane Smith, a government office. On 13 May 2008 the acting President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The parties requested an oral hearing. However, the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, Mr John Doe, is a national who was born in 1954 and lives in a town. The facts of the case, as submitted by the applicant, may be summarised as follows. In 1989 the applicant joined a military organization as a clerk, a civilian position, carrying out duties such as filing, photocopying, and maintaining a stationery store. In July 1993 the applicant was informed that he was to be made redundant, following organizational changes in the military organization pursuant to a process of civilianization. He was subsequently informed that the clerical post which he had occupied was to become a civilian post and was to be converted to that of a technical storeman. The applicant applied for this new post, but was informed in February 1994 that he could take it only if he undertook a training course, but that all relevant training courses had been cancelled. He also applied for a number of other clerical posts within the organization but was refused for them all. The applicant was therefore made redundant. His discharge from the organization, dated 18 February 1994, was formally made, incorrectly, on the basis that his services were no longer required. The applicant later discovered that his former duties were being carried out by an untrained civilian, while the technical storeman post remained vacant. On 3 May 1994 the applicant complained about his redundancy to an industrial tribunal, but his claim was rejected because the industrial tribunal did not have jurisdiction over matters involving military personnel. On 19 December 1994 the applicant claimed redress in respect of his redundancy from his commanding officer, under sections 180 and 181 of the Army Act 1955. On 22 March 1995 the commanding officer issued a brief in which he concluded that the applicant had a weak case for redress. He further requested the Army Board of the Defence Council to determine whether the applicant was subject to military law. The applicant's solicitors, on 6 December 1996, submitted observations in reply.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/08) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Novak (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2007. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr X. Y., a lawyer practising in Berlin. The European Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. W., of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the domestic authorities had failed to take effective steps to enforce his right to respect for his family life in respect of his two sons, as guaranteed by Article 8 of the Convention. On 12 October 2009 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1). The President also gave priority to the application, pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1967 and lives in Berlin. The applicant married in 1997 and has two sons, C, born on 3 December 1997, and D, born on 4 February 2004. In November 2002 the applicant's wife moved to her parents' house, taking C with her. One month later she instituted divorce proceedings. The applicant visited them on several occasions. However, most of these visits were disrupted by the couples' mutual hostility. In February 2003 the applicant's wife informed him that she would not allow further visits, but the applicant continued to go to her flat, sometimes with other members of his family. On 3 August 2003 the applicant, during one of the visits, took his son C away with him, without his wife's consent and apparently by force. Afterwards C lived with the applicant in Berlin until 8 March 2007. The applicant submitted that C had been neglected and that he had acted in the best interests of his son. C subsequently received dental treatment, psychological support and speech therapy, and started going to school. The Government submitted that the child's psychological problems had been caused by the trauma of being kidnapped by his father, which had also led to the aggravation of his stutter. They relied on the reasoning of the Regional Court judgment of 30 June 2006 (see paragraph 16 below). In August 2003 the applicant's wife informed the prosecutor that her son had been kidnapped by the applicant. The applicant's wife also applied to the court for sole residence of C; however, on 19 November 2003 the Regional Court decided to make a temporary residence order for C with the applicant. The applicant's wife was granted contact rights. The Government submitted that the applicant had been hindering her contact with C; the applicant denied this.

PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 12345/11 and 67890/14) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals, Mr John Doe and Mr Richard Roe (“the applicants”), on 15 July 2010 and 28 November 2013 respectively. The first applicant was born in 1962 and is currently detained in a prison in a region. He was represented by a law firm of solicitors practising in a city. The second applicant was born in 1976 and is currently detained in a prison in a region. He was represented by another law firm of solicitors practising in the same city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Smith of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The applicants’ complaints concerning the length of their criminal proceedings were communicated to the Government on 13 November 2012 and 17 December 2012 respectively. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. The initial investigation On 16 February 1998 Mr X reported his ex-wife, Ms Y, missing. On 24 February 1998 police carried out an initial forensic investigation of an apartment which Ms Y and her son had shared with the applicants in June 1997, the date she had last been seen. An Interim Missing Persons report was prepared by police and submitted to the Procurator Fiscal on 1 May 1998, with later reports following on 31 August 1998 and 8 September 1998. On 30 June 1998 police obtained a search warrant in respect of the apartment Ms Y had shared with the applicants. However, a full forensic examination of the property does not appear to have disclosed any relevant evidence. On 18 August 1998 the applicants were sentenced to periods of imprisonment of eight years’ and six years’ respectively following their conviction for various sexual offences. The complainer in relation to some of those offences was Ms Y’s son. Following conviction, both applicants were placed on the Sexual Offenders’ Register. By September 1998 Ms Y’s disappearance was being referred to by the Procurator Fiscal at Kilmarnock as “suspicious” and Crown Counsel described the police inquiry into her disappearance as a “murder inquiry”. On 14 September 1998 the police sought authorisation for the release of the applicants from a prison into their custody so that they could be interviewed with regard to the disappearance and suspected murder of Ms Y. On 17 September 1998, while serving their sentence at a prison, the applicants were detained by the police under section 14 of a law and removed to a police office in a city. On the same day the applicants were interviewed separately by police officers for over five hours. During these interviews they were directly accused of the murder of Ms Y. Both applicants asked police officers if they were going to be charged with the murder, but received indications to the contrary.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against a country (Country X) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (National Y) of Country X, on 15 September 2007. The national was represented by a lawyer practising in a city (City Z). The Government of Country X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, a person from the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The national alleged that he had been deprived of effective access to court in contravention of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. On 3 October 2008 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). On 2 March 2011 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1 of the Rules of Court) and the above application was assigned to the newly composed Sixth Section. The Government submitted a unilateral declaration which did not offer sufficient basis for finding that respect for human rights as defined in Article 37 § 1 the Convention had been fulfilled (Prencipe v. Monaco, no. 43376/06, §§ 62-63, 16 July 2009). The Court was therefore required to continue the examination of the case. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The national was born in 1945 and lives in a city (City A). By letter dated 10 September 2005, an authority (Authority B) informed the national that its representative would come to his home on 18 September 2005 to attach property to secure his tax debts amounting to 100,000 (approximately 11,000). It noted that he had previously been informed about his debts but that, since he had not paid, an attachment would be carried out. It is not known when the letter was sent or when the national received it. On 20 September 2005 the authority attached 1,000 (approximately 100) from a bank account belonging to the national. A document called Proof of Attachment was sent to the national confirming this and advising him how to go about appealing against the decision and that this had to be done within three weeks from the date that the decision was served on him. The national, who was on holiday at the time, did not receive the Proof of Attachment until he returned home on 9 October 2005 and was formally served the decision. In a decision of 25 September 2005 the authority distributed and paid the attached money to the creditor, in this case, the State itself. The decision was open to appeal within three weeks from the date of the decision. On 21 October 2005 the national requested the authority to rectify the decision concerning attachment as he considered it to be incorrect.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/95) against the Republic of X ("the Republic") lodged with the European Human Rights Commission ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms Convention ("the Convention") by a national, Mr John Doe ("the applicant"), on 1 May 1995. The applicant was represented by Mr A. B., a lawyer practising in Y. The Republic did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Convention institutions. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a "reasonable time". He further submitted that his right to a fair hearing had been breached because of his conviction by the Y Military Court, which lacked independence and impartiality. He finally contended that he had been convicted on the basis of the statements he had made to the police under duress. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 October 1997, when Protocol No. 10 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 10). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 October 2000 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 22 August 2002, the Court declared the application partly admissible. It retained the applicant's complaints concerning his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal and declared the remainder of his complaints inadmissible. The applicant and the Republic each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Y. On 15 January 1980 the applicant was arrested and placed in police custody by police officers from the Y Security Agency. He was accused of membership of an illegal organisation, the Z. On 13 March 1980 the Y Military Court ordered the applicant's detention on remand. On 24 January 1981 the Military Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Y Military Court against the applicant and 700 other defendants. The prosecution requested that the applicant be convicted and sentenced pursuant to Article 167 § 2 of the Criminal Code on account of his membership of an illegal armed organisation whose aim was to undermine the constitutional order and replace it with a Marxist-Leninist regime, contrary to Articles 145 § 1 and 167 § 2 of the Criminal Code. On 30 November 1982 the applicant was released pending trial.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an European national, Mr Eduard Novak (“the applicant”), on 20 December 2004. The applicant was represented by Mr K. Müller, a lawyer practising in Bergdorf. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr G. Weber, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 20 October 2006 the Court decided to communicate the complaints concerning the length of the proceedings and the lack of remedies in that respect to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. In this respect, the Court decided to reject the Government's request to discontinue the application of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Bergdorf. On 22 December 1995, while driving his car in reverse gear, he knocked a pedestrian over and drove off. On 9 February 1996 the Salzburg District Court (Bezirksgericht) issued a provisional penal order (Strafverfügung), following which the applicant was found guilty under Article 89 of the Criminal Code (Strafgesetzbuch) of having negligently caused bodily harm and under Article 95 of the Criminal Code of having abandoned the victim. The applicant was ordered to pay a fine of 13,000 Austrian schillings (ATS) (approximately 950 euros (EUR)). The applicant objected and the District Court opened ordinary criminal proceedings. On 12 July 1996 the court held a hearing in which it examined several witnesses, the applicant and an expert who submitted that the applicant had not necessarily noticed the accident. Subsequently, on 13 August 1996, the court convicted the applicant of having negligently caused bodily harm and acquitted him of having abandoned the victim. It sentenced him to a fine of ATS 3,500 (approximately EUR 240), suspended on probation. The applicant did not appeal. Meanwhile, having interviewed the applicant in March 1996, the Salzburg Federal Police Authority (Bundespolizeidirektion) issued a penal order on 18 May 1996 whereby the applicant was found guilty under section 4(2) in conjunction with section 100(2)(a) of the Road Traffic Act (Straßenverkehrsordnung) of having failed to inform the next police station about the accident. The applicant was ordered to pay a fine of ATS 4,500 (approximately EUR 300). He appealed on 7 June 1996. On 20 February 1997 the Salzburg Independent Administrative Panel (“the IAP” – Unabhängiger Verwaltungssenat), having held a public hearing on 15 February 1997 in which it heard evidence from several witnesses in the presence of the applicant's counsel, dismissed the applicant's appeal. It found that the applicant should have looked behind him when he reversed his car and, therefore, was to be blamed for carelessly failing to notice the accident.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/11) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alex Anon (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2010. The applicant was represented by Mr B. Client, a lawyer practising in a city. The government of the country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms C. Counsel of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that his right to respect for family life and his right to marry and found a family had been breached. On 15 June 2014 the application was communicated to the government. The applicant and the government each filed written observations on the admissibility and merits. In addition, third‐party comments were received from a centre for justice and human rights (Centre for justice and human rights), which had been given leave by the President to intervene in the written procedure (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 3 of the Rules of Court). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in a city. In 1998 the applicant married R. In 2003 R. underwent infertility treatment so she could conceive a child with him. In autumn 2003 the applicant met A.H. In January 2004 he moved out of the flat he had lived in with R. On 30 October 2005 A.H. gave birth to their daughter, M. On 25 August 2006 the applicant filed a petition for divorce. At first he requested a no-fault divorce. In his petition the applicant referred to various marital misunderstandings and quarrels for which he blamed the respondent. He admitted that he had moved out of the matrimonial home, but did not mention his involvement with a new partner. At a hearing held on 15 September 2006 the applicant refused to undergo the mediation process provided for by divorce law. R. did not agree to a divorce, declared that she loved the applicant and asked the court to dismiss the divorce petition. Subsequently, the applicant requested a divorce on fault‐based grounds. During the proceedings thirteen witnesses were heard. Most of them were of the opinion that the marriage seemed happy until autumn 2003. Only the applicant’s mother, his two colleagues and his cousin recalled minor arguments between the spouses. During the final hearing on 9 March 2009 the respondent reiterated her refusal to divorce. On 17 March 2009 the regional court refused to grant the divorce to the applicant. The court held that he was the only person responsible for the breakdown of his marriage because he had failed to respect the obligation of fidelity. The court did not find it credible that problems had already begun within the first year of the marriage. It observed that until 2003 the applicant had not wanted children. In that year he had changed his mind.

PROCEDURE The case of X and others was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (hereinafter called “the Commission“). The case originated in an application against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission on 11 June 1971 under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (hereinafter called “the Convention“) by five German citizens, namely X, Y, Z, W and V. The Commission’s request, which referred to Articles 44 and 48, paragraph (a) (art. 44, art. 48-a), and to which was attached the report provided for in Article 31 (art. 31), was lodged with the registry of the Court on 15 July 1977, within the period of three months laid down in Articles 32 para. 1 and 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47). The purpose of the request is to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 para. 1, 8 and 13 (art. 6-1, art. 8, art. 13) of the Convention. On 28 July, the President of the Court drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of five of the seven judges called upon to sit as members of the Chamber; Mr. X, the elected judge of German nationality, and Mr. Y, the President of the Court, were ex officio members under Article 43 (art. 43) of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 3 (b) of the Rules of Court respectively. The five judges thus designated were Mr. X, Mr. Y, Mr. Z, Mr. W and Mr. V (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4 of the Rules of Court) (art. 43) . Mr. Y assumed the office of president of the Chamber in accordance with Rule 21 para. 5. The President of the Chamber ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Government and the Delegates of the Commission regarding the procedure to be followed. By an Order of 12 August, the President decided that the Government should file a memorial within a time-limit expiring on 28 November and that the Delegates of the Commission should be entitled to file a memorial in reply within two months of receipt of the Government’s memorial. At a meeting held in private on 18 November in Strasbourg, the Chamber decided under Rule 48 to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court, on the ground “that the case raise(d) serious questions affecting the interpretation of the Convention“. The Government filed their memorial on 28 November.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by an international body on 18 September 1995, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 of the Convention (art. 32-1, art. 47). It originated in an application (no. 21335/93) against a state lodged with the body under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national, Mr X, on 2 September 1992. The body’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby the state recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent state of its obligations under Article 5 paras. 1 and 3 of the Convention (art. 5-1, art. 3). In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The government, having been informed of their right to intervene (Article 48 (b) of the Convention and Rule 33 para. 3 (b)) (art. 48-b), did not indicate any intention of so doing. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr Y, the elected judge of national origin (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr Z, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 4 (b)). On 29 September 1995, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr A, Mr B, Mr C, Mr D, Mr E, Mr F and Mr G (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 5) (art. 43). As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 6), Mr Z, acting through the Registrar, consulted the agent of the government, the applicant’s lawyer and the delegate of the body on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the government’s memorial on 3 April 1996 and the applicant’s memorial on 13 May 1996. In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 28 August 1996. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the government Mr H, (b) for the body Mr I, (c) for the applicant Mr J. AS TO THE FACTS I.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2009. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr X Y (“the Government”). The applicant complained that he had been unable to present his civil case to the courts on an equitable basis vis-à-vis the opposite party. On 12 November 2010 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in a city. From 2001 until 2005 the applicant ran a business, a shoe shop, with his wife. In October 2005 he started serving a prison sentence. On 5 August 2007 he lodged a civil action against his wife with a district court, claiming that she should transfer the lease of the shop to him, together with the merchandise which had been left there at the time of his arrest. He also claimed compensation for damage which he had allegedly sustained as a result of her having unlawfully taken over the business after his arrest, in the amount of 2,500 local currency units (LCUs) per month since October 2005. He further requested exemption from court fees. In the statement of claim he informed the court that his opportunity to represent himself properly had been curtailed by the fact that he was serving a prison sentence. The proceedings were conducted under the procedural provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure pertaining to commercial disputes, providing, in particular, for certain restrictions as regards time-limits for proposing evidence to be examined by the first-instance court (prekluzja dowodowa). On 18 December 2007 the regional court exempted the applicant from the obligation to pay court fees in the amount of 5,500 LCUs but maintained his obligation to pay other court fees as they arose in the future. The court noted that the applicant was poor and did not have any savings which would secure his procedural interests in the proceedings. On 20 February 2008 the applicant requested that witness A B, the owner of the shop, be heard by the court to testify on the lease. On 8 May 2008 the court issued a decision dismissing the applicant’s request for the witness A B to be heard. The court reiterated that according to the Code of Civil Procedure the applicant’s request had to be refused, as he had failed to submit it with his statement of claim. The court further noted that the requested evidence was of no importance for the case. The decision was sent to the applicant. It was served on him on 31 May 2008. A date for the hearing was scheduled for 12 June 2008.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by four European nationals, Mr Alex Smith, Mrs Jane Doe, Mr John Brown and Mrs Mary Jones (“the applicants”), on 15 September 2005. The applicants were represented by Mr David Lee, a lawyer practising in Berlin. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Robert Green of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 13 July 2007 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1947, 1953, 1953 and 1953 respectively and live in Berlin. A. Main proceedings On 7 December 2001 the Consumer Protection Association (Związek Obrony Konsumentów) acting on behalf of the applicants lodged a claim for payment with the Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy). In a letter of 22 May 2003 the applicants’ legal adviser complained about the delay in the proceedings and asked for a hearing date to be fixed. On 15 December 2003 the court held the first hearing. From January to March 2003 the court held 2 hearings. On 10 February 2004 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) declared the defendant insolvent. Consequently, at a hearing held on 4 March 2004 the trial court stayed the proceedings ex lege. The proceedings were resumed on 9 May 2007. On 11 May 2007 the Regional Court discontinued the proceedings in the case. B. Proceedings under the 2004 Act On 4 February 2005 the Consumer Protection Association acting on behalf of the applicants lodged a complaint with the Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time (Ustawa o skardze na naruszenie prawa strony do rozpoznania sprawy w postępowaniu sądowym bez nieuzasadnionej zwłoki) (“the 2004 Act”). The applicants sought a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings before the Regional Court had been excessive. They asked for an award of just satisfaction in the amount of 10,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) (approx. EUR 2,500). On 15 March 2005 the Court of Appeal dismissed the complaint. The court found that the 2004 Act produced legal effects as from the date of entry into force (17 September 2004), its provisions applied retroactively to all proceedings in which delays had occurred before that date and had not yet been remedied. It acknowledged that there had been a delay at the initial stage of the proceedings but found that this situation had ceased to exist when the 2004 Act entered into force.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the United Republic of A against the United Republic of A lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of A, Ms Hilde Lohmann (“the applicant”), on 1 May 2003. The applicant was represented by Mr J.H. Müller, a lawyer practising in A. The Government of A (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs B. Schmidt, a lawyer, of the Ministry of Justice. On 2 May 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in A. From 1960 to 1979 she worked as a ballet dancer for the X Company, a national company of the United Republic of Y. In 1979 she terminated her career on stage and worked for the company as a set and costume designer. The X Company paid the applicant her wages as a costume and set designer and, in addition, a monthly allowance in the amount of 588 Y marks (hereafter “the allowance”). The allowance was paid by virtue of the regulation of the Minister of Culture (Anordnung über die Gewährung einer berufsbezogenen Zuwendung an Ballettmitglieder in staatlichen Einrichtungen der Y) of 1 September 1976. Pursuant to this regulation former members of ballets in the Y were paid an allowance at the end of their career on stage. The allowance accrued after reaching the age of 35 and having worked for at least 15 years as a dancer. It was paid, irrespective of other earnings, by the former employer. Once the former dancer received an old-age or invalidity pension the allowance was regularly paid by the National Insurance of the Y (Staatliche Versicherung der Y). After the reunification of the Y and the United Republic of A the X Company which formerly belonged to the National People's Army (Nationale Volksarmee) of the Y was incorporated into the organisation of the Ministry of Defence of the United Republic of A. The Ministry took over the contracts with the company's staff and continued to pay the applicant her wages and the allowance. The allowance and the retirement pensions were moreover converted and paid in A Marks (AEM). On 1 January 1992 the Ministry discontinued all allowance payments to former ballet dancers with reference to Article 9 § 2 in conjunction with Appendix II, Chapter VIII, Section H, paragraph III Nr. 6 of the A Unification Treaty. In December 1992 the applicant brought an action with the Social Court of A claiming the payment of the allowance. On 24 August 1994 the Social Court of A ruled in a leading judgment that the social courts had no jurisdiction over disputes concerning the allowance.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Andorran nationals, Mr Alvaro Garcia and Mrs Silvia Garcia (“the applicants”), on 15 July 1998. The applicants were represented by Mr P.J. Martinez, a lawyer practising in Andorra. The Republic of Andorra (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicants complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of compensation proceedings. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 15 October 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 15 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). The case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. THE FACTS The applicants were born in 1950 and 1957 respectively and live in Andorra. In 1985 the applicants' daughter, D.G., was severely injured in an accident. Her hair was burned and part of her scalp was damaged. On 20 December 1989 D.G. underwent surgery at the Andorra University Plastic Surgery Department to repair the damage to her scalp. Prior to the operation, the doctors informed the applicants about the risks involved. Following the operation, the applicants' daughter caught an infection. On 10 January 1990 the doctors carried out a second operation on D.G. following a deterioration of her health. However, her physical appearance did not improve following the operation. On 20 December 1991 the applicants filed an action with the Andorra Civil Court of First Instance against the doctors who performed the operation and claimed compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary loss sustained as a result of medical malpractice. On 25 January 1992 the Andorra Court of First Instance issued a decision of non-jurisdiction on the ground that it was not competent to examine the acts of civil servants carried out in the exercise of their duties. On 12 February 1993 the applicants filed an action with the Andorra Administrative Court against the Andorra University Medical Department (hereinafter “the defendant”) and claimed compensation for medical malpractice. On 22 March 1993 the Andorra Administrative Court conducted a preliminary examination of the case file. On 10 April 1993 the defendant submitted its observations to the court. On 12 May 1993 the applicants submitted their response. On 28 January 1994 the Andorra Administrative Court held a hearing and gave an interim decision ordering the defendant to submit all the files concerning the operation performed on the applicants' daughter. On 20 March 1994 the defendant submitted additional observations.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 28 May 1996, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 of the Convention. The Government also applied to refer the case to the Court on 27 August 1996. It originated in an application against a State lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by a citizen on 22 April 1992. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the State recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8, 10, 13 and 14 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent her. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio a judge of British nationality and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court. On 10 June 1996, in the presence of the Registrar, the President of the Court drew by lot the names of the other seven members. As President of the Chamber, Mr Bernhardt, acting through the Deputy Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings. Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the Government’s memorial on 2 January 1997 and the applicant’s memorial on 6 January 1997. On 20 August 1996 Mr Bernhardt had granted leave to a non-governmental human rights organisation based in London to submit written comments on specified aspects of the case. These were received on 2 January 1997. On 21 February 1997, the Chamber decided to reject the Government’s application to refer the case to the Court, on the grounds that it was received after the expiry of the three-month period laid down by Articles 32 para. 1 and 47 of the Convention and that there was no exceptional reason for extending the time-limit.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by nationals, Mr Ali Mustafa and Mrs Sevgi Mustafa, on 27 June 2002. The applicants were represented by Mr Halil Tan, Mr Selim Yilmaz and Mrs Ayşe Tan, lawyers practising in City. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 12 July 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants, Ali Mustafa and Sevgi Mustafa, were born in 1985 and 1948 respectively and live in City. The second applicant is the mother of the former. When the first applicant (“the applicant”) was 17 years old, on 25 May 2002 at about 2 p.m. he was arrested at his home by police officers from the Department of Peace and Order attached to the City Security Directorate, on suspicion of involvement in various incidents of bag snatching in City. According to the report drafted by the police, the arrest took place on 26 May 2002 at 9.50 p.m. on the street outside his residence. The report stated that the police had acted upon the information of a certain M.D., a fellow detainee, who had cited the applicant's name during his interrogation in relation to the bag snatching in City. The report also stated that the applicant's mother had been informed of the arrest and detention. On 26 May 2002 the applicant was given a medical examination at the Forensic Medicine Institute. A subsequent medical report revealed that there were some blade cuts on his left arm which were three or four days old but, apart from those injuries, no signs of possible ill-treatment were noted. The applicant was then taken into custody at the Peace and Order Department. On 27 May 2002 at 3.30, 4.15, 4.45, 5.10, 5.35 and 6 p.m., the applicant and M.D. were taken to on-site inspections. A lawyer assigned by the City Bar Association was present during these inspections, when the applicant gave detailed statements as to how he and M.D. had planned and committed the offences. Around 6.15 p.m. the same day, he was again given a medical examination. The medical report drafted on that occasion recorded no signs of beatings or the use of physical force on the applicant's body. The same day, at the request of the police, the public prosecutor, without seeing the applicant, extended his custody period by two more days under Article 128 § 2 of the former Code of Criminal Procedure.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against a country (Country X) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals (John and Mary Smith) (“the applicants”) on 1 October 2002. The applicants were represented by Mr A. Brown, a lawyer practising in a city (City Y). The Government of Country X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador C. White, Head of the International Law Department at the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. On 12 November 2003 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS The applicants were born in 1935 and 1939 respectively and live in a town (Town A). On 11 April 1994 the applicants applied for a building permit for an adjoining building with a garage on their property. On 16 August 1994 the Mayor (Bürgermeister) of the town granted the building permit. On 31 August 1994 the applicants’ neighbours appealed. On 30 March 1995 the Municipal Council granted the appeal and refused the building permit. On 12 July 1995 the Regional Government (Landesregierung) dismissed the applicant’s appeal (Vorstellung). On 27 February 1996 the Administrative Court (Verwaltungsgerichtshof), upon the applicants’ complaint, quashed this decision. Subsequently, on 25 June 1996, the Regional Government quashed the Municipal Council’s decision and remitted the case back to the Municipal Council. On 10 February 1997 the applicants lodged an application with the Administrative Court against the Municipal Council’s failure to decide (Säumnisbeschwerde). On 21 April 1997 the Municipal Council again dismissed the applicants’ request for a building permit. On 17 June 1997 the Regional Government dismissed the applicants’ appeal. On 31 July 1997 the applicants filed a complaint with the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof). In October 1997 the Regional Government and the Mayor of the town submitted their observations. On 28 September 1999 the Constitutional Court instituted proceedings for the review of the lawfulness of the ordinance (Verordnungsprüfungsverfahren) upon which the Municipal Council had based its decision. On 15 March 2000 the Constitutional Court found that the ordinance at issue was unlawful. On 6 April 2000 this decision was served on the applicants’ counsel. On 26 May 2000 the Regional Government quashed the Municipal Council’s decision and remitted the case back to the Municipal Council. In January 2001, following negotiations, the applicants reached an agreement with the Municipal Council to the effect that the latter accepted to pay the fees incurred by the applicants’ representation in the proceedings so far, on the condition that the applicants amended their request for a building permit in accordance with the newly established building scheme (Bebauungsplan). On 6 February 2001 the applicants amended their request for a building permit. Subsequently, on 28 May 2001, the Municipal Council quashed the building permit of 16 August 1994 and remitted the case back to the Mayor of the town.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 35019/97) against the Republic of a European country lodged with a regional human rights body (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 16 January 1997. THE FACTS On 19 March 1991 the District Administrative Authority, referring to the relevant provisions of the Forestry Act, ordered the applicant to reforest a plot of land owned by him. In its decision, the authority specified that the applicant should plant 270 larches. In its reasoning, it noted that until October 1986 the northern part of the plot of land had been fully covered with larches and robinias and that the previous stock of trees was shown by the still existing stumps. The decision was served on 17 July 1996.
