PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123456/02) against the Republic of XYZ lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 August 2002. The applicant was represented by Mr B. Smith, a lawyer practising in City. The Government of XYZ (“the Government”) did not designate an agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 3 September 2006 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1937 and lives in City. In 1986 the applicant obtained a contract from the Provincial Administration of City to carry out repair work in twelve public schools in District in order to render them operational. At a later date, however, he noticed that some of the schools had not yet been fully constructed. He applied to the Governor's Office in City and requested the contract to be annulled. He submitted that the payment agreed on for the repairs was too low, given the amount of work needed to complete the construction of those schools. The Governor's Office requested the applicant to start the construction and the repairs, reassuring him that he would be reimbursed for his additional work. After having completed the construction, the applicant applied to the Provincial Administration of City and requested additional compensation of 50,000,000 local currency units (LCUs). However, his repeated efforts proved fruitless as no payment was made. On 18 July 1990 he filed an action with the City Civil Court and claimed the outstanding amount of LCUs 50,000,000 plus interest. On an unspecified date, the court appointed an expert to determine the amount of additional payment that the applicant was entitled to recover. However, the expert failed to submit his report. In the absence of the expert report, the court ordered on-site visits to the schools in order to establish the additional work carried out by the applicant. On 3 October 1999 the members of the court, accompanied by new experts, conducted an on-site examination at the schools. On an unspecified date, the experts submitted their calculation of the sums incurred by the applicant for the additional work. On 27 April 2000 the City Civil Court awarded the applicant LCUs 50,000,000 plus interest calculated at three different rates depending on the relevant period of time, i.e., 30% per annum running from 18 July 1990 to 1 January 1999; 50% per annum from 1 January 1999 to 1 January 2001; and at the rediscount rate running from 1 January 2001 until the date of payment. The applicant appealed.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by three Xanadu nationals, Mr Ali Xan, Mr Mustafa Xan, and Mr Yilmaz Zan (“the applicants”), on 27 June 2002. The applicants were represented by Mr N. Vefa, a lawyer practising in Yonder. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purpose of the proceedings before the Court. On 25 September 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaint concerning the length of the applicants' remand in custody and the criminal proceedings brought against them. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1982, 1984 and 1982 respectively and live in Zanadu. The applicants were arrested and taken into custody on 19 and 20 March 1998 respectively on suspicion of their involvement in the throwing of Molotov cocktails at various public buildings. On 23 March 1998 the Yonder Magistrates' Court ordered their remand in custody. The applicants were aged sixteen (Mustafa Xan) and eighteen (the other applicants) at the time of the events. On 23 April 1998 the public prosecutor at the Yonder State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicants and four other persons, accusing them of throwing Molotov cocktails at the Yonder primary school and the Yonder public garage on 18 March 1998 and of attempting to throw a Molotov cocktail at the Yonder Atatürk primary school with a view to supporting the activities of an illegal organisation, namely the Zan (the Zan Workers' Party). The charges were brought under Article 168 § 2 of the Xanadu Criminal Code. On 7 May 1998 the criminal proceedings against the applicants and four other accused commenced before the Yonder State Security Court. On 12 June 1998 the court heard the applicants who refuted the allegations against them and their earlier submissions given before the police, public prosecutor and the Magistrates' Court. They also challenged the accuracy of the arrest protocol and the report on the reconstruction of the events. The court decided to secure the testimony of those who had attended the arrest and the reconstruction of events and the submissions of the accused who were not detained. It further ordered that the birth date of Yilmaz Zan and another accused be determined since they had claimed that they were actually born in 1987. Between 12 June 1998 and 22 January 2001, the Yonder Security Court held fifteen hearings where it took various procedural decisions and postponed the trial as the procedure concerning the determination of the age of two accused had not been completed.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 25 May 2010. The applicant was initially represented by Ms Jane Smith, his sister, and subsequently by Mr Ali Ahmed, a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs Anna Vogel, and by their permanent Deputy Agent, Mr Hans-Joachim Behrens, of the Ministry of Justice. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the retrospective extension of his preventive detention from a period of ten years, which had been the maximum for such detention under the legal provisions applicable at the time of his offence, to an unlimited period of time violated Article 5 of the Convention. On 23 June 2010 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government, requested them to submit information on changes in the applicant’s detention regime and adjourned the examination of the application until the judgment in the case of M. v. Country, no. 12345/04, had become final. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). In view of the fact that the judgment of 18 November 2009 in the case of M. v. Country became final on 11 June 2010, the President decided on 19 June 2010 that the proceedings in the application at issue be resumed and granted priority to the application (Rule 41 of the Rules of Court). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and was in a prison until his preventive detention was declared terminated and his provisional detention in a suitable institution under the Therapy Detention Act was ordered on 29 November 2011. He is currently detained in a psychiatric hospital. A. The applicant’s previous convictions and the order for his preventive detention and execution thereof Since the age of sixteen, the applicant was sentenced to terms of imprisonment several times and spent only some four years outside prison. On 21 June 1990 the Regional Court convicted the applicant of rape. It sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment and ordered his placement in preventive detention pursuant to Article 66 § 1 of the Criminal Code (see paragraphs 32-33 below). The court found that in July 1989, some four months after his release from prison, the applicant had raped a woman whom he had come across in a city at night. The Regional Court had consulted a psychiatric expert, S., on the applicant’s criminal responsibility and his propensity to commit further sexual offences and endorsed his findings. The expert had found that the applicant did not suffer from a mental illness diminishing his criminal responsibility.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by five Xanadu nationals, A. X, B. X, C. X, D. X and E. X (“the applicants”), on 13 July 1998. The applicants were represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in Yonder. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Convention institutions. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). The case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section. By a decision of 27 November 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 November 2004 the case was transferred to the newly composed Second Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1952, 1979, 1981, 1983 and 1985 respectively and live in Zan Zan. On 15 April 1991 terrorists raided the applicants' village in Zan Zan and killed the men of the village, including the first applicant's husband and the father of the other applicants, A. O. On 15 April 1992 the applicants brought an action before the Yonder Administrative Court against the Ministry of Internal Affairs, (hereinafter “the defendant”), claiming a breach of the State's responsibility to protect the life and security of its citizens. They requested the court to award them compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage in respect of A.O's death. On 29 April 1992 the case was notified to the defendant. On 28 May 1992 the defendant submitted its observations to the court. On 16 June 1992 the observations were sent to the applicants. On 22 June 1992 the applicants submitted their response to the observations of the defendant. On 20 August 1992 the applicants' reply was sent to the defendant. PROCEDURE 11 The case originated in an application (no. 61908/00) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”), on 23 July 2000. 2. The applicant was represented by Mr. Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. 3. A. had been detained. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Ms. Jane Doe (“the applicant”) on 15 September 1999. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Federal Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 March 2002. The applicant was represented by A. Smith, a lawyer practising in Berlin. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Peter Jones, Director, Ministry of Justice. The applicant complained, inter alia, that the length of the court proceedings before the Federal Constitutional Court exceeded a reasonable time within the meaning of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 16 March 2003 the Fourth Section declared the application partly inadmissible. On 22 March 2004, the Fourth Section declared the applicant's complaint about the length of the proceedings admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), the parties replied in writing to each other's observations. THE FACTS The applicant lives in Großbottwar, Germany. He owned four shares in a company, the XYZ AG. 99 % of this company's shares were held by the company ABC GmbH. On 7 August 1993, following a majority decision of the shareholders' meeting, the XYZ AG sold all its company assets to a newly founded company, the XYZ GmbH, and was subsequently liquidated. The majority shareholder offered to buy the minority shareholders' shares at a price of 620 EUR per share. On 23 August 1993, the applicant and other private shareholders challenged the decision of 7 August 1993 before the Berlin Regional Court. They submitted that the main shareholder had circumvented rules aiming at the protection of minority shareholders inherent in the German Act on Stock Companies (Aktiengesetz). They further complained that the price per share offered by the main shareholder was too low and that minority shareholders had not been able to buy parts of the assets. On 23 February 1994, the Regional Court rejected the claim on the grounds that the decision in question was lawful and that there had been no violation of the applicant's and other shareholders' rights. On 22 December 1994, the Berlin Court of Appeal rejected the appeals lodged by the applicant and the other minority shareholders. On 4 December 1995, the Federal Court of Justice refused to entertain their appeals on points of law. On 13 January 1996, the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Federal Constitutional Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Novak (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2000. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr M. Smith, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 15 January 2003 the Fifth Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. It also gave priority to the application, pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1920 and lives in Novo City, Europe. The applicant was involved in administrative proceedings concerning the amount of the veteran benefit he had been receiving since 1975. On 10 September 2000 the Supreme Administrative Court gave a judgment in his case. The court, inter alia, ordered the Office for Veterans and Victims (Urząd do Spraw Kombatantów i Osób Represjonowanych) to pay the applicant a sum of EUR 10 as reimbursement of the court fees. In June 2002 the applicant received from the Office for Veterans and Victims only a half of the awarded sum (EUR 5). In May 2002 the applicant lodged with the Novo City District Court (Sąd Rejonowy w Novo City) a civil action against the Office for Veterans and Victims. He claimed compensation and payment of, inter alia, the remaining sum of EUR 5. On 15 June 2002 the Novo City District Court transmitted the case to the Warsaw District Court. The Warsaw District Court held one hearing and on 31 December 2003 it gave a default judgment (wyrok zaoczny) against the defendant ordering it to pay EUR 50 in compensation and EUR 30 as a reimbursement of the court fees. The court ordered that the judgment should be immediately enforceable. On 30 March 2004 the defendant lodged an objection against this decision. On 18 October 2004 the Warsaw District Court suspended the enforcement order in respect of the judgment of 31 December 2003. The applicant asked the court to order again that the judgment of 31 December 2003 be immediately enforceable. On 29 October 2004 the Warsaw District Court dismissed his request. The applicant appealed against this decision and was ordered to pay the court-fees. On 22 August 2005 his appeal was rejected due to the applicant's failure to pay the court fees. In the appeal procedure against this decision he was also ordered to pay the court‐fees. Finally, the applicant paid the court-fees and on 16 December 2006 the Warsaw Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) examined his appeal against the decision of 29 October 2004 and dismissed it.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 47117/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (“the applicant”), on 19 November 1998. PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court on 9 September 1993 by the European Commission of Human Rights ("the Commission") and on 11 October 1993 by the Government of a Kingdom ("the Government"), within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of a Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention"). It originated in an application (no. 15890/89) against a State lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national, Mr X, on 25 July 1989. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby the State recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46); the Government’s application referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48). The object of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 (art. 10) of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr Y, the elected judge of a nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr Z, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On 24 September 1993, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr A, Mrs B, Mr C, Mr D, Mr E, Mr F, and Mr G (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43). By letter of 29 October the Agent of the Government notified the Registrar of the appointment of Mr H as an ad hoc judge; in a letter of 16 November the Agent informed the Registrar that Mr H had withdrawn and that they had therefore appointed Mr I to replace him (Article 43 of the Convention and Rule 23) (art. 43). PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of that country, Ms Alice Brown (“the applicant”), on 10 November 2004. The applicant was represented by Ms K. Miller, a lawyer working for Human Rights Association, a city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr E. Green, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a city. The applicant complained of the lack of legal recognition of her change of gender and the refusal of the Social Security Department to pay her a retirement pension at the age of 60 as was the case for other women. She relied on Article 8 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 20 June 2005, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE According to the applicant’s birth certificate, she is male. She served in the army for three years from the age of 18 and then worked as a police officer. Aged 25, she gave up attempting to live as a man, and had gender reassignment surgery two years later. She has presented as a woman since 1964, is identified as a woman on her National Insurance card and paid contributions to the National Insurance scheme at the female rate (until 1976, when the difference in rates was abolished). In 1973 she became self-employed and started paying into a private pension fund. By a letter dated 23 September 1998, the applicant applied to the local government benefits office for State pension payments. She wished these to commence on 23 December 1998, her 60th birthday. Her application was refused by a decision of the Adjudication Officer issued on 30 October 1998. He stated that she had applied “too early”, and was only entitled to a State pension from the age of 65, the retirement age applicable to men. Her appeal against this decision was heard by Social Security Appeal Tribunal on 13 April 1999, which dismissed it on the basis of established case-law. At this time she claimed that she was no longer able to work due to a spinal collapse fracture of osteoporotic origin. On 1 November 1999 the applicant submitted her appeal to the Social Security Commissioner.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Xana (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national from Yland (a fictional country), Ms X Yzzy (“the applicant”), on 15 April 2004. 2. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr A Bcd, a lawyer practising in Z City (a fictional city). The Yland Government, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings (Article 36 § 1 and Rule 44), did not indicate that they wished to exercise that right. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE 1. Background to the case The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Z City. 6. She is the mother of a daughter T., born in wedlock on 20 October 1991. 7. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two European nationals, Mr Alex Novak and his son, Mr Mark Novak (“the applicants”), on 10 June 2002. The applicants were represented by Mr T. Smith, a lawyer practising in Berlin. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr K. Jones of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 20 June 2009 the President of the Third Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3 of the Convention). On 19 July 2009 the Government requested the Court to sever the complaints of the applicants. On 17 August 2009 the Court granted the Government's request and decided to sever the complaints of Alex Novak (“the applicant”) from the rest of the application. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the restrictions placed on his contacts with his close family members when he was detained amounted to a violation of his right to respect for family life under Article 8 of the Convention. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1930 and lives in Berlin. A. The applicant's arrest and detention On 29 June 2001 the Berlin District Court remanded the applicant in custody for two months. The court relied on a statement given on 28 June 2001 by the applicant's mentally ill son, J.N., who accused the applicant of homicide. The court also referred to the likelihood that a heavy penalty would be imposed on the applicant. On an unspecified date the applicant appealed and requested that the preventive measure imposed on him be reduced in severity. He relied on his age (he was seventy years old at the time) and on the fact that he was undergoing medical treatment. On 13 July 2001 the Berlin Regional Court, relying on the same grounds as the District Court, upheld the challenged decision. On 24 August 2001 the Berlin Regional Prosecutor requested the court to extend the applicant's detention. On 26 August 2001 the Berlin District Court granted the request and extended the applicant's detention for another month, until 29 September 2001. On an unspecified date the applicant's lawyer appealed against that decision. On 13 September 2001 the Berlin Regional Court upheld the challenged decision. The court recognised that the only evidence against the applicant was the statement by the applicant's son, who had undergone a psychiatric examination. It stressed, however, that according to the results of the psychiatric report, the applicant's son's mental condition had improved. The court also relied on the risk that the applicant could obstruct the proceedings.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 13017/02) against a State (referred to as "the Republic of Turkey") lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a national (referred to as "a national"), Mr X ("the applicant"), on 7 March 2002. The applicant was represented by lawyers practising in a city (referred to as "Istanbul"). The State (referred to as "the State") did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 13 October 2005 the Court decided to communicate the application to the State. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1963 and is currently detained on remand in a prison (referred to as "Edirne F-type prison"). On 28 November 1992 the applicant was taken into police custody by police officers from a department (referred to as "Anti-Terrorism Department of the Istanbul Security Directorate"). On 10 December 1992 the State Security Court ordered his detention on remand. On 5 January 1993 the Public Prosecutor at the State Security Court filed an indictment against the applicant and others, charging them with membership of an illegal organisation, contrary to the Criminal Code and the Law on Prevention of Terrorism. At the hearing of 22 November 1993 before the State Security Court, which included a military judge, the accused protested against the proceedings. Following the intervention of the security forces, they broke the windows of the court building. At the hearings held between 1993 and 1994 the court heard the testimony of several witnesses and took the statements of the accused. On 18 June 1999 the Constitution was amended and the military judges sitting on the bench of State Security Courts were replaced by civilian judges. At the end of almost every hearing the court dismissed the applicant’s request to be released pending trial and ordered his continued detention on remand, having regard to the nature of the offence and the content of the case file. At the hearings during which the applicant was absent the court considered his situation of its own motion and ordered his detention on remand, relying on the same reasons. At the hearing of 27 March 2000 the court finished taking the final statements of almost all the accused including the applicant and stated that no additional time would be given to those who had not yet submitted their final observations. On 30 July 2001 the applicant filed a petition with a different chamber of the State Security Court, complaining about the court’s order for his continued remand in custody. On 1 August 2001 his objection was dismissed on account of the nature of the offence and the content of the case file.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 67690/01) against a State (Republic of Poland) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, a Polish citizen (Mrs Michalina Kruk), on 2 October 2000. The State (Republic of Poland) was represented by their Agents, and subsequently, by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 9 October 2003 the President of the Fourth Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the State. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS The citizen was born in 1939 and lives in a town (Ołdrzychowice), Poland. A. Facts before 1 May 1993 On 2 April 1985 the citizen applied to a commission (Wrocław District Commission for Mining Damages) for compensation for damage caused to her house. On 25 September 1985 the Commission dismissed her application. The citizen appealed against this decision. Subsequently, on 7 July 1987 the Supreme Administrative Court (Naczelny Sąd Administracyjny) and on 24 August 1988 the Appellate Commission for Mining Damage (Odwoławcza Komisja do spraw Szkód Górniczych) quashed previous decisions given in the case. On 7 April 1992 the District Commission for Mining Damage gave its decision in which it partly allowed the citizen’s action. The citizen appealed against this decision. B. Facts after 1 May 1993 On 8 December 1993 the Wrocław Regional Commission held a hearing. On 2 September 1994 a new law entered into force which provided that the civil courts would be competent to examine applications for compensation for mining damage and abolished the Commission for Mining Damage (Ustawa z dnia 4 lutego 1994, Prawo geologiczne i górnicze). Accordingly, the citizen’s case was transferred to the Regional Court (Świdnica Regional Court). The first hearing was held on 24 April 1995. The court ordered that an expert opinion be prepared. The opinion was submitted to the court on 26 April 1996. Subsequently, hearings were held on 18 November 1996, 17 March and 19 September 1997, 13 February 1998 and 10 February 1999. The court ordered several new expert opinions. On 17 February 1999 the Regional Court gave judgment in which it dismissed the citizen’s action. On 10 March 1999 the citizen lodged an appeal against this judgment. On 11 May 1999 the Regional Court of Appeal (Wrocław Court of Appeal) quashed the impugned judgment and remitted the case. On 1 October 1999 the Regional Court held a hearing. The trial court ordered that new expert opinions be prepared. The hearing scheduled for 19 January 2000 was adjourned. At the hearing held on 16 February 2000 the Regional Court gave judgment. The court partly allowed the citizen’s action and granted her compensation. The citizen lodged an appeal against this judgment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xanadu, Mr Xanadu Citizen (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2000. The Government of Xanadu (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purpose of the proceedings before the Court. On 1 January 2003 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the administrative proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the remainder of the application at the same time. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in the district of Yonder in the province of Here. On 1 January 1989 the Yonder District Council (hereinafter “the Council”) and the applicant signed an agreement. By virtue of this agreement the Council unconditionally allocated part of the historic castle in Yonder to the applicant to open and run a museum for an indefinite period. On 1 January 1989 the applicant was issued with a special title deed to the property enabling him to open the museum. On 1 January 1990 the museum was opened to the public following the grant of a licence by the Ministry of Culture. On 1 January 1991 the Council annulled the agreement of 1 January 1989 on the ground that the applicant had not signed a protocol with the Mayor of Yonder within 15 days from the date of the opening of the museum. Pursuant to such a protocol the applicant would have undertaken to pay the Council 40% of the money generated from the sale of the entrance tickets to visitors to the museum. Items displayed in the museum were removed from the museum by the Council's employees. On 1 January 1991 the applicant brought an action before the Here Administrative Court requesting the annulment of the Council's decision of 1 January 1991. On 1 January 1991 the Here Administrative Court annulled the decision on the ground that the Council had never informed the applicant about the protocol or warned him about its intention to rescind the agreement. The Council appealed against the decision. On 1 January 1995 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the Here Administrative Court's decision of 1 January 1991. On 1 January 1995 the Here Administrative Court acceded to the Supreme Administrative Court's decision and rejected the applicant's request to annul the Council's decision. The court noted that a clause in the initial agreement between the Council and the applicant had stipulated that 40% of the income would be handed over to the Council. The court further observed that the applicant had been reminded by the Council about this clause on 1 January 1990 and had been urged to sign the protocol. On 1 January 1997 the Supreme Administrative Court rejected the applicant's appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Anderson (“the applicant”), on 5 December 2006. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Carter of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 21 February 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The Government submitted a unilateral declaration and invited the Court to strike the application out of the list, in accordance with Article 37 of the Convention. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in a city. A. Civil proceedings for dissolution of a partnership On 6 November 1992 the applicant lodged a claim with the Regional Court (Sad Okręgowy) for dissolution of a partnership. On 6 June 1995 the proceedings were stayed. On 26 September 1996 the Regional Court discontinued the proceedings. The applicant appealed against this decision. On an unspecified date the Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) quashed the decision on the discontinuance of the proceedings. On 23 July 1997 the Regional Court found that it was not competent to deal with the matter and referred the case to the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy). Between 26 February 1998 and 2 September 2002 the court scheduled eight hearings, two of which were adjourned. On 2 September 2002 the court ordered that an expert report be obtained. Between 25 November 2002 and June 2003 the expert witness prepared his report. On 8 April 2004 the proceedings were stayed. The applicant appealed. On 16 August 2004 the court rejected the applicant’s appeal. The proceedings are still pending before the District Court. B. Proceedings under the 2004 Act On 14 June 2005 the applicant lodged a complaint under the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time (Ustawa o skardze na naruszenie prawa strony do rozpoznania sprawy w postępowaniu sądowym bez nieuzasadnionej zwłoki) (“the 2004 Act”). On 29 September 2005 the Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) dismissed his complaint on the ground that on the date of the entry into force of the 2004 Act no undue delays in the court’s conduct could be discerned. The court acknowledged that the proceedings before 2004 had been unreasonably lengthy for various reasons such as the failure of witnesses and lawyers to appear on numerous occasions and the unreasonably long period taken up by the preparation of a report by the expert witness.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Norwegian national, Mr. Lars Nordberg (“the applicant”), on 30 August 2006. The applicant was represented by Mr. Hans Peterson, a lawyer practising in Oslo. The Norwegian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms. Ingrid Hansen from the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the administrative appellate courts had failed to hold an oral hearing in proceedings relating to his request for disability benefits. On 27 November 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The application was later transferred to the Sixth Section of the Court, following the re-composition of the Court’s sections on 1 February 2011. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Jonsbro. Since June 2001, the applicant has been on 100% sick leave due to various health problems. He has, inter alia, been operated on for cancer as the consequence of which he suffers from recurrent Erysipelas (a bacterial infection of the skin, which typically involves the lymphatic system) and lymphatic oedema in both legs. Hence, on 18 June 2002, the applicant applied for disability benefits (handikappersättning) retroactively from June 2000. He claimed that, due to his health problems, he had incurred, and still incurred, extra costs for, inter alia, medication, doctors’ visits, treatment, travel expenses, special clothes and shoes, special soap and creams, and for supplementary vitamins and minerals. He had calculated that these extra costs amounted, in total, to NOK 123,456 (approximately EUR 13,500) per year. On 3 May 2003 the Social Insurance Office (försäkringskassan –hereinafter “the Office”) of the County of Vestfold rejected the request. It accepted certain extra costs for medication, medical treatment and support material as well as for certain travel up to a specific amount. However, in the Office’s view, the total of the applicant’s extra costs per year amounted to no more than NOK 10,000 from September 2000, NOK 11,000 from January 2001 and NOK 9,000 from January 2002. Thus, the Office concluded that the applicant’s extra costs did not reach the minimum level established for each year to be granted disability benefits (namely NOK 12,374 for 2000, NOK 12,431 for 2001 and NOK 12,517 for 2002, which was equal to 28.5% of the basic amount in line with the price index [basbelopp]). It further noted that the applicant had claimed that he needed help with shopping and some cleaning and driving but that he had not stated that he had a daily need for assistance.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against a country (Country X) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Country X, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 4 August 2008. The applicant was represented by Mr Alex Brown, a lawyer practising in a city (City Y). The Government of Country X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Chris Green of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention, which amounted to interference with his private and family life. On 12 October 2009 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1971 and lives in City Y. On 14 January 1999 criminal charges were brought against the applicant. He was suspected of armed robberies, committed in an organised criminal group. The applicant was in hiding at the material time. On 29 January 1999 an arrest warrant was issued against the applicant by the authorities of Country X. After having been unsuccessfully sought for many months, he was eventually detained in a country (Country Z) on 23 October 2001 and remanded in custody. Subsequently, action was taken with a view to the applicant's extradition and on 21 October 2002, the authorities of Country Z handed him over to Country X. On 24 October 2002 the District Court of City W ordered that the applicant remain in custody, relying on the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences in question. The court considered that keeping the applicant in detention was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, given the risk that he might tamper with evidence and induce witnesses to give false testimony or go underground again (he had earlier been in hiding in Country Z). It further stressed the severity of the anticipated penalty and the fact that the applicant had been acting in an organised criminal group. The applicant's appeal against the detention order was dismissed by the Regional Court of City W on 23 December 2002. Likewise, his further appeals against decisions prolonging his detention and all his subsequent, numerous applications for release and appeals against refusals to release him were unsuccessful. In his applications and appeals he relied on his personal circumstances, in particular his poor health, stressing that he had been infected with an HCV virus. In the course of the investigation, the applicant's detention was prolonged on several occasions, namely by the decisions of the Regional Court of City W on 16 January, 20 March and 8 September 2003, 16 January and 20 September 2004, 14 January, 6 June and 14 November 2005, 24 April and 20 October 2006 and the decisions of the Court of Appeal of City W on 8 August 2007 and 6 February 2008.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of that country, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 May 2000. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr X. Y., a lawyer practising in a major city. The government of that country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. A., of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a major city. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his tariff as a discretionary life prisoner had not been set at trial by a judge but had been fixed by the Secretary of State after a long delay and without an oral hearing. He invoked Articles 6 § 1 and 5 § 4 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 28 October 2003, the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the government each filed brief observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and is currently serving a prison sentence in a prison, a county. On 30 December 1989, the applicant was convicted at a court in a major city of robbery, wounding with intent, possessing firearms with intent to endanger life and possessing ammunition with intent to endanger life. The offences arose out of a single robbery which occurred on 24 December 1988 at a shop in a city. One of the applicant’s associates entered the shop, snatched a bag containing 10,000 currency and held a loaded revolver to the head of a member of the shop’s staff. The applicant, armed with a loaded revolver, kept watch outside. During a changeover of cars in their flight from the crime, the applicant and his associates were intercepted by the police, who surrounded them and told them to lay down their arms. The applicant fired six shots, wounding one police officer in the leg. The police returned fire and one of the applicant’s associates was killed. The applicant received a superficial wound to his shoulder. He was arrested and immediately detained. The applicant was subsequently tried and was not represented at his trial. He stated that he was informed by his counsel that his defence was “political” in nature and could not be put by a professional advocate. His counsel then withdrew. The applicant was sentenced to life imprisonment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Xanadu national, Alex Smith (“the applicant”). The applicant was represented by Ms Johnson, a lawyer practising in Yonder. The Xanadu Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador G. Harkness, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant complained, in particular, that there was no public hearing in the disciplinary proceedings against him before the Administrative Court. On 1 December 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1939 and lives in Yonder. The applicant was, at the time of the events, a civil servant in a public employment relationship with the Regional Government of Xanadu (Landesregierung). He worked at the Department for Legal Affairs (Traffic Department). On 17 May 1993 the Department for Legal Affairs (Human Resources) laid disciplinary information against the applicant. The Disciplinary Commission at the Office of the Regional Xanadu Government (Disziplinarkommission des Amtes der Landesregierung) decided, on 21 June 1993, to institute the main disciplinary proceedings on account of seventeen specific charges dating from December 1990 to April 1993 and suspended the applicant from his duties (Einleitungs- und Suspendierungsbeschluss). On 21 September 1994 the Disciplinary Commission decided to hold a hearing (Verhandlungsbeschluss) in the disciplinary matter against the applicant, charging him on twenty-four counts. However, in the summons for the hearing the Disciplinary Commission informed the applicant on 2 October 2005 that only counts 1 to 14 would be subject matter of the hearing. A hearing was held in presence of the applicant and his counsel on 7 December 1995 following which the Disciplinary Commission held the applicant liable in respect of ten counts of misbehaviour. It imposed a disciplinary penalty of immediate retirement with a deduction of 20% of his pension benefits. On the remaining four counts the Disciplinary Commission found no reason to take further action. On 7 November 1996 the Senior Disciplinary Board at the Office of the Xanadu Regional Government (Disziplinaroberkommission des Amtes der Landesregierung) on the basis of the result of an oral hearing upheld this decision with regard to six counts, but found no reason for criticism as regards the remaining four counts. As a result the disciplinary penalty was reduced by setting the deduction of the applicant's pension benefits at 15%. The applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court on 9 January 1997. The applicant also requested the Constitutional Court to hold a public hearing.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/11) against a country in Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2010. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Legal Firm, a firm of lawyers based in City. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms Jane Smith, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that he did not have a speedy review of the lawfulness of his detention, in violation of Article 5 § 4 of the Convention, and that he had no effective remedy in respect of the violation of his rights as the domestic courts refused to grant a declaration and mandatory relief. On 15 January 2011 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960. At the time of the lodging of his application he was detained at Prison X, City. In 2006 the applicant was convicted of a crime. He was originally sentenced to life imprisonment with a tariff (i.e. minimum term to be served before eligibility for release arose) of five years. Upon appeal, this was reduced to a sentence of imprisonment for public protection (“IPP” – see paragraphs 22-23 below), which is also an indeterminate sentence, with a tariff of three and a half years, less 98 days spent on remand. A few months prior to tariff expiry, the Secretary of State referred the applicant’s case to the Parole Board, pursuant to section 239(2) of the Criminal Justice Act 2003 (see paragraph 27 below), to consider whether the applicant’s security category should be downgraded to allow him to go into open prison conditions. On 15 September 2008 the Parole Board notified the applicant of its decision in the following terms: “9. The panel, which included a psychologist and a psychiatrist among their number, noted the recommendations for open conditions made by report writers, but they also noted the identification of remaining areas of treatment need ... They feared that there had been an underestimate of risk ... and an insufficient attention to the sadistic elements of the offences in other assessments. They would therefore counsel against the formulaic approach in this case, which appears at least partly to be responsible for the conclusion that once RSOTP [a sexual offenders treatment programme] has been completed no further work is required and would recommend that further individual assessment should be undertaken, which takes account of their specified comments."

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/90) against the Republic of XYZ (the country) lodged with the European Human Rights Commission (the organization) under former Article 25 of the International Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms Convention (the document) by a national of XYZ, Mr John Doe (the applicant), on 15 September 1990. The applicant was represented by Mr James Smith, a lawyer practising in City (the country). The XYZ Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a “reasonable time” and that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the City Military Court which lacked independence and impartiality. He further submitted that he had been convicted on the basis of the statements he had made to the police under duress. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 October 1998, when Protocol No. 12 to the Convention came into force (Article 6 § 2 of Protocol No. 12). The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 53 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 28 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 27 § 1 of the Rules of Court. Mr Richard Brown, the judge elected in respect of XYZ, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr George White to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place (Article 28 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 30 § 1). By a decision of 10 January 2001, the Chamber retained the applicant’s complaints concerning his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal and declared the remainder of his complaints inadmissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 60 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Arrest and detention of the applicant On 20 December 1981 police officers from the City Security Directorate arrested the applicant on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organization, the Rev-Way (Revolutionary Path). On 20 January 1982 the City Military Court remanded the applicant in custody. B. Trial in the City Military Court On 22 January 1983 the Military Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Military Court against the applicant and 732 other defendants. The prosecutor accused the applicant of being one of the founding members and a leader of the Rev-Way, whose object was to undermine the constitutional order and replace it with a Marxist-Leninist regime.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xanadu, Mr Xanadu Xanadu (“the applicant”), on 15 August 2003. The applicant was represented by Mr Y Z, a lawyer practising in Yonder. The Government of Xanadu (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged that, as a result of unfair decisions given by the domestic courts, he had been deprived of his land which was the main source of income for his family. He relied on Articles 6, 13, 14 and 18 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. On 15 January 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in ZanZan. On 22 November 1985 Law no. 3084 came into force. Article 5 of this law provided the possibility of leasing State land to farmers who were in need and who fulfilled certain eligibility criteria (“right holders”). In particular, Article 24 § 1 of Law no. 3084 provided that those who had been convicted of certain offences were not entitled to benefit from this law (see paragraph 16 below). Following the promulgation of Law no. 3084, the applicant applied to the Commission which determined the eligibility of farmers to be right holders and requested to be provided with land in Yonder in the south-east of Xanadu. On 1 March 1999 the applicant was identified as a right holder and leased land from the Directorate General for Agricultural Reform (Tarım Reformu Genel Müdürlüğü) (“the Directorate General”) for an indefinite period on payment of a rent. The applicant earned his living by cultivating this land. On 11 May 2000, after conducting a “security investigation”, the Directorate General annulled the right holder status of the applicant. On 31 May 2000 the applicant brought an action in the Administrative Court requesting the stay of execution and reversal of the Directorate General’s decision. On 8 June 2000 the Administrative Court decided to request the defendant administration to indicate the reasons which grounded its decision to annul the right holder status of the applicant. The court invited the defendant administration to submit their response and relevant documents within thirty days. On 2 August 2000 the Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s request for a stay of execution of the decision, holding that necessary conditions were not met. On an unspecified date, the Directorate General refused to submit the information or documents requested by the Administrative Court.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Human Rights Commission (“the Commission”) on 15 May 1997, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 § 1 and Article 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 22410/93) against a European country lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by two citizens, Mr John Doe and Mrs Jane Doe, on 15 March 1993. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the country recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 § 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and sought leave to present their own case. However, the President of the Chamber, Mr Richard Smith, declined to grant the requested leave and the applicants subsequently designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30 § 1). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir John Freeland, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention), and Mr Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court (Rule 21 § 4 (b)). On 17 September 1996, in the presence of the Deputy Registrar, the President of the Court, Mr R. Ryssdal, drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr L.-E. Pettiti, Mr I. Foighel, Mr A.N. Loizou, Mr A.B. Baka, Mr L. Wildhaber, Mr D. Gotchev and Mr U. Lōhmus (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 § 5). As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 § 6), Mr Bernhardt, acting through the Deputy Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government (“the Government”), the applicants’ lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 § 1 and 38). Pursuant to the order made in consequence and subsequent extensions of the time-limit granted at the request of the applicants’ solicitors, the Registrar received the Government’s memorial on 2 April 1997 and the applicants’ memorial on 11 April 1997. On 25 April 1997 the Chamber decided to dispense with a hearing in the case, having satisfied itself that the conditions for this derogation from its usual procedure had been met (Rules 26 and 38). In the light of this decision, the Government, applicants and Commission were invited to submit written comments on the matters raised in the memorials. The Registrar subsequently received letters from the Government’s Agent and the applicants’ solicitors on the subject, inter alia, of the applicants’ claims under Article 50 of the Convention. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against the Kingdom of Andalusia lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by seven Spanish nationals, Ms Ana Garcia Lopez, Ms Carmen Garcia Lopez, Mr Jose Luis Garcia Lopez, Ms Maria Luz Sanchez Perez, Ms Daria Amelie Sanchez Perez, Ms Maria Teresa Sanchez Aige and Mr Javier Garcia Reverter (“the applicants”) on 25 August 1997. The application concerned the detention of the applicants, who are presumed members of a “sect”, for nearly ten days following a preliminary investigation directed by Seville investigating judge no. 6. The applicants relied on Articles 3, 5, 8 and 9 of the Convention. On 16 April 1998 the Commission (Second Chamber) decided to give notice of the application to the Spanish Government (“the Government”) under Rule 48 § 2 (b) of its Rules of Procedure and to invite the parties to submit written observations on its admissibility and merits. The Government submitted their observations on 15 July 1998, after an extension of time, and the applicants replied on 1 September 1998. Following the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention on 1 November 1998, and in accordance with the provisions of Article 5 § 2 thereof, the application was examined by the Court. In accordance with Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court, the President of the Court, Mr X, assigned the case to the Fourth Section. The Chamber constituted within that Section included ex officio Mr Y, the judge elected in respect of Spain (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 26 § 1 (a)), and Mr Z, President of the Section (Rule 26 § 1 (a)). The other members designated by the latter to complete the Chamber were Mr A, Mr B, Mr C, Mr D, and Mrs E (Rule 26 § 1 (b)). On 9 March 1999 the Chamber declared admissible the complaints of six of the applicants, namely Ms Ana Garcia Lopez, Ms Carmen Garcia Lopez, Ms Maria Luz Sanchez Perez, Ms Daria Amelie Sanchez Perez, Ms Maria Teresa Sanchez Aige and Mr Javier Garcia Reverter, concerning their deprivation of liberty (Article 5 of the Convention) and the interference with their right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion (Article 9 of the Convention). It declared the remainder of their application inadmissible. It also decided that if there was not a friendly settlement of the case, a public hearing would be held (Rule 59 § 2). On 26 March 1999 the Court sent the parties the text of its decision on the admissibility of the application (Garcia Lopez and Others v. Spain (dec.), no. 12345/97, ECHR 1999-II) and requested them to submit such further evidence and observations as they wished.

It originated in an application (no. 24645/94) against the Republic of Fictional Country (“the Republic”) lodged with the European Human Rights Commission (“the Commission”) by three Fictional Country nationals, Mr Fictional A, Mr Fictional B and Mr Fictional C, under former Article 25 on 17 November 1993. PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 16231/06 and 4890/08) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Turkish nationals, Mr. A and Mr. B (“the applicants”), on 3 April 2006 and 15 January 2008, respectively. The first applicant was represented by Mr. C, a lawyer practising in a city. The second applicant was represented by Mr. D, a lawyer practising in another city. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 13 May 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASES The applicants were born in 1980 and 1975, respectively, and live in a city and another city. The first applicant lost the sight of his right eye and the second applicant was injured in the legs during their compulsory military service. Upon the refusal of the Retirement Fund (Emekli Sandığı) to grant them special disability benefits, they applied to the Supreme Military Administrative Court, separately, for annulment of the Retirement Fund's decisions. On 6 October 2005 and 5 April 2007, respectively, the Supreme Military Administrative Court rejected their requests. In delivering its decision in respect of the first applicant, the Supreme Military Administrative Court relied on an old expert report which it had obtained during an action for damages filed previously by the applicant regarding the same disability. The written opinions submitted by the principal public prosecutor to the Supreme Military Administrative Court regarding their cases were not communicated to the applicants. The applicants' requests for rectification were rejected by the Supreme Military Administrative Court on 15 December 2005 and 5 July 2007, respectively. The decision of 5 July 2007 was served on the second applicant on 17 July 2007.

PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 12345/06 and 67890/06) against the Republic of Aland against the Republic of Aland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Alandan nationals, Mr Aland A. Aland and Mr Aland B. Aland (“the applicants”), on 10 August 2006. The applicants were represented by Mrs Aland C., a lawyer practising in Aland. The Alandan Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 15 October 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1978 and 1980 respectively. On 30 July 2004 a large group of demonstrators, including the applicants, gathered in Aland Street in front of the Aland High School in Aland to attend the reading out of a statement to the press in protest against the NATO summit which was being held in Aland on 28-29 July 2004. The demonstration was organised by Aland Union (Aland Trade Unions Confederation). A large group of police officers, all wearing helmets and gas masks and equipped with the necessary material, was also deployed to the area. Nearly 500 demonstrators took part in the demonstration and slogans were chanted against NATO. After the statement was read out by the representative of Aland Union, the demonstrators started to disperse. A small group of demonstrators, carrying the flags of their non-governmental organisation Aland Association, walked towards the police officers who had blocked Aland Street to prevent the group from approaching Taksim Square. The demonstrators attacked the police officers with sticks and stones and the police officers used tear gas and truncheons to disperse the group. Some of the nearby shops and vehicles were damaged during the incident. According to the incident report, six police officers were wounded during the incident. The applicants, who had listened to the press statement, were arrested during this incident. According to the applicants, they were beaten and insulted during and after their arrest. The same day, they were taken to the Aland Health Clinic for a medical examination. According to the applicants, the doctor examined them in the presence of the police officers. A copy of the medical report is not included in the case file. On 1 July 2004 the applicants were taken to the Aland Forensic Medicine Institute for a further medical examination. The doctor who examined the applicants concluded that both of them were unfit to work for seven days.

PROCEDURE . The case originated in an application (no. 61444/00) against a state lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 15 February 2000. 2. The applicant was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in a city, represented by Mr Z, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. 3. The applicant alleged that he had not had his case heard within a “reasonable time”, as required under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. He also alleged a breach of Article 13 of the Convention in that he had no effective domestic remedy in respect of the excessive length of the proceedings. 4. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. 5. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). 6. By a decision of 18 November 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. 7. The applicant and the state each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). 8. On 21 September 2004 the Chamber invited the parties to submit further observations on the merits of the complaint under Article 13. The state filed their observations on 23 November and 14 December 2004. The applicant’s representative lodged pleadings on 8 November 2004 and 3 January 2005 respectively. 9. On 2 February 2005 the applicant’s spouse, Mrs X, informed the Court’s Registry that the applicant had died on 30 December 2004. She stated that she wished to continue the proceedings before the Court in her late husband’s stead. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1934. He died on 30 December 2004. He lived in a city. In July 1994 the applicant and his wife concluded a contract with owners of a company, under that contract the company was to carry out building work on the applicant’s house. On 24 November 1994 the applicant, considering that the company was in breach of the contract, withdrew from it. On 1 February 1996 the applicant and his wife (“the plaintiffs”) sued the owners in a court, seeking compensation for the serious damage to the house allegedly caused by the defendants. On 13 March and 27 June 1996 the court held hearings and heard evidence from witnesses.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 10001/08) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”), on 19 February 2008. The applicant was represented by Mr. X.Y. Z., a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador A.B. C., Head of the International Law Department at the Ministry for European and International Affairs. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention because neither the Appeals Commission nor the Constitutional Court had held an oral hearing. On 23 September 2009 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in a city. The applicant worked for a tax authority as a civil servant. He was the head of a tax assessment division. As the tax authorities were to be reformed, the applicant was removed from his post as head of the tax assessment division by a decision of the tax authority of 29 March 2005. On 28 April 2005 the tax authority appointed the applicant to the post of specialist, a post that had a lower grade. Upon the applicant’s appeal the Appeals Commission at the Federal Chancellery set aside those two decisions on 28 July 2005. By letter dated 24 November 2005 the tax authority sent the applicant the job profiles for both the post of head of division and the post of specialist. The job profile for his former post as head of the tax assessment division stated that the applicant was responsible for, among other tasks, organising, coordinating and supervising the procedural requirements within the tax-assessment division, and dealing with case files in special circumstances. The applicant was also the supervisor of forty-three other civil servants and employees. The job profile for the new post of specialist stated that, among other tasks, the applicant would assist the leading specialist, especially in the areas of coordination, quality check and supervisory measures. He would further participate in several working groups and deal autonomously and on his own initiative with legal remedies. He was not entitled to directly assign that task to someone else. He would also have to take decisions on questions of procedural and material law, give advice in difficult cases in his area of expertise, and represent the authority before the Independent Finance Panel. The job profile did not state that any employees or civil servants were to be under his direct supervision.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against a country in Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr John Doe (“the applicant”) on 1 September 1999. The applicant was represented before the Court by Legal Firm, a city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr A. Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a city. The applicant complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that, because he was a man, he was denied social security benefits equivalent to those received by widows. By a partial decision of 15 September 2000 the Court decided to communicate the complaints concerning widows' benefits and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. By a decision of 1 May 2002 the Court declared the complaint regarding Widowed Mother's Allowance admissible and the remainder of the application inadmissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in a region. His wife died on 15 June 1998, leaving four children born in 1985, 1987, 1995 and 2001. His claim for widows' benefits was made in April 1999 and was rejected on 18 April 1999 on the ground that he was not entitled to widows' benefits because he was not a woman. The applicant did not appeal as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such social security benefits were payable to widowers under the country's law.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of that country, Ms Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 April 1996. The applicant was represented by Ms K. Smith of Liberty, London. The government of that country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr L. Brown of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The applicant complained about the use of a surveillance device in her home, invoking Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 30 October 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible, partly inadmissible. The applicant and the government each filed observations on just satisfactions (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965. In April 1994 the applicant was suspected by police officers in the Cambridge Constabulary of involvement in robbery. The view was taken by the Cambridgeshire Regional Crime Squad that it was necessary to place a hidden battery-powered listening and recording device in the applicant’s home. An application was therefore made to the Chief Constable for the installation of such a device, which was authorised on 15 June 1994, pursuant to the non-statutory Home Office Guidelines of 1984. In order to install the device, the police decided to arrest the applicant and her partner in connection with another matter (credit card fraud) and to remove them and their children from their home. Enquiries into the credit card fraud had previously lapsed without any arrest or questioning of the applicant or her partner. However, DC Jones of the Regional Crime Squad and WDC Smith, an officer in the intelligence bureau of the Cambridgeshire County Constabulary, decided to revive the investigation for the purpose of removing the applicant and her partner from their home for long enough to enable the installation of the listening device. WDC Smith briefed three officers about purported grounds for arresting the applicant and her partner for credit card fraud, without informing them of the intended installation of the device. At 6.30 a.m. on 10 July 1994 the three officers arrested the applicant’s partner in her home and shortly thereafter arrested the applicant. Both were taken to the police station. The officers seized the keys to the applicant’s home and car. Officers from the Regional Crime Squad then used the house key to enter the applicant’s home and install the listening device.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against a country lodged with a regional commission under former Article 25 of a human rights convention by a national, Mr John Doe Smith ("the applicant"), on 23 December 1996. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Brown, a lawyer practising in a city, and by Professor B. Green QC and Ms C. White, Counsel. The government of the country ("the government") were represented by their Agent, Mr D. Black, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, a city. The applicant alleged that the proceedings before the gaming board panel were in violation of Article 6 § 1 of the convention. The application was transmitted to the court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the court (Rule 52 § 1 of the rules of court).
