Within that section, the chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the rules of court. By a decision of 14 September 1999, the chamber declared the application admissible. The chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine), the parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE Between 1984 and 1992 the applicant was the sole managing director of company A, a company which owned and controlled six of the twenty casinos licensed to operate in a city. Company A was a subsidiary company of company B, of which the applicant was also managing director. Both companies will hereafter be collectively referred to as company C. In June 1991 a raid took place at the various premises of company A. The raid was carried out by the police in the presence of officials of the gaming board for a region ("the gaming board"), a statutory body which inspects and monitors the gaming industry. A large quantity of documents were seized. In March 1992 the gaming board lodged objections with the clerk to the licensing magistrates, with regard to company A’s annual application for renewal of the licences it held in respect of each of its casinos. The gaming board also made cancellation applications in respect of the existing licences held by company A. A meeting was held between the gaming board and the non-executive directors of company A and their legal advisors on 26 March 1992. As a result of this meeting, the applicant and the other executive directors (with the exception of the finance director) resigned with effect from 30 April 1992, on the understanding that such resignation was involuntary and constituted dismissal by company C.

PROCEDURE The case originated in four applications (nos. 46506/99, 46569/99, 46570/99 and 46939/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by four nationals, Mr A, Mr B, Mr C and Mr D (“the applicants”), on 8 December 1998. The applicants were represented by Ms E, a lawyer. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purpose of the proceedings before the Court. On 4 September 2001 the Court decided to join the applications, declared them partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the applicants’ right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal to the Government. On 7 November 2002 the Court further decided, under Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1980, 1977, 1979 and 1979 respectively. On 27 and 28 April 1998 respectively the applicants were taken into police custody by police officers. On 7 May 1996 the applicants were brought before the public prosecutor at the State Security Court and subsequently before the investigating judge. After taking their statements, the investigating judge ordered that the applicants be placed in detention on remand. In an indictment dated 23 May 1996, the public prosecutor at the State Security Court initiated criminal proceedings against the applicants and accused them of being members of an illegal armed organisation. The applicants were further accused of carrying out activities on behalf of the organisation, such as taking part in demonstrations on 1 May and 8 March (Women’s Day) during which they had chanted slogans and distributed leaflets. The public prosecutor asked the court to convict the applicants pursuant to Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code. On 9 October 1996 the State Security Court, composed of two civilian judges and a military judge, held that there was insufficient evidence to conclude that the applicants were members of the organisation, but found them guilty under Article 169 of the Criminal Code for aiding and abetting an illegal organisation. The first, second and third applicants were sentenced to two years and six months’ imprisonment, while the second applicant was sentenced to three years and nine months’ imprisonment. The applicants appealed. The chief public prosecutor at the Court of Cassation submitted his opinion on the merits of the appeal on 24 December 1997. This opinion was not served on the applicants, but read out during the hearing which took place on 18 March 1998. On 20 May 1998 the Court of Cassation, upholding the State Security Court’s reasoning and assessment of evidence, dismissed the applicants’ request for appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against the Republic of Xana (a fictional country) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (a fictional organization) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (a fictional convention) by two Xanian nationals, Ayla Xan and Mustafa Yuz (fictional names) on 22 November 1996. The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr Zan, a lawyer practising in Yuzan (a fictional city). The Xanian Government (a fictional government) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. Relying on Article 5 § 3 of the Convention the applicants complained that their detention in police custody lasted eight days without being brought before a judge or other officer authorised by law to exercise judicial power. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. Mr Wam, the judge elected in respect of Xana, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr A. B. C to sit as an ad hoc judge (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). On 14 November 2000 the Chamber retained the applicants' complaint under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 28 July 1996 police officers from the anti-terrorist branch of the Yuzan Security Directorate arrested the applicants on suspicion of membership of an illegal organization, the XYZ-Rızgari (a fictional organization). On 5 August 1996 the Yuzan State Security Court ordered the applicants' detention on remand. On 28 August 1996 the Chief Public Prosecutor filed an indictment with the Yuzan State Security Court charging the applicants with membership of the XYZ-Rızgari and undertaking actions against the indivisible integrity of the state. The charges were brought under Articles 125 and 168 of the Criminal Code. In a judgment dated 14 August 1997 the Yuzan State Security Court acquitted Ms Ayla Xan of the charges, holding that there was insufficient evidence to convict her. The court found Mr Mustafa Yuz guilty of the offences under Articles 125 and 168 and sentenced him to capital punishment. On 19 September 1997 Mr Yuz lodged an appeal with the Court of Cassation (a fictional court).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/03) against the Republic of Andria (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Andria (a fictional country), Mr Alex Andria (a fictional name). The applicant was represented by Mr and Mrs Baker (fictional names), lawyers practising in Andria (a fictional city). The Government of Andria (a fictional country) (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 15 November 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Andria (a fictional city). On 30 March 1995 the applicant was taken into custody by police officers from the anti-terror branch of the Andria Security Directorate on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the RevLeft (a fictional organization). On 10 April 1995 the applicant was brought before the Andria State Security Court and remanded in custody. He was placed in Andria Prison. On 3 May 1995 the public prosecutor at the Andria State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicant and nine other persons. The public prosecutor charged the applicant with attempting to undermine the constitutional order, an offence defined under Article 146 of the Criminal Code. Subsequently, the case brought against the applicant was joined with another case pending before the Andria State Security Court. Following the riots in the Andria Prison to protest against F-Type prisons, in December 2000 the applicant was sent to Andria F-type Prison. On 26 December 2000 in connection with the incidents that took place in the Andria Prison, the judge at the Andria Magistrate's Court ordered the applicant's detention on remand in absentia. In the detention order, it was stated that the applicant was accused of homicide, armed riot against prison administration and damaging prison property. On 12 January 2001 the applicant was brought before the Andria Magistrate's Court and the detention order dated 26 December 2000 was read out to him. He was also reminded that he could appeal against this decision before the Andria Assize Court. On 24 March 2001 the Andria public prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Andria Assize Court against the applicant and 400 other persons on account of the incidents in Andria Prison. The prosecutor requested the court to convict the accused persons under Articles 264, 304, 450, 456 and 457 of the Criminal Code of homicide, of having started a riot in the prison and of damage to public property. In the meantime, on 8 February 2001, the Andria State Security Court ordered the applicant's release pending trial within the context of the proceedings brought against him with the charge under Article 146 of the Criminal Code.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 July 2010. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The government of the country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Jones, of a department. The applicant mainly complained under Article 3 of the Convention that the system of primary education had failed to protect her from sexual abuse by a teacher in 1970 and, under Article 13, that she did not have an effective domestic remedy in that respect. She also relied on Article 8 and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1, both alone and in conjunction with Article 14. She also complained of the length of her civil proceedings and of the absence of an effective domestic remedy in that respect, relying on Article 6 alone and in conjunction with Article 13. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Ann Smith, the judge elected in respect of the country, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). On 15 July 2012 the President of the Chamber decided to appoint Mr Justice Brown to sit as an ad hoc judge (Article 26 § 4 of the Convention, and Rule 29 § 1). On 27 July 2012 a Chamber of that Section (composed of Dean Green, President, Mark Brown, Karel White, Boštjan M. Black, Ganna Red, André Green, judges, Peter Brown, ad hoc judge, and Claudia White, Section Registrar) examined the case. The Chamber, unanimously, struck out the complaints regarding the length of the domestic proceedings and the lack of an effective domestic remedy in that regard, given the friendly settlement reached between the parties on those issues. It also, unanimously, declared admissible the remaining complaints. On 21 September 2012 that Chamber (Angelika Blue, substitute judge, replaced Ganna Red who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case (Rule 24 § 3)) relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber, neither of the parties having objected to relinquishment (Article 30 of the Convention and Rule 72). The composition of the Grand Chamber was determined according to the provisions of Article 26 §§ 4 and 5 of the Convention and Rule 24, with Mr Justice Brown continuing to act as ad hoc judge (Article 26 § 4 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). The applicant and the government each filed further observations (Rule 59 § 1) on the merits.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 April 2002. The applicant was represented by Mr X. Y., a lawyer practising in Andria. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 30 October 2006 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. On 1 May 2007 this case was assigned to the newly constituted Sixth Section (Rule 25 § 5 and Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in Andria. A. Background to the case On an unspecified date, police officers at the Andria airport arrested two persons in possession of passports containing fake visas. In their statements to the police, these two persons submitted that they had paid 4,000 Andrian marks to the applicant and B.H. in order to have their passports stamped. Consequently, on 30 December 1997 police officers carried out a search at the applicant’s home in the presence of one of his siblings. The police officers seized five passports belonging to the applicant, his sibling and two other persons On 7 January 1998 the applicant surrendered to the police. He was then placed in custody. B. Proceedings before the domestic courts On 8 January 1998 the applicant was brought before a single judge at the Andria Magistrates’ Court who ordered his detention on remand. On 15 January 1998 the Andria Principle Public Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Andria Assize Court charging the applicant with the offence of forging passport, in particular arranging for false visa stamps for travelling abroad. On 10 March 1998 the Andria Assize Court heard the applicant and released him on bail. On 31 October 1999, following the qualification of the offence as committed by a criminal organisation, the Andria Assize Court issued a decision of lack of jurisdiction ratione materiae and sent the case-file to Andria State Security Court. On 12 November 1999 the Andria State Security Court issued a decision of lack of jurisdiction ratione materiae and referred the case to the Court of Appeals for determination of the competent court. On 26 December 1999 the Court of Appeals overturned the Andria Assize Court’s decision of lack of jurisdiction ratione materiae and held that the offence in question was within the latter’s jurisdiction. The case-file was therefore sent to the Andria Assize Court. Between 23 January 2001 and 4 November 2003 the Andria Assize Court held seven hearings.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 43631/09) against the Republic of Country A lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Country A, Ms Ana Novak (“the applicant”), on 10 August 2009. The applicant was represented by Mr J. Smith, a lawyer practising in City B. The Government of Country A (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms. C. Jones, Head of the Legal Department, Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that there had been a violation of Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention. On 15 September 2010 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1962 and lives in City C. Ana Novak was born on 3 November 2003 in Country D and was abandoned immediately by her biological mother, who gave birth anonymously. As her father was also unknown, Ana Novak became a ward of the State of Country D on 3 December 2003. The director of social services in City E (Country D) was appointed as her guardian. On 13 January 2004 the President of the court of City E granted the applicant, then aged 42 and unmarried, the right to take the child Ana Novak into her legal care (kafala). He also authorised Ana Novak to leave Country D and settle in Country A. In a decision of 19 January 2004, the President of the court of City F (Country D) admitted a request for the child to take the same name and authorised the change from Ana Novak to Novak Ana. Novak Ana arrived in Country A on 1 February 2004. Since then she has been living with the applicant and the applicant’s mother. On 8 November 2006 the applicant applied for the full adoption of Novak Ana. In support of her request she argued that to enable Novak Ana to be adopted was the solution most consistent with “the best interests of the child”, within the meaning of Article 3 § 1 of the Convention on the Rights of the Child of 20 November 1989 and Article 1 of the Hague Convention of 29 May 1993 on Protection of Children and Co-operation in Respect of Intercountry Adoption. In a judgment of 21 March 2007 the tribunal de grande instance of City B dismissed her application for adoption, after noting that kafala gave her parental authority, enabling her to take any decisions in the child’s interest. The court found that kafala gave the child the protection to which all children were entitled under the international conventions.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 10001/08) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by five Xanadanis, Mr Xanadu, Mr Xanadu, Mr Xanadu, Mr Xanadu, and Mr Xanadu (“the applicants”), on 15 January 2008. The applicants were represented by Mr Xanadu, a lawyer practising in Xanadu. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 12 June 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). By a letter sent in March 2009 the applicants’ representative informed the Court that the first applicant, Mr Xanadu, had died on an unspecified date and that his heirs could not be reached. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1921, 1941, 1946, 1948 and 1946 respectively and lived in Xanadu. In 2004 the General Directorate of Highways seized a plot of land belonging to the applicants without any formal expropriation, for the construction of a highway. The applicants brought an action before the Civil Court to obtain compensation for the de facto expropriation of their property. They requested 5,500 Xanadu liras (XAN) as compensation from the court and reserved their right to increase this claim in due course. On 15 June 2006 the Civil Court awarded the applicants XAN 5,500 as compensation for the de facto expropriation of their land, as requested, plus interest. The applicants initiated execution proceedings before the Execution Office to obtain that amount (file no. 2009/2819). On 13 March 2007 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. The applicants subsequently brought an additional action (“ek dava”) before the Civil Court to obtain further compensation for their land in the light of the expert report obtained during the previous proceedings, which had valued the land at a rate higher than that initially requested by them. On 24 May 2007 the Civil Court awarded the applicants XAN 372,445.25, plus interest. The applicants initiated another set of execution proceedings before the Execution Office to obtain the amount awarded (file no. 2007/6190). On 16 October 2007 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Civil Court, however reduced the amount awarded to the applicants to XAN 340,949.81. On 26 March and 13 November 2009 the administration paid XAN 8,925 and 485,173 respectively to the files before the Execution Office. According to the information provided by the applicants, there has been no debt outstanding in the execution files.

PROCEDURE The case originated in three applications (nos. 71912/01 and 26968/02 and 36397/03) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals, Mr A and Mr B (“the applicants”), on 15 June 2001, 7 May 2002 and 28 October 2003 respectively. The applicants were represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 23 September 2005 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the case at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1969 and 1979 respectively and live in a city. A. The arrest and detention of the applicants On 14 February 2001 two persons were shot and injured in a bus by a person who subsequently got off the bus. On the same day, upon receipt of information that the suspect of the shooting was in a car, police officers from a police headquarters arrested the applicants during a traffic control operation that they initiated on a motorway. The security forces further arrested four other persons, including the first applicant’s brother, in another car. The police officers confiscated the applicants’ telephones and both cars, in which 5 firearms were found. On the same day, the applicants were taken into police custody. On 15 February 2001 three police officers drafted a report containing the numbers dialled and calls received on the telephones of the first applicant, his brother and another suspect. On 19 February 2001 a single judge at a magistrates’ court extended the period of the applicants’ detention in police custody for a further three days. On the same day the applicants’ statements were taken by police officers from the organised crime unit of the police headquarters. According to the document containing their statements, the applicants were suspected of forming a criminal profit-making organisation proscribed by a law. According to the document, both applicants confessed to their involvement in a criminal organisation. On 15, 16 and 21 February 2001, the applicants were examined by doctors at a state hospital. The doctors noted in their reports that there were no signs of ill-treatment on the applicants’ persons. On 21 February 2001 the firearms found in the cars were brought before a single judge at the magistrates’ court, who ordered their detention on remand. Before the judge, the applicants refuted the accuracy of the documents containing their statements taken by the police. On 22 March 2001 the firearms found in the cars were subjected to a ballistic examination.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 10001/09) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 26 February 2008. The applicant was represented by Mr M. Smith, a lawyer practising in Brussels. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that the lustration proceedings in his case had been unfair, in violation of Article 6 of the Convention. On 24 November 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Brussels. On 11 April 1997 the parliament passed the Law on disclosing work for or service in the State’s security services or collaboration with them between 1944 and 1990 by persons exercising public functions (ustawa o ujawnieniu pracy lub służby w organach bezpieczeństwa państwa lub współpracy z nimi w latach 1944-1990 osób pełniących funkcje publiczne; “the 1997 Lustration Act”). It entered into force on 3 August 1997. Persons falling under the provisions of the 1997 Lustration Act, i.e. candidates or holders of public office such as ministers and members of parliament, were required to declare whether or not they had worked for or collaborated with the security services during the communist regime. The provisions of the Act extended to, inter alia, judges, prosecutors, advocates and members of the supervisory boards and boards of directors of the “European Television SA” and “European Radio SA” as well as their local branches. On 15 December 1998 the applicant, a member of the supervisory board of the Brussels Branch of the National Radio (Rada Nadzorcza Rozgłośni Regionalnej Polskiego Radia, Radio Brussels SA) declared that he had not collaborated with the communist-era secret services. In 2002 the applicant became a member of the board of directors of the same radio (Zarząd). In February 2005 the Commissioner of the Public Interest (Rzecznik Interesu Publicznego) informed the applicant that he had doubts as to the truthfulness of his lustration declaration. On 23 September 2005 the Brussels Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) decided to institute lustration proceedings against the applicant following a request made by the Commissioner on the grounds that the applicant had lied in his lustration declaration by denying that he had cooperated with the secret services. The Court of Appeal held hearings on 23 November, 8 December 2005 and 25 July and 20 September 2006. The applicant, who was not represented, attended the hearings although he lived in Brussels, 450 kilometres away from the court. The hearings were not open to the public.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123/03) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of that country, John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2002. The applicant was not represented. The government of that country (“the government”) were represented by their agent, Ms. Jane Smith of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, a city. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings, concerning his trial for a crime, exceeded a reasonable length of time. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 14 January 2003, the Court declared part of the application inadmissible and invited the respondent government to submit observations on the remaining complaints. On 6 September 2003, the Court declared the remainder of the application partly admissible. The applicant and the government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant is currently serving a sentence of life imprisonment in a prison. On 15 June 1994, John Smith was murdered in the flat he had shared with the applicant for the preceding eighteen months. He had been clubbed over the head with what was probably a hammerhead in a sock and possibly another weapon. The applicant was arrested and charged with a crime on 16 June 1994. On 10 July 1995, the applicant was tried for the murder of Mr. Smith, the issue for the jury being whether it was the applicant who was responsible for the murder. He was convicted on 26 July 1995 and on 26 September 1995 appealed against the conviction. On 26 February 1997, the conviction was quashed by the court of appeal on the basis that the judge had misdirected the jury. A retrial was ordered which took place between 20 July and 5 August 1997, when the jury was unable to reach a verdict and was discharged. The crown elected to proceed with a second retrial which began on 22 July 1998. At the outset counsel had unsuccessfully submitted that it was oppressive and an abuse of process to try the applicant again, after two unsuccessful trials. During the trial the applicant dispensed with the services of his counsel and solicitor and proceeded to defend himself, with assistance from a new solicitor. There came a point where he no longer felt able to do so and requested an adjournment. On 2 August 1998, the jury was duly discharged, and a further retrial began on 13 September 1998.

PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 12345/03 and 67890/03) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals, Mr John Doe and Mr Jane Smith (“the applicants”), on 26 May 2003. The applicants were represented by Mr Alex Brown, a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 14 September 2007 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility (Article 29 § 3). By a letter dated 9 July 2009, the respondent Government informed the Court that the first applicant, Mr John Doe, had died on 19 April 2008. By a letter dated 6 August 2009, the applicants' representative verified the first applicant's death on the said date and informed the Court that his heirs, namely Mr Mehmet Doe, Mr Şükrü Doe, Mr Ahmet Doe, Mr Abdurrahman Doe, Mr Harun Doe and Mr Musa Doe, wished to pursue his application. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASES The applicants were born in 1981 and 1961 respectively and lived in a city. On 5 May 1999 the applicants were laid off by a municipality (“the Municipality”), with which they had been temporarily employed. The applicants subsequently brought separate actions before a labour court in the city against the Municipality, claiming outstanding salaries, dismissal indemnities, severance pay and other pecuniary rights. On 23 December and 11 November 1999, respectively, the labour court granted the applicants' request and ordered the payment of 324,681,000 local currency units (LCU)1 to the first applicant and 927,531,0002 to the second applicant, together with interest. In the absence of an appeal, these judgments became final on 3 January 2000 and 22 November 1999, respectively. At the date of introduction of the applications, the judgment debts were still outstanding. However, in the meantime, friendly settlement agreements were reached between the applicants and the Municipality on 31 July 2008 and 10 February 2005, respectively, and the relevant payments were made to the applicants.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against the Kingdom of Xanadu lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Xanadu national, Mr X Y Z (“the applicant”), on 14 December 1995. The applicant was represented by Mr A B C, a lawyer practising in Yonder. The Xanadu Government (“the Government”) were represented by Mr D E F, who acted as Agent until he left the Attorney-General's Office (Civil Matters) in June 2002. Thereafter, they were represented by Mr G H I of that office. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 2 of the Convention on account of the reasoning relied on by the Xanadu courts in refusing his compensation claim with respect to damage sustained in criminal proceedings in which he had been acquitted. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the former Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 11 September 2001 the Chamber decided that, in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the case of J v. Xanadu, K v. Xanadu and L v. Xanadu (applications nos. 29327/95, 34964/97 and 56568/00 – Rule 43 § 2). By a decision of the aforementioned date the Court declared the application admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). However, this case was retained by the former Third Section. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 17 September 2002 (Rule 59 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr G H I, Attorney-General's Office, (Civil matters) Agent, Mr D E F, Advokat, Counsel/Adviser Mr J K L, Senior Public Prosecutor, Office of the Director of Public Prosecutors, Ms M N O, Attorney, Attorney-General's Office (Civil matters), Ms P Q R, Attorney, Attorney-General's Office, Advisers; (b) for the applicant Mr A B C, Advokat, Counsel, Mr X Y Z, Applicant. The Court heard addresses by Mr S T U (counsel for Mr J, who pleaded the common issues relevant to both his case and that of Mr X Y Z), Mr A B C and Mr D E F. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Zonder. On 10 March 1993 the head of the social services in the municipality of Zonder contacted the local police after having received reports from Vonder kindergarten indicating that the applicant, who was an assistant at the kindergarten at the time, had sexually abused one or more of the children there.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/04) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Bulgarian national, Mr Ivan Ivanov (“the applicant”), on 15 December 2003. The applicant was represented by Mr Peter Peterson, a lawyer practising in Vienna. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador George Green, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Under Article 8 of the Convention, the applicant alleged, in particular, that the imposition of an exclusion order on him and his expulsion to Bulgaria violated his right to respect for private and family life. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 1 June 2006 it was declared partly admissible by a Chamber of that Section, composed of Christos Rozakis, Snejana Botoucharova, Anatoli Kovler, Elisabeth Steiner, Khanlar Hajiyev, Dean Spielmann, Sverre Erik Jebens, judges, and of Søren Nielsen, Section Registrar. On 22 March 2008 a Chamber of that Section, composed of Christos Rozakis, Loukis Loucaides, Nina Vajić, Elisabeth Steiner, Khanlar Hajiyev, Dean Spielmann, Sverre Erik Jebens, judges, and Søren Nielsen, Section Registrar, delivered a judgment in which it held, by four votes to three, that there had been a violation of Article 8 of the Convention and that the respondent Government should pay the applicant 5,759.96 euros in respect of costs and expenses. On 24 September 2008, pursuant to a request by the respondent Government, the panel of the Grand Chamber decided to refer the case to the Grand Chamber in accordance with Article 43 of the Convention. The composition of the Grand Chamber was determined according to the provisions of Article 27 §§ 2 and 3 of the Convention and Rule 24. The applicant and the Government each filed a memorial. The Bulgarian Government did not make use of their right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention). A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 6 February 2009 (Rule 59 § 3). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr George Green, Agent, Ms Barbara Black, Adviser, Mr Carl Smith, Adviser; (b) for the applicant Mr Peter Peterson, Counsel. The Court heard addresses by Mr Peterson and Mr Green, as well as their answers to questions put by a number of judges. Subsequently, András Sajó, substitute judge, replaced Riza Türmen, who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case (Rule 24 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in October 1985 and currently lives in Bulgaria. In November 1991, at the age of six, the applicant lawfully entered Europe together with his parents and two siblings. Subsequently, he was legally resident in Europe. His parents, who were lawfully employed, acquired European nationality.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1001/05) against the European Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Pierre Dupont (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2004. The applicant was represented by Mr Y. Martin, of the Supreme Court and High Court Bar. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms F. Moreau, Director of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Justice. The applicant alleged that the additional time granted to the Chief Public Prosecutor for appealing against a judgment of the Criminal Court amounted to a breach of the principle of equality of arms as enshrined in Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. On 10 November 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the Convention). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Montreuil-sur-Mer. On 20 June 1996 the Paris Central Health Insurance Office (caisse primaire centrale d’assurance maladie) filed a criminal complaint stating that an investigation it had carried out in 1994 had revealed that the price charged for prosthetic knee joints by the Clinique de la Rive, of which the applicant was the manager, appeared abnormally high, especially in relation to the price charged in the public sector. It added that the prostheses were directly delivered to the operating theatre at the Clinique de la Rive but were billed by a company named Service Clinique, also managed by the applicant, with a systematic increase of 15% for the prostheses and 18.5% for the ancillary equipment, the increased price alone being charged to the Health Insurance Office. The Health Insurance Office therefore had doubts about the Service Clinique company, suspecting that its sole activity consisted in overbilling in this way. In the course of the investigation, complaints about similar acts were filed by various other health insurance funds or payment agencies. The preliminary investigation found, among other things, that the Service Clinique company had been established in particular to alleviate cash-flow problems resulting from the delay in reimbursement of health care under the third-party payment system. Under this system, in order to be fully reimbursed by the social security scheme for the health care provided, Clinique de la Rive had to wait for the invoice from the prosthesis supplier, which meant a delay of several days, if not weeks. It also transpired that Service Clinique used the same premises and staff as the Clinique de la Rive, that its sole customer was the Clinique de la Rive and that its manager, the applicant, was also the manager of the Clinique de la Rive together with his brother.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the International Human Rights Commission (“the Commission“) and by the Government of the Alpine Confederation (“the Government“) within the three-month period laid down in Article 32 § 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 12345/86) against the Alpine Confederation lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of the Alpine Confederation, Mr. Alain Durand, and a national of the Anatolian Confederation, Mr. Mustafa Kaya, on 5 December 1984. The Commission’s request referred to the declaration whereby the Alpine Confederation recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46) and to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48); the Government’s application referred to Articles 45, 47 and 48 (art. 45, art. 47, art. 48). Both sought a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 8 (art. 8). The Commission also sought a decision under Article 10 (art. 10). In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 § 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings. The President of the Court gave Mr. Durand leave to appear on his own behalf, while Mr. Kaya designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs. E. Bindschedler-Robert, the elected judge of the Alpine nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr. R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 3 (b)). On 15 June 1986, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other five members, namely Mr. L.-E. Pettiti, Sir V. Evans, Mr. R. Bernhardt, Mr. A. M. Donner and Mr. J. De Meyer (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 § 4) (art. 43). Subsequently, Mr. J. Cremona, substitute judge, replaced Mr. Donner, who was unable to attend (Rules 22 § 1 and 24 § 1). Mr. Ryssdal assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 § 5) and, through the Registrar, consulted those who would be appearing before the Court on the need for a written procedure (Rule 37 § 1). In accordance with the order made in consequence on 7 November 1986, the Registrar received the Government’s memorial on 20 December 1986 and the applicants’ memorial on 7 January 1987. On 18 February, the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. Having consulted - through the Registrar - the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the applicants, the President directed on 1 December 1986 that the oral proceedings should commence on 22 February 1987 (Rule 38). On 15 January 1987, he gave Mr. Durand and his assistant leave to plead in German (Rule 27 § 3).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/03) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Norwegian national, Ms. Anna Nordson (“the applicant”), on 11 February 2003. The applicant was represented by Mr. Ole Tvede, a lawyer practising in Oslo. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms. Ingrid Hovdahl-Andersen of the Ministry of Justice. The applicant alleged that civil proceedings initiated by her had not been determined within a reasonable time within the meaning of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was originally allocated to the First Section of the Court. By decision of 29 September 2005 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 April 2006 the case was assigned to the newly constituted Fifth Section (Rule 25 § 5 and Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court THE FACTS A. The circumstances of the case The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Stavanger. Subsequent to having suffered severe problems with her jaw, resulting in her being able to open her mouth only 5 millimetres, on 19 April 1988 at a hospital in Oslo the applicant underwent a jaw operation which entailed implanting a synthetic material in both her jaw-joints. Following the surgery, the applicant's ability to open her mouth was improved. She could thus open her mouth up to 20 millimetres. However, she experienced a lot of complications. Having regard thereto and due to a debate among doctors as to the potential danger related to the use of the synthetic material, in April 1990, the applicant had it removed. She continued to experience problems, and on 20 February 1992, alleging malpractice, she complained to the National Patients' Complaints Board (Sundhedsvæsenets Patientklagenævn) which is an impartial public authority which may express criticism of the medical staff or submit particularly serious cases to the public prosecutor with a view to taking the cases to court. In support of her complaint she maintained that subsequent to the operation in 1988 she had suffered from headache, and constant pain in the jaw-joints and the masticatory muscle. Before deciding on the issue, the applicant's complaint was sent for preliminary examination with the Medical Officer of Health of Akershus County (Embedslægeinstitutionen for Akershus Amt), the Medio-Legal Council (Retslægerådet) and the National Board of Health (Sundhedsstyrelsen). The Medico-Legal Council submitted their opinion on 5 March 1993 and the National Board of Health submitted their recommendation on 23 November 1993. By decision of 16 February 1994 the National Patients' Complaints Board found against the applicant. Consequently, on 4 March 1994 the applicant submitted a number of questions to the National Board of Health, which in return requested the Medico-Legal Council to prepare an opinion.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/12) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr. Alex Smith (“the applicant”), on 1 July 2012. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms. N. Brown, of the Foreign Office. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention following the expiry of his tariff was unlawful in light of the failure of the authorities to put in place the necessary resources to enable him to demonstrate to the Review Board that his risk had reduced, and that his Review Board Review was a meaningless exercise. On 15 October 2014 the complaint under Article 5 § 1 was communicated to the Government. A number of other complaints were declared inadmissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and is currently detained in Prison X. On 20 January 2008 he received an indeterminate sentence for public protection (“IPP sentence”) following his conviction of a crime against a minor. The offence had been committed while the applicant was on licence in the community following his release from a sentence for a crime and while he was undertaking a program in the community. A minimum term (“tariff”) of five years was fixed. The applicant was initially detained in Prison Y. It was recommended in 2008 that he complete the program. In July 2009 he was transferred to Prison Z. He completed a course in 2009 and the core program on 15 March 2010. On an unknown date, he completed a course. In October 2010 a report identified that further work was required to reduce the applicant’s risk of reoffending. It was recommended that he complete the extended program and, possibly, a program. The extended program consisted of seventy interactive sessions plus some individual work and generally lasted for around six months. At a Review Board review on 10 October 2010 the Panel said that much offending work still had to be done in order to reduce the applicant’s risk and that he should therefore remain in closed conditions. In October 2010 the applicant was transferred to Prison A. He claims that he had been informed that the extended program was available at that prison. A memo dated 20 September 2011 from the Department of Prison A confirmed that the applicant had been assessed as suitable to attend the extended program and that he would have to be transferred to another establishment to complete the course as it was not offered at Prison A. On 22 September 2011 the applicant completed the Thinking Skills Program at Prison A.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 49490/08) against a country, referred to as Country X, lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Country X, Ms X (“the applicant”), on 1 October 2008. The applicant was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in City A. The Government of Country X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Z of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 8 June 2009 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). On 23 December 2009 the Government submitted a unilateral declaration and invited the Court to strike out the application, in accordance with Article 37 of the Convention. The applicant filed an objection. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1957 and lives in City B, Country Y. A. Main proceedings [civil proceedings for division of matrimonial property] On 19 January 1987 the applicant lodged a request for the division of matrimonial property with the District Court of City A. A hearing, held on 14 December 1987, was adjourned to give the parties an opportunity to settle the case. However, they apparently failed to do so and on 13 April 1988 the first hearing on the merits was held. Between 18 May 1988 and 26 April 1993, the District Court scheduled 21 hearings, 13 of which were adjourned mostly due to the failure of witnesses to appear or for lack of documents which the parties were expected to supply. During that period the court asked experts to prepare six opinions and supplementary opinions on the value of the matrimonial property. In the meantime, on 2 February 1993, the case was assigned to another judge. Between 1 July 1993 and 28 May 2004 the District Court scheduled 49 hearings, 28 of which were adjourned. One hearing was adjourned due to the failure of the applicant to appear. During that period the court asked experts to prepare 10 reports and supplementary opinions on the value of the matrimonial property. On 4 June 2004 the District Court gave a decision. The applicant appealed. On 21 March 2006 the Regional Court of City A partly quashed the first-instance decision and remitted the case. Between 13 November 2006 and 18 February 2008 the District Court scheduled 6 hearings, during which the witnesses and the applicant were heard. On 17 March 2008 the District Court gave a decision. The applicant appealed. On 22 December 2008 the Regional Court dismissed the appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 36757/97) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of a country, Elvis Jakupovic (“the applicant”), on 8 April 1997. The applicant was represented by a lawyer practising in a city (Austria). The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, an Ambassador, Head of the International Law Department of the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant complained under Article 8 of the Convention that a residence prohibition imposed on him by the Austrian authorities violated his right to respect for his private and family life. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 15 November 2001 the Court declared the application partly admissible. Neither the applicant nor the Government filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1).The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1979 and lived at the time of the events in a city (Austria). He presently lives in a town (Croatia). In February 1991 the applicant arrived in Austria together with his brother, born in 1985, and joined his mother who had already been living and working there. Subsequently his mother remarried. The applicant's family now consists of his mother, his stepfather, his brother and two half sisters, born in 1993 and 1995. On 14 January 1994 the Police Authorities filed a criminal complaint against the applicant on suspicion of burglary. On 14 March 1994 the Regional Court (Landesgericht) provisionally discontinued the criminal proceedings and ordered the applicant to compensate the victims for the damage caused. On 11 May 1995 the District Administrative Authority issued a prohibition to possess arms (Waffenverbot) against the applicant as he had, in April 1995, attacked several persons with an electroshock device. On 31 May 1995 the applicant was remanded in custody on suspicion of having committed some fifty burglaries. On 28 August 1995 the Regional Court convicted the applicant of burglary and sentenced him to five months' imprisonment, suspended for a probationary period of three years. On the same day the applicant was released from detention on remand. On 28 September 1995 the District Administrative Authority issued a ten year residence prohibition against the applicant.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of XYZ lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of XYZ, Mr XYZ (the applicant), on 15 June 2001. The applicant was represented by Mr XYZ, a lawyer practising in XYZ. The XYZ Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 6 November 2007 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1947 and lives in XYZ. On 17 September 1981 the applicant was arrested and taken into custody for his suspected involvement in terrorist activities. Subsequently, he was remanded in custody until 7 April 1985, when, in the course of the criminal proceedings brought against him, he was released. On 16 May 1991 he was acquitted of all charges. The applicant submits that since this decision was not duly notified to him, he learned of his acquittal only in 1997. On 25 May 1997 the XYZ Assize Court, seeking compensation pursuant to Law no. 477. That Law provides, inter alia, for an award of damages to any person who has been unlawfully deprived of his or her liberty, or who, after being lawfully detained, was not subsequently committed for trial or was acquitted after standing trial. The applicant claimed 20,000,000,000 XYZ liras (approximately 256,706 US Dollars) for non-pecuniary damage. On 28 February 1999 the first-instance court awarded a certain amount of compensation. The Court of Cassation quashed that ruling on 31 December 1999 and remitted the file to the XYZ Assize Court for a more comprehensive examination. On 17 June 1999 the assize court dismissed the case on the ground that the applicant had failed to respect the statutory time-limit. This judgment was also quashed by the Court of Cassation on 2 May 2000. On 5 October 2000 the first-instance court handed down its third ruling where it awarded a certain amount of compensation. On 28 March 2001 the Court of Cassation quashed this judgment on the ground that the amount awarded was too low. On 7 September 2001 the assize court awarded the applicant 3,000,000,000 XYZ liras (approximately EUR 2,400) in respect of non-pecuniary damage. On 4 March 2002 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. In the course of the proceedings the assize court held investigatory sittings on a regular basis. Only on four occasions did it decide to notify the applicant’s lawyer of the date of its next session (30 April 1997, 10 February 1999, 1 June 2000 and 6 June 2001). However, no session was postponed on account of the applicant’s lawyer’s failure to attend.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against a generic country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of a generic treaty (“the Convention”) by a generic national, Mr Generic Person (“the applicant”), on 15 February 2006. The generic country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Generic Agent of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 1 October 2006 the President of the Fifth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The government requested that the present application be joined to application no. 12346/06, which was lodged by the applicant (Generic Person v. Generic Country (no. 1) and which concerned the length of another and unrelated set of civil proceedings. On 10 May 2008 the President of the Chamber decided not to join the applications. The government submitted a unilateral declaration and invited the Court to strike both of the above-mentioned applications out of the list, in accordance with Article 37 of the Convention. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in a generic city. A. Civil proceedings for payment On 15 November 2000 the applicant lodged a claim for payment with a generic district court. The applicant requested the court to make an order for payment against his business partner. The value of the claim was 1000 generic currency units (about 300 generic currency units). On 10 March 2005 the generic district court gave judgment and dismissed the applicant’s claim. On 9 April 2005 the applicant appealed against the first-instance judgment. On 30 December 2005 the generic regional court heard the applicant’s appeal and granted the claim for payment. B. Proceedings under the 2005 Act On 22 October 2005 the applicant lodged a complaint with the generic regional court under section 6 of the Law of 15 June 2005 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time (Ustawa o skardze na naruszenie prawa strony do rozpoznania sprawy w postępowaniu sądowym bez nieuzasadnionej zwłoki – “the 2005 Act”). He sought a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings before the generic district court had been excessive and that just satisfaction should be awarded to him. On 10 October 2005 the generic regional court gave a decision in which it acknowledged the excessive length of the proceedings (36 months and 7 days of inactivity on the part of the generic district court) but refused to grant the applicant any just satisfaction, holding that the applicant had failed to reason his request for just satisfaction and that the proceedings for payment of 1000 generic currency units did “not seem to be particularly important for the applicant, who is a businessman”. C. Application no.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 13024/05) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms X (“the applicant”), on 23 March 2005. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Y. On 3 October 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. It also gave priority to the application, pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1929 and lives in a city, Poland. In 1940 the applicant's father had been arrested and was sent with his family to a location. The applicant's mother died in 1940 and her father died in a city in 1967. In 1946 the applicant and her siblings returned to Poland. On 6 October 1948 the property belonging to the applicant's parents was taken over by the State. In 1990 the applicant and her sister were designated jointly as their father's heirs. On 29 November 2001 the applicant applied to a government official to have the 1948 decision annulled and her parents' property returned to her. The case was transferred to a ministry for consideration. Subsequently, the applicant wrote to the minister and other authorities complaining that the property had not been returned to her. On 28 November 2003 she complained to the minister about his inactivity. As she received no reply to her complaint, on 5 December 2003 the applicant, represented by a lawyer, lodged a complaint about the minister's inactivity with the Supreme Administrative Court. Following her complaint, on 5 January 2004 the Supreme Administrative Court requested the minister to provide it with the case file within thirty days. It appears that the minister did not comply with this order. However, the minister started examining the merits of the applicant's case and made several requests to various authorities asking them for documents. On 20 May 2004 the Regional Administrative Court, to which the case was transferred, informed the applicant that despite its repeated requests the minister had not complied with the order to provide the case file. The applicant was advised that she could therefore apply for a fine to be imposed on the minister. On 4 June 2004 the minister gave a decision in which he stayed the proceedings. The applicant lodged an appeal in which she asked for the decision to be reconsidered and the proceedings to be resumed.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1515/04) against a State (Republic of Turkey) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (Turkish national), Mr X (“the applicant”), on 25 September 2003. The applicant was represented by Ms Y and Mr Z, lawyers practising in a city (Izmir). The State (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 20 November 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1961 and lives in a city (Istanbul). On 3 September 2001 an arrest warrant was issued by a court (Izmir Criminal Court) in respect of the applicant due to his alleged involvement in an offence. On 13 August 2001 the prosecutor (Izmir Public Prosecutor) filed a bill of indictment charging the applicant with these offences. On 12 October 2001 the court (Bakırköy Magistrates' Court) ordered the applicant's detention on remand in accordance with the arrest warrant. On 10 December 2001 the court (Izmir Criminal Court) issued a decision of lack of jurisdiction and referred the case to another court (Izmir Assize Court). On 11 December 2001 the applicant was heard by the court (Bakırköy Magistrates' Court) upon the instruction of the court (Izmir Criminal Court). The applicant pleaded not guilty and requested his release. Between 19 December 2001 and 3 February 2003, the court (first-instance court) postponed nine hearings since the applicant, who was detained in a prison (Metris Prison), was not brought before it as he could not be transferred to another prison (Buca Prison) in the city (Izmir). Between 19 December 2001 and 7 July 2003, the court (Izmir Assize Court) examined the applicant's continued detention at the end of every hearing, either of its own motion or upon the applicant's requests. On each occasion, the court ordered the applicant's continued detention, having regard to the state of the evidence and nature of the offence. On 7 July 2003 the court ordered the applicant's release. On 8 November 2004 the applicant was acquitted for lack of evidence. On 10 February 2005 the applicant brought an action before the court (Bakırköy Assize Court) requesting compensation for his unjustified detention. On 8 October 2007, the court (Bakırköy Assize Court) partially granted the applicant's compensation claim. On 20 November 2008 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 8 October 2007. According to the information in the case file, the compensation proceedings are currently pending before the first instance court.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Human Rights Commission and by the Government of a European Country on 19 October 1996 and on 7 January 1997 respectively, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 § 1 and Article 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 24839/94) against a European Country lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by Ms Jane Doe, a citizen, on 11 March 1994. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 of the Convention and to the declaration whereby the European Country recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46). The object of the request and of the Government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 of the Convention. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 10001/09) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xanadu, Mr Xanadu Citizen (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2009. The applicant was represented by Mr Xanadu Lawyer, a lawyer practising in Xanadu. The Government of Xanadu (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 12 June 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1939 and lives in Xanadu. In 2005 the General Directorate of Highways seized a plot of land belonging to the applicant without any formal expropriation, for the construction of a highway. The applicant brought an action before the Civil Court to obtain compensation for the de facto expropriation of his property. He requested 5,000 local currency units (LCUs) as compensation from the court and reserved his right to increase this claim in due course. On 29 December 2006 the Civil Court awarded the applicant 5,000 LCUs as compensation for the de facto expropriation of his land, as requested, plus interest. The applicant initiated execution proceedings before the Execution Office to obtain that amount (file no. 2007/1234). On 29 May 2007 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. The applicant subsequently brought an additional action before the Civil Court to obtain further compensation for his land in the light of the expert report obtained during the previous proceedings, which had valued the land at a rate higher than that initially requested by him. On 2 November 2007 the Civil Court awarded the applicant 570,000.75 LCUs, plus interest. The applicant initiated another set of execution proceedings before the Execution Office to obtain the amount awarded (file no. 2010/3456). On 13 March 2008 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Civil Court. On 16 January 2010 the administration paid 9,410.32 LCUs to file no. 2007/1234 before the Execution Office in respect of the debt arising from the initial action. Subsequently, on 19 March 2010 they paid 789,091.92 LCUs to file no. 2010/3456 before the Execution Office in respect of the debt under the additional action. According to the information provided by the applicant, there has been no outstanding debt in the execution files.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 19 September 2000. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Ms Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in City. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr John Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that the court’s unreasoned decisions to refuse to grant him legal aid in connection with the preparation of an appeal against a first-instance judgment infringed his right to a fair hearing. On 10 October 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant owned and ran a company. On an unspecified date before 1998 the factory owned by the company burned down. Subsequently, the applicant was involved in a number of proceedings in connection with serious financial difficulties which had been caused by the fire. 1. Civil proceedings against the State Insurance Company (“PZU”) On 19 August 1999 the Regional Court in part dismissed and in part rejected the applicant’s compensation claim against the State Insurance Company, in connection with an insurance contract. On 14 September 1999 the applicant filed an appeal against this judgment with that court. On 21 September 1999 he requested the court to grant him full exemption from court fees. He referred to the fact that he had been partially exempted, by a decision of 30 September 1998, from the obligation to pay court fees. He submitted that his financial situation had further deteriorated since then. This request apparently remained unanswered. On 25 November 1999 the Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal. On 1 February 2000 the court, represented by a privately hired lawyer, lodged with that court a cassation appeal to the Supreme Court. On 21 February 2000 the Court of Appeal rejected the cassation appeal, finding that it failed to comply with the relevant formal requirements. On 16 March 2000 the applicant requested that a legal‐aid lawyer be assigned to the case for the purpose of preparing an appeal to the Supreme Court against that decision. On 20 March 2000 the Court of Appeal dismissed the request. This decision did not contain any grounds or reference to its legal basis. The applicant appealed. On 10 April 2000 the Court of Appeal rejected his appeal, holding that no appeal lay against the contested decision. It was only possible to submit an appeal to the Supreme Court against a decision rejecting a cassation appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against the Republic of Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Anna Nowak (“the applicant”), on 7 July 1999. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Smith, a lawyer practising in City, Country. The Country Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr B. Jones and subsequently Mr C. Brown, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 13 February 2003 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1954 and lives in City, Country. A. Proceedings for compensation and reinstatement The applicant worked as the head of the sales department in a company in City. On 24 August 1994 she was dismissed from her job. On 2 September 1994 she lodged a claim for compensation and reinstatement with the City District Court of Labour. Before 26 January 1995 the trial court held four hearings and heard evidence from one witness. On 2 March 1995 the parties reached a friendly settlement and the District Court discontinued the proceedings. On 16 March 1995 the applicant’s lawyer asked the court to resume the proceedings, as the defendant company had failed to comply with the terms of the settlement. On 27 June 1995 the Regional Court of Labour quashed the decision of 2 March and resumed the proceedings. On 21 September 1995 the District Court held a hearing. On 23 October 1995 it stayed the proceedings until the conclusion of criminal proceedings against the applicant (referred to below). The applicant’s further appeal against that decision was dismissed by the Regional Court of Labour on 28 December 1995. On 28 January 1999 the applicant asked the court to resume the proceedings.
