In a decision of 15 December 1996, the Office noted that the applicant had carried out heavy work as a generic occupation until 1982 when he had moved to a generic country and worked on renovating walls. In 1988 the applicant had informed the Office that he could no longer carry out his work because of his hip joint problems. Thus, in June 1988, he had been granted early retirement pension on the ground that he suffered from a degenerative joint disease. On the basis of the above, the Office considered that it was possible that the applicant’s work in the generic country had harmed him and, since it could only consider injuries which had occurred while working in the generic country, it could not examine the request. Upon request by the applicant, the Office, on 20 February 1997, reconsidered its previous decision but decided not to change it. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court of the County of Generic County, claiming that his injuries had been caused by his work in the generic country. He stated that he had created a company in the generic country to import generic goods but that, in order to get his business going, he had had to include measuring, installing and painting. However, since he already had pain in his hip joint and lower back, he had not been able to carry out the work and had sold the company.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 22341/09) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two applicants, on 25 March 2009. The applicants were represented by a charitable organisation based in Leeds. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 2 June 2009 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The first applicant arrived in the United Kingdom on 18 February 2004. He claimed asylum and that claim was accepted in March 2006. Prior to 30 August 2005, successful asylum seekers were granted Indefinite Leave to Remain in the United Kingdom along with refugee status. However, after 30 August 2005 the Immigration Rules were amended and refugees were granted an initial period of 5 years’ Leave to Remain, following which they could apply for Indefinite Leave to Remain. Consequently, the first applicant was granted five years’ leave to remain in the United Kingdom, to expire on 16 March 2011. At the same time, he was provided with a Refugee Convention Travel Document (“CTD”), also to expire on 16 March 2011. In June 2006 the first applicant was introduced to the second applicant through a friend. In February 2007 he travelled to Djibouti to meet her and they married on 5 April 2007. They lived together in Djibouti until the first applicant returned to the United Kingdom on 15 May 2007. The second applicant applied for a visa to join the first applicant in the United Kingdom. Although the first applicant was a refugee, the applicants did not qualify for “family reunion” under the Immigration Rules because paragraph 352A of the Immigration Rules only applied to spouses who formed part of the refugee’s family unit before he or she left the country of permanent residence. The second applicant therefore applied for leave to enter the United Kingdom under paragraph 281 of the Immigration Rules, as the spouse of a person present and settled in the United Kingdom. On 18 November 2007 the Entry Clearance Officer refused the application on the ground that the first applicant, having only been granted five years’ Leave to Remain, was not a person present and settled in the United Kingdom for the purposes of paragraph 281. On 17 February 2008 the second applicant gave birth to a son.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals, Ms. Jane Doe (“the first applicant”) and Mr. John Doe (“the second applicant”). The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr. X and Mr. Y of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 15 July 2003 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS The applicants are a married couple. The first applicant was born in 1950 and the second in 1945. They both live in a city, a country. Civil proceedings concerning delimitation of various plots of land belonging to the applicants began on 15 May 1980. On 15 September 1980 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) gave a decision. The applicants appealed. On 15 December 1980 the Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) set aside the first-instance decision and remitted the case. Following the remission of the case, the District Court held a number of hearings and ordered that several expert reports be prepared. On 15 September 1984 the District Court gave a decision. Upon the applicants' appeal, on 15 February 1985 the Regional Court set aside the decision and remitted the case for re-examination. Between 1985 and 1 May 1992 the District Court held 10 hearings. After 1 May 1992 the District Court held hearings on the following dates: 15 September, 15 November, 15 December 1992, 15 February, 15 March, 15 March and 15 April 1993. On 15 May 1993 the court held a viewing of the site. The next hearing was held on 15 October 1993. On 15 March 1994 the trial court held a hearing and stayed the proceedings because P.K., a party to the proceedings, had died. The applicants requested that the proceedings be resumed. On 15 January 1995 the court refused to resume the proceedings. On 15 March 1996 the applicants complained to the Ministry of Justice about the delay in the proceedings. On an unspecified date their complaints were referred to the President of the Regional Court, who replied thereto on 15 July 1996. He acknowledged that the proceedings were indeed lengthy and promised to supervise their conduct. On 15 June 1996, on the applicants' appeal, the Regional Court amended the decision of 15 January 1995 and resumed the proceedings. Subsequently, the District Court held hearings on the following dates: 15 December 1995, 15 September, 15 October and 15 December 1996. On 15 December 1996 the case file was sent to an expert who was to prepare an opinion. The expert returned the case-file on 15 May 1998.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Republic of Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 8 August 2006. The applicant was represented by Ms Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in City. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr John Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 27 September 2007 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1976 and lives in City. On 2 March 2003 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of armed robbery and theft committed as part of an organised criminal gang. On 3 March 2003 the Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) ordered his pre-trial detention. It referred to the likelihood that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged. It further considered that there was a reasonable risk that the applicant would obstruct the investigation by inducing witnesses to give false testimony. In the course of the investigation the applicant’s detention was prolonged by the Regional Court several times. The court referred to the likelihood of a severe sentence of imprisonment being imposed on the applicant and the complexity of the case. It relied on the fact that there were no circumstances to justify the application of a different preventive measure. On 20 November 2003 the Regional Prosecutor (Prokurator Okręgowy) indicted the applicant together with 13 other persons on charges of armed robbery, fraud, destruction of documents and theft committed as part of an organised criminal gang. The prosecutor asked the court to hear evidence from at least 120 witnesses. The trial began on 17 March 2004. The trial court held on average three hearings per month. In the course of the trial the applicant’s detention was prolonged by the Regional Court and the Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) several times. The court relied on the previous grounds. It also referred to the need to conclude the proceedings and in particular to ensure that the numerous co-accused and witnesses were questioned. The applicant’s appeals against the decisions extending his detention and against the detention order, and all his subsequent, numerous applications for release and appeals against refusals to release him, were unsuccessful. In particular, on 31 July 2006 the applicant made an application for his detention to be lifted or replaced by another preventive measure.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against the Kingdom of Andalusia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms Ana Martinez (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2009. The applicant was represented by Ms Begoña Lopez, a lawyer practising in Málaga. The Andalusian Government (“the Government”) were initially represented by their Agent, Mr Carlos Sanchez, and later by their Agent, Mr David Garcia. The applicant complained under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(d) of the Convention that she had not been given a proper and adequate opportunity, during either the investigative stage or the hearing, to challenge and question the victim, the sole witness against her in relation to all the crimes for which she had been convicted, with the exception of the forgery of official documents. On 25 February 2011 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). On 5 March 2011 the Court informed the European Government of their right under Article 36 § 1 of the Convention to intervene in the proceedings. The European Government did not inform the Court of their wish to intervene. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, Ms Ana Martinez, was born in 1980 and is currently serving a term of imprisonment in the Andalusian prison of San Pedro in Almeria (Almeria). On 10 March 2005, following reports to the police made by P., the applicant’s former partner and the mother of her son, the applicant was arrested at Malaga Airport and taken to a police station where she was informed of her right to appoint private legal counsel or, alternatively, to be provided with an officially appointed lawyer. The applicant opted for the latter. Investigating judge no. 3 of Almeria instituted a pre-trial investigation into allegations that the applicant had committed several serious offences of bodily harm, abduction and rape of P. On 12 March 2005 the applicant was brought before the investigating judge to be questioned about the offences of which she had been accused. She was accompanied by her officially appointed lawyer. The applicant was first informed by the judge of her right to appoint private legal counsel. She expressly appointed as private counsel the lawyer who had been officially assigned to her, who assisted her during her examination by the investigating judge. On 14 April 2005 the applicant was questioned again by the judge, in the presence of her counsel. On 28 April 2005 P. testified before the investigating judge; the applicant’s counsel failed to attend without providing a justification. P. confirmed the statement she had made to the police with the addition of some further details. This statement was written up and added to the case file.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Ms Alice Brown, Ms Clara Green, Ms Daisy White, Mr Edward Brown, Ms Fiona Black, and Mr George Brown (“the applicants”), on 15 November 2000. The applicants were represented by Mr Henry White, a lawyer practising in Andorra. The Andoran Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 15 September 2004 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants live in Andorra. On 9 February 1993 the General Directorate of National Roads and Highways expropriated two plots of land belonging to the applicants in Andorra in order to build a motorway. A committee of experts assessed the value of the plots of land and the relevant amount was paid to the applicants when the expropriation took place. Following the applicants’ request for increased compensation, on 10 November 1993, the Civil Court of First-instance in Andorra awarded them additional compensation of 443,710,000 local currency units, plus interest at the statutory rate, applicable at the date of the court’s decision, running from 9 February 1993, the date of the transfer of the title-deeds. On 26 October 1998 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Civil Court of First-instance in Andorra. On 17 May 2000 the General Directorate of National Roads and Highways paid the applicants 1,768,440,000 local currency units, including interest.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr. A. Novak (“the applicant”). The applicant was represented by Mr. B. Sidor, a lawyer practising in Warsaw. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. C. Nowakowski of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 15 October 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Gdynia. The applicant’s detention for the purpose of the first set of criminal proceedings On 10 October 2003 the applicant was arrested and placed in custody. He was suspected of having committed offences of kidnapping and acting in an organisation of a criminal character. On an unknown date the Warsaw District Court ordered that the applicant be detained until 15 December 2003. The court based its detention order on a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences and on the severity of the likely penalty, which gave rise to a fear that the applicant would obstruct the proceedings. The court also stressed his relapse into crime. Subsequent decisions as to the extension of the applicant’s pre-trial detention were taken on 20 November 2003, 10 December 2003, 10 February 2004, 1 June 2004, 29 September 2004, 22 December 2004 and 30 April 2005. In all the above-mentioned decisions the courts mainly relied on the same grounds for detention as those given for the making of the first detention order. In addition, they indicated the need to conduct further investigations and the probable collusion of the accused. On many occasions the applicant unsuccessfully requested his release from detention and, also unsuccessfully, appealed against decisions extending his pre-trial detention. On 5 February 2004 a bill of indictment was filed against the applicant and thirteen co-accused. The applicant was charged with kidnapping and acting in an organisation of a criminal character. From 30 October 2004 to 5 June 2005 the applicant was serving a prison sentence in respect of another conviction. On 30 July 2004 the first hearing was held before the Warsaw Regional Court. Hearings scheduled for 15 and 23 October 2004 were postponed due to the necessity of replacing one of the judges. On 7 November 2004 a new judge was assigned to the case.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against the Republic of Alfa (a fictional country) lodged with the European Human Rights Commission (a fictional organization) under former Article 25 of the Alfa Convention (a fictional document) by an Alfa national, Mr Alex Novak (a fictional person) (the applicant) on 15 January 1997. The applicant had been granted legal aid. The Alfa Government (the Government) were represented by their Agent, Mr John Doe, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings against him, relating to charges of threatening behavior, he did not have a public hearing as the trial was held in the prison where he was detained. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 12 to the Convention came into force (Article 6 § 2 of Protocol No. 12). 5. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 53 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 28 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 27 § 1. 6. By a decision of 20 July 2001 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible [Note by the Registry. The Court's decision is obtainable from the Registry.]. 7. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 60 § 1). 8. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Alfa City, on 30 September 2001 (Rule 60 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr Jane Smith, Head of the Constitutional Law Section at the Federal Chancellery, Agent, Mrs Mary Brown, Federal Ministry of Justice, Adviser; (b) for the applicant Mr Chris Green, of the Alfa Bar, Counsel. The Court heard addresses by Mr Green, Mr Smith and Mrs Brown. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant is serving a twenty-year prison term following his conviction for murder and burglary in 1988. He was first detained at Beta Prison, from which he escaped in 1992 but was rearrested within a day. In September 1995 he was transferred to Gamma Prison and on 10 May 1996 to Delta Prison, as the prison administration feared that he and a number of other inmates were devising an escape plan. On 10 May 1996, when prison personnel at Delta carried out the necessary reception formalities, the applicant refused to cooperate and demanded to be returned to Gamma Prison, threatening that otherwise he and other inmates would set fire to Delta Prison. On the following day, in the course of an interview with a senior prison officer, he again insisted on being returned to Gamma Prison and threatened the prison officer that otherwise someone would pay the officer "a private visit". A few days later he threatened a prison warder saying "that he should not turn his back on him".

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Xana lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Mr Ali Yılmaz (“the applicant”), on 1 April 2005. The applicant was represented by Ms C.D. Öztürk, a lawyer practising in Ankara. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 10 May 2008 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in Ankara. On 10 September 2001 the applicant was arrested and taken into custody on suspicion of membership of an organised criminal gang and involvement in kidnapping on behalf of that organisation. On 13 September 2001 he was remanded in custody. On 23 October 2001 the public prosecutor at the Ankara State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicant and twenty‐one other persons on the above-mentioned charges. On 10 November 2001 the criminal proceedings against the applicant and the twenty-one other accused commenced before the Ankara State Security Court. Eighteen hearings were held in total. Throughout the proceedings the applicant’s lawyer repeatedly requested that the applicant be released during trial, but those requests were dismissed at the end of each hearing by way of an interim decision using an identical expression, namely “having regard to the nature of the offence with which he is charged and the state of the evidence”. On a number of occasions the applicant’s lawyer objected to the interim decisions of the Ankara State Security Court extending the applicant’s detention, and in each case the objections were further dismissed by the Ankara State Security Court using the aforementioned identical expression. On 15 March 2005 the Ankara Assize Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him, in total, to 27 years and 4 months’ imprisonment. On 25 April 2006 the Court of Cassation held a hearing and upheld the first-instance court’s judgment in respect of the applicant’s membership of an organised criminal gang, but quashed the judgment in respect of the sentence imposed on the applicant for kidnapping. On 15 August 2006 the case was referred back to the Ankara Assize Court. On 25 November 2006 the Ankara Assize Court decided to release the applicant pending trial. He was accordingly released the next day. On 15 February 2009 the Ankara Assize Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to imprisonment for, in total, twelve years, eight months and fifteen days. The case is still pending before the Court of Cassation.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123456/01) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2001. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr A. Smith, and subsequently, Mr B. Jones of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 1 May 2003 the President of the Fifth Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The President of the Chamber further gave priority to the application, pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1925 and lives in a city, a country. On an unspecified date in 1995 the applicant asked an office to grant him “veteran status.” The President of the Office informed the applicant that his application was not complete and should be submitted first to a local veterans association. On 1 October 1996, after having contacted the city Veterans Association, the applicant lodged for the second time an application with the office concerning his “veteran status.” The Office failed to issue a decision and informed the applicant that he should first lodge an application with a different association. On 1 February 1997 the applicant lodged a complaint about the inactivity of the Office with the Supreme Court. On 1 June 1997 the Supreme Court allowed his complaint and ordered the Office to give a decision within two months. The court established that the applicant’s application of 1 October 1996 had satisfied legal requirements and that the Office should have given a decision on merits instead of asking the applicant to fulfil other conditions. On 1 February and 1 April 1998 the Office requested the applicant to submit additional documents concerning his case. The applicant complied with the requests. On 1 July 1998 the President of the Office gave a decision in which he refused to grant the applicant “veteran status.” The Office found that the applicant had failed to provide evidence of his participation in the country Defence War in September 1939. The applicant lodged a complaint against this decision with the Supreme Court. On 1 March 1999 the Supreme Court quashed the impugned decision and remitted the case to the first-instance authority. The court found that the Office had not examined the case properly and, in particular, had not heard the applicant despite his several applications and had not heard other soldiers who had allegedly fought with him.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/08) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Xanadu Citizen (“the applicant”), on 15 May 2008. The applicant was represented by Ms Y, his mother. The government of Xanadu (“the government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his right of access to court had been breached by the domestic court’s refusal to grant him legal aid. On 30 June 2010 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1980 and lives in Yonder. On 15 December 2003, after having completed his military service, the applicant was placed under the guardianship of his father, Z., by a decision of the Zephyr Magistrates’ Court as he was mentally ill and needed constant supervision. The applicant submitted several requests to the gendarmerie command claiming compensation for his illness which, according to him, began during his military service as a result of the treatment there. His requests were rejected on the basis of a medical report from the Zephyr Military Medical Academy, which indicated that such a condition could not have been caused merely by military service and that many other factors could have been involved in its development. Subsequently, under the guardianship of Z., the applicant initiated compensation proceedings before the Supreme Military Administrative Court, claiming that his illness had been caused by the ill-treatment to which he had been subjected in the army. He argued that his enrolment for military service after having passed several medical tests was proof that he had been healthy before. The applicant requested a total of 300,000 local currency units (LCUs) (approximately 150,000 euros (EUR) at the time) in respect of both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage, submitting the medical records from several hospitals in support of his claims. He also requested legal aid for the court fees, presenting a certificate from the office of the headman (muhtar) attesting to his father’s poverty. The certificate stated that neither Z. nor anyone else from his household was employed. It also indicated that he was ill, had no social security and depended on support from his neighbours. By two decisions of 20 July and 1 December 2006 respectively, the Supreme Military Administrative Court rejected the applicant’s legal aid request, stating that pursuant to the Code of Civil Procedure, a legal aid request must be supported by proof that the case is well-founded and that the plaintiff does not have the means to pay the required court fees. It concluded that the requirements had not been met in the applicant’s case.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 11036/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a French national, Mr Franck Ladent (“the applicant”), on 24 February 2003. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr L. Hincker, a lawyer practising in Strasbourg. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been deprived of his liberty in breach of Article 5 § 1 of the Convention. On 4 July 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The French Government were invited to intervene in the proceedings (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention). However, by a letter of 10 October 2006, they informed the Registry that they did not wish to exercise their right to intervene. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1972 and lives in a town in France. On an unspecified date he arrived in Poland. He married a Polish national on 15 March 2001. They initially lived in Kraków, but on 3 July 2001 they moved to France. Their two children were born in September 2001 and October 2002 respectively. The applicant is an artist and runs a small business in France which provides the only support for the family. On 21 March 2001 a certain B.M., an administrator of the building in which the applicant's wife had a flat, brought a private prosecution against the applicant for slander (zniewaga) under Article 216 § 1 of the Criminal Code. He alleged that the applicant had addressed him in obscene language in Polish. Subsequently, the private prosecution proceedings were commenced in the Kraków–Śródmieście District Court. It appears that following the applicant's departure for France the court sent him summonses in connection with the private prosecution but received no response. On 15 July 2002 the District Court ordered that the applicant be remanded in custody for a period of three months. It further ordered that a wanted notice (list gończy) be issued with a view to locating and detaining him. It invoked, inter alia, Articles 258 § 1(1) and 259 § 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (hereinafter “the CCP”). The District Court held as follows: “The accused has no permanent abode in Poland, [and] does not reside in any place known to the court, and is thus obstructing the proper conduct of the proceedings in the present case and the delivery of a proper judgment within a reasonable time. The need to issue a detention order in respect of the accused is required to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 69129/01) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Alice Green (“the applicant”). The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr John Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 13 October 2005 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1922 and lives in a village. On 23 February 1989 the applicant filed an action with a district court in which she sought a court order against third parties requiring them to remove an electricity cable they had installed on her land. Between May and August 1989 three hearings were held. An expert opinion was submitted to the court during that period. As the parties were subsequently invited to settle the case, between 15 November 1990 and 6 May 1991 the proceedings were stayed at their request in order to negotiate a settlement. On 29 June 1991 the district court delivered a judgment dismissing the applicant’s action. The applicant appealed on 28 August 1991. At the appeal hearing of 28 October 1991 the regional court decided to stay the proceedings pending the termination of other proceedings for the establishment of the defendant’s ownership of the land. Those proceedings ended on 26 October 1998 with the Supreme Court’s decision rejecting the applicant’s cassation appeal as inadmissible. On 3 December 1999 the proceedings were resumed upon the applicant’s request of 16 November 1999. On 23 December 1999 the regional court quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case for re-examination, indicating the need to obtain an expert opinion on the exact route of the electricity line across the land. A hearing was held on 9 February 2000; the court ordered the preparation of the expert opinion and ordered the applicant to pay the expert’s fee within 14 days. Between February and April 2000 the applicant repeatedly sought exemption from payment of the expert’s fee. She was ordered to pay the fee, failing which the evidence provided by the expert opinion would be excluded. The applicant failed to comply with the order. On 31 May 2000 the district court decided to omit the evidence contained in the expert opinion. It examined as evidence the case files of three other sets of related proceedings and on that basis delivered a judgment dismissing the action. On 7 September 2000 the regional court dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The court agreed with the first-instance court that the defendant had the right of co-ownership to the plot on the date on which the proceedings were instituted and that the applicant’s claim was accordingly inadmissible.

PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 19955/05 and 15085/06) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals, Alice Johnson and Brian Smith, on 20 May 2005 and 10 April 2006 respectively. The first applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr X. Brown, a lawyer practising in a city and the second applicant was represented by YZ Law Firm of another city. The country Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms W. Green, Foreign and Commonwealth Office. Each applicant alleged that, in confiscation proceedings following his conviction for drugs offences, the fact that the legal burden of proof was on him to show that he did not have realisable assets equivalent to the benefit figure offended the basic principles of a fair procedure, in breach of Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. Each applicant and the Government filed written observations. Under Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, the Chamber decided to examine the merits of each application at the same time as its admissibility. It also decided to join the applications (Rule 42 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. The first applicant (Ms Johnson) On 23 January 2002 the applicant and a co-defendant were convicted with intent to supply over 28 kilograms of pure heroin, which was seized by the police at the time of arrest. The heroin was assessed to have a wholesale value in excess of 1.2 million and a street value in excess of 4 million. The following day the applicant was sentenced to 22 years’ imprisonment. On 1 July 2002, after considering written and oral submissions from the applicant and the prosecution, the judge made a confiscation order under the Drug Trafficking Act 1994 (“the 1994 Act”: see paragraphs 20-22 below). He held that the applicant had benefited from drug trafficking. In assessing the amount of the benefit the judge took into account, inter alia, the following sums: 18,000 cash found on the applicant at the time of his arrest; 13,000 that the applicant had paid to his brother when a business partnership between them came to an end; 21,000 that he had spent, in cash, on buying two cars; a further 8,000 which he had spent on another two cars; and 620,445 which was the judge’s assessment of the cost to the applicant of purchasing the heroin which had led to the conviction. As regards this last sum, the judge, having heard all the evidence at trial, was satisfied that the applicant had been the principal participant in the offence and must have contributed to a large extent to the purchase of the drugs. However, to be fair to the applicant he took as his share one half of the wholesale value.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 31 December 1998. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Smith, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. He also complained under Article 6 § 1 in conjunction with Article 6 § 3 (c) of the Convention that for a certain period during the investigation he had been unable to communicate with his defence counsel out of earshot of a person appointed by the prosecutor. On 9 November 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the length of criminal proceedings, the length of detention, the alleged unfairness of the criminal proceedings and the refusal of access to the full statements made by anonymous witnesses. On 9 October 2007 the Court declared admissible the applicant’s complaints relating to the excessive length of his detention and the lack of unsupervised contacts with his lawyer at the investigation stage of the proceedings, and the remainder of the application inadmissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Detention on remand The applicant was arrested on 8 May 1996 on suspicion of having committed a crime while acting as a member of an organisation. On 9 May 1996 the prosecutor issued a detention order against him on charges of a crime involving use of a firearm and committed in conspiracy with other persons. The prosecutor referred to a reasonable suspicion, based on witnesses’ testimony, and the risk that the applicant might go into hiding or exert pressure on witnesses. Detention was imposed until 8 August 1996. The applicant was detained on the same date as two other accused persons. Yet another suspect was detained on 23 August 1996. The investigation and subsequent court proceedings were conducted against five persons jointly, four of them detained and one at liberty. On 10 May 1996 the applicant’s defence counsel appealed against the detention order. He challenged the credibility of the evidence in the applicant’s case, stating that it had been obtained illegally. In particular, he argued that the manner in which the applicant had been presented in an identification parade had not complied with the applicable procedural guarantees. This application was dismissed on 13 May 1996. In the course of the investigation, the applicant’s detention was prolonged twice, on 1 August, until 31 October 1996, and on 24 October, until 31 December 1996. The courts relied on a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had actually committed the offence with which he was charged and on the need to ensure the proper conduct of the investigation.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 April 1999. The applicant was represented by Mr C. Smith, a lawyer practising in Salzburg. The government of the country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador J. Brown, Head of the International Law Department at the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that the Regional Appeals Commission which decided on his claims for doctor’s fees lacked independence and impartiality. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 15 September 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in Salzburg. The applicant is a medical practitioner whose contract with the State Health Insurance Board was terminated by the latter on 31 December 1996. Subsequently the applicant was practising without a contract with the Health Insurance Board and is meanwhile retired. He complains about two sets of proceedings. A. The first set of proceedings On 30 October 1996 the applicant instituted proceedings against the State Health Insurance Board. He claimed that the defendant had to pay an additional amount of 120 Austrian schillings (ATS) for doctor’s fees. On 3 April 1997 the Joint Arbitration Committee dismissed the applicant’s claim. The applicant appealed against this decision. On 3 July 1998 the Regional Appeals Commission dismissed the appeal. On 25 September 1998 the applicant lodged a complaint with the Constitutional Court. He alleged, inter alia, that the general agreement between the Association of Health Boards and the Medical Association on which his doctor’s fees were based violated his constitutional right to non-discrimination. On 15 April 1999 he amended his complaint and alleged that the Regional Appeals Commission was no independent and impartial tribunal within the meaning of Article 6 of the Convention by virtue of its composition. On 17 December 1999 the Constitutional Court dismissed the complaint. It did not accept that the Regional Appeals Commission’s decision had violated the applicant’s constitutional rights. As regards the composition of the Regional Appeals Commission, the Constitutional Court noted that the applicant’s complaint had been lodged out of the statutory six months time-limit. However, referring to its constant case-law, it found that the applicant’s constitutional rights were not violated. B.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 8 December 1995, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application against a State lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by a citizen on 28 May 1993. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the State recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio a judge of a nationality and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. On 8 February 1996, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members. As President of the Chamber, Mr Ryssdal, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings. Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the applicant’s memorial on 28 June 1996 and the Government’s memorial on 4 July 1996. On 29 August 1996 the President decided to admit to the Court file an additional memorial submitted by the applicant which had been received by the Registrar on 7 August 1996. In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 25 September 1996. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government legal representatives, (b) for the Commission a Delegate, (c) for the applicant legal representatives.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/05) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 March 2005. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr X Y Z of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged in particular that his pre-trial detention had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 8 January 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the Convention). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in a city. On 15 July 2002 the applicant was arrested by the police on suspicion of having committed several burglaries and robberies together with several accomplices. On 16 July 2002 the District Court decided to place the applicant in pre-trial detention on the basis of a reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences. The court also considered that, given the likely severity of the penalty, it was probable that the applicant would interfere with the course of proceedings and he might go into hiding. Moreover, the court considered that there was a risk that the applicant would bring pressure to bear on witnesses or his accomplices. On 5 October and 21 December 2002 the Regional Court extended the applicant’s detention, finding that the original reasons for it were still valid. The court referred also to the risk of his absconding, considering that the applicant rarely stayed at his official place of residence and “had been avoiding contact with the police officers, who were looking for him”. On 17 June 2003 the Court of Appeal, upon an application from the Regional Prosecutor, further extended the applicant’s pre-trial detention. Subsequently, the applicant and ten co-accused were indicted before the Regional Court. On 18 September 2003 the Regional Court extended the applicant’s pre-trial detention. In a very brief reasoning the court stated that there was a reasonable suspicion against the applicant and that, given the likely heavy sentence and the fact that the applicant had acted in a criminal group, only his detention could secure the proper course of the proceedings. Subsequently, as the length of the applicant’s detention had reached the statutory time-limit of two years laid down in the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Regional Court applied to the Court of Appeal for the applicant’s detention to be extended beyond that term.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 September 2004. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent Mr A. Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. In addition, third-party comments were received from the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights (a city in Europe), which had been given leave by the President to intervene in the written procedure (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 2). The applicant alleged that the refusal to allow him to attend the funeral of his father was in breach of Article 8 of the Convention. On 8 October 2008 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in a town. On 10 January 2001 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) convicted the applicant of domestic violence and sentenced him to a one-year period of imprisonment suspended on probation for 4 years. The court found that between May 1999 and September 2000 the applicant had ill-treated his girlfriend in that he had beaten her and abused her verbally. It appears that the applicant breached the terms of his probation and on 15 March 2003 the District Court ordered that his sentence be enforced. On 1 April 2004 he started to serve it in the Detention Centre. On 15 June 2004 the applicant’s father died. The applicant submits that he immediately asked the prison authorities for leave to attend his father’s funeral. On 17 June the applicant’s girlfriend delivered him his father’s death certificate. On 18 June 2004, a Monday, the applicant made a formal application for leave to attend the funeral, which was to be held on 19 June 2004. On 18 June 2004 the Penitentiary Judge of the Regional Court (Sędzia Sądu Okręgowego Wydziału Penitencjarnego) refused the leave request. The reasons given for the judge’s decision were as follows: “The convicted person’s application cannot be allowed. The grounds relied on [by the applicant] to justify allowing him to leave the prison cannot be considered especially important. Consequently, since the conditions specified in Article 141 § 4 of [the Code of Execution of Criminal Sentences] had not been fulfilled, it has been decided as above.” The decision also included an instruction on the possibility to lodge an appeal against the decision with the Regional Penitentiary Court within 7 days of the date of notification of the decision. The decision was notified to the applicant on 19 June 2004.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/04) against the Republic of Xlodania lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Ms Xxandra Yarrows. The Republic of Xlodania (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. Wodders of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Haydock, a lawyer practising in City Y. On 27 October 2006 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, the owner of real property which she had been renting, filed a civil action for damages against the tenant. On 5 October 2001 her action was dismissed by a judgment of the City Y Regional Court. The applicant appealed against the judgment. On 20 February 2002 her appeal was dismissed by a judgment of the City Z Court of Appeal. Judge B. H. was the judge rapporteur in the case. The applicant lodged a cassation appeal against the judgment through a panel of the City Z Court of Appeal. On 23 April 2002 her cassation appeal was rejected by a decision of that panel. In its written grounds for the decision, the panel stated that the cassation appeal did not comply with a procedural requirement set out in Article 404 4 § 2 (4) of the Code of Civil Procedure in that it did not include “arguments showing that its examination [by the Supreme Court] would be justified” within the meaning of this provision (see paragraphs 15-17 below). The mere fact that the cassation appeal contained arguments to show the grounds on which it had been lodged was insufficient for the appeal to be declared admissible. The panel further stated that this shortcoming was serious and as such could not be remedied. Judge B.H. presided over the panel which gave this decision and also acted as the judge rapporteur on the admissibility issue. The applicant lodged an appeal with the Supreme Court against the decision of 23 April 2002, challenging inter alia the composition of the court. She submitted that the fact that the same judge had sat on a panel giving a second-instance judgment on the merits and subsequently on a panel rejecting a cassation appeal against that judgment rendered the proceedings unfair. On 8 June 2003 her appeal was dismissed by a decision of the Supreme Court. The court first noted the case-law of the Supreme Court on the interpretation of Article 404 4 § 2 (4) of the Code.

PROCEDURE The case originated in three applications (nos. 14352/05, 38484/05 and 38513/05) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by three nationals, Ms A. A., Mr B. B. and Mr C. C. (“the applicants”), on 4 April, 12 October and 7 October 2005. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Mr D. D., Ms E. E., Mr F. F. and Ms G. G., lawyers practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicants alleged in particular that they had been subjected to torture during their detention in police custody and that ensuing criminal proceedings against the police officers involved had been ineffective. The applicants relied on Articles 3, 6 and 13 of the Convention. On 22 May and 24 June 2009 respectively the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASES A. A. v Country (14352/05) The applicant was born in 1974 and lives in a city. On 21 and 22 February 1997 the applicant and a number of other suspects were taken into police custody by officers from the Anti-Terrorist Branch of the Security Headquarters, where they were kept until 6 March 1997 and allegedly ill-treated by police officers. The applicant stated in particular that she had been beaten, and subjected to sexual harassment and Palestinian hanging. On 26 February 1997 the applicant was taken to a hospital for a medical examination. The report drawn up by a doctor indicated that the applicant did not bear any signs of ill-treatment. On 4 March 1997 the applicant was taken to a forensic doctor who reported a lightly bruised area on her left shoulder, old scabs of various sizes on the lower parts of her legs, sensitivity in her thumbs and index fingers on both hands and pain in her arms. During the subsequent domestic proceedings, on 15 October 1999 the Forensic Institute established that the injuries noted on the applicant's body had rendered her unfit to work for three days. On 6 March 1997 the applicant was brought before the Public Prosecutor. She denied all accusations against her and mentioned the ill-treatment she had been subjected to. She was subsequently detained pending trial. Following the complaints of ill-treatment lodged by the applicant and fourteen other detainees, an investigation concerning eight police officers on duty at the time was initiated.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by six Andorran nationals, Ms Ana Garcia, Mr Juan Martinez, Mr Carlos Lopez, Mr David Sanchez, Ms Maria Rodriguez and Ms Carmen Gonzalez (“the applicants”), on 30 April 2003. The applicants were represented by Mr L. Garcia, Mr J. Martinez and Ms C. Lopez, lawyers practising in Andorra la Vella. The Andorran Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 5 November 2007 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1930, 1973, 1957, 1967, 1964 and 1954 respectively, and live in Andorra except for the third and the fourth applicants who reside in Andorra la Vella and El Mas de Sant Joan respectively. The first applicant’s son and the other applicants’ brother, Jose Garcia, was a student at the University of Andorra at the time of the events. On 15 March 1994 Jose Garcia was arrested and taken into police custody, together with his friend Mr X.Y.Z., at the Campus of the University of Andorra. They had flammable substances in their possession. On 16 March 1994, while in detention, Jose Garcia’s health deteriorated and he was admitted to the Hospital of Andorra. On the same day, he was transferred to the Hospital of Andorra. On his arrival, Jose Garcia was unconscious and had slight bruises and abrasions on various parts of his body. A brain scan revealed a subdural haematoma in the right fronto-temporo-parietal region. He was immediately operated on and remained in the hospital’s intensive care unit until 9 June 1994, without, it appears, regaining consciousness. Jose Garcia was later transferred, first to the Hospital of Andorra and later to the Hospital of Andorra where he died on 5 September 1994. He was twenty-one years old. On 8 September 1994, upon the request of the Public Prosecutor of Andorra, an autopsy was carried out on Jose Garcia at the Medical Faculty of the University of Andorra. According to the autopsy report, drawn up on 22 December 1994, the cause of death was attributed to pneumonia related respiratory insufficiency which had developed as a result of his transition from active to passive, following the subdural brain haemorrhage suffered from a head trauma. In the meantime, on 16 March 1994 Mr Y.Z. gave a statement to the police in which he claimed, inter alia, that he and Jose Garcia had been beaten both by the police officers who had arrested them and by the police officers at the Avcılar police station where they were interrogated, and that Jose Garcia’s poor health might have resulted from these beatings.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the International Human Rights Organization (“the Commission“) on 18 March 1995, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 16839/90) against the National Republic lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national, Mr X Y Z, on 16 May 1990. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby the National Republic recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr A B C, the elected judge of national nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr D E F, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 4 (b)). On 5 May 1995, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr G H I, Mr J K L, Mr M N O, Mr P Q R, Mr S T U, Mr V W X and Mr Y Z A (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 5) (art. 43). As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 6), Mr E F G, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the National Government (“the Government“), the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38). Pursuant to the orders made in consequence, the registry received the applicant’s and the Government’s memorials and the Delegate’s written observations on 7 August, 25 August and 2 October 1995 respectively. On 8 June 1995 the Secretary to the Commission had supplied the Registrar with various documents he had requested on the President’s instructions. In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, a city, on 21 November 1995. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/10) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Novak (“the applicant”), on 10 February 2010. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr M.Smith of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been unlawfully detained in a regular detention centre pending his transfer to a psychiatric hospital. He further complained about the length of his pre-trial detention. On 10 July 2010 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). In addition, the application was given priority, in accordance with Rule 41 of the Rules of Court. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in Zabrze. On 25 November 2008 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of domestic violence. On 27 November 2008 the Silesia District Court ordered his detention. The court considered that there was a reasonable suspicion that the applicant might commit another offence. On 15 and 26 December 2008 the applicant asked to be released from detention. On 17 December 2008 two expert psychiatrists considered that the applicant should be examined in a psychiatric hospital. On 31 December 2008 the District Court ordered that the applicant be observed for six weeks in a psychiatric hospital. On 18 February 2009 the court again extended the applicant's detention. The court relied on the grounds previously invoked, namely, the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offence with which he was charged and the need to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings. Between 28 January and 10 March 2009 the applicant was examined in a psychiatric wing of the Gliwice Detention Centre. On 10 March 2009 the experts delivered an opinion and considered that the applicant suffered from a delusional disorder and should be placed in a psychiatric hospital. On 30 March 2009 the Silesia District Prosecutor lodged a request with the District Court for the proceedings to be discontinued on the ground that the applicant could not be held criminally liable. On 14 April 2009 the applicant's detention was extended by the Silesia District Court. The court considered that there was a high probability that the applicant had committed the offence with which he was charged. On 18 July 2009 the court again extended the applicant's detention. The court held that there had been a delay in the proceedings resulting from the fact that the expert psychiatrists and the applicant's lawyer had been on holiday and could not have appeared before it. On 16 September 2009 the District Court extended the applicant's detention yet again.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/96) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Xanadan national, Mr Xanadu Citizen (“the applicant”), on 28 August 1996. The applicant was represented by Mr Xanadu Lawyer, a lawyer practising in Xanadu (Xanadu). The Xanadan Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. Mr Xanadu Judge, the judge elected in respect of Xanadu, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr Xanadu Judge to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints (applications nos. 12345/95, 12346/95, 12347/95, 12348/96, 12349/96, 12350/96, 12351/96, 12352/96, 12353/96, 12354/96, 12355/96, 12356/96, 12357/96, 12358/96, 12359/96, 12360/96, 12361/96, 12362/96, 12363/96, 12364/96, 12365/96, 12366/96, 12367/96 and 12368/96) (Rule 43 § 2). By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Arrest and detention of the applicant On 17 November 1980 police officers from the Xanadu Security Directorate arrested the applicant on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Xanadu Path (Revolutionary Way). On 20 February 1981 the Xanadu Martial Law Court (sıkıyönetim mahkemesi) ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. B. Trial in the Xanadu Martial Law Court On 26 February 1982 the Military Public Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Martial Law Court against the applicant and 722 other defendants. The Public Prosecutor accused the applicant, inter alia, of membership of the Xanadu Path, whose object was to undermine the constitutional order and replace it with a Marxist-Leninist regime. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Xanadan Criminal Code. On 14 December 1988 the Xanadu Martial Law Court ordered the applicant’s release pending trial.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 46284/99) against a state (Republic of Turkey) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 16 January 1999. The applicant was represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The state did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 31 January 2002 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the remaining complaints to the state. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, on 7 November 2002 the Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, who was born in 1971, lives in a city. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. On 12 November 1991 the applicant was arrested and placed in police custody by police officers from a security directorate on suspicion of his involvement in the activities of an illegal organisation. On 19 November 1991 the applicant gave a statement to the police, allegedly under duress and confessed that he had been involved in certain illegal activities organised by the illegal organisation. On 25 November 1991 the public prosecutor at a state security court questioned the applicant in relation to his involvement in the illegal organisation. The applicant denied the content of his written statement of 19 November 1991 and alleged that it had been taken under duress. On 26 November 1991 the applicant was brought before a single judge of the state security court, who after taking his statement ordered his release. On 30 December 1991 the public prosecutor at the state security court filed an indictment against the applicant and fourteen other defendants, accusing them of membership of an illegal organisation. The prosecution requested that the applicant be convicted and sentenced pursuant to a relevant article of the Prevention of Terrorism Act. On 13 April 1993 the state security court, composed of three judges including a military judge, convicted the applicant as charged. The court held that there was sufficient and satisfactory evidence to disclose that he had committed the alleged offences. It accordingly sentenced him to three years’ imprisonment. Both the applicant and the public prosecutor appealed. On 8 February 1994 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first instance court on the ground that the applicant should have been convicted under a relevant article of the Criminal Code on account of his membership to an illegal organisation. On 16 March 1994 the state security court, to which the case had been remitted, held its first hearing and asked the accused persons to submit their final observations.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 November 2001. The applicant was represented by Mr B. Smith, a lawyer working for Rights, City. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr C. Jones of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, City. The applicant alleged that the obligation imposed on him as a man in employment over age 60 to pay national insurance contributions, which did not apply to a woman in work of over that age, was in violation of Article 14 of the Convention in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 15 March 2004, the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). Following the judgment of the Grand Chamber in Doe and Others v. the country [GC], nos. 78901/02 and 79000/02, 15 April 2006, the applicant and the Government submitted further observations. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in a town, a county. Under current national law, the state pension age is 65 for men and 60 for women. Until these ages, men and women who work are required to pay national insurance contributions (“NICs”) if their earnings are above a threshold amount, currently 400 units of account (UA). The applicant is over 60 years old and works as an administrator. Since he has not reached the state pension age for men of 65, he is required to pay NICs on his earnings. At the time of introduction of the application, his monthly salary was 3,000 UA and he paid 10% of his earnings (between the primary threshold of 400 UA and the upper earnings limit of 2,500 UA) in NICs (Class 1), amounting to 400 UA per month and 4,800 UA per annum. From April 2003, NICs increased to 11% of the amount up to the upper earnings limit, plus an additional 1% on all earnings above the limit. The applicant’s NICs increased to 444.44 UA per month. The applicant will be required to pay national insurance contributions from his earnings until he reaches the age of 65. A woman of 60 years or more who continued to work would not be required to pay any NICs on her earnings.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against a country (Country X) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (National Y), on 16 November 2001. The Government of Country X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. A. (“the Agent”), of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 6 October 2005 the Court decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1941 and lives in a city (City A). A. Facts prior to 1 May 1993 On 8 December 1989 the applicant lodged a motion for the distribution of her parents’ estate with the court in City A. On 27 July 1990 the court assigned an expert to prepare an opinion on the case. His opinion was submitted on 20 August 1990. On 1 October 1990 the court held a hearing which was adjourned in order to establish the assets of the estate. On 7 October 1990 the court assigned an expert to establish the value of the estate. He submitted his opinion to the court on 17 December 1990. The delivery of the judgment was adjourned until 20 February 1991. On that date the hearings in the case were re-opened. Hearings were held on 14 May, 10 and 24 September 1991. On 24 September 1991 the court admitted an opinion of an expert in building matters. On 24 October 1991 an inspection of the property was conducted. On 12 November 1991 the expert submitted his opinion. On 2 December 1991 the court admitted an opinion of another expert, which was submitted on 10 December 1991. On 31 December 1991 the court delivered a decision on the distribution of the estate. The applicant appealed. On 27 March 1992 the second-instance court quashed the decision and remitted it to the court for re-examination. On 8 October 1992 the court assigned another expert. On 25 March 1993 the court assigned an expert in building matters. B. Facts after 30 April 1993 The court held hearings on 1 and 15 February and 1 March 1994. On 1 March 1994 the court admitted another opinion to be prepared by two experts in building matters. The opinion was submitted on 6 June 1994. On 15 February 1995 the court decided to admit evidence in the form of an inspection of the property to be carried out in the presence of an expert. The inspection was conducted on 26 May 1994. On 23 June 1995 the expert opinion was submitted to the court. On 20 December 1995 the court admitted an additional opinion of an expert and of an expert in building matters.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123456/99) against a country (Country X) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (National Y) of Country X, on 12 May 1999. The Government of Country X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. W. (“the Government’s Agent”). The national alleged that a delay in releasing him from prison had given rise to a violation of Article 5. On 17 March 2004 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The national was born in 1955 and lives in a town (Town A). The national was serving a prison sentence in a prison (Prison A) following three separate convictions. The overall term of his imprisonment was due to come to an end on 1 January 2003. Pursuant to the provisions of the Criminal Code applicable to re-offenders, the national became eligible for conditional release after having served three-quarters of the overall term of his imprisonment, namely on 1 January 2000. After that date, the national requested a court on several occasions to grant him conditional release. However, his requests were denied on grounds of insufficient progress in his rehabilitation. On 20 March 2000 the prison governor requested the Regional Court (Court B) to order the national's release (conditional early release) in view of his satisfactory rehabilitation. The Regional Prosecutor objected to that request. On 22 March 2000 the Regional Court gave a decision ordering the national's conditional release for a three-year probationary period. It placed the national under the court officer's supervision and imposed certain other obligations on him. The Regional Prosecutor appealed against that decision. The Regional Court did not amend its decision and transmitted the prosecutor's appeal to the Court of Appeal (Court C). The hearing before the Court of Appeal was scheduled for 12 April 2000 at 8.45 a.m. On that day the Court of Appeal upheld the decision of the Regional Court. No further appeal lay against the decision of the Court of Appeal. In the national's submission, the Court of Appeal's decision was delivered at 9 a.m. Later on 12 April 2000, a certified copy of the Court of Appeal's decision was sent to the Regional Court, which received it on 13 April 2000. On the same day the Regional Court ordered the governor of Prison A to release the national and served him with a copy of the Court of Appeal's decision. The governor received these documents on 14 April 2000. According to the official release certificate, the national was released on 14 April 2000.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/08) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Novak (“the applicant”), on 1 March 2008. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr S. Peterson of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 1 June 2008 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1980 and lives in a city. On 7 August 2005 the applicant was arrested by the police on suspicion of having committed, inter alia, several offences of drug trafficking.
