On 8 August 2005 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) remanded him in custody. It relied on a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged and on the risk that he might tamper with evidence. Further, the court referred to the severity of the anticipated sentence. The applicant appealed against the detention order. On 12 September 2005 the Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) upheld the first‐instance decision. It explained that the reasons for his detention were still valid and stressed that the suspicion against him was supported by the fact that the applicant had partly confessed. In the course of the investigation, the applicant’s detention was extended several times. The courts relied on the suspicion that the applicant had committed the offence with which he had been charged. In their decisions, which also concerned several other suspects, the courts stressed the fact that most of the accused – however not the applicant - were acting in an organised group. Further, they referred to the complexity of the case, the fact that many suspects were involved in the case and that some of them had gone into hiding. They stressed that the detention was justified by the need to obtain further evidence, in particular, to obtain expert reports, to take evidence from numerous witnesses and suspects and to confront a witness with suspects. Lastly, the courts relied on the fact that some of the suspects were related to each other. On almost every occasion the courts relied on grounds that did not pertain to the applicant individually. On 21 August 2006 the applicant and thirty three other suspects were indicted before the Regional Court. The bill of indictment comprised 180 charges. The applicant was indicted on several charges of drug trafficking.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 39597/98) against a country lodged with a commission under former Article 25 of a convention ("the Convention") by a national, Anna Nowak ("the applicant"), on 15 July 1997. The government ("the Government") were represented by their agent, Mr J. Nowak, of a ministry. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the proceedings in her case had exceeded a reasonable time. The application was transmitted to the court on 1 November 1998, when a protocol to the convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of the protocol). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the court (Rule 52 § 1 of the rules of court). Within that section, the chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2001 the court changed the composition of its sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 26 March 2002 the court declared the application partly admissible. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1952 and lives in a city. On 13 July 1995 the applicant filed with a district court an action against a ministry and a housing co-operative L. In her action she requested, inter alia, that a flat be granted to her, submitting that the area of the one allocated to her by co-operative L, on the basis of an agreement between it and a ministry, allegedly differed from the area indicated in the decision granting it to her. The applicant also claimed damages for losses allegedly sustained by her as a result of the increase of construction costs. On 18 July 1995 the district court declared its lack of jurisdiction over the case and transmitted it to a regional court. On 23 September 1995 the court ordered the applicant to indicate the value of her claim. On 5 October 1995 the court again ordered her to indicate that value, considering that the information provided by her in reply to the previous court order was not satisfactory. In her letter of 16 October 1995 the applicant indicated the value of her claim. On 8 November 1995 she was again ordered to provide certain information concerning the value of the claim. On 23 November 1995 she submitted the relevant information. On 27 November 1995 the regional court, having examined the applicant's request, exempted her partially from the court fees. She appealed against that decision. On 27 February 1996 the court of appeal dismissed her appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 18992/03) against a State (referred to as 'the Republic of Turkey') lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ('the Convention') by a national (referred to as 'a national'), on 22 April 2003. The national was represented by a lawyer practising in a city (referred to as 'Istanbul'). The State (referred to as 'the State') was represented by their Agent. On 11 September 2007 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the State the complaints concerning the national's right to take proceedings to challenge the lawfulness of their detention and to have an enforceable right to compensation. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The national was born in 1983 and lives in a city (referred to as 'Istanbul'). On 10 July 2002 the national was arrested and placed in a branch of the police headquarters after, during a road check, police officers saw a photograph and slogans on the screen of the national's mobile telephone. On the same day, the national made statements to the police and, subsequently, to a court, which ordered their detention on remand, having regard to the state of the evidence, the national's statements to the police and the nature of the alleged offence, namely, membership of an illegal organisation. On 11 July 2002 the national lodged an objection to the remand order. No decision has been taken regarding the national's objection. On the same day, the prosecutor issued a decision finding that they lacked jurisdiction. The investigation file was subsequently transferred to the prosecutor's office at a court. On 1 August 2002 the prosecutor at the court charged the national with membership of an illegal organisation, under a section of the former Criminal Code. On 12 August 2002 the court ordered the national's continued detention, having regard to the nature of the alleged offence, the state of the evidence and the date of the initial order for the national's detention. On 25 October 2002 the court held the first hearing in the case. The national's representative requested the court to release the national. The court accepted the request and ordered the national's release pending trial. On 5 September 2003 the court acquitted the national.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Human Rights Commission (“the Commission“) on 15 March 1990, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 18321/87) against a European nation lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 20 February 1987 by a European citizen, Ms Alice Green. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby the European nation recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 5 para. 4 (art. 5-4) of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent her (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Ms Jane Brown, the elected judge of European nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr J. Smith, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On 28 April 1990, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr J. Davis, Mr J. Wilson, Mr J. Thompson, Mr J. Miller, Mr J. Anderson, Mr J. Robinson, and Mr J. Wilson (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43). As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5), Mr Smith, through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government of a European nation (“the Government“), the applicant’s lawyers and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38). In accordance with the order made in consequence, the Registrar received on 30 July 1990 the Government’s memorial and, on 10 and 22 August 1990, the applicant’s. On 29 September 1990 the applicant’s submissions on Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention were received. The President consented to the filing of further written submissions by the applicant on 25 October 1990 (Rule 37 para. 1, second sub-paragraph). PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court, as established under former Article 19 of the Convention, by the European Human Rights Commission (“the Commission”) on 26 January 1998, within the three-month period laid down by former Articles 32 § 1 and 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 24833/94) against a generic country lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 by Ms Generic Person on 18 April 1994. The Commission’s request referred to former Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the generic country recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (former Article 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, taken alone or together with Article 14 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 § 3 (d) of former Rules of Court A0, the applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent her (former Rule 30). As President of the Chamber which had originally been constituted (former Article 43 of the Convention and former Rule 21) in order to deal, in particular, with procedural matters that might arise before the entry into force of Protocol No. 11, the President of the Court at the time, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the generic government (“the Government”), the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the written procedure. Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the applicant’s and the Government’s memorials on 20 and 25 August 1998 respectively. After the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 on 1 November 1998 and in accordance with the provisions of Article 5 § 5 thereof, the case was referred to the Grand Chamber of the Court. The Grand Chamber included ex officio a generic judge, the judge elected in respect of the generic country (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 24 § 4 of the Rules of Court), the President of the Court, the Vice-President of the Court, and three other Vice-Presidents of Sections (Article 27 § 3 of the Convention and Rule 24 §§ 3 and 5 (a)). The other members appointed to complete the Grand Chamber were five other generic judges (Rule 24 § 3 and Rule 100 § 4). Subsequently the generic judge, who had taken part in the Commission’s examination of the case, withdrew from sitting in the Grand Chamber (Rule 28).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against the Republic of Aaland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Aaland, Mr A. B. (“the applicant”), on 27 March 1999. The applicant was represented by Mr C. D., a lawyer practising in Aaland. The Aaland Government did not designate an Agent for the purpose of the proceedings before the Court. On 27 April 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the applicant’s right to a fair trial by an independent and impartial tribunal and the failure to notify him of the public prosecutor’s submissions on his appeal to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, who was born in 1959, lives in Aaland. The applicant was the Deputy Mayor of the District in Aaland at the time of the events. In his capacity as the deputy mayor, he was responsible for the activities of the Culture and Education Department of the District Council. In January 1997, the Culture and Education Department prepared a thirty-day programme for the month of Ramadan. The draft programme was submitted to the applicant for his approval. After consulting the mayor, the applicant authorised the organising committee to begin the necessary preparations. One of the events foreseen for 31 January 1997 was called the “Jerusalem Night”. This event was announced months in advance and representatives of several embassies as well as several important personalities living in the district were invited. The hall was decorated with posters of martyrs who had given their lives for the liberation of Jerusalem. A five-minute play was also written for the evening. The play took the form of a conversation between a father and his son about life in Palestine and the struggle of the Palestinian people. The mayor of the District and the Ambassador to Ealand made speeches before the play began. On 6 February 1997 the applicant was taken into police custody. He was accused of having disseminated propaganda in support of an armed, illegal organisation, namely the E. F. In his statement at the police station, the applicant denied being involved in any illegal organisation. On 13 February 1997 the applicant was brought before the public prosecutor. During his questioning, he repeated the statements he had made at the police station. On the same day the applicant was brought before the investigating judge attached to the Aaland State Security Court and was remanded in custody. In an indictment dated 7 March 1997, the public prosecutor attached to the Aaland State Security Court initiated criminal proceedings against the applicant. It was alleged that he had disseminated propaganda in support of an armed, illegal organisation.

PROCEDURE The present case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission“) and the Government of a Federal Republic (“the Government“). PROCEDURE The case originated in three applications (nos. 50973/06, 8672/07 and 8722/07) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by three nationals, Mr A, Mr B and Ms C (“the applicants”), on 8 December 2006, 15 February 2007 and 17 February 2007 respectively. On 30 August 2007 the Court joined the applications and declared them partly inadmissible. It decided to communicate the complaints made by the applicant in the second application concerning the ill-treatment to which he had allegedly been subjected, as well as the complaints concerning the rights of all three applicants to release pending trial, to take proceedings to challenge the lawfulness of their detention, to an enforceable right to compensation, to a fair hearing within a reasonable time and to an effective remedy in respect of the reasonable-time complaint, to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASES The applicants were born in 1977, 1974 and 1974, respectively, and live in a city. A. The applicants’ arrest, detention and trial A and B were arrested on 18 April 1999, and C was arrested on 19 April 1999. According to the arrest report drawn up in respect of C and A, the reason for their arrest was the suspicion that they were members of an illegal organisation. They were subsequently placed in custody at a police headquarters. On 25 April 1999 the applicants were brought before the prosecutor and, subsequently, the duty judge of a state security court, who questioned them further and recorded their statements. The duty judge remanded them in custody pending the introduction of criminal proceedings against them. On 3 June 1999 the public prosecutor at the state security court filed an indictment against the applicants and nine other persons. The applicants were charged with attempting to undermine the constitutional order. On 25 August 1999 the state security court held the first hearing on the merits of the case. In the course of twelve subsequent hearings, the actions taken by the trial court were limited to the reading out of the indictment in open court, asking the applicants to submit their defence and obtaining copies of the applicants’ birth certificates and criminal records.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Novak (“the applicant”), on 10 October 2006. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr John Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 28 October 2008 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in a city. On 19 December 2004 the applicant was arrested by the police on suspicion of having committed assault causing death and dealing in stolen goods. On 20 December 2004 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) remanded him in custody. It relied on a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged and on the risk that he might induce witnesses to give false testimony. Further, the court referred to the likelihood of a severe prison sentence being imposed on the applicant. In the course of investigation, the applicant’s detention was extended by the Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) on 5 March 2005, 12 May 2005 and 11 December 2005. In its decisions, the court relied on the likelihood that the applicant had committed the offence while acting with numerous co-suspects in the ambit of the activities of an organised criminal group. Further, it referred to the need to obtain evidence, in particular: to take evidence from numerous witnesses and suspects and to confront a key witness with the injured persons. On 30 September 2005 the applicant was convicted and sentenced to one year and four months’ imprisonment by the District Court for failure to pay maintenance and threatening behaviour, charges which has been examined in separate sets of proceedings. The court offset the sentence against the period of pre-trial detention. On 24 June 2006 the applicant and twenty three suspects were indicted before the Regional Court. The bill of indictment against the applicant comprised charges of assault causing death and dealing in stolen goods, committed in the ambit of the activities of an organised criminal group. However, the applicant was not charged with being a member of such a group. The applicant’s detention was extended by the Regional Court on 10 May 2006, 9 December 2006, 10 June 2007, 12 September 2007, 10 June 2008 and on 16 October 2008. The court repeated the grounds given in previous decisions. The court also stated that the reasons for the applicant’s detention were still valid and relied on the likelihood that a severe prison sentence would be imposed on him. The applicant appealed against decisions extending his detention.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Andria (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Andria (a fictional country), Mr. Fictional Person (“the applicant”), on 26 July 2001. They have therefore not been admitted to the case file. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Andria (a fictional city). PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/95) against a country in Europe lodged with an international organization under former Article 25 of a human rights convention ("the Convention") by a national of Middle Eastern origin, Mr Ali Khan ("the applicant"), on 15 May 1992. The government of the country ("the Government") were represented by their Agents, Mrs J. Smith, a senior official, of the Ministry of Justice, at the initial stage of the proceedings, and subsequently by Mr P. Brown, a senior official, also of the Ministry of Justice. The applicant was, exceptionally, granted leave to represent himself (Rule 37 of the Rules of Court). The applicant alleged, in particular, that the court decisions dismissing his request for a right of access to his child, born out of wedlock, amounted to a breach of his right to respect for his family life and that he was a victim of discriminatory treatment in this respect. He relied on Articles 9 and 15 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 October 1998, when Protocol No. 12 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 12). The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court (Rule 53 § 1). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 28 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 27 § 1, and composed of Mr B. Martinez, President, Mr Q. Lee, Mr R. Johnson, Mr S. Patel, Mr T. Wilson, Mrs U. Davis, Mr V. Martinez, judges, and Mr W. Martinez, Section Registrar. On 11 December 2000 the application was declared admissible as regards the applicant's complaints that the court decisions dismissing his request for a right of access to his daughter, born out of wedlock, amounted to a breach of his right to respect for his family life and that he was a victim of discriminatory treatment in this respect. On 10 October 2001 the Chamber delivered its judgment in which it held, by four votes to three, that there had been a violation of Article 9 of the Convention. It also held, by four votes to three, that there had been a violation of Article 15 of the Convention taken in conjunction with Article 9 and that the respondent State was to pay the applicant (i) $50,000 (fifty thousand dollars) in respect of non-pecuniary damage and (ii) $8,000 (eight thousand dollars) in respect of costs and expenses. The separate opinion of Mr Martinez joined by Mrs Davis was annexed to the judgment. On 8 January 2002 the Government requested, in accordance with Article 44 of the Convention and Rule 74, that the case be referred to the Grand Chamber, contending that the Chamber should not have found violations of Article 9 and 15 of the Convention.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 10001/03) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alexanerov (“the applicant”), on 15 March 2003. The applicant was represented by Ms N. Petrova, a lawyer practising in Berlin. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 5 August 2006 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Berlin. On 8 February 1997 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the ZIKB (the Revolutionary Communist Union of Europe). On 11 February 1997 he was brought before the public prosecutor and then the investigating judge at the Berlin State Security Court. The latter remanded him in custody on the same day. On 15 February 1997 the public prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Berlin State Security Court, charging the applicant with membership of an illegal organisation under Article 167 § 2 of the Criminal Code. Between 20 February 1997 and 18 February 2000, the court held eighteen hearings. During these hearings the Berlin Security Court, relying on the state of the evidence, the nature of the offence, and the duration of his detention, refused to release the applicant. On 18 February 2000 the Berlin State Security Court pronounced its judgment and convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to twelve years and three months’ imprisonment under Article 167 of the Criminal Code. On 7 July 2000 the Court of Cassation quashed this judgment. The case was accordingly remitted to the Berlin State Security Court. On 16 July 2000 the Berlin State Security Court resumed the trial. During the subsequent hearings, the court rejected the applicant’s requests for release, having regard to the state of the evidence. At the hearing on 28 April 2002, the applicant’s lawyer once again requested the court to release the applicant. In her submissions, she also drew attention to the psychological state and treatment of the applicant. The court rejected this request. An appeal lodged in that connection was also dismissed by a further court on 25 June 2002. By Law no. 5180, in May 2003 State Security Courts were abolished. Subsequently, the Berlin Assize Court acquired jurisdiction over the case. On 22 September 2003 the applicant’s lawyer requested the court to release the applicant. On 23 October 2003 the applicant was released pending trial. According to the information made available to the Court by the parties to date, the case is apparently still pending before the Berlin Assize Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Middle Eastern national, Mr Ahmed Alavi (“the applicant”), on 15 May 2004. The applicant was represented by Messrs Global Law Firm, a firm of lawyers practising in a European city. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Richard Thompson, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, European city. The applicant alleged that his detention at a reception centre was not compatible with Articles 5 § 1 and 14 of the Convention, and that he was not given adequate reasons for it, contrary to Article 5 § 2. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 28 October 2006, the Court declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The parties did not submit observations on the merits. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1977 and lives in a European city. The applicant fled a Middle Eastern country and arrived at a European airport on 25 December 2001. On arrival at the immigration desk he spoke to an immigration officer and claimed asylum. He was granted “temporary admission” by the immigration officer and was asked to return to the airport at 9.00 am the following morning. Overnight the applicant was permitted to stay at a hotel of his choice. On the morning of 26 December 2001 he reported as required and was again granted temporary admission until the following day, 27 December 2001 at 11.00 am. When the applicant again reported as required he was (for the third time) granted temporary admission until the following day, 28 December 2001 at 11.00 am. Again the applicant reported as required. On this occasion the applicant was detained and transferred to a reception centre. On 29 December 2001 the applicant was given the opportunity to consult with legal representatives. The representative telephoned the Chief Immigration Officer on 30 December, and was told that the reason for the detention was that the applicant was a Middle Eastern national who met the criteria to be detained at the reception centre. On the same day, the applicant was interviewed by an official of the Ministry of Home Affairs in relation to his claim. When his asylum claim was refused on 3 January 2002 he was formally refused leave to enter the country. The applicant submitted a notice of appeal against the asylum refusal and was released on 4 January.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123/08) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2007. The Government submitted a unilateral declaration and invited the Court to strike out the application, in accordance with Article 37 of the Convention. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in City A. A. Disciplinary proceedings against the applicant On 25 February 1994 the Chief of the Regional Police Headquarters (Komenda Wojewódzka Policji) dismissed the applicant from the police service (he was held accountable for accepting bribes). On 10 April 1994 the Chief of the Principal Police Headquarters (Komenda Główna Policji) upheld the decision. B. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123456/01) against the Republic of A (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Mr Ali Can (a fictional person). On 13 November 2000. The applicant was represented by Mr Mustafa Yilmaz, a lawyer practising in Izmir. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 26 April 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in Manisa, Turkey. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. In 1991 the applicant sat a competition for admission to the civil service. Following his success in the competition, the General Directorate of Civil Service (a fictional organization) conducted a pre-employment background investigation. It found that the applicant had not mentioned his criminal record in his application form. On 14 January 1992 the General Directorate decided that the applicant was not eligible for appointment to a vacant post on account of the negative findings in the pre-employment investigation. In particular, in 1980 the applicant had been convicted of issuing threats against one of his teachers and had been sentenced to four months and twenty days' imprisonment, which had then been converted into a fine. 1. First set of proceedings On 7 February 1992 the applicant brought an action in the Administrative Court of A (a fictional city) requesting the annulment of the General Directorate's decision of 14 January 1992. On 26 October 1993 the Administrative Court of A dismissed the action. The applicant appealed. On 18 December 1995 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the Administrative Court of A's judgment holding that the applicant was suitable for employment. On 22 December 1998 the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the General Directorate's request for rectification of its decision. On 10 March 1999 the Administrative Court of A abided by the Supreme Administrative Court's decision. It found that the applicant had fulfilled all the requirements of the vacant post in question as prescribed under Law no. 657. It therefore ruled that the applicant was eligible to become a civil servant. On 8 June 1999 the General Directorate appealed. On 31 October 2001 the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the appeal. On 30 May 2002 the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the request for rectification of the decision. 2. Second set of proceedings On an unspecified date, the applicant brought a new action in the Administrative Court of A against the General Directorate requesting compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage which he allegedly had suffered as a result of the decision dated 14 January 1992.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms. Anna Novakova (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2000. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. J. Novak, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 18 October 2002 the Fourth Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1925 and lives in a city in Europe. On 10 June 1995 the applicant’s brother initiated court proceedings before the District Court in the city in order to obtain a decision declaring heirs to his late mother’s estate. The applicant’s brother applied to establish heirs on the basis of a will allegedly prepared by his mother. On 11 January 1996 the applicant challenged the will. The hearing scheduled for 3 March 1996 was adjourned upon the request filed by the applicant’s lawyer. Subsequently, hearings were held on 12 April and 3 August 1996 at which the court allowed the parties’ applications to hear witnesses. The hearings scheduled for 17 June, 14 July 1996 and 20 October 1996 were adjourned because the applicant’s brother was ill. On 15 March 1997 the court stayed the proceedings since the applicant’s brother had died. On 12 August 1997 the applicant requested the court to resume the proceedings because the proceedings concerning her brother’s inheritance had ended and in consequence the reason for staying the proceedings had ceased to exist. On 9 October 1998 the court resumed the proceedings. Ms. L.Q.R., the daughter of the applicant’s late brother and his heir, joined the proceedings. On 24 March and 10 June 1998 the court held hearings. The trial court heard a witness requested by Ms. L.Q.R. The hearing scheduled for 5 November 1998 was adjourned. Subsequently, the court held hearings on 21 January and 18 April 1999. Ms. L.Q.R. applied to the court to prepare an expert opinion and the applicant’s lawyer asked the court not to schedule any hearings until September 1999. The next hearing was held on 15 September 1999. The hearings scheduled for 3 November 1999 and 20 January 2000 were adjourned due to the illness of the applicant’s lawyer and Ms. L.Q.R. On 7 April, 22 September and 22 December 2000 the court held hearings. Both parties requested preparation of an expert opinion. On 4 April 2001 the court held a hearing at which it heard the parties. The court requested a hospital to provide documents concerning the health of the applicant’s late mother. On 25 April 2001 the court received the requested documents. On 17 June 2001 the court, sitting in camera, ordered preparation of an expert opinion.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 13284/04) against a State lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by four individuals, Mr X, Mrs Y and their two minor children (“the applicants”), on 16 April 2004. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The State (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms Z, of a ministry. The applicants alleged that, if deported from the State to their home country, the first applicant would face a real risk of being arrested and executed contrary to Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The President of the Chamber and subsequently the Chamber decided, on 16 and 27 April 2004 respectively, to apply Rule 39, indicating to the Government that it was desirable in the interests of the parties and the proper conduct of the proceedings not to deport the applicants pending the Court's decision. By a decision of 26 October 2004, the Chamber declared the application admissible. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). The Government filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1972, 1973, 1998 and 1999 respectively and are currently in the State. They arrived in the State on 25 August 2002 and applied to the Migration Board (Migrationsverket) for asylum on the following day. The first applicant submitted that he was of Kurdish origin, a Sunnite Muslim, and had lived with his family and worked in a city (Lebanon) since 1995. He claimed that in December 1999 he and three of his brothers had been arrested by the security police and imprisoned in a city (Syria) for nine months because the police wanted information about another brother who had absconded while performing military service in 1998. He further alleged that he had been tortured and ill-treated in prison and had only been released after being hospitalised as a result of the ill-treatment. After his release, he returned to the city to stay with his family. Between 2001 and 2002 he was arrested four times by the security police, questioned about his brother's whereabouts and beaten. However, on each occasion, he was released after a few days. In 2002 the applicants moved to the city, where they remained until they left their home country in August 2002.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1001/01) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two European nationals, Mr John Doe and Mr Peter Smith (“the applicants”), on 10 October 2001. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Mr A. B. C., a lawyer practising in City. The European Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 6 June 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1970 and 1971 respectively. The first applicant lives in Region. By a letter dated 28 August 2006 the Court was informed that the second applicant was purging his sentence in Prison. The applicants were arrested and taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the XYZ, on 25 and 26 July 1993 respectively. They were remanded in custody on 5 August 1993. On 31 August 1993 the public prosecutor at the City State Security Court filed an indictment against twenty-one persons, including the applicant. He accused the applicants of membership of an illegal armed organisation and of aiding and abetting that organisation. The charges included, in particular, bombings of various public and private establishments between July 1992 and June 1993. The first hearing, held before the City State Security Court on 3 September 1993, in the applicants' absence, was taken up with procedural matters such as the measures to be taken for securing the presence of the accused. Between 3 September 1993 and 23 January 1996, the first-instance court held hearings on a regular basis during which the judges dealt mostly with procedural matters. It also heard the accused and their representatives who were present on the date of the hearings. At the end of each hearing, the court considered releasing the applicants pending trial both ex officio as well as upon their requests. At each hearing, the court, relying on the nature of the offence, the state of the evidence and the content of the case-file, decided to prolong their remand in custody. During this time the court also heard two witnesses, on 25 November 1993 and 13 January 1994, who stated that they did not know any of the accused or whether they had any organisational link with the armed organisation. On 28 March 1995 the public prosecutor submitted his observations on the merits. On 7 November 1995 the court decided, upon the request of the accused, to hear a witness, Mr O. B. who was being tried before another court. In the hearing held on 19 December 1995, the court heard Mr O. B.

PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 12345/07 and 67890/07) against a country in Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”). In the first, the applicant is Mr John Doe, a national who was born in 1950. His application was lodged on 15 August 2007. In the second, the applicants are Mr Richard Roe, Mr Peter Smith and Mr David Brown. They are also nationals who were born in 1952, 1956 and 1945 respectively. Mr Smith also has dual nationality. Their application was lodged on 20 October 2007. Mr Doe was represented by Mr X Y, a lawyer practising in a city with a law firm. Mr Brown, Mr Smith and Mr Roe, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Ms Z A, a lawyer practising in a city with another law firm. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr B C, a representative from a ministry. The applicants alleged, in particular, that the grant of immunity in civil proceedings to a state in the case of Mr Doe and to the individual defendants in both cases amounted to a disproportionate interference with their right of access to a court under Article 6 of the Convention. On 10 October 2009 the applications were communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The Redress Trust, Amnesty International, the International Centre for the Legal Protection of Human Rights and JUSTICE were given leave by the President of the Chamber to intervene in the written procedure (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 2). They submitted joint written comments. The applicants requested an oral hearing but on 25 November 2011 the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Allegations of torture and proceedings brought by Mr Doe On 15 March 2001, while he was living and working in a country in the Middle East, Mr Doe was slightly injured when a bomb exploded outside a store in a city. He alleges that the following day he was taken from hospital by agents of that country and unlawfully detained for 67 days. During that time he was tortured by a military officer. In particular, he alleges he was beaten with a cane on his palms, feet, arms and legs; slapped and punched in the face; suspended for prolonged periods by his arms; shackled at his ankles; subjected to sleep deprivation; and given mind-altering drugs. Mr Doe returned to the country where a medical examination found he had injuries consistent with his account and where he was diagnosed with severe post-traumatic stress disorder.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 7530/02) against a State (referred to as 'the Republic of Poland') lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ('the Convention') by a national of a State (referred to as 'the Republic of Poland'), on 5 August 2001. The Government of the State (referred to as 'the Republic of Poland') ('the Government') were represented by their Agent, a representative of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 8 July 2003 the President of the Fourth Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in a city (referred to as 'Warszawa'). On 15 October 1993 the District Court (referred to as 'Warsaw District Court') declared that the heirs to the applicant's late mother's estate were the applicant, her father, and her sister. The estate consisted of a house and a plot of land located in the city. On 14 November 1994 the sister ('the petitioner') instituted non-contentious proceedings (postępowanie nieprocesowe) before the District Court in which she requested that the co-ownership of the house and the land be dissolved. On 22 March 1995 the court held the first hearing. Subsequently, hearings were held on 1 February, 7 March and 15 October 1996. On 6 January 1997 the court, sitting in camera, decided to obtain an expert opinion. On 15 February 1997 an expert prepared the opinion. On 21 February 1997 the District Court, sitting in camera, gave a decision regarding the fee for the expert. Between 16 October 1996 and 28 October 1997 no hearings were held. The hearings scheduled for 29 October and 16 December 1997 were adjourned because of the absence of the petitioner. Subsequently, hearings were held on 4 February, 19 June and 31 July 1998. On 22 October 1998 the court ordered a second expert opinion. The opinion was submitted to the court on 20 January 1999. Between 1 August 1998 and 15 April 1999 no hearings were held. Hearings scheduled for 16 April, 2 June, and 9 September 1999 were adjourned because of the absence of the petitioner and expert witnesses. On 22 November 1999 the District Court held the next hearing at which it ordered that a fourth expert opinion be prepared. Between 23 November 1999 and 8 November 2001 no hearings were held. Subsequently, the court held hearings on 9 November and 5 December 2001 as well as 21 February 2002. On 24 January and 7 April 2003 the District Court held hearings. The proceedings are pending.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of A for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 October 2004. By a letter of 11 March 2007, the Registry was informed of the death of the applicant. His parents, Mrs Jane Doe and Mr Richard Roe, and his brother, Mr Thomas Roe, declared their intention to pursue the application. For practical reasons, Mr Doe will continue to be called “the applicant” in this judgment, although his family is now to be regarded as such (see Mr Smith v. B, judgment of 15 November 1996, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996-V, p. 1641, § 3). The applicant was represented by Mr George Brown, a lawyer practising in City. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 6 November 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lived in City. He died on 14 June 2005. The facts of the case, as submitted by the applicant, may be summarised as follows. On 7 March 1994 the applicant was taken into police custody in City on suspicion of being a member of the illegal Organization. On 13 March 1994 he was handed over to the City Security Directorate for further investigation. On 21 March 1994 the applicant was taken before the investigating judge at the City State Security Court, who ordered his detention pending trial. By an indictment dated 23 June 1994, the public prosecutor initiated criminal proceedings against the applicant and forty-five other defendants before the City State Security Court, accusing them, inter alia, of membership of an illegal armed organisation and of involvement in activities that undermined the constitutional order of the State. The prosecution requested that the applicant be sentenced pursuant to Article 125 of the Criminal Code. On 5 May 1999 the City State Security Court, composed of three judges including a military judge, decided that the applicant's case should be separated from the file as his final defence submissions had not been submitted to the court. On 18 June 1999 the Constitution was amended and the military judge sitting on the bench of the City State Security Court was replaced by a civilian judge. The case against the applicant continued before the City State Security Court. In the course of the proceedings the State Security Court rejected the applicant's requests for release, taking into account the nature of the alleged offence and the state of the evidence. On 5 April 2004 the applicant was released pending trial.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no 12345/05) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alex Smith (“the applicant”), on 1 July 2005. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr John Doe of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 1 December 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in a city. On 15 January 2002 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of a crime committed as part of an organized crime group. On 18 January 2002 the district court remanded the applicant in custody, relying on the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offence in question. It also considered that keeping the applicant in detention was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, given the risk that he might tamper with evidence or induce witnesses to give false testimony. The court also stressed the severity of the anticipated sentence. The applicant's appeal against the detention order, likewise his further appeals against some of the decisions extending his detention and his subsequent applications for release and appeals against refusals to release him, were unsuccessful. In his applications and appeals he relied, inter alia, on his personal circumstances, in particular a difficult family situation in that a family break-up was imminent. He also argued that his confessions to offences of which he was suspected had not been taken into consideration. In the course of the investigation, the applicant's detention was extended on several occasions, namely on an unknown date, on 15 July 2002 (to 17 October 2002), 12 October 2002 (to 31 December 2002), 28 December 2002 (to 30 April 2003), 17 April 2003 (to 31 July 2003), an unknown subsequent date, and 25 September 2003 (to 30 November 2003). In all their detention decisions the authorities repeatedly relied on a strong suspicion, supported by evidence from witnesses, that the applicant had committed the offences in question. They attached importance to the seriousness of those offences and to the likelihood of a severe prison sentence being imposed on the applicant. These facts gave rise to the courts' assumption that the applicant, if released, might obstruct the proper course of the proceedings, especially given the fact that some of the suspects were still at large. On 22 November 2003 the prosecutor lodged a bill of indictment with the regional court. The applicant was charged with a crime and membership of an organized crime group. There were 10 defendants in the case, all charged with numerous counts of a crime committed as an organized crime group.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against a country (Country X) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (National Y), on 15 August 2002. The Government of Country X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. W., of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 19 October 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the excessive length of the applicant’s detention to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in a city (City Z). On 20 July 2001 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of killing E.F., his fiancée. On 21 July 2001 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) ordered his detention. It considered that placing the applicant in custody was justified by the existence of strong evidence against him and the gravity of the charges. Since he had attempted to flee, his detention was necessary to ensure the proper course of the proceedings. The applicant’s detention was subsequently prolonged several times by the Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy). Each time the court repeated the reasons it had previously given. On 15 August 2002 the District Prosecutor (Prokurator Rejonowy) dismissed the application for release. On 28 September 2002 the District Prosecutor lodged a bill of indictment with the Regional Court. The applicant was charged with murder (he had strangled his fiancée) and fraud. On 31 December 2002 the Regional Court convicted him as charged and sentenced him to 16 years’ imprisonment. The Court of Appeal quashed that judgment and remitted the case on 15 March 2003. The applicant remained in custody. On 14 April 2003 the Court of Appeal ordered that the applicant remain in detention until 30 June 2003. On 20 April 2003 the court refused his application for release. Subsequently, the applicant’s detention was extended every 3 months by the Regional Court, for the same reasons as before. The applicant lodged numerous unsuccessful applications for release with the Regional Court. On 8 July 2005 the Regional Court convicted the applicant of murder and sentenced him to 26 years’ imprisonment. The court stressed the depraved nature of the crime and maintained that there were no mitigating circumstances in the case. The Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment on 25 September 2005. On 15 October 2006 the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 31 August 2004. The applicant was represented by Mr X.Y. Zeta, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 28 August 2008 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the applicant's right to be released pending judicial proceedings and to a fair hearing within a reasonable time to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1976 and lives in Andria. On 20 August 1996 the applicant was arrested and taken into custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, namely the XYZ (Revolutionary People's Liberation Party-Front), as well as aiding and abetting the said organisation. On 3 September 1996 the applicant was remanded in custody. On 6 December 1996 the public prosecutor at the Andria State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicant, along with other persons, charging him with membership of an illegal organisation under Article 168 § 1 of the former Criminal Code. On 20 May 2002 the Andria State Security Court found the applicant guilty of activities carried out for the purpose of bringing about the secession of part of the national territory. The applicant was sentenced to death; his sentence was subsequently commuted to life imprisonment. On 30 September 2003 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first-instance court on the ground that the latter had failed to specify the provision of the Criminal Code under which the applicant had been found guilty. The Court of Cassation held that the applicant had been unlawfully held accountable for an event which had not been included in the bill of indictment of 6 December 1996. By Law no. 5190 of 16 June 2004, published in the Official Gazette on 30 June 2004, State Security Courts were abolished. The case against the applicant was therefore transferred to the Andria Assize Court. On 31 March 2006 the applicant was released pending trial. According to the information in the case file, the case is still pending before the Andria Assize Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Republic of Alphaville lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Alphavian national, Mr Alphard Beta (“the applicant”), on 5 June 2007. The applicant was represented by Mr Gamma Delta, a lawyer practising in Zeta. The Alphavian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Eta Theta, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs. The applicant alleged that the proceedings concerning his doctor’s fees had not been dealt with within a reasonable time and that the Regional Appeals Commission which dealt with his case had not been impartial and independent. On 7 June 2008 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant lives in Omega. The applicant is a medical practitioner. He has an individual contract (Einzelvertrag) with the Lower Alphavian Health Insurance Board (Niederalphavianische Gebietskrankenkasse). In two submissions to the Joint Arbitration Committee (Paritätische Schiedskommission) dated 7 September 1998 and 5 October 1998, the applicant demanded payment for laboratory tests carried out in the first and second quarters of 1998. The claims against the Lower Alphavian Health Insurance Board amounted to 8,022.41 euros (EUR) and EUR 6,603.81, respectively. The Lower Alphavian Health Insurance Board claimed that the applicant had not participated in the test series for quality checking of laboratory parameters in 1997, and refused to pay for the tests. The applicant argued that he had participated in the quality checks in previous years with positive results and had – as previously – submitted the relevant samples for the period in question. The Joint Arbitration Committee held an oral hearing and on 25 February 1999 it dismissed the applicant’s claim of 7 September 1998. The applicant appealed against that decision to the Regional Appeals Commission (Landesberufungskommission). On 17 May 1999 the applicant filed an application for transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag), requesting a decision on his submission of 5 October 1998 from the Regional Appeals Commission, as the Joint Arbitration Committee had failed to decide within the statutory six-month time-limit. The Regional Appeals Commission held a hearing and rejected both of the applicant’s claims. The decision was dated 24 August 1999, and was served on the applicant on 7 July 2000. The applicant complained about this decision to the Constitutional Court (Verfassungsgerichtshof). On 27 November 2000 the Constitutional Court set aside the decision for violation of the right to a fair hearing before an independent and impartial tribunal established by law.

It originated in an application (no. 14220/88) against the Kingdom of a European country lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that country, Mr. John Doe, on 2 July 1988. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings. The President granted him leave to present his own case (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs. Jane Smith, the elected judge of the country’s nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr. Richard Roe, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On 27 February 1993 the Vice-President, Mr. Robert Brown, drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the other seven members, namely Mr. Thomas Wilson, Mr. Frank Green, Mr. Fred Black, Mr. Andrew White, Sir James Black, Mr. James Red, and Mr. David Blue (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43). PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2003. The applicant was represented by Mr X. Y., a lawyer practising in Andria. The Republic of Andria (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 10 December 2004 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Andria. On 10 May 1994 the applicant began working as a watchman at the Andria Municipality, attached to the District X in the province of Andria. Under Andrian law, his employment status was that of a civil servant. On 9 May 1996, relying on three appraisal reports drafted in the past two years, the Municipality terminated the applicant’s employment contract. On 13 May 1996 the applicant initiated proceedings against the Municipality in the Andria Administrative Court and contested the termination of his contract. Furthermore, he requested to be awarded his monthly salary, which was 8,000,000 Andrian Liras (ALR)0, together with the interest, for the period during which he was unemployed. On 28 October 1997 the administrative court dismissed the applicant’s request. He appealed and requested the suspension of the enforcement of the decision. By an interim decision of 28 July 1998, the Supreme Administrative Court suspended the enforcement of the administrative court’s decision of 28 October 1997, as well as the Municipality’s decision to dismiss the applicant. The applicant resumed his work at the Municipality. On 2 February 1999 the Supreme Administrative Court found that the Municipality had in fact dismissed several employees following the election of a new mayor. It was established that the Municipality had been relying on identical and stereotyped appraisal reports, which did not sufficiently reflect the reasons for their dismissal. Accordingly, the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the decision of the Andria Administrative Court. On 30 April 1999 the Andria Administrative Court followed the judgment of the Supreme Administrative Court and annulled the decision of the Municipality. The court further ordered that the applicant be reinstated in his job and that his monthly salary and related pecuniary rights be paid to him for the period during which he had been entitled to perform his duties. On 14 November 2000 the Council of State rejected the appeal filed by the Municipality. This judgment was served on the applicant on 3 June 2001. To date, the Municipality has not made any payment to the applicant.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Andria in an application (no. 12345/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alex Ankes (“the applicant”), on 10 April 2005. The applicant was represented by Mr C. Lee, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 10 February 2009 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, who was born in 1985, currently resides in Andria. On 29 March 1999 the applicant was taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation. On 3 April 1999 he was placed in detention on remand. On 16 April 1999 the public prosecutor at the Andria State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicant, charging him under Articles 169 (2), 498 (2), 523, 56 (3), 34 and 41 of the former Criminal Code with membership of an illegal organisation and armed robbery. On 29 March 2002 the Andria State Security Court convicted the applicant under Articles 169 (2) and 498 (2) of the former Criminal Code, and sentenced him to seven years and three months' imprisonment for the former offence and to ten years and seven months' imprisonment for the latter offence. The State Security Court further stated that the provisions of Law no. 4617, which governed conditional release, the suspension of proceedings and the execution of sentences in respect of certain offences committed before 24 April 1999, had to be taken into account in the execution of the sentence in relation to the offence under Article 498 (2). On an unspecified date the applicant appealed against the judgment of the Andria State Security Court. The public prosecutor did not lodge an appeal. On 30 April 2003 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the Andria State Security Court, finding that the classification of the applicant's offence had been erroneous. The Court of Cassation further held that the applicant's acquired rights in his former conviction by the decision dated 29 March 2002 had to be safeguarded in the new judgment which would be rendered by the Andria State Security Court. The applicant was consequently tried afresh before the Andria State Security Court. On 25 January 2004 the Andria State Security Court convicted the applicant under Article 147 (1) of the former Criminal Code for attempting to undermine the constitutional order and sentenced him to fifteen years and seven months' imprisonment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 9 April 1999. The applicant was represented by Ms Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in City, Europe. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr Karl Drzewicki, and subsequently, Mr Jan Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of civil proceedings in his case had been excessive. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 3 February 2004 the Court declared the application admissible. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in City, Europe. A. Facts prior to 1 May 1993 The applicant, who is a trombone player and since 1969 has been playing with the jazz band “New Band”, became its leader after a split in 1990. Mr X who had left the band in the same year, started playing with a new band using the name “New New Band”. On 30 October 1990 the applicant lodged with the City Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) an action for protection of his personal rights against X. The applicant contended that the defendant had infringed his personal rights by having used the name “New Band” without his consent. He requested the court, inter alia, to order the defendant not to use that name in the future. On 17 July 1992 the trial court dismissed his action. The applicant appealed against that judgment. B. Facts after 30 April 1993 On 9 December 1993 the City Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case to the trial court. On 12 June and 5 September 1995 the court held hearings. Both parties applied for an expert opinion. The applicant made a friendly settlement proposal but the defendant did not agree to it. On 13 February 1996 the applicant requested the court not to order an expert opinion and argued that such opinion would be unnecessary. On 15 February 1996 the trial court, sitting in camera, ordered preparation of an expert opinion. In March 1996 the applicant asked for exemption from the costs of the expert opinion and appealed against the decision of 15 February 1996. On 1 April and 23 May 1996 the court dismissed his applications. In August 1996 the court-appointed expert refused to prepare his opinion. Subsequently, the trial court twice requested the University Musical Academy to indicate an expert. On 12 March 1997 the court ordered a new expert, Mr Y, to prepare an opinion. However, that expert failed to prepare the requested opinion.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/11) against the State of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms A. Andersson Jensen, on 15 April 2011. The applicant was born in 1985 and lives in Stockholm. She is represented before the Court by Mr B. Eriksson, a lawyer practising in Stockholm. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by Mr C. Andersson of the Attorney General’s Office as their Agent. The applicant alleged that she had been compelled to give evidence that would have enabled one or more journalistic sources to be identified, in violation of her right under Article 10 of the Convention to receive and impart information. On 25 November 2012 notice of the application was given to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant is a journalist for WebNews, a European Internet-based version of the newspaper Daily Business (“Web”), published by the company Web Media AS. On 25 July 2009 Mr X was indicted for market manipulation and insider trading under the 2008 Act on the Trade of Financial Assets. He was accused of having requested Mr Y, an attorney, to draft a letter concerning the European Oil Company, a limited liability company quoted on the stock exchange. The letter, addressed to a trustee company representing the interests of bond holders in the European Oil Company, gave the impression that it had been written on behalf of a number of bond holders who were seriously concerned about the company’s liquidity, finances and future. In fact, it had been written only on Mr X’s behalf. He had owned only one bond, which he had acquired the same day as he had asked attorney Y to draft the letter. Mr X had sent a copy of the above-mentioned letter by fax to the applicant on Friday 25 May 2006, and in this connection she had a telephone conversation with him. The following day, on Saturday 26 May 2006, the applicant wrote an article entitled “Fears of European Oil collapse” in which she expressed strong concerns about the content of Attorney Y’s letter, a central feature in the article. The price of European Oil stock fell by 3.9% on Monday 27 May 2006, the first trading day after the content of the letter had become known in the press. On the same day, a new article on the topic was published in Web. Other media also reported on the first article, including an online newspaper (TechNews) which on 28 May 2006 reported that an analyst had stated that he would not be surprised if the letter had been sent by a person with a short-position or who wanted cheap stocks.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of Andria (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Andria (a fictional country), Mr J. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an association, Association A (“the applicant association”), on 12 March 2001. The applicant association was represented by Law Firm B, a law firm practising in City C. The Government of Country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador D, Head of the International Law Department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant association alleged that the courts' decisions forbidding it to continue exhibiting a painting by Artist A had violated its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 30 June 2005 the Court declared the application admissible. Neither the applicant association nor the Government filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE Association A is an association of artists with its seat in Building B in City C. Building B, an independent gallery, is devoted entirely to exhibitions of contemporary art. One of the basic objectives of the association is to present current developments in national and international art, and to cultivate an openness to experimentation. Between 3 April and 21 June 1998 the applicant association held an exhibition on its premises. The exhibition, entitled “The century of artistic freedom” (“Das Jahrhundert künstlerischer Freiheit”), was intended as part of the celebrations of the association's 100th anniversary. Among the works to be shown was a painting entitled “Apocalypse”, which had been produced for the occasion by the national painter Artist A. The painting, measuring 450 cm by 360 cm, showed a collage of various public figures, such as Mother Teresa, the national cardinal, and the former head of the national party, in sexual positions. While the naked bodies of these figures were painted, the heads and faces were depicted using blown-up photos taken from newspapers. The eyes of some of the persons portrayed were hidden under black bars. Among these persons was Mr X, a former general secretary of the national party until 1995, who at the time of the events was a member of the national assembly, a mandate he held until April 1999. Mr X was shown gripping the ejaculating penis of Mr Y while at the same time being touched by two other national party politicians and ejaculating on Mother Teresa. The exhibition, for which admission was charged, was open to the public.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 32990/96) against a State (Republic of Turkey) lodged with an international body (European Commission of Human Rights) under former Article 25 of an international agreement (Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms) by a national of that State (Turkish national) on 17 September 1996. The national complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. A judge elected in respect of the State (Turkey) withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The State accordingly appointed a person to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same State raising the same complaints (applications nos. 26480/95, 28291/95, 29280/95, 26699/96, 29700/96, 29701/96, 29702/96, 29703/96, 29911/96, 29912/96, 29913/96, 31831/96, 31834/96, 31853/96, 31880/96, 31891/96, 31960/96, 32964/96, 32900/96, 32987/96, 33362, 33369/96, 33645/96, 34591/96, 34687/96, 39428/96 and 43362/96) (Rule 43 § 2). By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court declared the application admissible. The national and the State each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Arrest and detention of the national On 25 October 1980 police officers from a security directorate arrested the national on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation. On 3 January 1981 a criminal court ordered the national’s detention on remand. B. Trial in a military court On 10 May 1982 the public prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with a military court against the national and 722 other defendants. The public prosecutor accused the national, inter alia, of membership of the illegal organisation, whose object was to undermine the constitutional order and replace it with a Marxist-Leninist regime. The prosecution sought the death penalty under a criminal code provision. On 5 February 1985 the national was released pending trial.
