PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2009. The applicant was represented by Mr Alex Smith, a lawyer practising in Uppsala. The government of the country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms Lisa Johnson, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the administrative courts had failed to hold an oral hearing in proceedings relating to his request for life annuity. On 1 March 2012 the application was communicated to the government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in Västerås. In 1990 the applicant was diagnosed with type II diabetes and vascular spasms. While riding a bicycle on work-related business on 15 December 2000, the applicant suffered a heart attack which caused him to fall. About two weeks later, he also suffered a cerebral stroke. On 5 March 2001 he reported the accident to the Social Insurance Office (Försäkringskassan) of the County of Västmanland which granted him early retirement pension as from 1 October 2001. The applicant also requested the Social Insurance Office to grant him life annuity (livränta) but, on 28 May 2003, the Social Insurance Office rejected the request. It found that the applicant’s medical problems could not be regarded as work-related and that his ability to support himself by working was not sufficiently reduced as a result of the accident. According to medical opinions given on 8 June and 18 July 2002 by Dr John Smith, the Social Insurance Office’s own medical doctor (försäkringsläkare), the main reason for the applicant’s inability to work was diabetes, from which he had suffered for 17 years at the time of the accident, and some other medical conditions from which he suffered and which together had caused the heart attack and the cerebral stroke. According to him, it was not probable that work-related factors, such as stress, had contributed to the deterioration of the applicant’s physical condition. By letter dated 7 April 2003 the applicant’s legal counsel appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of Västmanland, claiming that the applicant had a right to a life annuity since his illnesses had been work-related. At times he had had up to three different jobs, each one of which, had been hectic and thereby created a difficult and very stressful situation. He produced a medical opinion by Dr. Carl Eriksson, dated 4 March 2003, which stated that known risk factors for arteriosclerosis and heart attack were, among other factors, diabetes, smoking and high blood pressure. Recently, the feeling of severe stress, especially over a long period of time, had been shown to be an element that increased the risk of developing heart and vascular disorders as well.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/13) against the Kingdom of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms Amira Alfar (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2012. The applicant was represented by Ms J. Albers, a lawyer practising in a European city. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr K. Van Dyke, Senior Adviser, Federal Justice Department. The applicant complained that the ban on wearing in public places clothing designed to conceal the face deprived her of the possibility of wearing the full-face veil. She alleged a violation of Articles 8, 9 and 10 of the Convention, taken separately and in conjunction with Article 14 of the Convention. She alleged, further, that she had not had an effective remedy before the Conseil d’Etat (Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention). On 15 July 2015 the Government were given notice of the above-mentioned complaints and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The non-governmental organisation Freedom and the Human Rights Centre of a European University were given leave to submit written comments (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1980 and lives in a European town. The applicant stated that she was a Muslim and had decided, on her own initiative, to wear the niqab – a veil covering the face except for the eyes – in accordance with her religious beliefs. She said that she had taken the decision to wear the full-face veil when she was sixteen years old. She explained that her choice had been accepted by her family and friends and by her husband. She also stated that she had always agreed to remove her veil for identification purposes as required by the authorities, such as when issuing her identity card. On 1 March 2009 the Vesdre district administrative authorities proposed an amendment to the district regulations regarding the wearing of the burqa in public thoroughfares and in public places ... . The president of the police district invited the Verviers public prosecutor to express an opinion on that proposal. On 1 March 2009 the public prosecutor replied that he did not have any observations to make. The municipal councils of the three municipalities belonging to the police district – the municipal council of Pepinster on 1 June 2009, the European town on 4 June 2009 and Verviers on 8 June 2009 – enacted the following provisions of the consolidated by-laws of the Vesdre police district, which differed, moreover, from the original proposal. “Article 113.”

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the United Nations of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms. Aisha Khan (“the applicant”), on 10 July 2007. The applicant was represented by Ms. F. Ali, a lawyer practising in Lyon. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. B. Patel, Director, of the European Ministry of Justice. On 30 May 2008 the President of the Sixth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Villeneuve. A. Background to the case On 9 July 1995 the applicant had an accident at work – a cut of about one centimetre to his left wrist. The same day he was treated by the company doctor, Dr. C. On 11 July 1995 his general practitioner transferred him to hospital. That day and again on 25 July 1995 he was examined by a Dr. D. On his second examination Dr. D. diagnosed that the applicant was unable to flex his thumb. On 6 August 1995, following a further examination, he had surgery on a muscle, the flexor pollicis longus. B. Proceedings before the Regional Court On 27 January 1997 the applicant instituted proceedings in the Regional Court against Dr. C. and Dr. D., seeking an award of compensation for pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage in the amount of 50,000 euros (EUR). He argued that if the defendants had treated him properly, the operation would have been avoided, which in turn would have avoided severe pain and further problems, including reactive depression. In February 1997 the court scheduled a hearing for 20 April 1997. Submissions by the parties followed and in April the case was transferred to a single judge. On 11 May 1997, following the hearing, the Regional Court decided to hear the applicant's general practitioner and scheduled a new hearing for 27 July 1997. On account of the absence of the first defendant's legal counsel, it later postponed it to 23 November 1997. It refused a subsequent request for a further postponement. On 19 August 1997 the applicant's legal counsel ceased taking instructions from the applicant. On 25 October 1997 his new lawyer addressed the court. In November 1997 the parties agreed on written submissions. In February 1998 the applicant's second lawyer also ceased taking instructions from the applicant; subsequently, a new lawyer was appointed and requested access to the files. On 27 March 1998 the applicant requested the court to await the outcome of the social court proceedings, which were also pending, and returned the files. On 14 April 1999 the applicant's third lawyer also ceased taking instructions but was subsequently reappointed in June.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by five Andorran nationals, Mr Alvaro Garcia, Mr Jose Martinez, Mr Carlos Lopez, Mr Ignacio Sanchez and Mrs Maria Rodriguez (“the applicants”), on 15 June 2004. The applicants were represented by Mr J. Perez, a lawyer practising in Andorra. The Andorran Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 5 July 2008, the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 7 June 2000 the applicants were laid off by the Andorra Sur municipality, with which they had been employed. Each of the applicants brought an action in the Andorra Labour Court, claiming outstanding salaries, dismissal indemnities, severance pay and other pecuniary rights. On 13 December 2000 the court ruled in their favour and ordered the municipality to pay the applicants certain amounts in Andorran liras (AL), including costs, together with interest running from 20 June 2000. In the absence of an appeal the judgments became final on 28 December 2000. In the following months, as they did not receive any payment, the applicants requested the Andorra Governorship to intervene in order to facilitate the enforcement of the court’s judgments. The Governor’s Office informed the applicants that it had requested the municipality to redress their grievances. However, due to lack of funds, the municipality did not make any payment. At the date of introduction of the present application, the relevant judgment debts were still outstanding. Therefore, friendly settlement agreements were reached between the following applicants and the municipality on the dates indicated: Maria Rodriguez on 18 February 2006; Jose Martinez on 26 January 2007, and Carlos Lopez on 12 October 2008. No settlement was reached in respect of the other applicants. However, the municipality deposited a partial amount in the relevant account at the local enforcement office, which was made available to the remaining applicants. On 22 March 2006 Ignacio Sanchez was paid 934 New Andorran liras (NAL).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Andria (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr X Y Z (“the applicant”) on 15 December 2001. The applicant was represented by Mr A B C, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Andrian Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 15 October 2005 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1948 and lives in Andria. On 12 April 1997 the General Directorate of National Roads and Highways expropriated two plots of land belonging to the applicant in Andria in order to build a motorway. A committee of experts assessed the value of the plots of land and the relevant amount was paid to the applicant when the expropriation took place. Following the applicant’s request for increased compensation, on 30 November 1997 the Andria Civil Court of First-instance awarded him additional compensation of 962,996,880 Andrian liras (AL), plus interest at the statutory rate, applicable at the date of the court’s decision, running from 12 April 1997, the date of the transfer of the title-deeds. On 29 May 1999 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Andria Civil Court of First-instance. On 16 March 2001 the General Directorate of National Roads and Highways paid the applicant the amount of AL 2,861,840,000, including interest.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Ana Novakova (“the applicant”), on 3 August 2010. The applicant was represented by Ms B. Petrova, lawyer practising in Andria. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the refusal by the domestic courts to allow her to bear only her maiden name unjustifiably interfered with her right to protection of her private life under Article 8 in conjunction with Article 14 of the Convention. On 22 November 2010 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Andria. On 30 October 1992 the applicant, who is a university professor, got married and took her husband’s surname pursuant to Article 153 of the Civil Code. As she was known by her maiden name in her academic and professional life, she continued using it. However, she could not use it in official documents. Following the amendment made to Article 153 of the Civil Code on 14 May 1997 that entitled married women the right to put their maiden name in front of their husband’s surname, the applicant started to avail herself of this possibility in official documents. Following the adoption of new Civil Code on 22 November 2001, Article 187 was worded identically to the former Article 153. On 5 December 2007 the applicant brought proceedings before the Court of First Instance for permission to use only her maiden name, “Novakova”. On 31 January 2008 the Court of First Instance dismissed the applicant’s request on the ground that, under Article 187 of the Civil Code, married women had to bear their husband’s name throughout their marriage and were not entitled to use their maiden name alone. The applicant appealed. On 14 July 2008 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment. On 4 December 2008 the applicant’s rectification request was further rejected by the Court of Cassation on the ground that it failed to meet the requirements foreseen in the law and the applicant was fined the equivalent of EUR 80 (euros) as a result. The latter decision was delivered to the applicant on 9 January 2009.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/96) against the Republic of X (X) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of X, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 12 January 1996. The applicant was represented by Mrs Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in City (X). The X Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. Mr John Smith, the judge elected in respect of X, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr John Doe to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaint (applications nos. 12345/95, 12345/95, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96, 12345/96) (Rule 43 § 2). By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1) THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Arrest and detention of the applicant On 15 March 1978 police officers from the Security Directorate of City arrested the applicant on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the XYZ (X). On 22 March 1978 the Assize Court of City ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. B. Trial in the Martial Law Court of City On 4 March 1981 the Public Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Martial Law Court of City against the applicant and 127 other defendants. The Public Prosecutor accused the applicant, inter alia, of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the XYZ, whose object was to undermine the constitutional order and replace it with a Marxist-Leninist regime.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 10 May 2009. The applicant was represented by Ms A. Brown, a lawyer practising in a city. The government of the country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Green, of the Department of Foreign Affairs. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention that his trial was unfair because of the non-disclosure of the sources of the evidence of a Chief Superintendent without adequate counterbalancing measures. On 15 June 2012 the application was communicated to the government. Written submissions were received from a human rights commission, which had been granted leave by the President to intervene as a third party (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 2 of the Rules of Court, as in force at the material time). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1980 and has a permanent address in a city. A. Background facts The criminal proceedings against the applicant to which this application relates arose, inter alia, from his association with the following events. On 15 November 2003, an off-duty police detective attached to a special unit - who lived in a housing estate near the city called Maple Grove - noticed suspicious activity and contacted a local police station. From shortly after 10 pm, he watched the movements of three cars (a blue Ford Focus, a dark Volkswagen Golf and a yellow van) and he noticed the occupants of the three cars acting in what appeared to be a coordinated manner. At one stage, five men got out of the Volkswagen Golf and three of them got into the back of the yellow van, where there was already a driver and a man in the passenger seat. The other two got back into the Volkswagen Golf and it was driven off. A taxi arrived and its sole passenger got out and joined the other group. These six men were gathered together at the side of the van. An unmarked police vehicle manned by two police officers arrived in response to the off-duty detective’s call and approached the van. One of the men walked away from the group while four of them got into the back of the van and one into the driver’s seat. The Ford Focus remained on the estate parked near the van. One police officer spoke to the driver of the van who gave a false name (referred to below as XY). While speaking with him, the police officers noted a black balaclava and the handset of a portable radio on the floor of the van.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Human Rights Commission on 1 January 1999, within the three-month period laid down by former Articles 32 § 1 and 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 25594/94) against a European country lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 by two nationals, Mr John Doe and Ms Jane Smith, on 19 August 1994. The applicants were represented by Mr J. Bate, a solicitor practising in a city. The Commission’s request referred to former Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the country recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (former Article 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 of the Convention. In accordance with the provisions of Article 5 § 4 of Protocol No. 11 taken together with Rules 100 § 1 and 24 § 6 of the Rules of Court, a panel of the Grand Chamber decided on 20 January 1999 that the case would be examined by the Grand Chamber of the Court. The Grand Chamber included ex officio Sir Nicolas Bratza, the judge elected in respect of the country (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 24 § 4), Mr L. Wildhaber, the President of the Court, Mrs E. Palm, Vice-President of the Court, and Mr J.-P. Costa and Mr M. Fischbach, Vice-Presidents of Sections (Article 27 § 3 of the Convention and Rule 24 §§ 3 and 5 (a)). The other members appointed to complete the Grand Chamber were Mr A. Pastor Ridruejo, Mr G. Bonello, Mr J. Makarczyk, Mr P. Kūris, Mr R. Türmen, Mrs F. Tulkens, Mrs V. Strážnická, Mr P. Lorenzen, Mr V. Butkevych, Mr A.B. Baka, Mr R. Maruste and Mrs S. Botoucharova (Rule 24 § 3). Subsequently Sir Nicolas Bratza, who had taken part in the Commission’s examination of the case, withdrew from sitting in the Grand Chamber (Rule 28). On 13 May 1999 the Government of the country (“the Government”) appointed Lord Reed to sit as an ad hoc judge (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). Later Mr Makarczyk, who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case, was replaced by Mr J. Casadevall (Rule 24 § 5 (b)). In accordance with the President’s decision, a hearing took place in public in a Human Rights Building, a city, on 23 June 1999. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr M. Eaton, Agent, Mr J. Morris QC, Attorney General, Mr R. Singh, Ms M. Demetriou, Counsel, Ms C. Stewart, Mr S. Bramley, Home Office, Advisers; (b) for the applicants Mr P. Codner, Counsel. The Court heard addresses by Mr Codner and Mr Morris.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/11) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alex Brown (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2011. The applicant was born in 1985 and is currently detained at a prison. He is represented before the Court by Mr H. Clark, a lawyer practising in a city with a law firm. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr K. Davis of the Foreign Ministry. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The present case concerns the applicant’s trial and conviction before a judge and jury at a court for the murder of a Mr Chris Davis. A co-defendant, Mr Sam Green, was tried and acquitted of assisting an offender. The facts of the case may be summarised as follows. A. The murder Mr Davis was shot dead at about 8.00 pm on 1 April 2007. According to witnesses the gunman was wearing a cap and drove off in a silver car. In the early hours of 2 April 2007 a silver car was set alight a short distance from the scene of the shooting. Shortly after the murder the applicant fled to a country. He was subsequently extradited from that country to the country to stand trial for Mr Davis’s murder. B. The applicant’s defence On 2 April 2009 the applicant formally served a Defence Statement in which he alleged that Mr Davis had been murdered by Mr White, a man who had previously been convicted of serious offences and who was at that time serving a prison sentence for murder. The applicant’s case was that he had been involved in a drug deal with Mr White and Mr Davis. On the morning of 1 April 2007 Mr White and Mr Davis had asked him to provide a car so they could collect a shipment of drugs. Later that day he purchased the car in the presence of Mr Green and Mr White, but Mr White had driven off in it. The applicant met Mr White again at 7.30 p.m. to give him his share of money for the drugs. Mr White was driving the car. The applicant left the meeting with Mr Green, who was driving a van. After this meeting the applicant went to his parents’ home. During the night he went to a service station and while he was there he called a friend whose mother lived near the road where the burning car was discovered. C. Mr White’s evidence On 5 August 2009 the police interviewed Mr White about the applicant’s allegations. He answered “no comment” to the questions asked. That evening he telephoned his son and told him he had never heard of the applicant and knew nothing of the murder.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court, in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”), by a regional human rights body on 30 October 1999 and by a national government, on 10 December 1999 (Article 5 § 4 of Protocol No. 11 and former Articles 47 and 48 of the Convention). The case originated in an application (no. 24876/94) against a country lodged with the regional body under former Article 25 of the Convention by two nationals, Mr John Doe and Mrs Jane Doe (“the first applicant” and “the second applicant” respectively), on 19 May 1994. The applicants alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against them in respect of their occupation of their land in their caravans violated their right to respect for home, family life and private life contrary to Article 8 of the Convention. They complained that these measures also disclosed an interference with the peaceful enjoyment of their possessions contrary to Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention and deprived their children of education contrary to Article 2 of Protocol No. 1. They further complained that they were subject to discrimination contrary to Article 14 of the Convention. The regional body declared the application admissible on 4 March 1998. In its report of 25 October 1999 (former Article 31 of the Convention), it expressed the opinion that there had been no violation of Article 8 of the Convention (18 votes to 8), that there had been no violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (19 votes to 7), that there had been no violation of Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 (21 votes to 5) and that there had been no violation of Article 14 of the Convention (18 votes to 8). Before the Court, the applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by a law firm, solicitors practising in a city. The national government were represented by their Agent, Mr Smith of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. On 4 February 2000, the panel of the Grand Chamber determined that the case should be decided by the Grand Chamber (Rule 100 § 1 of the Rules of Court). The composition of the Grand Chamber was determined according to the provisions of Article 27 §§ 2 and 3 of the Convention and Rule 24 of the Rules of Court. Sir Richard Brown, the judge elected in respect of the country, who had taken part in the regional body’s examination of the case, withdrew from sitting in the Grand Chamber (Rule 28). The government accordingly appointed Lord Justice Jones to sit as an ad hoc judge in his place (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). The applicants and the government each filed a memorial.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 60553/00) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 30 June 2000. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Y, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 21 March 2002 the First Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS A. The circumstances of the case The applicant was born in 1963 and lives in a city (Austria). He is a practising lawyer by profession. On 18 June 1993 a colleague, Mr Z, laid a disciplinary information against the applicant alleging that he had infringed the profession’s honour and reputation in the context of administrative criminal proceedings relating to traffic offences. He was suspected of having misbehaved towards intervening police officers during a traffic control by threatening them with job-related troubles in case they charged him with traffic offences. Subsequently, on 10 September 1993 the Bar Chamber appointed an Investigating Commissioner. On 16 September 1993 the Investigating Commissioner informed the applicant that disciplinary proceedings against him were opened and requested him to file observations as regards the charges against him. On 4 October 1993 the applicant complied with this request. On 13 June 1994 the Investigating Commissioner submitted a report to the Disciplinary Council. On 7 October 1994 the Disciplinary Council discontinued the proceedings against the applicant. The Bar Chamber filed an appeal against this decision. On 15 December 1994 the applicant submitted his observations on the appeal. On 20 February 1995 the Appeals Board allowed the Bar Chamber’s appeal and remitted the case to the Disciplinary Council. In August 1995, after the case had been taken over by another Investigating Commissioner, the latter agreed with the police to question the officers involved in the traffic control by way of letters rogatory. On 3 November 1995 he filed letters rogatory with the District Court which were subsequently transferred. On 13 December 1995 the officers were questioned. On 8 February 1996 the Investigating Commissioner submitted his report to the Disciplinary Council. On 3 June 1996 the Disciplinary Council, upon the Investigating Commissioner’s report, decided to open the main proceedings. This decision was served on the applicant on 31 July 1996. On 30 August 1996 the applicant filed his observations.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/11) against a national entity (referred to as "the Respondent") lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a national of a different country (referred to as "the applicant"), on 15 February 2011. The applicant was represented by Mr D. Müller, a lawyer practising in Geneva (Canton of Geneva). The Respondent was represented by their Deputy Agent, Mr B. Schmid, of the European Law and International Human Rights Protection Unit, Federal Office of Justice. The applicant alleged that he was the victim of a violation of his right to respect for private and family life, as guaranteed by Article 8, on account of an order by the Federal Court, in a judgment of 15 March 2011, prohibiting him from re-entering the Respondent's territory for a period of ten years. On 25 May 2011 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Respondent. It was also decided, under Article 29 § 1, that the Chamber would rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The President further decided, under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court, that the application would receive priority treatment. The national government did not avail themselves of their right to intervene in the proceedings (Article 36 § 1). On 1 March 2012 the Court’s Sections were reorganised. The application was assigned to the third Section (Rules 25 § 1 and 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1985 and currently lives in Berlin (Germany). He entered the Respondent's territory with his parents on 15 October 1987. On 15 May 1991 he obtained a one-year residence permit, which was subsequently renewed on a regular basis. On 15 October 1998, 15 August 2000 and 15 May 2003 he received, respectively, a suspended prison sentence of two and a half months, a six-month suspended prison sentence and a sentence of five months’ imprisonment, for a number of offences committed between 1994 and 2000 (wounding, grievous bodily harm, assault, theft, robbery, damage to property, receiving stolen goods, proffering insults and threats, disturbance, a weapons offence and a serious breach of road traffic regulations). In a decision of 15 April 2004 the Aliens Department for the Canton of Geneva ordered the applicant’s administrative removal for an indefinite duration. His appeals against that decision were dismissed, first on 15 December 2004 by the Administrative Court for the Canton of Geneva (the “Administrative Court”), then on 15 April 2005 by the Federal Court. On 15 October 2005 the applicant was deported to his home country. After returning to the Respondent's territory illegally in May or June 2006, he was arrested and taken into custody on 15 July 2006 pursuant to arrest warrants issued on the basis of his criminal convictions.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 6544/05) against a State (referred to as 'the Republic of Poland') lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ('the Convention') by a national of a State (referred to as 'the Republic of Poland'), on 15 December 2004. The Government of a State ('the Government') were represented by their Agent, a representative of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The national alleged, in particular, that the length of his pre-trial detention had exceeded a 'reasonable time' within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 5 July 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). On 16 June 2009 the judgment was adopted. The Court found no violation of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The judgment was delivered on 7 July 2009. On 5 October 2009 the national challenged the inadmissibility part of the Court's judgment in so far as it declared his complaint about the unfairness of his criminal proceedings inadmissible. On 19 January 2010 the Chamber decided to restore to the list this particular complaint and to re-examine it. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The national was born in 1974 and lives in a city (referred to as 'Lębork'). He is currently serving a prison term. On 19 November 2002 the national was arrested on suspicion of forgery of documents as well as armed robbery and drug trafficking, committed in an organised criminal group. Since September 2002 he had been in hiding. On 21 November 2002 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) remanded him in custody, relying on the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences in question. It also considered that detaining the national was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, because the national had threatened the victim at the time of the commitment of the alleged offence. The court also stressed the severity of the anticipated sentence and the fact that the national had a previous criminal record. An appeal by the national against the detention order was unsuccessful. On 16 December 2002 the Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) upheld the challenged decision, basically repeating the arguments of the District Court and relying additionally on the fact that in September 2002 the national had gone into hiding. The argument that the national had gone into hiding was repeated by the District Court in its decisions of 18 February 2003 and 3 June 2003, extending the national's detention. Numerous appeals by the national against decisions extending his detention and all his subsequent applications for release were unsuccessful. Subsequently, the national's pre-trial detention was prolonged on several occasions (on 18 February, 6 March, 3 June, 28 August and 5 December 2003 and on 16 February, 8 June and 17 August 2004).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/09) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 4 March 2009. The applicant was represented by Mr Alex Smith, a lawyer practising in Berlin. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Peter Jones of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that his detention had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 6 October 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1957 and lives in Berlin. On 20 May 2003 the Regional Prosecutor instituted an investigation into illegal trading in liquid fuel. On 8 June 2005 the applicant was charged with, inter alia, establishing and leading an organised criminal group engaged in money laundering, illegal trading in liquid fuel and the falsification of tax documents. On 9 June 2005 the Berlin District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) remanded him in custody, on the basis of reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offence in question. It also considered that keeping the applicant in detention was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, given the risk that he might tamper with evidence. The court also stressed the severity of the anticipated sentence. The applicant's appeals against decisions prolonging his detention were unsuccessful. In his appeals, he argued that the charges against him were based on unreliable and fabricated evidence. He also relied on his personal circumstances, in particular the need to ensure that his wife, who suffered from psychiatric problems, was cared for. In the course of the investigation, the applicant's detention was prolonged on 30 August and 30 November 2005 and 2 March 2006. Further decisions extending the applicant's detention were taken by the Berlin Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) on 19 May, 9 August 2006 and 22 November 2006, 14 February, 16 May, 17 August, 19 September and 19 December 2007. In all their detention decisions the authorities repeatedly relied on a strong suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences in question, which was supported by evidence from witnesses and experts. They attached importance to the complexity of the case, the significant number of persons involved and the voluminous documentation. They further considered that the need to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, especially the need to verify evidence from suspects and witnesses, justified holding the applicant in custody.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms. Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 December 2003. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr. X Y Z of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Capital City. The applicant alleged that as a woman she was unable to receive invalidity benefit after the age of 60, whereas a man could receive such benefit until the age of 65. The case raised issues under Article 14 in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 30 April 2004, the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). Following the judgment of the Grand Chamber in Case X v. Country [GC], nos. 78901/02 and 78902/02, 15 April 2006, the Government, but not the applicant, submitted further observations. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in City. In August 2004 the applicant turned 60 years of age. Prior to that date she was in receipt of long-term incapacity benefit (IB), a benefit payable to people incapable of work who satisfy the eligibility criteria. She had qualified for the rate of 80.00 units (U) per week. She was also paid 40.00 U per week in disability living allowance (DLA) and 15.00 U in DLA care. At age 60, which is the date of entitlement to the State pension for women, she ceased to be eligible for IB. In its place she became entitled to draw her state retirement pension which, based upon her contribution record, entitled her to 55.00 U per week (about 60% of the maximum rate as she had only contributed for 24 years out of 39). She continued to draw DLA. As a result, the applicant claimed that she was some 25.00 U per week worse off as a result of her transition from IB to the State pension. The applicant complained to the Ministry of Social Affairs concerning the differential treatment but was informed that nothing could be done.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/03) against the Kingdom of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms Ana Garcia Lopez (“the applicant”), on 15 December 2002. The applicant was represented by Mr Carlos Sanchez Martinez, of the Barcelona Bar. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by Mr Juan Lopez Garcia, Agent of the Government and Head of the Legal Department of the Human Rights Office at the Ministry of Justice. The applicant alleged a breach of her right to respect for her home, contrary to Article 8 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 30 July 2005 the Chamber declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 18 October 2005 the applicant lodged a written reply to the Government’s observations and her claim for just satisfaction. The Government did not lodge any comments on her claim. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Barcelona. A. Background to the case The applicant has lived in a flat in a residential quarter of Barcelona since 1975. Since 1978 the Barcelona City Council has allowed licensed premises such as bars, pubs and discotheques to open in the vicinity of her home, making it impossible for people living in the area to sleep. Local residents first complained about vandalism and noise in the locality before 1985. In view of the problems caused by the noise, the Barcelona City Council resolved on 25 December 1986 not to permit any more night clubs to open in the area. However, the resolution was never implemented and new licences were granted. In 1994 the City Council commissioned a report by an expert. The expert found that the noise levels were unacceptable and exceeded permitted levels. At 3.45 a.m. on Saturdays they were in excess of 100 dBA Leq (decibels), ranging from 101 to 116.9 dBA Leq. In a report of 3 February 1996 the police informed the Barcelona City Council that nightclubs and discotheques in the sector in which the applicant lived did not systematically close on time. They said that they were able to confirm that the local residents’ complaints were founded. On 30 June 1997 the City Council approved a new bylaw on noise and vibrations, which was published on 15 July 1997 in the Official Gazette of Barcelona province.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Commission on 4 July 1996 and by the Government on 11 September 1996, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 § 1 and Article 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 22714/93) against Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by a national, Mr X, on 28 July 1993. The Commission's request referred to Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby Austria recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46); the Government's application referred to Articles 44 and 48. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 35 § 3 (d) of Rules of Court B, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 31). The lawyer was given leave by the President to use the German language (Rule 28 § 3). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr Y, the elected judge of national origin (Article 43 of the Convention), and Mr Z, the Vice-President of the Court (Rule 21 § 4 (b)). On 7 August 1996, in the presence of the Registrar, the President of the Court, Mr A, drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr B, Mr C, Mr D, Mr E, Mr F, Mr G and Mr H (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 § 5). As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 § 6), Mr Z, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant's lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 39 § 1 and 40). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the applicant's and the Government's memorials on 21 and 28 February 1997 respectively. The Commission produced the file on the proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar on the President's instructions. In accordance with the President's decision, the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 22 April 1997. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against the Republic of XYZ (the "Republic") lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a Turkish national, Mr Ali Yilmaz ("the applicant"), on 1 January 1997. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Hakan Yilmaz and Mr Levent Can, lawyers practising in Ankara. The Republic did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Convention institutions. The applicant alleged under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that he had been denied a fair hearing on account of the presence of a military judge on the bench of the Ankara State Security Court which tried and convicted him. He further complained under Article 6 § 3 (b) that the written opinion of the chief public prosecutor at the Court of Cassation had never been served on him, thus depriving him of the opportunity to put forward his counter-arguments. He finally contended that he had been convicted merely on account of his association with a left-wing magazine, in violation of his rights under Articles 9 and 10. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 15 January 2004 the Court declared the application partly admissible. It retained the applicant’s complaints concerning his right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal and his right to have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The applicant and the Republic each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 24 May 2004 the case was assigned to the Third Section of the Court. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1972 and lives in Ankara. On 23 March 1995 the applicant was arrested and placed in police custody by police officers from the Ankara Security Directorate. He was accused of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation, the XYZ (Revolutionary People’s Liberation Party-Front).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/03) against a country (Country X) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (National Y) of Country X, on 15 February 2003. The Government of Country X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr Z. Alpha and subsequently Mr A. Beta of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 20 March 2003 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. It also gave priority to application, pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1920 and lives in a city (City A), Country X. On 20 March 1967 the applicant and his wife obtained a divorce decree. On 10 June 1976 the applicant's ex-wife filed with the City A District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) a petition for division of the matrimonial property. On 25 September 1978 the City A District Court gave a decision. Both parties appealed. On 15 December 1979 the City A Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) quashed the first-instance decision and remitted the case. In 1983 the applicant's ex-wife donated her share in the disputed property to C.H. and D.H., who became parties to the proceedings. On 15 November 1990 the applicant sent a letter to the Minister of Justice, complaining about the slow progress of the proceedings. On 25 January 1991, in reply to his complaints, the President of the City A Regional Court acknowledged that the proceedings were indeed lengthy. Prior to 1 May 1993, the City A District Court held a number of hearings and obtained several expert reports. On 15 November 1993 the District Court held a hearing. On 30 May 1994 the applicant challenged the impartiality of the presiding judge. On 20 July 1995 the District Court ordered that expert evidence be obtained. On 15 October 1995 the expert informed the court that he had been unable to prepare a report due to the applicant's conduct. On 5 September and 15 October 1995 the trial court held inspections of the site. On 1 October 1996 the City A District Court gave a decision. The court granted ownership of the entire property (plot of land and the house) to C.H. and D.H. The court also ordered them to pay off the applicant's share in the estate. On 15 March 1997, on the applicant's appeal, the City A Regional Court partly amended the first-instance decision. On 15 June 1997 the applicant lodged a cassation appeal. On 25 February 1998 C.H. and D.H. sold their share in the property to a certain E.S. On 15 April 1999 the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) quashed the decision of 15 March 1997 and remitted the case to the City A Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 5270/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 30 December 2003. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Y of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 19 April 2005 the President of the Fourth Section Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1963 and is presently detained in a detention centre. A. The proceedings before the Regional Court On 17 July 2001 the Regional Court ordered that the applicant be remanded in custody in view of a reasonable suspicion that he had committed an offence acting in an organised criminal group. The court also considered that the measure was justified by the severity of the penalty that could be expected and the need to secure the proper conduct of the investigation. Subsequently, the Regional Court prolonged the applicant’s detention on several occasions. On 5 September 2002 the Court of Appeal, upon the prosecutor’s request, decided to prolong the applicant’s detention relying, in addition to the earlier grounds, on the complexity of the case. On 21 December 2002, the applicant was indicted before the Regional Court. The bill of indictment was directed against 22 co‐accused. On 30 December 2002 the Regional Court prolonged the applicant’s detention relying on the strong probability that the applicant and 13 co-accused had committed the offences with which he had been charged and the severity of the sentence that could be imposed. The court further submitted that only detention would secure the applicant’s appearance at the trial. On 14 May 2003 the Regional Court made an application under the Code of Criminal Procedure to the Court of Appeal asking that the applicant’s detention be prolonged beyond the statutory time-limit of two years. On 21 May 2003 the Court of Appeal granted that application and prolonged the detention of the applicant until 27 November 2003. The Court justified its decision with reference to the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences and the complexity of the case which concerned an organised criminal group and involved several co‐accused. At the hearing held by the Regional Court on 22 October 2003 the applicant’s application for release was dismissed. On 26 November 2003 the Court of Appeal, upon another application under the Code of Criminal Procedure, prolonged the applicant’s detention until 22 January 2004. It reiterated the grounds previously given for keeping him in custody.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 32971/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr X (“the applicant”). The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Y of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of his right of access to a court. On 5 September 2006 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, Mr X, was born in 1957 and lives in a city, X. On 1 August 2000 and 13 February 2002 there was a fire at a street in X, where the applicant’s business was located. On 15 November 2002 he sued an insurance company, X S.A., before a regional court for compensation of 545,918.65 X (approx. 136,500 euros (EUR)). At the same time, he also asked to be exempted from court fees. On 9 December 2002 the court ordered the applicant to pay X 28,896 (approx. EUR 7,228) in court fees. On 22 January 2003 the regional court refused to exempt the applicant from court fees. The court’s reasons for this decision read, in so far as relevant, as follows: “... Despite the court’s request, the applicant has failed to provide information concerning his business activities. The documents submitted concern a manufacturing and servicing company (Zakład produkcyjno-uslugowy) located at the street in X. However, from the insurance policies submitted, it appears that the applicant insured two companies, both located at the street in X: a manufacturing and servicing company and a private car transport company (Przedsiębiórstwo Prywatnej Komunikacji Samochodowej). ... It is therefore not clear what type of business activities the applicant is involved in at the street in X (...). The documents submitted by the applicant show that he has already received X 360,572.68 [approx. EUR 90,142] as partial compensation from X S.A. According to the applicant, this amount did not compensate him for the damage actually incurred. However, there are no reasons to believe that the applicant’s business collapsed because he received only partial compensation. It further appears from the submitted tax return forms concerning the manufacturing company’s business for January to October 2002 that the applicant made an eight-digit gross profit and a seven-digit net profit in that period. This leads the court to the conclusion that the applicant can afford to pay the court fees because he has sufficient funds. However, lack of information concerning all his assets prevents the court from making an objective assessment of his financial situation.” On 3 February 2003 the applicant filed an interlocutory appeal (zażalenie) against this decision.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 10001/01) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr Adam Novak (“the applicant”), on 15 March 2001. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr P. Zielinski, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his right to a “hearing within a reasonable time”, guaranteed by Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, had not been respected. On 20 April 2001 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in Bielawa, Poland. A. Facts before 1 May 1993 Between 15 and 18 February 1992 a local newspaper published letters of certain X.Y. and Z.A. The authors accused the applicant, at the time the Deputy Mayor of Bielawa, of fraud and called him a “liar”. On 2 March 1992 the applicant brought a private prosecution on charges of libel against X.Y. and Z.A. to the Dzierżoniów District Court (Sąd Rejonowy). The trial began on 15 May 1992. The court adjourned the hearing due to the absence of one of the defendants. Further hearings were listed for 10 June, 20 July, 20 August and 22 September 1992, 11 February and 28 April 1993, but most of them were adjourned because of the parties' or their lawyers' absence. B. Facts after 1 May 1993 On 20 May 1993 the Court adjourned the trial because the defendants had failed to appear. The next hearing, set down for 24 June 1993, was cancelled because of the absence of the lay judge. Further hearings, scheduled for 8 July 1993, 25 March 1994, 31 May and 14 June 1995 were adjourned because of the absence of the defendants, their counsel, a witness and the applicant. The court decided to impose a fine on one of the witnesses who had failed to appear. At the hearing on 29 June 1995 the defendants' counsel informed the court that he would not represent them any longer. On 20 July 1995 the trial was adjourned because the defendants had failed to appear. The court ordered that both defendants be subjected to police supervision in order to ensure the proper course of the proceedings. On 18 October 1995 the court lifted police supervision in respect of X.Y. A hearing set down for 1 March 1996 was adjourned since the defendants and a witness had failed to appear before the court. The court ordered that Z.A. be detained on remand to ensure his presence at hearings. A hearing scheduled for 29 March 1996 was adjourned because X.Y., the applicant and witnesses had failed to appear.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against the Republic of X ("the Republic") lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a national of X ("the applicant"), on 1 July 1997. By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Arrest and detention of the applicant On 17 April 1985 police officers from the Security Directorate of X arrested the applicant on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Y Organization. On 6 February 1985 the Martial Law Court of X ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. B. Trial in the Martial Law Court of X On an unspecified date in 1985 the Public Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Martial Law Court against the applicant. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by three Xanadu nationals, Ali Xanadu, Nazmi Xanadu and Doğan Xanadu (“the applicants”), on 15 November 2000. The applicants were represented by Mr Mahmut Xanadu, a lawyer practising in Xanadu. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 15 September 2004 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 29 August 1995 the General Directorate of National Roads and Highways (General Directorate) expropriated plots of land belonging to the applicants in Xanadu in order to build a motorway. A committee of experts assessed the value of the plots of land and the relevant amount was paid to the applicants when the expropriation took place. Following the applicants’ requests for increased compensation, on 26 November 1996, the Xanadu Civil Court of First-instance awarded them additional compensation of 290,000,000 Xanadu Liras (Xanadu Liras), plus interest at the statutory rate, applicable at the date of the court’s decision, running from 29 August 1995, the date of the transfer of the title-deeds. On 1 June 1998 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. On 16 May 2000 the General Directorate of National Roads and Highways paid the applicants 973,920,000 Xanadu Liras (approximately 1,739 Xanadu Euros (Xanadu Euros)), including interest.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 May 2000. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr X. Y and subsequently Ms Z. A of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that the labour law proceedings in his case exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 By a decision of 10 August 2004 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 15 November 2002 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Steelville, Europe. In October 1993 the applicant was dismissed from work. On 21 October 1993 he filed with the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) a petition in which he requested that he be reinstated in his former post and awarded compensation. On 18 June 1994 the court stayed the proceedings until the completion of criminal proceedings against the applicant, considering that the courts’ findings in those proceedings could affect the outcome of the employment dispute. On 30 August 1994 the criminal court gave judgment. On 25 October 1994 the second-instance court quashed it and remitted the case for re-examination. On 22 March 1997 the District Court discontinued the labour law proceedings, because three years had passed since the date of staying them. On 25 May 1997 it allowed the applicant’s appeal and quashed that decision. On 3 November 1997 the criminal court discontinued the proceedings against the applicant, considering that the theft of two boxes of glue committed by him was of an insignificant nature. On 23 February 1998 the second-instance court acquitted the applicant. On 15 May 1998 the District Court gave judgment in respect of part of his claim. It reinstated the applicant in his former post. On 6 August 1998 the second-instance court dismissed his employer’s appeal against that judgment. On 4 March 1999 the District Court ordered an expert opinion concerning the calculation of the applicant’s lost earnings. It was submitted on 26 August 1999. In September 1999 the court ordered a supplementary opinion. At the hearing held on 14 January 2000 it requested the preparation of another supplementary opinion. It was submitted on 16 June 2000. The court held a hearing on 5 February 2001.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alex Smith (“the applicant”), on 25 February 1999. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Brown, a lawyer practising in a city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Green of a government department. The applicant alleged that his detention on remand pending his trial by court martial was in breach of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. By a decision of 25 October 2005, the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), the parties replied in writing to each other's observations. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in a city. The applicant joined the Army in 1990. In 1999 he was serving as a soldier with a regiment and was stationed in a country. On 1 November 1999 a woman alleged that she had been raped and on 2 November the applicant was arrested, along with two other soldiers, by the service police. The service police interviewed the applicant on 4 November 1999 and it appears that he was assisted by a lieutenant from legal services. On that date he also signed a certificate acknowledging that he had been informed of his right to have the assistance of an “accused advisor” during any summary hearing before his commanding officer (“CO”). On 5 November 1999 he was charged by his CO, pursuant to a section of the Army Act 1955 (“the 1955 Act”), with indecent assault contrary to a section of the Sexual Offences Act 1956. It appears that his two co-accused were charged with rape. The charge was read; the CO said that the matter was to be referred to a higher authority given the seriousness of the charge; the applicant was asked if he had anything to say and he replied that he had not. He was given a document immediately before that hearing, which document was taken back from him immediately thereafter. A certificate dated 6 November 1999 and signed by the applicant has been submitted: it confirms that the applicant received a pamphlet and that he had had the opportunity to be advised by an officer of his choice. On the same date, the CO referred the case to the Higher Authority and remanded the applicant in close arrest. A short note by the CO (“referred to Higher Authority”) constitutes the sole record before the Court of that hearing.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against the Republic of X (a fictional country) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of X (a fictional country), Mr Ali Xan (“the applicant”), on 21 May 1996.
