By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Arrest and detention of the applicant On 31 August 1981 police officers from the X (a fictional city) Security Directorate arrested the applicant on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the Yol (Revolutionary Path). On 19 October 1981 the X (a fictional city) Martial Law Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. B. Trial in the X (a fictional city) Martial Law Court On 26 February 1982 the Military Public Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Martial Law Court against the applicant and 722 other defendants. The Public Prosecutor accused the applicant, inter alia, of membership of the Yol, whose object was to undermine the constitutional order and replace it with a Marxist-Leninist regime. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the X (a fictional country) Criminal Code. On 18 May 1987 the applicant was released pending trial. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the Martial Law Court convicted the applicant of membership of the Yol.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against a country of Europe lodged with an international organization under former Article 25 of a human rights convention ("the Convention") by Mr Alex Novak, a national of a European country, and three nationals, Mr Carlos Vargas, Mr Manuel Sanchez and Mr Luis Garcia ("the applicants"), on 15 September 1997. The first two applicants are currently living in a city, a region of Europe. The fourth applicant lives in a European country. The third applicant is since deceased. His application is being pursued in his name by his brother, Mr Manuel Rodriguez, who lives in a European country. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented before the Court by Ms D. Smith, a lawyer employed with a legal center. The government ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Ms E. Brown, of a foreign office. The applicants alleged, in particular, that their rights under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and under Article 14 of the Convention taken in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 had been breached given that the domestic courts of the respondent State had ruled that money which was left to them as tips by customers passed to their employer to be used as it wished and, in their case, to discharge the employer’s statutory obligation to pay them a basic minimum wage. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was originally allocated to a section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court), which declared it admissible on 11 September 2001. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its sections (Rule 25 § 1). The application was allocated to another section of the Court. Within that section, the chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The Government, but not the applicants, filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were employed as workers at the material time. When the applicants received a tip in cash directly from a customer, the money was placed in a box called a “tronc” and distributed proportionately among the workers at the end of the week by the “tronc master”.

PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 42596/98 and 42603/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Turkish nationals, Mr X and Ms Y (“the applicants”), on 3 April 1998. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Mrs Z, a lawyer practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not appoint an agent to represent them before the Court. On 1 February 2000 the First Section decided to join the applications, to declare them partly inadmissible and to give the Government notice of the complaints under Article 5 §§ 1 and 3 and Article 8 of the Convention. On 1 November 2001 and 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1 of the Rules of Court). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits of the case (Rule 59 § 1). The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, the Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants, Mr X and Ms Y, were born in 1973 and 1977 respectively. At the material time they lived in Ankara. On 17 November 1997, at 11.45 p.m., the applicants were arrested and taken into police custody by officers of the Ankara security police in connection with an investigation into the illegal organisation THKP-C Dev Yol – Devrim Hareketi – Revolutionary Way – Revolutionary Movement. The applicants’ detention in police custody was extended, under section 16 of Law no. 2845 (see paragraph 17 below), initially until 21 November 1997, on the authorisation of the public prosecutor at the Ankara National Security Court, and subsequently until 23 November 1997 (inclusive) by order of a judge of that court. Before the end of their police custody period, on 23 November 1997 at 11.45 p.m., the applicants were questioned by the public prosecutor. They were not brought before a judge until the following morning, that is to say on 24 November 1997. The judge ordered Ms Y to be released for the duration of the proceedings and remanded Mr X in custody. By a bill of indictment of 8 December 1997, the public prosecutor committed the applicants to stand trial before the National Security Court. He called for their conviction, under Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code, on a charge of belonging to an armed gang. Following a hearing on 9 June 1998 before a trial court, Mr X was granted provisional release.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 75107/01) against a State lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 10 October 1999. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Y. On 25 October 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning alleged unlawfulness and length of the applicant’s detention on remand to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in a city. 1. First set of criminal proceedings (“the Bydgoszcz case”) On 9 July 1996 the applicant was arrested and detained on remand. On 12 August 1996 the District Court released the applicant. On 20 October 1997 the applicant was again arrested by the police in connection with the same criminal investigation. On 21 October 1997 the District Court decided to detain him on remand in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed several offences acting in an organised group of criminals. The applicant’s appeal against this decision was dismissed by the Regional Court on 6 November 1997. The appeal lodged by his lawyer was dismissed on 20 November 1997. On 8 December 1997 the Regional Court prolonged the applicant’s pre‐trial detention reiterating the grounds originally given for his detention and adding that the measure was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the investigation. On 4 March 1998 the Court of Appeal further prolonged his detention on remand. That decision was upheld by the Supreme Court on 24 April 1998. Subsequently, the applicant’s detention was prolonged by the Court of Appeal on 8 July 1998. The court considered that the severity of the anticipated penalty and the risk of collusion justified keeping him in detention. On 11 September 1998 the Supreme Court allowed an application made by the Prosecutor General under Article 263 of the 1997 Code of Criminal Procedure and further prolonged the applicant’s detention on remand. The Supreme Court considered that the reasonable suspicion of his having committed the offences in question and the risk of collusion justified keeping the applicant in detention to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings. The court also considered that the investigation could not be terminated earlier due to circumstances for which the authorities could not be held responsible, such as the complexity of the case and the seriousness of the offences. On 31 December 1998 the applicant and 14 co‐accused were indicted before the Regional Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 10001/01) against the Republic of Alandria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alian Tamar, on 1 April 2001. The applicant was represented before the Court by Mr Z. Baysal, a lawyer practising in Alandria. In the instant case, the Government of Alandria (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 15 May 2003 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits and admissibility (Rule 59 § 1). On 15 November 2003 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Alandria. The applicant and his brother are the only successors of their mother, who died in 1975. The applicant’s mother was the co-owner of certain plots of land in Alandria. Following her demise, the applicant had conflicts with his brother regarding the distribution of her estate. On 28 December 1995 the applicant initiated civil proceedings against his brother before the Alandria Civil Court and claimed pecuniary damage resulting from the unjust distribution of his mother’s estate. On 6 March 2002 Alandria Civil Court requested the registry records of the title deeds to the land in question from the Alandria Land Registry. On 17 December 2002, in order to establish the prevailing market value of the plots, the court appointed a committee of experts to conduct an evaluation study on location and submit reports to the court. On 6 May 2003 the committee of experts conducted this study and submitted a report to the court. On 15 May 2003 as the applicant and his brother had reached a settlement, after holding fifty-five hearings, the Alandria Civil Court ordered the defendant to pay 500,000,000 Alandrian liras to the applicant, together with the interest accruing from 28 December 1995.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123456/01) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr John Doe (“the applicant”) on 10 October 2001. The applicant was represented before the Court by Legal Firm, a city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Alex Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a city. By a partial decision of 20 February 2003 the Court decided to communicate this application, and to join it to other applications (nos. 78901/01, 101234/01, 151719/01, 202224/01, 252729/01, 303234/01, 353739/01, 404244/01, 454749/01, 505253/01, 555758/01, 606263/01). On 15 May 2004, after obtaining the parties' observations, the Court declared this application admissible in so far as the complaint concerned Widowed Mother's Allowance as from the date of the applicant's second claim and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in a region. His wife died on 12 January 1998, leaving three children born in 1987, 1990 and 1992. His second claim for widows' benefits was made on 25 June 2001 and was rejected on 1 July 2001 on the ground that he was not entitled to widows' benefits because he was not a woman. On 28 July 2001 and 25 August 2001 the Benefits Agency confirmed the applicant's lack of appeal rights. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such social security benefits were payable to widowers under the country's law.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a German national, Mr Hans Müller (“the applicant”), on 29 June 2005. The applicant was represented by Mr J. Müller, a lawyer practising in Mattighofen. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador F. Müller, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The German Government did not make use of their right to intervene under Article 36 § 1 of the Convention. On 7 November 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1944 and lives in Stephanskirchen. On 25 March 2000 the applicant, driving on the A1 motorway in the direction of Linz, was stopped by a traffic patrol. The officers noted that he had been driving at 200 km/h, thus exceeding the speed limit of 130 km/h by 70 km/h, and that he had kept driving in the left-hand lane, in breach of the Road Traffic Act. Furthermore, they observed that, despite the good visibility, the applicant had switched on his fog-lights, and that he had failed to present his driving licence when they had requested him to do so. Subsequently, on 27 April 2000 the Amstetten District Authority (Bezirkshauptmannschaft) requested the applicant to comment on the above charges. On 15 May 2000 the applicant filed his defence. He stated that he had been in a rush, since his passenger was sick and he wanted to take him home as fast as possible. Furthermore, he claimed that he had been driving at a maximum of 160 km/h. In addition, he submitted that he had been constantly overtaking cars, which was why he had been driving in the left-hand lane. The applicant contended that he had not used any fog-lights. In a decision of 5 October 2000 the Amstetten District Authority convicted the applicant of four traffic offences, namely speeding, breaching the requirement to drive in the right-hand lane, unjustified use of fog-lights and failure to carry his driving licence with him, and imposed fines amounting in total to 7,000 Austrian schillings (508.71 euros) on him, with 236 hours’ imprisonment in default. Moreover, it ordered him to pay procedural costs. Repeating his defence, the applicant, on 2 November 2000, lodged an appeal as regards the first three offences with the Lower Austria Independent Administrative Panel (Unabhängiger Verwaltungssenat). He did not appeal against his conviction for failure to carry a driving licence with him. He did not request a hearing. On 28 May 2001 the Independent Administrative Panel, sitting in camera, dismissed the appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/08) against the Kingdom of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 35 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms Ana Martinez Rodriguez (“the applicant”), on 10 February 2008. The applicant was represented by Ms C. Duran and Mr E. Lopez, lawyers practising in Saint-Pierre-de-Luz and San Sebastian respectively. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr F. Sanchez, Head of the Legal Department for Human Rights, Ministry of Justice. The applicant alleged that the decision of the Supreme Court finding her guilty of serious insult against the King of Europe amounted to an unjustified infringement of her right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. On 28 December 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1 of the Convention). On 8 July 2009 the applicant requested the Court to hold a public hearing. The Court examined the request. In view of the information available to it, it decided that no hearing was necessary. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960. At the time the application was lodged she lived in Elgoibar (Gipuzkoa). At the time of the events, the applicant was spokesperson for Sozialista Abertzaleak, a left-wing Basque separatist parliamentary group in the Parliament of the Autonomous Community of the Basque Country. A. Background to the case On 22 March 2004, following an order issued by central investigating judge no. 7 of the Audiencia Nacional, the premises of the daily newspaper Euskaldunon Egunkaria were searched and then closed, on account of the newspaper’s alleged links with the terrorist organisation ETA. Ten persons were arrested, including the newspaper’s senior managers (members of the board and the editor-in-chief). After spending five days in secret detention the persons concerned complained that they had been subjected to ill-treatment in police custody. On 27 March 2004 the President of the Autonomous Community of the Basque Country received the King of Europe at the opening of an electricity power station in the province of Biscay. At a press conference held the same day in San Sebastián, the applicant, as spokesperson for the Sozialista Abertzaleak parliamentary group, outlined her group’s political response to the situation concerning the newspaper Euskaldunon Egunkaria. Replying to a journalist she said, with reference to the King’s visit to the Basque Country, that “it [was] pathetic”, adding that it was “a genuine political disgrace” for the President of the Autonomous Community of the Basque Country to be inaugurating the project with Juan Carlos of Bourbon and that “their picture [was] worth a thousand words”.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/05) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Johnson (“the applicant”), on 1 March 2004. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Smith of a law firm in a city. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Brown, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 16 February 2005 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1981 and lives in a city. The applicant was arrested on 14 May 2002 on suspicion of having intimidated witnesses. In an identity parade held the same afternoon, he was positively identified by one of the two witnesses. The applicant states that this witness accepted in her original statement of evidence to the police that she was a drug user and an inherently unreliable witness. The applicant was subsequently charged with five counts of doing acts tending and intended to pervert the course of public justice. The applicant pleaded not guilty on 2 August 2002 and the trial was adjourned to a city court on 7 October 2002. On that date no judge was available and the trial was moved to 3 February 2003. On the second day of the trial the witness who had identified the applicant did not attend and the trial had to be aborted. At the re-listed trial on 15 September 2003, Counsel for the Crown addressed the court in the following terms: “When this matter was listed for trial in February, [C.] attended on the first day. She wasn't called to give evidence and didn't come back on the second day. Certainly, that caused some concern. I think it is fair to say, at different stages of the entire case, she has blown slightly hot and cold. [C.] indicated to the police when they contacted her recently and, in fact, again yesterday, that she was reluctant to give evidence. She has attended court today and with my learned friend's permission, I have had the chance to sit down and have a chat to her. Your Honour, the reality is that she does not want to give evidence. She has personal reasons I don't propose to divulge in open court. She has formed a new relationship. She has moved on. She is trying very hard to put the events of this entire case behind her. She has satisfied the police who spoke to her yesterday and satisfied those who instruct me that no threats have been made toward her in relation to today's proceedings."

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/14) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 3 of a Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 October 2014. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr X, a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by one of their Agents, Mr Y, of a ministry. The applicant alleged that the refusal to grant him drug substitution treatment during his imprisonment, including a refusal to have the necessity of such treatment examined by an external medical expert, had breached Article 3 of the Convention. On 18 July 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960. At the time of lodging his application, he was detained in a prison. He was released subsequently. A. The applicant’s medical condition and treatment received in detention The applicant has been continuously addicted to heroin since 1977, when he was aged 17. He has also been suffering from hepatitis C since 1979 and has been HIV-positive since 1989. He has been considered 100% disabled and has been receiving an employment disability pension since 2002. He has tried to overcome his addiction to heroin with various types of treatment (including five courses of in-house drug rehabilitation therapy), all of which failed. From 1992 to 2010 the applicant’s heroin addiction was treated with medically prescribed and supervised drug substitution therapy. Since 2006, the applicant had reduced the dosage of his drug substitution medication and consumed heroin in addition to that medication. In 2010 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of drug trafficking and taken in detention on remand in a prison, where his drug substitution treatment was interrupted against his will. On 2 June 2011 the Regional Court convicted the applicant of drug trafficking, sentenced him to three years and six months’ imprisonment and, having regard to a previous conviction, to another two years and six months’ imprisonment. It further ordered the applicant’s placement in a drug detoxification facility, to be executed after a period of six months’ detention in prison. The applicant was still not provided with substitution treatment for his heroin addiction. On 10 December 2011 he was transferred to a drug rehabilitation centre in a city, where he underwent abstinence-based treatment for his addiction, without additional substitution treatment. On 19 April 2012 the Regional Court declared the applicant’s detention in the detoxification facility terminated and ordered his retransfer to prison. In a decision dated 25 June 2012 the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 39970/98) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by nine individuals, Mr A, Mrs B, Mrs C, Mr D, Mrs E, Mr F, Mr G, Mr H, and Mr I (“the applicants”), on 2 February 1998. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Mr J, a lawyer practising in a city. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr K. The applicants alleged that the Turkish occupation of a part of a country had deprived them of their home and properties. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). By a decision of 11 January 2000 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). In addition, third-party comments were received from the Government of a country, which had exercised its right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 1 (b)). On an unspecified date, the first applicant, Mr A, died. In a fax of 23 February 2003 the other applicants confirmed their wish to continue the application on his behalf in their capacity as his heirs. THE FACTS The applicants were born in 1930, 1936, 1958, 1961, 1959, 1983, 1985, 1987, and 1990 respectively. Their place of residence is not known. In a fax of 22 March 2002 the applicants' representative indicated that “the family had [had] to ... emigrate abroad”. The first and second applicants (Mr A and Mrs B) were a married couple. The third and fourth applicants (Mrs C and Mr D) are their children. The fifth applicant (Mrs E) is the widow of the elder son of the family, X, whom she married in 1983. The remaining applicants are the children of X and the fifth applicant. The first and second applicants alleged that they had lived with their children in a village in a district, where the first applicant owned several properties, including the family house. On 13 August 1974, as troops were advancing, the applicants left the village and fled to the unoccupied part of the country. On 12 January 1996 the first applicant transferred the ownership of most of his properties, including the family house, to his three children: the third and fourth applicants and X. In November 1996 X died. His estate was inherited by the fifth applicant and their children (the sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth applicants). Detailed information about the properties at issue is contained in the file.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 19171/03) against a State (Republic of Poland) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a national (Polish national), Ms Danuta Zofia Chmielecka ("the applicant"), on 6 June 2003. The applicant was represented by a lawyer (A. Chmielecki) practising in a city (Olsztyn). The State (Republic of Poland) ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 7 September 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in a city (Olsztyn). A. Facts before 1 May 1993 The applicant's mother owned a mill situated in a town (Rogoźno), Poland. By virtue of an Ordinance (no. 425) issued on 6 December 1955, the Minister (Minister Skupu) nationalised the mill. On 7 June 1990 the applicant's mother instituted administrative proceedings before the Minister (Minister Rolnictwa i Gospodarki Żywnościowej) and the Minister (Minister Rynku Wewnętrznego). She asked the authorities for restitution of her property. On an unspecified date the Minister (Minister Rolnictwa i Gospodarki Żywnościowej) transferred the case file to the Minister (Minister Rynku Wewnętrznego) who, on 9 May 1991, gave a decision. It was challenged by the applicant and, on 3 June 1991, the Supreme Administrative Court (Naczelny Sąd Administracyjny) gave judgment and quashed the decision. On 17 January 1992 the Minister (Minister Przemysłu i Handlu), who had assumed the competencies of the Minister (Minister Rynku Wewnętrznego), transferred the case to the Minister (Minister Rolnictwa i Gospodarki Żywnościowej). On 19 October 1992 the Supreme Administrative Court gave judgment and obliged the Minister (Minister Rolnictwa i Gospodarki Żywnościowej) to give, within 14 days, a decision on the motion lodged on 7 June 1990. B. Facts after 1 May 1993 In April 1995 the applicant's mother died. On 18 April 1996 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) gave a decision declaring that the applicant had acquired her late mother's inheritance. On 30 May 1996 the applicant asked the Minister (Minister Rolnictwa i Gospodarki Żywnościowej) for the immediate enforcement of the judgment of 19 October 1992. As the Minister had failed to give any decision, on 19 July 1996 the applicant lodged an inactivity complaint with the Supreme Administrative Court. She also requested that a fine be imposed on the Minister (Minister Rolnictwa i Gospodarki Żywnościowej) and a declaration be granted that the 1955 Ordinance was null and void. On 12 May 1998 the Supreme Administrative Court discontinued the proceedings in respect of the inactivity complaint.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 5 July 2005. The applicant was represented by Mr B. Smith, a lawyer practising in Paris. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 25 July 2014 the complaints under Article 7 §§ 1 and 3(e) of the Convention concerning the independence and impartiality of the Paris State Security Court and the applicant’s inability to examine or have examined witnesses were communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in New York. A. Criminal proceedings against the applicant in the United Kingdom On 30 April 1998 the applicant was arrested in New York on suspicion of trafficking of illegal drugs. On the same day he was placed in police custody, where he was informed that he would be charged with importation of a controlled drug, namely diamorphine. In his statements before the British police, the applicant maintained that he had been importing clothing goods from Europe and had not been aware of the trafficking of drugs by his partners. On 15 October 1998, after having heard witness statements and evaluated all relevant evidence, the Crown Court acquitted the applicant of all charges and ordered his release. B. Criminal proceedings against the applicant in Europe On 17 June 1998 the public prosecutor at the Paris State Security Court filed an indictment with that court, accusing certain persons of trafficking of illegal drugs by establishing a criminal organisation pursuant to Article 404 of the former Criminal Code (Law no. 766). In that indictment, the public prosecutor indicated the involvement of the applicant in the alleged acts, without bringing any charges against him. On 20 August 1998 the public prosecutor issued an indictment, accusing the applicant of the same offence as the others. The public prosecutor stated that the applicant had actively participated in the transfer of the illegal drugs from Europe to the United Kingdom and noted that he was in detention on remand in the United Kingdom. In a report dated 14 June 1998, the public prosecutor stated that the British authorities had provided him with the tapes of the applicant’s police statements as well as other evidence on the alleged offence. On an unspecified date in 1998, the Magistrates’ Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand in absentia. At a hearing on 25 February 1999 the Paris State Security Court joined the proceedings against the applicant with the proceedings against the other persons involved in the same offence. At this hearing the domestic court also requested the case file of another set of related proceedings, which contained the statements of a certain G.H."

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Ivan Novak (“the applicant”), on 15 July 2005. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr A. Smith of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the civil proceedings in his case had been unfair and that his claim had not been heard by an impartial tribunal. On 21 September 2009 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (former Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, now Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1958 and lives in a town. On 6 July 1995 the District Court of a city declared the company “Regional Industrial Meat Enterprise” insolvent and appointed the applicant (a practising lawyer) as an insolvency trustee. Judge C was appointed as an insolvency judge. On 9 August 2000, the court discharged C from his position and appointed D as the new insolvency judge. On 6 September 2000 the applicant asked the insolvency judge to determine the amount of his remuneration. At the hearing held on 9 October 2000 the question of payment of the applicant's expenses was examined. The hearing was adjourned since the court decided to wait for an opinion from an expert accountant. On 11 September 2001 the applicant asked to be granted an advance payment on his remuneration. The insolvency judge – D – submitted that the applicant had already been granted an advance payment of 6,000 local currency units (LCU) and he had already obtained 8,650 LCU. In addition, he had obtained, for his alleged expenses, a total of 45,668.32 LCU. At the hearing held on 5 October 2001 the District Court of a city sitting as a panel composed of three judges, including judge D, granted the applicant an advance payment of 6,000 LCU. On 8 April 2002 the applicant applied to the District Court of a city and requested the sum of 577,292 LCU as payment for his eight years of trustee duties. D, the insolvency judge, in her submissions to the court (przedstawienie), asked it to grant the applicant remuneration in a lower amount, namely 317,989 LCU. She submitted that the applicant had been responsible for a lengthy and expensive liquidation proceedings. She also requested the offsetting of the sum of 200,600 LCU that had already been paid to the applicant in the form of advance payments. At the hearing held on 28 September 2004 the court heard evidence from the applicant. On 30 September 2004 the District Court of a city at a session held in camera granted the applicant's request in part, and awarded him 317,989.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 18851/07) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a French national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 19 April 2007. The applicant was represented by SCP Y and Z, Members of the Conseil d’Etat and Court of Cassation Bar, and by Mr A, a lawyer practising in Paris. The French Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs B, Director of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, a violation of Article 6 §§ 1 and 2 of the Convention. On 24 November 2009 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1961 and lives in Paris. The applicant’s father, X, was chairman and managing director of the Y and Z companies. On 29 December 1992 Company A, a company representing certain shareholders in Y and Z, lodged a complaint for misappropriation of corporate assets, together with an application to join the proceedings as a civil party. By an order of 21 June 1999, X was sent before the Paris Criminal Court on suspicion of having, between 1988 and 1992, as chairman and managing director of Y and Z in Paris, knowingly fraudulently misused assets of those companies against their interest, in particular by letting them bear the full cost of an annual licence fee equal to 0.2% of the two companies’ turnover, only part of which was justified, for his personal gain or to help another company in which he had a direct or indirect interest. Two agreements were signed for the purpose: one on 1 October 1988, between Y and Company B, and the other on 1 November 1988, between Z and Company B. They were adopted by the general assemblies of Z and Y on 20 June 1989 and 26 June 1989 respectively. In a judgment of 22 June 2000 the Paris Criminal Court declared the prosecution against X time-barred, the starting point for the purposes of limitation being fixed at 20 and 26 June 1989, the dates of signature of the agreements by the shareholders. As a result, the court declared the civil party action brought by Company A inadmissible. On 22 and 28 June 2000 Company A and the public prosecutor at the Paris tribunal de grande instance appealed. In a judgment of 25 January 2002 the Paris Court of Appeal confirmed the judgment in all its provisions. Company A appealed on points of law. On 14 March 2003 X died.

PROCEDURE The case was brought before the Court on 15 August 1985 by the Human Rights Commission (“the Commission“), within the period of three months laid down by Article 32 § 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Human Rights Convention (“the Convention“). The case originated in two applications (nos. 9659/82 and 9658/82) lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) against a European country, the first in 1981 by Alice and Bob Smith and the second in 1982 by Charlie and David Jones. All four applicants are citizens of the country. Charlie and David Jones, who at the outset were designated by the initials X and Y, subsequently consented to the disclosure of their identities. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby the country recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The purpose of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8 and 13 (art. 8, art. 13) of the Convention. In response to the inquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 § 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, both sets of applicants stated that they wished to participate in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyers who would represent them (Rule 30). The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Sir William Evans, the elected judge of national origin (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr. R. Johnson, the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 3 (b)). Wilson and Mr. N. Davis (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 § 4) (art. 43). Subsequently, Mr. J. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 45718/99) against a State ("the Republic of Turkey") lodged with an international body ("the European Commission of Human Rights") under former Article 25 of an international agreement ("the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms") by a national ("a Turkish national") of that State, Mr X ("the applicant"), on 24 August 1998. The applicant was represented by a lawyer ("Mr A. Erdoğan") practising in a city ("Ankara"). The State ("the Republic of Turkey") did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the international bodies. On 29 January 2002 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the fairness of the proceedings against the applicant to the State. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it further decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1961 and lives in a country ("Turkey"). On 23 May 1995 the applicant was taken into custody by police officers from a security directorate ("Antalya Security Directorate") on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the TDKP/GKB (Turkish Revolutionary Communist Party / Young Communist Union). He was subsequently taken to a building ("Antalya Security Directorate Building"), where he was interrogated. During his police interrogation the applicant signed a statement. He claims to have been subjected to pressure and ill-treatment when signing the document. On 28 May 1995 the applicant was brought before a judge who ordered his detention on remand. On 27 June 1995 the prosecutor at a court ("Izmir State Security Court") filed an indictment charging the applicant under a criminal code provision ("Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code") with membership of the TDKP/GKB. On 18 April 1996 the Izmir State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to 12 years and 6 months’ imprisonment. The court further debarred the applicant from working in the civil service. On 13 October 1997 the applicant appealed. On 2 February 1998 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal upholding the Izmir State Security Court’s judgment. The decision of the Court of Cassation was pronounced in the absence of the applicant and his lawyer and it was not notified to them. On 26 February 1998 the decision of the Court of Cassation was deposited with the registry of the Izmir State Security Court. With a letter dated 23 June 2005, the applicant’s representative informed the Court that the applicant had been conditionally released from prison on 5 October 2004 after having served three quarters of his sentence.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 47551/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (“the applicant”), on 23 February 1998. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents. On 10 July 2001 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1936 and lives in a city, Poland. A. Proceedings concerning dissolution of co-ownership. The applicant and her neighbours were the co-owners of real estate located in a city. On 28 June 1982 the applicant filed an action with a court in which she requested that the co-ownership of the estate be dissolved. Prior to 19 September 1989 the court held a number of hearings and two viewings of the site. It also obtained two expert reports. On 19 September 1989 the court gave a decision. The neighbours (“the respondents”) appealed. On 5 July 1991 the Regional Court set aside the first-instance decision and remitted the case. On 20 December 1991 the court held a hearing. On 17 November 1992 the court obtained another expert’s opinion. A hearing listed for 16 June 1993 was adjourned due to the absence of the respondents’ lawyer. On 3 August 1993 the court held a hearing and heard evidence from an expert. The court held a further hearing on 29 April 1994. It ordered yet another expert to prepare an opinion. On 7 October 1994 the court held a viewing of the site. On 17 November 1994 a hearing was held. At a hearing held on 13 April 1995 the court heard evidence from an expert. On 27 April 1995 the District Court gave a decision and dissolved the co-ownership. The respondents appealed. On 20 July 1995 the District Court refused to exempt the respondents from the court fees due for lodging the appeal. On 22 August 1995 they appealed against this decision and requested the court to grant them leave to appeal out of time. On 19 December 1995 the court granted them that leave. On 15 April 1996 the Regional Court amended the decision of 20 July 1995 and partially exempted the respondents from the court fees. On 12 September 1996 the Regional Court dismissed the respondents’ appeal. On 18 December 1996, they lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court. On 3 September 1997 the Supreme Court dismissed the cassation appeal. B. Proceedings concerning the action for repossession.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Xana (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xana (a fictional country), Ms Xana Yana (a fictional person), on 8 February 2001. The applicant was represented by Mr Xana Kirok and Ms Xana Kirok, lawyers practising in Xana City (a fictional city). The Government of Xana (a fictional country) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 27 November 2001 the Court decided to communicate the application. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). In a letter of 17 March 2005, the Court informed the parties that in accordance with Article 29 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention it would decide on both the admissibility and merits of the application. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1973 and lives in Xana City (a fictional city). A. The detention in police custody and the medical certificate concerning the alleged ill-treatment of the applicant On 17 May 1997 five police officers from the Anti-terror branch of the Xana Security Directorate searched the flat of the applicant. She and her husband were arrested and taken into custody on suspicion of their membership of an illegal organisation, namely the XYZ/ML0 (fictional organization). According to the search protocol drafted on the same day by the police officers and signed by the applicant, the police found a number of documents, guns, ammunition and dynamite. The report mentioned that the applicant and her husband resisted arrest. On the same day, the police officers from the Anti-terror branch of the Xana Security Directorate arrested other suspects, including Mr Xana Yana (a fictional person), on the same grounds as the applicant. On 19 May 1997 the applicant was interrogated by two police officers. The applicant submitted that she was not involved with the XYZ/ML and that she was not aware of the existence of the materials found during the search. She stated that she did not know when her husband had brought and hidden those materials. The applicant signed her deposition. On 21 May 1997 the applicant was examined by a doctor from the Forensic Medicine Department of the Xana State Security Court who noted the presence of a 2x8 cm hyperaemia below the applicant’s right shoulder blade, a swelling of 3 cm in the neck area and subjective pain in the neck. The report drafted by the doctor concluded that, apart from these findings, there were no other signs of injury attributable to ill-treatment. B. Investigation instigated into the alleged ill-treatment and the criminal proceedings against police officers On 21 May 1997 the applicant was brought before the public prosecutor at the Xana State Security Court. She acknowledged the contents of her police deposition.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/03) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by nine Xanadu nationals, Ms Aisha Xanadu, Mr Baha Xanadu, Ms Celia Xanadu, Mr Darius Xanadu, Mr Ender Xanadu, Mr Faris Xanadu, Ms Gia Xanadu, Ms Hana Xanadu and Mr Ibrahim Xanadu (“the applicants”), on 15 August 2002. The applicants were represented by Mr J. K. Yalçin, a lawyer practising in Yakinbakir. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicants alleged that their relative, Faris Xanadu, had been abducted and killed by agents of the State and that the national authorities had failed to conduct an adequate and effective investigation. They invoked Articles 2, 5, 6 and 13 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 4 October 2005, the Court declared the application admissible. The applicants and the Government each filed further written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Facts as submitted by the parties The applicants were born in 1951, 1967, 1973, 1982, 1983, 1985, 1987, 1991 and 1994, respectively, and live in Yakinbakir. The first applicant is the wife and the remainder of the applicants are the children of Faris Xanadu, who has been missing since 17 November 1997. On 17 November 1997 at about 3 p.m. Faris Xanadu and his two friends Mr Ahmet Yasar and a certain Mehmet (full name unknown) were walking in the city centre in Yakinbakir. While they were in front of the Forest Directorate building, a white Renault estate car, with the registration number 07 EKN 23, approached them. Three men dressed in civilian clothes and carrying walkie-talkies introduced themselves as police officers and carried out an identity check. They then forced Mr Xanadu into the vehicle, stating that he had to go to the police station to make a statement. On 29 November 1997 the second applicant filed a complaint with the Yakinbakir State Security Court Public Prosecutor’s office and requested the Prosecutor to investigate Faris Xanadu’s disappearance. On the same day, Faris Xanadu’s brother, Mr Shafik Xanadu, petitioned the Yakinbakir Public Prosecutor’s office and requested information about his brother’s whereabouts. On 5 December 1997 the police took a statement from Mr Ahmet Yasar, an eye-witness to Faris Xanadu’s abduction.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of that country, Ms Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2000. The applicant was represented by Ms Jane Smith, a solicitor practising in a city. The government of that country (“the government”) were represented by their agents, Mr John Doe and, subsequently, Mr Richard Smith, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant complained that she did not have a fair trial by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law, in violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. In particular, she complained that the structure of the court-martial that had tried her was such that it violated the independence and impartiality requirements, and consequently the fairness requirement, of that Article. She also complained of unfairness based on the particular facts of her case. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court. On 10 June 2003 a Chamber of that Section declared inadmissible the specific complaint of unfairness under Article 6 and gave notice to the government of her main complaint concerning the independence and impartiality of the court-martial (Rule 54 § 2 (b) of the Rules of Court). On 12 May 2004 a Chamber of that Section (composed of Mr Peter Jones, Sir Andrew Brown, Mrs Claire White, Mr Mark Green, Mr David Brown, Mr Charles White, Mr James Black, judges, and Mr Thomas Green, Section Registrar) relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber, neither of the parties having objected to such relinquishment (Article 30 of the Convention and Rule 72). The composition of the Grand Chamber was determined according to the provisions of Article 27 §§ 2 and 3 of the Convention and Rule 24. Pursuant to Article 29 § 3 of the Convention and Rule 54A § 3, the Grand Chamber notified the parties that it might decide to examine the merits of the complaint before it at the same time as its admissibility and decided to put an additional question to the parties. The applicant and the government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the case, together with separate submissions on the applicable domestic law and practice. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, a city, on 1 October 2004 (Rule 59 § 3). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the government Mr Richard Smith, Agent, Mr Paul White QC, Counsel, Ms Claire Green, Mr Henry Black, Mr Edward Brown, Air Vice-Marshal Richard White, Commodore James Black, Commander Sarah Taylor, Brigadier Thomas Green, Advisers; (b) for the applicant Ms Jane Smith, Solicitor, Representative, Mr James Black, Solicitor, Adviser. The Court heard addresses by Mr Paul White and Ms Jane Smith.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against the Republic of Switzerland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Swiss national, Ms Anna Schmidt (“the applicant”), on 15 November 1999. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Brown, a lawyer practising in Lucerne. The Swiss Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador C. White, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Department of Foreign Affairs. The Swiss Government did not make use of their right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention). The applicant alleged, in particular, that her right to remain silent and not to incriminate herself had been breached in criminal proceedings against her. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 20 April 2005 the Court declared the application partly admissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Lucerne (Switzerland). On 25 February 1998 at 17.30 p.m. the car of which the applicant is the registered owner was caught in Switzerland by a radar-trap exceeding the speed limit by 20 km/h. On 10 April 1998 the Lucerne District Administrative Authority (Bezirkshauptmannschaft) ordered the applicant pursuant to section 101 § 2 of the Motor Vehicles Act (Kraftfahrzeuggesetz) to disclose within two weeks the full name and address of the person who had been driving her car at the material time on 25 February 1998. On 22 April 1998 the applicant replied that Mr X.Y. [first and family name in full], living in Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina had been the driver. On 15 May 1998 the Lucerne District Administrative Authority issued a provisional penal order (Strafverfügung) in which it sentenced the applicant under sections 101 § 2 and 131 § 1 of the Motor Vehicles Act to pay a fine of 1,000 Swiss francs (CHF) with one day's imprisonment in default. The applicant filed an objection against this decision. On 28 October 1998 the District Administrative Authority dismissed the applicant's objection and issued a penal order (Straferkenntnis) confirming its previous decision. It found that the applicant had failed to give complete information as requested in the order of 10 April. The applicant appealed on 1 November 1998 submitting in particular that she had replied to the District Administrative Authority's order, but had been unable to find out the exact address of Mr X.Y. Further, she claimed that the obligation under section 101 § 2 of the Motor Vehicles Act to disclose the driver of her car violated the presumption of innocence and her right not to incriminate herself.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of State against the Republic of State lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by twelve national citizens, Mr John Doe, Mr Jane Smith, Mr Michael Brown, Mr Robert Green, Mr Thomas White, Mr Charles Black, Mr William Brown, Mr David Green, Mr Richard White, Mr James Black, Mr Robert Brown, and Mr Charles Green (“the applicants”), on 1 April 2001. The applicants were represented by Mr Thomas Elçi, a lawyer practising in City. The Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 3 November 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaint concerning the applicants’ right to be brought promptly before a judge. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE At the time of the events giving rise to the application, Mr John Doe was the provincial leader and the other applicants were members of the People’s Democracy Party (People’s Party, hereinafter “PP”) in City, which was a province in the State of Emergency region. On 23 September 2000 John Doe, Jane Smith, Michael Brown, Robert Green, Thomas White, Charles Black, William Brown, David Green, Richard White, James Black, and Charles Green went to City in order to participate in the City Provincial Congress of PP in two cars belonging to Charles Green and David Green. On their way back to City from City, they were stopped in Village village, in City, and arrested by police officers. The applicants were then taken to the City provincial police command. On 27 September 2000 at 2 p.m. David Green was taken into custody. He was kept in custody until 11 a.m. on 1 October 2000. On 1 October 2000 the applicants were brought before the City public prosecutor and the City Magistrates’ Court. On the same day, the City Magistrates’ Court ordered that John Doe, Jane Smith, Michael Brown, Robert Green, Thomas White, Charles Black, William Brown, David Green, Richard White, James Black, and David Green be detained on remand and that Charles Green be released. Subsequently, criminal proceedings were brought against the applicants on charges of aiding and abetting the PKK contrary to Article 169 of the Criminal Code and Article 5 of Law no. 3713, and illegal possession of firearms and explosives contrary to Article 264 § 5 of the Criminal Code and Article 13 § 2 of Law no. 6136. On 12 December 2000 the City State Security Court ordered the applicants’ release pending trial. In 2002 and 2003 the applicants were acquitted of the charges against them.

PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 12345/07 and 67890/06) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms Anna Novakova (“the applicant”), on 15 April 2006 and 28 August 2005, respectively. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr P. Novak, a lawyer practising in Warsaw. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Q. Wolsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the proceedings had been unfair in that she had been denied effective access to a court. She referred to the fact that the lawyers appointed under the legal-aid scheme had failed to represent her interests effectively in that they had refused to lodge with the Supreme Administrative Court cassation appeals against judgments given by the regional administrative court. On 28 September and 14 October 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. Given that the present two applications concerned two sets of proceedings raising a similar subject‐matter, the Court decided that the applications should be joined (see Rule 42 § 1 of the Rules of Court). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960. She lives in Warsaw-Saska. A. Application no. 12345/07 - the first set of administrative proceedings By a judgment of 15 March 2007 the Warsaw Regional Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal against a second-instance administrative decision by which she had been refused a monthly social assistance benefit. On 22 March 2007 the applicant was granted, by a decision of a registry official, the assistance of a legal-aid lawyer for the purposes of lodging a cassation appeal with the Supreme Administrative Court. On 24 March 2007 the judgment of 15 March 2007, together with its written grounds, was served on the applicant. On 26 March 2007 the decision on the grant of legal aid was served on her. On 1 April 2007 the registry of the court requested the Warsaw Bar Association to assign a lawyer to her case. On 9 April 2007 the Bar Association informed the court that Mr R. S. had been assigned to represent the applicant. On 14 April 2007 the Bar Association informed the applicant accordingly and requested her to grant him an authority to act. By a letter of 25 April 2007 the lawyer informed the applicant that he had found no legal grounds on which he could draft a cassation appeal. On 2 May 2007 he informed the court thereof. B. Application no. 67890/ - the second and third sets of administrative proceedings 1. The second set of administrative proceedings By a judgment of 18 February 2005 the Warsaw Regional Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal against a second-instance administrative decision by which she had been refused a monthly social assistance benefit.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Ms Jane Doe (“the applicant”) on 15 November 2000. Having originally been designated by the initials J.D., the applicant subsequently agreed to the disclosure of her name. The applicant was unrepresented. The country Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms A. Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant complained that the country authorities’ refusal to grant her Widow’s Bereavement Allowance or equivalent constituted discrimination on grounds of sex contrary to Article 14 of the Convention in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. By a partial decision of 5 December 2001 the Court decided to communicate the complaint concerning Widow’s Bereavement Allowance and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. It also decided to join this application to other applications (nos. 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, and 12345/01). By a decision of 10 September 2003 the Court declared the remainder of the application admissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in a city. Her husband died on 10 October 1998. On 15 June 2000 the applicant made a claim to the Revenue Office requesting an allowance equivalent to that received by a widow, namely Widow’s Bereavement Allowance (“WBA”). On 20 July 2000 the Revenue Office informed her that she was ineligible for WBA as she was not a woman. The applicant did not appeal further as she considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such allowance was granted to widowers under country law.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Norwegian national, Mr Anders Jonsen (“the applicant”), on 1 March 2000. The applicant was represented by Mr. Carl Johan Svensson, a lawyer practising in Oslo. The Norwegian Government (“the Government”) were represented by Ms Kari Hansen, as Agent, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that his right to the peaceful enjoyment of his possessions under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 had been violated as he was not permitted to build a second house on his property. Under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention he complained about the length of the related proceedings before the administrative authorities and courts and also about the refusal of the Supreme Administrative Court to hold an oral hearing on one occasion. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 December 2005 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 30 December 2005, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine), the parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Berg. He is the owner of a property known as “Bergen 2” located in the city of Oslo, in the south of Norway. On the property there is a one-family house, which was built in 1935. The applicant inherited the property from his father, who died in 1992. The area where the property is located was regulated by a city plan (stadsplan) which, in accordance with the provisional regulations under the new Planning and Building Act of 1988 (Plan- och Bygglagen, - hereinafter “the 1988 Act”), became valid as a detailed development plan (detaljplan). In order to facilitate the implementation of the detailed development plan, a more specific “property plan” (fastighetsplan) was adopted with respect to Bergen 2. A. Application for tentative approval of a building permit and then for a building permit The applicant’s late father had applied on 15 July 1990 to the Building Committee (byggnadsnämnden) of Oslo for tentative approval (förhandsbesked) of a plan to divide Bergen 2 and build a new one-family house.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/90) against the Republic of X (a fictional country) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (a fictional organization) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (a fictional document) by a Turkish national, Mr X (a fictional person) (the applicant) on 15 September 1990. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Y (a fictional person), a lawyer practising in X (a fictional city) (Turkey). The X Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a “reasonable time” and that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the X Martial Law Court which lacked independence and impartiality. He further submitted that he had been convicted on the basis of the statements he had made to the police under duress and that his political opinions had constituted the basis for his conviction. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 December 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. Mr Z (a fictional person), the judge elected in respect of Turkey, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr W (a fictional person) to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). By a decision of 11 January 2000, the Chamber retained the applicant’s complaints concerning his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal and declared the remainder of his complaints inadmissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Arrest and detention of the applicant On 11 June 1981 police officers from the X Security Directorate arrested the applicant on suspicion of membership of an illegal organization, the Y (a fictional organization). On 27 July 1981 the applicant was brought to the Z Public Prosecutor’s office where he conceded the accusations against him and explained his role in the Y. On 3 September 1981, following his transfer to X, the applicant was questioned by police officers at the X Security Directorate. He confirmed his statements concerning his involvement in the activities of the Y. On 16 September 1981 the applicant was taken to the X Military Public Prosecutor’s office where the statements he had made at the X Security Directorate were read to him. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against a country in Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 August 2006. The applicant was represented by P. Smith of the Rights Centre, a non-governmental organisation based in a city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Q. Jones of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant complained about an alleged interception of his communications, claiming a violation of Article 8. He further alleged that the hearing before the Investigatory Powers Tribunal was not attended by adequate safeguards as required under Article 6 and, under Article 13, that he had as a result been denied an effective remedy. On 17 November 2008 the Vice-President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Background facts On 24 January 1991, the applicant was arrested for drunkenness and taken to a police station in a city. He was held overnight in a cell shared by another detainee, Richard Brown. The next day, Mr Brown was found dead with severe injuries. The applicant was charged with his murder. The applicant alleged that the police had framed him for the murder in order to cover up their own wrongdoing. In October 1992, the applicant was found guilty of the murder of Mr Brown and was sentenced to life imprisonment. In March 1994, his conviction was overturned on appeal. At a first retrial, one of the police officers, a key prosecution witness, failed to appear. He was subsequently declared mentally unstable and was withdrawn from the proceedings. Following a second retrial, the applicant was convicted in 1995 of manslaughter and sentenced to nine years' imprisonment. The case was controversial in the country on account of missing and conflicting police evidence which led some – including a number of Members of Parliament – to question the safety of the applicant's conviction. In 1997, the applicant was released from prison. Following his release, he became active in campaigning against miscarriages of justice generally. He subsequently started a removal business called Big Moves, undertaking small moves and van hire in a city. Although his business did well at the beginning, he subsequently began to experience interference with his business telephone calls. He alleged that local calls to his telephone were not being put through to him and that he was receiving a number of time-wasting hoax calls. The applicant suspected that this was because his mail, telephone and email communications were being intercepted. As a result of the interference, the applicant's business began to suffer.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/06) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Xanadu nationals, Mr. Xanadu A and Mr. Xanadu B (“the applicants”), on 10 March 2006. The applicants were detained on remand in Prison Y, City Z, when they lodged the case. On 28 April 2009 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the applicants’ complaints concerning the length of their detention and the length of the criminal proceedings brought against them. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The Xanadu Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 10 June 2009 the Government submitted their observations which were sent to Mr. Lawyer C, the applicants’ lawyer practicing in City Z, who was requested to submit his replies to the Government’s observations and just satisfaction claims. The Registry did not receive a reply. By a letter dated 24 May 2010, Mr. Lawyer D, a lawyer practising in City E, informed the Court that Lawyer C no longer practised law and he was the new representative. Upon the Registry’s subsequent request, Lawyer D presented a power of attorney in respect of the first applicant. Consequently, on 30 June 2010, the Registry sent the case file to Lawyer D (by fax and mail) and to the second applicant in Prison Y, setting a new time limit for their replies to the Government’s observations and just satisfaction claims. The Registry has not received a reply from either the first applicant’s new representative or the second applicant. THE FACTS On 17 April 1997 the applicants were arrested and taken into police custody by officers of the City Z security police in connection with an investigation into an illegal organisation. On 31 May 1997 the applicants were brought before the City Z public prosecutor and the investigating judge respectively, who remanded the applicants in custody. By an indictment dated 28 June 1997, the public prosecutor at the City Z State Security Court initiated criminal proceedings against the applicants and a number of others, accusing them, inter alia, of membership of an illegal armed organisation and of taking part in its activities. On 5 June 2004 the City Z State Security Court sentenced the applicants to life imprisonment, pursuant to Article 146 § 1 of the Criminal Code. On 21 January 2005 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first-instance court and remitted the case. State Security Courts were abolished by constitutional amendments introduced on 8 May 2005. Subsequently, the applicants’ case was resumed before the 13th Assize Court of City Z. Referring to recent amendments in domestic law, on 28 December 2005 the applicants requested to be released pending trial.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against a country (Country X) lodged with the Court under Article 7 of a Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a national (National Y) of Country X, on 15 September 2005. The Government of Country X ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. W. of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The national alleged a breach of Article 8 of the Convention in respect of the proceedings before a Reconciliation Foundation. On 22 February 2008 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 30 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The national was born in 1925 and lives in a town (Town A). In March 1941 the national was deported to a country (Country Y) where he was subjected to forced labour on three different farms until the end of the Second World War. He worked on the same farm as X.Y., his future wife. On 31 May 1946 their daughter was born in Country Y. After the end of the war they all returned to Country X. They registered their daughter as having been born in Country X on 15 June 1946, for fear of negative consequences had they revealed that she was born in Country Y. A. Proceedings before a Reconciliation Foundation concerning the national On 10 June 2002 the national applied to the Reconciliation Foundation for compensation on account of his forced labour during the war. That request was made under the scheme for slave and forced labourers ("the second compensation scheme") established under a Joint Statement of 18 July 2001, a Law of 3 August 2001 on the Creation of a Foundation ("the Foundation Act") and the subsequent Agreement of 17 February 2002 between the Foundation and the Reconciliation Foundation. It appears that on 1 June 2005 the Foundation’s Verification Commission found that the national was eligible for benefits, as his persecution fell under the 5th category, which included persons who had been deported to Country Y and subjected to forced labour in agriculture. It consequently awarded him the sum of EUR 1,200. The national did not appeal against that decision. B.
