Proceedings before a Reconciliation Foundation concerning the national’s daughter On an unspecified date the husband of the national’s daughter applied to the Reconciliation Foundation for compensation on account of her birth at a time when her parents had been forced labourers in Country Y. That request was made under the second compensation scheme. On 29 August 2004 the Foundation’s Verification Commission refused the request by the national’s daughter. The national appealed against that refusal. He relied on a number of statements provided by his fellow forced labourers.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against a national government (the "Government") lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (the "Convention") by a national, Ms. Alice Brown ("the applicant"), on 7 December 1999. The applicant was represented by Ms. Claire Green, a lawyer practising in a city. The Government ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, initially Mr. John Doe, and then Mr. Richard Smith. Relying on Article 8 of the Convention, the applicant complained of a violation of her right to respect for her private and family life owing to the fact that she had been unable to attend the funeral of her stillborn child and that her baby's body had been transported in an ordinary delivery van. By a decision of 2 May 2006, the Fifth Section declared the application admissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in a town (in a canton). A. The events giving rise to the case The facts of the case, as presented by the parties, may be summarised as follows. The applicant arrived in the country on 10 June 1996 as an asylum seeker. On 17 June 1996 she was placed in an accommodation centre for asylum seekers in a canton. On 12 March 1997 she was moved to an accommodation centre in a town. On 4 April 1997 the applicant gave birth to a stillborn baby, the father of whom was a national. The autopsy established that the foetus had died two days before delivery, at twenty-six weeks and two days. At the request of the midwife, the applicant, who was in a state of shock, was taken from the accommodation centre to a hospital. When asked by the midwife, both the applicant and the baby's father said that they did not want to see the baby's body. On the same day the social worker and the registrar of births of the municipality were informed of the child's birth. Believing that it was not compulsory in the case of a child stillborn at the start of the twenty-seventh week of pregnancy to be buried with an attendant ceremony, they ordered a burial without a ceremony, in the absence of the applicant. They based their decision in particular on the fact that the parents had not expressed a wish to see the body before the autopsy and took the view that, given her mental state, the applicant was not fit to attend the burial.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/01) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2001. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr X Y (“the representative”), on 15 April 2005. On 15 May 2006 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in a town. A. The first set of criminal proceedings against the applicant The applicant was charged with attempted theft. On 15 October 2000 the District Court of a town convicted him as charged and sentenced him to 18 months’ imprisonment, taking into account that he was a habitual offender. The applicant appealed. On 1 April 2001 the Regional Court of a city quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case. On 15 March 2002 the District Court of a town again convicted the applicant of attempted theft and sentenced him to 16 months’ imprisonment. The applicant appealed. On 15 July 2002 the Regional Court of a city upheld the District Court’s judgment, finding that the correctness of the conviction was borne out by the evidence before the trial court. On 15 September 2002 the legal-aid counsel refused to file a cassation appeal in his case for lack of appropriate grounds. Throughout the proceedings, except for the retrial, the applicant was represented by a counsel. B. The second set of criminal proceedings against the applicant In October 2003 the applicant was arrested and charged with aiding and abetting the sale of stolen goods. He was remanded in custody from 15 October 2003 to 15 February 2004. On 15 March 2004 the District Court of a city convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to 16 months’ imprisonment. It took into account that the applicant was a habitual offender. The applicant appealed against the trial court’s judgment. On 15 August 2004 the Regional Court of a city upheld the first-instance judgment. The applicant was represented by a counsel. It appears that he did not lodge a cassation appeal against the Regional Court’s judgment. C. The alleged censorship of the applicant’s correspondence with the Court The envelope in which the applicant’s letter dated 15 December 2003 was sent to the Court from the Detention Centre of a city bears two stamps that read: “censored” (ocenzurowano) and “Detention Centre, City” (Areszt Śledczy, Miasto). It appears that the envelope was cut open and subsequently resealed with adhesive tape.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Janusz Nowak (“the applicant”), on 10 June 2001. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Nowak, a lawyer practising in Gdynia, Europe. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr B. Nowak and Mr C. Nowak of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 15 March 2003 the Court decided to communicate the application. to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Kraków, Europe. On 20 January 1995 the applicant sued a certain F.K. (“the defendant”) in the Kraków Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy), seeking payment for works which he had carried out for her. On 18 February 1995 the applicant was partly exempted from the payment of court fees. The first hearing was fixed for 25 January 1996, but was eventually adjourned since the defendant was ill. On 21 February 1996 the defendant lodged a counterclaim. The trial court held hearings on: 2 February, 18 March, 6 May and 3 September 1996 and on 16 February and 16 May 1997. The court heard evidence from several witnesses and from the defendant. On 16 May 1997 the court ordered that expert evidence be obtained. On 10 June 1997 the expert submitted his opinion to the court. On 24 December 1997 the court held a hearing and heard evidence from the expert. The applicant requested the court to take new expert evidence. During the hearing held on 24 June 1998 the court heard several witnesses. The applicant asked the court to appoint another expert. On 16 August 1998 the applicant applied for an exemption from the costs involved in obtaining an expert opinion. His request was granted on 28 February 1999. On 28 February 1999 another expert submitted his opinion to the trial court. On 17 September 1999 the applicant asked the court to set a date for a hearing. He stressed that the court had only held two hearings per year. The next hearing was fixed for 9 March 2000, but was adjourned at the parties' request. On 16 June 2000 the applicant again asked the court to obtain new expert evidence and set a date for a hearing as soon as possible. He submitted that he had been suffering from various ailments and for that reason the court should give priority to his case. On 8 December 2000 the court, sitting in camera, decided to obtain an opinion from another expert. On 14 February 2001 the expert submitted his opinion to the court. On an unspecified later date the applicant complained to the Ombudsman about the length of the proceedings.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Commission on an unspecified date within the three-month period laid down by the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 12345/90) against the State in question lodged with the Commission under the Convention by a citizen of the State in question, on an unspecified date. The Commission's request referred to Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the State in question recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 § 1 and 13 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 35 § 3 (d) of the Rules of Court B, the applicant designated the lawyer who would represent her (Rule 31). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio the elected judge of the State in question (Article 43 of the Convention), and the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 4 (b)). On an unspecified date, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely the lawyer, Mr X, Mr Y, Mr Z, Mr W, Mr V, and Mr U (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 § 5). Subsequently Mr A, the first substitute judge, replaced Mr Y, who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case (Rules 22 § 1 and 24 § 1). On an unspecified date, the Agent of the State in question wrote to the Registrar to inform him that it was the opinion of the State in question that the present case and the case of X v. the State in question (no. 6789/95) should be considered by the same Chamber and that both cases should be considered by a Grand Chamber in accordance with Rule 53 § 1. On an unspecified date the Registrar informed the Agent that, before drawing lots in the two cases, the President had considered whether to constitute a single Chamber. However, bearing in mind, inter alia, that none of those taking part in the proceedings had asked that the case be examined by the same Chamber, he decided to constitute a separate Chamber for each case. On an unspecified date the Chamber decided not to relinquish jurisdiction in favour of a Grand Chamber. As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 § 6), the President, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the State in question, the applicant's lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 39 § 1 and 40). Pursuant to the order made in consequence on an unspecified date, the Registrar received the applicant's and the State in question's memorials on an unspecified date and an unspecified date respectively.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 29871/96) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 15 December 1995. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in Z. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 14 December 1999 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The parties then replied in writing to each other's observations. On 1 March 2005, under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, the Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1953. At the time he lodged his application he was living in A. In 1975 he went to B, where he enrolled at the University of C. In 1979 he married a Turkish national. The applicant and his wife both held residence permits and were employed as social workers. They had two children, one born in 1981 and one in 1986, who attended school in B. In a secret message dated 19 March 1984, the Turkish Ministry of Foreign Affairs informed the Turkish Ministry of Defence that the applicant was a member of the Union of Turkish Students and a sympathiser of the Kurdistan Committee, two organisations active in C. According to the message the applicant had links with D (the European Organisation of Kurds of Revolutionary Turkey), was one of the leaders of E (the Federation of Workers' Associations of Federal Germany) and had taken part in a demonstration organised by left-wing separatists in protest against the military intervention of 12 September 1980. On 28 March 1984 the Ministry of Defence brought the above-mentioned facts to the attention of the Commander of the 8th district of the state of emergency region of F province. In a secret message on 3 April 1984 the latter reported the applicant to the military prosecutor's office attached to the headquarters of the Commander of the state of emergency region, which opened a preliminary investigation in respect of activities detrimental to the national interest committed abroad, an offence under Article 140 of the Criminal Code. On 13 March 1986 the National Assembly lifted the state of emergency in F province.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against a country (Country X) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (National Y) of Country X, on 15 July 2008. The Government of Country X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. A. of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The national complained, in particular, that he had been deprived of access to the Supreme Court. On 23 July 2010 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). In accordance with Protocol No. 14, the application was allocated to a Committee. The Government objected to the examination of the application by a Committee. After having considered the Government’s objection, the Court decided that the case should be examined by a Chamber. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The national was born in 1962 and lives in a city (City A). On 6 June 2007 the District Court of City A convicted the national of several robberies and sentenced him to 3 years and 6 months’ imprisonment. By a judgment of 28 December 2007 the Regional Court of City A upheld the first-instance judgment. On 4 January 2008 the national requested the Regional Court of City A to grant him a legal-aid lawyer for the purpose of lodging a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court. On 7 February 2008 a legal-aid lawyer was assigned. By a letter of 14 March 2008 the lawyer informed the court in a one sentence-long opinion that he had not found any grounds on which to prepare a cassation appeal. This statement did not include any reasons for the refusal to lodge a cassation appeal. By a letter of 17 March 2008 the court forwarded the lawyer’s statement to the national. The letter read as follows: “...The Regional Court of City A informs you that your legal-aid lawyer, advocate Mr B., informed the court in writing that he had not found any grounds to prepare a cassation appeal. In consequence, the time-limit for lodging a cassation appeal by a lawyer of your own choice expires on 7 April 2008.” The letter as well as the opinion were served on the national on an unspecified date. On 27 March 2008 the Regional Court of City A refused to assign a new legal-aid lawyer to the national. The court stated that because the previous legal-aid lawyer had not found any grounds on which to draw up a cassation appeal, the mere fact that the national disagreed with this decision could not require the verification of this opinion by successive lawyers.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals, Ms X and Mr Y (“the applicants”), on 15 September 2010. The applicants were represented by Mr Z, a lawyer practising in a city. The Government were represented by Mr W, an attorney at the Office of the Attorney General (Civil Affairs), as their Agent. The applicants alleged that their deportation from the country to a country would entail a violation of their rights under Article 8 of the Convention. On 8 July 2011 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The first and second applicants, who are sister and brother, were born in a country in 1987 and 1988 respectively and live in a city. A. Factual background to the present application In 1990 the applicants arrived in the country with their mother and were in view of the children’s particular situation granted a residence permit on 3 March 1993 on the ground of strong humanitarian considerations (section 8(2) of the former 1990 Immigration Act, see paragraph 46 below). During the summer of 1993 the mother returned with the children to a country, where the children first lived with their grandparents and then with their father and his wife. There they stayed until the turn of the year 1996‐1997, when the mother resettled in the country with the children. In the meantime, on 3 August 1996 the Directorate of Immigration had granted them a settlement permit, while being ignorant about their stay in the country from 1993. In 1997 the applicants’ father applied for family reunification. His application, which was refused, prompted an investigation by the immigration authorities which revealed that for most of the period from 1993 to early 1997 the applicants and their mother had lived in a country. The authorities further observed that the applicants had strong attachment to a country since they had lived and gone to school in that country from 1993 to early 1997 and because their father still lived there. On 24 February 1999 the Directorate of Immigration decided to withdraw the applicants’ and their mothers’ settlement permit, on the ground that the permit had been granted on the basis of false information provided by the mother about her and the children’s residence in the country. It was also decided to refuse them further residence in the country. On 24 September 1999 the Ministry of Justice upheld the Directorate’s decision. Several successive requests for reconsideration were rejected. In June 2002 the children were apprehended with a view to being deported to a country. However, the police decided not to do so, based on their information that they had no contact with the mother or with the family in a country.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Mr Ali Erden (“the applicant”), on 10 April 2002. The applicant was represented by Ms T. Aslan, a lawyer practising in Izmir. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 12 September 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Antalya. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. On 7 October 1999 the applicant was taken into custody for his suspected involvement in terrorist activities. On the same date the Magistrates' Court of Antalya ordered his detention pending trial. At a hearing held on 25 November 1999, the State Security Court of Izmir ordered the applicant's release. On 29 June 2000 he was acquitted of all charges. On 10 August 2000 he applied to the Antalya Assize Court, seeking compensation pursuant to Law no. 466. That Law provides, inter alia, for an award of damages to any person who has been unlawfully deprived of his or her liberty, or who, after being lawfully detained, was not subsequently committed for trial or was acquitted after standing trial. The applicant claimed a total of 6,050,000,000 Turkish Liras (TRL) in pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages, comprising lost wages as a construction worker, legal costs and fees and moral damages. On 13 June 2002 the court handed down a judgment awarding the applicant an unspecified sum of money. Upon separate appeals by the applicant as well as the Treasury, the Court of Cassation quashed that ruling on 12 May 2003 and remitted the file to the Antalya Assize Court for a more comprehensive examination. The assize court resumed the proceedings by broadening the scope of its examination of the damage which the applicant had suffered. On 23 September 2003 the court gave a second judgment, which the Court of Cassation quashed on 18 October 2004. Once again the Court of Cassation directed the court to conduct a more thorough research into the applicant's entitlement to damages. On 18 February 2005 the assize court handed down its third ruling, awarding the applicant 681 New Turkish liras. The parties appealed separately. The applicant learned through his verbal contacts with the assize court's registry that on 6 February 2006 the Court of Cassation had upheld the latter judgment with certain rectifications.

PROCEDURE The case was brought before the Court by an organization on 13 July 1989, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 § 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in three applications (nos. 12244/86, 12245/86 and 12383/86) against an unnamed state lodged with the organization under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention on 16 June 1986 by individuals and on 2 September 1986 by another individual. The organization's request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby the state recognized the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent state of its obligations under Articles 5 and 13 (art. 5, art. 13) of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 § 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio an individual, the elected judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 3 (b)). On 23 August 1989, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other five members, namely individuals (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 § 4) (art. 43). Subsequently, a substitute judge replaced an individual who was unable to take part in the consideration of the case (Rule 24 § 1). The President assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 § 5) and, through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the unnamed government (“the Government“), the Delegate of the organization and the representative of the applicants on the need for a written procedure (Rule 37 § 1). Thereafter, in accordance with the orders and directions of the President, the registry received the Government’s memorial on 19 December 1989, the applicants’ memorial on 10 January 1990, the appendices to that memorial two days later and the applicants’ claims for just satisfaction under Article 50 (art. 50) of the Convention on 9 March 1990. By letter received on 8 February 1990 the Secretary to the organization advised the Registrar that the Delegate did not propose to file a memorial in reply. After consulting, through the Registrar, those who would be appearing before the Court, the President directed on 21 December 1989 that the oral proceedings should open on 26 March 1990 (Rule 38).

PROCEDURE The case originated in six applications (nos. 12345/07, 12346/07, 12347/07, 12348/07, 12349/07 and 12350/07) against a country of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by six nationals, Mr John Doe, Mr Richard Roe, Mr Peter Parker, Mr James Bond, Mr Sean Connery and Mr Roger Moore (“the applicants”), on 15 August 2007. The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr David Jones, a lawyer practising in a city. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr James Bond, State Counsel. In their applications, the applicants complained, among other things, that they had been dismissed by way of reprisal for belonging to a trade union and on account of its demands, on the pretext of allegedly offensive content in the union’s newsletter. They relied on Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention. The applications were allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 12 December 2008 the President of the Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time, as allowed by former Article 29 § 3 (now Article 29 § 1) of the Convention and Rule 54A. On 18 November 2009 the Chamber, composed of Josep Casadevall, President, Elisabet Fura, Corneliu Bîrsan, Alvina Gyulumyan, Egbert Myjer, Luis López Guerra and Ann Power, judges, and Santiago Quesada, Section Registrar, decided, under Rule 42 § 1, to join the proceedings in the applications registered under nos. 12349/07, 12345/07, 12346/07, 12347/07, 12348/07 and 12350/07. It declared admissible the applications (nos. 12345/07, 12346/07, 12347/07, 12348/07) lodged by Mr John Doe, Mr Richard Roe, Mr Peter Parker and Mr James Bond (“the applicants”) and inadmissible those (nos. 12349/07 and 12350/07) lodged by Mr Sean Connery and Mr Roger Moore. On 9 December 2009 the Chamber delivered a judgment (Connery and Others v. Country) in which it held, by six votes to one, that there had been no violation of Article 10 of the Convention and that no separate question arose under Article 11 of the Convention. On 8 March 2010 the applicants requested the referral of the cases to the Grand Chamber in accordance with Article 43 of the Convention and Rule 73, arguing that there had been a violation of Articles 10 and 11. On 11 May 2010 the panel of the Grand Chamber granted that request. The composition of the Grand Chamber was determined according to the provisions of Article 26 §§ 4 and 5 of the Convention and Rule 24. The applicants and the Government filed memorials before the Grand Chamber.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/08) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Xanadu nationals, Mr X Y and Mr Z W (“the applicants”), on 1 October 2007. The applicants were represented by Mr A B, a lawyer practising in Yonder. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 11 December 2009 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). Following the communication of the application, the Government, but not the applicants, filed further written observations (Rule 54 § 2). However, the applicants indicated their wish to pursue their application. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1986 and 1980 respectively and live in Zonder. On 21 March 2006 the applicants attended the Newroz celebrations in Ptnos, a district of Zonder. During the gathering, the crowd shouted slogans. Subsequently, the Ptnos Security Directorate initiated an investigation on account of the fact that some of the participants had shouted slogans praising the imprisoned leader of the XYZ (an illegal organisation). Following an examination of a recording of the gathering, it was reported that the first applicant had shouted “Long live President ABC”, while the second applicant was seen as shouting slogans such as “Long live President ABC” and “Youth are the guardsmen of ABC”. On 28 March 2006 the applicants were taken into police custody. In police statements taken from them on the same date, they both denied shouting slogans in support of the XYZ. They maintained that they had shouted slogans in support of peace. Again on the same date, the applicants were subsequently taken before the public prosecutor and the investigating judge in turn. In their statements to the prosecutor and the judge, they maintained that they had only shouted “Kurds and Turks are brothers” and denied the accusations. The investigating judge released the applicants when the interrogation was over. On 29 March 2006 the Ptnos Public Prosecutor initiated criminal proceedings against the applicants in the Ptnos Criminal Court, charging them with disseminating the propaganda of an illegal organisation, based on the slogans shouted during the Newroz celebrations. The prosecution accordingly called for the applicants to be sentenced pursuant to Article 220 § 8 of the Criminal Code. On 15 August 2006 the court received an expert report regarding the video footage of the event. According to this report, the second applicant was seen shouting slogans in Kurdish and Turkish such as “Rise up again and again, our president is ABC”, “Long Live President ABC” and “Youth are the guardsmen of ABC”.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 December 2009. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Smith, a lawyer practising in a city with a law firm, assisted by Mr B. Jones QC and Ms C. Brown, counsel. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms D. Lee, Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his whole life sentence gave rise to a violation of Article 3 of the Convention. On 15 July 2014 the complaint under Article 3 was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and is detained in a prison. In October 1985, the applicant broke into a family home, stabbed to death a man, his wife and their adult son and repeatedly raped their 19 year‐old daughter, having first dragged her past her father’s body. He was arrested several weeks later and charged with the offences. At trial he pleaded not guilty, denying the killings and claiming that the sex had been consensual. On 15 September 1986, at a crown court, he was convicted of aggravated burglary, rape and three counts of murder. The trial judge sentenced the applicant to a term of life imprisonment and recommended a minimum tariff of 20 years to the Secretary of State for the Home Office. When asked to give his opinion again on 18 January 1990, the judge wrote that “for the requirements of retribution and general deterrence this is genuinely a life case”. On 20 January 1990 the Lord Chief Justice recommended that the period should be set at a whole life term stating that “I do not think that this man should ever be released, quite apart from the risk which would be involved”. On 21 December 1995, the Secretary of State informed the applicant that he had decided to impose a whole life term. Following the entry into force of a criminal justice act 2004, the applicant applied to the High Court for a review of his minimum term of imprisonment. On 22 May 2009, a judge handed down judgment in the applicant’s case ([2009] EWHC 860 (QB)), finding that there was no reason for deviating from the Secretary of State’s decision. The seriousness of the offences alone was such that the starting point was a whole life order. In addition, there were a number of very serious aggravating factors. The judge made express reference to an impact statement from the surviving victim, which described “sadistic as well as sexual conduct”. There were no mitigating factors. On 7 October 2009, the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against a country of Central Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals, Ms. Anna Novak (“the first applicant”) and Mr. Jan Novak (“the second applicant”), on 15 June 1998. The government of the country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. P. Smith, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicants alleged, in particular, that their right to a “hearing within the reasonable time” had not been respected. On 20 November 2002 the Court decided to communicate the application to the government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS The applicants were born in 1955 and 1957 respectively and live in a town of Central Europe. The applicants bought a second-hand car on 20 July 1992. Their car was seized by a border guard on 10 April 1993, as it appeared that it had been stolen. On 12 April 1993, at the second applicants' request, the local police instituted criminal proceedings against a car dealer from whom the applicants had bought the car. On 13 July 1993 the second applicant informed the local prosecutor that he wished to join the proceedings as a civil party and asked the prosecution to forward his civil claim to the court together with the bill of indictment. The local court convicted the accused on 18 August 1993. The local prosecutor forwarded the applicant's claim to the local court on 26 August 1993. Since the criminal proceeding had already been terminated, the criminal court could not deal with the claim. Accordingly, it referred the claim to the civil division of the local court on 15 June 1994. On 14 November 1994 the president of the local court informed the applicant that his statement of claim and accompanying documentary evidence had been lost. He asked the applicant to provide copies of documents in order to reconstruct the case-file. On 5 December 1994 the court found that it was not competent to deal with the claim and referred the case to the regional court. On 14 January 1995 the second applicant asked the court to exempt them from payment of the court fees. The court partly granted his request on 1 February 1995. On 26 February 1995, at the applicant's request, the court issued an interim order to secure his claim. On an unspecified date the second applicant appointed the first applicant as his representative. From then on she took part in the proceedings. The first hearing before the regional court was set down for 15 May 1995. The court held hearings on 27 June and 12 September 1995. They were adjourned because witnesses, M.N. and M.M., had failed to appear.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123/08) against a State (hereinafter referred to as "the State") lodged with the Court under Article 7 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a national, Ms Jane Doe ("the applicant"), on 15 January 2007. The applicant was represented by Mr John Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The State were represented by their Agent, Ms Mary Johnson of a Ministry. The applicant complained about the length of civil proceedings and lack of an effective remedy under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention. The applicant and the State each filed observations on the admissibility and the merits. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in a town. During the period from 1985 to 1989 the applicant received treatment at a Unit of a Hospital in a city. In May 1990, the applicant underwent two examinations at a Hospital in another city. In October 1990 she underwent a diagnostic examination at a Hospital in a city. 1. Administrative proceedings Alleging malpractice on the part of the consultant who performed the examinations, on 30 June 1991 the applicant’s insurance company, acting on her behalf, filed a grievance with a Board. The latter found against her by decision of 28 September 1993. On 9 September 1995, alleging malpractice on the part of the consultant who performed the diagnostic examination, the applicant requested that an Association grant her compensation. The latter refused her request on 28 January 1996 finding that her troubles were caused by the disorder for which she sought treatment, rather than the examination and treatment received in that connection. On appeal, on 20 January 1998 the Appeals Board upheld the Association’s decision. 2. Proceedings before the courts On 29 June 1994, alleging malpractice, the applicant instituted civil proceedings before a High Court against the medical consultant who performed the examinations in May 1990. On 7 September 1994 the applicant changed the defendant from the medical consultant to a County, being responsible for a Hospital. She amended the writ accordingly and requested that the County be ordered to acknowledge its liability in damages for the injuries allegedly incurred in connection with the examinations carried out at the Hospital. During the proceedings before the High Court, which ended on 13 November 2001, the applicant changed counsel at least five times. Moreover, during the proceedings a significant amount of time was spent on the drafting and discussion of various questions to be submitted to a Council for an expert opinion. From September 1994 to March 1995 pleadings were exchanged.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Andria (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Andria (a fictional country), Mr. X Y Z (“the applicant”), on 15 August 2004. The applicant was represented by Mr. A B C, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Government of Andria (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 16 October 2008 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Andria. On 15 October 1991 the applicant had an accident while entering a lift in the Andria Business Centre in Andria. The applicant subsequently learned that the lift had been under repair at the material time, despite the lack of any warning signs to this effect in the building, and that the accident had been caused by her attempt to operate the lift under those circumstances. Following the accident the applicant was taken to the Andria General Hospital where she received medical treatment. According to the report drawn up by an orthopaedist in that hospital on 25 July 1992, the applicant suffered a thoracic vertebral fracture as a result of the accident, was unfit for work for 60 days and was required to undergo 240 days of treatment. Criminal proceedings were subsequently brought against the two workers who had been repairing the lift at the time (case no. 1991/978), on charges of causing injury through professional negligence. On 12 January 1994 the Andria Criminal Court acquitted the workers, holding that they were not responsible for the injuries which the applicant had suffered. The Andria public prosecutor then brought criminal proceedings before the Andria Criminal Court of First Instance against the manager and the concierge of the Andria Business Centre, on charges of causing injury through negligence (case no. 1994/789). Meanwhile, on 9 August 1992 the applicant brought civil proceedings (case no. 1992/345) before the Andria Civil Court against the management of the Andria Business Centre and Elmas Electrical Maintenance Co. (the lift maintenance company), seeking compensation for the pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage that she had suffered as a result of the accident. On 3 January 1994 the first-instance court dismissed the case in so far as it concerned the management of the Andria Business Centre, as the latter had no legal status. Following the decision of 3 January 1994, on 23 October 1994 the applicant brought a second case before the Andria Civil Court against the owners of the apartments in the Andria Business Centre and its manager (case no. 1994/567). Case no. 1994/567 was subsequently joined to case no. 1992/345. On 1 January 1995 the Andria Civil Court ordered that the file concerning case no. 1994/789 be obtained from the Andria Criminal Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/90) against a country of Europe lodged with an international organization under former Article 2 of a convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms by a national of a European country, Ms. Jane Doe ("the applicant"), on 1 December 1990. The applicant was represented before the Court by Ms. A. Smith, solicitor to the National Rights Commission, Dublin. The government of the country ("the government") were represented by their Agent, Mr. B. Jones. The applicant complained of the circumstances in which her application for a post in the civil service was rejected and her complaints of discrimination on grounds of religion blocked by a certificate issued under section 42 of the Fair Employment Act. She invokes principally Article 6 of the convention, as well as Articles 8, 9, 10, 13 and 14 of the convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 January 1995, when Protocol No. 10 to the convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 10). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 1 May 2000, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The applicant and the government each filed observations. The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE In July 1990, the applicant applied for a position as an administrative assistant with the civil service, the lowest grade in the non-industrial civil service. She passed a written test but was not invited for interview at that stage. In 1991, the applicant was invited for interview, and was informed on 15 August 1991 that she was being recommended for appointment "subject to the satisfactory outcome of various pre-appointment enquiries". She was informed on 20 September 1991 that she had been unsuccessful. No reasons were given. The applicant believed that the decision not to appoint her must have been taken on grounds of her religious beliefs – she is a Protestant and a member of an association known as the National Foresters – and not for any legitimate security ground. A number of her relatives are involved in public service in various capacities, and neither she nor any member of her family had ever been involved in any form of criminal activity. She had some unpleasant encounters with the police, but there was no question of proceedings against her.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/95) against the Republic of XYZ (the country) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (the organization) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (the document) by a national of XYZ (the country), Mr John Doe (the applicant), on 15 May 1995. The applicant was represented by Mrs Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in City (the city) (the country). The XYZ Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a “reasonable time” and that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the City Military Court which lacked independence and impartiality. He further submitted that he had been convicted on the basis of the statements he had made to the police under duress. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. Mr Richard Brown, the judge elected in respect of XYZ, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr Frank Green to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). By a decision of 11 January 2000, the Chamber retained the applicant’s complaints concerning his right to a fair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal and declared the remainder of his complaints inadmissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Arrest and detention of the applicant On 6 March 1981 police officers from the City Security Directorate arrested the applicant on suspicion of membership of an illegal organization, the Rev-Way. On 7 March 1981 the police officers conducted a search in a vacant area indicated by the applicant in City. They found pistols, several bullets and cartridge clips. On 28 March 1981 the applicant was questioned by the police officers at the City Security Directorate where he admitted that he had been involved in the Rev-Way. On 11 May 1981 the City Military Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. In his questioning by the investigating judge he denied the allegations against him and submitted that the police officers took his statements under duress.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123456/02) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”), on 20 July 2001. The applicant was represented by Mr. X, a lawyer practising in Andorra. The Government of Andorra (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant complained, in particular, about the excessive length of the civil proceedings, the non-enforcement of the court decision, as well as the authorities’ subsequent delay in paying the additional compensation awarded by the domestic courts. On 14 February 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1948 and lives in Andorra. On 25 June 1987 the Municipality of Andorra decided to expropriate two houses that belonged to the applicant and located in Andorra. The applicant filed an action before the Andorran Administrative Court to annul the decision of the Municipality. On 22 December 1993 the Administrative Court dismissed his request. A committee of experts assessed the value of the property at 11.590.000 local currency units, and this amount was consequently paid to the applicant when the expropriation took place. On 18 January 1994 the applicant filed an action before the Civil Court of General Jurisdiction for increased compensation. On 28 May 1998 there was a hearing attended by neither the applicant nor his lawyer. Subsequently, the court decided to close the case until the applicant renewed his petition. On 5 June 1998, following the new petition filed by the applicant’s lawyer, the case was resumed. Twenty three hearings were held before the Civil Court of General Jurisdiction, during six of which neither the applicant nor his lawyer were present. On 16 July 1998 the court awarded the applicant 11.590.000 local currency units of additional compensation, plus interest at the statutory rate, as of 22 December 1993. Following the applicant’s appeal, on 19 December 2000 the Court of Cassation upheld the decision of the Civil court. This decision was notified to the applicant on 26 January 2001. The applicant requested the Court of Cassation to rectify its decision. On 23 March 2001 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s request. In his observations dated 30 June 2006, the applicant informed the Registry that he had not yet been paid the award determined by the first-instance court on 16 July 1998.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 22922/03) against a State lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 4 February 2003. The applicant was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in a city. The State (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 28 September 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaint concerning the lack of legal assistance to the applicant during his police custody. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1983 and lives in a city. On 31 December 2000 at about 00.15 a.m. the applicant, who was seventeen years old at the time, was taken into police custody in a city on suspicion of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation by way of chanting slogans in favour of that organisation and by burning tyres in the streets. The same day he was interrogated by the police and the public prosecutor respectively, in the absence of a lawyer. According to the information in the file, the applicant was released on the second day of custody. On 10 January 2001 the Public Prosecutor at the State Security Court filed an indictment accusing the applicant and three others of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation, an offence under Article 169 of the Criminal Code and Section 5 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713). Between 10 January and 13 August 2001, the court held thirty-four hearings, during which the applicant was not represented by a lawyer. A lawyer was assigned to the applicant for the hearing of 3 September 2001. On 3 December 2001 the State Security Court delivered its judgment. It convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to two years and six months’ imprisonment. In convicting the applicant, the court had regard to the applicant’s statements to the police and the public prosecutor, which were taken in the absence of a lawyer. On 8 July 2002 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s appeal, without holding a hearing on the merits. The decision dated 8 July 2002 was deposited with the registry of the State Security Court on 21 August 2002. Subsequently, on 11 September 2002 the applicant was sent to prison to serve his sentence. In the meantime, on 30 July 2003 Law no. 4963 entered into force, which amended Article 169 of the Criminal Code. Relying on the fact that the new law provided more favourable provisions for the applicant, on 29 August 2003 the applicant’s lawyer requested the re-opening of the proceedings. On 15 September 2003 the Criminal Court decided to re-open the case and ordered the applicant’s release from prison.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”), on 10 June 2003. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 8 June 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the excessive length of the applicant's detention to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1980 and lives in a city. On 12 March 2003 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of having committed a crime. On 13 March 2003 the District Court remanded him in custody until 12 June 2003 on reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offence in question. The court also considered that keeping the applicant in detention was justified by the existence of strong and substantial evidence, in particular testimonies of a victim and witnesses. It also gave as a ground for detention the severity of the likely sentence. Further, the court considered that, given the risk that the applicant might tamper with evidence, in particular intimidate witnesses, keeping him in detention was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the investigation. On 9 April 2003, following an appeal by the applicant, the Regional Court upheld that decision. The applicant's further appeals against decisions extending his detention and all his subsequent, numerous applications for release and appeals against refusals to release him, were unsuccessful. In the course of the investigation, the applicant's detention was extended on four occasions. The relevant decisions were given by the District Court on 10 June and 10 September 2003, and later on 10 February and 7 May 2004. In all their detention decisions the authorities repeatedly relied on the original grounds given for the applicant's detention. They also attached importance to the need to extend the investigation in the light of new charges against the applicant, and to obtain fresh evidence, in particular evidence from experts. On 18 May 2004 the District Court held the first hearing. It subsequently scheduled twelve hearings in the case. Four of them were cancelled for various reasons.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/08) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2008. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr X Y (“the Government”), on 30 July 2009. On 15 August 2009 the President of the Fifth Section Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). On 2 October 2010 the Government submitted a unilateral declaration and invited the Court to strike out the application, in accordance with Article 37 of the Convention. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in City A. A. Main proceedings On 28 August 1993 the applicant and K. P., disguised as police officers, requested A. J. and Z. T. to present their car registration documents for inspection. Subsequently, as it transpires from the case file, the applicant, assisted by K. P., seized the car and drove away. On 28 August 1993 a criminal investigation was opened against the applicant and K. P. by the City A District Prosecutor's Office. On an unspecified date in 1994 the applicant was committed for trial before the City A District Court on a charge of car theft. On 19 February 1996 a burglary was committed at the City A District Court building and the case documents were stolen. On 20 March 1996 proceedings to have the case documents reconstructed were initiated and the criminal proceedings against the applicant were suspended. On 28 December 1997 the City A District Court decided that the case documents had been partly reconstructed. The applicant appealed. On 10 February 1998 the City A Regional Court upheld the District Court's decision. On 21 February 1998 the City A District Court scheduled a first hearing for 5 March 1998. On 5 March 1998 the criminal proceedings against the applicant were reopened and the first hearing took place. Several subsequent hearings in the case, inter alia those of 12 April, 25 June and 1 October 1998 and 25 June 1999, were adjourned because witnesses or the accused failed to appear. On 15 December 1999 the City A District Court decided to have the proceedings suspended as one of the accused, K. P., had gone into hiding. On 27 January 2008 the criminal proceedings were reopened by decision of the City A District Court, as K. P. had been found. He was taken to a hearing under police escort. On 24 May 2008 the City A District Court decided to discontinue the proceedings as the charges against the applicant had become time‐barred. That decision became final on 30 May 2008. B.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Novak (“the applicant”), on 15 November 2006. The European Government were represented by their Agent, Mr M. Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his pre-trial detention had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 31 October 2008 the President of the Fifth Section of the Court decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant’s pre-trial detention to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in City. On 16 November 2004 the applicant was arrested by the police. On 17 November 2004 the City Court decided to place the applicant in pre-trial detention in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed a robbery by punching P.Q. and taking a “Brand” watch from him worth 100 European euros (EUR). The court also relied on the severity of the penalty that was likely to be imposed on the applicant and the fact that he had been previously convicted of another robbery, for which he had been sentenced to two years’ imprisonment. On 9 January 2005 the applicant’s pre-trial detention was extended. On 27 March 2005 the applicant was indicted before the City Court. The prosecutor established that on 16 November 2004, in City train station, P.Q., a homeless person, had been stopped by an individual who had taken a can of beer from him. The individual had then returned, hit P.Q. in the face, causing a bruise, and taken his watch. When the police arrived, P.Q. identified the applicant as the perpetrator. On his arrest the applicant had dropped the watch and it had been returned to its owner, P.Q. On 7 April 2005 the City Court further extended the applicant’s detention, finding that the grounds previously given remained relevant. Moreover, the court did not find any circumstances that would point in favour of the applicant’s release. On 15 June 2005 the Starogard City Court, to which the case had been transferred, dismissed the applicant’s request for release and further extended his pre-trial detention. It relied on the reasonable suspicion against the applicant and on the likelihood that a severe sentence would be imposed. It appears that on 28 June 2005 the trial court held the first hearing. Subsequently, hearings were held at regular intervals. On 13 October 2005 the District Court extended the applicant’s detention, relying solely on the likely severity of the sentence. On 11 January and 10 April 2006 the applicant’s detention was further extended.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 23 July 2001. The applicant was represented by Ms Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr Richard Brown and, subsequently, Mr Michael Green. The applicant alleged that the length of civil proceedings in his case had exceeded a reasonable time. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 31 May 2005 the Court declared the application partly admissible. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1936 and lives in a city. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. On 1 September 1992 the applicant signed a lease contract with a co‐operative. On 22 April 1993 the contract was terminated by the lessor and the applicant was barred from entering the leased premises. On 21 July 1993 the applicant brought a civil action against the co‐operative before a regional court. He claimed that the lease contract had been terminated in breach of its provisions. He further alleged that as a result of the early termination he had suffered serious financial losses. He sought pecuniary damages and reimbursement of amounts he had paid in taxes in connection with the contract. The first hearing in the case took place on 16 February 1994. The following two hearings were held on 12 June 1995 and 2 February 1996. An expert was appointed at the latter hearing. The first-instance judgment was given on 30 April 1997. On 25 July 1997 the applicant lodged an appeal with the appellate court. On 13 November 1997 the court quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case for re-examination. It pointed out that the first-instance court had erred in the assessment of the evidence and that certain facts relevant for the outcome of the case required further clarification. The regional court, having re-examined the case, dismissed the applicant’s action on 30 June 1998. The applicant appealed on 29 July 1998. On 13 January 1999 the court again quashed the judgment of the regional court and remitted the case for re-examination. It stated that the first-instance court had partly failed to assess the evidence which was crucial for the case. No hearings were held throughout 1999.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 34030/07) against the Republic of a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 3 August 2007. The applicant was represented by Ms Y, a lawyer practising in a city. The Government of a European country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Z of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that the lustration proceedings in his case had been unfair, in violation of Article 6 of the Convention. On 25 February 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1946 and lives in a city. On 3 August 1997 the Law of 11 April 1997 on disclosing work for or service in the State’s security services or collaboration with them between 1944 and 1990 by persons exercising public functions entered into force. On 14 April 2004 the applicant, a candidate for the European Parliament, declared that he had not collaborated with the communist-era secret services. He was subsequently elected as a Member of the European Parliament. On 9 December 2004 the Court of Appeal decided to institute lustration proceedings against the applicant following a request made by the Public Interest Commissioner on the grounds that the applicant had lied in his lustration declaration by denying that he had cooperated with the secret services. On 17 February 2006 the Court of Appeal, acting as the first-instance lustration court, found that the applicant had submitted an untrue lustration declaration since he had been an intentional and secret collaborator with the State’s secret services. The court established that the applicant had met on probably two occasions in 1973 with agents of the secret services and had agreed to help them as a consultant. The applicant appealed against the decision. He submitted that he had never collaborated with the secret services and the meeting in question had been in connection with the preparation of an article. The applicant also referred to his subsequent activity in a movement for which he had been persecuted and detained by the communist authorities. Subsequently, he was allowed to leave the country and between 1985 and 1994 he was a deputy of a section of Radio Free Europe in a city. On 6 June 2006 the Court of Appeal, acting as the second-instance lustration court, upheld the impugned judgment. On 1 February 2007 the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 19582/02) against a State (Republic of Turkey) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (Turkish national), Mr Ali Çimen (“the applicant”), on 8 December 2001. The applicant was represented by a lawyer (Mr M. İşeri) practising in a city (Izmir). The State (Republic of Turkey) (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 13 March 2007 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the lack of legal assistance to the applicant during his police custody and the non-communication of the written opinion of the Principal Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1969 and lives in a city (Izmir). On 17 April 2000 the applicant was taken into custody by police officers from a branch (Anti-Terrorist Branch) of a directorate (Security Directorate) on suspicion of his involvement in the activities of an illegal organisation. On the same day, the applicant was interrogated at the branch in the absence of a lawyer. According to a form explaining arrested persons’ rights which the applicant had signed, he had been reminded of the charges against him and of his right to remain silent. In his statement, the applicant admitted to his involvement in the illegal organisation. On 20 April 2000 the applicant was brought before a prosecutor and subsequently a judge at a court (State Security Court). Before the prosecutor and the judge, again in the absence of a lawyer, the applicant admitted that he had participated in certain activities of the illegal organisation. On the same day, the applicant’s lawyer requested to visit him; however this request was rejected by the prosecutor. On 2 May 2000 the prosecutor at the court filed a bill of indictment, accusing the applicant of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation. He requested that the applicant be sentenced and convicted under a code (Criminal Code) and a section (Prevention of Terrorism Act) of a law (Law no. 3713). On 5 December 2000 the court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to three years and nine months’ imprisonment. In its decision, the court attached particular importance to the applicant’s statements to the judge. On 25 December 2000 the applicant appealed. On an unspecified date, the Principal Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation submitted his written opinion. This opinion was not served on the applicant or his representative. On 11 June 2001, the Court of Cassation, upholding the reasoning and assessment of the court, dismissed the applicant’s appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/05) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Zephyr Windward (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2005. The applicant was represented by Ms A Breeze, a lawyer practising in Yonder. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 5 January 2008 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the lack of legal assistance to the applicant during his police custody to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and is serving his prison sentence in the Yonder H-type Prison. On 28 April 1999 the applicant was taken into custody during a military operation carried out by the armed forces on suspicion of being a member of an illegal armed organisation, namely the KKK. The applicant was detained at a gendarme station, where he was questioned in the absence of a lawyer and his detailed statement was recorded verbatim. In the statement the applicant was quoted as having said that he had joined the KKK on 14 March 1996 and that he had carried out a number of armed activities since that date. On 7 May 1999 the applicant was brought before the public prosecutor and subsequently the investigating judge. When questioned by the prosecutor and the judge, in the absence of a lawyer, the applicant confirmed the accuracy of the information contained in the statement he had made at the gendarme station, and repeated that he had carried out a number of armed activities. The applicant was placed in detention on remand on the order of the investigating judge. On 16 June 1999 the public prosecutor at the State Security Court filed an indictment, charging the applicant with the offence of carrying out activities for the purpose of bringing about the secession of part of the national territory. He sought the death penalty under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. The trial of the applicant and his seven co-defendants began on 21 August 1999 before the State Security Court. In the course of the trial, the applicant was represented by his lawyer. He informed the court that he had joined the KKK in 1996 and had received military training. He further admitted to certain charges brought against him. The applicant also stated, during the hearings, that he had been forced to put his thumbprint on the statement taken from him at the gendarme station. On 29 November 2002 the State Security Court found the applicant guilty as charged and sentenced him to death. The death penalty was commuted to a life sentence.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against a country of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of that country, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 October 2003. The government of that country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr X Y (“the government’s representative”), on 30 November 2006. The President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to communicate to the government the complaint concerning the issue of the possible monitoring of the applicant's correspondence. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. The criminal proceedings against the applicant The applicant, Mr John Doe, is a national of that country who was born in 1980 and lives in a town. The applicant was charged with drug trafficking and detained on remand from 5 April 2003 to 22 May 2005. He was detained in a detention centre. On 30 May 2004 the regional court of that country found the applicant guilty of drug trafficking and sentenced him to three years' imprisonment. The applicant appealed. On 30 December 2004 the appellate court of that country amended the judgment and sentenced the applicant to two years and four months' imprisonment. The judgment is final. B. The monitoring of the applicant's correspondence On 1 October 2003 the applicant sent a letter to the European Court of Human Rights. It was received by the Court on 21 October 2003. It bears a stamp “censored on” (cenzurowano dnia ...), a handwritten date “1 October” and an illegible signature. The envelope also bears a stamp of the regional court of that country. On 4 December 2003 the applicant sent another letter to the European Court of Human Rights. It was received by the Court on 17 December 2003. It bears a stamp “censored on”, a handwritten date “4 December” and an illegible signature. The envelope also bears a stamp of the regional court of that country. It also appears that both envelopes had been cut open and resealed with adhesive tape. The applicant submitted a photocopy of an envelope sent to him on 24 October 2003 by an organization. It bears a stamp “censored on”, a handwritten date “31 October 2003” and an illegible signature. The envelope also bears a stamp of the regional court of that country. The applicant claimed that he had received the letter in an opened envelope. The applicant also produced a photocopy of an envelope sent to him on 22 November 2003 by an organization. It bears a stamp “censored”, a handwritten date “28 November 2003” and an illegible signature. The envelope also bears a stamp of the detention centre of that country, with a date of receipt (25 November 2003) and a stamp of the regional court of that country.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals, Ms Applicant1 and Mr Applicant2 (“the applicants”), on 4 March 2003. The applicants were represented by Mr Lawyer1, a lawyer practising in City. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 18 January 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1979 and 1951 respectively and currently reside in City1 and City2 respectively. The second applicant, Mr Applicant2, and the first applicant, Ms Applicant1, were, respectively, the owner and the editor of Newspaper1, a weekly newspaper. In its 31st edition, in January 2002, Newspaper1 published an article entitled ‘Öcalan1’s reply to Akçam2‘. It concerned Öcalan’s response to Akçam’s accusations on issues concerning the establishment of the PKK and its development which was published in another newspaper. It also featured Öcalan’s thoughts on various issues such as education and cultural activities in Kurdish. Various parts of the article read as follows: “ Response to Akçam ....Öcalan replied to one of the ex-leaders of DEV-YOL, Akçam...It is not a coincidence that they are making him talk. It is important...Those that Akçam claimed to have saved from the hands of the PKK, he had them murdered...he caused great damage...they had them murdered. This person’s identity and personality is dubious. He also caused great damage to the PKK...We were at ADYÖD together in 1975...In 1982 he provoked the anti-fascist front. You can ask Tore this, he knows this period. He said that, at that time, Apo wanted to kill him. No, I never had any intention of killing him. On the contrary, we have suspicions that it was that front who attempted to kill or assassinate us. He very openly dissolved DEV-YOL. He is swearing to his past...he has one foot in America, the other in Yerevan. It is not known to whom and what he adheres...He is dangerous... Identity notice Öcalan also referred to the desires for a Kurdish education and the State’s response to these requests and said: It would be better to establish special learning houses in villages and streets to learn Kurdish on a scientific basis rather than the State giving permission for it. I am saying do literary and cultural work and activities...If Turkey prohibits it then it cannot make progress... “May it be a democratic year” If there are no developments in the democratic expansion then there will be deadlock.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 August 2009. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Richard Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that his detention on remand exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention.
