On 25 January 2010 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided that the merits of the application be examined at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, Mr John Doe, is a European national who was born in 1960 and who lives in Warsaw, Europe. On 8 May 2007 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of being a member of an organised criminal group, tax fraud, perjury and other related offences. On 10 May 2007 the Warsaw District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) remanded him in custody. That decision was justified by the strong evidence against the applicant, the gravity of the offences with which he had been charged and the severity of the penalty which could be imposed if convicted. In addition, the court relied on the risk that the applicant would induce witnesses to give false testimony and also go into hiding if released. The latter ground was justified in the light of the fact that the applicant did not have a fixed residence prior to his arrest. It appears that the applicant’s interlocutory appeal against the above detention order was dismissed on 22 May 2007. Subsequently, the applicant’s pre-trial detention was extended by the decisions of the Warsaw District Court issued on 24 July, 23 October and 15 December 2007, 15 February, 28 April and 15 June 2008 and by the decisions of the Gliwice Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) issued on 21 September and 28 December 2008 and 24 March 2009. The domestic courts relied on the original grounds for the applicant’s detention. In addition it was noted that the proceedings were complex and involved a large number of witnesses and voluminous evidence. The investigating authorities had to obtain expert reports on accountancy, finance and forensics. Lastly, it was noted that new aspects of the alleged criminal activities of the applicant were being revealed in the course of the progressing investigation. On 23 March 2009 the prosecutor lodged a bill of indictment against the applicant and his two alleged accomplices with the Warsaw Regional Court. The applicant was indicted of numerous counts of tax fraud, money laundering and perjury, allegedly committed within an organised criminal group. The first hearing took place on 24 September 2009. It appears that since then the trials have been taking place once a month or more frequently.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr John Doe (“the applicant”) on 1 October 2000. The applicant was unrepresented before this Court. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr A. B. C. of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, a city. The applicant complained that the authorities' refusal to grant him a benefit constituted discrimination on grounds of sex contrary to Article 14 of the Convention in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. By a partial decision of 1 December 2001 the Court decided to communicate this application. It also decided to join this application to other applications (nos. 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00, 12345/00 and 12345/00). On 1 August 2003, after obtaining the parties' observations, the Court declared this application admissible in so far as the complaint concerned a benefit and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1944 and lives in a county. His spouse died on 1 June 1995. On 1 September 2000 the applicant made a claim to a department requesting an allowance equivalent to that received by a widow, namely a benefit for the years 1995/6 and 1996/7. On 1 September 2000 the department informed him that he was ineligible for the benefit as he was not a woman. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such benefit was payable to widowers under the country's law.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xanadu, Mr Xanadu Man (“the applicant”), on 15 July 2010. The applicant was represented by Mr Xanadu Lawyer, a lawyer practising in Xanadu City. The Republic of Xanadu (“the government”) were represented by their Agent. On 17 July 2012 the application was communicated to the government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Xanadu City. On 25 April 2007, in the course of a military operation, several terrorists were killed by the security forces in Yonderland. On 29 April 2007 a large group of people assembled at their funeral and protested against the security forces. The demonstrations continued and in the course of the events about 1,500 to 2,000 people resisted the police, attacking them with stones, blocking the traffic by burning tyres and damaging nearby shops and public buildings by throwing stones. Many demonstrators were arrested by the police. According to the documents in the case file, the applicant was among those who were arrested on the night of 30 April 2007. At 3.30 a.m. on 1 May 2007 the applicant was examined by a doctor at the Xanadu City State Hospital. In his report, the doctor noted that there were ecchymoses on the applicant’s back, lumbar area and the side of his left knee. At 10.12 p.m. on 2 May 2007 the applicant was examined by another doctor at the Xanadu City State Hospital. The medical report indicated large ecchymoses on the applicant’s back and on the outer part of his left femur. At 2.46 a.m. on 3 May 2007 the applicant was examined for a third time, by another doctor from the same hospital. According to the report, no new signs of physical violence were found on the applicant. Following those medical examinations, the applicant was brought before the Xanadu City Public Prosecutor, where he denied the charges against him. On the same day the applicant, along with ten other persons, was questioned by the Xanadu City investigating judge. The medical report was read to the applicant. He stated that the injuries had not occurred during the incidents but had been inflicted by police officers while he had been in police custody. The judge remanded the applicant in custody. On 3 May 2007 the Xanadu City Public Prosecutor issued an indictment charging the applicant with involvement in the activities of an illegal organisation. On 25 May 2008 the Xanadu City Assize Court convicted the applicant under Article 314 of the Criminal Code and sentenced him to six years and three months’ imprisonment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/04) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Bulgarian national, Mr Ivan Petrov (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2003. The applicant was represented by Mr Georgi Ivanov, a lawyer practising in Brussels. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Anna Petrova, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Bulgarian Government did not make use of their right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention). The applicant alleged, in particular, that the residence prohibition against him violated his right to respect for his private and family life. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 1 June 2005 the Court declared the application partly admissible. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1985 and currently lives in Bulgaria. In October 1991 the applicant lawfully entered Europe together with his parents and two siblings. Subsequently, he was legally resident in Europe. His parents were lawfully employed and have meanwhile acquired European nationality. The applicant attended school in Europe. In late 1999 criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant. He was, inter alia, suspected of having broken into cars, shops and vending machines, of having stolen empties from a stock ground, of having forced another boy to steal 1,000 European schillings from the latter’s mother, of having beaten this boy and thereby having bruised him, and of having used a motor vehicle without the owner’s authorisation. On 10 August 2000 the Brussels Juvenile Court (Jugendgerichtshof) convicted the applicant of some 20 counts of partially completed and partially attempted aggravated gang burglary (gewerbsmäßiger Bandendiebstahl), of extortion (Erpressung), of partially completed and partially attempted assault (Körperverletzung), and of the unauthorised use of a vehicle (unbefugter Gebrauch eines Fahrzeugs) committed between November 1988 and June 2000. He was sentenced to 18 months’ imprisonment, 13 of which were suspended on probation. Moreover, he was instructed to start drug therapy. On 12 March 2001 the applicant was arrested and further criminal proceedings were opened against him relating to a series of burglaries committed between July 2000 and February 2001. The applicant and his accomplices were suspected of having broken into shops or restaurants, where they stole cash and goods. On 12 March 2001 the Brussels Juvenile Court remanded him in custody. On 26 August 2001 the Brussels Juvenile Court convicted the applicant of 18 counts of partially completed and partially attempted aggravated burglary and sentenced him to 15 months’ imprisonment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Xana lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Xanian national, Mr Xan Y. Zer-Reissig (“the applicant”), on 11 March 2004. The Xanian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Mr Xan Y. Trauttmannsdorff, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Administrative Court failed to hold an oral hearing, which was in breach of Article 6. On 30 November 2005 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1921 and lives in Xanburg. He is a lawyer practising in Xanburg and the owner of a parcel of land in the municipality of Kingstetten, which is designated as “forest” land in the zoning plan. On parts of this parcel – approximately 1,500 square meters – he runs an organic farm on a part-time basis, breeding sheep and goats. Besides that, he keeps bees and grows herbs. On 18 August 1998 the applicant applied to the mayor of Kingstetten for a building permit for a shed, to be used as a shelter for sheep and goats in summer and beehives in winter. It is also designed as a refuge for farm workers. He therefore submitted construction plans for the planned shed and a map of the land in question. The mayor rejected the applicant's request on 16 February 2000. Relying on a report by an agricultural expert at the Regional Government of Xanland, he stated that, in view of its shape, size and design, it would not qualify as a farm building and that even if it was an agricultural construction, it could not be erected on the land in question, as the latter had been designated as forest and grassland. The applicant lodged an appeal with the municipality of Kingstetten on 10 April 2000. On 3 July 2000 the municipality dismissed his appeal on the same grounds. Subsequently, on 13 September 2000, the applicant filed an objection (Vorstellung) with the Regional Government of Xanland and requested it to hear representatives of the District Farmers' Association (DFA, Bezirksbauernkammer) and the Austrian Beekeepers' Association (ABA, Österreichischer Imkerbund) as experts who would prove that the building he intended to erect was necessary for the intended agricultural enterprise. The Regional Government quashed the municipality's decision on 10 January 2001 and referred the case back to the municipal council. It stated that the municipality had failed to address all the points of appeal. The applicant lodged further grounds in support of his appeal on 19 March, 4 and 24 April 2001.

PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 12345/05 and 67890/08) against a State (the "State") lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a national, Mr John Doe ("the applicant"), on 15 August 2005 and 5 October 2008 respectively. 2. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Alex Smith, a lawyer practising in Karlsruhe. The State ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Ms Jane Doe, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. 3. The applicant alleged in both applications, in particular, that the retrospective extension of his preventive detention from a maximum period of ten years, which had been the maximum for such detention under the legal provisions applicable at the time of his offence, to an unlimited period of time breached the prohibition of retrospective punishment under Article 7 § 1 of the Convention. In his application no. 67890/08, he further complained under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention about his continued preventive detention beyond the ten-year period. 4. On 18 April 2008 a Chamber of the Sixth Section decided to adjourn the examination of application no. 12345/05 pending the outcome of the proceedings in the case of X v. State, no. 23456/05. On 25 February 2010 the President of the Sixth Section decided to give notice of the applications no. 12345/05 and no. 67890/08 to the Government, requested them to submit information on changes in the applicant's detention regime and adjourned the examination of the applications until the judgment in the case of X v. State, no. 23456/05, has become final. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time (Article 29 § 1). In view of the fact that the judgment of 20 March 2010 in the case of X v. State became final on 15 June 2011, the President decided on 19 June 2011 that the proceedings in the two applications at issue be resumed and granted priority to the applications (Rule 41 of the Rules of Court). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Karlsruhe. A. The applicant's previous convictions and the order for his preventive detention and execution thereof On 7 February 1986 the Karlsruhe Regional Court convicted the applicant of two counts of rape and abduction and of one count of attempted rape and deprivation of liberty committed in 1985. It sentenced him to five years' imprisonment and ordered his placement in preventive detention pursuant to Article 66 of the Criminal Code (see paragraphs 37-38 below). The court found that the applicant, acting with full criminal responsibility, had raped two young women and had attempted to rape another woman all of whom he had taken with him in his car.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/01) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms. Anna Novak (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2002. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. Ivan Petrov, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 10 October 2003 the President of the Fourth Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The President of the Chamber further gave priority to the application, pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1925 and lives in a city in Europe. I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. Since 1960, the applicant’s relatives, X.Y. and Z.A., have occupied a part of the applicant’s property, with the agreement of the applicant. It appears that X.Y. and Z.A. carried out construction work on the property which provoked a conflict between them and the applicant. On 10 January 1993 the applicant lodged a civil action with the local court in which he asked the court to order the eviction of X.Y. and Z.A. from his property. On 30 January 1993 the trial court held a hearing at which it gave a default judgment. The court allowed the applicant’s action and ordered that the judgement be immediately enforceable. The defendants lodged an objection against the judgment. On 8 March 1993 the local court held a hearing at which it allowed the applicant’s motions to hear witnesses and to hold a viewing of the property. Subsequently, the trial court requested a copy of the case-file concerning another set of civil proceedings instituted by the defendants against the applicant. On 25 April 1993 the court decided to stay the proceedings until the termination of the second set of proceedings, instituted by the defendants, in which they claimed that they had acquired the title to the property in question by prescription. The applicant appealed against the decision to stay the proceedings; however, on 5 July 1993 the Regional Court dismissed his appeal. Subsequently on several occasions, the applicant applied to resume the proceedings. In August 1993, February 1994, February, June, October and December 1995 and May 1996 the trial court requested the local court to provide information concerning the state of the proceedings concerning the acquisition of property by prescription. On 10 October 1995 the applicant applied to resume the proceedings. He submitted that the second set of proceedings for acquisitive prescription had ended on 23 September 1995 with the second-instance court’s decision.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Human Rights Commission (“the Commission“) on 15 January 1988, within the three-month period laid down in Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 12345/85) against the State of Xanadu lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr Alex Johnson, a citizen of Xanadu, on 10 February 1985. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) of the Convention and to the declaration whereby Xanadu recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). It sought a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 13, 17 and 18 (art. 6, art. 13, art. 17, art. 18) of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 (P1-1) to the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Article 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr H. Anderson, the elected judge of Xanadu nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr S. Thompson, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On 25 February 1989, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the five other members, namely Mr J. Brown, Mr K. Lee, Mr L. Davis, Mr M. Wilson and Mr N. Clark (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43). Subsequently, Ms O. Wilson, who had taken up her duties before the hearing, replaced Mr Anderson who had resigned from the Court (Rule 2 para. 3). Mr Thompson, who had assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5), consulted - through the Registrar - the Agent of the State of Xanadu (“the Government“), the Delegate of the Commission and the applicant on the need for a written procedure (Rule 37 para. 1). In accordance with his order, the Government’s memorial and the applicant’s memorial were received by the registry on 3 and 10 June 1989, respectively. On 7 April 1990 the Secretary to the Commission notified the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. Having consulted - through the Registrar - those who would be appearing before the Court, the President directed on 22 March 1990 that the oral proceedings should commence on 25 June 1990 (Rule 38). The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Xanadu, on the appointed day. The Court had held a preparatory meeting immediately beforehand.

PROCEDURE The case originated in three applications (nos. 12345/02, 12346/02, and 12347/02) against the Republic of Aaland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by three Aaland nationals, Mr A Aaland, Mr B Baland, and Mr C Caland (“the applicants”), on 18 June 2002. The applicants were represented by Mr D Daland, a lawyer practising in Aaland. The Aaland Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicants complained that the non-enforcement of court decisions in their favour had given rise to a violation of Article 6 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. On 12 September 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the applications. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants are all Aaland nationals and live in Aaland. Until 4 May 1999 the applicants were employed as manual workers by the Aaland Sur Municipality (“the Municipality”). On that date, the Municipality discharged 153 employees, including the applicants, without paying their wages, a dismissal indemnity or any other pecuniary rights to which they were entitled pursuant to domestic labour law. On 2 June 1999 the applicants brought separate actions for compensation against the Municipality before the Aaland Labour Court. On 11 November 1999 the court ruled in their favour and ordered the Municipality to pay 743,859,795 Aaland liras to Mr A Aaland, 1,000,000,000 Aaland liras to Mr B Baland, and 774,821,795 Aaland liras to Mr C Caland, plus statutory interest running from 2 June 1999. It also ruled that the legal costs and expenses of the proceedings should be borne by the Municipality. In the absence of an appeal, the judgments became final on 11 November 1999. On an unspecified date, the applicants initiated enforcement proceedings against the Municipality. However, their efforts proved futile as the Municipality refused to comply with the judgments. On 15 February 2001 and 21 March 2001 the applicants' representative requested the Aaland Governor's Office and the Ministry of Internal Affairs to intervene on their behalf in order to facilitate the enforcement of the court's judgments. On 9 May 2001 the Aaland Governor's Office informed the applicants' representative that they had written to the Municipality requesting them to redress the applicants' grievances. However, the Municipality did not make any payment since it was underfunded. On 20 June 2002 Mr B Baland reached a friendly settlement agreement with the Municipality. The friendly settlement protocol stipulated that the applicant would waive all of his claims, including the principal amount of compensation determined by the Labour Court, interest and all costs and fees, if he were to be paid 1,025,815,000 Aaland liras. The protocol also stated the applicant would receive this sum in five instalments.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Norwegian national, Mr Andersson Johnson (“the applicant”), on 1 September 2007. The applicant was represented by Ms Hansen Jensen, a lawyer practising in Oslo. The Norwegian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms Olsen Hansen of the Ministry of Justice. By a decision of 10 October 2007 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The applicant submitted his claims for just satisfaction and the Government made their comments on that matter. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Stavanger. At the beginning of the 1990s a new concept called “tax asset stripping cases” (company stripping cases) came into existence in Norway. It covered a criminal activity by which the persons involved committed aggravated debtor fraud by buying up and selling numerous inactive solvent private limited companies within a short period and, for the sake of their own profit, “stripping” the companies of assets, including deposits earmarked for payment of corporation tax. The persons involved were usually intricately interconnected and collaborated in their economic criminal activities, which concerned very large amounts of money. According to surveys made by the customs and tax authorities, approximately one thousand six hundred companies with a total tax debt exceeding two billion Norwegian kroner (NOK) were stripped in the period from the late 1980s until 1994. Following a number of legislative amendments, the trade in inactive, solvent companies largely ceased in the summer of 1993. At the relevant time the applicant was part owner of a private limited stockbrokers company ([C] and [the applicant] A/S] - hereafter “the company”). On 20 January 1994 he learnt that the tax authorities were about to check the company’s accounts for the years 1989 to 1992. On 8 May 1994 the tax authorities informed the applicant that the question of whether any criminal liability had occurred would be decided on later. The tax authorities also reported various potential co-offenders to the police. During 1994, 1995 and at the beginning of 1996 the police carried out an investigation comprising, among other things, discovery orders against banks, international letters of request, search warrants and numerous interviews of witnesses. On 22 June 1996, the Oslo City Court (Oslo Byret – hereafter “the City Court”), sitting in camera, granted the police a warrant to search the premises of the applicant’s business and those of the company. On 3 July 1996 the search was carried out by the police.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 66354/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Abdullah Altun (“the applicant”), on 25 July 2000. The applicant was represented by Mr M.S. Enez, a lawyer practising in Ankara. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 24 March 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the applicant's right to a fair trial by an independent and impartial tribunal. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1972 and lives in a town. The applicant was a student in the Medical Faculty of a university at the time of the events giving rise to the present application. On 23 March 1995 the applicant was notified by an arrest warrant, which he signed, about the basis and the reasons for his arrest. On the same day he was taken into custody by the police officers from the Anti-Terror Branch of the Security Directorate on suspicion of his involvement in an organization. On 5 April 1995 the police officers drafted a report of the re-construction of events, which was signed by the applicant. On 9 April 1995 the applicant gave a statement to the police, where he confessed that he had been involved in certain activities for the organization. On 10 April 1995 he was brought before the judge who ordered his detention on remand. On 13 April 1995 the chief public prosecutor at the State Security Court filed a bill of indictment with the latter charging the applicant under Article 125 of the Criminal Code with carrying out activities for the purpose of bringing about the secession of part of the national territory. On 3 June 1999 the State Security Court composed of two civilian judges and a military judge, convicted the applicant of the charges against him and sentenced him to death under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. Taking into account the applicant's behaviour during the trial, the death penalty was commuted to a life sentence. It is to be noted that the State Security Court held thirty hearings and heard nineteen witnesses. On 21 February 2000 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Security Court. On 1 March 2000 the decision of the Court of Cassation was pronounced in the presence of the applicant's lawyer. On 25 April 2000, the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant's request for rectification of decision.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 29766/03) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals, Mr X and Ms Y (“the applicants”), on 22 August 2003. The applicants were represented by a lawyer practising in the city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicants alleged that the treatment to which they had been subjected by police officers during their arrest had amounted to a breach of Article 3 of the Convention. On 8 December 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1975 and 1978 respectively and live in the city. On 1 September 2001 at about 7 p.m. the applicants went to a park in the suburb to attend a meeting, namely the so-called “peace festivities” organised by the branch of a political party. While they were about to enter the park, the applicants were stopped and searched by the police. The officers found a number of copies of a bulletin in a bag. As the applicants appeared suspicious, the police officers arrested them. The applicants were allegedly beaten up, insulted and threatened with death during their arrest. In particular, two police officers applied pressure to their necks from behind and made them lie down. Following the arrival of two more police officers, they dragged both applicants along the ground, kicked and slapped them and put them in a police car. Once in the car, the police officers continued to punch and slap them, hit them with sticks, insult and threaten them. One of the police officers first sat on the head of Ms Y and then hit her against the roof of the car. When the applicants asked where they were being taken, one of the officers said: “We are taking you to a stream where your corpses will be found”. However, according to the arrest and seizure report drafted by two police officers, the applicants were arrested because they had been acting suspiciously. The report further stated that the applicants had resisted the police officers, and had self-inflicted certain scratches and bruises on their bodies during the incident. In particular, Mr X had hit his elbow on the wall of the park and Ms Y had bruised her left elbow whilst resisting getting into the police car. The applicants refused to sign this report. On the same day at about 8 p.m. the applicants were taken to a hospital for a medical examination. The doctor who examined the applicants drafted a provisional report.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of that country, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 April 2001. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr T. Brown, a solicitor practising in a city. The government of that country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms F. Green of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, a city. The applicant, serving a sentence of life imprisonment, alleged that the Parole Board did not provide the guarantees and procedures required by Article 5 § 4 when examining whether he should be released and that he had no enforceable right to compensation for any breach of his rights as required by Article 5 § 5. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 25 August 2003, the Court declared the remainder of application admissible. The applicant filed observations on just satisfaction and the government replied (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and is serving a sentence of life imprisonment in a prison. The applicant was convicted in or around 1980 for an offence. He was sentenced to mandatory life imprisonment, and his tariff (the minimum period of imprisonment required to satisfy the requirements of retribution and deterrence) was set at 10 years. At the time of the applicant's latest Parole Board review in 2002, he was detained in a prison as a “Category B” prisoner (prisoners being given a security category classification ranging from Category A (highest risk) to Category D (suitable for open conditions)). The Parole Board recommended that the applicant should be transferred to open conditions, and that his detention should be reviewed after two years. By letter dated 10 July 2002 the Secretary of State informed the Prison Service that he did not accept the Parole Board's recommendation for transfer to open conditions, and that the next review should begin after 12 months. In the letter to the applicant which accompanied the decision it was stated that: “... [t]he Secretary of State attaches particular weight to the psychologist's report, it has highlighted in some detail, the need for further exploration of your insight into, and responsibility for, the index offence and the apparent lack of empathy towards the victim.” In May 2002 the applicant was transferred to a prison. He claimed that he did not receive notification of the parole decision until sometime after 15 September 2002.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Zephyr Wind (“the applicant”), on 15 August 2010. The applicant was represented by Mr Vortex Gale, a lawyer practising in Yonder. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been denied access to a lawyer while in police custody and that his police statements had been relied on by the trial court to convict him. On 19 July 2014 the complaint concerning restriction on access to a lawyer was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. On 7 November 2016 the Vice-President of the Second Section invited the Government to submit further observations, if they so wished, following the judgment in Ibrahim and Others v. the United Kingdom ([GC], nos. 50541/08 and 3 others, 13 October 2016). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1985 and lives in Zephyria. On 17 February 2004 the applicant was arrested and taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation. On 18 February 2004 his statements were taken by the police in the absence of a lawyer. The applicant confessed to being a member of an illegal organisation. He gave a detailed account of its structure and his acts within the illegal organisation. On the same day the applicant was heard by a public prosecutor and an investigating judge respectively. In these statements to the public prosecutor and the investigating judge, he denied his police statements and argued that they had been taken under duress. Following his questioning, the investigating judge ordered that the applicant be held on remand. On 28 February 2004 a public prosecutor at the Yonder State Security Court filed an indictment with that court, charging the applicant under Article 146 of the former Criminal Code. State Security Courts were later abolished by Law no. 5190 of 16 June 2004, and the case was transferred to the Yonder Assize Court. On 10 July 2008 the Yonder Assize Court found that, inter alia, on the basis of the applicant’s statements to the police, the public prosecutor and the investigating judge, the applicant had committed the offence under Article 314 of the Criminal Code and sentenced him to two years and one month’s imprisonment. On 27 April 2009 the applicant’s lawyer appealed against the judgment, arguing that the applicant had been convicted on the basis of statements taken under duress. On 3 February 2010 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by twenty Norwegian nationals, Ms Anna Andersson, Mr Per Bernhardson, Ms Gunilla Bring, Mr Ulf Backlund, Mr Berndt Eriksson, Ms Carina Granberg, Ms Agneta Holmstrom, Mr Gustaf Harestal, Mr Bjorn Hojer, Ms Inga-Britt Hojer, Mr Christer Johansson, Mr Curt Lindgren, Mr Hakan Olsson, Mr Roger Olsson, Mr Goran Osterman, Mr Lars Sjostedt, Mr Christer Skog, and Mr Olle Stenlund (“the applicants”), on 4 June 2010. The applicants were represented by Mr J. Ebbesson, a professor of environmental law, and Mr B. Rosengren, a lawyer, both practising in Oslo. The Norwegian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr A. Ronquist, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had been denied effective access to court in relation to decisions taken on the construction of a railway, in violation of their rights under Articles 6 and 8 of the Convention. On 21 May 2012 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants own property close to Trondheim, in the vicinity of a Natura 2000 area, the European network of nature protection areas established under the EU Habitats Directive of 1992 (see further below at paragraph 33). Most of them live there (permanently or on a part-time basis). A. Proceedings on permissibility of railway project On 15 October 1999, the National Rail Administration (Banverket; hereinafter “the NRA”) applied to the Government for permission, under the Environmental Code (Miljöbalken), to construct a 10 km long railway section in a river area in the north of Norway (constituting the final section of a railway called “Botniabanan”, the total length of which is 190 km). The NRA presented some alternative railway stretches, all located in a specified “corridor”, but recommended the one named “alternative east”. The proposed railway construction concerned certain areas which were or were going to be part of Natura 2000. It appears that six of the present applicants own houses or land within the mentioned “corridor”: Ms Carina Granberg, Ms Agneta Holmstrom, Mr Gustaf Harestal, Mr Bjorn Hojer, Ms Inga-Britt Hojer, and Mr Christer Skog. Ownership of Mr Skog’s property was transferred to Ms Granberg on 7 January 2011. The properties of the other twelve applicants – houses and land in their ownership or owned houses located on non-freehold sites – are situated outside the “corridor”. The distance from their properties to the “corridor” or the specific stretch of the railway fixed in later proceedings vary; the houses appear to be situated 300 – 2500 metres away whereas the closest piece of land is located about 50 metres from the “corridor”.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/95) against the Republic of X (the respondent State) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of X (the applicant), on 15 January 1995. The applicant was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in City (X). The X Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. Mr Z, the judge elected in respect of X, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Mr A to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaint (applications nos. 12345/95, 12346/95, 12347/95, 12348/95, 12349/95, 12350/95, 12351/95, 12352/95, 12353/95, 12354/95, 12355/95, 12356/95, 12357/95, 12358/95, 12359/95, 12360/95, 12361/95, 12362/95, 12363/95, 12364/95, 12365/95 and 12366/95) (Rule 43 § 2). By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1) THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Arrest and detention of the applicant On 21 April 1979 police officers from the Security Directorate of X arrested the applicant on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the YZ (X People’s Liberation Party/Front). On 28 April 1979 the Martial Law Court of X (sıkıyönetim mahkemesi) ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. B. Trial in the Martial Law Court of X On 15 January 1980 the Public Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Martial Law Court against the applicant and 127 other defendants. The Public Prosecutor accused the applicant, inter alia, of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the YZ, whose object was to undermine the constitutional order and replace it with a Marxist-Leninist regime, under Article 146 § 3 of the Criminal Code.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court, in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”), by the Government of a European Country (“the Government”) on 5 July 1999 (Article 5 § 4 of Protocol No. 1 and former Articles 47 and 48 of the Convention). It originated in an application (no. 28501/95) against a European Country lodged with the European Human Rights Commission (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention by the applicant, a national of a European Country, John Doe (“the applicant”) on 21 July 1994. The applicant was represented by Mr X Y, a lawyer practising in a European City (Germany). The Government were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Z W, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Agent of the Government of a European Country, having been informed by the Registrar of their right to intervene (former Article 48 (b) of the Convention and former Rule 35 § 3 (b)), indicated that they did not intend to do so. The Government’s application referred to former Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby a European Country had recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (former Article 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c). On 20 September 1999 the Panel of the Grand Chamber decided, pursuant to Article 5 § 4 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention and Rules 100 § 1 and 24 § 6 of the Rules of Court, that the applications would be examined by one of the Sections. It was, thereupon, assigned to the Third Section. Within that Section, the Chamber was constituted in accordance with Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. In accordance with Rule 59 § 3 of the Rules of Court, the President of the Chamber invited the parties to submit a memorial on the issues in the case. The Registrar received the Government’s memorial on 9 December 1999 and the applicant’s memorial on 7 April 2000. After consulting the Agent of the Government and the applicant, the Chamber decided not to hold a hearing in the case. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 8 March 1993 the Public Prosecutor's Office at the Regional Court filed an indictment charging the applicant with murder. It was alleged that the applicant, in December 1991, had killed his wife and had then buried her decapitated corpse in a field where it had been discovered in May 1992.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/11) against the European Republic lodged with the Court under Article 7 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Xavier Dubois (“the applicant”), on 15 February 2011. The applicant was represented by Ms C.-N. Fontaine, a lawyer practising in Dax. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Durand, Director of Legal Affairs with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his conviction for having refused to undergo DNA profiling had amounted to an unjustified infringement of his right to respect for his private life within the meaning of Article 7 of the Convention. On 22 April 2013 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Villeneuve. On 20 February 2009 he attended a rally organised by a regional agricultural trade union and by the GFA (a mutual-benefit land alliance), the “Lura”, on the occasion of a meeting of the Technical Committee of the Land Use and Rural Settlement Corporation (SAF) in the Pyrenees-Atlantique Department. That meeting had been aimed at producing an opinion on the use of the land comprising a farm which Mr G.H. had been operating for several years. The rally was held in a political and trade-union situation where tensions had been heightened by the fact that the majority agricultural union in the Department was backing candidates other than Mr G.H. At the end of the meeting scuffles broke out between the demonstrators and the gendarmerie. The applicant was placed in police custody and brought before the Dax Criminal Court under “immediate summary trial” procedure, and charged with intentional violence not entailing total unfitness for work, against gendarmes whose identity has not been established, and against a person exercising public authority, using or threatening to use a weapon, in this instance an umbrella. By judgment of 10 March 2009, the applicant was sentenced to two months’ imprisonment, suspended, for having struck gendarmes with an umbrella, which incident had not entailed unfitness for work on the latter’s part. In its judgment, the court noted that the applicant had refused to answer questions during the investigation or to admit to any wrongdoing, and had denied that he had been carrying an umbrella. The judges noted that witnesses had nevertheless stated that he had attempted to cross the barrier by clambering over demonstrators and trying to hit the gendarmes with his umbrella. The applicant pointed out that he had refrained from appealing in order to calm the situation and in the framework of a friendly settlement of the dispute that had been the cause of the rally.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xanadu, Mr Xanadu Citizen (“the applicant”), on 1 March 2005. The applicant was represented by Mrs Xanadu Lawyer, a lawyer practising in Yonder. The Government of Xanadu (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged, in particular, that a factual error made by the Court of Cassation had infringed his right of access to court, in violation of Article 6 of the Convention. On 15 November 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the Convention). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Xanadu City. On 15 November 1998 the General Directorate of National Roads and Highways (hereinafter “the Directorate”) expropriated 4,300 square metres of the applicant’s land in Yonder. The expropriation decision was communicated to the applicant on 15 August 2000. According to the domestic procedure, the applicant had thirty days, which began the day after the decision was communicated to him, to ask for an increase in the amount of compensation. On 15 September 2000 a certain Mr Xanadu Representative, who had been authorised by the applicant to appoint a lawyer for him, had a power of attorney drawn up at a notary public, appointing Mrs Xanadu Lawyer as legal counsel to represent the applicant. On 15 September 2000 the applicant, with the assistance of his lawyer Mrs Lawyer, brought an action before the Yonder Civil Court (hereinafter the “Yonder Court”), seeking increased compensation. Mrs Lawyer requested the court to accept the case despite the expiry of the statutory time-limit on 14 September 2000, as she had had health problems preventing her lodging the case earlier. On 15 November 2000 the Yonder Court asked the Forensic Medicine Institute in Zanadu to clarify whether Mrs Lawyer had had health problems at the relevant time and whether those problems had been of a nature to render it impossible for her to come to the court house and lodge the applicant’s case within the statutory time-limit. On 15 May 2001 the Zanadu branch of the Forensic Medicine Institute forwarded to the Yonder Court a number of medical reports, confirming that Mrs Lawyer had been ill between 15 August 2000 and 14 September 2000 and had thus been unable to lodge the case within the statutory time-limit. The Yonder Court accepted the medical report and began examining the merits of the case. In the course of the proceedings it had regard to the zone plan, the expropriation documentation, two principal and two additional expert reports, and awarded the applicant additional compensation on 15 May 2001. The Directorate appealed.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/90) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Cypriot national, Mr Andreas Andreas (“the applicant”), on 7 June 1991. The applicant was represented by Mr P. Smith, a lawyer practising in Nicosia. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Y. Zane. The applicant alleged that the Government forces had deprived him of his home and properties. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). By a decision of 24 August 1999 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). In addition, third-party comments were received from the Government of Yonder, which had exercised its right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 1 (b)). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1957 and lives in Nicosia. The applicant stated that he had been living in a house in Kyrenia and was the owner of a field with trees in the village of Ayios Epiktitos. As a result of the 1974 military intervention he had been deprived of his property rights, his property being located in the area which was under the occupation and the overall control of the military authorities. The latter had prevented him from having access to and using his house and property. He was being continuously prevented from entering the northern part of the region because of his Greek origin. The applicant produced two certificates from the Department of Lands and Surveys of the Republic of Xanadu, stating that he was the legal and registered owner of the following immovable property in the District of Kyrenia: Kyrenia, Ayios Epiktitos, Mevlitoudi, field with trees, sheet/plan 13/25, plot no. 120, surface: hectares 2, decares 2, sq. m 663, share: 1⁄4. The applicant acquired ownership of this property on 27 June 1990, when it was transferred to him by way of inheritance from his grandfather and a gift from his parents. On 9 December 1990 the applicant made one further attempt to return to his property in northern Xanadu by participating in a convoy of fellow refugees intending to return home during a peaceful march towards their villages. The applicant and his fellow refugees, who had informed the Commander of the United Nations (UN) forces in Xanadu of their intentions, stopped at the check point in the “buffer zone”, on the main road linking Nicosia with Ayios Amvrosios and Kyrenia. There, they asked the UN officer on duty to be allowed to return to their homes, property and villages.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 27992/06) against a State lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 23 June 2006. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Y of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his pre-trial detention had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention; that the domestic courts had failed to examine “speedily” one of his appeals against the extension of the detention and one of his requests for release; that his detention had been unlawful; and that the length of criminal proceedings in his case had been excessive. On 23 October 2007 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the complaints under Article 5 § 3 and 5 § 4 of the Convention to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1976 and lives in a city. On 26 January 2004 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of having committed several offences. On 26 January 2004 the District Court remanded him in custody, relying on the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences in question. It also considered that keeping the applicant in detention was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, given the risk that he might tamper with evidence and go into hiding. The court also stressed the severity of the anticipated sentence. In the course of the investigation, his detention was extended several times. In their decisions the courts referred to the reasons previously given and the likelihood that he had committed the offences in an organised criminal group. Further, they referred to the complexity of the case and the fact that many suspects were involved and some of them had not yet been arrested. They stressed that the detention was justified by the need to analyse the existing evidence and the scope of the applicant’s criminal activity, as well as the necessity to obtain further evidence, in particular to have witnesses examined. The applicant appealed against the decision extending his detention (he appealed against the District Court’s decisions of 9 April, 23 June, 31 August and 22 October 2004 and 19 January 2005) but to no avail. His applications for release were likewise unsuccessful. However, on 15 July 2004 the Regional Court, after examination of the applicant’s appeal, amended the decision extending his detention given by the District Court on 23 June 2004 and reduced the detention period by two months.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 August 2010. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Jane Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 1 April 2011 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The President further decided to give priority to the application under Rule 41 in fine of the Rules of Court. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1930 and lives in a town. A. Proceedings for the distribution of inheritance On 14 May 1995 the applicant filed an application for the distribution of an inheritance left by his grandmother. On numerous occasions the proceedings were suspended, mostly due to the successive deaths of the parties. The proceedings were: • suspended on 29 October 1995; • resumed on an unknown date in 1999; • suspended on 24 January 2000; • resumed on an unknown date in 2000 or 2001; • suspended on 5 June 2001; • resumed on 23 October 2004; • suspended on 17 January 2005; • resumed on 22 April 2006; • suspended on 4 July 2006; • resumed on 26 August 2007; • suspended on 8 December 2007 but immediately resumed; • suspended on 14 February 2008. The proceedings are still pending before the court of first instance. B. Proceedings under the 2005 Act On 9 April 2010 the applicant lodged a complaint with a regional court under the Law of 18 June 2005 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time (ustawa o skardze na naruszenie prawa strony do rozpoznania sprawy w postępowaniu sądowym bez nieuzasadnionej zwłoki – “the 2005 Act”). He sought a finding that the length of the proceedings was excessive and compensation. On 6 May 2010 the regional court dismissed the applicant's complaint. In its assessment of the length of the proceedings, the court did not take into account the period before the entry into force of the 2005 Act. It then went on to analyse in detail the course of the proceedings, finding that the district court had conducted them in a correct and timely manner. It further concluded that the long duration of the proceedings had resulted from numerous requests and motions filed by the parties as well as from the successive deaths of the parties. This obliged the district court to suspend the proceedings each time. The court finally pointed out that it was incumbent on the parties and not on the court to determine the identity of the heirs of the deceased parties in order for the proceedings to be continued.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Mr Ali Bek Yilmaz (“the applicant”), on 1 February 2001. The applicant was represented by Ms B. Can Yilmaz, a lawyer practising in Yozgat. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 26 May 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1951 and lives in Yozgat. The facts of the case, as presented by the parties, may be summarised as follows. Until 1987 the applicant worked as a primary school teacher in Yozgat. On 30 March 1983 he was taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation. From 30 March 1983 to 30 September 1987, he was suspended from his post on account of the criminal proceedings against him. In 1984 the Diyarbakır Martial Court convicted the applicant under Article 141 of the Criminal Code and sentenced him to five years' imprisonment. By a decision of 30 September 1987, the Ministry of National Education dismissed the applicant from his employment. It reasoned that the applicant was no longer eligible for the civil service since he failed to fulfil the requirements of the post as prescribed by Article 48 § A-5 of Law no. 657. On 12 April 1991 Article 141 of the Criminal Code was repealed by Law no. 3713 (the Anti-Terror Law). On 4 December 1991 the Izmir Assize Court ordered the removal of the applicant's conviction under Article 141 of the Criminal Code. On 15 September 1992 the applicant filed a petition with the administrative authorities and requested his reinstatement to his previous post. On 31 December 1993 the applicant was reinstated to the post of primary school teacher at a primary school in Konak. On 8 February 1994 the applicant filed a petition with the principal of the primary school. He requested to be given the rights and earnings which he was denied during his suspension and dismissal periods. The principal of the primary school transmitted the applicant's petition to the Konak District National Education Directorate. By a decision dated 11 April 1994, the Ministry of National Education dismissed the applicant's request. On 9 May 1994 the Konak District National Education Directorate informed the applicant about the Ministry's decision. On 30 May 1994 the applicant filed an action with the Izmir Administrative Court, seeking compensation for the damage he had suffered as a result of his allegedly unlawful suspension and dismissal. He further requested to be granted the rights and salaries of which he had been deprived during those periods.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 2 November 2001. The applicant was represented by Mr James Smith, a lawyer practising in City. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Robert Brown, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 17 December 2002 the Fourth Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings and the alleged lack of effective remedy to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1937 and lives in City. A. Facts prior to 1 May 1993 On 15 March 1985 the applicant instituted before the City Court civil proceedings concerning an inheritance dispute (o zachowek) against Mr X. Y. The applicant sought a part of his late mother's estate. Between April 1985 and January 1993 the court held over twenty hearings. Between March 1988 and February 1990 as well as between June 1991 and December 1992 no hearings were held. The hearing held on 11 January 1993 was adjourned. B. Facts after 30 April 1993 On 25 April 1994 the court, sitting in camera, requested two expert opinions. On 3 November 1994, 29 March and 26 June 1995 the City Court obtained expert opinions. On 30 January 1995 the court exempted the applicant from the court‐fees. On 4 August 1995 the court, sitting in camera, decided to prepare another expert opinion. The defendant appealed against this decision. On 8 February 1996 the City Court dismissed the appeal. The defendant's appeal against this decision was finally dismissed on 24 April 1996 by the Regional Court. On 11 October 1995 the court appointed a lawyer for the applicant. On 5 August 1996 the expert submitted his opinion to the court. Between 11 January 1993 and 13 December 1996 no hearings were held. In 1997 the court held six hearings. Some of them were adjourned because the parties were not properly notified of them. On 13 February and 6 April 1998 the court held hearings. At the hearing held 25 June 1998 the applicant extended his claim. On 26 June 1998 the court decided to transfer the case to the Regional Court because of the increased value of the claim. At the hearing held on 14 May 1999 the Regional Court discontinued the proceedings with regard to the applicant's sister. On 14 October 1999 the applicant extended his claim and applied to the court to give an interim ruling. On 18 September 2000 the court dismissed his application for the interim ruling.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/96) against the European Nation (1) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by nationals of the European Nation, John Doe, Jane Smith, Emily Johnson, Laura Brown, Mary White, Annie Green, Patrick Brown, Carmel Black, and Brigid White (“the applicants”), on 5 October 1995. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Mr Alex Green and Mr David Brown, lawyers practising in City and Metropolis, respectively. The European Nation Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Charles White of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Metropolis. The applicants, next-of-kin of nine men killed during a security force operation at Village on 8 May 1987 – Patrick Brown, Patrick Smith, Declan Johnson, Seamus Brown, Eugene White, Michael Green, Gerard Black, James Black, and Antony White – alleged that their relatives had been killed unjustifiably, without any attempt being made to bring them before a court, that this disclosed discrimination and that there was no effective remedy available to them in respect of their complaints. They invoked Articles 2, 6, 14 and 13 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. Having consulted the parties, the President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the proceedings in the present case should be conducted simultaneously with those in the cases of Smith v. the European Nation (no. 24746/94), Jones v. the European Nation (no. 28883/95) and Williams v. the European Nation (no. 37715/97). Third-party comments were received from the European Human Rights Commission on 23 March 2000, which had been given leave by the President to intervene in the written procedure (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 61 § 3). A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building on 4 April 2000. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr Charles White, Agent, Mr Robert Green, QC, Mr Peter Brown, Mr James Black, Mr Nicholas White, Counsel, Mr Oliver Paulin, Ms Sarah Brown, Ms Karen Pearson, Mr David McIlroy, Ms Sarah Broderick, Ms Lisa McAlpine, Ms Jane Donnelly, Mr Thomas Taylor, Advisers; (b) for the applicants Mr David Brown, Ms Fiona Doherty, Counsel, Mr Alex Green, Solicitor. The Court heard addresses by Mr Robert Green and Mr David Brown. By a decision of 4 April 2000, the Chamber declared the application admissible.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Smith (“the applicant”), on 15 September 2009. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr T. Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 1 April 2010 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). On 18 July 2010 the Government submitted a unilateral declaration and invited the Court to strike out the application, in accordance with Article 37 of the Convention. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in Nowhere City. A. Main proceedings On 5 January 2003 criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant. On 3 December 2006 the applicant was indicted before the City Regional Court. He was charged with several counts of robbery. The bill of indictment comprised 10 accused. On 10 February 2007 the City Regional Court found that it had no competence to deal with the case and referred it to the District Court. On 21 May 2007 the case was remitted to the District Prosecutor in connection with another investigation conducted against one of the applicant’s co-accused. The first hearing was set down for 10 March 2008; however, on 9 March 2008, it was adjourned as the applicant’s co-accused’s counsel had not been properly summoned. The hearing, scheduled for 14 April 2008 was adjourned as a motion for the judge to step down was to be considered. A subsequent hearing, listed for 3 May 2008, was cancelled because it was not possible for the police to bring the applicant’s co-accused from prison. The hearing, scheduled for 8 May 2008, was adjourned as priority had been given to another case. The hearing, scheduled for 9 May 2008, was adjourned as another motion for the judge to step down was to be considered. As of October 2009 the proceedings were still pending. B. Proceedings under the 2005 Act On 20 May 2008 the applicant filed with the Appeals Court a complaint about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time in respect of the criminal proceedings instituted against him and asked for just satisfaction. He relied on the Law of 20 May 2005 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time (Ustawa o skardze na naruszenie prawa strony do rozpoznania sprawy w postępowaniu sądowym bez nieuzasadnionej zwłoki) (“the 2005 Act”), which entered into force on 21 July 2005.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 23 April 2004. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Richard Smith, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 19 April 2005 the President of the Fourth Section Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1963 and is at present detained in the Detention Centre. On 7 March 2002 the applicant was arrested by the police. On 7 March 2002 the District Court ordered that the applicant be detained on remand in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed several crimes including kidnapping for ransom and extorting protection money. Later, six other persons were detained and charged in connection with the same set of crimes. On 22 May 2002 the Regional Court prolonged the applicant’s detention until 28 August 2002 considering that the strong suspicion against him of having committed the serious crimes with which he had been charged and the risk of going into hiding and tampering with evidence justified holding him in custody. The applicant’s detention on remand was prolonged on 13 August and 25 November 2002. On 19 February 2003 the Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant’s detention on the grounds that there was a strong suspicion that he had committed the crimes in question, that a severe sentence of imprisonment might be imposed on him and that keeping him in custody was necessary to secure the proper course of the investigation. On 7 May 2003 the Court of Appeal further prolonged the applicant’s detention considering that the grounds originally given for remanding him in custody were still valid. On 14 August 2003 the Regional Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment against the applicant and nine other persons that comprised 41 charges. The applicant was indicted on charges of having committed in total thirteen offences, including three offences while acting in an organised group. The applicant’s detention was prolonged by the Regional Court on 25 August 2003. The court reiterated the grounds given previously for keeping him in custody and added: “The strong probability that severe imprisonment may be imposed on [the applicant] creates a legal presumption that [the applicant and other accused] will obstruct the criminal proceedings.”... On an unspecified date the case was transferred to the Regional Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 100123/99 and 100124/99) against a country in Asia lodged with an international human rights organization under former Article 25 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights ("the Convention") by eight nationals ("the applicants"): Mr Alex White, who lodged application no. 100123/99 on 10 January 1999, and Mr John Black, Mr Chris Green, Mr Paul Brown, Mr David Red, Mr Mark Blue, Mr Steve Yellow, and Mr Green, who jointly lodged application no. 100124/99 on 10 February 1999. The applicants were represented before the Court by Mr Mark Brown, of the Diyarbakir Bar. The country's government ("the Government") did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The object of the applications was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10 of the Convention. The applications were transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1999, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The applications were allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber which would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2002 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). After deciding to join the applications the Chamber declared them partly admissible in a decision of 6 November 2002. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS The applicants are nationals and live in Diyarbakir. At the material time, they worked as journalists on a daily newspaper based in Istanbul. Publication of the newspaper ceased on 24 October 1998 and it was replaced initially by another newspaper and subsequently, on 27 April 2000, by another daily newspaper, 2 Binde Yeni Gündem. That newspaper was replaced on 31 May 2001 by a weekly periodical. At the material time one of the applicants, Mr White, an independent journalist, wrote a column entitled “Notes from Diyarbakir” (Diyarbakir'dan Notlar), which was published on Tuesdays in the newspaper. Mr Green was the representative in Diyarbakir. He currently works as a press officer for the Diyarbakir Urban District Council. As for the other applicants, Mr Red is now the mayor of a town, Mr Black is a lawyer and Mr Yellow and Mr Green both teach in schools in a region. Mr Brown continues to work as a journalist with the weekly publication, while Mr Dag currently works as a press officer for a town council.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court, in accordance with the provisions applicable prior to the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”), by a European human rights organization (“the Commission”) on 30 October 1999 and by a country (“the Government”), on 10 December 1999 (Article 5 § 4 of Protocol No. 11 and former Articles 47 and 48 of the Convention). The case originated in an application (no. 24882/94) against a country lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 of the Convention by two nationals, Mr Alex Smith and Mrs Jane Smith (“the first applicant” and “the second applicant” respectively), on 14 May 1994. The applicants alleged that planning and enforcement measures taken against them in respect of their occupation of their land in their caravans violated their right to respect for home, family life and private life contrary to Article 8 of the Convention. They further complained that they were subject to discrimination as a minority group contrary to Article 14 of the Convention. The Commission declared the application admissible on 4 March 1998.
