PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of that country, Ms Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 April 2000. The applicant was represented by Ms L. Smith, a lawyer practising in Cambridge. The government of that country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr A. Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, London. The applicant complained of the installation and use by the police of a covert listening device at her place of work. The case as declared admissible raises complaints under Article 8 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 22 October 2002, the Court declared the application partly admissible, partly inadmissible. The applicant and the government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and is currently serving a sentence of imprisonment in a correctional facility. The applicant owned a workshop in a region and had business connections in a foreign country. She had two vehicles each of which had a false compartment in the fuel tank. The false compartments could hold up to 45 kilograms of a substance. From 1995 she was suspected by the police of being involved in the trafficking of a substance. The police also suspected her of being involved in the handling of stolen goods, including stolen vehicles. On 23 March 1996 she was arrested by the local police in relation to their suspicions of her handling stolen goods. Whilst she was in custody, a listening device was installed at her workshop premises which remained there and active until 30 August 1996 when it was discovered. On 31 January 1997 an indictment was signed charging the applicant with conspiracy to import a substance and conspiracy to supply a substance, namely cannabis. The prosecution evidence against the applicant relied on tape recordings made from the listening device which had been installed by the police at the applicant’s workshop premises. It was acknowledged by the prosecution that without the evidence from the tapes, there was no prima facie case against the applicant. The applicant objected to the admission of the tape recordings as evidence in her trial.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 4819/02) against a State (Republic of Turkey) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (Turkish national), Mr X (“the applicant”), on 6 June 2001. The applicant was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in a city (Istanbul). The State (Republic of Turkey) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 13 September 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the State. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in a city (Istanbul). The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. On an unspecified date in 1993, a detained member of an organisation (Workers' Party of Kurdistan) confessed to the authorities that a number of lawyers, among whom was the applicant, had been operating as undercover members of the organisation. Upon his confession, the public prosecutor attached to the State Security Court of a city (Diyarbakır) initiated a criminal investigation. On 23 November 1993 the applicant was taken into custody, where he denied any association with the organisation. On 20 December 1993 he was brought before a judge, who ordered his release pending trial. On 22 December 1993 the prosecutor filed an indictment, charging the applicant, together with twenty-two other lawyers, with being a member of the organisation. The specific charges against him included the transmission of messages, documents and money among the incarcerated members, the sheltering and healing of a wounded militant and the delivery of 2 kilograms of a substance belonging to the organisation from a city (Diyarbakır) to a city (Istanbul). The prosecutor subsequently charged nine other persons with similar crimes. Their cases were also joined to that of the applicant. With a hearing on 17 February 1994, the State Security Court of a city (Diyarbakır) began the trial. At the same hearing, it ordered the release of all the accused who had not been already released by then. On 19 September 1996 the prosecutor filed his observations on the merits. On 18 June 1999 the Constitution was amended and the military judge sitting on the bench of the State Security Court of a city (Diyarbakır) was replaced by a civilian judge. On 21 December 2000 Law no. 4616 governing conditional release, discontinuation of proceedings and suspension of the execution of sentences for offences committed before 23 April 1999 came into force. On 22 February 2001 the court held that all of the accused were eligible, under the new legislation, for the discontinuation of the proceedings against them. Accordingly, it discontinued the proceedings against the applicant, to be resumed only if he were to be convicted of an offence of the same or a more serious kind within a five-year period.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 36887/97) against Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 6 March 1997. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in a city. The Government were represented successively by their Agents, Ms Z, Mr A, and Dr B, all of the Department of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that section 52 of the Offences Against the State Act 1939 constituted a violation of the rights guaranteed by Articles 6, 10 and 13 of the Convention. On 1 July 1998 the Commission decided to communicate to the Government the applicant’s complaints under Articles 6 and 10 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. Mr C, the judge elected in respect of Ireland, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Government accordingly appointed Ms D, the judge elected in respect of Croatia, to sit in his place (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). By a decision of 21 September 1999, the Court declared admissible the applicant’s complaints under Articles 6 and 10 of the Convention. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) and the parties replied in writing to each other’s observations on the merits. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 7 June 1996, at approximately 6.00 a.m., two police officers left a city in an unmarked police car escorting a van carrying significant sums of money on its way to a village. When the two vehicles arrived at the post office in the village, the police car was rammed from behind by a stolen vehicle and immediately surrounded by five heavily armed and masked individuals dressed in paramilitary style uniforms. One of the five opened fire at point blank range on the police officers. One of those officers died instantly and the other was seriously wounded. The police suspected a local unit of an unlawful paramilitary organisation and the organisation later claimed responsibility for the murder.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/09) against the Republic of Andria (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Andrian nationals, Ms Alice Andria and Ms Beatrice Borealis (“the applicants”), on 15 January 2008. The applicants were represented by Mr Charles Dexter, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Andrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 12 June 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1927 and 1933 respectively and live in Andria. In 2004 the General Directorate of Highways seized a plot of land belonging to the applicants without any formal expropriation, for the construction of a highway. The applicants brought an action before the Andria Civil Court to obtain compensation for the de facto expropriation of their property. They requested 5,500 Andrian liras (AND) as compensation from the court and reserved their right to increase this claim in due course. On 22 June 2006 the Andria Civil Court awarded the applicants AND 5,500 as compensation for the de facto expropriation of their land, as requested, plus interest. The applicants initiated execution proceedings before the Andria Execution Office to obtain that amount (file no. 2009/2799). On 13 March 2007 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. The applicants subsequently brought an additional action (“ek dava”) before the Andria Civil Court to obtain further compensation for their land in the light of the expert report obtained during the previous proceedings, which had valued the land at a rate higher than that initially requested by them. On 24 May 2007 the Andria Civil Court awarded the applicants AND 34,529, plus interest. The applicants initiated another set of execution proceedings before the Andria Execution Office to obtain the amount awarded (file no. 2007/6186). On 16 October 2007 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Andria Civil Court. On 25 March and 13 November 2009 the administration paid AND 8,878 and 53,411 respectively. According to the information provided by the applicants, there has been no outstanding debt in the execution files.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms. Anna Novakova (“the applicant”) on 15 October 2002. The applicant was not legally represented. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. K. Zawadski of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 28 July 2007 the President of the Fifth Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Warsaw. A. Facts prior to 1 May 1993 On 3 May 1990 the applicant asked the Warsaw District Court to declare that she had been the beneficiary of an inheritance from a certain N.K. on the basis of a will made before a notary on 25 February 1975. On 28 September 1990 the other party to the proceedings, a certain W.X., lodged her own inheritance claim and asked the same court to declare that she had received an inheritance from her sister – N.K. – on the basis of the above-mentioned will made before a notary on 22 November 1988. On 13 November 1990 a hearing was held. The applicant asked for the annulment of a will made on 22 November 1988 in favour W.X. On 16 March 1991 a psychiatric opinion (opinia sądowo‐psychiatryczna) concerning the testator's state of health between 1975 and 1988 was obtained. At hearings scheduled between 1 October 1992 and 1 February 1993 evidence was heard from over 20 witnesses. B. Facts after 30 April 1993 On 30 October 1994 the court obtained a second psychiatric opinion prepared by an expert from the Warsaw Medical Academy (Akademia Medyczna). On 11 February 1995 the Warsaw District Court asked the Poznan Medical Academy for an expert report to be prepared by the Institute of Psychiatry – the so-called “institute opinion” (opinia instytucjonalna). On 21 April 1995 the Poznan Medical Academy informed the Warsaw District Court about the state of preparation of the report. On 11 July 1995 the Poznan Medical Academy informed the Warsaw District Court that, due to the holiday season, it was not possible to prepare the above-mentioned “institute opinion”. It asked the Warsaw District Court whether it would accept an expert opinion given by two experts in psychiatry. On 22 July 1995 the President of the Warsaw District Court agreed. The opinion was submitted on 9 May 1996. The fourth expert's report in the case was submitted on 25 September 1997. At a hearing held on 24 December 1997 the Warsaw District Court gave a decision. It was served on the applicant's lawyer on 28 January 1998. On 25 February 1998 the applicant appealed.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 37770/97) against a country lodged with an organization under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms by a national, John Doe, on 19 July 1997. The government of the country were represented by their Agent, Mr. X Drzewicki and subsequently Mr. Y of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The national alleged, in particular, that his right to “a hearing within a reasonable time” had not been respected. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 12 November 2002 the Court declared the application admissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The national was born in 1952 and lives in a city. On 31 July 1992 the national sued a co-operative in a regional court, seeking repayment of his indexed membership shares. On 29 April 1993 the national asked the court to list a hearing. On 21 September 1993 the court held the first hearing and requested the national to submit certain documents. On 25 September 1993 the national submitted to the court his pleadings together with the relevant documents. On 17 May 1994 the court held the second hearing. It ordered an accountant of the co-operative to provide information about the management of the co-operative's assets. The documents were submitted to the court on 1 October 1994. The third hearing was held on 23 March 1995. On 4 May 1995 the national requested that the court issue an interim order and restrain the co-operative from selling or encumbering its property in order to safeguard his claim. On 5 July 1995 the court refused to issue the interim order. The national appealed against this decision. On 7 September 1995 the Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance decision. On 16 November 1995 the regional court held the fourth hearing. The accountant of the co-operative summoned as a witness failed to appear due to illness. The next hearing, listed for 16 April 1996, was adjourned on the ground that the presiding judge was ill. On 20 April 1996 the national complained, invoking Article 6 of the Convention, about the length of the proceedings to the President of the regional court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1448/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two individuals, Mr X and Miss Y (“the applicants”) on 2 January 2004. The applicants were granted legal aid. The applicants maintained, in particular, that the manner in which the compulsory lessons in religious culture and ethics were taught infringed their rights as guaranteed by the second sentence of Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 9 of the Convention. In a decision of 6 June 2006, the Chamber declared the application admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 3 October 2006 (Rule 59 § 3 of the Rules of Court). There appeared before the Court: – for the Government Mr M. Özmen, Co-Agent, Mr H. Ünler, Ms Z.G. Acar, Ms E. Esin, Ms D. Kilislioğlu, Mr İ. Aycan, Mr S. Duman, Advisers; – for the applicants Mr K. Genç, Counsel, Mr A.Ş. Yakişan, Ms İ. Melikoff Mr T. Öker, Advisers, Mr X, First applicant. The Court heard addresses by Mr Genç and Mr Özmen. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE Mr X, who was born in 1960, and his daughter Ms Y, who was born in 1988, live in a city. At the time Mr X lodged the application on his own and his daughter's behalf, she was attending the seventh grade of the state school in a district of the city. A. Background to the case Mr X stated that his family were adherents of a belief system. This belief system originated in central Asia but developed largely in Turkey. Two important figures had a considerable impact on the emergence of this religious movement. This belief system, which has deep roots in Turkish society and history, is generally considered as one of the branches of Islam, influenced in particular by Sufism and by certain pre-Islamic beliefs. Its religious practices differ from those of the Sunni schools of law in certain aspects such as prayer, fasting and pilgrimage. According to the applicant, this belief system is a belief or philosophy influenced by other cultures, religions and philosophies. It represents one of the most widespread faiths in Turkey after the Hanafite branch of Islam. It advocates close contact with nature, tolerance, modesty and love for one's neighbour, within the Islamic faith. The adherents of this belief system reject the sharia (code of laws in orthodox Islam) and the sunna (forms of behaviour and formal rules of orthodox Islam) and defend freedom of religion, human rights, women's rights, humanism, democracy, rationalism, modernism, universalism, tolerance and secularism. The adherents do not pray by the Sunni rite (in particular, they do not comply with the obligation to pray five times daily) but express their devotion through religious songs and dances (semah); they do not attend mosques, but meet regularly in cemevi (meeting and worship rooms) for ritual ceremonies.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 September 2002. The applicant was represented by Mr X.Y. Z and Ms A.B. C, lawyers practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 12 January 2007 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in a city. The applicant owns a flat in a city. Based on a construction permit issued by the city municipality on 15 January 1992, construction works were commenced on neighbouring land to build an apartment block. The limitations concerning the height of the building were not respected and, as a result, the sea view from the applicant’s flat, which is situated on the sixth floor, was blocked by the new building. On an unspecified date, the applicant initiated administrative proceedings against the city municipality for the annulment of the construction permit. He maintained that the permit was in breach of city planning regulations. On 28 June 1996 the city administrative court found in the applicant’s favour and annulled the construction permit. On 15 March 1997 the supreme administrative court upheld the decision of the city administrative court. The applicant asked the city municipality to enforce the decision of the city administrative court, but his request was rejected. On 18 October 1999 the applicant initiated compensation proceedings before the city administrative court on account of the municipality’s failure to implement the court order of 15 March 1997. He requested both pecuniary and non-pecuniary compensation, stating that the non-enforcement of the final court decision which had annulled the construction permit had diminished his flat’s value. On 19 November 1999 the city administrative court partially upheld the applicant’s claim, awarding him pecuniary compensation, but refusing non-pecuniary damages. On 26 April 2001 the supreme administrative court upheld the city administrative court’s decision in respect of pecuniary damage. However, finding that the applicant was also entitled to non-pecuniary compensation, it quashed the judgment in this respect. Subsequent to this decision, the municipality paid the pecuniary compensation to the applicant. On 1 November 2001 the city administrative court awarded 250,000,000 local currency to the applicant in respect of non-pecuniary damage. On 16 April 2003, considering the amount of non-pecuniary compensation insufficient, the supreme administrative court quashed the judgment of the city administrative court once again. On 19 December 2003 the city administrative court insisted on maintaining its judgment. The applicant appealed. On 16 June 2006 the supreme administrative court quashed the judgment of the city administrative court of 19 December 2003.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 November 2004. The applicant was represented by Mrs Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in Cityville. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Jane Doe, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs. The applicant alleged that the relevant provisions of the Civil Code relating to custody and their application by the courts had discriminated against him as the father of a child born out of wedlock. Furthermore, he alleged that the District Court had failed to hold a hearing to discuss the decisive expert opinion and, more generally, that it had failed to hear him in person. By a decision of 30 September 2008 the Court declared the application admissible. Neither party filed further observations on the merits of the case. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1977 and lives in Townsville. The applicant’s son K. was born out of wedlock on 30 May 2001. The child was given the applicant’s family name by decision of the District Administrative Authority of 30 June 2001. At that time K.’s mother was living as a tenant in the applicant’s house, in a separate apartment. The applicant was sharing an apartment with his long-term partner, U., who later became his wife, and their son D. aged six at that time. During K’s first year the applicant took parental leave and took care of him together with U. Subsequently, K’s mother took parental leave. In early January 2003 K’s mother moved out of the applicant’s house. On 29 January 2003 the applicant asked the District Court to transfer sole custody of K. to him under Article 176 of the Civil Code. He submitted in particular that he and U. had mainly taken care of K. and that the child’s mother was not capable of doing so. The latter opposed the transfer of custody. At that stage and at all subsequent stages of the proceedings the applicant was assisted by counsel. By letter of 15 February 2003 the Youth Office, which had been following the case since summer 2002, expressed the view that both parents were capable of exercising custody. On 15 March 2003 the applicant and K’s mother appeared before the District Court and were heard by the judge. According to the minutes, the applicant requested that the opinion of an expert in child psychology be taken. K’s mother agreed to that request.

PROCEDURE The case originated in four applications (nos. 12345/01, 12346/01, 12347/01 and 12348/01) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by four nationals, Mr John Doe, Mr Richard Roe, Mr William Smith and Mr George Brown (“the applicants”), on 27 October 2001 (Mr Doe), 26 September 2001 (Mr Roe), and 29 September 2001 (Mr Smith and Mr Brown). The European country Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Charles Smith of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, London. Mr Roe, Mr Smith and Mr Brown were represented by Ms Patricia Green, a solicitor practising in London. Mr Doe was not represented before the Court. By decisions dated 18 June 2002 (application no. 12345/01) and 8 April 2003 (nos. 12346/01, 12347/01 and 12348/01), the Court declared the applications partly admissible. In September 2003 the applications were adjourned pending the conclusion of related domestic proceedings (see paragraph 26-28 below). On 1 July 2005 the Court invited the parties to submit observations on the merits. The Government and the applicants represented by Ms Green requested a hearing on the merits. On the date of the adoption of the present judgment the Court decided that a hearing would not be necessary. By a letter dated 2 August 2006, Mr Smith, Mr Brown and Mr Roe informed the Court that they had reached a friendly settlement with the Government in respect of their claims for Widowed Mother’s Allowance and/or Widow’s Payment, for the following sums: GBP 19,164.94 damages plus GBP 2,469.84 costs for Mr Roe; GB 7,767.59 damages plus GBP 2,699.40 costs for Mr Brown; GBP 11,783.98 damages plus GBP 1,860.00 costs for Mr Smith. By a letter dated 24 July 2006, the non-governmental organisation Liberty sought leave to submit third-party observations in the case. The request was rejected by the President of the Chamber on 28 August 2006. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASES The facts of each case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. A. Mr Doe, no. 12345/01 Mr John Doe is a European national, born in 1922 and living in a city. The applicant’s spouse died on 25 February 1999. On 11 October 2000 he contacted the Revenue (“R”) and applied for widow’s bereavement allowance (“WBA”: see paragraph 21 below) for the years 1998/9 and 1999/2000. He was informed that he did not qualify for the tax allowance, since he was a man and the law provided only for payments to widows. B. Mr Roe, no. 12346/01 Mr Roe was born on 21 May 1958 and lives in a town. He was widowed on 14 October 1996. There were two children of the marriage, born in 1988 and 1994. In around November 1996 the applicant telephoned the Revenue requesting an allowance equivalent to that received by a widow.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Ali Xan. On 15 March 2001. The applicant was represented before the Court by Mr John Doe, a lawyer practising in Yonder. The Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 10 June 2003 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the length of detention on remand, the right to a fair trial by an independent and impartial court within a reasonable time, the right to be presumed innocent and the right to examine witnesses. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant filed observations on the merits and admissibility on a timely basis (Rule 59 § 1). The Government submitted their observations outside the time limit. They have therefore not been admitted to the case file. On 15 October 2003 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 14 May 1992 the applicant was taken into custody in Zephyr by police officers from the Delta Security Department on suspicion of membership of a terrorist organisation, and he was held in custody until 9 June 1992. On 9 June 1992 the Alpha Civil Court of First Instance ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. On 17 June 1992 the Beta State Security Court filed a bill of indictment accusing the applicant of membership of an illegal terrorist organisation and aiding and abetting the said organization, contrary to Article 125 of the Xanadu Criminal Code. On 25 June 1992 the Beta State Security Court commenced the trial against the applicant and two other suspects and prolonged the applicant’s detention. The State Security Court considered the applicant’s continued detention on 50 occasions, either on its own motion or upon the applicant’s request. On each occasion, the applicant’s continued detention was ordered having regard to the nature of the offence, the state of evidence and the content of the file. On 28 November 2000, after holding 50 hearings, the Beta State Security Court convicted the applicant under Article 146 of the Criminal Code and sentenced him to death, since commuted to life imprisonment. On 10 December 2001, upon the applicant’s appeal, the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the State Security Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of X (hereinafter "the State") lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a stateless person, Mr X Y Z ("the applicant"), on 2 December 2001. The applicant was represented by Mr A B C, a lawyer practising in Y. The State Government ("the State Authorities") were represented by their Agent, Ms D E F, of the Ministry of Justice. On 22 December 2006 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. On 1 May 2007 this case was assigned to the newly composed Sixth Section (Rules 25 § 1 and 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, Mr X Y Z, was born in 1960 in Z. At the time of lodging his application, he was detained in Y. He is currently living in Z. On 1 August 1985 the Y Z District Court issued an arrest warrant in respect of the applicant on the ground that he was strongly suspected of having murdered A. On 19 July 1991 the Y Z District Court issued a further arrest warrant in respect of the applicant and five other suspects, born in Z, L, or M. The court accused the applicant of having prepared, with others, a bomb attack at the "B" discotheque in Y on 5 April 1987 in order to kill as many members of the American armed forces as possible. During this terrorist attack, three people had been killed and 104 seriously injured. On 1 September 1993 the applicant was arrested by the police in Z and was subsequently taken into detention with a view to extradition. On 21 June 1995 a Z court acquitted the applicant of A.'s murder but convicted him of forgery and sentenced him to one year and six months’ imprisonment. On 24 May 1997 the applicant was extradited to the State and subsequently held in detention on remand on account of the arrest warrant issued in 1991. On 25 November 1997 the Y Court of Appeal ordered the applicant’s continued detention on remand. It held that the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged resulted, among other things, from the confession of one of the other suspects. The danger of his absconding still persisted because the applicant had been extradited to the State only in May 1997 and had neither a fixed dwelling nor social ties in the State which would prevent him from absconding if released. The court moreover referred to the lifelong prison sentence the applicant faced and underlined that more lenient preventive measures would not be suitable. Lastly, there had been no breach of the obligation to proceed speedily (Beschleunigungsgebot).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Anonymous (“the applicant”), on 3 April 2003. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr John Doe of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 17 September 2007 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1931 and lives in a city. A. Background of the case The applicant’s testators owned a piece of real property in a city. By virtue of the 1945 Decree on the Ownership and Use of Land in a City (Dekret o własności i użytkowaniu gruntów na obszarze m. st. a City) all land in a city was nationalised. The applicant’s testators filed an application for the grant of a right of perpetual use of the real property. On 6 July 1972 the Board of the National Council (Prezydium Rady Narodowej) refused the application. On 12 February 1973 the competent Minister upheld that decision. Simultaneously, the applicant’s testators lodged a claim for compensation. On 22 November 1972 the Board of the National Council dismissed the claim as according to the 1957 Law on exclusion of detached houses and apartments in housing cooperatives’ buildings from public management (Ustawa o wyłączeniu spod publicznej gospodarki lokalami domów jednorodzinnych oraz lokali w domach spółdzielni mieszkaniowych), the real property in question was not a detached house. Consequently, the 1965 Cabinet Resolution allowing for nationalised detached houses to be compensated was not applicable. The applicant’s testators appealed unsuccessfully against this decision. B. Administrative proceedings for compensation On 24 February 1997 the applicant instituted administrative proceedings against the State Treasury for compensation for nationalised family real property. It appears that on several occasions between 1997 and 2000 the applicant lodged complaints, alleging inactivity on the part of the first‐instance authority. On 25 February 2000 the Mayor of a District informed the applicant that the administrative proceedings were in their final stage and in the near future a decision would be issued ordering valuation of the real property. Consequently, the assessment of the amount of compensation would then be possible. On an unspecified date the applicant lodged a complaint about inactivity on the part of the Mayor of the District with the Supreme Administrative Court. On 17 November 2000 the Supreme Administrative Court admitted that the proceedings in question had been lengthy and ordered the Mayor to deal with the case within two months of the judgment being served on the parties.

PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 8319/07 and 11449/07) against the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two individuals, Mr A. Adow Sufi and Mr A. Ibrahim Elmi (“the applicants”), on 21 February 2007 and 14 March 2007 respectively. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Ms N. Mole of the Aire Centre, a lawyer practising in London. The United Kingdom Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr D. Walton of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The applicants alleged that if returned to an unspecified country they would be at real risk of ill-treatment contrary to Article 3 and/or a violation of Article 2 of the Convention. They also complained that their removal would disproportionately interfere with their rights under Article 8 of the Convention. On 23 February 2007 and 14 March 2007 the Acting President of the Chamber to which the cases were allocated decided to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Government that it was desirable in the interests of the parties and the proper conduct of the proceedings that the applicants should not be expelled to the unspecified country pending the Court’s decision. The Court also decided to grant priority to the applications under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court. On 23 February 2007 and 26 March 2007 the Acting President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the case (Rule 59 § 1). At the Government’s request the cases were adjourned on 7 October 2008 pending the decision of the Court of Appeal in HH (Unspecified), AM (Unspecified), J (Unspecified) and MA (Unspecified) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2010] EWCA Civ 426. The adjournment was lifted when the Court of Appeal delivered its judgment on 23 April 2010. The applicants and the Government each filed further observations in October 2010. The Chamber decided to join the applications (Rule 42 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The facts of the case, as submitted by the applicants, may be summarised as follows. A. The first applicant The first applicant, Mr A. Adow Sufi, is a national who was born in 1987 and is currently in detention in an unspecified centre. On 30 September 2003 he entered the United Kingdom clandestinely using false travel documents. On 3 October 2003 he claimed asylum on the ground that as a member of a sub-clan of a minority clan, he had been subjected to persecution by an unspecified militia, who had killed his father and sister and seriously injured him.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 78027/01) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 13 November 2001. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The object of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 5 and 13 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 6 February 2003 the Chamber declared the application admissible and decided to join to the merits its examination of the Government's preliminary objections. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1978 and lives in a city. On 28 October 2001 he was arrested and taken into custody at the gendarmerie command. On 30 October 2001 the gendarmes took a statement from him. He was suspected of having assisted and supported an illegal organisation. He allegedly signed his statement while blindfolded. At the end of his detention in the gendarmes' custody, he was examined by a forensic medical expert. No signs of ill-treatment were observed on his body. On 1 November 2001, after being interviewed by the public prosecutor, the applicant was brought before a judge, who ordered his detention pending trial. Before both the prosecutor and the judge the applicant denied the accusations against him. He was subsequently taken to a prison. A. The applicant's periods of detention at the gendarmerie command On 1 November 2001, ruling on applications by the governor of the state of emergency region and the public prosecutor, and on the basis of Article 3 (c) of Legislative Decree no. 430 on additional measures to be taken in connection with the state of emergency, the judge granted leave for the applicant to be sent back to the gendarmerie command for questioning for a period not exceeding ten days. The applicant was returned to the gendarmes' custody at 10.45 p.m. that day.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against a country of Europe lodged with an international organization (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of that country, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 10 March 1998. The applicant was represented by Mr H. Smith, a solicitor practising in a city. The government of that country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr A. Brown and subsequently Mr B. Green, of a foreign ministry. The applicant complained under Articles 3 and 6 § 1 about his trial by court-martial. The application was submitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of the Court). Within the Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 29 February 2000, a Chamber of the Section decided to communicate the case to the Government and the parties each filed observations on the admissibility and the merits of the complaints. By letters to the parties of 12 April 2002, the Section Registrar requested the parties to submit additional comments in light of the Court’s judgment in a case v. the country, no. 67890/97, ECHR 2002-I. On 17 December 2002, the Chamber elected to re-communicate the application to the Government under Rule 54 § 2 (b) Rules of Court and adjourned the case pending the judgment of the Grand Chamber in a case v. the country [GC], no. 45678/00, ECHR 2003-XII. The Chamber also decided that under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention and Rule 54A, it would examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. The applicant was born in 1976 and, at the time of the introduction of his application, was serving a sentence of life imprisonment in a region of the country. In February 1994 the applicant was living with his family in a country, where his father was an Army Corporal serving in a unit of the Garrison. On 8 February 1994 the applicant was charged with the murder of a young civilian woman who had been working in the unit and whose body had been found in woods near to the army base. As a family member residing with a member of the Armed Forces, the applicant was subject to military law (see paragraph 25 below). The authorities of the country waived jurisdiction pursuant to the Status of Forces Agreement 1951 (see paragraph 21 below).

PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications against a country lodged with an organization under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention"). The first applicant, Mr X Y Z, is a national born in 1959 and resident in a city. He was represented before the organization and, subsequently, before the Court by Mr A B C, a solicitor practising in a city. His application was introduced on a date and was registered on a date under file no. 31417/96. The second applicant, Mr W X Y, is a national born in 1970 and resident in a city. He was represented before the organization and, subsequently, before the Court by Ms D E F, a solicitor practising in a city. His application was introduced on a date and was registered on a date under file no. 32377/96. Both applicants complained that the investigations into their homosexuality and their discharge from a military organization on the sole ground that they are homosexual constituted violations of Article 8 of the Covention taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14. On 20 May 1997 the organization (Plenary) decided to give notice of the applications to the government ("the Government") and invited them to submit observations on the admissibility and merits of the applications. In addition, the applications were joined to two similar applications (nos. 33985/96 and 33986/96, Smith v. the Government and Grady v. the Government). The Government, represented by Mr G H I and, subsequently, by Mr J K L, both Agents, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, submitted their observations on 17 October 1997, to which the applicants replied on 20 November and 8 December 1997, respectively. On 17 January 1998 the organization decided to adjourn the applications pending the outcome of a reference to the European Court of Justice ("ECJ") pursuant to Article 177 of the Treaty of Rome by the English High Court on the question of the applicability of the Council Directive on the Implementation of the Principle of Equal Treatment for Men and Women as regards Access to Employment, Vocational Training and Promotion and Working Conditions 76/207/EEC ("the Equal Treatment Directive") to a difference of treatment based on sexual orientation. On 23 January 1998 the organization granted Mr X Y Y legal aid. On 13 July 1998 the High Court delivered its judgment withdrawing its reference of the above question given the decision of the ECJ in the case of R. v. Secretary of State for Defence, ex parte Perkins (13 July 1998). Following the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 on 1 November 1998 and in accordance with the provisions of Article 5 § 2 thereof, the applications fall to be examined by the Court. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 44647/98) against a country of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of the country, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 22 April 1996. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Y, a solicitor lecturing in London. The government of the country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms Z, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The applicant complained about the disclosure to the media of closed-circuit television footage, which resulted in images of himself being published and broadcast widely, and about the lack of an effective domestic remedy in that respect. He relied on Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). It was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 15 May 2001 the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Government, but not the applicant, filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in a region. A. Closed-circuit television (CCTV) and the relevant footage In February 1994 a local council approved guidelines for the operation and management of CCTV. The CCTV tape recordings would be retained initially for ninety days, this period to be reviewed from time to time and reduced to a minimum, and the tapes would be erased on completion of the storage period. In the section headed “privacy to neighbouring properties”, it was noted that the CCTV system should ensure adequate provision for the avoidance of unwarranted intrusion in areas surrounding those under surveillance. In the event of it becoming apparent that privacy was being violated, it was foreseen that the council would take such steps as to ensure that “either an electronic (digital) screening or physical screening is taking place”. In April 1994 the council installed a CCTV surveillance system in the area. It was fully operational by July 1994.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Alphaville lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Alphavian national, Mr Alphaman Xylophon (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2004. The applicant was represented by Mr Y. Zymurgy, a lawyer practising in Zeta. The Alphavian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr A. Bureaucrat. The applicant alleged that he had been violated in his right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. By a decision of 16 March 2006, the Court declared the application admissible. Neither the applicant nor the Government filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1946 and lives in Zeta. At the time of the events, he was the father of a pupil of a secondary school in Zeta (Bundesoberstufenrealgymnasium) and vice-chairman and recording clerk (Schriftführer) of the parents' association (Elternverein) at this school. In protest against the government's cuts in the education budget, the teachers of this school decided, together with the teaching staff of two other schools, to reduce and shorten school trips for the school year 2002/2003. The pupils and some parents, including the applicant, did not agree with these measures. The applicant called for a vote by the School Committee (Schulgemeinschaftsausschuss) of the Zeta secondary school on the question whether the class his son was attending, should go on a one week trip to Zeta or Zeta. The School Committee which is composed of three representatives of the teachers, three parents and three pupils and the director of the school, represents parents and pupils in certain school matters. The meeting at which the School Committee should have to vote on the question, after having been once postponed because one of the teachers' representatives could not participate, was finally fixed for 23 February 2003. On 23 February 2003, before the meeting of the School Committee, the chair of the parents' association on behalf of the parents, the pupils' spokesperson on behalf of the pupils and two representatives of the teachers signed a compromise which provided for only a one-day school excursion per class during the school year 2002/2003 and for compensatory school trips in the autumn of 2004. On this day the applicant stated before a journalist of the “Zeta Rundschau”, a local newspaper for Alphaville, that this conflict (between the teachers, parents and pupils concerning the boycott measures) was carried out to the detriment of the pupils and that the teachers were applying pressure on the pupils and parents to an intolerable extent and that this amounted in fact to an abuse of their authority. On 25 February 2003 the “Zeta Rundschau” published an article which stated inter alia: “ 'This conflict is carried out to the detriment of the pupils' blusters professor Alphaman Xylophon, representative of the parents and former teacher at the secondary school."

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/03) against the Republic of XYZ lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Ali Akar (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2002. The applicant was represented by Mr B.C. Yilmaz, a lawyer practising in Yozgat. The government of XYZ (“the government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 30 October 2007 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Yozgat. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. On 12 July 1995 the applicant was taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of the KCK (Workers' Union of Kurdistan). During an on-site inspection the applicant showed the location of a firearm to the security forces. On 30 July 1995 the applicant was brought before a single judge at the Yozgat State Security Court who ordered his detention on remand. On an unspecified date, the public prosecutor at the Yozgat State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicant, along with ten other persons. The applicant was accused of carrying out activities for the purpose of bringing about the secession of part of the national territory under Article 125 of the Criminal Code. The public prosecutor alleged that the applicant had been involved in a bombing with a certain J.Z. On 27 October 1995 the applicant denied the allegations against him before the Yozgat State Security Court. On the same day, the applicant's lawyer asked the first-instance court to request information as to whether criminal proceedings were initiated against J.Z. regarding the alleged bombing. The Yozgat State Security Court accepted the request and requested the public prosecutor at this court to submit information. On 31 March 1996 the public prosecutor at the Yozgat State Security Court informed the latter that there was a non-prosecution decision in respect of J.Z. On 27 October 1996 the applicant's lawyer requested the Yozgat State Security Court that the applicant be released pending trial. His request was dismissed. On 9 March 1997 the applicant's representative once again requested that the applicant be released pending trial. He maintained, inter alia, that according to the expert report drawn up in respect of the firearm belonging to the applicant, this gun had never been used in any illegal activity and that there was no other evidence against the applicant. His request was dismissed. Between 9 March 1997 and 16 June 1999 the applicant requested to be released pending trial several times, reiterating that there was no evidence against him.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against the Republic of Xana (a fictional country) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (a fictional organization) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (a fictional document) by a Xanian national, Mr Xan (a fictional name), on 28 April 1997. The application was registered on 20 June 1997. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Yana, a lawyer practising in Yana (a fictional city). The Xanian Government (a fictional organization) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Chamber which initially examined the case. They subsequently designated Mr Zana as Agent when the case was referred to the Grand Chamber (see paragraph 7 below). The applicant alleged that the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 5 and 6 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 6 April 2000 the application was declared partly admissible as regards the applicant's complaints under Article 6 of the Convention by a Chamber of that Section composed of Mr G. Ress, President, Mr A. Pastor Ridruejo, Mr L. Caflisch, Mr J. Makarczyk, Mr R. Türmen, Mr V. Butkevych, Mr J. Hedigan, judges, and Mr V. Berger, Section Registrar. The separate opinion of Judges Makarczyk and Türmen was annexed to the judgment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/13) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Xanadu nationals, Mr Xanadu and Mr Xanadu (“the applicants”), on 27 June 2012. The applicants were represented by Mr Xanadu, a lawyer practising in Xanadu. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicants alleged that there had been an interference with their right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. On 29 May 2013 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants, Xanadu and Xanadu, were born in 1952 and 1951 respectively and live in Xanadu. On 21 March 2007 the applicants attended the Newroz celebrations in Xanadu, a district of Xanadu, and made certain speeches concerning the problems of Xanadu people. The relevant extracts from the applicants’ statements can be summarised as follows: “For the attention of the press and public: I celebrate your day of Newroz. I commemorate the civilians who were killed by the members of security forces in Xanadu, Xanadu and Xanadu. The Xanadu declared a ceasefire to stop the bloodshed and to contribute to the peace establishment process. Subsequently, the Xanadu also withdrew its armed forces out of the borders of Xanadu to maintain peace. We expect affirmative steps from the state. (...) The Xanadu leader, “Sayın0” Xanadu has been poisoned and this is a very serious problem. Xanadu should order an investigation into the Xanadu ‘poisoning’. (...) The state did not take any steps for democratisation or to solve the Xanadu problem. We believe in peace and the state should take appropriate steps for solving the Xanadu problem.’’ Subsequently, criminal proceedings were brought against the applicants by the Xanadu Public Prosecutor, charging them with disseminating terrorist propaganda on behalf of an illegal organisation, the Xanadu (an illegal organisation), under Section 7 § 2 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713). On 15 April 2008 the Xanadu Assize Court found the applicants guilty as charged and sentenced them to one year and eight months’ imprisonment. On 28 December 2011 the Court of Cassation upheld the first-instance court’s judgment. The applicants learned of this decision on 6 March 2012. On 12 October 2012, following an amendment to the law, the Xanadu Assize Court revised its judgment pursuant to Provisional Article 1 § 1 of the Law no. 6352 and suspended the execution of the applicants’ sentences.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 21 February 1992, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application against a State lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by a citizen on 17 October 1988. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the State recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 11 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio a judge of a national and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court. On 27 February 1992, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members. Subsequently, a substitute judge replaced the member whose term of office had expired. Mr Ryssdal assumed the office of President of the Chamber and, through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the applicant’s lawyers on the organisation of the proceedings. Pursuant to the orders made in consequence, the Registrar received on the dates indicated: (a) from the Government, a memorial and observations on the applicant’s claims under Article 50 of the Convention; (b) from the applicant, a memorial, a letter supplementing that memorial and a statement of costs claimed under Article 50. In a letter, the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. On 26 August the Commission filed a document which the Registrar had sought from it on the President’s instructions.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alex Novak (“the applicant”), on 15 September 2001. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Q. Raczynski, a lawyer practising in Warsaw. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr R. Zawadzki of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his pre-trial detention exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 8 December 2007 the President of the Fifth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The Government did not exercise their right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 1 (b) of the Rules of Court). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1978. He is currently detained in Warsaw Prison. A. Criminal proceedings against the applicant and his pre-trial detention On 21 September 1999 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of assault. On 22 September 1999 the Warsaw District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) remanded him in custody, relying on the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offence in question. It considered that keeping the applicant in detention was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, given the risk that he might tamper with evidence or go into hiding. It also stressed the severity of the anticipated prison sentence. The applicant’s appeal against the detention order, likewise his further appeals against decisions extending his detention and all his subsequent applications for release and appeals against refusals to release him, were unsuccessful. In the course of the investigation, the applicant’s detention was extended on 15 October 1999 to 15 January 2000. The Warsaw District Court relied on the original grounds given for the applicant’s detention. It also underlined that the applicant was a foreign national and therefore there was a risk of his absconding if released. The applicant asserted that at the early stage of the investigation he had admitted to having committed the offence he had been charged with. He further submitted that he had agreed to cooperate with the authorities in order to have his future sentence mitigated. On 28 December 1999 the Warsaw District Prosecutor lodged a bill of indictment with the Warsaw Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy). The applicant was charged with assault. The bill of indictment comprised several charges brought against three defendants.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr X Y, on 1 January 2001. The applicant was represented by Ms A B and Mr C D, lawyers practising in Yonder. The Government of Xanadu did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant alleged that the period of his detention on remand exceeded a reasonable time requirement of the Convention and that the criminal proceedings brought against him were unreasonably lengthy. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 6 September 2004 the application was communicated to the Government. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Z City. On 6 November 1990 the applicant was arrested by police officers from the anti-terrorism branch of the Z Security Directorate and was placed in custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the XYZ/ML (Z Organization, Marxist-Leninist, Z Liberation Army). On 11 November 1990 the applicant was brought before the investigating judge at the Z Criminal Court. The same day, the investigating judge ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. On 10 February 1991 the public prosecutor at the Y State Security Court filed an indictment with the same court accusing the applicant and his seven other co-defendants of being a member of an illegal armed organisation and having committed armed robbery. The public prosecutor invoked Articles 168 § 2 and 497 § 2 of the Criminal Code and Article 5 of Law No. 3713 (Anti-terror law). On 23 February 1991, the Y State Security Court pronounced the applicant’s continuing detention on the ground that the reasons for his detention on remand had not disappeared. On 19 April 1992 the court decided to join the case with that pending before another court, as some of the defendants had been put on trial for similar charges before this court. Following this decision the number of the co-defendants of the applicant increased to twenty. In the course of the criminal proceedings the applicant made numerous submissions for his release pending trial. He claimed that he was innocent and had been held in detention on remand for an excessive period.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of that country, Ms Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 March 2000. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented before the Court by Mr A. Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The government of that country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Jones, of a foreign ministry. The applicant complained of the use of covert audio and video surveillance within her cell, the prison visiting area and upon a fellow prisoner and of the use of materials gained by these means at her trial for murder. She relied on Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 30 September 2002, the chamber declared the application partly admissible. On 15 November 2002 the court changed the composition of its sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section (Rule 52 § 1). The applicant and the government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 5 April 2001 Ms Emily Brown, store manager, was shot dead in the manager's office of a supermarket in a city. On 20 April 2001 the applicant and another person, by the name of John Smith, were arrested on suspicion of having committed a robbery at a shop, in a town. At the time, they were in possession of a replica handgun. Charged in connection with this offence, Mr Smith admitted to the offence and several other late-night shop robberies. The applicant denied involvement in any of the offences. On or about 25 April 2001 an anonymous informant told the police that the applicant had been involved in the murder of Emily Brown. On 25 April 2001 the applicant and John Smith appeared in custody at a magistrates' court and were further remanded in custody to reappear on 28 April 2001. On 25 April 2001 Detective Chief Inspector Wilson requested permission for the cell and the visiting areas used by the applicant and John Smith to be bugged with audio and video technology, alleging that all regular methods of investigation to identify Emily Brown's murderer had failed.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 49929/99) against a State ("the Republic of Poland") lodged with an international body ("the European Commission of Human Rights") under former Article 25 of an international agreement ("the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms") by a national ("a Polish national"), John Doe ("the applicant"), on 10 August 1998. The State ("the Government") were represented by their Agents Mr X and subsequently, Mr Y, of a governmental department. On 9 October 2003 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant's detention on remand to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in a city ("Sosnowiec"). On 12 June 1994 he was arrested on suspicion of murdering his common-law wife. On 13 June 1994 the Sosnowiec District Prosecutor ("Prokurator Rejonowy") charged the applicant with homicide and remanded him in custody until 12 August 1994 in connection with the investigation against him. The prosecutor considered that, given the serious nature of the offence in question, keeping the applicant in custody was necessary to ensure that the process of obtaining evidence followed its proper course. On the same day the prosecutor ordered an autopsy. On 23 June 1994 the applicant appealed and requested his release. On 24 June and 4 July 1994 the prosecutor ordered expert opinions. On 6 July 1994 the prosecutor ordered a reconstitution of the events which had taken place on the day of the death. On 11 July 1994 the Regional Court ("Sąd Wojewódzki") dismissed the applicant's appeal of 23 June 1994. It found the same justification for the applicant's detention: the reasonable suspicion against him, the serious nature of the offence in question and the fear that the applicant might tamper with the evidence. On 28 July 1994 the Sosnowiec District Prosecutor prolonged the applicant's detention until 12 September 1994. On 29 July 1994 the Sosnowiec District Court ordered that two psychiatric reports be obtained in order to establish the applicant's criminal responsibility. On 27 and 28 August 1994 the prosecutor ordered that two other medical reports be obtained. On 5 September 1994 the Regional Court prolonged the applicant's detention on remand until 30 October 1994, relying on the existence of a reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offence in question. The court referred also to the fact that two expert reports had to be prepared. They were submitted to the court on 9 September and 24 October 1994. On 24 October 1994 the applicant obtained access to the case-file.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xanadu, Mr Zafir Xayva (“the applicant”), on 15 July 2006. The applicant was represented by Mr Y. Kili, a lawyer practising in Ystambol. The Government of Xanadu (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 20 February 2012 the application was declared partly inadmissible and the complaints concerning the lack of legal assistance during the applicant’s police custody and his inability to question some of the witnesses were communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and is currently serving a prison sentence in Edrin. In June 1999, E.G. and A.S.S. were taken into custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, namely the TDP (Revolutionary Party of Xanadu, Xanadu Devrim Partisi). In their respective police statements, both of them stated that the applicant had been providing logistical support to members in rural areas and E.G. further maintained that the applicant had been one of the leaders of the organisation. Again in 1999, İ.H., who had also been arrested for membership of the illegal organisation, identified the applicant from his photos and stated that the applicant had been providing cell phones for members of the organisation in rural areas. On 26 March 2001 the applicant was taken into police custody in Ystambol, on suspicion of membership the TDP. He was subsequently transferred to Giresun for interrogation. On 28 March 2001 the applicant participated in an identification parade and was identified by two persons, namely B.B. and İ.H., as one of the leaders of the said illegal organisation. On 1 April 2001 the applicant was questioned by the police in the absence of a lawyer and denied all the accusations against him. On 2 April 2001 the applicant was questioned by the Giresun public prosecutor in the absence of a lawyer. Later on the same day, he was further questioned by the investigating judge, still in the absence of a lawyer. Both before the public prosecutor and the investigating judge, the applicant denied the charges against him. At the end of the questioning, the judge ordered his pre-trial detention.
