He was a partner in a commercial partnership, a banking and stockbroking firm called Partnership X (hereafter “the Partnership”). In addition to the applicant, the Partnership had five other partners: X, Y, Z, and two private limited companies, namely Company A and Company B. Subsequently, in legal proceedings it was established that a further partner, W, had not formally resigned from the Partnership and therefore was also to be considered a partner. On 29 March 1988, due to financial difficulties, proceedings were initiated before the Bankruptcy Court (Skifteretten under Sø- og Handelsretten) concerning the Partnership and the partners for suspension of payments. On 29 August 1988, the Bankruptcy Court decided to discontinue the suspension of payments. At the same time, having heard two bankruptcy petitions against the applicant, who did not object to the claim that the bankruptcy conditions had been met, the Bankruptcy Court commenced bankruptcy proceedings against his estate. A trustee in bankruptcy was appointed to sort out the estate and to settle the accounts and the applicant was divested of the right to administer or to deal with his assets. The Bankruptcy Court formally commenced the examination of claims on 17 November 1988, but found that it was appropriate to wait until the claims against the Partnership had been lodged and examined. On 8 December 1988, bankruptcy proceedings commenced against the Partnership and by the end of 1988 bankruptcy notices regarding all the co‐partners had been issued as well. The Partnership’s assets, including the individual partners’ assets, were estimated at about 8 million fictional currency, while its liabilities were estimated at 15 million fictional currency. The Partnership estate was closed on 5 December 1995 with distribution of dividends. In the meantime, as regards the applicant’s bankruptcy estate, in the period between 1988 and 1990 various court sessions were held with a view to determining the applicant’s assets and considering creditor claims. In the beginning of 1991 a new trustee was appointed. Court hearings were held in April and December 1991. Moreover, the trustee held several meetings with the applicant and the partners in 1991 and 1992.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of that country, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 January 1999. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr A. Brown, a lawyer practising in Edinburgh. The government of that country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, London. The applicant alleged that his criminal proceedings exceeded a reasonable time contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 20 June 2000, the Court rejected part of the application as inadmissible. On 15 November 2000, the Court changed the composition of its sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. By a final decision of 30 January 2002, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant and the government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1965 and is currently serving a sentence of imprisonment in HM Prison Greenfield, Edinburgh. The applicant was arrested on a charge of attempted murder arising out of a high speed car chase which occurred in the early hours of 15 November 1994. On 16 November 1994, he was arrested again, interviewed and cautioned in respect of a separate incident of rape and assault which also occurred during the early morning of 15 November 1994. On 17 November 1994, the applicant appeared in court in respect of the various road traffic offences and the attempted murder of a police officer. On 22 November 1994, he was fully committed and remanded in custody on those charges (of which he was later acquitted). On 15 December 1994, the applicant appeared before the Sheriff and was committed in respect of the rape charge. On 10 June 1995, the trial began in the High Court. On 11 July 1995, the applicant was convicted, by a majority verdict, of all charges and sentenced to 8 years 9 months' imprisonment. On 13 July 1995, the applicant lodged an intention to appeal with the High Court sitting as an appeal court. On 25 August 1995, a Note of Appeal was lodged. On 30 September 1995, a single judge refused the appeal. The applicant appealed.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms. Anna Kowalska (“the applicant”), on 15 December 1998. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr. P. Nowak of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 25 March 2006 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. It further gave priority to the application in view of the applicant’s age, pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On an unspecified date in 1978 the applicant’s neighbour cut several trees on a plot of land which allegedly belonged to the applicant’s mother. Consequently, proceedings aimed at the determination of ownership of the controversial strip of land were initiated. On 10 March 1982 administrative proceedings concerning the ownership of the land were reopened. On 15 May 1984 the administrative organ referred the dispute to a civil court. On 30 March 1984 the applicant’s mother died and the applicant became a party to the proceedings. On 15 June 1989 the Sucha Beskidzka District Court gave a decision. Upon the applicant’s appeal, on 10 February 1990 the Bielsko Biała Regional Court quashed this decision and remitted the case. On 15 June 1990 the court stayed the proceedings as the applicant had failed to indicate the addresses of some of the parties to the proceedings. The applicant on six occasions unsuccessfully requested the court to resume the proceedings. The proceedings were finally resumed by the Sucha Beskidzka District Court on 10 June 1996. On 11 and 29 June 1996 the court held hearings. On 6 June 1997 the proceedings were again stayed. They were resumed on 12 September 1997. On 8 and 22 January 1998 the Sucha Beskidzka District Court held hearings. On the latter date the court ordered that an expert opinion be obtained. On 18 November 1998 the court ordered the expert to pay a fine because he had failed to submit his report within the prescribed time-limit. Further hearings were held on 18 December 1998, 24 September 1999 and 3 October 1999. On 3 October 1999 the Sucha Beskidzka District Court gave a decision. On 15 April 2000 the District Court rejected the applicant’s appeal for failure to comply with formal requirements. On 28 May 2000 the Bielsko Biała Regional Court rejected the applicant’s interim appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 287/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two applicants, Mr A and Mr B (“the applicants”), on 23 September 2002. The applicants were represented by Mr C and Mr D, lawyers practising in Istanbul. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 7 May 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1955 and 1957 respectively and live in Istanbul. On 3 and 15 March 1981 the applicants were arrested. On 26 May 1981 the Ankara Martial Law Court ordered their detention on remand. On 16 June 1981 the public prosecutor attached to the Adana Martial Law Court filed a bill of indictment against 343 persons, including the applicants, and charged the latter with membership of an illegal organisation. On 17 June 1986 the Adana Martial Law Court convicted the applicants as charged. On an unspecified date the applicants appealed. On 20 March 1991 the Military Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first-instance court and remitted the case to the Ankara Martial Law Court, since in the meantime the former court had been abolished. On an unspecified date in 1991 the applicants were released pending trial. Subsequent to the promulgation of Law no. 3953 on 27 December 1993, which abolished the jurisdiction of the Martial Law Courts, the Ankara Assize Court acquired jurisdiction in the applicants’ case. On 18 June 2001 the Ankara Assize Court convicted Mr B under Article 146 § 1 of the Criminal Code and sentenced him to death. This sentence was subsequently commuted to life imprisonment. Regarding Mr A, the first-instance court ordered that the criminal proceedings against him be terminated on the ground that the statutory time-limit under Articles 102 and 104 of the Criminal Code had expired. The judgment of the Ankara Assize Court was automatically referred to the Court of Cassation insofar as it concerned Mr B, since the latter’s sentence exceeded 15 years’ imprisonment. On 24 July 2002 Mr A and Mr B allegedly learned about the outcome of the proceedings before the Ankara Assize Court through a friend. By a letter dated 7 February 2003, the applicants’ former lawyer informed the Court that the judgment of 18 June 2001 had been served on Mr A on 3 February 2003 upon his request, and that the proceedings against Mr B were still pending before the Court of Cassation. (From the case file it appears that the State had attempted to serve the judgment on Mr A earlier, but had mistakenly sent it to the wrong address.)

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 46004/99) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (“the applicant”), on 6 August 1998. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr K. Drzewicki and subsequently Mr. J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that the civil proceedings in his case exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 6 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 24 June 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1935 and lives in a city, Poland. On 28 March 1991 a person filed with the District Court an action in which she sought the distribution of an inheritance and the dissolution of the co-ownership of the inherited property. The applicant was one of the heirs to that property. The court held hearings on various dates. On 4 March 1999 the hearing was adjourned because of the absence of the applicant's lawyer. Further hearings were held on various dates. The hearing scheduled for 8 September 1999 was adjourned because of an illness of a court expert. The court held hearings on various dates. On 20 June 2000, in reply to the applicant's complaint about the excessive length of the proceedings, the President of the Regional Court noted that the delay resulted from the complexity of the case, the parties' numerous requests concerning evidence and their petitions challenging expert opinions. She admitted that the court experts had failed to issue their opinions within the time-limits.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of that country, Ms Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2003. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr John Smith, a solicitor practising in Hertford. The government of that country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms Mary Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, London. Insofar as the case was declared admissible, the applicant alleged that the statements obtained under compulsion in bankruptcy proceedings should not have been admitted in criminal proceedings against her. She invoked Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 29 January 2004, the Court communicated the applicant's complaint about self-incrimination to the respondent government and declared inadmissible the remainder of the application. By a decision of 25 October 2004, the Court declared the remainder of the application admissible. The applicant but not the government filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Manchester. From 1980, the applicant ran a company which operated 15 retail shops. Following financial problems, the company went into liquidation in March 1988. On 22 June 1988, a bankruptcy petition was presented against the applicant and on 10 April 1989, a bankruptcy order was made. On 28 August 1989, the applicant was publicly examined by the official receiver. Under section 291 of the Insolvency Act 1988, the applicant was obliged to answer the questions put to her by the official receiver and if she failed to comply without reasonable excuse, she would have been guilty of contempt of court and liable to punishment by a fine or imprisonment. On 15 April and 22 April 1989, a bank advanced 120,000 euros (EUR) and EUR 95,000 respectively to the applicant. On 22 April 1989, the applicant's spouse collected part of the advance, EUR 80,000, and took it to another country in a suitcase. The applicant was subsequently charged with two offences of obtaining property by deception contrary to section 15(1) of the Fraud Act 1971 on the grounds that she had misled the bank into advancing money by false representations regarding her income, her debts and the bankruptcy proceedings against her.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court, as established under former Article 19 of the Convention, by the European Human Rights Commission (“the Commission”) and by the Country Government (“the Government”) on 24 and 27 October 1998 respectively, within the three-month period laid down by former Articles 32 § 1 and 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 12345/96) against the Country of Country lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 by a Country citizen, Mr John Doe, on 25 August 1995. The Commission’s request referred to former Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby Country recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (former Article 46); the Government’s application referred to former Article 48. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 10 and 13 of the Convention. After the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 on 1 November 1998 and in accordance with the provisions of Article 5 § 5 thereof, the case was referred to the Grand Chamber of the Court. The Grand Chamber included ex officio Mr X. Yz, the judge elected in respect of Country (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 24 § 4 of the Rules of Court), Mrs A. B and Mr C. D, the Vice-Presidents of the Court, and Mr E. F and Mr G. H, Vice-Presidents of Sections (Article 27 § 3 of the Convention and Rule 24 §§ 3 and 5 (a)). The other members appointed to complete the Grand Chamber were Mr I. J, Mr K. L, Mr M. N, Mr O. P, Mr Q. R, Mrs S. T, Mr U. V, Mrs W. X, Mrs Y. Z, Mr A. B, Mr C. D and Mr E. F (Rule 24 § 3 and Rule 100 § 4). The applicant designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 36). The lawyers were given leave by the President of the Grand Chamber, Mrs B, to use the German language (Rule 34 § 3). As President of the Grand Chamber, Mrs B, acting through the Deputy Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant’s lawyers and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the written procedure. Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the applicant’s memorial on 25 February 1999 and the Government’s memorial on 30 March 1999. In accordance with the decision of the President of the Grand Chamber, a hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, City, on 2 June 1999. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr X. Y, Attorney, Co-Agent, Mr Z. A, Mr B. C, Mr D. E, Mr F. G, Counsel; (b) for the applicant Mr H. I, Rechtsanwalt, Mr J. K, Rechtsanwalt, Counsel. Mr Doe was also present.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/05) against the Republic of Andria (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Andria (a fictional country), Mr Andria Citizen (a fictional person) (“the applicant”), on 5 March 2005. The applicant was represented by Mr O. Lawyer (a fictional person), a lawyer practising in Andria (a fictional city). The Government of Andria (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 15 March 2007 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in Andria (a fictional city). On 31 October 2002 the Court found that there had been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention, following an application lodged by the applicant on 22 July 1996 (a fictional case) concerning the length of criminal proceedings brought against him for his membership of Revolutio Way (a fictional organization). By then the proceedings had lasted for over nineteen years. The Court awarded the applicant 100,000 euros in compensation. At the time of the Court’s judgment, the criminal proceedings against the applicant were still pending before the Andria Assize Court (a fictional court). The facts of the case thereafter, as submitted by the applicant, may be summarised as follows. On 15 May 2003 the applicant attended a hearing before the Andria Assize Court, gave a statement and submitted the Court’s judgment of 31 October 2002 in order to ensure that his case would be heard within a reasonable time. On 17 July 2003 the Assize Court sentenced the applicant to death, and then commuted his sentence to life imprisonment. The judgment was subject to appeal. In the meantime in October 2002, Article 39 of the Constitution was amended so that the death penalty could no longer be ordered or implemented other than in time of war or of imminent threat of war, or for acts of terrorism. Subsequently, by Law no. 4772, which was published on 10 August 2003, the Government resolved, inter alia, to abolish the death penalty in peacetime. On 29 May 2005 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first-instance court on the ground that the death penalty had been abolished during the course of the proceedings. On 24 December 2005 the Andria Assize Court resumed the trial. On that day it ordered, in absentia, the provisional detention of the applicant in order to secure a statement from him. On 28 December 2005 the Andria Assize Court heard a statement from the applicant as regards the state of the case and revoked the detention order as having served its purpose. Subsequently, the Andria Assize Court held thirteen more hearings.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 39163/06) against a State (the Republic of Poland) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (a Polish national), Ms X (“the applicant”), on 12 September 2006. The Government (the Polish Government) were represented by their Agent, Mr Y of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that her detention on remand had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 30 January 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) and to examine it simultaneously with the case of X v. State (no. 24023/06), which concerned the same criminal proceedings. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1952 and lives in a town (Józefosław). On 10 June 2003 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of fraud, committed in an organised criminal group. On 11 June 2003 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) remanded her in custody, relying on the reasonable suspicion that she had committed the offence in question. It also considered that keeping the applicant in detention was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, given the risk that she might tamper with evidence and induce witnesses to give false testimony. The court also stressed the severity of the anticipated sentence. The applicant’s appeal against the detention order, likewise her further appeals against decisions prolonging her detention and her application for release, were unsuccessful. In the course of the investigation, the applicant’s detention was prolonged on several occasions by the District Court (on 11 June 2003, 3 September 2003, 3 December 2003 and 3 March 2004) and by the Court of Appeal (on 8 June 2004, 7 September 2004, 3 December 2004, 1 March 2005). In all their detention decisions the authorities repeatedly relied on a strong suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences in question, which was supported by evidence from witnesses and experts. They attached importance to the grave nature of those offences and the likelihood of a severe sentence of imprisonment being imposed on the applicant. They further considered that the need to secure the proper conduct of the investigation, especially the need to verify evidence from suspects and witnesses and the need to obtain fresh evidence from experts justified holding her in custody. On 12 May 2005 the District Prosecutor (Prokurator Rejonowy) lodged a bill of indictment with the District Court. The applicant was charged with fraud and forgery of documents, committed in an organised criminal group. There were 16 defendants in the case, all charged with numerous counts of fraud committed in an organised criminal group.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against the Republic of A (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of A (a fictional country), Mr Ali Yılmaz (a fictional person) (“the applicant”), on 15 December 1999. The applicant was represented by Mr J.K. Yılmaz, a lawyer practising in B (a fictional city). The Government of A (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 1 October 2004 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in B. He was the deputy chairman of the pro-Kurdish HDP (Halkın Demokrasi Partisi – People’s Democracy Party) prior to the events giving rise to the present application. On 16 June 1998 the applicant was taken into custody by police officers from the anti-terror branch of the B Security Directorate. According to the arrest protocol (yakalama tutanağı) signed by four police officers and the applicant, a search warrant had been issued in respect of the applicant. When the officers saw the applicant, they asked him to show his identity card. The applicant however attempted to escape. On 18 June 1998 the deputy director of the B Security Directorate sent a letter to the public prosecutor at the B State Security Court requesting that the applicant’s custody period be extended. The deputy director maintained, inter alia, that the applicant had been taken into custody on 16 June 1998 during the course of a police operation carried out against the PKK and that the police had not yet completed the detailed questioning of the applicant and the gathering of evidence. The public prosecutor referred the security directorate’s request to the B State Security Court. On the same day, the single judge of the State Security Court decided to extend the custody period for three days starting from 19 June 1998, including 21 June 1998. The applicant did not appear before the judge. On 20 June 1998 two police officers from the anti-terror branch of the B Security Directorate took statements from the applicant. The applicant was questioned, in particular, about his statements made in several television programmes, broadcast on MTV, a pro-Kurdish channel, in which he had taken part in his capacity as deputy chairman of the HDP. On 22 June 1998 the applicant was brought before the public prosecutor at the B State Security Court, who questioned him about his statements during the same television programmes. Subsequently, the public prosecutor requested the B State Security Court to order the applicant’s detention on remand.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/08) against the State of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by four European nationals, Mr Alex Green, Mr Sam Brown, Mr John White, and Mr Chris Black (“the applicants”), on 5 February 2008. The applicants were represented by Mr P. Smith, a lawyer practising in London. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs C. Jones, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicants alleged that the Supreme Court judgment of 8 August 2007 constituted a violation of their freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. They further submitted that they were punished without law in violation of Article 7 of the Convention. On 28 December 2009 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The application was later transferred to the Sixth Section of the Court, following the re-composition of the Court’s sections on 2 March 2012. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). In addition to written observations by the applicants and the Government, third-party comments were received jointly from the International Centre for the Legal Protection of Human Rights and the International Commission of Jurists, whom the President had authorised to intervene in the written procedure (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1980, 1983, 1989, and 1988 respectively. The first applicant lives in Manchester and the other applicants live in Birmingham. In January 2005 the applicants, together with three other persons, went to a secondary school and distributed approximately a hundred leaflets by leaving them in or on the pupils’ lockers. The episode ended when the school’s principal intervened and made them leave the premises. The originator of the leaflets was an organisation called National Youth and the leaflets contained, inter alia, the following statements: “Homosexual Propaganda (Homosexpropaganda) In the course of a few decades society has swung from rejection of homosexuality and other sexual deviances (avarter) to embracing this deviant sexual proclivity (böjelse). Your anti-European teachers know very well that homosexuality has a morally destructive effect on the substance of society (folkkroppen) and will willingly try to put it forward as something normal and good. -- Tell them that HIV and AIDS appeared early with the homosexuals and that their promiscuous lifestyle was one of the main reasons for this modern-day plague gaining a foothold. -- Tell them that homosexual lobby organisations are also trying to play down (avdramatisera) paedophilia, and ask if this sexual deviation (sexuella avart) should be legalised.” For distributing the leaflets, the applicants were charged with agitation against a national or ethnic group (hets mot folkgrupp).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 5 April 2004. The applicant was represented before the Court by Ms Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in Warsaw. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Alex Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his correspondence with the Court had been opened and read by the prison authorities. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 8 September 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, Mr John Doe, is a European national who was born in 1975 and lives in Nowhere. By a decision of the Warsaw District Court of 15 September 2003 the applicant was arrested and remanded in custody on suspicion of illegal production and sale of alcohol, selling cigarettes without payment of excise duty and membership of an organised criminal group. According to the applicant's submissions, police officers used force against him during his arrest and insulted him. When ordering his detention, the court found that the evidence obtained in the case, in particular the testimonies of the other suspects and of a witness, bills, minutes of searches and telephone conversations, indicated a high probability that the applicant had committed the offences. The applicant's detention was therefore necessary in order to prevent collusion and to avert the risk that he would exert pressure on witnesses or that the suspects would coordinate their testimonies. During the investigation the applicant's detention was successively prolonged by detention orders issued by the Inowrocław District Court or the Warsaw Court of Appeal and dated 12 December 2003, 12 March and 28 August 2004. The applicant submits that the decision of 12 December 2003 was served on him on 17 December 2003 and that for 5 days he had been kept in custody without having been provided with a relevant detention order. In his letter of 5 April 2004 the Warsaw Regional Prosecutor admitted that the service of the applicant's motion for release had been delayed for 6 days before reaching the Prosecutor Office. In further letters, the Regional Prosecutor stated among other things that the applicant's correspondence with the prosecutor had not been delayed by the Prosecutor Office.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by four European nationals, Ms Alice Smith, Mr John Doe, Mr Peter Green and Mr Richard Brown (“the applicants”), on 5 September 2006. The applicants were represented by Ms Jane White and Ms Sarah Black, lawyers practising in London. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicants alleged, in particular, that the intervention of a number of police officers and the force used by those police officers against them in a demonstration in which they were taking part had been in violation of their rights under Articles 3 and 11 of the Convention. On 7 April 2009 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1985, 1981, 1956 and 1980 respectively and live in London. On 18 October 2004 the applicants took part in an anti-war demonstration in London. The gathering was dispersed by police officers and the applicants were arrested and taken into police custody where they remained until their release the following day. The applicants allege that they were subjected to ill-treatment during their arrest and their detention in custody. According to an incident report drawn up by a number of police officers on 18 October 2004, fifty to sixty persons, including the applicants, gathered in a square in London at 8.00 p.m. and chanted anti-war slogans, protesting against the Government’s proposals to send soldiers to participate in the invasion of Iraq. The police had warned them with loudspeakers that they were disturbing the flow of traffic and had unsuccessfully asked them to disperse. When the police had attempted to arrest some of the demonstrators and put them into the police vehicles, a number of the demonstrators had displayed “rowdy behaviour” and the police had had to use force against them. A total of six persons, including the applicants, had been arrested and taken to a police station at 9.00 p.m. the same evening. This incident report was signed by six police officers who were only referred to in the report with their identification numbers. The same day the applicants were examined by a doctor. According to the medical reports, the second and third applicants had no signs of ill-treatment on their bodies. The first applicant had bruising on her lower lip and on her lower right leg. The fourth applicant had bruising on the left side of his lower back and on the back of his right ear. His legs were also sensitive and he had redness in his left eye.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/02) against a country (Country X) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (National Y) of Country X, on 1 January 2002. The Government of Country X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. W. of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 1 July 2005 the President of the Fourth Section decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in a city (City A) in Country X. On 1 January 1993 the applicant was involved in a car accident as a result of which one person died. Subsequently, the prosecution service opened an investigation in the case. On 1 February 1994 the prosecution service discontinued the investigation. Subsequently, an auxiliary prosecutor appealed and the investigation was resumed. On 1 March 1994 the applicant was charged with manslaughter. It appears that the applicant had by then left the country and was not notified of the decision. On 1 April 1994 the applicant was indicted before the local court. On 1 May 1995 the trial court decided to stay the proceedings on the grounds that the applicant’s address could not be established as he had left the country. On 1 June 1997 the District Court issued an arrest warrant against the applicant. On 1 July 1997 the applicant was arrested by the police while crossing the border. On 1 August 1997 the trial court resumed the proceedings and held a hearing. Subsequently, the District Court held hearings on 1 September and 1 December 1997 and 1 February and 1 June 1998. In 1999 the court held hearings on 1 February, 1 April, 1 September and 1 October. On 1 October 1999 the District Court gave judgment. The trial court acquitted the applicant. On 1 February 2000 the Regional Court examined the appeal lodged by the auxiliary prosecutor. The appellate court quashed the judgment and remitted the case. On 1 November 2000 the District Court held a hearing. In 2001 the trial court held one hearing on 1 January and ordered that an expert opinion be prepared. On 1 May 2001 the next hearing was held. At the hearing on 1 June 2001 the applicant pleaded guilty. On the same day the District Court found the applicant guilty and sentenced him to a suspended prison sentence. The judgment is final.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Zara Novak (“the applicant”), on 15 August 1999. The Government of Xanadu (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr A. Bolek, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant was exceptionally granted leave to be represented by Mr C. Dolek (Rule 36 § 4 of the Rules of Court). The latter was also granted leave to use the national language in the proceedings before the Court (Rule 34 § 3 of the Rules of Court). The applicant alleged in particular, that her right to a “hearing within reasonable time” had not been respected. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. On 30 April the Fifth Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings and an alleged interference with the applicant’s property rights to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. It also gave priority to application, pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. THE FACTS The applicant, Ms Zara Novak, is a national, who was born in 1950 and lives in Zabrze, Xanadu. A. Proceedings concerning a claim for restitution and compensation. In 1955 the applicant’s property was expropriated. On 28 June 1996 the Minister of Economy (Minister Gospodarki) annulled the expropriation order. On 23 December 1996 the applicant brought a claim against a company “Xanadu Metal Works” before the Regional Court, seeking restitution of her property. The court held hearings on 30 May, 10 July and 17 October 1997. On 30 January 1998 the applicant modified her claim and filed an action for compensation for loss of profits caused by the prolonged impossibility of using her property. On 8 March 1999 the Regional Court held a hearing and gave an interlocutory judgment. It ordered that the property be restored to the applicant. On 9 December 1999 the court was to hold a hearing, but an expert failed to appear because he had not been duly summoned. On 27 January 2000 and 23 March 2000 the court held further hearings. A hearing listed for 15 February 2001 was cancelled since the expert and the defendant failed to appear. The hearing listed for 29 March 2001 was adjourned as the court had ordered the expert to prepare a supplementary report. On 21 February 2002 the court held a hearing. On 8 March 2002 the Regional Court gave judgment and awarded the applicant compensation.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 37075/97) against a State ("the Republic") lodged with an international human rights body ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of an international human rights treaty ("the Convention") by a national ("the applicant"), on 28 May 1997. The applicant was represented before the Court by a lawyer ("Mrs S. Schubert") practising in a city ("Vienna"). The State ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, a diplomat ("Ambassador H. Winkler"), from a government department ("International Law Department" at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs). The applicant alleged in particular that disciplinary proceedings against him lasted unreasonably long. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when a protocol to the Convention came into force. The application was allocated to a section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 21 November 2000 the Court declared the application partly admissible. As of 1 November 2001 the application was allocated to another section of the Court. Within that section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. THE FACTS The applicant was a professional ("accountant"). He retired in 1998. On 2 April 1986 a professional body ("Chamber of Accountants") instituted disciplinary proceedings against the applicant. Subsequently, the proceedings were adjourned having regard to criminal proceedings pending against the applicant. On 14 April 1986 the applicant was convicted of a crime ("aggravated fraud") by a court ("Vienna Regional Criminal Court"), which conviction was confirmed by a higher court ("Oberster Gerichtshof") on 3 October 1988. By the end of 1990 the file relating to the criminal proceedings reached a disciplinary body ("Disciplinary Court") and on 8 November 1991 the hearing date was set down for 8 May 1992. On 8 May 1992 the Disciplinary Court, having regard to the applicant's conviction, found that he had infringed the profession's reputation and ordered the suspension of the applicant's right to practise for one year. On 19 October 1992 the applicant appealed this decision. On 7 May 1993 the Appeals Board dismissed the appeal stating that the suspension should last for one year. This decision was served on 30 January 1995. On 15 March 1995 the Constitutional Court ("Verfassungsgerichtshof") refused to deal with the applicant's complaint and transferred the case to an administrative court ("Verwaltungsgerichtshof"). On 30 March 1995 the Chamber of Accountants declared the suspension to be effective from 31 January 1995 to 30 January 1996. On 17 May 1995 the Administrative Court granted the applicant's complaint suspensive effect. On 28 February 1997 it dismissed the complaint. The decision was served on 22 March 1997.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/11) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2011. The applicant was represented by Mr X Y, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 30 December 2013 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1990 and lives in Andria. On 28 March 2003 the applicant, who was eighteen years old at the time, was arrested by police officers in Andria, on suspicion of theft. On the same day, he was examined by a doctor at the Andria State Hospital, and no signs of injury were reported. At the police station, the applicant was allegedly forced to make self-incriminating statements. During his interrogation, the applicant claims that the police officers pulled his ears and he was beaten and subjected to falaka (beating on the soles of his feet). On 30 March 2003, following the complaint of the applicant’s representative, the Andria Public Prosecutor went to the police station to see the applicant. According to his report, there were several widespread bruises on the soles of the applicant’s feet and oedema behind his ears. The public prosecutor also noted that the applicant had stated that he had been ill‐treated and that he could identify the police officers who had ill‐treated him. The same day, the applicant identified the four police officers who had ill‐treated him. Following his interrogation by the public prosecutor, the applicant was released. The applicant was subsequently taken to the Andria State Hospital for a medical examination. According to the doctor’s report, there were several scars on his left arm, bruises and oedema behind his left ear, and bruises on both of his palms and on the soles of his feet. It was noted that his injuries would heal in five days. On 2 May 2003 the Andria Public Prosecutor initiated criminal proceedings against four police officers, accusing them of ill-treating the applicant under Article 245 of the former Criminal Code. The applicant joined the proceedings as a civil party. On 10 May 2003 the Andria Criminal Court declared that it lacked jurisdiction, holding that the proceedings should be initiated before the Assize Court on account of torture under Article 243 of the former Criminal Code. The proceedings therefore resumed before the Andria Assize Court. At the end of the trial, on 16 June 2011 the Andria Assize Court, on the basis of the evidence in the case file, found the police officers guilty of inflicting torture pursuant to Article 243 of the former Criminal Code. The court found it established that the police officers had intentionally ill-treated the applicant to extract a confession.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 29724/08) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national. The applicant was represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 6 September 2010 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant is a Turkish national who was born in 1972 and lives in a town. On 20 June 2003 the applicant, who is of Kurdish origin, was arrested in a city and taken into police custody with three other individuals on suspicion of acting as a courier for an illegal armed organisation. The applicant was in possession of a false identity card at the time of his arrest. On 21 June 2003 a person arrested with the applicant on suspicion of attempting to participate in the armed activities of the illegal organisation was questioned at a police headquarters, in the absence of a lawyer. The person claimed that he had met the applicant the day before in a town and that at the time they were arrested the applicant was taking him to the mountains to join members of the illegal organisation. On 22 June 2003 the applicant was taken for questioning at a police headquarters. Before his questioning the applicant signed a form which explained the rights of arrested persons, by which he was informed of the charges against him and his right to remain silent. In his statement, given in the absence of a lawyer, the applicant denied any affiliation with the illegal organisation and contested the person's allegations. He also stated that he was a shepherd and at the time of his arrest he was in the mountains looking for lost sheep. He also explained that he had been carrying a false identity card as he was an army deserter. An interpreter was present during this questioning. A confrontation was held between the applicant and the person, without any legal assistance. On 23 June 2003 the applicant was brought before a Public Prosecutor, where he reiterated the statement he had made to the police. Later the same day the applicant was also questioned at a Magistrates’ Court in the absence of a lawyer. At the end of that questioning the judge remanded the applicant in pre-trial custody. On the same day the person also made statements before the Public Prosecutor and the Magistrates’ Court, in which he repeated his allegations about the applicant. On 7 July 2003 the Public Prosecutor at a State Security Court filed an indictment with that court accusing the applicant of aiding and abetting the illegal organisation, and the person of membership of that organisation.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alex Anonym (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2001. By a letter dated 15 March 2005, the Registry was informed of the death of the applicant on 10 June 2004 and the applicant’s mother, Mrs Mary Anonym, declared her intention to pursue the application. The applicant’s mother was represented by Mr and Mrs Smith, lawyers practising in Andria. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 15 September 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960. On 10 October 1993 the applicant was arrested by police officers from the Anti-Terror branch of the Andria Security Directorate in the course of a police operation carried out against the illegal organisation the XYZ (a political party). On 20 October 1993 the applicant was brought before a single judge at the Andria State Security Court, who ordered his detention on remand. On 15 December 1993 the public prosecutor at the Andria State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicant and ten other persons. The public prosecutor charged the applicant with membership of an illegal organisation under Article 168 § 1 of the Criminal Code. On 1 February 1994 the Andria State Security Court held the first hearing on the merits of the case (no. 1993/123). On 13 October 1996 the public prosecutor at the Andria State Security Court filed a further bill of indictment against the applicant, accusing him of attempting to undermine the constitutional order, contrary to Article 146 of the Criminal Code. Between 1 February 1994 and 27 August 1998, the Andria State Security Court held 28 hearings in the case. Throughout these hearings, the applicant and his representative requested that the applicant be released pending trial. They contended that the length of the applicant’s detention on remand was excessive and that he suffered from health problems. The court dismissed the requests on each occasion, holding that the applicant’s detention pending trial should continue having regard to the nature of the offence with which he was charged, the state of the evidence and the date of the remand decision. On 27 August 1998 the Andria State Security Court decided to disjoin the proceedings against the applicant from case no. 1993/123 and to join them to a case brought against him in 1996 (no. 1996/456).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Janusz Nowak (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2003. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Adam Nowak of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 20 January 2008 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the administrative proceedings to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, Mr Janusz Nowak, is a European national who was born in 1945 and lives in Warsaw. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. On 15 October 2000 the applicant lodged with the Mayor of Warsaw (Urząd Miasta) an application to transform his right of perpetual use (prawo użytkowania wieczystego) of a piece of real property into a right of ownership. He relied on the provisions of the 4 September 1997 Law on Transforming Perpetual Use Vested in Individuals into Ownership (ustawa o przekształceniu prawa użytkowania wieczystego przysługującego osobom fizycznym w prawo własności) (“the 1997 Act”). On 3 November 2000 the Mayor informed the applicant that, due to a judgment of the Constitutional Court (Trybunał Konstytucyjny) which found some provisions of the 1997 Act to be incompatible with the Constitution, he could not give a decision in the case within the statutory time-limit of one month, and set a new time-limit of 31 July 2001. On 27 November 2001 the Mayor informed the applicant that, due to some changes to the 1997 Act, a valuation report concerning the property (operat szacunkowy) had to be drawn up and a new time-limit set, 31 March 2002. On 6 August 2002 the applicant complained to the Warsaw Self‐Government Board of Appeal (Samorządowe Kolegium Odwoławcze) about inactivity on the part of the administrative authority. On 17 January 2003 the Warsaw Self-Government Board of Appeal found the applicant's complaint well-founded and ordered the Mayor to give a decision on the merits within one month of the delivery of its decision. The Mayor did not give the decision within the prescribed time‐limit. Instead, on 6 March 2003, the Mayor issued a procedural decision (postanowienie) setting another time-limit, 31 December 2003, and informing the applicant that the decision could not be appealed against and that it could be challenged only when a decision on the merits had been given. On 20 August 2004 the applicant again asked the Mayor to give a decision in his case.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 51279/99) against the French Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two French nationals, Mr A and Mr B, and the company C (“the applicants”) on 19 April 1999. The applicants were represented by Mr D, of the Conseil d’Etat and Court of Cassation Bar. The French Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr E, Head of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicants alleged, in particular, a violation of their freedom of expression, as guaranteed by Article 10 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 4 September 2001 the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). The Government, but not the applicants, filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The first two applicants were born in 1948 and 1960 respectively and live in a city. In order to consider an application by a State for membership of the European Union, the European Commission decided it would need very precise information on the issue of drug production in that State and the measures being taken to eradicate it, that being the avowed political aim of the King of that State in person. To that end, the Secretariat General of the Commission requested an observatory to prepare a report on drug production and trafficking in that State. Investigations and reports by the observatory were considered authoritative. The tribunal and the public prosecutor’s office of the capital city were among the subscribers to its publications. The observatory delivered its report to the European Commission in February 1994. The report contained the names of people implicated in drug trafficking in that State. However, the Commission asked the observatory for a revised version of the report, with the names of the drug traffickers deleted in order to make it more suitable for the discussions that were scheduled with the authorities of that State. This expurgated version of the initial report was published, notably in a book sold by the observatory entitled Etat des drogues, drogue des Etats (“State of drugs, drugs of States”) and containing a chapter on that State. The book was referred to in a newspaper on 25 May 1994. After initially remaining confidential, the original version of the report began to circulate. The newspaper learnt of its existence in the autumn of 1995.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/05) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alex Brown (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2005. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr D. Green of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Capital City. By a decision of 2 October 2007 the President of the Third Section of the Court decided to communicate the application. Subsequently, under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in a region. The applicant and his wife had two children, born in 1983 and 1988. The applicant’s wife died on 3 June 1998. On 6 October 2000 the applicant applied to the Benefits Agency for the payment of social security benefits. He applied for benefits equivalent to those which a widow, whose husband had died in similar circumstances to those of his wife, would have been entitled, namely a Widow’s Payment (“Wpt”) and a Widowed Mother’s Allowance (“WMA”), payable under the Social Security and Benefits Act 1991 (“the 1991 Act”). On 18 October 2000 his application was rejected as these benefits were only available to women. This decision was reconsidered without alteration on 26 October 2000. The applicant appealed to the Social Security Tribunal on 11 July 2001 and again his claim was rejected. In December 2001 the applicant applied for leave to appeal to the Appeal Commissioner. Eventually permission was granted but his appeal was again rejected on 27 May 2004. The applicant again appealed to the Commissioner who rejected the applicant’s appeal on 14 December 2006. Finally, the applicant submitted an appeal to the Court of Appeal (Civil Division), which was refused on 17 March 2007. At the time of his claim in 2000 the applicant was in receipt of child benefit.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by four Andorran nationals, Ms Ana Garcia, Mr Jose Martinez, Mr Carlos Sanchez and Ms Maria Lopez (“the applicants”), on 15 July 2000. The applicants were represented by Mr Luis Rodriguez and Mr Juan Perez, lawyers practising in Andorra la Vella. The Andorran Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 28 June 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning insufficient interest payable in respect of additional compensation, the delay of the authorities in payment of the additional compensation and the length of the proceedings to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1950, 1940, 1952 and 1942 respectively and live in Andorra la Vella and Sant Julià de Lòria respectively. In 1994 the applicants' plots of land in Andorra la Vella were expropriated by the General Directorate of Public Works. A committee of experts assessed the value of these lands and the determined amounts were paid to them when the expropriation took place. On 22 September, 12 October and 23 November 1995 respectively, the applicants filed separate actions for compensation with the Andorra la Vella Civil Court of First Instance. On 20 October 1996 the first-instance court ordered the administration to pay Mr Martinez 42,410,845,000 Andorran liras (AL) plus interest at the statutory rate, running from 8 September 1995, the date on which the ownership of the property was transferred to the National Water Board. On 26 October 1996 the first-instance court ordered the administration to pay Ms Garcia AL 6,467,500,000 plus interest at the statutory rate, running from 10 September 1995, the date on which the ownership of the property was transferred to the National Water Board. On the same day, the first-instance court ordered the administration to pay Ms Lopez AL 80,274,368,000 plus interest at the statutory rate, running from 24 October 1995, the date on which the ownership of the property was transferred to the National Water Board. On 8 October 1996 the first-instance court ordered the administration to pay Mr Sanchez AL 13,075,000,000 plus interest at the statutory rate, running from 10 September 1995, the date on which the ownership of the property was transferred to the National Water Board. The Court of Cassation upheld the above-mentioned judgments of the Andorra la Vella First Instance Court on 12 May, 22 May and 27 May 1997 respectively. On 9 March, 14 March, 13 April and 5 May 1998 respectively, the administration paid the applicants the amounts due together with interest.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Andria (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Andria (a fictional country), Mr Andria Andrian (a fictional name), on 10 June 2002. The applicant was represented by Mr K. Kost (a fictional name), a lawyer practising in Andria (a fictional city). The Government of Andria (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 17 November 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Andria (a fictional city). On 16 July 1989 the applicant brought a case before the Erdek Civil Court (a fictional court) against the Treasury (a fictional organization), requesting to be registered as the owner of a certain plot of land. On 18 March 1991 the Erdek Civil Court granted the applicant’s request. The Treasury appealed. Whenever he inquired about the outcome of the appeal proceedings, the applicant was informed by the registry of the first-instance court that the proceedings were still pending. In 1997, however, the applicant was informed by the Court of Cassation (a fictional court) that the latter had actually rendered its decision long before, on 30 November 1991. The Erdek Civil Court declared, in response to a petition from the applicant, that the case file had never been sent back to it and it had subsequently attempted to recreate the case file, which appeared to have been lost. On 9 April 1997 the Treasury filed a petition with the Court of Cassation requesting that the decision of 30 November 1991 be rectified. On 29 August 1997 the Court of Cassation decided that it could not examine the Treasury’s request as the reconstituted file was not sufficient and it needed the original case file for such an examination. It therefore decided to send the file back to the Erdek Civil Court. According to the information submitted by the parties to the Court, the proceedings are still pending. In 2000 the Land Registry Commission attached to the General Directorate of Land Registration conducted a land registry survey and registered the title to the relevant plot under the name of a certain Kostantin (a fictional name) and the Treasury. On 31 July 2000 the applicant brought a case before the Erdek Cadastral Court (a fictional court), challenging the land registry survey. On 19 July 2003 an on-site inspection of the land was carried out, and on 21 December 2003 the Erdek Cadastral Court allowed the applicant’s request in part. On 11 January 2005 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of 21 December 2003 and on 27 March 2007 it dismissed the Treasury’s rectification request.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of A. against the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms A. (“the applicant”), on 15 August 2004. The applicant was represented by Mr B., a lawyer practising in B. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 25 December 2008 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the civil proceedings. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in B. On 3 and 4 May 1996 the applicant deposited a total of 1,547,000,000 local currency (LC) with Company C., a private brokerage firm, and requested the firm to buy Treasury bonds for her. In September 1996 the applicant contacted D., the broker to whom she had given the money, and asked her whether she had bought the Treasury bonds on her behalf. D. informed the applicant, by way of a handwritten document, that she had. On 16 March 1997 when the applicant went to the office of Company C. A.Ş., she learned that D. had used her money not to buy Treasury bonds but to buy stocks, which had lost their value and therefore the firm had caused her to lose money. On 30 September 1997 the applicant brought a case against Company C. A.Ş. and D. before the Commercial Court (Ticaret Mahkemesi), requesting the defendants to reimburse the money which she had deposited with the firm. On 28 May 1999 the Commercial Court partially granted the applicant’s request and ordered the defendants to pay her 942,000,000 LC with simple interest. Both the applicant and the defendants appealed. On 25 October 2001 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 28 May 1999. The case was subsequently remitted to the Commercial Court. On 8 November 2002 the Commercial Court once again partially granted the applicant’s request and ordered Company C. A.Ş. and D. to pay her 1,512,000,000 LC with simple interest. The applicant and Company C. A.Ş. appealed. On 10 September 2003 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of 8 November 2002. On 14 January 2004 the applicant requested rectification of the Court of Cassation’s decision of 10 September 2003. On 12 April 2004 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s request.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against a country lodged with a regional commission under former Article 25 of a human rights convention by a national, Mr Smith ("the applicant"), on 1 February 1998. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by a law firm practising in a city. The government ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Mr Jones of the foreign ministry. The applicant alleged that there had been undue delay between the reviews by a parole board of his continued detention as a prisoner serving a sentence of discretionary life imprisonment. He invoked Article 5 § 4 of the convention. The application was transmitted to the court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the court (Rule 52 § 1 of the rules of court). Within that section, the chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the rules of court. By a decision of 21 March 2000, the chamber declared the application partly admissible. Neither party filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 11 February 1980, the applicant pleaded guilty to manslaughter on the ground of diminished responsibility in respect of the death of his 62‐year-old landlady whom he had battered with an axe. He was sentenced to life imprisonment. The court acted on medical evidence that the applicant had a gross personality disorder to such a degree that he was amoral. The consultant psychiatrist said in his report at the trial that: “... although [the applicant’s] instability might get less over the years as he matured, should he be sent to prison, his eventual release should be approached with great caution.” The applicant was initially sent to a Category A prison due to concerns about his dangerousness and risk of escape. He was involved in work to address his offending and other problems. He successfully completed an anger management and skills program in or about 1989 and his conduct was noted as significantly improving from that point. In 1993, he was transferred to a Category B prison. The applicant’s tariff period of 15 years expired on 25 June 1994 (this was the minimum period fixed by the secretary of state concerning the requirements of retribution and deterrence). The parole board in that month agreed to the transfer of the applicant from a Category B to Category C prison.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/12) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Central Asian national, Mr. Alex Novak (“the applicant”), on 28 November 2012. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Ms. Jane Smith and Mr. John Doe, lawyers practising in London. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 4 June 2012 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1985 and, according to the latest information available to the Court, lives in Aksaray. On 2 April 2011 the applicant, who had been living in Europe since 2008, was taken into custody in the context of an investigation into murder by a person or persons unknown. He was placed in the Yedikule Security Directorate in London. On 4 April 2011 the applicant delivered his witness statement before a criminal court in relation to the aforementioned investigation. However, he was not released after delivering the statement; instead he continued to be detained in the Yedikule Security Directorate for having outstayed his visa. On 5 April 2011 the applicant was transferred to Fatih police station in London (“Fatih police station”), where he was placed in a custodial cell for the next five days. On 10 April 2011 the applicant was sent to Removal Centre with a view to being deported. According to the applicant’s account, Removal Centre was severely overcrowded at the time of his detention. He had to share a dormitory measuring approximately 30-35 sq. m with twenty-four to forty-five other people and the overcrowding of the centre resulted in hygiene problems. The building was infested with insects and the quality and quantity of the food provided was also fairly poor. Moreover, there was no provision for outdoor exercise. On 12 April 2011 the applicant lodged an application with the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) for refugee status. On 27 April 2011 he claimed asylum from the Ministry of the Interior. On 29 April 2011 the applicant was granted a temporary residence permit in the province of Aksaray as an asylum seeker and he was released from Removal Centre on the same day. It appears that the applicant was subsequently permitted to reside in Konya. According to the latest information provided to the Court, the applicant’s applications for asylum and refugee status are still pending before the domestic authorities and the UNHCR respectively.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national from a West African country, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 July 2009. The applicant was represented by Ms. Jane Smith of Legal Services, a lawyer practising in a major city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr. Richard Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 28 June 2009 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). On 8 January 2011 the Acting President of the Section to which the case was allocated decided to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Government that it was desirable in the interests of the parties and the proper conduct of the proceedings that the applicant should not be expelled to the country of origin pending the Court’s decision. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. The applicant was born in 1980 and is currently detained in a prison. The applicant arrived in the country on 10 March 1996 and claimed asylum. The asylum claim was refused but he was granted exceptional leave to remain until March 2001. On 25 June 1999 the applicant was convicted of offences of rape and indecency with a child and sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment. On 18 April 2003 the Secretary of State for Home Affairs issued the applicant with a decision to make a deportation order and on 22 April 2003 he issued an authority for detention until the making of a deportation order. On 24 May 2003 the applicant appealed against the decision to make a deportation order and made a fresh claim for asylum. The appeal was unsuccessful and his appeal rights were exhausted on 5 October 2004. In early 2004 the applicant was interviewed by probation officers who found that he was not suitable for parole. During his time in prison he had received ten charges relating to offences against prison discipline. Four of these offences involved fighting. Moreover, he was assessed as presenting a high risk of sexual offending and a medium risk of general offending on release. On 2 September 2004 the applicant’s release became automatic. However, he remained in detention pursuant to the authority issued on 22 April 2003. On 6 March 2005 the Secretary of State for Home Affairs issued a deportation order which included a paragraph authorising the applicant’s detention until his deportation. The order was served on the applicant on 21 March 2005. The applicant had claimed to be a member of the Doe tribe, which comes from a region in West Africa.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 48095/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr. X (“the applicant”), on 17 April 1999. The applicant was represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 29 April 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the applicant's right to a fair trial by an independent and impartial tribunal to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). The case was assigned to the newly composed Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in a city. In 1988 the applicant was convicted of membership in an illegal organisation. On 15 April 1991 he was conditionally released from prison. On 16 March 1996 the applicant was arrested and taken into custody by the police. On 9 April 1996 the applicant was interrogated by the police officers at a security directorate. On 9 April 1996 the State Security Court ordered his detention on remand. On 22 April 1996 the public prosecutor at the State Security Court filed an indictment with the latter, accusing the applicant of membership in an illegal armed organisation. In the meantime on 7 May 1996 the public prosecutor at another State Security Court filed an indictment accusing the applicant of being an accessory to a bank robbery and murder. On 26 December 1996 the two cases were joined and the criminal proceedings continued before the State Security Court. On 16 December 1997 the State Security Court, composed of two civilian judges and a military judge, convicted the applicant and sentenced him to life imprisonment. On 30 November 1998 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment without conducting a hearing. On 10 October 2002 the applicant's representative informed the Court that the applicant was released from prison due to ill-health. Accordingly, the applicant was imprisoned, in total, for about six years and six months.
