On 25 October 1999 the applicant was heard first by the public prosecutor and later by a judge at the State Security Court. The latter ordered his release from custody. Following the applicant’s complaint, the public prosecutor instigated an investigation into the events. On 26 November 1999 the public prosecutor decided not to prosecute the police officers at the Security Directorate. In its decision the prosecution noted that none of the persons put forward as witnesses by the applicant were able to confirm the applicant’s version of events, that the applicant was unable to identify the alleged perpetrators and that none of the medical reports, dated 19 October 1999, 23 October 1999 and 25 October 1999 save for one dated 11 November 1999, i.e.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against a national government (X) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”), on 27 June 1999. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr. Charles Brown, a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. James Green, a former official in charge of human rights and European affairs. On 26 October 2003 the President of the Fourth Section decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the right to respect for private life. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in a city. On 15 July 1940, before the applicant’s birth, the State-appointed guardian brought an action against B.X., the applicant’s putative biological father, seeking a declaration of paternity and payment of a contribution towards his maintenance. B.X. admitted that he had had sexual relations with the applicant’s mother but denied paternity. On 27 July 1940, after the applicant’s birth, his mother declared on registering the birth that the father was B.X., with whom she had had sexual relations during the period of conception. On 31 January 1948 the Court of First Instance dismissed the action for a declaration of paternity. In the absence of an appeal, the judgment became final. In 1959 the applicant, who had been placed with a foster family, met his mother, who informed him that his father was B.X. According to the applicant, he had regular contact with his father and received presents from him and a monthly payment of 10 local currency units ((CHF) – 6.40 euros (EUR)) until he reached the age of majority. B.X. and his family denied those allegations. Only B.X.’s legitimate son admitted that he had received a telephone call from the applicant after B.X.’s death. Furthermore, B.X. always refused to undergo tests to establish his paternity. In 1977, shortly after his death, a blood-type analysis carried out at the applicant’s request did not rule out his being the latter’s father. In 1998 the applicant contacted a university institute to have a private paternity test carried out, but his request was refused. On 3 December 1998 the applicant successfully applied to renew the lease for B.X.’s tomb until 2017 for the sum of CHF 2,600 (EUR 1,657). On 7 May 1999 the applicant applied to the Court of First Instance for revision of the judgment of 30 January 1948.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/08) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Ana Martinez Rodriguez (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2008. The applicant was represented by Mr C. Sanchez, a lawyer practising in Barcelona. The Andorran Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the refusal by the domestic courts to allow her to bear only her maiden name unjustifiably interfered with her right to respect for her private life under Article 8 of the Convention. She claimed that the fact that Andorran law allowed married men but not married women to bear their own surname after marriage constituted discrimination on grounds of sex and was incompatible with Article 14 of the Convention. On 25 November 2010 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Barcelona. Following her marriage to Juan Martinez on 7 June 1997, the applicant, whose surname was “Rodriguez” prior to her marriage, had to take her husband’s surname pursuant to Article 154 of the Andorran Civil Code. As she was known by her maiden name in her academic and professional life, she continued to use it; however, she could not use it in any official documents. An amendment to Article 154 of the Civil Code on 15 June 1998 meant that married women acquired the right to put their maiden name in front of their husband’s surname. The applicant preferred not to make use of that option because, in her view, the amendment in question did not satisfy her request, which was to use her maiden name on its own. Following the enactment of the new Civil Code on 25 December 2002, Article 188 was worded identically to the former Article 154 (see “Relevant domestic law and practice” below). On 28 October 2006 the applicant brought proceedings before the Barcelona Court of First Instance seeking permission to use only her maiden name, Rodriguez. On 7 January 2007 the court dismissed the applicant’s request on the grounds that, pursuant to Article 188 of the Civil Code, married women had to bear their husband’s name throughout their marriage and were not permitted to use their maiden name alone. The applicant appealed against that judgment and on 22 April 2007 it was upheld by the Court of Cassation. A request by the applicant for the proceedings in her case to be reopened was further rejected by the same court on 15 August 2007. That decision was served on the applicant on 12 September 2007.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 2311/04) against a State lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms X (“the applicant”), on 22 December 2003. The applicant was represented by Ms Y, a lawyer practising in a city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. On 16 November 2006 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1951 and lives in a city. A. Main proceedings On 3 June 1991 the applicant instituted civil proceedings for dissolution of a co-ownership and division of an inheritance before a court in a city. On 18 November 1992 the case was transmitted to a court in another city. Between 24 February 1993 and 28 May 2003 the court held 18 hearings. On 7 June 2004 the court in another city gave a partial decision in the case. The court held that, following further proceedings, a final decision concerning the distribution of the estate would be given at a later stage. The applicant appealed. On 9 June 2005 the court in a city, having examined the partial decision, remitted the case to the court in another city. According to the applicant’s submissions, from June 2005 until March 2006 no hearing was listed in her case. On 22 August 2007 the court in another city gave a decision and divided the inheritance. It is unclear whether the applicant appealed against that decision. B. Proceedings under the 2004 Act On an unspecified date the applicant lodged a complaint with the court in a city, under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time. On 8 March 2005 the court in a city rejected her complaint for a procedural mistake. On 11 April 2005 the applicant again lodged a complaint with the court in a city under section 5 of the 2004 Act. She sought a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings before the court in another city had been excessive and that just satisfaction in the amount of 10,000 local currency units (approx. 2,500) should be awarded to her.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 32849/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 17 June 2004. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Y. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of his detention on remand had been unreasonable. On 13 September 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the unreasonable length of the applicant's pre-trial detention to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1954 and lives in a city, Poland. On 21 August 2001 the applicant was arrested by the police. On 22 August 2001 a court decided to detain the applicant on remand in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had been involved in an offence. On 20 December 2001 the Regional Court prolonged the applicant's pre-trial detention. The court relied on the severity of the sentence that might be imposed and held that keeping the applicant in detention was justified by the need to secure the proper conduct of the investigation. The applicant's appeal against this decision was dismissed on 29 January 2002. On 8 April 2002 the Regional Court further prolonged the applicant's detention reiterating the grounds originally given for his detention and adding that the measure was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the investigation. Subsequently, on 24 July and 25 September 2002, the Court of Appeal prolonged the detention of the applicant and several co-accused. The court considered that the strong suspicion against the accused of having committed serious offences made it probable that they would obstruct the course of the proceedings. It found that a presumption established a likelihood that the accused might obstruct the proceedings. With regard to the applicant, the court underlined the risk of a severe penalty being imposed on him. On 22 November 2002 the applicant and several co-accused were indicted before a Regional Court. On 27 November 2002 the pre-trial detention of the applicant and several others was further extended. The Regional Court considered the risk of the accused tampering with evidence high, basing itself on the fact that they had been charged with an offence. The applicant's request to lift his pre-trial detention was dismissed on 9 June 2003.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/05) against the Republic of Andria (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Andria (a fictional country), Mr John Doe (a fictional person), (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2005. The applicant was represented by Mr M. A. Smith and Mrs M. Smith, lawyers practising in Andria (a fictional city). The Government of Andria (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 10 September 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1980 and is currently detained in the Andria F Type Prison (a fictional prison) pending the criminal proceedings against him. On 7 May 1998 the applicant was arrested and taken into custody on suspicion of being involved in the activities of an illegal organisation known as the XYZ (a fictional organization). On 10 May 1998 he was brought before a single judge at the Andria State Security Court who ordered his pre-trial detention. On 20 May 1998 the public prosecutor at the Andria State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicant and another person, charging them with attempting to undermine the constitutional order under Article 146 § 1 of the former Criminal Code. On 27 September 2002 the Andria State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to death. On 14 May 2003 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first-instance court. The case was remitted to the Andria State Security Court for further examination. On 25 December 2003 the Andria State Security Court convicted the applicant for a second time on the same charge and sentenced him to life imprisonment. On 5 July 2004 the Court of Cassation once again quashed the judgment of the Andria State Security Court. By Law no. 5190 of 16 June 2004, published in the Official Gazette on 30 June 2004, State Security Courts were abolished. The case against the applicant was subsequently resumed before the Andria Assize Court. According to the information in the case file, the case is still pending before the Andria Assize Court. Throughout the proceedings, the first-instance courts examined the applicant's continued detention at the end of every hearing, either on their own motion or upon the applicant's request. Each time the courts ordered his continued detention having regard to the state of evidence and the content of the file.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 38811/97) against a country (A) lodged with an organization (B) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a national (C) ("the applicant"), on 12 December 1996. The government (D) of country (A) ("the Government") were represented by their Agents, Mr X and subsequently Mr Y. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his right to a "hearing within a reasonable time" had not been respected. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 19 November 2002 the Court declared the application partly admissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1946 and lives in a town (E). A. Proceedings concerning the action for damages against a cooperative and a company. On 30 July 1987 the applicant lodged a claim for payment against a cooperative with a court (F) on 3 November 1987 the company joined the proceedings as a second defendant. Prior to 1 May 1993 the trial court held several hearings and ordered an opinion from an expert. On 30 December 1993 the applicant modified his claim and applied for an exemption from court fees. At the hearing held on 21 February 1994 the court ordered the applicant to pay the court fees due for the submission of the modified claim. On 28 February 1994 the applicant again asked the court to exempt him from court fees. On 28 March 1994 the court (F) rejected his application. On 1 April 1994 the applicant appealed against that decision. On 30 September 1994 the court (G) dismissed his appeal. On 8 November 1994 the applicant paid the required court fees. On 7 January 1995 the applicant modified his claim for the second time. On 8 February 1995 the court (F) partly exempted him from the court fees. On 8 March 1995 the court (F) held a hearing. On 28 May 1995 the applicant modified his claim for the third time. On 12 February 1997 the court ordered that expert evidence be obtained. The expert opinion was completed on 19 May 1997 and submitted to the court. On 2 July 1997 the court ordered that a new expert opinion be obtained.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/08) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 29 May 2007. The applicant was represented by Mr Alex Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Bob Jones of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 21 April 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1954 and lives in a town. A. Criminal proceedings against the applicant and his detention on remand On 9 August 2005 the applicant was arrested by officers of an agency on suspicion of revealing secrets and bribery. As submitted by the applicant, the officers had handcuffed and beaten him. He was taken to the agency and subsequently to a prosecutor’s office where he was again beaten and urged to confess. At the same time another group of armed officers had broken into his apartment and handcuffed and terrorised his wife. Their apartment was ransacked during the search for documents and other evidence. On 11 August 2005 the court remanded him in custody, relying on the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences in question. It also considered that it was necessary to keep the applicant in detention in order to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, given the risk that he might tamper with evidence or induce witnesses to give false testimony. The court also stressed the severity of the likely sentence to be imposed and the complexity of the case. The court found that there was a reasonable suspicion that the applicant, while at liberty, would have had unlimited opportunities to contact other persons who were directly linked to his criminal activities. In the course of the investigation, the applicant’s detention was prolonged on several occasions, inter alia on 7 November and 29 December 2005 by a court, on 17 March and 12 September 2006 by a court, on 19 February and 27 April 2007 by a court, and on 4 July 2007 by a court (until 15 October 2007). In all their decisions regarding detention the authorities repeatedly relied on the original grounds given for the applicant’s detention.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against the Republic of Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national from Country, Ms X Y Z (“the applicant”), on an unspecified date in 2008. The applicant was represented by Mr A B C, a lawyer practising in City. The Government of Country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On an unspecified date in 2008 the President of the Chamber to which the case was allocated decided, in the interests of the parties and the proper conduct of the proceedings before the Court, to indicate to the Government of Country, under Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, that the applicant should not be deported to Country until the Court comes to a conclusion regarding the application. On 18 April 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided that the admissibility and merits of the application would be examined together (Article 29 § 3) and that the case would be given priority (Rule 41). The applicant and the Government each submitted written observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in City. A. The applicant's arrival in Country and the deportation proceedings On an unspecified date the applicant was divorced from her husband in Country. The applicant's ex-husband was appointed the legal guardian of the couple's children. On 2 October 2005 the applicant arrived in Country with her children, whom she had brought without the consent of her ex-husband. According to her submissions, the applicant had escaped from the violence of her ex-husband. The applicant applied to the national authorities and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (“the UNHCR”) requesting temporary and permanent asylum soon after her arrival in Country. On 28 September 2006 the applicant married an Iranian national who had converted to Christianity. In October 2006 the applicant also converted to Christianity. On an unspecified date the UNHCR dismissed the applicant's asylum request. On 22 December 2006 the applicant and her husband were served with the decisions of the Ministry of Interior rejecting their temporary asylum requests. The Ministry of the Interior considered that the applicant and her husband wished to use the temporary asylum system in Country in order to go to a European country where they could improve their financial situation. The applicants were also informed that they had the right to object to the decisions concerned. On 7 November 2007 the applicant was informed that she would be deported. On the same day she was granted a residence permit for fifteen days in order to facilitate her departure from Country.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1820/08) against a country of the European region of Great Britain and Northern Ireland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of a non-European country, Mr X Y Z (“the applicant”), on 9 January 2008. The applicant was represented by Ms N. Mole of the Aire Centre, a lawyer practising in London. The Government of the United Kingdom (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms H. Upton of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. On 25 November 2008 the President of the Chamber decided to give notice of the application to the Government of the United Kingdom. It was also decided to judge on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, Mr X Y Z, is a national of a non-European country who was born in 1960. He currently lives in a non-European country. The facts of the case, as submitted by the applicant, may be summarised as follows. The applicant was born in a non-European country and lived there until 1982. He was educated in a non-European country and for a period he was employed by a company in a non-European country. On 9 September 1982, when he was twenty-two years old, he was granted two months' leave to enter the United Kingdom as a student. His leave was subsequently extended to 15 January 1986. In 1983 the applicant was joined by a partner, who was also a national of a non-European country. The applicant married his partner in the United Kingdom in 1987. They had three children, who were born on 11 February 1986, 28 October 1991 and 16 September 1992. The children were born in the United Kingdom and all are British citizens. The oldest child has a daughter, who is now two years old. Prior to the expiry of his leave in January 1986, the applicant applied for a further extension. The following day, however, he was caught returning from the Netherlands with a visitor's passport obtained by deception. Although he was not prosecuted for the offence, the application to extend his leave was refused. On 12 March 1987 the applicant was informed of his liability for deportation. He was served with a deportation order on 31 July 1987. He attempted to appeal against the order and a second deportation order was served on 4 December 1990. The applicant appealed against the second order, but the appeal was subsequently withdrawn. The applicant was convicted of theft and conspiracy to defraud on 7 March 1989. He was sentenced to four years' imprisonment. Other convictions the same day resulted in five terms of twelve months' imprisonment to run concurrently. On 24 October 1995 the applicant claimed asylum by post, but on 12 January 1998 the application was refused for non-compliance. On 28 September 2000 the applicant and his wife applied for leave to remain under an overstayer's regularisation scheme.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms Anna Novakova (“the applicant”), on 5 September 2002. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr M. Petrovic of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that she had been deprived of access to the Supreme Court. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1949 and lives in a city. On 5 November 2000 the applicant filed a claim for payment against a housing co‐operative of which she was a member. By a judgment of 27 February 2001 the Regional Court of a city dismissed the claim. The judgment was upheld on 7 September 2001 by the Court of Appeal of a city. On 21 November 2001 the applicant was served with that judgment together with its written grounds. On 10 December 2001 she filed a request with the Regional Court of a city to be granted a legal-aid lawyer for the purpose of lodging a cassation appeal. Her request was subsequently forwarded to the Court of Appeal of a city as the Regional court lacked jurisdiction to deal with it. The request was allowed by a decision of 17 December 2001. On 18 December 2001 the decision of 17 December 2001 was served on the local Bar Association. At the same time the Court of Appeal of a city informed the Bar about the date on which the applicant had been served with the second-instance judgment. On 3 January 2002 the Bar Association informed the applicant that a legal-aid lawyer had been assigned to her case. By a letter of 19 January 2002 to the court the lawyer refused to lodge a cassation appeal, finding no grounds to do so. The letter read: “Having examined the file in detail, I have not found grounds for lodging a cassation appeal. The judgment given on 7 September 2001 by the Court of Appeal did not breach any provisions of substantive law. Nor were any provisions of procedural laws violated during the proceedings. The findings of fact made by the courts show without any ambiguity that the applicant had never had the right to a co-operative apartment which could be assimilated to ownership. She had admitted, both before the first-instance and the appellate court, that at the time of the exchange of apartments she had been aware that her right was only assimilable to the rights arising out of a rental contract. (...) It had been open to her to take steps in order to have her right transformed into an ownership-like right, but she had not done so. Hence, the first instance court was right in finding that the defendant housing co-operative was not obliged to pay compensation to the applicant.”

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 38227/02) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 2 October 2002. The applicant was represented by a lawyer practising in Warsaw. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Y, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 4 May 2004 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1979 and lives in a town. On 13 July 2000 the applicant was arrested by the police on suspicion of having committed burglary. On 15 July 2000 the court ordered that the applicant be remanded in custody for a period of three months in view of the strong suspicion that he had committed burglary. It considered that there was a reasonable risk that the applicant would tamper with evidence, given the fact that he had only partly confessed. Further, the court referred to the risk that the applicant might obstruct the proper conduct of the proceedings by going into hiding. In that regard, the court relied on evidence from one of the applicant’s co-suspects, who had stated that, shortly before having been arrested, the applicant had tried to leave for a foreign country in order to evade serving a sentence of imprisonment which had been previously imposed on him. Finally, the court had regard to the severity of the anticipated penalty. Subsequently, the applicant was charged with multiple counts of burglary. He confessed to some counts. On 30 January 2001 the prosecutor terminated the investigation. On the same day he filed a bill of indictment with the court. The applicant had been indicted on multiple charges and one charge of assault. There were other defendants in the case. The prosecution asked the court to hear evidence from multiple witnesses. From 1 June 2001 to 19 December 2002 the trial court listed multiple hearings. The trial began on 17 January 2003. The subsequent hearings were held on multiple dates. At the hearing held on the latter date the court fined multiple witnesses who had failed to appear.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals, Mrs Alice Smith and Mr Bob Smith (“the first and second applicants”), on 15 November 2010. The applicants were represented by Mr X. Y., a lawyer practising in a city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms Z. W., of a government department. The applicants mainly complained under Article 2 that there had been an unlawful use of lethal force against the deceased, Mr John Doe, and that the State had not fulfilled its procedural investigative obligations in that respect. On 22 November 2012 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). On 12 December 2013 the Government declined to exercise their right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1962 and 1934, respectively, and live in a city. They are the wife and father, respectively, of Mr John Doe. A. The death of Mr John Doe The applicants maintained that, at 2 a.m. on 8 June 1998, John Doe was walking home when he was passed by persons who were being chased by police officers from the Green Operational Support Unit (“Green OSU”) of a police force. They also contend that one of those officers hit John Doe on the face with a truncheon and that he fell to the ground where he was kicked on the left side and hit on the back with a truncheon by the officers. He went home and informed his wife. He then went to hospital and it is alleged that police officers taunted him about the incident on the way there. He was treated for undisplaced fractures to both sides of his right jaw bone. Following an article in a local newspaper about the incident, two witnesses (one an allegedly direct witness) came forward. Having experienced headaches and tingling in one arm in late November/early December 1998, on 28 December 1998 John Doe began vomiting and complained of severe headaches. He collapsed and was transferred to hospital where he died on 2 January 1999. B. The police investigation and the inquest On 3 January 1999 a pathologist found that John Doe died from a cerebral infarction and it was not possible to correlate the recent thrombosis causing the fatal cerebral infraction with a facial injury in 1998. On 8 January 1999 the police began an investigation supervised by an independent commission. On 30 April 1999 the Coroner registered the death as he considered, given the pathologist’s report, that an inquest was not necessary.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2004. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. Richard Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 8 March 2007 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1967 and lives in a town. A. The applicant’s pre-trial detention On 11 February 1998 the applicant was arrested by the police on suspicion of murder, involvement in drug trafficking and illegal possession of a firearm. On 13 February 1998 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) remanded him in custody in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences in question and having regard to their seriousness. It further considered that there was a risk that he would obstruct the proper conduct of the investigation and influence witnesses and other members of the criminal group to which he belonged. In the course of the investigation, the applicant’s detention was extended several times. On 4 August 1998 the applicant was indicted before the Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy). As the bill of indictment did not meet the formal requirements a second bill of indictment was served on 22 August 1998. The bill of indictment comprised charges of murder, drug trafficking and illegal possession of a firearm and concerned four accused. From 13 November 1998 until 2 January 1999 the applicant served a prison sentence imposed on him in other criminal proceedings. From 17 February 1999 to 10 August 1999 the court held eight hearings during which it heard evidence from sixty-six witnesses, as the applicant and the co-accused asked for all the witnesses to be heard during the hearing and for their testimony not merely to be read from the investigation file. The hearings scheduled for 10 September 1999 and 12 October 1999 were postponed due to the illness of a lay judge (ławnik) and the absence of one of the lawyers. On 13 October 1999 the court decided to hear the case from the beginning because of the inability of the lay judge to continue to sit in the case. From 13 October 1999 to 13 January 2000 the court held thirteen hearings. In a number of hearings witnesses failed to appear. On 13 January 2000 the court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to life imprisonment and forfeiture of his civic rights. He appealed.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Norwegian nationals, Mr Ali Hassan and Mrs Lina Alameddine (“the applicants”), on 12 June 2006. The applicants were represented by Mr V. Andersson, a lawyer practising in Oslo, and by Mr P. Nilsson and Ms S. Johansson, lawyers of the Oslo Tenants' Association. The Norwegian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr H. Jensen, Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicants alleged that their eviction from their flat following their refusal to remove a satellite dish resulted in violations of Articles 8 and 10 of the Convention. On 22 June 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants, a married couple of Syrian origin, were born in 1958 and 1964 respectively and live in Stavanger. They have three children, who are now eighteen, sixteen and eight years of age. From 1 November 1999 they rented a flat in Sandviken, a suburb of Oslo. Rule 13 of the special provisions of the tenancy agreement stipulated the following: “The tenant undertakes not to erect, without specific permission, placards, signs, sunblinds, outdoor aerials and such like on the house.” The agreement further stipulated, as a general condition, that the tenants were obliged to take proper care of the flat and to maintain good sanitary conditions, order and good practice in the house. It appears that when the applicants moved in, there was a satellite dish mounted on the façade, next to one of the windows of the flat. The applicants made use of this in order to receive television programmes in Arabic and Farsi. In October 2003 the applicants' landlord changed. The new landlord, a real-estate company, demanded that the satellite dish be dismantled. The applicants did not comply and, by letter of 2 April 2004, the company gave the applicants notice of termination of the tenancy agreement with effect from 31 July 2004. Further, in April 2004, the landlord initiated proceedings before the Rent Review Board (hyresnämnden) in Oslo against the applicants and some other tenants who had installed satellite dishes in the same house. The landlord sought execution of the notice of termination, claiming that the applicants' satellite installation violated the express ban in Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement and that, by not complying with the instruction to dismantle the dish, they had failed to maintain good sanitary conditions, order and good practice.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 10 June 2010. The applicant was represented by Mr Richard Smith and Ms Jane Doe, lawyers practising in Andorra. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 15 January 2015 the complaint concerning alleged interference with the applicant’s right to freedom of expression and of assembly was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Andorra. At the time of the events in question the applicant was the vice‐president of Party X (Party for Rights and Freedoms). On 5 January 2005 the party held its first ordinary congress at a restaurant in Andorra, where the applicant was elected by the delegates to act as the meeting’s chairman. On 28 March 2006 a public prosecutor at the Andorra public prosecutor’s office filed an indictment with the Andorra Criminal Court of First Instance against thirteen members of Party X, including the applicant, for acting in violation of section 82 (c) of Law no. 2830 during the congress on the grounds, inter alia, that there had been banners in a language other than the official language and that most of the speeches given by the delegates had been in that language. The applicant acknowledged before the first-instance court that he had not intervened as the chairman when certain delegates had spoken in that language. In this connection, he submitted that, as a founder member of Party X, he believed that that language should be used in all areas of life; that those who spoke that language were speaking in their mother tongue; and that he believed it was neither legal nor ethical for him to intervene to force people to speak in a language other than their mother tongue. He maintained that such speeches could not have constituted an offence, when taking into account laws that had been enacted in compliance with the conditions for membership of the European Union, and the provisions of the European Convention on Human Rights. In this connection, the applicant also submitted that the relevant provisions of Law no. 2830 were contrary to the Constitution. On 7 December 2006 the first-instance court dismissed an application from the defendants to suspend the proceedings and transfer the case to the Constitutional Court for examination of the compatibility of the relevant provisions with the Constitution. On 14 March 2008 the Andorra Criminal Court of First Instance convicted the applicant of the charges.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ali Mustafa, (“the applicant”), on 8 March 2010. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 7 June 2013 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in a city. On 19 July 1999 the applicant started working for a company owned by the city council (“the City Council”). On 20 April 2008 he resigned from his job to perform his military service. On 21 May 2008 the applicant was paid 17,000 local currency units (LCU) in respect of severance pay and he signed a release (ibraname) discharging the City Council from all liability. Following his discharge from the military on health grounds shortly after he was enlisted, on 22 April and 30 May 2008 the applicant requested his reinstatement in his previous job. However, his requests were rejected by the City Council. On 29 June 2008 the applicant initiated proceedings before the labour court of the city, seeking reinstatement. He relied on clause 20 of the collective bargaining agreement in force at the company (“the collective agreement”), which provided for the reinstatement of employees who had quit their jobs to perform their military service, provided that they applied within three months of their discharge from the armed forces. On 10 September 2008, in a decision rendered orally in the presence of the parties, the labour court of the city found in favour of the applicant. The court held that the applicant’s discharge from the military shortly after he had been enlisted fell under the provision of the collective agreement, which called for the suspension of the employment contract when an employee was conscripted (silah altına alınma) for reasons other than compulsory military service, such as being recalled to the armed forces in times of war. Therefore it held that the applicant was entitled to be reinstated in accordance with the terms of the collective agreement. The court informed the parties that they could appeal against this decision within the time-limits set out in the applicable procedure. On 16 September 2008 the City Council appealed against the decision and reserved its right to submit additional observations once the reasoned judgment of the first-instance court had been served on it. That appeal was not communicated to the applicant. On 14 October 2008, the registry of the first-instance court forwarded the file to the court of cassation for appeal on points of law. On 24 October 2008 the City Council submitted its additional observations. It argued, inter alia, that the first-instance court’s interpretation of the collective agreement had been erroneous. These observations were also not communicated to the applicant.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 May 2007. The applicant was represented by Ms A. Smith, a lawyer practising in City. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador J. Brown, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Europe, Integration and Foreign Affairs. The applicant complained, in particular, that in the proceedings for the withdrawing of his driving licence he did not have a hearing before the Administrative Court. On 20 June 2008 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in City. On 5 November 2000 the applicant was stopped by the police at 10.30 p.m. while driving his car on a public road. He was ordered to undergo a breathalyser test. After nine attempts to measure the amount of alcohol, among which only one was valid, the test was discontinued. The applicant’s conduct was considered to amount to a refusal to undergo the breathalyser test and his driving licence was temporarily withdrawn. Two different sets of proceedings were initiated against the applicant. On 10 December 2000 the City District Administrative Authority (Bezirkshauptmannschaft, DAA) issued a decision to withdraw the applicant’s driving licence for a period of four months as a preventive measure to secure road safety. The DAA observed that, according to the case-law of the Administrative Court, it amounted to a refusal to undergo a breathalyser test if the person who had been ordered to undergo the test had made four invalid attempts out of five. According to the statements of police officers X. and Y. and the paper print outs of the test results, the applicant had been allowed to make much more attempts, namely nine and only one had produced a valid result. When the applicant had claimed that the breathalyser had been defective, police officer Y had made himself two attempts using the same mouthpiece as the applicant and both attempts had produced valid results. The DAA also noted that technical tests of the breathalyser had been carried out on 15 May 2000 and on 9 November 2000 and each time the breathalyser had been found fully functioning. On the basis of this evidence it was safe to conclude that the applicant had refused to undergo the breathalyser test. The DAA also ordered that an appeal had no suspensive effect because it was necessary to avoid the risk that a person lacking trustworthiness for road traffic might drive. Moreover the applicant was ordered to follow driver improvement training before his driving licence would be returned.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 32987/96) against a State lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 25 June 1996. The applicant was represented by a lawyer practising in a city (State). The State did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. A judge elected in respect of the State withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The State accordingly appointed an ad hoc judge to sit in his place (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). The President of the Chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same respondent State raising the same complaints (applications nos. 26480/95, 28291/95, 29280/95, 26699/96, 29700/96, 29701/96, 29702/96, 29703/96, 29911/96, 29912/96, 29913/96, 31831/96, 31834/96, 31853/96, 31880/96, 31891/96, 31960/96, 32964/96, 32900/96, 33362/96, 33369/96, 33645/96, 34591/96, 34687/96, 39428/96 and 43362/96) (Rule 43 § 2). By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the State each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Arrest and detention of the applicant On 3 November 1980 police officers from a Security Directorate arrested the applicant on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation. On 30 January 1981 a Martial Law Court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. B. Trial in a Court On 10 May 1982 the Public Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with a Martial Law Court against the applicant and 722 other defendants. The Public Prosecutor accused the applicant, inter alia, of membership of an illegal organisation, whose object was to undermine the constitutional order. The prosecution sought the death penalty. In a judgment of 24 August 1988 the Martial Law Court convicted the applicant on account of his involvement in the illegal organisation.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the State of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a German national, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”), on 28 April 2004. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr. E. Smith, a lawyer practising in Bonn. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs. B. Jones, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The applicant complained that, in the proceedings for review of his pre-trial detention, the Court of Appeal, by remitting his case back to the court of first instance instead of quashing the detention order which it had found not to comply with domestic law, had unlawfully deprived him of his liberty and had unduly delayed the judicial review proceedings. Furthermore, he claimed that his defence counsel had been refused access to the investigation files. He relied, in particular, on Article 5 of the Convention. On 29 October 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1964. At the date the application was lodged, he was living in Bonn. 1. The District Court’s detention order On 26 July 2003 the applicant was arrested. On the same day the Bonn District Court, after hearing representations from the applicant, ordered his detention on remand. The applicant was assisted from this point on by counsel. The District Court found that there was a strong suspicion that the applicant had evaded taxes on some twenty occasions between 1997 and July 2003. He had been working as a self-employed commercial agent for several firms in Germany since 1995 and been running a telephone service since 2001. In 2002 the company XYZ Aachen had paid him commission amounting to 125,000 euros. The court found that, according to the documents before it at that date, the applicant was suspected of having evaded turnover taxes of 57,000 euros, income taxes of 133,000 euros and trade taxes of 20,000 euros. The District Court noted that the applicant, who had availed himself of the right to remain silent, was strongly suspected of tax evasion on the basis of the business records that had been seized when his home was searched. He had to be placed in pre-trial detention because of a danger of collusion (Verdunkelungsgefahr) (see section 112 § 2 no. 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure – paragraph 41 below). The documents seized were incomplete. There was therefore a risk that the applicant, if released, might destroy the missing documents or conceal further business transactions and accounts.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/90) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Cypriot national, Mr Andreas Kyriacou (“the applicant”), on 30 May 1990. The applicant was represented by Mr E. Evripidou, a lawyer practising in Nicosia. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Z.M. Necatigil. The applicant alleged that the Turkish occupation of the northern part of Cyprus had deprived him of his home and properties. The applicant died on 3 November 1994. No letters of administration having been granted for his estate, his lawful heirs are his wife, Mrs Andriana Yianni Kyriacou and his two sons, Andreas Ioannou and Kyriakos Ioannou. In September 1999 the applicant’s heirs informed the Court that they wished to pursue the application on behalf of the deceased. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). By a decision of 8 June 1999 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). In addition, third-party comments were received from the Government of Cyprus, which had exercised its right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 1 (b)). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1900. The applicant grew up in Trypimeni, a village in the District of Famagusta. He alleged that he was the owner of the following immovable properties in the village: (a) registration no. 5147, plot no. 20, sheet/plan 13/40, house with two rooms and one kitchen, one veranda, oven, trees and yard; the applicant alleged that two extra rooms and one kitchen had been added later; area of the plot of land: 530 sq. m; area of the house: 230 sq. m; (b) registration no. 2597, plot no. 442, sheet/plan 13/40, field with olive trees; area: 13,713 sq. m. In support of his claim of ownership, the applicant submitted copies of the original title deeds. It appears from these documents that the applicant owned five twelfths of the property described above under paragraph 9 (a) and half of the property described above under paragraph 9 (b). However, in his observations of September 1999, the applicant’s lawyer alleged that his client had had full ownership of the whole of the two plots. He submitted that from 1920 onwards only the applicant, his wife and his two children had been living in the house built on plot no. 20. This house had been the marital home from the time of his wedding and the applicant had had the absolute and unrestricted use and occupation of it. Moreover, from August 1927 the applicant had been cultivating and taking care of the whole of plot no. 442.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 3 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Nigerian national, Ms Aisha Aden (“the applicant”), on 20 August 2010. The applicant was represented by the Rights Centre, an NGO situated in Stockholm. The Norwegian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Lars Jensen, from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and their Co-Agent, Ms Maria Andersson, from the Ministry of Justice. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Norwegian authorities’ refusal to reinstate her residence permit in Norway was in breach of Articles 2 and 6 of the Convention. On 28 January 2010 the acting President of the Sixth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 28 § 1). On 15 March 2011 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court) and the above application was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in Nigeria on 15 October 1988 as the youngest of six siblings. Currently she lives in Stavanger. From 1992 to 1996 the applicant lived with her family in Uganda. In May 1995 the applicant’s father and a sister were granted asylum in Norway. Having been granted a residence permit in December 1995, on 12 March 1996 the applicant, who at the relevant time was seven years old, her mother and four siblings joined them. A few years later, the applicant’s parents divorced. The parents maintained joint custody of the applicant, who lived with her mother. From 1996 until August 2003, the applicant attended various schools, some of which expelled her due to disciplinary problems. The applicant also had difficulties with her parents, who disapproved of certain aspects of her behaviour. Consequently, in June 2004, when the applicant was fifteen years old, her father decided to take her to Uganda to take care of her paternal grandmother, who was living at the Kibera refugee camp in eastern Uganda. It appears that the applicant’s mother did not want her to go but reluctantly agreed on the understanding that it would be a short trip. It also appears that the applicant believed that she was going on a short trip to visit her grandmother. When the applicant’s father returned to Norway, he was summoned for an interview with the Immigration Service on 12 October 2004 because the latter had been informed that he, who had been recognised as a refugee, had visited his country of origin. On 19 November 2004 the Immigration Service (Utlendingsdirektoratet) took the stand that the applicant’s father’s residence permit had not lapsed. In that connection, the applicant’s father was advised on the regulation regarding lapse of residence permits.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 7 April 1993, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application against Ireland lodged with the Commission under Article 25 on 1 May 1990 by an Irish citizen. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby Ireland recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6, 8 and/or 14 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio a judge of Irish nationality and the President of the Court. On 23 April 1993, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members. On 25 May 1993, a judge withdrew from the Chamber. By letter of 30 June 1993, the Agent of the Government notified the Registrar of the appointment of an ad hoc judge. As President of the Chamber, through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the procedure. Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the applicant’s memorial and the Government’s on 23 September 1993 and 14 October 1993, respectively. The Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 November 1993. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 47328/99) against a State (Republic of Turkey) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (Turkish national), Mr X (“the applicant”), on 15 March 1999. The applicant was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in a region (Middlesex). The State (Republic of Turkey) did not designate an Agent for the purpose of the proceedings before the Court. On 27 April 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the applicant’s right to a fair trial by an independent and impartial tribunal and the failure to notify the applicant of the public prosecutor’s submissions on his appeal to the State (Republic of Turkey). Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, who was born in 1964, resides in a city (Istanbul). On 31 January 1997 the applicant made a speech about the liberation movement in a region (Palestine) and praised the leaders who worked for the liberation of a place (Jerusalem) during a meeting which was organised by a local council in a city (Ankara). On 6 February 1997 the applicant was taken into police custody. In his statement, he explained that he supported a regime and that he longed for a regime that was based on a religious text (Koran). On 13 February 1997 the applicant was questioned by a prosecutor attached to a court (State Security Court) in the city (Ankara). During his questioning by the prosecutor, the applicant repeated his police statement. On the same day the applicant was brought before an investigating judge attached to the court (State Security Court) and he was subsequently placed in detention on remand. In an indictment dated 7 March 1997, the court (State Security Court) public prosecutor initiated criminal proceedings against the applicant. Before the court (State Security Court), which was composed of three judges including a military judge, the applicant contested the charges against him. On 15 October 1997 the court (State Security Court) convicted the applicant of being a member of an illegal organisation and sentenced him to seventeen years and six months’ imprisonment pursuant to a law (Criminal Code). On 6 January 1998 the applicant appealed to a higher court (Court of Cassation). The public prosecutor at the higher court (Court of Cassation) submitted his written opinion on the merits of the appeal. The opinion was not notified to the applicant, but was read out during the hearing before the higher court (Court of Cassation). On 21 September 1998 the higher court (Court of Cassation) dismissed the applicant’s appeal, upholding the court (State Security Court)’s assessment of evidence and its reasons for rejecting the applicant’s defence. On 24 December 1998 the public prosecutor attached to the higher court (Court of Cassation) rejected the applicant’s request for rectification.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 48001/99) against a country of Europe ("the Republic") lodged with an international organization ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of a convention ("the Convention") by a national of the country, John Doe ("the applicant"), on 6 July 1999. The applicant having died on 2 December 2001, the Court accepted that his son, Alex, was entitled to pursue the application. The applicant was not represented before the Court. The government of the country ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Mr. Smith, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his right to a "hearing within a reasonable time" had not been respected. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1999, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 23 October 2001 the Chamber of the Fourth Section declared the application admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1905 and lived in a city. He was the co-owner of a plot of land and a house in the city. On 23 September 1980 John G. ("the petitioner") filed with a local court an application for division of the property. On 2 August 1984 the court gave a decision and divided the property. On 21 January 1985, on the applicant's appeal, a higher court quashed the decision and remitted the case to the local court. On 24 September 1986, at the request of the petitioner, the local court issued an interim order enjoining third parties from entering the attic of the house. On 27 May 1988 the court issued another interim order enjoining the applicant and his wife from carrying out any work to the house. On 24 November 1989 the court rejected another request of the petitioner for an interim order. Having obtained a number of expert reports, the local court gave a preliminary decision on 22 December 1989. It determined that the house in question consisted of two apartments, basements and an attic. On 9 July 1990, on the applicant's appeal, the higher court quashed this decision. On 24 December 1990 the applicant filed with the local court an application for permission to carry out works on the gas supply to his apartment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1182/05) against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a German national, Mr Ingo Hub (“the applicant”), on 4 January 2005. The German Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs A. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. On 22 April 2008 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE 1. Background to the case The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in a city. The applicant is the father of a child (S.), born on 30 July 1990. In 1997 the applicant and the child’s mother separated. S. remained with his mother. In 1998 the applicant and S.’s mother were divorced. On 21 January 1998 the court awarded the mother sole custody of the child and decided that the applicant would be entitled to personal contact with the child every other weekend. In September 1998, however, the applicant ceased to have contact with the child. 2. Proceedings before the court On 7 October 1998 the applicant requested the court to impose a coercive fine on the mother to enforce his access rights. The court registered his request under file number 11 F 4813/98. Between 9 November 1998 and 10 March 1999 the parties and the Youth Office submitted observations. On 17 May 1999 the applicant withdrew his request and stated that he now wished the court to mediate between the parents with a view to reaching an agreement on the applicant’s contact rights according to section 52a of the Non-Contentious Proceedings Act (see “Relevant Domestic Law” below). The court pursued the applicant’s modified request under the same file number (11 F 4813/98). On 13 August 1999 the court heard the child, who declared that he wished to see his father only occasionally under the supervision of a third person. At a hearing held on 23 August 1999 the parents agreed on supervised contact for the applicant. On 18 October 1999 the court held a further hearing at which the parties declared that the court currently did not need to take any action. On 22 February 2000 the applicant applied for the appointment of a guardian ad litem and a contact supervisor arguing that the mediation proceedings had failed. On 10 March 2000 the court appointed a guardian ad litem and set down the case for hearing on 5 April 2000. However, that hearing was postponed to 15 May 2000 as agreed with the parties.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against a country of Western Europe and Northern Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2007. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Smith of Legal Associates, a lawyer practising in London. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Jones of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant complained, among other things, that he had been dismissed on account of his political views and membership of a political party. On 8 December 2008 the Acting President of the Fifth Section decided to communicate the complaints concerning Articles 10, 11 and 14 of the Convention to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Manchester. The applicant was employed by Global Services from 5 January 2004 to his dismissal on 31 July 2005. Global Services provided transport to local authorities, including Manchester City Council. The applicant, who is white European, was employed formerly as a driver’s assistant and latterly as a driver. As such, he was responsible for transporting children and adults with physical and/or mental disabilities within the Manchester area. The majority of his passengers were of Asian origin. There had been no complaints about his work or his conduct at work and his supervisor, who was of Asian origin, had nominated him for the award of “outstanding employee”. On 25 June 2005 a local newspaper article published in Manchester and the surrounding areas identified the applicant as a candidate for the Nationalist Party in the forthcoming local elections. On the same day, the applicant was temporarily assigned to deliver mail to local council offices. At the relevant time the Nationalist Party only extended membership to white nationals. According to its constitution it was: “wholly opposed to any form of integration between European and non-European peoples. It is therefore committed to stemming and reversing the tide of non-white immigration and to restoring, by legal changes, negotiation and consent, the overwhelmingly white makeup of the European population that existed in Europe prior to 1950.” On 26 June 2005 the Workers’ Union sent a letter to Global Services stating that many of its members found the applicant’s continued employment a “significant cause for concern, bearing in mind the Nationalist Party’s overt and racist/fascist agenda.” The letter advised Global Services that 70-80 percent of its customer base and 35 percent of its workforce were of Asian origin. The Workers’ Union asked that Global Services take immediate action to ensure its members were not subjected to racial hatred. Another union, the Labour Union, and a number of employees also made representations to Global Services about the applicant’s continued employment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against the Republic of X (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an X national, John Doe (the applicant), on 29 April 1999. The applicant was represented before the Court by Mr. X Y, a lawyer practising in City Y. The Government of X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Z W, Head of the International Law Department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that criminal proceedings against him lasted unreasonably long. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 21 November 2000 the Court declared the application admissible. As of 1 November 2001 the application was allocated to the First Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided for in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. THE FACTS On 3 June 1994 an action in defamation was brought against the applicant. He was suspected of having abused another person in the course of an altercation. Trial hearings were held on 8 November 1994, 8 May 1995 and 3 October 1995 before the District Court. On the latter date the applicant was convicted of defamation and sentenced to a fine. On 4 March 1996, following the applicant’s appeal, the Regional Court quashed the sentence because of errors of procedure and law, and referred the case back to the District Court. It found, inter alia, that the District Court had relied on evidence that had been precluded. On 17 February 1997, after hearings on that date and 10 January 1997, the District Court convicted the applicant again, qualifying the incriminated behaviour this time as an insult. On 8 January 1998, following the applicant’s appeal, the Regional Court quashed the sentence again and referred the case back to the District Court. The Court of Appeal found that the District Court had failed to take evidence concerning the applicant’s intentions. On 18 May 1998 the District Court again convicted the applicant of insult. On 25 January 1999 the Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal. The decision was served on 27 April 1999.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against a Republic (name omitted) lodged with an international organization ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of a human rights convention ("the Convention") by a national, Mr. John Doe ("the applicant"), on 31 August 1995. The applicant was represented by Mr. James Smith, a lawyer practising in a city (name omitted). The Republic's government ("the Government") were represented by their Agents, Mr. Robert Brown and, subsequently, by Mr. Michael Green. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand had been unreasonably long. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 By a decision of 21 October 2004, the Court declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1946 and lives in a city (name omitted). The applicant was arrested on 24 August 1994 on suspicion of extorting protection money from an escort agency. By a decision of 26 August 1994 given by a prosecutor (name omitted) the applicant and other suspects were detained on remand. On 2 September 1994 the applicant's lawyer appealed against the decision of 26 August 1994. His appeal was dismissed by a court on 8 September 1994. On 24 October 1994 the prosecutor (name omitted) dismissed the applicant's lawyer's appeal of 19 October 1994 against the detention decision, considering that a number of witnesses had given evidence incriminating all the suspects. On 24 October 1994 the prosecutor (name omitted) ordered the applicant to undergo psychiatric observation. On 10 November 1994 the court prolonged the applicant's detention on remand until 21 January 1995, considering that the charges against the applicant were of a serious nature and that they had been supported by the evidence gathered in the proceedings. The court pointed out that the investigation had not yet been completed and that the group the applicant belonged to had brought improper pressure upon the witnesses to change their testimony. On 21 November 1994 an expert opinion on the state of the applicant's mental health was issued. On 7 December 1994 the court of appeal dismissed the applicant's lawyer's appeal of 24 November 1994 against the decision of 10 November 1994 prolonging the applicant's detention on remand.
