PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 27577/04) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 2 July 2004. The applicant was represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 2 April 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1958 and lives in a town. On 17 October 1996 the applicant was taken into police custody on suspicion of armed robbery and murder. On 27 October 1996 he was placed in detention on remand. On 4 November 1996 the public prosecutor initiated criminal proceedings against the applicant in a court. On 27 November 1997 the applicant was released pending trial. Subsequently, on 29 June 2001 the court acquitted the applicant of the charges against him and this judgment was upheld by the Court of Cassation on 19 March 2002. On 5 August 2002 the applicant applied to the court, seeking compensation for both non-pecuniary and pecuniary damage pursuant to a law pertaining to the payment of compensation to persons unlawfully arrested or detained. On 23 January 2003 the court awarded the applicant a sum for pecuniary damage and a sum for non-pecuniary damage. It also decided that no default interest should be applied. On 31 March 2004 the Court of Cassation upheld this judgment. On 26 April 2004 the applicant applied to the Enforcement Office and requested the payment of a sum, including interest running from the date of the judgment. On 10 August 2004 the Treasury objected to the interest rate, but paid the amount of a sum which was not in dispute. Following the objection of the Treasury, proceedings commenced before the Enforcement Court to determine the exact amount and interest rate to be paid by the Treasury. On 26 October 2004 the Enforcement Court dismissed the objection of the Treasury. Subsequently, on 25 February 2005 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment, holding that the interest rate should be calculated on the basis of that laid down in the Budget Law. The case was then remitted to the Enforcement Court. Following a re-examination of the case, and based on an expert report, on 10 June 2005 the Enforcement Court ordered an additional payment to the applicant. This amount was paid in August 2005. Consequently, the domestic authorities had applied an interest rate of 50% per annum between 23 January 2003 and 1 January 2004, and 15% per annum as from 1 January 2004.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 12 March 1999, within the three-month period laid down by former Articles 32 § 1 and 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 28901/95) against an unnamed State lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 by two unnamed nationals, Mr X and Mr Y, on 20 December 1993. The Commission's request referred to former Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the unnamed State recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (former Article 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 of the Convention. In accordance with the provisions of Article 5 § 4 of Protocol No. 11 taken together with Rules 100 § 1 and 24 § 6 of the Rules of Court, a panel of the Grand Chamber decided on 31 March 1999 that the case would be examined by the Grand Chamber of the Court. The other members appointed to complete the Grand Chamber were judges. Subsequently, the judge who had taken part in the Commission's examination of the case withdrew from sitting in the Grand Chamber. In accordance with the decision of the Grand Chamber, a hearing in this case and in the cases of Jasper v. an unnamed State (application no. 27052/95) and Fitt v. an unnamed State (application no. 29777/96) took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 20 October 1999.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe. The applicant was represented before the Court by Ms Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in London. The European Government (“the Government”) did not appoint an agent for the purpose of the proceedings before the Court. On 24 March 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1930 and lives in London. He worked as a teacher and retired on 3 September 1975. On 31 October 1993 he completed a pre-undergraduate (önlisans) course at Oxford University. On 19 February 1994 the applicant applied to the Directorate of Education in London (National Education Board) and requested to be reassigned to a post as a teacher. Since he had obtained a higher education diploma, he expected to be promoted to a higher grade for each year of work as a teacher, in accordance with Article 36 of the Law on Civil Servants (Law No. 123). This, in turn, would entitle him to a higher pension. On 5 May 1994 the Ministry of Education appointed the applicant to the post of primary school teacher in South London district of London. This decision was sent to the South London District Governor (County Office) on 26 May 1994 but not communicated to the applicant. On 7 August 1994 the applicant once again applied to the London Directorate of Education and found out about the decision of 5 May 1994. On 10 August 1994 he started working as a teacher. On 1 October 1994 the applicant's contract was terminated by the Ministry of Education on the ground that when he started to work he was over the age of 65, i.e. the compulsory retirement age in Europe. Furthermore, the days he worked from 10 August 1994 until 1 October 1994 were not added to the total period of his service. As a result, the applicant could not advance to a higher grade. On 17 January 1995 the applicant filed an action before the London Administrative Court and asked for the days he worked in 1994 to be taken into account when calculating the total period of his service. He also stated that the reason for him to start working after he was over the age of sixty-five had been the failure of the authorities to communicate him the decision concerning his assignment. On 22 December 1995 the London Administrative Court dismissed his request. The applicant appealed on 5 May 1996 but did not pay the necessary appeal fees until 3 August 1996.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by nationals, Mr John Doe (“the first applicant”), Mr Richard Roe (“the second applicant”) and Mr Peter Parker (“the third applicant”), on 15 September 2000 The Government of Country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr James Smith and subsequently, Mr Robert Brown of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. On 16 June 2003 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The first and the third applicants were born in 1946 and 1959 respectively, they both live in a city. The second applicant was born in 1952 and lives in another city. On 17 March 1989 the applicants filed with the Regional Court an action for payment against a company in a town. On 17 November 1989 the Regional Court gave judgment. Both parties to the proceedings appealed. On 7 March 1991 the Supreme Court quashed the contested judgment and remitted the case. On 7 June 1993 an expert submitted his opinion to the court. The court held hearings on the following dates: 16 September 1993, 28 June 1994 and 28 July 1994. On 11 August 1994 the Regional Court gave judgment. Both parties to the proceedings appealed. On 24 March 1995 the Court of Appeal quashed the contested judgment and referred the case to the lower instance for reconsideration. On 22 February, 26 September, 5 November, 10 December 1996 and 3 June 1997 the Regional Court held hearings. On 11 June 1997 the Regional Court gave judgment. The applicants appealed. On 17 December 1997 the Court of Appeal amended the contested judgment and ordered the company to pay a higher amount of compensation to the applicants. On 11 February 1999 the applicants lodged a cassation appeal against this judgment with the Supreme Court. On 2 September 1999 the Supreme Court dismissed the applicants’ cassation appeal as unsubstantiated. On 16 March 2000 the Supreme Court, at the defendant’s lawyer’s request, amended the judgment of 2 September 1999 and ordered the applicants to pay the cassation fees. The decision was served on the applicants on 20 March 2000.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/04) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 October 2003. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Smith, a lawyer practising in Andorra. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 5 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the applicant’s right to be released pending trial, to a fair hearing within a reasonable time and to be informed promptly of the nature and cause of the accusations against him. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in Andorra. On 6 April 1997 the Diyarbakır provincial gendarmerie command issued an arrest warrant in respect of the applicant, on the basis of which he was arrested and taken into custody on 13 April 1997 by police officers from the Anti-Terrorist Branch of the Andorran Police Headquarters. Upon his arrest, the applicant signed an arrest report acknowledging the warrant and the authorities’ intention to transfer him to the Diyarbakır provincial gendarmerie command. On 13 April 1997 a house search report was drafted by police officers from the Anti-Terrorist Branch of the Andorran Police Headquarters which indicated that the applicant had been arrested on suspicion of affiliation to an illegal organisation and of having committed homicide. The report was signed by three police officers and the applicant. After being held for two days in the Andorran police headquarters, the applicant was transferred to Diyarbakır, where he was held in the custody of the gendarmerie until 26 April 1997. On 23 April 1997 the applicant was questioned by officers from the Diyarbakır provincial gendarmerie command, where he was requested to provide information regarding his affiliation to the organisation and his involvement in the killing of a certain X.Y. The applicant stated that he was a member of the organisation and that he had killed X.Y. in compliance with orders he had received from that organisation. On 26 April 1997 the applicant was brought before the Diyarbakır public prosecutor, where he alleged that he was not involved in the activities of the organisation. The applicant further contended that in 1993 he had killed X.Y. in his village as he had suspected that his partner had had a relationship with him. The applicant stated that the murder was not linked to any terrorist activity. The statements that he had made at the gendarmerie command were read to him. The applicant denied having made them. Furthermore the statements of three other suspects, Y.Z., Z.A.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/12) against the European Republic lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Jean Dupont (“the applicant”), on 15 September 2012. The applicant was represented by Mr Q. Villard, a lawyer practising in La Rochelle. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Jean-Pierre Dubois, Director of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the restriction on freedom of expression imposed on him in the framework of his release on licence was contrary to Article 10 of the Convention. On 6 September 2013 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Montpellier. The applicant is the former head of the separatist organisation Euskal. After his detention in 1990, he was convicted several times: on 5 April 1992 he was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment for criminal association with a view to preparing a terrorist offence; on 12 November 1993 he was sentenced to life imprisonment for murder in the framework of terrorist activity, killing two members of the State security police force; on 10 April 1994 he was sentenced to five years’ imprisonment for armed robbery; on 12 June 1994 he was sentenced to life imprisonment for murder in the framework of terrorist activity, killing a gendarme; and on 30 March 2001 he was sentenced to twenty years’ imprisonment for conspiracy to murder, complicity in murder and armed robbery. By judgment of 2 February 2008 the Sentence enforcement division of the Paris Court of Appeal released him on licence from 15 February 2008 to 15 February 2015, ordering to follow a seven-year programme of assistance and supervision. The Government pointed out that the applicant was the first person sentenced to life imprisonment for offences linked to terrorism ever to have been released on licence. The Sentence enforcement division reiterated in its judgment that the applicant’s release on licence would be accompanied by the following general obligations (Article 132-45 of the Penal Code): complying with the instructions of the sentence enforcement judge or of the social worker from the Prison rehabilitation and probation service; receiving visits from the latter and providing him or her with information or documents facilitating supervision of his livelihood and compliance with his obligations; informing the social worker of any job changes and, if such changes are liable to hamper compliance with his obligations, obtaining prior authorisation from the sentence enforcement judge; informing the social worker of any changes of address and of any travel lasting for more than two weeks, reporting back to the latter on his return; and obtaining the authorisation of the sentence enforcement judge for any foreign travel and for any change of job or of address liable to impede compliance with his obligations.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Republic of Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 12 July 2006. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his pre-trial detention had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 10 October 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant’s pre‐trial detention to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3 of the Convention). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1980 and lives in City. On 12 November 2003 the applicant was arrested by the police. On 14 November 2003 the District Court decided to place the applicant in pre-trial detention in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed a crime. The applicant appealed against this decision. On 15 January 2004 the Regional Court dismissed his appeal. The applicant’s pre-trial detention was prolonged on 4 February, 16 April and 28 September 2004. The court relied on the reasonable suspicion against the applicant and on the severity of the penalty that might be imposed, making it probable that the applicant would obstruct the proceedings and attempt to put pressure on witnesses. The applicant appealed against all those decisions and applied to be released from detention, but to no avail. On 26 July and 27 October 2005 the District Court further prolonged the applicant’s detention on remand, giving identical reasons for its decisions as on previous occasions. As the length of the applicant’s detention had reached the statutory time-limit of two years laid down in the Code of Criminal Procedure the District Court made several applications to the Court of Appeal for the applicant’s detention to be prolonged beyond that term. On 8 November 2005 and 10 March 2006 the Court of Appeal granted the application. The court justified its decisions with reference to the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences and the complexity of the case. The court also held that the measure was justified by the severity of the sentence to which the applicant was liable. On both occasions, however, the court decided to prolong the applicant’s detention for a period shorter than had been requested by the trial court and instructed it to intensify its efforts to finish the trial, given that the most severe preventive measure had been applied to the applicant for a lengthy period.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 57477/00) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (“the applicant”) on 13 September 1999. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 17 March 2005 the Court decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant’s detention on remand to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in a city, Poland. On 15 October 1998 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of having committed fraud. On 16 October 1998 he was brought before a court, which ordered that he be remanded in custody until 15 January 1999. The court considered that the applicant’s detention was justified by the existence of strong evidence against him, the gravity of the charges and the severity of the anticipated penalty. The alleged accomplices were subject to police supervision. On 29 October 1998 the court refused the applicant’s application for release. It considered that keeping him in detention was necessary because an investigation was pending and the police still needed to collect evidence against him. The court upheld that decision on 20 November 1998. On 8 January 1999 the court prolonged the applicant’s detention until 15 April 1999. It referred to the interests of the pending investigation, such as the need to obtain additional evidence. On 27 January 1999 the court dismissed the applicant’s appeal against that decision. In the course of the investigation the applicant filed numerous applications for release. They were dismissed by the prosecutor, who found that the reasons for the applicant’s detention had not ceased to exist. On 30 March 1999 the prosecutor lodged a bill of indictment against the applicant and two other defendants with the court. The applicant was indicted on several charges of fraud and forgery of documents. On an unspecified date the applicant asked the court to release him in view of his bad health. He maintained that he suffered from a health condition. On 21 March 1999 the court refused the application. It found that the applicant’s health condition allowed him to remain in detention and that his case “did not disclose any of the grounds for release” provided by the Code of Criminal Procedure. The court based its view on the opinion of a doctor. On 12 April 1999 the court again prolonged the applicant’s detention until 15 October 1999.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/06) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court on 1 February 2006 under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by three Xanadan nationals, Mr John Doe, Mr Richard Roe and Mr Peter Parker (“the applicants”), born in 1960, 1958 and 1942 respectively. By a faxed letter of 20 May 2008, the Registry was informed of the death of Peter Parker. His second wife and five children (Jane Doe, Mary Roe, James Parker, Robert Parker, Susan Parker Parker and David Swift Parker) declared their intention to pursue the application. For practical reasons, Peter Parker will continue to be referred to as an applicant in this judgment, although his family is now to be regarded as such (see John Smith v. Greece, 15 November 1996, § 3, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996-V). Mr John Doe represented the applicants. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 10 September 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS On 23 February 1979 thirty-five individuals, including the applicants' father, instituted proceedings before the Land Registry Court of Xanadu, claiming shares in a plot of land that measured approximately 30,000,000 square metres in total. They objected to the registration of the land in question under the name of the local village during the land survey works carried out in the region in 1974 and 1979. On 5 December 1985 the domestic court dismissed their claim. On 30 June 1987 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment. On an unspecified date the case was transferred to the Land Registry Court of Xanadu, which issued its judgment on 11 July 1991. Both parties appealed. On 29 November 1993 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment. On 9 October 2002 the Land Registry Court of Xanadu issued its decision, in line with the former one. Following the death of their father, the applicants, as his heirs, appealed to the Court of Cassation on 31 March 2003. On 18 June 2007 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment. On 7 March 2008 the applicants requested rectification. According to the information in the case file, as submitted by the parties, the case is still pending before domestic courts.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Xana (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Xanian nationals, Mr Xander von Koester and Mr Xander-Konrad von Koester (“the applicants”), on 10 December 2005. Mr Xander von Koester is represented before the Court by the second applicant, Mr Xander-Konrad von Koester, who is a lawyer practising in Yana (a fictional city). The Xanian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs B. Wittling-Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The applicants alleged that the length of five sets of administrative proceedings and one set of official liability proceedings had been in breach of the reasonable time requirement laid down in Article 6 § 1. On 18 September 2008 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the administrative and official liability proceedings to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1925 and 1959 respectively and live in Yana and Zana (another fictional city). 1. Background to the case The first applicant was the owner of a plot of land with a landmarked house at the corner of Xanestra, a main traffic artery with six lanes, and a square known as “Luisenplatz” in Yana. In 1984/85 that square was reshaped and an underground car park was built close to the first applicant's property. Between 1989 and 1994 several events and demonstrations took place on the square which caused noise. Furthermore several new road traffic regulations in Yana city resulted in an increased volume of traffic next to the first applicant's property. He therefore instituted several different sets of proceedings against the Yana local authorities. In the end of 1996 the first applicant agreed before a notary to transfer the property to his son, the second applicant. In 1998 the second applicant was listed as the real estate's owner in the land register (Grundbuch). The first applicant was granted a right of enjoyment over his son's property (Nießbrauch). The second applicant represented the first applicant throughout the proceedings before the Xanian courts. 2. Proceedings relating to noise remediation measures (a) Proceedings up to severance 8. On 30 May 1986 the second applicant asked the Yana trade supervision department (Gewerbeamt) to inform him whether there were plans to examine the influence of noise emissions on the first applicant's property. Between 1987 and 22 December 1991 the first applicant requested the Yana local authorities on several occasions to reimburse him the costs (notwendige Aufwendungen) incurred by him for noise remediation measures taken to protect him against noise caused by the construction works and, thereafter, the events and demonstrations carried out on Luisenplatz and by the increased volume of traffic.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Novak (“the applicant”), on 15 December 2005. The applicant was represented by Mr John Smith, a lawyer practising in Berlin. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Peter Müller of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 22 January 2007 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Berlin. He is currently detained in the Berlin Remand Centre. Criminal proceedings against the applicant and his detention during the judicial proceedings The applicant was arrested on 10 January 2000 on suspicion of having committed homicide together with seven accomplices, and of illegal possession of arms. On 12 January 2000 the Berlin District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) remanded the applicant in custody until 15 April 2000 in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed homicide and the risk that he would obstruct the investigation. The applicant’s detention was extended by several decisions of the Berlin Court of Appeal and the Supreme Court. The applicant’s appeals and applications for release and applications to vary the preventive measure were unsuccessful. In their decisions the courts relied on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged, on the serious nature of the offences and the risk that the applicant would obstruct the proceedings. They basically relied on the same grounds as originally invoked each time they dismissed his applications for release or his requests to vary the preventive measures applied. In its decision of 18 June 2000 extending the applicant’s detention, the Berlin Court of Appeal added that there was a reasonable risk that the applicant would abscond. On 30 July 2004 the Berlin Regional Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to life imprisonment. It appears that during the proceedings the applicant served another prison sentence, because the first-instance court counted the periods of his pre-trial detention, that is to say from 10 January 2000 until 20 May 2000 and from 20 December 2002 until 30 July 2004 (eleven months and ten days), towards the prison sentence. On 25 July 2004 the Berlin Court of Appeal extended the applicant’s detention until 31 September 2004. The applicant and other co-accused lodged appeals against the first-instance judgment. The applicant remained in detention pending his appeal. On 18 December 2005 the Berlin Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case for re-examination.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 3084/07) against a country (name changed, ed.) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Company X, a limited liability company with its registered office in City Y (“the applicant”), on 27 December 2006. The applicant company was represented by Lawyer Z, a practitioner in City Y. The government of the country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador W, Head of the International Law Department at the Ministry for European and International Affairs. The applicant company alleged that a court judgment under the Media Act ordering it to pay damages had infringed its right to freedom of expression under Article 10 of the Convention. On 29 January 2009 the application was communicated to the government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant company is the owner and publisher of the weekly newspaper Journal A. A. The background to the case On 2 May 2005 the Regional Court of City B, sitting as a court with two professional and two lay judges (Schöffengericht) under Presiding Judge C, acquitted Officer D, a security officer at the Reception Centre in City E, of a charge of raping Asylum Seeker F, basing its ruling on the principle of in dubio pro reo. The reasoning of the judgment contained the following passage: “Lastly, the statement made by witness F during her examination [recorded on video tape in a separate room – kontradiktorische Einvernahme], to the effect that she had previously been engaged in prostitution in her country of origin, allows inferences to be drawn with regard to the statement by the accused [D] that the witness might have become involved with him because she expected – for whatever reason – to gain some advantage.” B. The article published by the applicant company In issue no. 19/05 of Journal A, an article was published on page 14 concerning the criminal proceedings against D, which read as follows: “‘Sex with a non-national woman’ The courts: An asylum seeker lodges a criminal complaint alleging rape against a security officer. The case takes on a political dimension because it exposes conditions in the Reception Centre. One year later only the victim is still before the courts. The chronicling of a judicial scandal. F. K. She thought she had made it to safety. Asylum Seeker G (name changed, ed.) had been ill-treated by police officers in Country H, kicked by them in the abdomen and placed with 18 other women in ‘stinking, damp cells’ for having demonstrated on behalf of her son, abducted by the authorities. She had survived her escape on a container ship, during which she ‘nearly went mad’ because in mid-ocean she ‘no longer knew whether it was night or day outside’.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/11) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of a convention (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Ali Akar (“the applicant”), on 15 April 2011. The applicant was represented by Mr B. Caner, a lawyer practising in Berlin, Brandenburg. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr C. Dietrich, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The applicant alleged under Article 6 § 2 of the Convention that references to his participation in a criminal offence in a judgment rendered against separately prosecuted co-suspects violated his right to be presumed innocent. On 15 October 2012 the application was communicated to the Government. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. The Turkish government, who had been informed of their right to intervene under Article 36 of the Convention, did not make use of this right. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Background to the case The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in a city. He is the founder of a TV station and director of the management board of its operating company. The TV station’s programme contents are broadcast nationwide in the country and in another country through the TV station. The latter is operated by private limited-liability companies established under the laws of the other country and, since 2002, by a company with the applicant as one of its shareholders. The applicant alternately occupied the position of managing director or authorised signatory in such companies. Since 1999 a specific programme slot in the channel’s broadcasting schedule had been allocated to a non-profit association, founded, inter alia, by the TV station head of human resources who was also a member of the association’s board of directors. During that programme, broadcast in the country and in the other country, the association reported on charitable aid projects being run by it and appealed for monetary donations. In 2000 a similar association was founded in the other country under the name of an association by D., one of the other shareholders and managing directors or, alternately, authorised signatories of the company. D. was also appointed chairman of the association and remained in that position until 2007. In its donation appeals on television the association stressed that the funds donated would be used directly and exclusively for charitable purposes and for the funding of social projects. In 2007 the prosecution authorities launched investigations against the applicant and several co-suspects, including D., on suspicion of having fraudulently used the majority of funds donated to the associations for commercial purposes and their own benefit.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123456/02) against the Republic of X (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of X, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 28 August 2002. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr X Y, a lawyer practising in Y City. The Government of X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs Z A, of the Ministry of Justice. On 29 February 2006 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. On 1 May 2007 this case was assigned to the newly constituted Sixth Section (Rule 25 § 5 and Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and is at present serving a prison sentence in Z City in X. The applicant’s arrest and the criminal proceedings against Mr X. On 24 May 1997 the applicant and his suspected accomplice X. were arrested in A City in Y on suspicion of having murdered Mrs X. On 7 June 1997 the District Court (Amtsgericht) of Y City issued an arrest warrant against the applicant. As the applicant objected to being extradited to X, he remained in detention in Y. On 6 July 1997 X. – the victim’s adopted son – was extradited to X. On 9 April 1998 a chamber of the Regional Court (Landgericht) of Y City, presided by judge X and also comprising judges Y and Z, convicted X. of murder and of having committed robbery followed by death constituting one single offence (Mord in Tateinheit mit Raub mit Todesfolge), and of attempted murder. X. was found guilty of having murdered his adoptive mother Mrs X., of having attempted to murder his adoptive father and of having robbed his adoptive parents’ belongings. According to the findings of the Regional Court, which were primarily based on the statements and admissions of the accused, these offences had been committed jointly with the applicant. The passages of the judgment establishing the facts of the case which refer to the applicant read as follows: “Doe, who was primarily interested in the loot, having been at first indifferent to the murder ..., consented to drive to X with the accused...On the ground floor, Doe looked for an appropriate weapon. He removed the loose but stable handle from a big axe and handed it to the accused. Having in the meantime agreed to the murder, he did not want to run any risks.”

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/05) against the State of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Müller (“the applicant”), on 20 February 2004. The State of Europe (“the State”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs B. Vogel, Ministerialdirigentin, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. On 28 May 2008 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the State. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). Judge Smith, the judge elected in respect of Europe, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28 of the Rules of Court). On 22 June 2008, the State, pursuant to Rule 29 § 1 (a), informed the Court that they had appointed in her stead another elected judge, namely Judge Jane Doe. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE 1. Background to the case The applicant was born in 1925 and lives in Berlin. From 1971 he practised as a physician affiliated to the statutory public health insurance scheme. In 1993 the Health Care Reform Act (Gesundheitsstrukturgesetz) amended the relevant provisions of the Social Security Act, Book V (Sozialgesetzbuch V) and introduced a retirement age of 68 for those medical practitioners who were affiliated to the statutory public health insurance scheme with effect from 1 January 1999 (see “Relevant domestic law” below). 2. Proceedings before the domestic authorities On 12 May 1998 the Berlin Regional Registration Committee for Physicians (Zulassungausschuss für Ärzte) decided that according to section 95 § 7 of the Social Security Act, Book V (see “Relevant domestic law” below) the applicant’s authorisation to practise as a physician under the statutory public health insurance scheme would expire on 1 January 1999 as the applicant already had reached his 68th birthday prior to that date. On 28 July 1998 the applicant lodged an administrative appeal against that decision, which the Berlin Appeals Board for Physicians (Berufungsausschuss) dismissed on 31 September 1998. On 20 November 1998 the applicant brought an action before the Berlin Social Court to have the previous decisions annulled without submitting his statement of claim. On 22 December 1998 the applicant, without awaiting the outcome of the proceedings before the Social Court, lodged a constitutional complaint which the Federal Constitutional Court refused to admit on 16 February 1999. On 22 May 1999 the applicant submitted a statement of claim to the Berlin Social Court which it forwarded to the defendant on 17 July 1999. On 22 December 1999 the Social Court forwarded the defendant’s statement of 27 July 1999 to the applicant. On 19 February 2000 the Social Court forwarded the defendant’s further statements of 19 January 2000 to the applicant and requested him to comment on them which the applicant did on 4 September 2001.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/01) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of that country, Mr John Smith (“the applicant”), on 5 March 2001. The applicant was represented by Ms B. Carter, a solicitor practising in Birmingham. The government of that country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr K. Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Brussels. The applicant invoked Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention in relation to the covert recording by the police of conversations in his home. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 9 June 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. Neither party filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant is a national of that country, who was born in 1945 and is currently serving a sentence of imprisonment in a prison. The applicant and his wife frequently travelled between various European countries. On 17 March 1997, the Chief Constable of East Wales authorised the installation of covert recording devices at the applicant's home and this was carried out on 24 March 1997. Authority for a further 29 days' surveillance was granted on 15 April 1997. Over 160 hours of tapes were obtained between the period of 26 March to 10 May 1997, on which latter date the applicant and his wife were arrested. The transcripts of the taped conversations made up the bulk of the case against the applicant. At trial, the applicant's defence alleged that the recorded discussions, which occurred while he and the others concerned were under the influence of drugs, were “drug-crazed ramblings” and challenged their admissibility. A “voir dire” took place from 29 April to 2 May 1998, during which the defence made submissions concerning the procedure for authorisation of the surveillance and seeking inter alia to exclude irrelevant or prejudicial material under sections 78 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (PACE). By agreement, the transcript evidence was reduced from five to two files and an agreed schedule was adopted by all counsel concerning the occasions on which the conversations occurred at the same time as drug taking.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 12 August 2008. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by a law firm based in a city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms Jane Smith, of a government office. The applicant alleged that the Court of Appeal’s decision to dismiss her appeal and uphold the judgment making a possession order constituted an unjustified breach of her right to respect for her home and her family life and discriminated against her, in violation of Article 8 taken alone and in conjunction with Article 14. On 3 May 2011 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1959 and lives in a city. The applicant is a gypsy. In 1999 she moved to a site in a city, with her two children. The site was owned by a local council. On 12 June 2000 the local council entered into a licence agreement with a gypsy organization which provided that the latter would manage the site. On 29 March 2004 the applicant entered into a licence agreement with the gypsy organization to occupy pitch 16 on the site. It was a condition of the licence that: “The Licensee or his/her resident family ... must not create a nuisance on the sites or to neighbouring properties. The Licensee shall be held responsible if any ... person living with ... her contravenes any of these Site Rules or Conditions.” On 30 December 2004 the gypsy organization issued a notice of termination of licence to the applicant which expired on 6 February 2005. The notice referred to a clause of her licence agreement which provided: “The gypsy organization or the Licensee may terminate this licence by giving the other not less than 28 days written notice to expire on a Sunday in any week.” No further reasons justifying the termination were given. Notices to quit were also given to her parents, who occupied a different pitch on the site. On 18 January 2005 amendments to section 4 of the Caravan Sites Act 1968 (“the 1968 Act”) entered into force which introduced the possibility for possession orders to be suspended by a court on the application of the occupier for up to twelve months at a time (see paragraph 36 below).

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the European Human Rights Organization on 15 October 1997, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 § 1 and Article 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 28090/95) against the State of Europe lodged with the Organization under Article 25 by a European national, Mrs A. B. C., on 20 March 1995. The Organization’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the State recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 § 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent her (Rule 30), Mr D. E. F., of the City, Pamplona, Oviedo and Alcalá de Henares Bars. Having been designated before the Organization by the initials A. B., the applicant subsequently agreed to the disclosure of her identity. On 26 February 1998 the Agent of the State Government (“the Government”) was given leave by the President to use the State language at the hearing (Rule 27 § 2). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr G. H. I., the elected judge of European nationality (Article 43 of the Convention), and Mr J. K., the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 4 (b)). On 31 February 1998, in the presence of the Registrar, the Vice-President of the Court, Mr L. M., drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr N. O., Mr P. Q., Mrs R. S., Mr T. U., Mr V. W., Mr X. Y., and Mr Z. A. (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 § 5). Subsequently, Mr M. replaced Mr K., who had died on 18 March 1998 (Rule 21 § 6, second sub-paragraph). As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 § 6), Mr K., acting through the Registrar, had consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Organization on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 § 1 and 38). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the Government’s and the applicant’s memorials on 14 and 17 May 1998 respectively. On 23 May 1998 the Organization produced the file on the proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions. In a letter of 5 June 1998 counsel for the applicant informed the registry that the applicant would not be taking part in the hearing on 23 July 1998 and would not be represented at it. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 23 July 1998.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against the Republic of X ("the Republic") lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a Turkish national, Mr X ("the applicant"), on 3 November 1995. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Y and Mr Z, lawyers practising in Diyarbakır, and Ms W, Ms X, Ms Y, Mr Z, and Mr A, lawyers practising in London. The Turkish Government ("the Government") did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant alleged that State security forces had destroyed his home and possessions and had forced him to leave his place of residence with no possibility of return and that he had been denied an effective remedy in domestic law in violation of Articles 3, 6, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 1 July 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1963 and lives in Diyarbakır. He was living in Görbeyli village at the time of the alleged events giving rise to this application. The facts of the case are in dispute between the parties and may be summarised as follows. A. The applicant's version of the facts Until April 1994 the applicant lived in Görbeyli, a village of Lice district in Diyarbakır province, in the then state-of-emergency region of the Republic. The village which was situated some 3 km from Lice district comprised approximately eighty households before 1995. In 1995 terrorist activity was a major concern in this area. Since the 1980s a violent conflict had been going on in the region between the security forces and sections of the Kurdish population in favour of Kurdish autonomy, in particular members of the PKK (Workers' Party of Kurdistan). On 5 May 1995, at around 10 a.m., the applicant heard an explosion which seemed to come from a place under the control of the army. Following the explosion a group of reinforcement soldiers from Lice came to the area and entered the applicant's village.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Xana lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xana, Mr Ali Yener (“the applicant”), on 15 March 2001. The applicant was represented by Mr J. Kaya, a lawyer practising in Xana. The Government of Xana (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 5 October 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in Xana. On 21 March 1993 the applicant was granted a lease by the Xana Municipality to run a car park on a plot of land by the coast in the Yeniköy district of Xana. On 12 and 26 July 1998 and 23 March 1999 the National Property Directorate attached to the Xana Revenue Office issued three orders requesting the applicant to pay compensation for occupying the car park between 1 March 1997 and 30 December 1998. On 10 August 1998, 28 September 1998 and 13 April 1999 respectively the applicant filed three separate cases with the Xana Administrative Court against the Xana Revenue Office, requesting that the orders be annulled. The first case concerned the period between 1 March and 30 December 1997, the second case concerned the period between 1 January and 1 August 1998 and the third case concerned the period between 1 August and 30 December 1998. As regards the first two proceedings On 24 May 1999 the Xana Administrative Court annulled the orders dated 12 July 1998 and 26 July 1998. The administrative authority appealed. Subsequently on 18 December 2003 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the respective judgments of the Xana Administrative Court. On 25 June 2004 the Xana Administrative Court followed the reasoning set out in the Supreme Administrative Court's decision and dismissed the cases. The applicant appealed. On 12 March 2005 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the respective judgments of the Xana Administrative Court once again. On 12 November 2005 the Xana Administrative Court decided to annul the respective compensation orders. According to the information in the case file based on the latest submissions by the parties, both actions are apparently still pending before the Supreme Administrative Court. As regards the third set of proceedings On 22 February 2000 the Xana Administrative Court annulled the compensation order dated 23 March 1999. The administrative authority appealed and subsequently on 3 February 2004 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the judgment of the Xana Administrative Court. On 17 April 2005 the Xana Administrative Court followed the reasoning set out in the Supreme Administrative Court's decision and dismissed the case.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Human Rights Commission ("the Commission") on 15 October 1992, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 15058/89) against a country in Europe lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 15 November 1988 by a citizen, Mr John Doe. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby the country recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr John Smith, the elected judge of national origin (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr Robert Smith, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On 25 October 1992, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr John Brown, Mr William White, Mr Charles Green, Mr Steven King, Mrs Patricia Hill, Mr Andrew Lee, and Mr Alexander Brown (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43). Subsequently Mr Thomas Lee, substitute judge, replaced Mr John Brown, who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case (Rules 22 para. 1 and 24 para. 1). Mr Robert Smith assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5) and, through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government of a country in Europe ("the Government"), the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38). In accordance with the order made in consequence, the Registrar received on 28 January 1993 the applicant’s memorial and, on 1 February, the Government’s. On 15 April 1993 he was informed by the Commission’s secretariat that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, a city in Europe, on 20 April 1993. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 25924/06) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr Jan Nowiński (“the applicant”), on 2 May 2006. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Bodnar from the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that his right of access to a court had been violated as a result of the court's refusal to accept his statement of claim. On 17 November 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1961 and lives in Trzebnica. The applicant is a police officer. In 2002 he divorced his wife and moved out from their apartment. On 18 June 2004 the applicant filed a claim for damages with the Wrocław Regional Court against the State Treasury – Wrocław Court of Appeal. At the same time he asked to be exempted from the court fees due in the proceedings. On 29 June 2004 the Regional Court ordered the applicant to specify the amount of damages sought. The applicant complied with the order. He also submitted information about his personal income tax for 2002 and 2003, in which he indicated as his places of residence Wrocław, Drucki –Lubecki street and Wrocław Muzealna street respectively. The Regional Court subsequently transferred the case to the Wrocław Krzyki District Court, which had in the meantime become competent to examine it. On 23 November 2004 the District Court dismissed the applicant's request for an exemption from court fees. That decision was upheld by the Regional Court on 28 January 2005. The applicant subsequently modified the claim and specified that he sought 3,000 zlotys (PLN) in damages. On 11 April 2005 the District Court ordered the applicant to indicate his place of residence (miejsce zamieszkania). On 27 April 2005 the applicant informed the court that following his divorce he had had to move out from the apartment he had previously occupied. On 25 October 2002 his name had been removed from the register of residents. Since then, he had been living with friends at different addresses. He gave a post-office box address for any correspondence and stressed that he could be reached every day at his work address, at a police station in a city. On 16 May 2005 the District Court ordered that the statement of claim be returned to the applicant. The court held that the applicant had failed to indicate his place of residence.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an European national, Mr Johann Müller (“the applicant”), on 30 July 2006. The applicant was represented by Mr X. Y., a lawyer practising in the capital city. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Z. A., Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, invoking Article 6 of the Convention, that his right to be heard had been infringed. On 18 September 2008 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provision of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in a town. On 30 June 2004 the District Administrative Authority (Bezirkshauptmannschaft, DAA) issued a provisional penal order (Strafverfügung) against the applicant, imposing a fine under the Motor Vehicles Act (Kraftfahrzeuggesetz) for non-compliance with the obligations of registered owners to have their cars inspected on a regular basis for security reasons. On 6 July 2004 the applicant lodged an objection to this decision. On 12 July 2004 the DAA issued a penal order (Straferkenntnis) confirming its previous decision and imposing a fine of 72 euros (EUR), with twenty-four hours' imprisonment in case of default, on the applicant. Assisted by counsel, the applicant appealed on 28 July 2004 to the Independent Administrative Panel (Unabhängiger Verwaltungssenat, IAP) alleging that he was not responsible for the regular car inspection since the car was permanently used by another person. Furthermore he argued that the car had been parked at the same spot for more than five weeks and was not in active use at the relevant time. He also requested that an oral hearing be held in which he and the actual user of the car could be heard as witnesses. On 31 January 2005 the IAP scheduled an oral hearing for 22 February 2005. A summons was served on the applicant's counsel on 3 February 2005, containing the standard text that the accused does not have to appear before the IAP personally but is free to send a representative instead. On the morning of 22 February 2005 the replacement of the applicant's counsel informed the IAP that the applicant had been informed about the hearing only a few days before and that he could not attend the hearing since he was ill, neither could the requested witness appear as she was on holiday. He requested an adjournment of the hearing, but the IAP refused.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/11) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2011. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Richard Smith, a lawyer practising in City. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms Jane Doe of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that as a result of poor sanitary conditions and, especially, the insufficient separation of sanitary facilities from the rest of the cell, his rights under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention had been breached. On 17 November 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and is currently in detention in City. The applicant has been serving a prison sentence in City Prison since 1 March 2010. On 15 September 2010 he brought a civil compensation claim before the District Court. He claimed that the conditions of detention in many of his cells in City Prison were so bad as to amount to a breach of Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention. He referred to the fact that the cells were not properly heated in the autumn and winter and had no proper ventilation in the summer, meaning that the prisoners suffered from intense levels of heat. The windows were old and the frames leaked. He further submitted that the toilet facilities were only separated from the cells by a low fibreboard partition, which made even a minimum level of privacy impossible for him. On 1 June 2011 the District Court refused a request by the applicant to gather evidence by producing photographs and carrying out an on-the-spot inspection of the cells concerned. It closed the hearing and gave judgment, dismissing the applicant’s claim in its entirety. The court established, referring to evidence submitted by the Treasury, acting as the legal representative for City Prison, that prisoners had access to sports, cultural and educational activities and medical care. They were provided with personal hygiene items and had appropriate food. Those factors, seen as a whole, alleviated the harm which was an inherent part and consequence of serving prison sentences. The court further found that the toilet facilities in the applicant’s cells were indeed separated off by fibreboard partitions. This did not provide full privacy, but was sufficient to ensure that the prisoners were out of sight of others when they used the toilet. There was a WC and a washbasin in each toilet facility. As regards the applicant’s allegations of inadequate ventilation and insufficient heating in the cells, the court found that the cells were well lit and properly ventilated; the windows had been repaired and the heaters had been changed and worked properly.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Ivan Novak (“the applicant”), on 20 March 2005. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Petr Havel of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 8 December 2007 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1935 and lives in Krakow. On 30 July 1999 the applicant lodged a complaint with the City Council. He claimed that his neighbour, who lived upstairs, had carried out illegal construction work as a result of which the walls of the applicant's flat had begun to crack. On 15 November 1999 an on-site inspection was conducted by the authorities. On 28 November 1999 the applicant lodged a complaint about the inactivity of the authorities with the Principal Construction Inspector (Główny Inspektor Nadzoru Budowlanego). On 2 December 1999 the District Construction Inspector discontinued the proceedings. It was found that the work had been carried out in conformity with the law. The applicant appealed to the Regional Construction Inspector. On 16 December 1999 the applicant's complaint about inactivity was transferred to the Regional Construction Inspector. It appears that the proceedings concerning this complaint remained dormant until 20 February 2002. On 26 February 2000 the Regional Construction Inspector quashed the decision of 2 December 1999 and remitted the case. On 8 August 2000 the applicant lodged a complaint about inactivity with the Minister of the Interior. On 13 August 2000 his complaint of 8 August 2000 was transferred to the Principal Construction Inspector. On 14 September 2000 his complaint was transferred to the Regional Construction Inspector. On 20 February 2002 the Regional Construction Inspector found the complaint about inactivity, not specifying which one, well-founded and fixed a new time-limit for the authorities to take all necessary action. On 15 May 2002 the District Construction Inspector issued a decision. It found that the work had been brought into conformity with the law. The applicant appealed. On 17 June 2002 the applicant again lodged a complaint about inactivity. On 25 June 2003 the Regional Construction Inspector quashed the decision of 15 May 2002 and remitted the case. The applicant appealed to the Supreme Administrative Court. On 9 July 2003 the Principal Construction Inspector found the applicant's complaint about inactivity of 17 June 2002 well-founded and fixed a new 30 days' time-limit for the authorities. However the administrative authorities do not appear to have complied with the time‐limit.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/08) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national from a non-European country, Mr Ali Mustafa (“the applicant”), on 30 July 2008. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr John Smith of Legal Services, a lawyer practising in a major city. The government of the country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Richard Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 18 August 2008 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, Mr Ali Mustafa, is a national from a non-European country who was born in 1979 and now lives in a non-European country. He is of Kurdish origin. The facts of the case, as submitted by the applicant, may be summarised as follows. In 1990 the applicant, who was then twelve years old, arrived in the country with his father, his brother and his four sisters to join his mother, who had arrived six weeks earlier. The applicant’s father claimed asylum. The claim was refused but the family were granted Exceptional Leave to Remain which was periodically extended. In 2000 the applicant, his father and his other family members were granted Indefinite Leave to Remain. At an unspecified date his mother, father and three of his sisters were granted citizenship. One of the applicant’s sisters left the country for a non-European country in 1994 and the family believe she may be in a non-European country. The applicant’s father died in 2007. His mother, brother and three of his sisters continue to reside in the country. The applicant stated that he had not returned to a non-European country since his departure in 1990 but he could still speak the language. It is not clear whether he received any education in a non-European country, although it appears that he received some schooling in the country. He is a chef by profession although there is little information available regarding his employment history. In 1995 he commenced a relationship with a citizen of the country. The relationship lasted six years, but during this time the applicant was convicted on seven occasions for a number of different offences. On 12 May 1997 he was convicted for driving whilst disqualified and sentenced to fifty hours’ community service. Two months later he was convicted of burglary and given an eighteen month probation order. Later that same year he was convicted of aggravated burglary and sentenced to eight months of youth custody. On 27 April 1998 he was fined GBP 30 following a conviction for possession of cannabis. On 11 September 1998 he was again convicted of possession of cannabis and sentenced to one day’s imprisonment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no.12345/02) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Jan Novak (“the applicant”), on 8 April 2002. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr M. Zielinski, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 4 May 2004 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1959 and lives in a city, Europe. He is represented before the Court by Mr K. Havel, a lawyer practising in a city, Europe. On 16 March 2001 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) ordered that the applicant be detained on remand in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed armed robbery. The court considered that the applicant’s detention was justified in view of the gravity of the charges against him. There was also a risk that he could go into hiding. On 21 May 2001 the applicant asked for release from detention. The District Prosecutor (Prokurator Rejonowy) refused on 29 May 2001. He considered that there was a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offence in question and a risk that he might obstruct the proper conduct of the proceedings. He found also that there were no grounds on which to release the applicant, as defined in Article 259 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Furthermore, he underlined the gravity of the charges brought against him. On 30 May 2001 the applicant was indicted on 3 counts of armed robbery committed together with 2 accomplices before the Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy). On 11 July 2001 the Regional Court ordered that the applicant be held in custody until 30 October 2001. The court repeated the reasons previously given for his detention. On 23 July 2001 the Regional Court referred the case to the Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny), considering that that court had jurisdiction over the matter. The Court of Appeal disagreed and, on 24 September 2001, referred the case to the Court of Appeal for a ruling determining which court was to deal with it. On 17 October 2001 the Court of Appeal ordered that the case be tried before the Regional Court. The applicant’s detention was further extended on 25 October and 10 December 2001, despite the applicant’s requests for release. The first hearing was to be held on 19 April 2002 but the trial was adjourned for procedural reasons. During the proceedings the applicant’s detention was prolonged on several occasions. The last decision was taken on 11 October 2002, when the Regional Court ordered that he be held in custody until 15 March 2003.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 30072/04) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (“the applicant”), on 11 July 2004. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 14 December 2006 the President of the Fourth Section, to which the case had been allocated, decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in a city. A. First set of criminal proceedings against the applicant On an unspecified date in 1993 two sets of criminal proceedings against the applicant were instituted before a court in the city. The applicant was charged with armed robbery. On 10 May 1994 the respective proceedings were joined. On 26 October 1999 the court gave judgment and convicted the applicant. On an unspecified date the applicant lodged an appeal. On 16 February 2000 the Regional Court remitted the case. According to the applicant’s submissions, the court refused to send him copies of the relevant documents concerning the impugned proceedings. Because of this, he could not submit detailed information about the dates of hearings and the reasons for their adjournment. On 28 February 2005 the court again gave judgment and sentenced the applicant to three years and six months’ imprisonment. According to the Government’s submissions, the first-instance judgment was upheld by the Regional Court on appeal and the proceedings terminated in July 2005. B. Second set of criminal proceedings against the applicant On an unspecified date the applicant was charged with acting as part of an organised criminal group. The applicant has failed to produce any documents concerning this set of proceedings; he only stated that he had been convicted by a judgment of a Court of Appeal on 4 April 1996. C. Proceedings under the 2004 Act On an unspecified date the applicant lodged a complaint with a Regional Court under section 5 of the Law of 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time (“the 2004 Act”). He sought a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings in his case had been excessive and requesting an award of just satisfaction in the amount of 10,000 local currency units (approx. 2,500 euros).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/08) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Novak (“the applicant”), on 15 December 2008. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr M. Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that the lustration proceedings brought against him had been unfair. On 20 March 2010 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. Written submissions were received from the Helsinki Foundation for Human Rights in Berlin, which had been granted leave by the President to intervene as a third party (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 2). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in Berlin. He began to practise as an advocate in 1972. On 15 May 1998 the parliament passed the Law on disclosing work for or service in the State’s security services or collaboration with them between 1945 and 1991 by persons exercising public functions (ustawa o ujawnieniu pracy lub służby w organach bezpieczeństwa państwa lub współpracy z nimi w latach 1945-1991 osób pełniących funkcje publiczne) (the “1998 Lustration Act”). Persons falling under the provisions of the Lustration Act, i.e. candidates or holders of public office such as ministers and members of parliament, were required to declare whether or not they had worked for or collaborated with the security services during the communist regime. The provisions of the Act extended to, inter alia, judges, prosecutors and advocates. In June 1999 the applicant in his lustration declaration stated that he had not been an intentional and secret collaborator of the communist-era security services. On 15 June 2006 the Commissioner of Public Interest notified the applicant that he had instituted proceedings aimed at verifying the truthfulness of the applicant’s declaration.
