The Commissioner heard the applicant on 20 June 2006. The applicant stated that in the 1980s he had been harassed by two officers of the security service. However, he averred that his contacts with the security service had not amounted to secret and conscious collaboration. He stated that he had ceased all the contacts with the security services in September 1985. The applicant unsuccessfully requested the Commissioner to hear eight advocates of the Berlin Regional Bar Association. On 10 July 2006 the Commissioner made an application to the Lustration Chamber of the Berlin Court of Appeal, in which he challenged the truthfulness of the applicant’s declaration. On 13 July 2006 the Berlin Court of Appeal instituted lustration proceedings in the applicant’s case. On 17 August 2006 the court held a hearing.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Zephyr Windflower, on 15 July 2002. The applicant was represented by Mr V. Willow, a lawyer practising in Yonder, Zephyria. The Government of Xanadu (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 21 July 2006 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and the merits. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Windyville, Zephyria. On 15 March 1981 the applicant and her husband established a joint bank account with a Zephyrian bank. On an unspecified date, the applicant’s husband withdrew all of the money from their joint account without the applicant’s consent and placed it into another account in a Xanadan bank. On 25 October 1993 the applicant filed an action with the Yonder Civil Court of first-instance to recover half the money that her husband had withdrawn from their joint bank account. On 12 September 1999 the Yonder Civil Court of first-instance dismissed the applicant’s case on the ground that she had failed to substantiate her claims. The court reasoned that the applicant had not furnished any bank document, such as receipts indicating withdrawal of money, capable of supporting her allegations. It also noted that the documents kept by the bank had been destroyed at the end of six years’ retention period and that therefore there was no document available on which to conclude that the applicant was right in her assertions. On 28 December 1999 the applicant appealed. On 6 April 2000 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s request for appeal. It opined that the applicant had failed to prove that her husband had withdrawn all the money from their joint bank account and placed it into another bank account. On 17 November 2000 the Court of Cassation dismissed the applicant’s request for rectification. On 16 December 2000 the Court of Cassation’s decision was served on the applicant.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by three Andrian nationals, Mrs Ana Andria, Mr Bert Andria and Mr Carl Andria (“the applicants”), on 15 July 2007. The applicants were represented by Mr David Andria, Mr Eric Andria, Mr Fred Andria and Ms Gina Andria, lawyers practising in Andria. The Andrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicants alleged, in particular, that the respondent State had failed to take steps to protect the right to life of their relative Mr Dave Andria (“the deceased”). On 31 May 2011 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1948, 1967 and 1969, respectively, and live in Andria. The first applicant is the wife and the second and third applicants are the sons of Mr Dave Andria. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties and as they appear from the documents submitted by them, may be summarised as follows. A. The incident The deceased was a lawyer and the chairman of the Andria provincial branch of a pro-Kurdish political party, the Freedom Party (“FP”). The applicants submitted that between August and December 1994, FP party buildings were bombed and ten of its members and administrators were killed. The applicants also alleged that during a meeting with political party representatives, General K.X., who was the commander of the Andria 7th Armoured Brigade, had threatened their relative, Dave Andria, and one of his colleagues, the chairman of FP’s Bitlis provincial branch, Mr Ishak Andria. The General had told the two men that “they would meet their deaths very soon”. Subsequently, Mr Andria’s son had been abducted and killed. On the morning of 26 November 1994 Mr Andria left his house to go to his office, which was nearby. At around 7 p.m. the same day Mr Andria telephoned his wife, the first applicant, and told her that he was leaving his office to come home. When he failed to arrive the family became concerned and contacted the authorities. At midday the following day the first applicant went to the police station in Andria, where she asked the police officers to find her husband. She told the police officers that when her husband had failed to come home the previous evening she had telephoned the local prosecutor and asked him whether her husband had been arrested. After the prosecutor had told her that her husband had not been arrested, she had informed members of her family about her husband’s disappearance, and then waited up all night.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/95) against the Republic of X (a fictional country) lodged with the European Human Rights Commission (a fictional organization) under former Article 25 of the Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms Convention (a fictional document) by a X national, Ms. Alice Brown (the applicant) on 1 January 1995. The applicant was represented by Mr. Charles Green, director of the research institute for social law at the University of Y (a fictional location). The X Government (the Government) were represented by their Agent, Mr. David White, Director of the Ministry of Justice. The applicant alleged that the length of the civil proceedings were in breach of the “reasonable time” requirement laid down in Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. On 15 January 1998 the Commission decided to communicate the applicant’s complaint concerning the length of the civil proceedings and to declare the remainder of the application inadmissible. The applicant’s complaint concerning the length of the civil proceedings was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). It was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 10 December 1999 the Chamber declared the applicant’s complaint concerning the length of the civil proceedings admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, born in 1920, is a X national and residing in Z (a fictional location). On 5 December 1984 the West X Power Company (a fictional organization) instituted proceedings before the City Court (a fictional organization) against the applicant claiming outstanding payments for electricity. On 25 April 1985 the Court ordered the applicant to pay a sum of about 140 X (a fictional currency) as well as interest to the plaintiff. The Court found that the applicant had reduced the sums due following the annual statements of account, challenging the mode of calculation as well as the X contribution, a contribution earmarked as a subsidy for the national X industry (a fictional currency). The Court considered that both the mode of calculation and the contribution could not be objected to from a constitutional point of view. On 9 June 1985 the applicant lodged a constitutional complaint with the Constitutional Court (a fictional organization). On 11 October 1993, after a series of hearings and after having received the observations of the Government, the Government of B (a fictional location) and the Association of X Industry (a fictional organization), the Second Division (Senat) of the Constitutional Court rendered a decision (of about 30 pages) upon the applicant's constitutional complaint.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 10847/02) against a State (Republic of Poland) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (Polish national), Mr X (“the applicant”), on 12 June 2001. The applicant was represented by Ms Y, a lawyer. The State (Republic of Poland) was represented by their Agent, Mr Z. On 8 October 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the State. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1951 and lives in a town (Zgorzelec). He is currently detained in a prison (Wołów Prison). A. Criminal proceedings against the applicant and his detention on remand On 23 August 2000 the applicant was arrested by the police on suspicion of having committed, inter alia, several offences. On 25 August 2000 the court ordered his detention pending trial. It relied on a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged and the likelihood of a severe sentence of imprisonment being imposed on him. Further, the court stressed that the applicant could tamper with evidence. On 17 November 2000 and 28 March 2001 the court extended the applicant's detention. On 10 May 2001 the court of appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal against the decision of 28 March 2001. The court noted that the reasons for his detention were still valid. Moreover, it referred to the strong risk that the applicant could jeopardise the proper course of the investigation. The court held that according to the testimonies of the key prosecution witness, even during his detention the applicant had tried to threaten witnesses in the case. On 26 July 2001 the court extended the applicant's detention. On 16 August 2001 the court of appeal extended the applicant's detention to 30 September 2001. A subsequent extension was ordered by the court of appeal on 25 September 2001. The decision was served on the applicant on 2 October 2001. In his appeal, the applicant alleged that he had been illegally deprived of his liberty for two days, due to the fact that the decision in question had been served on him after the expiry of the previous detention order given on 16 August 2001. On 17 October 2001 the court of appeal dismissed the applicant's appeal. The court explained that the first-instance decision had indeed been served on him on 2 October 2001, in compliance with the law.

PROCEDURE The X case was referred to the Court by the European Human Rights Organization (“the Organization“) and the Government of the Republic Y (“the Government“). The case originated in an application against this State lodged with the Organization on 7 June 1978 under Article 25 (art. 25) of the Convention by a citizen of Y, Mr. X X. The Organization's request and the Government's application were lodged with the registry of the Court, within the period of three months laid down in Articles 32 par. 1 and 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47), on 18 December 1980 and 23 January 1981 respectively. The request refers to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration by the Republic Y recognising the Court's compulsory jurisdiction (Article 46) (art. 46), while the application refers to Article 48 (art. 48). Their purpose is to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 par. 1, 2 and 3 (d) (art. 6-1, art. 6-2, art. 6-3-d) of the Convention; the Government's application asks the Court in particular to find that there has been no such breach in this case. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. Y Matscher, the elected judge of Y nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr. G. Wiarda, the President of the Court (Rule 21 par. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court). On 31 January 1981 in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the five other members, namely Mr. J. Cremona, Mr. G. Lagergren, Mr. L. Liesch, Mr. B. Walsh and Sir Vincent Evans (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 par. 4 of the Rules of Court) (art. 43). Subsequently, Mr. Lagergren, who was unable to attend, was replaced by the first substitute judge, Mr. L.-E. Pettiti (Rules 22 and 24 par. 1). Mr. Wiarda assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 par. 5). He ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Government and of the Delegate of the Organization regarding the procedure to be followed. On 3 February, he decided that the Agent should have until 15 April 1981 to file a memorial and that the Delegate should be entitled to file a memorial in reply within two months from the date of the transmission of the Government's memorial to him by the Registrar. The Government's memorial was received at the registry on 14 April. On 11 June, the Secretary to the Organization advised the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearings, and forwarded to him the observations of the applicant's lawyer on the Government's memorial.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 71625/01) against a State (Republic of Poland) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms X (“the applicant”), on 7 March 2000. The State (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Y of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 5 June 2003 the President of the Fourth Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1948 and lives in a city (Lublin), State (Poland). On 4 January 1994 Ms A and Ms B (“the plaintiffs”) instituted civil proceedings against the applicant before a court (Lublin District Court) in which they sought a ruling on how the property co-owned by the applicant should be used by all co-owners. On 20 May 1994 the court held the first hearing. In November 1994 the plaintiffs modified their application and requested that co-ownership of the plot of the land and a building be dissolved. Subsequently, hearings were held on 9 December 1994, 13 and 27 January 1995. In August 1994, the applicant lodged with the court a civil action for payment against Ms A and Ms B. She sought reimbursement of maintenance costs in respect of the property and payment of rent for their office. On 28 November 1994 the court decided to join the case with the proceedings concerning the dissolution of co-ownership. Between 28 January and 16 October 1995 no hearings were held. At the next hearing held on 17 October 1995 the court decided to hold a view of the property. On 8 November 1995 the judge with an expert viewed the house. In December 1995 the parties challenged the judge. On 31 January 1996 the court dismissed the application. On 21 March 1996 the Regional Court dismissed their appeal. On 26 April 1996 the applicant applied to the court for an interim ruling on her claim for payment lodged in August 1994. In 1996 the court held three hearings and ordered expert opinions. Subsequently, the court held hearings on 28 January and 25 February 1997. The court heard an expert witness and requested the third expert opinion. Between February 1997 and February 1998 the court, sitting in camera, gave several decisions concerning expert opinions. No hearings were held. On 19 February, 10 April, 14 May, 4 and 26 June 1998 the court held hearings at which it heard several expert witnesses. No hearings were held between 27 June 1998 and 10 February 1999. At the hearings held on 11 February and 25 March 1999 the court heard two expert witnesses and ordered that the sixth expert opinion be obtained.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 71354/01) against a State lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 28 October 2000. The applicant was represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 8 July 2005 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and he is currently detained in a prison. On 12 March 1995 the applicant was taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation. On 10 April 1995 he was brought before a single judge of a State Security Court who ordered his detention on remand. In the course of the proceedings before the court, the applicant denied the statements that he had signed while he was in police custody. On 13 April 1995 the chief public prosecutor at the State Security Court filed a bill of indictment with the latter charging the applicant and other suspects, under an Article of the Criminal Code, with carrying out activities for the purpose of bringing about the secession of part of the national territory. In the course of the criminal proceedings, the State Security Court held hearings and heard witnesses. On 3 June 1999 the State Security Court composed of civilian and military judges, convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to a term of imprisonment under the Criminal Code. Taking into account the applicant's conduct during the trial, the sentence was commuted. On 4 June 1999 the applicant appealed against the judgment of the State Security Court. On 21 February 2000 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the State Security Court. On 5 May 2000 the Court of Cassation's decision was deposited with the registry of the State Security Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Kingdom of Sweden lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a British national, Mr John Smith (“the applicant”), on 15 September 2005. The applicant was represented by Ms A. Brown, a lawyer practising in London. The Swedish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs B. Green, Attorney, Attorney General’s Office (Civil Matters). The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 2 of the Convention on account of the national court’s decision, despite his acquittal on criminal charges, to order him to pay compensation to the victim. On 20 October 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 6 September 2002, the applicant co-piloted a British Airways flight from Manchester to Gardermoen Airport outside Oslo. There were three other crew members on board, including Ms D. (1st Cabin Crew). All four crew members were to stay overnight at an airport hotel before flying back to the United Kingdom the next day. On 1 December 2003 the Eidsvoll District Court (tingrett) convicted the applicant of having raped D and sentenced him to 2 years’ and 6 months’ imprisonment and ordered him to pay her NOK 75,000 for non-pecuniary damage and NOK 160,000 for pecuniary damage. On an appeal by the applicant, the Eidsivating High Court (lagmannsrett), sitting with a jury, held a fresh hearing in the case. The jury answered the questions relating to the charges in the negative (no reasons are given by a jury). The professional judges decided to pass judgment on the basis of the jury’s verdict and acquitted the applicant by a judgment of 20 March 2004. Ms D. maintained the claim that the applicant was civilly liable to pay compensation under the Damage Compensation Act 1969. The High Court, consisting of the professional judges, considered the claim the next day. By two votes to one the High Court concluded, in the same judgment, that the applicant was liable and ordered him to pay NOK 74,000 in compensation for pecuniary damage and NOK 25,000 for non-pecuniary damage. The High Court’s judgment included the following account and reasoning: “The High Court jury was asked one main question, which concerned forcible coitus. The jury answered the question in the negative. Thereafter the jury was asked one main question as to whether the accused was guilty of obtaining, by gross negligence, sexual relation by violence or threatening behaviour. There was additionally put a supplementary question as to whether the sexual relation mentioned in the main question constituted coitus. The jury answered the main question in the negative. The court bases the judgment on the jury’s verdict."

PROCEDURE The Müller case was referred to the Court by the Government of a Federal State (“the Government“). On 4 October, the Registrar received from the Secretary to the Commission forty copies of the latter’s report. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. H. Müller, the elected judge of national origin (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr. G. Balladore Pallieri, the President of the Court (Rule 21 par. 3) (b) of the Rules of Court). Bindschedler-Robert, Mr. F. Matscher and Mr. E. García de Enterría (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 par. 4) (art. 43). Mr. Balladore Pallieri assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 par. 5). He ascertained, through the Deputy Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Government and the President of the Commission regarding the procedure to be followed. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against a country in Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 July 1999. The applicant, who was granted legal aid, was represented by Mr John Smith, a firm of solicitors practising in a city in Europe. The Government were represented by their Agents, Mr A.B. Jones and, subsequently, Mr K. Brown, both of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant’s admissible complaints concerned the compliance with Article 6 of prison adjudication proceedings against her. By a decision of 15 October 1999, a Chamber of the Fourth Section of the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in a city in Europe. In or around late 1998 the applicant breached an earlier probation order (concerning a charge of deception) and was sentenced to six months’ imprisonment. It was her first time in prison. Her term of imprisonment began in November 1998. She was accorded an unconditional release date of 15 January 1999. A. The applicant’s disability The applicant suffered from a neurological disorder which can inhibit voluntary muscle control. She used a wheelchair and could only walk a few steps with assistance. She did not have voluntary control of her bladder meaning that on occasion she either could not urinate for several hours or she urinated uncontrollably and required medication to restrain this. The condition did not affect her intelligence but rather her ability to process information so that she required explanations in plain language and sufficient time for full comprehension. A short medical report from a general practitioner dated 15 August 1999 noted that the applicant was a patient of the relevant practice and that her condition could have affected her ability to produce a urine sample on demand as voluntary control of the nervous system is always affected by the disorder. While he suggested obtaining a specialist’s report on these matters, the applicant stated that she could not afford to obtain one. The prison psychologist’s report of 31 January 1999 noted that the applicant had been referred in December 1998 given her distress and difficulties in coping with her imprisonment. It noted as follows: “Largely confined to a wheelchair, [the applicant] manifests obvious physical symptoms of the disorder as well as somewhat less obvious mental ones. [The applicant] possesses an excellent vocabulary and a reasonably well-developed capacity to think logically that places her well in the highest range of mental functioning for those who have the condition from which she suffers."

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 3 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two European nationals, Ms Alice Smith and Ms Betty Jones (“the applicants”), on 10 November 2001. The Government of the country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr John Brown, Director of Legal Affairs at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicants alleged a violation of Article 7 of the Convention, taken together with Article 13, and of Article 2 of Protocol No. 2 to the Convention, taken together with Article 13 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 53 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 28 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 27 § 1. On 10 November 2002 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 26 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 53 § 1). By a decision of 12 April 2005 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 60 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1970 and 1935 respectively and live in a city. The first applicant was born on 7 December 1970 of a relationship which began in 1966 between the second applicant, a widow and the mother of a daughter born in 1958, and Mr John Doe, a married man and the father of four children born in 1941, 1943, 1944, and 1946. At the time her birth, her father and mother had been living together since 1966. Her father formally acknowledged paternity on 8 December 1973 and she has borne his name since 18 May 1986. On 12 May 1981 the first applicant's father drew up a private deed dividing his movable property between his five children. The document was signed by the four legitimate children and by the father on the first applicant's behalf. On 12 October 1985 he made a manuscript will in which he left to the first applicant the disposable portion of his estate which, pursuant to Article 914 of the Civil Code, came to one quarter. He stipulated that it was to be taken free of his wife's life interest. In a second manuscript will dated 18 June 1986 he stated that he wished the estate to be divided into five parts to be allocated by the drawing of lots in the presence of all his children, for the disposable portion of the estate to pass to the first applicant after an account had been taken of any gifts that had been made and for his wife's life interest to attach only to the share of the four legitimate children.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123/45) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by three Xanadu nationals, Mr Xanadu, Mr Xanadu, and Mr Xanadu (“the applicants”), on 1 January 2000. The applicants were represented by Mr Xanadu, Mr Xanadu, and Mr Xanadu, lawyers practising in Xanadu. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 1 January 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1940, 1944 and 1933 respectively and live in Xanadu. In 1995 the Provincial Private Administration Office expropriated a plot of land belonging to the applicants in order to expand the organised industrial zone. A committee of experts assessed the value of the plot of land and the relevant amount was paid to the applicants following the expropriation. On 1 January 1996 the applicants brought an action in the Civil Court of First Instance requesting additional compensation. The applicants argued that the plot of land in question should have been considered as urbanised land (arsa) instead of rural land. Three on-site inspections were conducted and three separate expert reports were received by the court. The applicants requested the court to dismiss two experts who took part in the preparation of a report, alleging that these experts were not impartial since they were civil servants. During the hearing on 1 January 1997, the applicants stated that they agreed to base the additional compensation on the lowest amount submitted in the expert reports. On 1 January 1997 the First Instance Court decided that the plot of land in question should be classified as urbanised land and awarded the applicants a certain amount of additional compensation. When deciding on the amount of additional compensation, the court relied on the outcome of another action which qualified the same plot of land as urbanised land. On 1 January 1998 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment on the ground that the expert reports were not sufficient basis for a judgment. On 1 January 1998 the Civil Court of First Instance challenged the decision of the Court of Cassation (direnme kararı). The case file was transferred to the Grand Chamber of the Court of Cassation for Civil Law Matters (Hukuk Genel Kurulu). On 1 January 1998 the Grand Chamber of the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 1 January 1998. On 1 January 2000 the Civil Court of First Instance decided that the plot of land was of rural nature.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 31 August 2006. The applicant was represented by Mr Richard Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms Jane Doe of a ministry. On 5 September 2007 the Acting President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in a town, a country. At the beginning of the 1990s a new concept called “tax asset stripping cases” came into existence in a country. It covered a criminal activity by which the persons involved committed aggravated debtor fraud by buying up and selling numerous inactive, solvent private limited companies within a short period and, for the sake of their own profit, “stripping” the companies of assets, including deposits earmarked for payment of corporation tax. The persons involved were usually intricately interconnected and collaborated in their economic criminal activities, which concerned very large amounts of money. According to surveys made by the customs and tax authorities, approximately one thousand six hundred companies with a total tax debt exceeding two billion local currency were stripped in the period from the late 1980s until 1994. Following a number of legislative amendments, the trade in inactive, solvent companies largely ceased in the summer of 1993. In 1994, the applicant learnt via a local newspaper that he was the subject of an investigation, as was a private limited stockbrokers company, of which he was part owner. By letter of 9 June 1994 he informed the police that he was available for an interview, if required. By letter of 14 June 1994 the police confirmed that they were in the process of investigation and informed the applicant that they would talk to him at a later stage. From November 1994 to September 1995, six discovery orders were issued against two banks, four search warrants were issued and numerous interviews were held. On 19 September 1995 the applicant was arrested and charged, inter alia, with aggravated debtor fraud. On the same day he was detained in solitary confinement, which was prolonged at regular intervals until he was released on 22 December 1995. On the latter date, an oral hearing took place before a city court, during which the prosecution stated that the investigation was concluded and that the indictment could be expected at the beginning of 1996.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, John Doe (“the applicant”), on 10 May 2005. The applicant was represented by Mr B. Smith, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 6 January 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in Andria. At the time of the events the applicant was employed as an electrician in a private company. On 3 August 1992 the scaffolding on which the applicant was working collapsed and resulted in the applicant’s total disability. On 18 September 1992 the applicant brought an action for damages in the Andria Labour Court. On 4 February 1995 the Andria Labour Court partially upheld the applicant’s claims and awarded 10,000,000 local currency units (LCU) for pecuniary damage and LCU 30,000,000 for non-pecuniary damage, plus interest at the statutory rate, running from the date of the incident. The defendant appealed. On 12 October 1995 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment and remitted the case to the Andria Labour Court. It found that the Labour Court had incorrectly calculated the amount of compensation and interest. The Andria Labour Court rendered its second judgment on 13 September 1996, awarding the same amounts as before. On 24 January 1997 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment. It held that, although the Andria Labour Court had decided to conform to the Court of Cassation’s previous decision, it had reached the same conclusion as before. On 30 November 1997 the applicant lodged an additional claim with the same court, requesting further damages. These two cases were later joined. The Andria Labour Court issued its third judgment on 14 June 1998. It upheld the applicant’s additional claim lodged on 30 November 1997 and granted LCU 1,574,919,236 for pecuniary damage and LCU 30,000,000 for non-pecuniary damage, plus interest at the statutory rate, running from the date of the judgment and from the date of the incident respectively. The defendant appealed. On 22 October 1998 the Court of Cassation quashed the Labour Court’s decision for the third time on the same ground as before. On 4 November 1999 the Andria Labour Court issued its fourth judgment, dismissing the applicant’s pecuniary damage claims as a whole. In its reasoning, the court held that the Court of Cassation’s assessment method was inapplicable to the incident. It also pointed out that its previous decision regarding the applicant’s non-pecuniary damage claims had become final on 4 February 1994 as the defendant had not challenged it. The applicant appealed.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123456/01) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 November 1998. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador J. Smith, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 7 June 2004 the Court decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS In April 1994 welding work was carried out in the applicant’s fashion boutique. On 28 June 1996 the applicant filed an action for damages against the company which had carried out the welding work. She alleged that the welding work had soiled stored clothes and the salesroom of her boutique and had affected her health. The Regional Court (Landesgericht), upon her request, had previously granted her legal aid for these proceedings on 5 June 1996. On 30 September 1996 the Regional Court held a first hearing. On 7 November 1996 it appointed an expert and instructed him to prepare a report. The expert delivered his report on 28 February 1998. On 2 June 1998 the court held a further hearing. It heard some witnesses and then adjourned the proceedings to hear the expert and further witnesses. On the same day the defendant challenged the expert for bias. The court dismissed this motion on 18 September 1998. On 16 December 1998 the court held another hearing and heard further witnesses and the expert. It also ordered the parties to submit their extensive questions in writing and, on 2 February 1999, instructed the expert to supplement his opinion. On 5 July 1999 the expert delivered his supplementary opinion. On 15 November 1999 the court held a hearing and, upon the applicant’s request, decided to appoint a further expert in order to assess the amount of damages. It further requested the applicant to declare whether she still claimed damages for injuries to her health. The proceedings were adjourned in order to appoint the expert and to hear a witness who had not appeared. In a statement of 13 January 2000 the applicant declared that she maintained her claim for damages as regards injuries to her health. On 1 March 2000 the court, noting that the applicant had made incorrect statements when declaring her financial situation, withdrew the legal aid granted to her. On 19 April 2000 the Regional Court of Appeal confirmed this decision. Subsequently, on 17 May 2000 the Regional Court imposed a fine on the applicant for abuse of process. It further informed the parties that it considered it necessary to decide first whether the claim for damages was well-founded in principle before ordering further expert opinions.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/95) against a European country lodged with an international human rights organization (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the European Convention on Human Rights (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms. Jane Doe, on 10 June 1995. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. John Smith, Director, Ministry of Justice. The applicant alleged that court decisions refusing her claims for reimbursement of gender transition measures and also the related proceedings were in breach of her right to a fair trial and of her right to respect for her private life and that they amounted to discrimination on the ground of her particular psychological situation. She relied on Articles 6 § 1, 8, 13 and 14 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 15 November 1998, when Protocol No. 10 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 10). The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court (Rule 51 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 26 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 27 § 1. By a decision of 20 October 2000, the Chamber declared the application admissible. On 15 November 2000 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 24 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in a city. At birth, she was registered as male, with the forenames Michael Henry. A. The proceedings for the change of the applicant’s forenames In 1992 the applicant instituted proceedings before a district court, asking it to change her forenames to Jane Elizabeth. On 15 December 1993 the District Court granted the applicant’s request. The court found that the conditions under section 1 of the Gender Transition Act (Gesetz über die Änderung der Vornamen und die Feststellung der Geschlechtszugehörigkeit in besonderen Fällen) were met in the applicant’s case. The District Court, having heard the applicant and having regard to the written opinions of the psychiatric experts Prof. G. and Dr. H. of 25 August 1993, and of the psychological expert Prof. I. of 1 October 1993, considered that the applicant was a male-to-female transsexual. It noted that, although Prof. G. and Dr. H. had indicated that the applicant was not a typical transsexual, the Gender Transition Act required only that the condition of transsexuality be met, irrespective of the particular form it took. Moreover, the court found that the experts had convincingly shown that the applicant had been for at least the last three years under the constraint of living according to these tendencies and that there was a high probability that she would not change these tendencies in the future. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/05) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Ali Anon (“the applicant”), on 3 September 2003. The applicant was represented by Mr B. Mungan and Ms A. Anon, two lawyers practising in Ankon, and Ms G. Doyduk, a lawyer practising in Strasbourg. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 16 September 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1951 and lives in Ankon. On 11 August 1994 the applicant, a building contractor, was charged by the Ardahan public prosecutor with forgery of official documents for his personal financial benefit to the detriment of the administrative authorities. On 18 October 1994 the Ardahan Assize Court held the first hearing on the merits of the case (case no. 1994/48). During the second hearing held on 29 November 1994, the Ardahan Assize Court decided to await the outcome of certain administrative proceedings against a civil engineer working at the Kars governor’s office. On 21 May 1998 criminal proceedings brought against the aforementioned civil engineer were joined to the case against the applicant. On 2 March 1999 the first-instance court was notified of the outcome of the administrative proceedings against the civil engineer. On 13 February 2001 the Ardahan Assize Court convicted the applicant as charged. On 15 November 2002 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. On 9 January 2003 the Principal Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation objected to the decision of the Court of Cassation, arguing, inter alia, that the first-instance court had failed to conduct a graphological examination of the allegedly forged documents. On 1 April 2003 the Plenary Court of Cassation (Criminal Divisions) dismissed the Principal Public Prosecutor’s objection regarding the graphological examination, holding that such an examination was not justified by the facts of the case, and upheld the judgment of 13 February 2001 with one minor technical amendment (düzelterek onama). On 23 June 2003 the decision of the Plenary Court of Cassation (Criminal Divisions) was deposited with the registry of the first-instance court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1520/06) against a state (Republic of Turkey) lodged with an international court under Article 34 of a human rights convention ("the Convention") by a national (Turkish national), Mr X ("the applicant"), on 30 December 2005. The applicant was represented by Ms Y, a lawyer practising in a city (Istanbul). The state ("the Government") were represented by their Agent. On 18 June 2009 the President of a section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in a town (Bartın). On 13 January 1982 the applicant, a primary school teacher in a city (Kahramanmaraş) at the material time, was discharged from his duties and on 10 March 1989 he was reinstated. The applicant subsequently requested a ministry to reimburse him for the salaries and other financial rights he had been unfairly deprived of during the period of inactivity. The ministry rejected this request. The applicant lodged an action before an administrative court, requesting this court to quash the ministry's decision and to order the payment of his entitlements. On 6 November 1991 the administrative court partially granted the applicant's request and ordered the calculation and payment of the applicant's salaries and other financial benefits, solely for the period falling between 15 March 1985 and 10 March 1989. The administrative court did not order payment of interest on the relevant amount. On 16 April 1992 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the judgment of the administrative court. Following the final decision of the Supreme Administrative Court, the applicant petitioned the ministry on numerous occasions for the execution of the judgment of the administrative court and the payment of his money. On 14 January 2001 the applicant applied to an administrative court, requesting the clarification (tavzih) of its decision dated 6 November 1991. The applicant asked the court to declare, in particular, the exact amount that he was entitled to receive from the ministry. He explained that without this information, he could not request the enforcement of the impugned judgment by execution offices. On 20 March 2002 the administrative court rejected the applicant's request for clarification. On 30 June 2005 the applicant was paid 4.35 Turkish liras (TRY0)0, which corresponded to the salaries and other financial benefits he would have received during the specified period of his discharge. The applicant was not paid any default interest on this amount to compensate the effects of inflation, pursuant to the instructions of a ministry of finance dated 24 May 2005 and the judgment of the administrative court dated 6 November 1991.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/04) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 November 2002. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 18 October 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant's detention to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1969 and lives in a city. On 21 April 1999 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of armed robbery. On 22 April 1999 the court remanded him in custody in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed several offences of armed robbery. Later, several other persons were detained and charged in connection with the same investigation conducted by the Department of Organised Crime of the Regional Prosecutor's Office. In the course of the investigation, the applicant's detention was prolonged several times. On 13 December 2000 the Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's and his eight co-suspects' detention until 31 March 2001. On 7 March 2001 the Court of Appeal prolonged the applicant's detention until 31 May 2001. It relied on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged and the severity of the anticipated penalty. The Court of Appeal further held that the detention on remand was the only measure which could secure the proper conduct of the proceedings given the nature of the charges and the relations between the suspects, who had acted in an organised group. It also considered that the prolongation of detention was justified by the need to obtain DNA evidence in order to corroborate evidence previously obtained. On 15 May 2001 the prosecution filed a bill of indictment with the Regional Court. The applicant was charged with several dozen counts of armed robbery which had been committed in an organised armed criminal group. The bill of indictment listed 120 charges brought against 19 defendants, who were all detained on remand. The case file comprised 114 volumes. The prosecution asked the court to hear evidence from 366 witnesses. On 23 May 2001 the Court of Appeal ordered that the applicant be kept in custody until 31 October 2001. In addition to the grounds previously invoked, it referred to the complexity of the case, the significant number of defendants and the number of witnesses to be heard in the trial. On 24 October 2001 the Court of Appeal extended the applicant's detention until 31 March 2002, relying on the same grounds as in its earlier decisions.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/06) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alex Anon (“the applicant”), on 1 March 2006. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Coder of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 15 January 2007 the President of the Fifth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in a city. He is a driver by profession. On 5 January 1975 he had a car accident in a country. On 30 October 1996 he was involved in another car accident in the city. A. Proceedings concerning disability pension On 6 July 1997 the applicant lodged a claim for a disability pension in connection with both accidents. On 18 September 1997 the city Social Security Board gave a decision. On 22 November 1997 the applicant appealed against it. On 15 October 1998 the Regional Court stayed the proceedings with respect to the disability caused by the accident of 30 October 1996 pending the termination of criminal proceedings against the applicant. The applicant’s interlocutory appeal against that decision was dismissed by the Court of Appeal on 19 November 1998. As regards the disability resulting from the accident which had occurred in 1975, the Regional Court has still not determined the matter. On 24 August 1998 the applicant filed another motion with the city Social Security Board to be granted a disability pension in connection with the 1975 accident. On 25 March 1999 he lodged a complaint with the Regional Court alleging inactivity on the part of the Social Security Board. On 4 October 2005 the Regional Court severed part of the applicant’s claim concerning the 1975 accident. On 11 October 2005 the Social Security Board gave a decision in respect of the 1975 accident. On 26 October 2005 the applicant appealed against it. On 30 May 2006 the Regional Court gave judgment in the criminal proceedings against the applicant concerning the accident which had occurred in 1996. The judgment is final. On 24 April 2006 the Regional Court gave a judgment upholding the decision issued by the city Social Security Board in 2005 in connection with the 1975 accident. The judgment is final. On 1 March 2008 the Regional Court gave judgment granting the applicant a right to a disability pension in connection with the 1996 accident. Both parties appealed against that judgment. On 15 October 2008 the Court of Appeal gave judgment in which it rejected the applicant’s appeal and entertained the appeal lodged by the Social Security Board.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 August 2001. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr X Y, a lawyer practising in Brussels. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Z W, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 2 May 2003 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant’s pre-trial detention to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. On 1 October 2003 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Strasbourg, Europe. On 15 February 2000 the applicant was arrested by the police on suspicion of having committed homicide. On 16 February 2000 the Strasbourg District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) ordered that he be detained on remand in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offence in question, the serious nature of that offence, the severity of the anticipated penalty and the need to secure the proper conduct of the investigation, in particular the process of obtaining evidence. During the investigation the applicant’s detention was extended on several occasions. He filed numerous but unsuccessful applications for release and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against the decisions prolonging his detention. The applicant made repeated applications for release on personal grounds, submitting that he had to secure the care and well-being of his 2 year old son. He also contested the reasonableness of the charge against him, maintaining that it was solely based on evidence from his common-law wife who was his alleged accomplice. On 7 May 2000 the Strasbourg Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) prolonged his detention until 15 August 2000. On 8 August 2000 it ordered that he be kept in custody until 15 November 2000. On 6 November 2000 it extended that period until 15 February 2001. The court reiterated the grounds originally given for the applicant’s detention. It also considered that the need to take further evidence from experts justified the continuation of that measure. On 1 February 2001 the applicant, together with his common-law wife, was indicted on charges of homicide, attempted homicide, assault occasioning actual bodily harm, uttering threats, theft, burglary, fraud and illegally possessing explosives and dangerous substances before the Strasbourg Regional Court. In all, 20 charges were brought against the applicant. The prosecution asked the court to hear evidence from 90 witnesses. The Regional Court continually prolonged the applicant’s detention pending trial.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/03) against the Republic of Diğer lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by six Diğer nationals, Mr A B C, Mr D E F, Mr G H I, Ms J K L, Mr M N O and Mr P Q R (“the applicants”), on 28 October 2001. The applicants were represented by Mr S T U and Mr V W X, lawyers practising in a city. The Republic of Diğer (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 15 May 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1979, 1978, 1980, 1984, 1981 and 1979 respectively and live in a city. On 28 May 2001 the applicants were taken into custody by police officers from the Anti-Terrorism Branch of the Security Directorate in a city. According to the arrest and search protocols, the applicants were arrested in the course of a police operation carried out against an illegal organisation, namely the XYZ (the Revolutionary People's Liberation Party-Front) as they were considered to be involved in the activities of this organisation at the university. On 30 May 2001 the deputy director of the Anti-Terrorism Branch of the Security Directorate in a city requested the public prosecutor at the State Security Court in a city to extend the applicants' custody period for two days. The public prosecutor at the State Security Court in a city granted the requested extension. On 1 June 2001 the Security Directorate in a city requested the State Security Court in a city to extend the custody period for a further six days. The single judge of the State Security Court in a city duly extended the custody period for six days starting from 1 June 2001. On 3 June 2001 the applicants made statements before the police. On 4 June 2001 the applicants were brought before a doctor, who noted that there were no signs of ill-treatment on their bodies. On the same day, the applicants made statements before the public prosecutor at the State Security Court in a city and subsequently, a single judge of the state security court, who ordered that A B C, D E F and G H I be detained on remand and the other applicants be released. Before the judge, one of the applicants, D E F alleged that he had been subjected to ill-treatment while in custody. On 8 June 2001 the applicants' representative filed an objection with the court requesting that A B C, D E F and G H I be released. In his petition, the representative maintained, inter alia, that the applicants had been subjected to different types of ill-treatment while in custody.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms. Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 September 2007. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Ms. Claire Wilson, a lawyer practising in Uppsala. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. John Smith, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged a breach of Article 8 of the Convention in relation to the contact restrictions following the taking into public care of her three children. On 18 January 2010 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the contact restrictions to the Government. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). On 2 February 2012 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1 of the Rules of Court) and the above application was assigned to the newly composed Sixth Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in a European country. A. Background and taking into public care The applicant is the mother of three children, X. born in December 2000, Y. born in June 2002, and Z. born in August 2004. In April 2005, the applicant separated from the children’s father, W., and she was eventually granted sole custody of the children, while W. was granted contact rights. The applicant married V. in December 2006. The applicant and her children have been known to the social services since 2003 when a first investigation into their home environment was carried out. During April and May 2006, the personnel at the children’s day care centre felt that the applicant was distracted and stressed and the children were hungry and dirty when they arrived at day care in the mornings and were behaving in a wild and hyperactive manner. In view of this, they reported the situation to the social services in a city. In April the applicant herself contacted a psychiatric clinic for help, as she considered the situation to be chaotic and she needed help for her daughter, Y., who she claimed destroyed everything at home. The clinic reported the family’s situation to the social services. On 5 May 2006 the applicant contacted the clinic in a state of despair and, in response, a social emergency unit went to the applicant’s home, accompanied by police and a chief physician from the adult psychiatric clinic. The authorities found the interior of the home completely destitute; there was hardly any furniture and there was no electricity or running water.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Government on a date within the three-month period and by the Commission on a subsequent date, within the three-month period laid down in the Convention. It originated in an application against a State lodged with the Commission under the Convention on a date by two citizens, Mrs X Y and her daughter Z, hereinafter referred to as the first and second applicant respectively. The Government’s request referred to Articles 32 and 48; the Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the State recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30). The President gave the lawyer leave to use the language (Rule 27 para. 3). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr A B, the elected judge of national origin (Convention) (art. 43), and Mr C D, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On a date the President drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the other seven members, namely Mr E F, Mr G H, Mr I J, Mr K L, Mr M N, Mr O P and Mr Q R (Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43). Mr D assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5) and, through the Deputy Registrar, consulted the applicants’ lawyer, the Agent of the Government and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received, on a date, the Government’s memorial and, on a subsequent date, the applicants’ observations. Various documents were produced by the Commission on a date and by the Government on a subsequent date, at the request of the Registrar. On a date the Registrar was informed that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. In accordance with the decision of the President - who had also given the Agent of the Government leave to plead in the language (Rule 27 para. 2) - the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, a city, on a subsequent date.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against a country in Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 November 2002. The applicant was represented by Law Firm Rdw, solicitors in a city. The Government of the country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr A. Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a city. The applicant complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that, because he was a man, he was denied social security benefits equivalent to those received by widows. On 10 December 2006 the Court decided to communicate the complaints concerning widows’ benefits. Subsequently, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in a county. His wife died on 15 December 2001. They had no children from the marriage. His claim for widows’ benefits was made on 1 January 2002 and was rejected on 30 May 2002 on the ground that he was not entitled to widows’ benefits because he was not a woman. The applicant did not appeal as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such social security benefits were payable to widowers under the country’s law.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two European nationals, Ms Anna Nowak (“the first applicant”) and Mr Paweł Nowak (“the second applicant”), on 29 July 2004. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr T. Kowalski of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 30 March 2007 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was further decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The President also gave priority to the application, pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants, Ms Anna Nowak (“the first applicant”) and Mr Paweł Nowak (“the second applicant”) were a married couple. They were born in 1925 and 1923 respectively and lived in Warsaw. The second applicant died on 1 March 2006. By letters of 14 September and 19 November 2007 the first applicant informed the Court of the identity of the second applicant's heirs, Ms Marta Nowak, Ms Teresa Kowalska, Ms Anna Wójcikowska and Mr Stanisław Nowak. They expressed a wish to continue the application in the second applicant's stead. A. Civil proceedings for the division of inheritance and dissolution of co-ownership (“the first set of civil proceedings”) 1. Facts before 1 May 1993 On 20 January 1980 the applicants brought an action for the division of an inheritance with the Warsaw District Court (Sąd Rejonowy). Between 12 September 1981 and 7 January 1983 the court held ten hearings in the proceedings. On 31 August 1983 the Warsaw District Court stayed the proceedings. They were resumed on an unknown date in 1984. On 17 October 1986 the applicants challenged the impartiality of the judge dealing with the case. The challenge was dismissed as unfounded by the Warsaw District Court on 3 February 1987. On 14 January 1992 the court stayed the proceedings. On 22 March 1992 an expert who had been called to give an opinion informed the court that he had not been admitted to the applicant's property. On 1 October 1992 another expert submitted his opinion. 2. Facts after 1 May 1993 On 22 April 1997 the applicants asked the court to resume the proceedings. On 30 June 1997 the proceedings were resumed. By a decision of 11 July 1997 the Warsaw District Court discontinued the proceedings because no motion for the resumption of the proceedings had been lodged within a period of three years. On 5 February 2000 the applicants lodged an interlocutory appeal against this decision. By a decision of 25 April 2000 the District Court rejected the interlocutory appeal, as lodged outside the prescribed time-limit. On 16 August 2000 the Warsaw Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) quashed the above-mentioned decision and remitted the case.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/95) against a country lodged with an international organization under former Article 25 of a convention ("the Convention") by a national of that country, Mr. Zhang Li ("the applicant"), on 22 July 1996. The applicant was represented by Mr. Wang Wei, a lawyer practicing in a city. The government of the country ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Ms. Zhao Mei, of a ministry. The applicant complained that his case had not been heard by an impartial tribunal because, allegedly, the jury had been racially prejudiced. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when a protocol to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of the protocol). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By a decision of 29 June 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE In March 1995 the applicant, an ethnic group, appeared together with Mr. A and Mr. B before a court, composed of a judge and a jury, to be tried for conspiracy to defraud. After the defense had stated its case, the judge started his summing-up, which he had almost completed by Friday evening when he adjourned. On Monday morning a juror arrived at the court and handed an envelope to the court usher containing the following complaint: "I have decided I cannot remain silent any longer. For some time during the trial I have been concerned that fellow jurors are not taking their duties seriously. At least two have been making openly racist remarks and jokes and I fear are going to convict the defendants not on the evidence but because they are [ethnicity]. My concern is the defendants will not therefore receive a fair verdict. Please could you advise me what I can do in this situation." The juror who had written the complaint was asked not to join the other jurors. The judge discussed the complaint with counsel in chambers and then adjourned and listened to submissions in open court. The defense asked the judge to dismiss the jury on the ground that there was a real danger of bias. The judge, however, decided to call the jury back into court, at which stage the juror who had written the complaint joined the others.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr Alex Novak, represented before the Court by Mr Ivan Novak, his father and legal guardian. The Xanadu Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr John Doe of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his right to the respect for his correspondence, guaranteed by Article 8 of the Convention, was breached. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 28 September 2004, the Court declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a further decision of 28 June 2005 the Court declared inadmissible the applicant’s complaint about the length of criminal proceedings against him. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 15 April 1998 the applicant was arrested and charged with attempted extortion of money by threats. On 16 April the District Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the detention order, finding that in the light of the evidence the arrest was justified. On 17 April 1998 the District Court decided to detain the applicant on remand. Subsequently, throughout the initial period of his detention, at least until 2 July 1998, the applicant remained in the detention centre City-Area. On an unspecified date after 2 July 1998 the applicant was transferred to the detention centre City-Center. On 26 July 1998 the applicant sent his first letter to the European Commission of Human Rights. A letter of 24 August 1998, sent by the Commission to the applicant, was intercepted, opened and read by the prosecutor conducting the investigations in the applicant’s case. The envelope in which the letter was delivered bears the following stamps: Detention Centre City-Area, 8 September 1998; Detention Centre City 10 September 1998, Detention Centre in Town 12 October 1998, the Prison 14 October 1998. It also bears a note: Censored, 15 September 1998 (“Ocenzurowano”) signed by an illegible signature. The applicant requested that criminal proceedings be instituted in respect of the interference with his correspondence from the European Commission of Human Rights.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 30358/04) against a State lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 4 August 2004. The applicant was represented before the Court by Ms Y, a lawyer practising in a city. The State’s (“the Government”) representative was Mr Z of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant complained, in particular, under Article 6 of the Convention about the lack of access to a court in that a domestic court refused to appoint him a legal aid lawyer for the purpose of lodging a cassation appeal. On 6 December 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, Mr X, is a national who was born in 1970 and is currently serving a prison sentence in a prison. A. Conditions of the applicant’s detention 1. Period of the applicant’s detention The applicant has been in continuous detention from an unspecified date in September 2000 until the present day. 2. Description of the applicant’s detention conditions He was initially committed to a remand centre. In November 2000 he was transferred to a remand centre, where, as he submitted, he had been detained together with two or three other detainees in cells measuring 6 or 10 square metres. In July 2001 the applicant was transferred back to a remand centre, where he had been detained in overcrowded cells. In addition, the applicant, who was a non-smoker, had been exposed to cigarette smoke because smoking inside the cell was allowed. From 31 December 2003 until an unspecified date in July 2005 the applicant was detained in a remand centre. He was assigned to a cell measuring 6 square metres which he had shared with two other detainees. On an unspecified date in July 2005 the applicant was committed to a remand centre. He submitted that, initially, the conditions of his detention had been satisfactory. In his letter of 19 June 2006, however, he claimed that the establishment had become overcrowded just like all the other detention facilities. The Government submitted that as of 26 November 2009 the applicant had been detained in a prison, in a cell in which the statutory minimum space of 3 square metres per person had been respected. B. The applicant’s actions concerning the conditions of his detention On 7 October 2004 the applicant complained to the remand centre’s administration about overcrowding and bad living conditions. He did not complain to the penitentiary authorities in connection with the living conditions as regards the more recent period of his detention.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms Anna Novak (“the applicant”), on 1 July 2009. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr M. Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 15 May 2010 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in Berlin. A. Main proceedings On 16 January 2000 the applicant lodged with the Berlin District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) a counterclaim for payment against the “Lawyer” Housing Co-operative (Spółdzielnia Mieszkaniowa “Lawyer”). The proceedings for payment instituted by the housing co-operative had been pending since 10 October 1998. On 2 March 2000 the applicant lodged a motion for joinder of the cases. On 18 June 2000 the court held a hearing; however it did not give any decision on the applicant's motion. After three years and ten months, on 20 February 2003, the court gave a decision that the case should be examined separately in another set of proceedings and returned the statement of claim to the applicant because of procedural shortcomings.
