The applicant lodged an interlocutory appeal. On 31 January 2004 the Berlin Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) quashed the first-instance decision and remitted the case. On an unspecified date the Berlin District Court again returned the statement of claim to the applicant because of procedural shortcomings. The applicant lodged another interlocutory appeal. On 15 October 2006 the Berlin Regional Court quashed the contested decision and remitted the case. Hearings scheduled for 25 January and 6 March 2008 were adjourned as another case had been given priority. On 12 May 2008 the Berlin District Court gave a default judgment. On 9 June 2008 the court supplemented the judgment by ordering its immediate enforceability. On 30 June 2008 the defendant filed an objection (sprzeciw) against the default judgment. On 8 July 2008 the Berlin District Court quashed the order of immediate enforceability. On 19 August, 30 September, 18 November, 16 December 2008 the Berlin District Court held hearings. Hearings scheduled for 19 February and 2 April 2009 were adjourned due to the absence of one of the witnesses. On 26 June and 17 November 2009 the court held hearings. The case is still pending before the first-instance court. B.

PROCEDURE The case originated in three applications (nos. 1234/02, 56789/02, 91011/03) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Xanadu nationals, Ms X Y and Mr Z A (“the applicants”), on 23 October 2001, 13 July 2002 and 6 May 2003, respectively. The applicants were represented by Mrs A B, a lawyer practising in Y City. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 5 January 2006 the Court declared the applications partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the applicants’ alleged ill-treatment in police custody, the right to an effective remedy in this regard, the length of their detention in police custody, the alleged deprivation of their right to challenge the lawfulness of their detention, and their right to compensation in this respect. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1978 and 1980 respectively and live in Y City. A. The events concerning the applicants’ arrest and detention On 29 July 2001 the applicants were arrested on suspicion of having participated in an illegal demonstration which took place in Z City. They were subsequently taken to the Z Security Directorate. According to the arrest reports drafted by the police officers and signed by the applicants on the day of the incident, in Z City a group of fifteen people closed the main street to traffic by blocking the side streets with dustbins, and they initiated a protest rally. They were carrying torches and shouting slogans in support of the PKK0. When they noticed that policemen were approaching, they started to run away. The first applicant, who was identified by the police as one of the protesters, was arrested on the spot. The second applicant was arrested following a chase. The police prevented him from being lynched. It was further noted in the arrest report that the second applicant’s lip was injured. Following his examination by a doctor at the H Numune Hospital, the medical report dated 29 July 2001 concluded that the second applicant had an abrasion on his upper lip and a 5-15 centimetre hyperaemia on the right side of his chest. It was noted that it was necessary to consult cardiothoracic and ear, nose and throat specialists. Thereafter, the applicants were handed over to the Anti-Terrorism Department of the Y Security Directorate. On 31 July 2001, upon the request of the Anti-Terrorism Department, the public prosecutor at the Y State Security Court prolonged the applicants’ detention in police custody until 2 August 2001. On 1 August 2001, the public prosecutor extended the applicants’ detention for three more days.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Smith (“the applicant”), on 8 November 2006. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr John Doe of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that his right to respect for his family life had been infringed. On 11 December 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (former Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, now Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in City. On 11 October 2005 the applicant was arrested on charges of aggravated assault and theft. On 13 October 2005 the City District Court ordered his pre-trial detention, which was subsequently extended on several occasions. The applicant's mother and wife were witnesses during the investigation stage of the proceedings. On 30 March 2006 a bill of indictment was lodged with the City District Court. The applicant was charged with aggravated assault and theft. On an unknown date the applicant's wife and mother applied to be allowed to visit the applicant in prison. Their applications bear handwritten notes “refusal, the person is a witness”, illegible signatures and the date of 3 April 2006. On 17 July and 2 August 2006 the applicant requested to be allowed to maintain personal contact with his family. His applications were rejected. The authorities noted that the family members themselves should apply for permission to visit the applicant in prison. On 14 November 2006 the applicant's mother applied for permission to visit the applicant in prison. Her application bears a note “refusal, witness in the case”, an illegible signature and the date of 14 November 2006. During a hearing held on 3 April 2007 the applicant's mother and wife stated that they refused to testify at the trial. On the same day, the applicant's mother was granted permission to visit the applicant in prison. On 27 June 2007 the applicant and his wife were granted a divorce. On 29 July 2008 the City District Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to two years' imprisonment. The applicant's pre-trial detention was lifted on 8 October 2008. After that date he was visited by his mother on 11 occasions.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/08) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Smith (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2008. The applicant was represented by Mr J.K. Brown, a lawyer practising in London. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged a violation of Articles 10 and 14 of the Convention respectively, in conjunction with Article 3 of Protocol No. 1, and a violation of Article 13 of the Convention. On 22 April 2012 the applications were communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Brussels. The applicant, who was a professor of social science at the University of Brussels, had stood for the parliamentary elections of 25 June 2008, in the third electoral district of Paris, as an independent candidate. He had not been a member of any political party at the material time. A. The legislative background to the present applications With a view to a deeper understanding of the background to the present applications, the Court considers it useful to outline the circumstances under which the parliamentary elections of 25 June 2008 took place. Accordingly it will refer to the relevant passages of Smith and Jones v. Europe ([GC], no. 11111/04, §§ 27-31, ECHR 2009), which read as follows: “27. In early April 2008 the European Parliament decided to hold early parliamentary elections, choosing 25 June 2008 as the date. The decision followed a political crisis resulting from Parliament’s inability to elect a new President of the Republic to follow on from John Doe before the expiry of his single seven-year term of office, on 18 April 2008. In the normal course of events, these elections should have been held on 5 October 2008. Fifteen political parties took part in the elections, which were marked by two characteristics. Firstly, a strong mobilisation of the electorate was observed following the presidential crisis, since the participation rate rose to 85%. Secondly, political parties used two pre-electoral strategies to circumvent the national 10% threshold. The Party of Democratic Left (DLP) took part in the poll under the banner of the CEP, a rival party, and by that means managed to win fourteen seats. The Party for Democratic Society (DPS, pro-Kurdish, left-leaning) presented its candidates as independents using the slogan ‘A thousand hopes’; it also supported certain left-wing European candidates. This movement was backed by other small left-wing groups such as the EMEP, the SDP and the ODP (the Liberty and Solidarity Party, socialist). More than sixty independent candidates stood for election in about fifty provincial constituencies. In the elections the AKP, the CEP and the MHP managed to get over the 10% threshold. With 47.58% of the votes cast, the AKP won 345 seats, 63% of the total."

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms Ana Novakova (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2009. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr M. Kowalski of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 16 January 2010 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). On 20 June 2010 the Government submitted a unilateral declaration and invited the Court to strike out the application, in accordance with Article 37 of the Convention. The applicant filed an objection. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Greenfield. A. Main proceedings On an unspecified date in August 2002 criminal proceedings were instituted against the applicant. On 30 August 2003 the applicant was indicted before the Greenfield District Court. She was charged with several offences of fraud. The bill of indictment comprised 12 accused. On 10 September 2003 the case was remitted to the Greenfield District Prosecutor. On 22 October 2003, the court ordered that the applicant undergo a psychiatric examination and that an expert's opinion on her health be prepared. The hearing was adjourned until 31 March 2004. Between 7 April 2004 and 15 November 2005 the court held nine hearings, four of which were cancelled. The applicant failed to appear at one of these hearings. During hearings listed for 15 October, 10 and 22 November 2004 witnesses were heard. On 7 December 2004, upon the request of the applicant's co-accused's lawyer, the hearing was cancelled. At hearings, set down for 15 December 2004, 5 January, 2 and 23 February, 14 March, 1 and 22 April 2005, witnesses were heard. Between 13 May 2005 and 20 December 2006 the court held 17 hearings, six of which were adjourned since witnesses had failed to appear before the court. The next hearing, scheduled for 22 January 2007, was adjourned as the applicant's co-accused's counsel had not been properly summoned. The subsequent hearing, scheduled for 9 March 2007, was cancelled due to the judge's illness. On 2 April 2007, due to the judge's prolonged illness, the case was assigned to another judge. In consequence the case had to be reheard from the beginning and the first hearing was set down for 28 November 2007. On 5 October 2007 the case was assigned to a third judge because of the new division of work in the court. The trial was listed for 12 May 2008. The proceedings are still pending before the Greenfield District Court. B.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 38978/97) against the Kingdom of X ("the Kingdom") lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a X national, X Xsson ("the applicant"), on 15 September 1997. The applicant was until 31 May 2000 represented by Mr Y Antal and thereafter by Mr Z Jacobson, both lawyers practising in X. The X Government ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Ms A Jagander, Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his rights under Article 6 of the Convention had been violated on account of the lack of an oral hearing before the Administrative Court of Appeal and the Supreme Administrative Court in proceedings concerning social security benefits. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 4 May 2000 the Court declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 17 October 1994 the applicant, who was born in 1937 and had been on early retirement since 1989, applied for disability benefits under the Social Insurance Act (Lagen om allmän försäkring, 1962:381; hereinafter "the 1962 Act"). He claimed that he had extra costs following an operation on his intestines in September 1994 due to, inter alia, an increased consumption of fluids. By a decision of 28 December 1994 the Social Insurance Office (försäkringskassan; hereinafter "the Office") of the County of X rejected the application, finding that the applicant's costs were not such as to make him eligible for benefits. The applicant later made a new application, which was rejected by the Office on 8 February 1995. The applicant appealed to the County Administrative Court (länsrätten) of the County of X. On 16 May 1995 the court rejected his appeal. The court did not hold an oral hearing nor did the applicant request one. Following the applicant's further appeal, the Administrative Court of Appeal (kammarrätten) in X, by a decision of 17 November 1995, refused him leave to appeal. On 5 December 1995 the applicant made yet another application for disability benefits. On 3 April 1996 the application was rejected by the Office, which again found that the applicant's costs did not attain the required level. The Office had at its disposal three medical certificates issued by different physicians.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the State of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alexander Novak (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2002. The applicant was represented by Mr J. Miller, a lawyer practising in Strasbourg. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs B. Schmidt, a representative of the Ministry of Justice. On 14 November 2005 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The applicant died on 25 May 2006. On 12 June 2006 his lawyer informed the Registrar that his wife from a second marriage, Mrs Marynka Novak, wished to continue with the case. By letter of 13 August 2006, the Government objected to her being allowed to do so. On 1 May 2007 this case was assigned to the newly composed Sixth Section (Rule 25 § 1 and Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, Mr Alexander Novak, was born in 1945 and lived in Luxembourg. He worked between 1970 and the beginning of 1980 with asbestos insulators for the X Company in Luxembourg. During this period, the workers of this company who were exposed to asbestos dust while working had to clean their clothes themselves. This was done by the applicant's first wife Mrs Elisa Novak. On 1 May 1980, after the applicant had stopped working for the X Company, an accident prevention regulation (Unfallverhütungsvorschrift) entered into force pursuant to which the company was put in charge of cleaning the working clothes. Having contracted a mesothelioma, an asbestosis related disease, Mrs Elisa Novak applied on 7 February 1992 to the Strasbourg Health Insurance Association for compensation payments, claiming that her illness was the consequence of the daily cleaning of her husband's work clothes. On 7 July 1992 the Health Insurance Association dismissed her request holding that her activity was not covered by the industrial health insurance, since she had acted on a strictly private basis and not as an employee. On 6 August 1992 Mrs Elisa Novak filed an objection against this decision which was rejected on 14 November 1992 by the Appeals Board of the Health Insurance Association. In February 1993 Mrs Elisa Novak commenced proceedings before the Luxembourg Social Court. After her death on 14 August 1993, her husband Alexander Novak, the applicant, continued the proceedings as legal successor of the deceased. The Social Court decided to await the decision in the precedent which was pending from May 1993 until February 1994 before the Social Court of Appeal and from March 1994 until December 1994 before the Federal Social Court. From March 1994 until October 1994 the proceedings were formally suspended.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against the Republic of X (the "Republic") lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by an Austrian national, Mr. John Doe ("the applicant"), on 20 March 1998. The applicant was represented by Law Firm A, a law firm practising in City B. The Republic was represented by their Agent, Ambassador C, Head of the International Law Department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings against him lasted unreasonably long in breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 52 § 1). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 23 May 2002 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Republic each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1938 and lives in City C/Republic. He is an auditor and tax consultant. In December 1989, the Tax Office in City D, in the course of investigations into a large scale fraud relating to the "XYZ" group, instituted criminal proceedings against 97 persons, requesting them to submit in writing their comments as suspects. On 14 December 1989 the applicant, who in his professional capacity assisted the "XYZ" group, wrote a letter to the Tax Office in City E. Therein he asked that his income tax declarations for the years 1985 to 1987 be corrected, so that the losses declared be cancelled, in particular 541,585 for the year 1985; 1,000,000 for 1986 and 220,000 for 1987. He further asked that following a re-calculation of his income, new tax assessment orders be issued. Investigations by the Tax Authorities against the applicant for tax evasion On 27 and 28 December 1989 the Tax Office in City D informed the applicant that he was suspected of tax evasion in that he had acted as a sham holder of shares in three cases concerning the years 1985–87. It further invited him to submit his comments in writing. After the applicant's request of 15 January 1990 for an extension of the time-limit had been granted, he submitted his comments on 31 January 1990. Until 29 October 1992 the Tax Office in City D for the Audit of Large-scale Companies examined the "XYZ" group."

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123456/99) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr. Zephyr Zephyrov. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Ms. A. Wind and Ms. B. Cloud, lawyers practising in Xanadu. The Xanaduian Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he was subjected to ill-treatment in police custody and that he had no effective remedy under domestic law for his allegation of ill-treatment. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 5 October 2004, the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The parties replied in writing to each other’s observations. The Chamber, after consulting the parties, decided that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1979 and lives in Xanadu. A. The detention in police custody and the medical certificates concerning the alleged ill-treatment of the applicant On 6 February 1999 the applicant was arrested and taken into police custody by police officers from the Anti-Terror Branch of the Xanadu Security Directorate on suspicion of his membership of an illegal organisation, namely the PKK (the Workers’ Party of Kurdistan). On the same day the public prosecutor granted the request of the Anti-Terror Branch to place the applicant in police custody for four days at the Anti-Terror Branch of the Xanadu Security Directorate. On 10 February 1999 the Xanadu State Security Court extended the custody period for a further two days. On 10 February 1999 the applicant was taken to Haseki Hospital, where he was issued with a medical report. In the report ‘surface erythema and scrapes on the proximal part of both arms’ were noted. On the same day the applicant was allegedly forced to sign a statement explaining that the bruises on his arms had been caused by a dust allergy. On 12 February 1999 the applicant was brought before the public prosecutor of the Xanadu State Security Court and then before a judge at the Xanadu State Security Court, where he stated that he had been subjected to physical and emotional violence. The court ordered the applicant’s detention on remand.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against a country (Country X) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (National A) of Country X (the applicant), on 1 January 2000. The Government of Country X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Person B of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 1 January 2010 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the length of the applicant’s detention on remand and censorship of his correspondence with his lawyer. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in City A, Country X. 1. The applicant’s detention on remand On 1 January 1998 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of having committed fraud and forgery while being a member of an organised criminal group. On 1 January 1998 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) detained the applicant and two other co-suspects on remand. The Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) upheld that decision on 1 January 1998. The courts considered that the applicant’s detention was justified by the existence of strong evidence against him and the gravity of the charges. They also relied on the risk that the applicant might attempt to tamper with evidence. On 1 January 1998 the Regional Court ordered that the applicant be kept in custody until 1 January 1998. The court repeated the reasons previously given for the applicant’s detention and noted that the applicant had attempted to influence his co-suspects to change their statements. The applicant’s detention was prolonged several times by the Regional Court for the same reasons as before. The applicant’s appeals against those decisions were dismissed. On 1 January 1999 the applicant and 12 other persons were indicted on several counts of fraud and forgery, and participation in an organised criminal gang. The applicant remained in detention. The first hearing before the Regional Court was scheduled for 1 January 1999. Subsequently, the court held 34 hearings. On 1 January 2000 the Regional Court decided to ask the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) to prolong the applicant’s detention. The applicant’s detention was subsequently prolonged numerous times by the Regional Court and the Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) for the same reasons as before. The applicant’s appeals against those decisions were dismissed. On 1 January 1999 and 1 January 2001 the applicant lodged unsuccessful applications for release with the Regional Court. On 1 January 2002 the Regional Court asked the Court of Appeal to prolong further the applicant’s detention until 1 January 2002. On 1 January 2002 the Court of Appeal refused the application. The court noted that the applicant had already been detained for 3 years and 8 months.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national from a Commonwealth country, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2000. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Legal and Co., solicitors in London. The government of the country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms Smith, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that his expulsion to the Commonwealth country placed him at risk of torture or inhuman or degrading treatment, that he would not receive a fair trial if he were returned to the Commonwealth country and that he had no effective remedy available to him in respect of these matters. He relied on Articles 3, 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. The President of the Chamber and subsequently the Chamber decided to apply Rule 39, indicating to the Government that it was desirable in the interests of the parties and the proper conduct of the proceedings that the applicant should not be expelled to the Commonwealth country pending the Court’s decision. By a decision of 10 March 2000, the Chamber declared the application admissible [Note by the Registry. The Court’s decision is obtainable from the Registry]. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in a city, one of the islands, in 1965. The islands are part of a Commonwealth country. It has its own President, parliament and government and enjoys considerable autonomy. According to the applicant, in 1993 he joined a political party in the islands. He was an active member, attending meetings and contributing money to the party funds. In August 1995 the applicant was arrested by the ruling party officers because of his involvement with the opposition party. He was detained at a police station in the islands for three months, where he was tortured. He was repeatedly locked in a cell full of water for days at a time so he was unable to lie down. He was hung upside down with his feet tied together until he bled through the nose, and he was also subjected to electric shocks. In November 1995 the applicant stated that he was released from detention following pressure from the opposition party leaders on the government.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 38414/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 2 October 2002. The applicant was represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he did not receive a fair and public hearing, as he was not informed promptly of the accusation against him, he did not have adequate time and facilities for the preparation of his defence and that he was not allowed to defend himself in person or through a lawyer. On 13 December 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. On 30 May 2006 the Government filed observations on the admissibility and merits. On 19 October 2006 the President of the Third Section refused to include in the case file the applicant's observations in reply to Government's observations and his just satisfaction claims which were filed outside the time-limit (Rule 38 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1984 and lives in a city. On 26 June 2002 the applicant, together with a friend, quarrelled with a man in a park. The quarrel had turned into a fight and the applicant stabbed the man in his leg. The police and the public prosecutor took the statements of the parties, including the applicant. The applicant denied having injured the man. Following their questioning, they were all released. On 3 July 2002 the Public Prosecutor at the Magistrates' Court filed an indictment against the applicant, on account of assault with a knife and occasioning actual bodily harm. The indictment was not notified to the applicant. After having examined the case file, on 17 July 2002 the Magistrates' Court issued a penal order, convicting the applicant and sentencing him to pay an amount. On 30 August 2002 the penal order was notified to the applicant. On 6 September 2002 the applicant challenged the decision of the Magistrate's Court, before the Criminal Court of First Instance. He argued that he had been deprived of his right of defence in violation of the Convention. On 11 September 2002 the Criminal Court of First Instance upheld the decision of the Magistrate's Court, maintaining that it was in accordance with the law and procedure. On 25 September 2002 the Public Prosecutor issued a payment order under which the applicant was obliged to pay the relevant amount.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/05) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2005. The applicant was represented by Mr Chris Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Jane Doe of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that his detention on remand exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 8 June 2007 the President of the Fifth Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in a city. He is currently detained in a remand centre. On 20 February 2003 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of having been involved in drug trafficking as a member of an organised criminal group. On 22 February 2003 the District Court ordered that the applicant be detained on remand until 20 May 2003 in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences in question. The court considered that keeping the applicant in detention was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings given the risk that he might obstruct them. This suspicion was, in the court’s view, justified by the fact that the applicant had been acting in an organised criminal group, “the members of which had not been identified”. The court also stressed the severity of the likely sentence. The applicant’s detention was repeatedly extended by several decisions of the Regional Court and the Appeal Court. In their decisions, the courts repeatedly relied on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged, the serious nature of the offences and the risk that the applicant, as a member of an organised criminal group, would obstruct the investigation. On 15 December 2005 the prosecutor lodged a bill of indictment with the Regional Court against the applicant and 30 other co-accused. The prosecutor requested 20 witnesses to be heard. On 10 December 2006 the Court of Appeal, extending the applicant’s detention for a further three months, noted that the length of the investigation had already been excessive and ordered that, by the end of the extended detention (that is, by 15 March 2007), the Regional Court commence the trial and hear all the defendants in the proceedings. On an unspecified date the applicant appealed. On 20 December 2006 the Court of Appeal confirmed its decision. It appears that the Court of Appeal’s instructions were not followed by the Regional Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 29503/03) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 3 April 2003. The applicant was represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the criminal proceedings against him had not been fair and that they had not been concluded within a reasonable time. On 7 May 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1958 and lives in a city. On 19 March 1992 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of obtaining property by deception. The same day he was placed in police custody in a city, where a statement was taken from him. In that statement the applicant admitted having committed the offence. The applicant was released from police custody on 21 March 1992 and was brought before a judge the same day. The judge questioned the applicant further and ordered his detention in prison pending the institution of criminal proceedings against him. When he was questioned by the judge, the applicant denied the accusations against him. While being questioned in police custody and subsequently by the judge, the applicant was not represented by a lawyer. On 24 March 1992 a prosecutor filed an indictment with a court, charging the applicant and another person with the offences of forgery and perverting the course of justice. On 25 March 1992 the applicant's legal representative submitted a petition to the court, arguing that there was no evidence against the applicant other than the police-custody statement taken from him. The same day the applicant asked to be examined by a doctor. According to the report drawn up by the doctor, there were injuries to his mouth. On 30 March 1992 the applicant's trial began before a court. During the third hearing, held on 22 May 1992, the court decided that it lacked jurisdiction and transferred the case file to another court. In the course of the criminal proceedings the applicant was represented by a lawyer. He alleged that he had been ill-treated in police custody and submitted that the only evidence against him was the statement taken from him in police custody. On 3 December 1992, after having been detained for eight and a half months, the applicant was released from prison on bail.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against a country of Central Europe lodged with an international human rights organization under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms by a national of that country, Ms. Jane Doe ("the applicant"), on 10 March 1997. The government of that country ("the government") were represented by their Agent, Mr. John Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the civil proceedings in her case exceeded a reasonable time, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 11 October 2001 the Court declared the application admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant is a national of that country, born in 1930 and living in a city of Central Europe. On 2 November 1987 the applicant lodged a motion with a local court, claiming division of conjugal property, consisting, as she claimed, of 42 pieces of movable property. Subsequently, hearings were held on, inter alia, 18 May 1988, 11 January 1989 and 17 February 1989. In 1990 an expert submitted a report concerning the value of movable property. Apparently, on an unspecified later date, the President of the local court, following the applicant’s complaints about the lack of progress in the case, ordered that the conduct of the proceedings be supervised by him. On an unspecified date in 1991 the case was transferred to another judge rapporteur. On 1 April 1992 the applicant again complained about the excessive length of the proceedings. On an unspecified date the defendant claimed that a house in which the applicant lived should be included in the property concerned. On an unspecified date four years after the beginning of the proceedings he submitted certain documents to prove that his family had borne certain costs relating to the construction of the house. On 15 January 1992 a hearing was held and the court ordered that an expert report be prepared to estimate the value of the house. On 9 February 1993 the defendant proposed that a court settlement be concluded. The applicant did not accept the proposed terms. On the whole, 22 hearings were held until 1 May 1993, the date on which the country recognized the right of individual petition became effective.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 9 March 2000. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr X Y Z. On 16 June 2003 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1957 and lives in a town. On 20 April 1993 the applicant lodged a petition for a divorce with a regional court. The regional court held hearings on 24 August and 7 October 1993, 13 January and 26 April 1994. On 1 June 1994 the court ordered an expert opinion. It was submitted to the court on 29 August 1994. Further hearings were held on 15 November 1994, 7 February 1995, 25 April 1995, 10 August 1995, 7 November 1995 and 16 May 1996. On 5 June 1996 the applicant specified his claim and accepted that custody rights be granted to his wife. On 13 September 1996 the court ordered fresh expert evidence. The court requested a psychology department to expedite the preparation of the opinion on the applicant's child's emotional development. On 21 January 1997 the hearing was adjourned, in order to give the experts more time to prepare the opinion. On 24 January 1997 the court requested the psychology department to send back the case file and to submit the opinion. The file was sent back on 21 March 1997; however, no opinion was submitted. On 21 April 1997 the applicant complained to a ministry about the length of the proceedings. On 3 June 1997 the ministry examined the facts and considered that the applicant's complaint was justified. The court held further hearings on 26 June 1997, 23 July 1997, 18 September 1997, 24 November 1997, 26 January 1998, 16 March 1998, 20 April 1998, 8 June 1998 and 13 July 1998. On 26 August 1998 the applicant sent another letter to the ministry complaining about the length of the proceedings. In September 1998 the case was put under the administrative supervision of a ministry. The psychology department failed to submit the relevant expert opinion. As a consequence, the court ordered a new expert opinion on 6 October 1998. On 4 December 1998, upon the applicant's further complaint, the ombudsman examined the case and considered the complaint justified. The ombudsman requested the president of the regional court to take the necessary steps to accelerate the proceedings. On 22 February 1999 and 8 March 1999 the court held hearings.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against a country lodged with an international organization ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a national, Ms Jane Doe ("the applicant"), on 3 October 1996. PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 4149/04 and 41029/04) against the Republic of Alanda lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr A. Anon (“the applicant”), on 23 January 2004 and 4 August 2004 respectively. The applicant was represented by Ms B. Lawyer, a lawyer practising in Ankon. The Government of Alanda (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 29 April 2008 the Court decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility (Article 29 § 3). Third-party comments were received from the Alanda Helsinki Monitor, which had been given leave by the President to intervene in the procedure (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 2 of the Rules of Court). The Government replied to those comments (Rule 44 § 5). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1931 and lives in Ankon. A. Concerning application no. 4149/04 1. The compensation proceedings initiated by the applicant In 2000 the Ministry of Culture published a book entitled “The Gypsies of Alanda”, written by Associate Professor C. Scholar. On 15 June 2001 the applicant filed a petition with the Ministry of Culture on behalf of the Gypsy associations. In his petition, he stated that in twenty-four pages of the book, the author had stated that Gypsies were engaged in illegitimate activities, lived as “thieves, pickpockets, swindlers, robbers, usurers, beggars, drug dealers, prostitutes and brothel keepers” and were polygamist and aggressive. Furthermore, Gypsy women were presented as being unfaithful to their husbands. The applicant also submitted that the book contained several other expressions that humiliated and debased Gypsies. Claiming that the expressions constituted criminal offences, he requested that the sale of the book be stopped and all copies seized. On the same day, the head of the publication unit at the Ministry of Culture ordered that all copies of the book be returned to the publication unit as there were corrections to be made. On 11 October 2001 the applicant wrote a letter to the Ministry of Culture enquiring whether the copies of the book had been seized. On 17 October 2001 the head of the publication unit at the Ministry of Culture informed the applicant that the publications advisory board of the Ministry, composed of seven professors, had decided that the book was scientific research and that the expressions in the book did not contain any insults or similar expressions. The applicant was also informed that the author of the book would not permit any amendments to the text and that, in accordance with the author’s request, the Ministry had transferred the copyright of the book to him. On 4 February 2002 the applicant sent letters to the Ministry of Culture and to Associate Professor C. Scholar and repeated his initial request. He received no reply.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of XYZ lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two XYZ nationals, Mrs Aisha Xan and Ms Bisma Xan, on 15 June 2003. The applicants were represented by Mrs Zara Yilmaz, Mr Ali Bay, Mr Can Aydin and Mr Berk Kaya, lawyers practising in Diyarbakir. The XYZ Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 22 June 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints brought by Aisha Xan concerning the lawfulness and length of her detention in police custody on the basis of Law-Decree no. 430 and her right to an effective remedy whereby she could have challenged the lawfulness of this detention. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The first applicant, Aisha Xan (hereafter referred to simply as “the applicant”), was born in 1965 and lives in Siirt. On 15 October 2002 the applicant was arrested and taken into police custody on suspicion of aiding members of an illegal armed organisation. She was remanded in custody on 18 October 2002. However, at the request of the Governor of the State of Emergency Region and the public prosecutor, pursuant to Article 3 (c) of Law-Decree 430, which allowed them to take further measures within the framework of the state of emergency, a single judge at the Van State Security Court authorised, on 20 November 2002, the applicant's transfer from prison to the Diyarbakir gendarmerie command for further interrogation for a duration not exceeding ten days. This period was extended by the same court for another ten days on 30 November 2002. The objection lodged by the applicant's lawyer against this decision was dismissed on 2 December 2002. Between 20 November and 9 December 2002, the applicant was held in the Diyarbakir and Siirt gendarmerie command. On 9 December 2002 the applicant was returned to prison. The subsequent criminal proceedings brought against the applicant ended with her acquittal.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Commission and by the Government on 8 December 1994 and 9 January 1995, within the three-month period laid down by the Convention. It originated in an application against the Government lodged with the Commission under the Convention by a national, Mr X, on 6 November 1991. The Commission’s request referred to the Convention and to the declaration whereby the Government recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court; the Government’s application referred to the Convention. The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr Y, the elected judge of the nationality (the Convention), and Mr R. Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On 27 January 1995, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr Z, Mr A, Mr B, Mr C, Mr D, Mr E and Mr F (the Convention). On 6 February 1995 Mr Y withdrew pursuant to Rule 24 para. 2, as the case raised issues similar to those in the cases of X - in which he had acted as Agent and Counsel for the Government (judgment of 17 January 1970, Series A no. 11, p. 5, para. 7) - and Y, from which he had withdrawn (judgment of 30 October 1991, Series A no. 214-B, p. 25, para. 3). On 31 March 1995 the delegate of the Agent of the Government informed the Registrar that Professor G had been appointed to sit as ad hoc judge (the Convention and Rule 23) (the Convention). As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5), Mr R. Ryssdal, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant’s lawyers and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 31 May 2005. The applicant was represented by Mr Alex Brown, a lawyer practising in City. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 11 May 2009 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1961 and is currently serving his prison sentence in City Prison. A. The applicant’s detention in police custody and the medical reports issued in his respect On 16 January 2004 at 6.30 p.m. the applicant was taken into police custody in connection with a murder investigation. At 6.35 p.m. he met a lawyer from the City Bar Association at the City Security Directorate. The applicant was then taken to the doctor, who did not find any signs of physical ill-treatment on his body. On 17 January 2004 the applicant was questioned by the police in the absence of a lawyer. According to a form signed by the applicant, he was reminded of his right to the assistance of a lawyer but he did not make such a request. In his statement to the police, the applicant confessed that he had been involved in the murder of a certain Person A. He explained that on 11 October 2003, together with Person A and Person B, he had gone to Location to have dinner in a picnic area. Subsequently, a fight broke out between Person A and Person B, and, as a result, Person A fell and hit his head on some rocks. When they saw that he was dead, they panicked and tried to get rid of his body. They tied heavy iron bars to his legs and placed his body on a tyre inner tube that they had taken from the boot of Person B’s car. Then they swam far from the shore with the body, and dropped it into the sea. The applicant subsequently took part in a reconstruction of events with the police at the scene of the incident. On the same day at about 5.30 p.m. the applicant was once again examined by a doctor, who did not find any signs of ill-treatment on his body. The applicant was subsequently taken before the public prosecutor and the judge. Still waiving his right to legal assistance, the applicant repeated the statement he had given to the police. The judge ordered his pre-trial detention and the applicant was placed in City Prison. On 19 January 2004, at 4.15 p.m., at his request, the applicant was examined by a doctor in City State Hospital.

PROCEDURE The case originated in three applications (nos. 12345/05, 67890/06 and 11223/07) against the Federal Republic of a Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 29 May 2005, 6 June 2006 and 11 July 2007 respectively. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Ms Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mrs Mary Brown, Ministerialdirigentin, Federal Ministry of Justice. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of two sets of proceedings concerning custody of his children had been excessive. On 9 December 2009 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1980 and lives in a city. A. Background to the case The applicant and his former wife married in 1995. They have two children, a son born in December 1990 and a daughter born in May 1995. Until 1996 the applicant assumed a major part of the child care while the mother completed her studies. In July 1997 the couple separated and the children remained with the mother. The applicant had regular contact with his children until the beginning of 1998 when the mother and children moved from a city to a city in a region. Following the move the mother's parents assumed a large part of the child care because the mother was in full-time employment. The applicant subsequently found that his regular contacts with the children were obstructed by the mother and her parents and lodged an application for the regulation of his contact rights with a court in March 1998. By a court decision of 23 July 1998 (file no. 123/98) he was granted contact with his children every second and fourth weekend of the month from 6 p.m. Friday to 6 p.m. Sunday. Since disputes regarding the applicant's contact with his children persisted, the applicant instituted further proceedings for the regulation of his contact rights. At the same time, proceedings for a provisional decision on custody were opened, as well as divorce proceedings which also dealt with the issues of custody and contact rights as ancillary matters (Folgesachen). The proceedings were to a large extent conducted jointly until the applicant's former wife's petition for divorce was granted by a judgment dated 29 November 2000 and custody of the children was decided as an ancillary matter to the divorce. However, no decision on the applicant's contact rights was taken at that time. The parties continued to argue about the applicant's contact rights with the children and regular contact was interrupted repeatedly and for longer intervals.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/95) against the Republic of X (the "Republic") lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by an X national, Mr X ("the applicant"), on 15 March 1989. The applicant was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in City (X). The Republic of X ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Mr Z, Head of the International Law Department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that in criminal administrative proceedings against him he did not have a determination of his case by an independent tribunal. The application was transmitted to the Court on 15 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted in accordance with Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 15 November 1998 the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Chamber decided, after having consulted the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 15 March 1988, the applicant was instructed to inform the police who had parked a car belonging to the applicant in the Street in City on 15 March 1988 at 5.30pm. He failed to provide the information, and on 15 October 1988 was fined 1,000 X currency (XC) for the failure, pursuant to sections 134 (1) and 103 (2) of the X Act 1967 (X Law). The penal notice (X notice) was confirmed by the Regional Government (X Government) on 15 May 1989. On 15 November 1989 a minor error in the penal order was corrected. The applicant's administrative complaint to the Administrative Court (X Court) was ultimately dismissed on 15 January 1990. The Administrative Court found that the correct provisions of the X Act had been applied, and further confirmed that the reasons given by the applicant for not having supplied the required information were inadequate.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by twelve European nationals, Mr Alex Smith, Mr John Doe, Mr Peter Brown, Mr David Green, Ms Lisa Blue, Mr Robert White, Mr Charles Black, Mr Thomas Gray, Mr William Brown, Mr James Green, Mr Robert White, and Ms Lisa Blue (“the applicants”), on 30 October 2000. The applicants were represented by Mr John Doe, a lawyer practising in London. The European Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purpose of the proceedings before the Court. On 23 September 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1968, 1972, 1964, 1966, 1973, 1962, 1976, 1962, 1963, 1971, 1970, and 1969 respectively. They were detained in the Prison, in London, at the time of the events giving rise to the present application. A. Events in Prison On 20 July 1995 the applicants, along with ten other prisoners, were taken from their cells to an area of the prison in order to be brought before the London State Security Court for trial. According to the applicants, while they were waiting to be collected, they were attacked by prison administrators, prison warders, and gendarmes using truncheons and wooden planks, because they had objected to being searched. According to the Government the applicants had resisted the search, attached themselves to one another and subsequently fallen down the stairs and injured themselves. The applicants were then taken to the London State Security Court in prison vehicles. At the hearing before the State Security Court, the applicants' complained that they had been beaten before being brought before the court. The court noted the applicants' condition and decided to postpone the proceedings on the ground that it was impossible to hold a hearing in such circumstances. It ordered that the applicants be medically examined and that the results be sent to the London public prosecutor's office with a view to the opening of an investigation. A letter to that effect was sent the same day to the public prosecutor. B. The investigation concerning the incident in Prison A preliminary investigation was instigated by the London public prosecutor's office into the allegations of the applicants. On 20 July and 14 August 1995 the prosecutor took statements from the applicants who reiterated that they were beaten by the gendarmes and the prison wardens. On 20 July 1995 a forensic expert examined Alex Smith, Peter Brown, David Green, Lisa Blue, Robert White, Charles Black, William Brown, James Green, Robert White, and Lisa Blue in prison.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Alphaville lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Alphavian national, Mr Alphard Alpherson (“the applicant”), on 10 June 2006. The applicant was represented by Mr X.Y. Zephyr, a lawyer practising in Alphabad. The Alphavian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Mr Gamma Delta, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant complained, in particular, about a breach of Article 6 of the Convention on account of unreasonably lengthy proceedings in which no oral hearing before a tribunal was held. On 10 April 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant is the owner of a farm in Alphaville. On 21 April 1999 he asked the Mayor (Bürgermeister) of Alphaville to grant him a permit for the building of roofing between two buildings in order to create a tool shed on his farm. On 12 July 1999 the Mayor, acting as building authority of first instance, dismissed this request as the project was contrary to the relevant area zoning plan (Flächenwidmungsplan). On 22 July 1999 the applicant appealed and submitted in particular that permits had been granted for the building of the other two buildings. He had constructed the roofing at issue at the same time and then sought a building permit for it as in the other cases. He further requested, should it be necessary, that the Municipal Council grant him an exemption permit under Section 22 of the Regional Planning Act (Raumplanungsgesetz). Under this provision a land owner may be exempted under certain conditions from the application of the relevant area zoning plan. The Municipal Council (Gemeindeamt) remitted the case back to the Mayor. Having held a hearing on 15 March 2000, the Mayor, on 13 September 2000, again dismissed the applicant's request for a building permit. He referred to the relevant area zoning plan (Flächenwidmungsplan) and further noted that the local council (Gemeindevorstand) had not granted an exemption permit. The Mayor finally observed that for the construction of the two other buildings there had been proceedings for re-designation of the concerned land. The applicant had then promised to demolish the already existing roofing which had been built without the authorities' consent and the relating demolition order had not been challenged by the applicant. By a decision of 15 January 2001 the local council dismissed the applicant's request for an exemption permit. It noted that the building project concerned 60 square metres while the relevant provisions of the Alphaville Regional Planning Act (Raumplanungsgesetz) provided such an exemption only for a small-sized project of around 25 square meters.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against a country lodged with an international organization under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms by a national, Mr John Doe (the applicant), on 16 July 1998. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Adams, a solicitor practising in a city. The government of the country (the Government) were represented by their Agent, Ms Jane Smith of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, a city. The applicant alleged that neither he nor his legal representative were given the opportunity to address the magistrates' court prior to the imposition of a binding over order in respect of which he was later committed to prison for failure to comply with its terms. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 21 October 2003, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 3 January 1997 the applicant appeared before the magistrates' court, charged with assault occasioning actual bodily harm and failing to answer bail. He was legally represented. The applicant elected to be tried in the Crown Court. The stipendiary magistrate therefore adjourned the proceedings to enable a committal hearing to take place at a later date and proceeded to consider whether the applicant should be granted bail. During the course of that consideration, the applicant “reacted adversely” in court, causing a disturbance which led the magistrate to conclude that there existed a future risk of a breach of the peace by him. The magistrate therefore made an order binding the applicant over to keep the peace and to be of good behaviour under the Justices of the Peace Act 1361. The applicant was “bound over” in his own recognisance of 50 pounds sterling together with a surety of 250 pounds sterling. The precise terms of the order were found by the Divisional Court (in the later judicial review proceedings) to be unclear. However, the Divisional Court proceeded on the assumption that the order of the magistrates' court had fixed a period of 28 days' imprisonment in default of the applicant's own recognisance and/or a suitable surety.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/08) against the Kingdom of Andalusia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Spanish national, Mrs Ana García Pérez (“the applicant”), on 28 November 2008. The applicant was represented by Ms P. Sánchez López, a lawyer practising in Seville. The Spanish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. García Pérez, Head of the Human Rights Department at the Ministry of Justice. The applicant, a Rom of Spanish nationality, complained about a refusal to grant her a survivor’s pension, following the death of X.Y., also a Rom of Spanish nationality, on the sole ground that they were not a married couple under Spanish law. She alleged that there had been a violation of Article 14 of the Convention taken in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Article 12 of the Convention. On 14 June 2008 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. As provided for by Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was also decided that the Chamber would examine the admissibility and merits of the case at the same time. The parties filed their observations. In addition, third-party comments were received from Union Roma which had been given leave by the President to intervene in the written procedure as amicus curiae (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 2 of the Rules of Court). A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Brussels, on 27 June 2010 (Rule 59 § 3). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr J. García Pérez, Head of the Human Rights Department at the Ministry of Justice, Agent; (b) for the applicant Ms P. Sánchez López, Mr A. García Pérez, Counsel; (c) for the third party Mr J. Ramírez Heredia, Chairman of Union Roma. The Court heard addresses by Mr García Pérez, Ms Sánchez López and Mr García Pérez and their replies to questions from Judges García and Myer. It also heard statements by Mr Ramírez Heredia and by Mrs García Pérez, the applicant. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Seville. The applicant and X.Y., both members of the Roma community, were married in December 1980 according to their community’s own rites. The marriage was solemnised in accordance with Roma customs and cultural traditions and was recognised by that community. For the Roma community, a marriage solemnised according to its customs gives rise to the usual social effects, to public recognition, to an obligation to live together and to all other rights and duties that are inherent in the institution of marriage.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/08) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2007. The applicant was represented by Ms. Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. Peter Brown, of a ministry. The applicant complained that the courts’ protracted custody proceedings, including their handling of his request for the return of his daughter under the Hague Convention, and the decision to remove his daughter from the population register, violated Articles 6, 8 and 13 of the Convention. On 26 June 2008 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). On 1 February 2011 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1 of the Rules of Court) and the above application was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in a city. In 1999 the applicant married L., a national holding permanent residence permits in a country and in the country. In February 2004 she obtained nationality. In August 2003 their daughter, N., was born. She is also a national. Between May and August 2005 L. visited her parents in a city together with N. Upon their return, the applicant’s relationship with L. quickly deteriorated and, in September 2005, she returned to her parents’ home in a city with N. They have remained there ever since. A. The proceedings relating to custody and rights of contact In September 2005 the applicant submitted an application for divorce from L. to a court in a city. He further requested sole custody of N. or, if the court decided that the parties should have joint custody, that N. should live with him. In any event, if the court were to decide that N. should live with her mother, he wanted contact rights to be exercised on a regular basis according to a specific schedule. L. agreed to the divorce but opposed the applicant’s requests in relation to their daughter. She wanted sole custody of N. but agreed, pending the final outcome of the proceedings, that the applicant could visit N. in a city for a few hours every other weekend with her or her mother (N.’s maternal grandmother) present.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 45712/99) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by three applicants on 12 November 1998. The applicants were represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 17 June 2004 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. In a letter of 22 June 2004, the Court informed the parties that in accordance with Article 29 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention it would decide on both the admissibility and merits of the application. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1956, 1954 and 1955 respectively and live in a city. In 1995 the Sakarya Governor’s office expropriated a plot of land belonging to the applicants. A committee of experts assessed the value of the plot of land and the relevant amount was paid to them when the expropriation took place. Following the applicants’ request for increased compensation, on 11 September 1997 the Sakarya Civil Court of First-instance awarded them an additional compensation plus interest at the statutory rate running from 12 December 1995. In the course of the proceedings, the court conducted on-site visits and requested expert reports which concluded that the land in question was development land. In view of a judgment rendered by the Court of Cassation which ruled that the lands within the vicinity of the Sakarya organised industrial zone should be considered as agricultural lands, the court decided not to take the expert reports into account. It therefore relied on a fourth expert report which served as a conciliation report for a calculation of the amount due to the applicants. The applicants appealed against the judgment of the Sakarya Civil Court of First-instance. In their submissions, the applicants contested the court’s decision to take solely the last expert report into consideration. On 12 February 1998 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Sakarya Civil Court of First-instance. On 1 April 1998 the Sakarya Governor’s Office paid the amount to the applicants. On 26 May 1998 the Court of Cassation rejected the applicants’ request for rectification.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of A (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of A (a fictional country), Mr Ali Mustafa (“the applicant”), on 15 August 2005. Until March 2009 the applicant was represented by lawyers at the Human Rights Initiative (HRI) in B (a fictional city). Subsequently, he was represented by Mr Mehmet Can, a lawyer practising in C (a fictional city). The Government of A (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the refusal of the national courts to lift a confiscation order for a number of books published by his company violated his right to freedom of expression within the meaning of Article 10 of the Convention. On 20 April 2010 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in C. He is the owner of “X Books and Publishing”, a small independent firm that has published numerous books in A. In the 1990s a number of books published by the applicant's company were found to contain propaganda in breach of various provisions of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3713), as well as “insults to the memory of Atatürk” in breach of Law no. 5817. He was convicted and served a total period of one year, six months and ten days in prison and paid the equivalent of 6,234 local currency units (LCU) in fines. Most of the books in question were confiscated. On 25 November 1995 he introduced an application with the Court in relation to that conviction and the confiscation of the books. On 10 May 2006 the Court found a violation of Articles 7 and 10 of the Convention (see Ali Mustafa v. A, no. 30456/96, 10 May 2006). Following the repeal of section 9 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act in August 2004, the applicant made applications to the Second Chamber of the State Security Court on various dates in 2004 and asked for the confiscation orders to be lifted. The Second Chamber of the State Security Court rejected the claims and the applicant lodged objections against those rejections with the Third Chamber of the same court. The Third Chamber of the State Security Court lifted the confiscation orders in respect of a number of the books but held that, as the confiscation orders had already been executed, there were no books to return.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by Ms. Amelia Reader ("the applicant"), a European national, on 17 June 1999, within the three-month period laid down by former Articles 32 § 1 and 47 of a certain Convention. It originated in an application (no. 30428/96) against a country lodged with a commission under former Article 25 by the applicant. The government of the country are represented by their Agent, Ambassador C. Writer, Head of the International Law Department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant's request to the Court referred to Article 48 as amended by Protocol No. 9, which the country had ratified. The object of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention.
