Having consulted, through the Registrar, those who would be appearing before the Court, the President directed on 15 November 1990 that the oral proceedings should open on 22 April 1991 (Rule 38).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against a country in Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 April 2010. The applicant was represented by Ms A. Brown, a lawyer practising in a city in Italy. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Green, of a government department. The applicant alleged that his disenfranchisement as a result of his residence outside the country constituted a violation of Article 3 of Protocol No. 1 to the Convention, taken alone and taken together with Article 14, and Article 2 of Protocol No. 4 to the Convention. On 15 December 2010 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1922 and lives in a city in Italy. He left the country in 1983 following his retirement and moved to Italy with his wife, an Italian national. Pursuant to primary legislation, citizens residing overseas for less than fifteen years are permitted to vote in parliamentary elections in the country (see paragraphs 10-11 below). The applicant does not meet the fifteen-year criterion and is therefore not entitled to vote. In particular, he was unable to vote in the general election of 5 June 2010.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against the Republic of Alfa (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Alfa nationals, Mr Alfa and Mrs Beta (“the applicants”), on 15 October 1998. The applicants were represented by Mr Gamma, a lawyer practising in Delta (a fictional city). The Alfa Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Xi, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 10 July 2001 the First Section declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS The applicants were born in 1930 and 1935, respectively, and live in Echo, Alfa. The applicants run a fishing farm in Echo since 1975. Before that date the parents of the first applicant had run the fishing farm. Between 1955 and 1970 the Alfa River Engineering Directorate (Flussbauleitung) carried out regulation works on a small river in the vicinity of the applicants' estate without permission under the Water Act (Wasserrechtsgesetz 1958). In October 1969 the former owners of the estate requested the Alfa District Authority (Bezirkshauptmannschaft) to order the Municipalities of Foxtrot and Echo (“the Municipalities”) to re-establish the former state of the river bed maintaining that the regulation works had damaged the well which supplied their fishing farm with water. They submitted that the original capacity of the well had been 800 litres of water per second. After the regulation of the river the capacity of the well had been reduced to 100 litres of water per second. This constituted an interference with their water-rights. In case that the regulation could not be reversed they requested that the Municipalities be ordered to take other steps to ensure the water supply of the fishing farm. On 12 January 1970 the District Authority dismissed this request. On 18 May 1970 the Upper Alfa Regional Governor allowed the appeal and remitted the case to the District Authority to decide on the request. On 12 January 1971 the applicants' predecessors filed a request for transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag) as the District Authority failed to decide within the statutory six months time-limit. On 10 February 1971 the Regional Governor dismissed this request. On 3 September 1971 they filed again a request for transfer of jurisdiction and the Regional Governor again dismissed this request. The applicants' predecessors filed an appeal against this decision. On 9 February 1972 the Federal Minister for Agriculture and Forestry (Bundesminister für Land- und Forstwirtschaft) allowed the appeal as a consequence of which the Regional Governor had to take a decision on the merits.

PROCEDURE The present case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 16 May 1983, within the period of three months laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 of the Convention. The case originated in an application against a State lodged with the Commission on 19 July 1979 under Article 25 by a citizen. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the State recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention. In response to the inquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the citizen stated that he wished to participate in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyers who would represent him. The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, an elected judge of a nationality (Article 43) and the President of the Court. On 27 May 1983, the President of the Court drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the five other members. Mr. Zekia and Mr. Bernhardt, who were prevented from taking part in the consideration of the case, were subsequently replaced by substitute judges. Mr. Wiarda assumed the office of President of the Chamber. He ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission, and the lawyers for the applicant regarding the need for a written procedure. On 24 June, he directed that the Agent and the lawyers for the applicant should each have until 16 September to file a memorial and that the Delegate should be entitled to file, within two months from the date of the transmission to him by the Registrar of whichever of the aforesaid documents should last be filed, a memorial in reply. On 14 September, the President extended until 14 October each of the time-limits granted to the Agent and the applicant’s lawyers.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Xanadan nationals, Mr X Y and Ms Z W (“the applicants”), on 1 August 2002. The applicants were represented by Mr A B, a lawyer practising in Yonder. The Xanadan Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 29 June 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1979 and 1951 respectively and live in Yonder. The first applicant was the editor-in-chief of a weekly newspaper, The Weekly News, and the second applicant was its owner. In August 2001, in the tenth issue of the newspaper, an article which contained an interview with C X, who was one of the leaders of an illegal organisation, namely the Z Group, was published. The relevant parts of the interview read as follows: “Three years have passed since the Z Group declared a ceasefire to stop the bloodshed and to contribute to the peace process. Subsequently, the Z Group withdrew its armed forces out of Xanadu to maintain peace. However, the state did not take any steps for democratisation or to solve the Z problem. ... The case brought against our leader A B is a case against the Z people. Therefore, it is not our Prime Minister who wishes to be tried before the European Court of Human Rights, but it is our people. The law was violated in Yonder and, consequently, the death penalty imposed on A B and on our people is not legitimate. All things considered, it is natural that our people have expectations from the European Court of Human Rights, the court of Europe which defends democracy, human rights and the rule of law. ...” On 10 September 2001 the public prosecutor at the Yonder State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicants. By referring to the above-mentioned paragraphs of the interview, the public prosecutor accused the applicants of having allowed the publication of the declarations of an illegal armed terrorist organisation. The charges were brought under Article 6 §§ 2 and 4 of the Law on the Prevention of Terrorism (Law no. 12345), additional Article 2 of the Press Law (Law no. 6789) and Article 36 of the Criminal Code. On 27 December 2001 the Yonder State Security Court, composed of three civilian judges, convicted the applicants as charged and fined them 1,000,000,000 Xanadan liras and 2,000,000,000 Xanadan liras respectively. The first instance court further ordered temporary closure of the newspaper for a period of ten days. The applicants appealed.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/07) against the Republic of Xana lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Xanian nationals, Mr Xan and Mr Yana (“the applicants”), on 1 January 2007. The applicants were represented by Mr Zan, a lawyer practising in Yana. The Xanian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 15 July 2008 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS The first applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Zana. By a letter dated 15 July 2008, the applicants’ representative informed the Court that the second applicant had died on 10 April 2007 and that his son Mr Yana wished to pursue the application. In 1975, a third person named C.D. inherited a plot of land from her mother, a Syrian national. However, she did not have the land registered in her name at the time. On 10 July 1997 C.D.’s representative signed an agreement with the applicants before a notary public, promising to sell the land to them. The applicants paid the amount due and were told that C.D. would finalise the relevant formalities and transfer the ownership of the land to the applicants in the shortest possible time. On 1 August 1997 the applicants brought an action against C.D. before the Yana Civil Court of General Jurisdiction. They claimed that she had failed to transfer the ownership of the land to them, although they had paid the purchase price. They requested that the land be registered in their names. On 31 December 2003 the court dismissed the action. It held that on 1 November 1966 the Cabinet of Ministers had issued a decree seizing the property of Syrian nationals living in Xana, including the land in question. As the land had been owned by the State since 1966, the court concluded that the sale agreement of 10 July 1997 signed by C.D. was void. Both parties appealed against that decision. C.D. also put forward a plea of unconstitutionality against the decree of 1966. On 28 March 2005 the Court of Cassation dismissed the plea of unconstitutionality and upheld the first instance court’s decision. On 8 July 2005 the Court of Cassation rejected the applicants’ request for rectification. This decision was not served on the applicants and they learned about the outcome of the proceedings by tracking their application through the Court of Cassation’s web site.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Xanaqua lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xanaqua, Mr Xan Yana (“the applicant”), on 10 March 2006. The applicant was represented by Mr Zan Aya, a lawyer practising in Xanaqua. The government of Xanaqua (“the government”) were represented by their Agent. On 25 July 2008 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (former Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Xanaqua. On 10 January 2001 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of theft. On 15 March 2002 he was released pending trial. On 30 August 2006 the Xanaqua Assize Court sentenced the applicant to one year and six months' imprisonment. On 15 June 2005 the Supreme Court upheld the judgment of 30 August 2006.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X Y Z (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2001. The applicant was represented by Law Firm, solicitors in a city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr A B C of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a city. The applicant complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that, because he was a man, he was denied social security benefits equivalent to those received by widows. On 10 February 2002 the Court decided to communicate the complaints concerning widows’ benefits relating to the period after the date on which the applicant lodged his relevant claim and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. Subsequently, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in a city. His wife died on 15 November 1995 leaving dependent children. His claim for widows’ benefits was made in February 2000 and on 1 March 2000 it was determined that he was entitled to Widowed Parent’s Allowance as from 1 April 2000. The applicant however requested that the claim be treated as from the date of his wife’s death, or alternatively that he be allowed to claim the equivalent widow’s benefit. On 10 November he made a formal application for widow’s benefit which was rejected on 15 January 2001 on the ground that he was not entitled to widows’ benefits because he was not a woman. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such social security benefits were payable to widowers under the country’s law.

PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 31145/96 and 35580/97) against a country lodged with an international human rights body under former Article 25 of a human rights convention by two nationals, Mr A and Mr B, on 13 April 1996 and 1 April 1997, respectively. The applicants were represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The government of the country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr X and Mr Y, both of a government department. The applicants alleged, as regards their trial by court-martial, that they did not have a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. On 31 May 1999 the international body found a violation of a specific article of the convention. By letter dated 27 September 1999 the Government referred the cases to the court explaining that the reference had been made not to contest the breach but to seek a ruling on what just satisfaction, if any, should be awarded to the applicants. In accordance with the protocol and rules of court, a panel of the grand chamber decided on 13 December 1999 that the applications should be considered by a chamber constituted within one of the sections of the court. The applications were then allocated to the third section of the court. Within that section, the chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in the rules of court. A judge elected in respect of the country withdrew from sitting in the case. While the government initially appointed an ad hoc judge, by letter dated 9 November 2000 they agreed that another judge, elected in respect of another country, would sit in place of the withdrawn judge. The chamber decided to join the proceedings in the applications. The applicants and the government each filed observations on the merits. The chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASES At the time of the events in question, both applicants were serving in the army and were tried by district courts-martial convened pursuant to the Army Act 1955. Mr A pleaded guilty to the armed forces’ disciplinary offence of absence without leave (contrary to section 38(a) of the Army Act 1955).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Andorra, Mr Alvaro Verde (“the applicant”), on 10 June 2001. The applicant was represented by Mr T. Blanco, a lawyer practising in Andorra. The Andorran Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 1 October 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaint concerning the alleged ill-treatment of the applicant during police custody and his right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1976 and was serving his prison sentence in Andorra prison at the time of his application to the Court. The applicant was arrested and taken into police custody on 27 December 1994 on suspicion of membership in an illegal organisation, namely the Red Star. The applicant claims that he was subjected to ill-treatment while in police custody. In particular, he claims to have been beaten, given electric shocks, deprived of food and water, immersed in cold water and subjected to falaka (beating of the soles of the feet). On 8 January 1995 the applicant, together with twelve other suspects, was taken to the Andorran Forensic Institute for a medical examination. The doctor noted that there were no physical signs of ill-treatment on the applicant's body. On the same day the applicant was brought before the public prosecutor at the Andorran State Security Court where he denied the statements he gave to the police and alleged that he had been subjected to torture whilst in custody. Later that day the applicant was brought before a judge who ordered his remand in custody. The public prosecutor, in view of the complaints of ill-treatment of the applicant and other suspects arrested in the course of an investigation into the Red Star, forwarded the case file to the Andorran public prosecutor's office. The latter, after having instigated an investigation into the complaints, issued a decision of non-prosecution against two police officers for lack of evidence on 11 May 1995. On an unspecified date the public prosecutor at the Andorran State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicant accusing him of membership in an illegal organisation and committing arson under Articles 168 § 2 and 369 of the Criminal Code. The proceedings against the applicant were subsequently joined with the criminal proceedings against nineteen other persons who had been charged with membership of the same organisation.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/13) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Alice Smith (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2013. The applicant was represented by Ms B. Jones, a lawyer practising in a city. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by two of their Agents, Mr C. Brown and Mrs D. Green, of the Ministry of Justice. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the conditions of her detention for preventive purposes in two police stations had violated Article 3 of the Convention. On 1 March 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. The Government of the country, having been informed of their right to intervene in the proceedings (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 of the Rules of Court), indicated that they did not wish to exercise that right. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1982 and lives in a city. A. The applicant’s arrest, the order for her detention, its termination and the conditions of its execution The applicant is an anti-nuclear and environmental activist. She has repeatedly used her climbing skills to draw public attention to her protest. 1. The applicant’s arrest On 1 October 2008 around 11 a.m. the applicant and three further persons belonging to an environmental protection group, an organisation, climbed on the arch of a railway bridge. The group fixed banners expressing protest against the transport, by train, of radioactive waste from a location, France, to the interim storage facility in a city, scheduled from 7 to 9 November 2008. The members of the group refused to have themselves roped down by the police, who had dissolved their assembly. They were finally roped down by a police’s mountain rescue team. The police then arrested only the applicant at 2.40 p.m. while the other three participants remained at liberty. They further seized the banners and the climbing equipment. 2. The detention order against the applicant On 1 October 2008 at 5.30 p.m. a district court, having heard the applicant and the police, ordered the applicant’s detention for preventive purposes under section 18 § 1 no. 2 of the Public Security and Order Act. That detention was to last until the arrival of the “castor”0 containers in a train station and until 10 November 2008, 0.00 p.m. at the most. The court found that the applicant, who had been represented by counsel throughout the proceedings before the domestic courts, and three further persons had let themselves down on a rope on a railway bridge. They had unrolled banners protesting against the castor transport. A commuter train had to be stopped because its passage would have put the protesters at risk.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against a country lodged with an international organization ("the Commission") under Article 34 of a convention ("the Convention") by a national, Mr John Doe ("the applicant"), on 24 April 1997. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Smith, a legal officer with a non-profit organization, a city. The government ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Jones. The applicant alleged that social-security legislation discriminated against him and his late wife on grounds of sex, in breach of Article 14 of the Convention taken in conjunction with both Article 8 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 11 May 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible [Note by the Registry. The Court's decision is obtainable from the Registry]. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections. This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant is a national born in 1956 and living in a city. In December 1984 the applicant married Mary Doe. They had two children: Emily Grace, born on 24 March 1989, and Daniel Leo, born on 2 August 1990. Mrs Doe died of cancer on 7 June 1996, at the age of 39. The applicant is the administrator of her estate. Mrs Doe had been employed as a local authority housing officer. For the greater part of her married life, she was the primary breadwinner. She had paid full social-security contributions as an employed earner until 1994, and was subsequently entitled to contribution credits as a person unfit for work. On 3 November 1995 the applicant gave up work to nurse his wife and care for their children. Following his wife's death, he worked part time between 2 September 1996 and 6 November 1996, for an annual salary of 4,393 pounds sterling (GBP), but since this proved uneconomic he stopped working to care full time for the children. On 4 November 1996 the applicant applied to the Benefits Agency for the payment of social-security benefits. He applied for benefits equivalent to those which a widow whose husband had died in similar circumstances to those of Mrs Doe would have been entitled, namely a widow's payment and a widowed mother's allowance, payable under the Social Security and Benefits Act 1992.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 May 2000. The applicant was represented by Mr Alex Smith, a lawyer practising in Andorra. The Government of Andorra (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 22 June 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. On 23 July 2005 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). The case was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Andorra. On 15 July 1986 the applicant was seriously injured in an explosion of a bomb placed in the garden of the Military barracks in Andorra district of Andorra. He was ten years old at the time of the events. On 10 March 1987 the applicant’s father, acting as his legal guardian, filed a petition with the Ministry of Internal Affairs requesting compensation for the damage the applicant had sustained. The Ministry of Internal Affairs rejected this request on 15 May 1987. On 3 July 1987 the applicant’s father brought an action for compensation before the Andorra Administrative Court against the Ministry of Internal Affairs (hereinafter “the respondent”). On 16 July 1987 the case was notified to the respondent which submitted its observations on 11 September 1987. On 3 February 1988 the Andorra Administrative Court dismissed the respondent’s preliminary objection. Between 3 February 1988 and 4 October 1989 the first-instance court took certain procedural decisions on 4 October 1988, 27 April 1989 and 16 July 1989. On 4 October 1989 the Andorra Administrative Court considered that there was neither fault nor negligence attributable to the authorities and dismissed the case. On 30 January 1990 the applicant appealed against the aforementioned decision and requested the suspension of the execution of the judgment. On 30 January 1990 the applicant paid the expenses pertaining to the appeal procedure. The applicant was warned that the amount paid was insufficient and on 30 March 1990 he paid the remaining costs of the appeal procedure. On 3 May 1990 the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the applicant’s request for a suspension of the execution of the judgment of 4 October 1989. On 16 November 1990 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the judgment of the first-instance court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against the Republic of Aalandia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 November 2010. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Brown, a lawyer practising in City. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 25 July 2013 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in City. On 28 August 1991, when the applicant was a conscript in the army, a clash broke out between the security forces and a group of terrorists. During the incident the applicant was severely wounded by gunshots. Subsequently, he was treated in different military hospitals. According to a medical report, dated 15 October 1992, the applicant’s work capability had been reduced by 35%. Consequently, on 3 May 1993 he was declared to be suffering from a permanent disability and discharged from the army. He was also awarded a sixth-degree disability pension. In the following years the applicant started suffering from persistent headaches and dizziness, and had sleeping problems. In 2005 a CT scan revealed an unidentified metallic object in the left orbital area. Subsequently, in 2008, the applicant was admitted to the neurosurgery department of the H Military Hospital and another CT scan revealed that he had a bullet in his head, measuring 17 x 12 mm. The doctors stated that removing the bullet was potentially life-threatening. On 20 August 2008 the applicant applied to the Ministry of Defence for compensation in respect of his injury. He alleged that, on account of medical negligence, the bullet in his head had remained unnoticed and that he had sustained further pecuniary damage as this fact had not been taken into account in calculating his disability pension. Following tacit dismissal of the claim by the administrative authorities, on 12 February 2009 the applicant instituted two separate actions in the Supreme Military Administrative Court, one for the pecuniary damage and the other for the non-pecuniary damage he had sustained on account of the bullet which had been found in his head in 2008. On 17 March and 14 April 2009 respectively the Supreme Military Administrative Court, by a majority, rejected both actions as being out of time. In both decisions the court held that notwithstanding the fact that the applicant had not been aware of the bullet in his head until 2008, pursuant to section 44(1) of the Supreme Military Administrative Court Act, his compensation claims should have been lodged within five years of the incident. On 19 May 2009 the Supreme Military Administrative Court rejected a rectification request lodged by the applicant.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 18152/11) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of an unspecified origin, Mr [Last Name] (“the applicant”), on 14 January 2011. The applicant was represented by lawyers practising in Istanbul. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 25 September 2014 the applicant’s complaints under Article 3, Article 5 §§ 1, 2, 4, and 5 and Article 13 of the Convention regarding his detention at the Foreigners’ Removal Centre were communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible, pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. The Government, who were informed of their right to intervene under Article 36 of the Convention, did not make use of this right. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1972. He was detained at the Foreigners’ Removal Centre at the time of the events giving rise to this application. His current address is unknown. In 2000 the applicant fled to Turkey because he was being searched for by authorities. It appears that shortly before his escape, he had lost his right leg in a bomb attack. Subsequent to his departure from the country, criminal proceedings were brought against the applicant by the authorities before a court on the following charges: (i) participation in an armed insurrection and membership of an armed organisation with the purpose of overthrowing the constitutional order and violating the territorial integrity of the country and (ii) possessing firearms and ammunition. It appears that the court issued a detention order in respect of the applicant in his absence. On 24 January 2008 the applicant was taken into police custody in the context of an operation. He was subsequently taken to a prison, where he was placed in pre-trial detention upon the order of a court. On an unspecified date criminal proceedings were commenced against the applicant before a court. On 28 January 2009 the court ordered the applicant’s release from the prison. There is no further information in the case file as regards the outcome of the criminal proceedings. Following his release from prison on 28 January 2009, the applicant was placed in detention at the Foreigners’ Removal Centre, which is attached to a security directorate. On an unspecified date the authorities requested the extradition of the applicant.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 21890/03) against a State (referred to as 'the Republic of Poland') lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ('the Convention') by a national of a country (referred to as 'the applicant'), on 23 May 2003. The Government of the country ('the Government') were represented by their Agent, a representative from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 14 September 2006 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in a town (referred to as 'Rejowiec Fabryczny'). A. The alleged ill-treatment of the applicant It appears that in November 2002 the District Prosecutor of a district (referred to as 'Chełm District') charged the applicant with armed robbery. On an unspecified date in November 2002 the court ordered his detention on remand. He was detained in a prison (referred to as 'Chełm Prison'). In connection with the criminal investigation against the applicant, the District Prosecutor ordered the applicant to provide a sample of his body odour. According to the applicant, on 13 March 2003 he was called to an interrogation room in the prison where he was informed that he was to provide the required samples. However, the applicant stated that he would provide them only in the presence of his lawyer. According to the applicant, he was then knocked over and kicked by two police officers and a prison guard. During that time he also lost a valuable item (referred to as 'gold neck chain'). Subsequently, the applicant agreed to provide the samples. The applicant claimed that as a result of the beating he had bruises on his abdomen, his back and his waist. He also had pain in his spine. On 24 March 2003 the applicant filed a criminal complaint with the District Prosecutor, alleging that he had been beaten on 13 March 2003 by two police officers and a prison guard. He further alleged that his gold chain had been stolen during the incident. On 24 April 2003 the District Prosecutor opened an investigation. She heard the applicant and the two police officers and prison guard involved in the alleged incident. She also heard two other police officers who had been working in a neighbouring room at the time of the alleged incident. The District Prosecutor established that the applicant had been told to provide the samples and, if he refused, that they would be taken against his will. After some persuasion, the applicant had agreed to provide the samples. All the officers confirmed that version of events and stated that force had not been used. The District Prosecutor obtained other relevant evidence which did not corroborate the applicant's allegations of ill-treatment. Between 13 March and 1 April 2003 the applicant was seen by a prison doctor on five occasions.

Alpaslan"), an agent ("Mr S. Güran"), a counsel ("Mr B. Yildiz"), an adviser ("Ms D. Kilislioğlu"), an adviser ("Ms B. Özaydin"), an adviser ("Ms M. Gülşen"); – for the applicant a counsel ("Mr S. Circular of 23 February 1998 On 26 August 1997 the applicant, who was then in her fifth year at a university ("University of Bursa"), enrolled at a faculty ("Cerrahpaşa Faculty of Medicine") at a university ("University of Istanbul").

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 73988/01) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 3 April 2000. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Y of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 4 July 2005 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1962 and lives in a town. A. The first set of criminal proceedings against the applicant On 8 February 2000 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of having committed three burglaries. On 10 February 2000 the District Court ordered that the applicant be remanded in custody until 8 May 2000. It found that there were reasonable grounds for believing that the applicant had committed the offences in question and that he would obstruct the proper course of the proceedings. The applicant’s detention was subsequently prolonged by the District Court on unspecified dates. On 31 August 2000 the bill of indictment was filed with the court. On 11 December 2000 the District Court convicted the applicant of six counts of burglary and sentenced him to five years’ imprisonment. The applicant appealed against that judgment. On 11 April 2001 the Court quashed the first-instance judgment and ordered a retrial. The applicant was released on the same day. On 19 February 2003 the District Court convicted the applicant of five counts of burglary and sentenced him to four years’ imprisonment. B. The second set of criminal proceedings against the applicant On an unspecified date in February 2000 the applicant was charged with homicide. On 20 March 2000 the District Court ordered that the applicant be detained for three months in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offence at issue. On 30 June 2000 the District Court ordered the applicant’s release. On 15 November 2000 the criminal proceedings against the applicant were discontinued. C. The third set of criminal proceedings against the applicant On 25 March 2002 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of burglary. On 27 March 2002 the District Court ordered his detention on remand until 25 May 2002. It found that there was a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed burglary, having regard to the evidence obtained in the investigation. It also relied on the severity of the likely sentence given the fact that the applicant was a habitual offender. Lastly, it held that there was a risk that the applicant would tamper with evidence.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms. Anna Novak (“the applicant”) on 15 June 1998. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. M. Smith, and subsequently, Mr. N. Jones of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of civil proceedings in her case had been excessive. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 7 June 2004 the Court declared the application admissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in Berlin, Germany. The applicant used to work in the Berlin office of the company “B.A.R.” registered in Europe. On 18 June 1994 she was dismissed from her job. On 28 June 1994 she lodged a claim for reinstatement with the Berlin District Court (Sąd Rejonowy). The court held hearings on 28 August and 5 January 1995. On 1 March 1995 the applicant asked the court to issue an interim order to safeguard her claim in the proceedings. On 3 May 1995 the court refused her request. On 15 June 1995 the Berlin Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) dismissed the applicant's appeal against that decision. On 3 May 1995 the court held a hearing. At the next hearing held on 22 August 1995 the applicant modified her claim. As a consequence, the case was transferred to the Regional Court. The court held further hearings on 4 October and 16 November 1995. It also decided that two witnesses should be heard by two other courts. The witnesses were heard by the Munich District Court and the Düsseldorf District Court on 30 April and 3 July 1996, respectively. On 27 November 1996 and 15 January 1997 the Regional Court held hearings. The hearing listed for 2 February 1997 was cancelled. At the hearing held on 10 April 1997 the Regional Court ordered the applicant to specify her claim. On 28 April 1997 the applicant modified her claim. On 28 May 1997 the court stayed the proceedings on the ground that the applicant had not complied with the order of 10 April 1997. Upon the applicant's appeal, on 10 July 1997 the Berlin Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) quashed the decision of 28 May 1997. On 29 March 1998 the Regional Court ordered the applicant to specify her claim. On 3 April 1998 she submitted her pleading to the court. On 1 June 1998 the court held a hearing.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xanadu, Mr Ali Reşit Arslan (“the applicant”), on 21 August 2001. The applicant was represented by Ms T. Gürcan, a lawyer practising in Xanadu. The Government of Xanadu (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 1 June 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the alleged ill-treatment of the applicant and the length of the proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, the Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1966 and was serving a prison sentence in Xanadu prison at the time of his application to the Court. On 4 April 1993 the applicant was taken into custody by police officers from the Anti-Terrorist Branch of the Xanadu Security Directorate on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation the XYZ (the Kurdistan Workers' Party). According to the arrest report, the applicant resisted the arrest and the police officers had to use force to apprehend him. On 19 April 1993 the applicant was brought before the investigating judge at the Xanadu State Security Court, where he denied the allegations against him. The judge ordered the applicant's detention on remand. On 29 April 1993 the applicant was examined by a doctor at the ABC State Hospital who noted that there was a restriction in the functioning of the right shoulder and elbow. On 4 May 1993 a doctor from the DEF Forensic Medicine Institute drew up a report, according to which there were numerous ecchymoses and lesions on the various parts of the applicant's body and there was a reduced functioning of the right arm. In a further report dated 9 July 1993, it was concluded that the injuries on the applicant's body rendered him unfit for work for ten days. On 5 May 1993 the public prosecutor at the Xanadu State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicant, along with twenty-seven other persons, charging him with membership of an illegal organisation under Article 168 § 1 of the Criminal Code. On 12 July 1993 the applicant maintained before the Xanadu State Security Court that his statements had been taken under torture while in police custody. At the end of the hearing, the court concluded that the applicant's representative could file a complaint with the authorities about the applicant's allegations of ill-treatment. On 22 January 1997 the public prosecutor proposed to alter the charge against the applicant to treason against the integrity of the State, a capital offence under Article 125 of the Criminal Code.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 73604/01) against a State entity lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 13 June 2001. The applicant was represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The State entity (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, a former official in charge of a section. On 26 October 2004 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1951 and lives in a city. He is a journalist with a national company. At the material time he was responsible for a programme. On 6 and 11 March 1997, as part of that programme, the national company broadcast on its channel a report by the applicant concerning the position of the country during the Second World War. The report began by discussing the history of the country during the Second World War, as supposedly experienced by the people at the time and taught for many years in schools. The country had been portrayed as a brave country which, despite its neutrality, had been on the side of democracy and thus of the Allies. After this recounting of the “myth”, the journalist stated: “There has been a somewhat rude awakening.” The programme continued with severe criticism of the country’s position by prominent figures and with contrasting opinions of citizens who had lived through the war. The journalist said that historians had made efforts to uncover a significant part of the truth. The programme then described the attitude of the country and its leaders, emphasising their alleged affinity with the far right and their inclination towards rapprochement with a foreign country. This was followed by an analysis of the question of anti-Semitism in the country and of the country’s economic relations with the foreign country, focusing on the laundering of Nazi money by the country and on the role of companies in the matter of unclaimed assets. The programme provoked objections from groups of citizens, who filed complaints with an authority. In the course of its investigation into the complaints, the authority interviewed two experts.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 24 September 2008. The applicant was represented by Ms Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms Mary Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant complained of the ineffectiveness of the investigation into the circumstances of his brother’s death. On 13 February 2012 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in a town. A. The investigation into the circumstances of J.K.’s death The applicant’s brother J.K. worked as a night guard at a bus terminus in a city. On 12 November 2003, at around 4 a.m., his clothes caught fire. Drivers at the station raised the alarm and managed to extinguish the fire. J.K. was subsequently taken to hospital. However, because of his serious injuries he died on 26 November 2003. On 31 December 2004 the district prosecutor discontinued the investigation into the circumstances of J.K.’s death. During the investigation it was established that J.K. must have either fallen asleep or fainted and that his clothes had caught fire when they came into contact with an electric heater. The prosecutor concluded that it had been an unfortunate accident and that no offence had been committed. On 24 January 2005 the applicant appealed. He argued that the prosecution authorities had failed to establish the circumstances of his brother’s death. He submitted that witnesses had given different versions of the events. In addition it had not been established how J.K’s clothes could have caught fire and where the electric heater had been placed. He further stressed that J.K. had suffered from serious diabetes and should not have been allowed to work night shifts. On 25 May 2005 the Chief Inspector of the regional command, in reply to the applicant’s complaint, stated that the investigation into the circumstances of J.K.’s death had indeed been too long. The officer in charge had already been disciplined. On 22 August 2005 the applicant again complained to the regional prosecutor about delays in the proceedings. Subsequently, on 19 October 2005 he complained to the appellate prosecutor about the fact that he had not received any reply from the Regional Prosecutor. On 21 November 2005 the appellate prosecutor confirmed that the proceedings had indeed been too long. He further informed the applicant that the Regional Prosecutor had been reproached for not having replied to his complaint in a timely manner. On 29 November 2005 the district prosecutor reopened the investigation into the circumstances of J.K.’s death. On 22 April 2005 the applicant complained about the actions taken by the police officers on 12 November 2003.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 3042/05) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 19 November 2004. The applicant was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 20 January 2011 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, who was born in 1964, is currently serving a prison sentence in a prison. On 26 March 1998, following a house search and the seizure of certain items, the applicant was taken into police custody on suspicion of being a member of an illegal organisation. According to the applicant’s statements, he was questioned by police officers on an unspecified date but exercised his right to remain silent. During the questioning, he was not provided with a lawyer. In the meantime, on 29 March 1998, a certain co-accused was confronted with the applicant, in the absence of a lawyer, and identified him. On 1 April 1998, the applicant and other accused persons were examined by a doctor who noted that none of them showed signs of physical violence apart from a few. On the same day, the applicant was brought before the public prosecutor and the investigating judge at a court where he denied the allegations, in the absence of his lawyer. In his statements, the applicant also mentioned that he had not been provided with a lawyer during his police custody despite his request to that effect. He also denied the confrontation and identification records in his statements made to the public prosecutor. After the questioning was over, the investigating judge remanded the applicant in custody. On 21 April 1998 the public prosecutor issued an indictment, charging the applicant with being a leader of an armed organisation. On 6 July 1998 the applicant was released pending trial. On 26 October 2001 the first-instance court convicted the applicant as charged. On 19 November 2001 the applicant was detained to serve his prison sentence. On 14 February 2002 the Court of Cassation quashed the conviction for lack of reasoning. On 26 December 2003 the court once again convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to a number of years’ imprisonment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/90) against a country of Europe lodged with an international organization ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of a convention ("the Convention") by a national of that country, Ms Jane Doe ("the applicant"), on 10 June 1990. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Legal Firm, solicitors practising in a city. The government of that country ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Mr X of the Foreign Ministry, in the capital city. The applicant alleged violations of Articles 8, 12, 13 and 14 of the Convention in respect of the legal status of transsexuals in that country and particularly their treatment in the sphere of employment, social security, pensions and marriage. The application was declared admissible by the Commission on 1 December 1997 and transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1999 in accordance with Article 5 § 3, second sentence, of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention, the Commission not having completed its examination of the case by that date. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 11 September 2001, a Chamber of that Section, composed of the following judges: Mr A, Mr B, Mr C, Mrs D, Mr E, Sir F and Mr G, and also of Mrs H, Section Registrar, relinquished jurisdiction in favour of the Grand Chamber, neither of the parties having objected to relinquishment (Article 30 of the Convention and Rule 72). The composition of the Grand Chamber was determined according to the provisions of Article 27 §§ 2 and 3 of the Convention and Rule 24 of the Rules of Court. The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the case should be assigned to the Grand Chamber that had been constituted to hear the case of Case X v. a country (application no. 12345/90) (Rules 24, 43 § 2 and 71). The applicant and the Government each filed a memorial on the merits. In addition, third-party comments were received from Organization Y, which had been given leave by the President to intervene in the written procedure (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 61 § 3).
