There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr X, Agent, Mr Y, Counsel, Mr Z, Mr A, Ms B, Ms C, Advisers; (b) for the applicant Ms D, Q.C., Counsel, Mr E, Counsel, Ms F, Solicitor.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against the Republic of Alfa (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Alfa national, Mr John Doe (the applicant), on 1 November 2000. The applicant was represented by Mr X. Y., a lawyer practising in Alfa City. The Alfa Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Z. Alpha, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged in particular that the proceedings relating to his request for an industrial licence for chimney sweeping lasted unreasonably long. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 16 June 2005, the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Alfa City. He is a chimney sweeper by profession. On 4 August 1988 the applicant filed a request for an industrial licence (Konzession) for chimney sweeping in Alfa City. On 31 March 1989 he filed an alternative request to start chimney sweeping in a specified administrative area (Kehrgebiet). Following a new regulation concerning the division of those administrative areas which entered into force in December 1991, the applicant, on 14 January 1992, modified his request into one for an industrial licence as a chimney sweeper in a different specified administrative area. As the Upper Austria Regional Governor (Landeshauptmann) did not deal with his request, the applicant, on 20 July 1992, filed a request for the transfer of jurisdiction (Devolutionsantrag) with the Federal Minister of Economic Affairs (Bundesminister für wirtschaftliche Angelegenheiten). On 3 June 1993 the Federal Minister allowed his request for transfer but dismissed his application for the industrial licence under the Trade Act (Gewerbeordnung). Referring to the submissions of the competent municipalities, he noted that there was no need for further chimney sweepers in the concerned area. On 20 July 1993 the applicant filed a complaint with the Administrative Court. He complained in particular that the Federal Minister had not made sufficient investigations for his findings. On 20 December 1994 the Administrative Court (Verwaltungs-gerichtshof) quashed the decision on procedural grounds. On 3 February 1995 the Federal Minister rejected the applicant’s request for a transfer of jurisdiction, finding that, according to the amended Trade Act (Gewerbeordnung), the authority now competent for applications of the applicant’s kind was the Administrative District Authority, namely the Alfa City Municipal Office (Magistrat).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Xana lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Turkish national, Mr Xan Yana (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2005. The applicant was represented by Ms Zan Xana, a lawyer practising in Yana. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 30 December 2008 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Yana. He was detained at the Xana prison at the time of the events. Upon the applicant’s request he was examined by a doctor at the prison clinic on 16 February 2005. According to the prison clinic’s registry provided by the Government, the applicant was examined by the prison doctor who considered that he was suffering from a tension headache. The doctor decided to transfer the applicant to a neurology department of a hospital. The Government submitted that, since there was no neurology department at Xana State Hospital, the applicant was transferred to Kastamonu State Hospital where he was examined by a doctor at the Neurology Department on 26 April 2005. In the meantime, on 20 February 2005 the applicant filed a petition with the Xana Judge for the Execution of Sentences, after an oral refusal by the prison authorities, requesting copies of the doctor’s report issued after his medical examination of 16 February 2005 and the relevant pages of the prison clinic’s registry. On 22 February 2005 the Xana Judge of Execution ordered the prison authorities to provide the applicant with copies of the requested documents. The applicant was so provided. On 27 February 2005 the Xana public prosecutor filed an objection against the above decision. Referring to the spirit and purpose of a circular dated 6 January 2006, he claimed, inter alia, that the delivery of the originals or copies of any official prison documents to detainees or convicted persons was not permitted, in practice, on grounds of security and public order. On 28 February 2005 the Xana Assize Court accepted the prosecutor’s objection on these grounds. On 1 March 2005 the documents in question were reclaimed by the prison authorities. On 26 April 2005, the applicant requested the prison authorities to provide him with a copy of the medical report and prescription issued at the Kastamonu State Hospital following his medical examination on 26 April 2005. On the same day he received them. The applicant’s further request from the Ministry of Justice to quash the Assize Court’s judgment by a written order (yazılı emir) was also rejected on 5 June 2005. On 25 December 2005 the applicant was released from prison.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr John Doe (“the applicant”) on 10 December 2001. The applicant was represented by Mr Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Andrian Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 10 July 2005 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in Andria. On 3 December 1994 the General Directorate of National Roads and Highways expropriated a plot of land belonging to the applicant in Andria in order to build a motorway. A committee of experts assessed the value of the plot of land and the relevant amount was paid to the applicant when the expropriation took place. Following the applicant’s request for increased compensation, on 28 April 1998 the Andrian Civil Court of First-instance awarded him additional compensation of 300,000,000 local currency units (LCUs), plus interest at the statutory rate, applicable at the date of the court’s decision, running from 3 December 1994, the date of transfer of the title-deeds. On 22 March 1999 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Andrian Civil Court of First-instance. On 15 May 2001 the General Directorate of National Roads and Highways paid the applicant 1,000,000,000 LCUs, interest included.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights on 11 December 1995, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 of the Convention. It originated in three applications against the United Kingdom lodged with the Commission under Article 25 on 14 December 1992 by three applicants. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the United Kingdom recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 8 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent them. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio a judge of British nationality and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court. On 8 February 1996, in the presence of the Registrar, the President of the Court drew by lot the names of the other seven members. As President of the Chamber, Mr Bernhardt, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the United Kingdom Government, the applicants’ lawyers and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings. Pursuant to the orders made in consequence, the Registrar received the Government’s and the applicants’ memorials on 2 and 15 July 1996 respectively. On 17 July 1996, the President granted leave to a non-governmental human rights organisation to submit written comments on specified aspects of the case. The comments were received on 16 August 1996. In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 October 1996. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/13) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms Ana Novak (“the applicant”), on 15 August 2013. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Ms Q. Kowalski, a lawyer practising in Berlin. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr R. Nowak, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, a breach of Article 3 of the Convention on account of the imposition on her of the so-called “dangerous detainee” regime. On 10 October 2015 the complaint under Article 3 of the Convention was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1988 and lives in Gdynia. A. Criminal proceedings against the applicant On 12 March 2008 the applicant was arrested and remanded in custody. She was charged with, inter alia, murder, attempted murder, and illegal possession of firearms. On 15 November 2010 the Gdynia Regional Court convicted the applicant of battery and attempted murder and sentenced her to twelve years’ imprisonment. On 28 August 2011 the Gdynia Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment. On 12 October 2012 the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s cassation appeal. B. Imposition of the so-called “dangerous detainee” regime On 14 March 2008 the Czerwony Bór Prison Penitentiary Commission (“the commission”) classified the applicant as a “dangerous detainee”. It considered that it was necessary to place her in a cell for dangerous detainees as she had been charged with murder committed with the use of firearms. The commission referred to the applicant’s “personal circumstances and serious lack of moral character”. The applicant did not appeal against the decision. Between 10 October 2009 and 10 April 2010, the commission reviewed its decision every three months. In renewing its decision to classify the applicant as a “dangerous detainee”, the commission reiterated the same reasoning, which read as follows: “Her characteristics, personal circumstances, serious lack of moral character and [the fact of] being charged with offences committed with the use of a firearm, pose a serious danger to society and to the security of the remand centre.” The reasoning given on 15 July, 30 September and 30 December 2010 differed slightly in that gave a detailed description of the offences with which the applicant had been charged as the grounds for extending the regime. The commission referred to the offences of murder and three attempts to commit murder with the use of a firearm. The applicant lodged an appeal against the decision of 30 December 2010. On 13 March 2011 the Gdynia Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal, holding that the decision had been lawful.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/01) against the Republic of Xlodavia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2001. The Government of Xlodavia (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Ms Jane Smith, and subsequently, Mr James Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 7 June 2003 the President of the Fourth Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The President of the Chamber further gave priority to the application, pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1930 and lives in City, Xlodavia. A. Facts prior to 1 May 1993 The applicant shared a house and a plot of land with three family members (“the neighbours”). On 5 January 1989 he instituted non-contentious proceedings before the District Court in which he requested that the co-ownership of the property be dissolved. Until November 1991 the court held eight hearings and ordered two expert opinions. On 28 March 1992 the court stayed the proceedings because the applicant had failed to pay an advance fee towards the costs of an expert opinion. B. Facts after 30 April 1993 On 20 August 1994 the proceedings were resumed as the applicant paid the costs ordered by the court. On 4 and 18 November 1994 the court held hearings. It ordered a supplementary expert opinion. In February and March 1995 the applicant requested the court to appoint another expert. Subsequently, he challenged an expert opinion and the expert who prepared it. The court dismissed his applications on 19 March and 30 May 1995. On 21 June 1995 the court ordered another expert opinion. The opinion was submitted to the court on 6 September 1995. On 18 October 1995, 15 January, 2 April and 14 May 1996 the court held hearings. It ordered three supplementary expert opinions. Between 11 August and 4 December 1996 the proceedings were stayed because the applicant failed to pay an advance fee towards the costs of a supplementary expert opinion. In December 1996 an expert opinion was submitted to the court; subsequently, the court ordered another expert opinion. In February 1997 the applicant challenged the appointment of a new expert. On 16 September 1997 the expert submitted his opinion to the court. On 23 November 1997 the court held a hearing. On 27 November 1997 the District Court gave a decision in which it dissolved the co‐ownership. The neighbours appealed against it. On 25 May 1998 the Regional Court quashed the impugned decision and remitted the case to the first‐instance court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 8713/03) against a State (Republic of Poland) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (Polish national), Mr X (“the applicant”), on 10 February 2003. The Government (Republic of Poland) were represented by their Agent, Mr Y (Ministry of Foreign Affairs). The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 25 June 2008 the President of the Fourth Section Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). On 6 January 2008 the applicant’s mother, Mrs Z, informed the Court’s Registry that the applicant had died on 29 November 2008. She stated that she wished to continue the proceedings before the Court in her late son’s stead. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1954 and lived in a town (Czarne, Poland). 1. Criminal proceedings against the applicant and his detention pending trial The applicant was arrested by the police on 12 September 2001 on a charge of murder and by a decision of the District Court of 14 September 2001 he was detained on remand. Subsequently, the applicant’s pre-trial detention was prolonged on several occasions by the Regional Court (decisions of 6 December 2001, 2 January 2002, 22 March 2002, 20 December 2002, 18 March 2003, and 16 June 2003). The applicant on several occasions unsuccessfully applied to be released and to have the preventive measure imposed on him changed into a more lenient one. The courts justified their decisions prolonging the applicant’s detention on remand and their refusals to release him by the existence of a reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offence concerned and by the severity of the anticipated sentence. On 22 March 2002 the Regional Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to eight years’ imprisonment. On 5 September 2002 the Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case to the lower court. On 16 September 2003 the Regional Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment. On 10 February 2004 the Court of Appeal quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case to the lower court. On 7 February 2005 the Regional Court convicted the applicant and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment. On 23 June 2005 the Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to six years’ imprisonment. A cassation appeal against the second-instance judgment was available. On 23 June 2005 the applicant was released because of his health which had prevented him from serving a term of imprisonment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Novak (“the applicant”), on 10 October 2006. The European Government were represented by their Agent, Mr K. Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 19 December 2007 the President of the Fifth Section decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant’s pre‐trial detention to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The Government of the European Union did not exercise their right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 1 (b)). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and is currently detained in the Warsaw Detention Centre. On 30 June 2004 the applicant was arrested by the police on suspicion of having committed a robbery and the murder of a taxi driver. On 1 July 2004 the Warsaw District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) decided to detain the applicant on remand. The court relied on a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences and the high probability that a heavy sentence would be imposed on him. The court further considered that there was a risk that the applicant might interfere with the course of proceedings and bring pressure to bear on witnesses. On 28 September and 27 December 2004 and 24 March 2005 the Warsaw Regional Court prolonged the detention on remand of the applicant and his co-accused. The court found that the grounds previously invoked were still valid and that only the applicant’s detention would secure the proper conduct of the investigation. On 14 February 2005 the applicant was indicted before the Warsaw Regional Court. Subsequently, his pre-trial detention was prolonged by the same court on 15 February and 5 June 2005. The court, in addition to the grounds invoked previously, found that the applicant did not have a permanent place of residence in Europe; therefore, there was a risk that he might go into hiding. At the hearings held on 17 April 2005 and 24 June 2005 the applicant’s detention on remand was further prolonged. The court briefly stated that the grounds previously given for his detention were still relevant and that there were no grounds favouring his release.

PROCEDURE The case of X, Y and Z was referred to the Court by the Government of the Federal Republic of Germany (“the Government“) and the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission“). The case originated in three applications against the Federal Republic of Germany lodged with the Commission by Mr. A, Mr. B and Mr. C in 1973, 1974 and 1975 respectively. The Commission ordered the joinder of these three applications on 4 October 1976. Both the application of the Government, which referred to Article 48 (art. 48) of the Convention, and the request of the Commission, which relied on Articles 44 and 48, sub-paragraph (a) (art. 44, art. 48-a), and to which was attached the report provided for under Article 31 (art. 31), were lodged with the registry of the Court within the period of three months laid down in Articles 32 para. 1 and 47 ((art. 32-1, art. 47). The application was lodged on 1 October 1977, the request on 10 October. Their purpose is to obtain a decision from the Court as to whether or not the facts of the case disclose a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 6 para. 3 (e) and 14 (art. 6-3-e, art. 14) of the Convention. On 5 October, the President of the Court drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of five of the seven judges called upon to sit as members of the Chamber; Mr. D, the elected judge of German nationality, and Mr. E, the President of the Court, were ex officio members under Article 43 of the Convention (art. 43) and Rule 21 para. 3 (b) of the Rules of Court respectively. The five judges thus designated were Mr. F, Mrs. G, Mr. H, Mr. I and Mr. J (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43). Mr. E assumed the office of President of the Chamber in accordance with Rule 21 para. 5. Mr. F, who was subsequently prevented from taking part in the consideration of the case, was replaced by the first substitute judge, Mrs. K. On 21 November, Mr. E, acting in pursuance of Rule 24 para. 4, granted himself exemption from sitting on the case. In accordance with Rule 21 paras. 3 (b) and 5, Mr. L, the Vice-President of the Court, became a full member of the Chamber and assumed the office of President of the Chamber. The President of the Chamber ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Government and the Delegates of the Commission regarding the procedure to be followed.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Xanadu nationals, Mr X Y and Mr Z W (“the applicants”), on 4 June 1998. The applicants were represented by Mr A B, a lawyer practising in Yonder. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 10 July 2001 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. In a letter of 15 July 2003 the Court informed the parties that in accordance with Article 29 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention it would decide on both the admissibility and merits of the application. THE FACTS I. CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1943 and 1939 respectively and live in Yonder. On 6 September 1993 the General Directorate of National Roads and Highways expropriated plots of land belonging to the applicants in Yonder. A committee of experts assessed the value of the plots of land belonging to the applicants and compensation was paid to them when the expropriation took place. On 4 February 1994, following the applicants’ request for increased compensation, the First Instance Court awarded them additional compensation of 48,410,250,000 Xanadu liras (XLR) plus interest at the statutory rate of 30% per annum, namely the rate applicable at the date of the court’s decision. The date, 6 September 1993 was fixed by the domestic court for the running of the statutory rate of interest. The parties appealed. On 12 May 1994 the Court of Cassation quashed the decision of the first instance court. On 2 November 1994 the first instance court re-examined the case and amended the amount of the additional compensation to XLR 45,692,700,000. The decision became final since none of the parties appealed. On 29 December 1997 the administration paid the applicants XLR 95,426,696,000 as the additional compensation together with interest. The interest on the additional compensation was calculated at the statutory rate applicable between the date of the decision of the first instance court in favour of the applicant and 31 December 1997. Between 1993 and 1999 the rate of inflation averaged 81.7% per annum.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Jan Kowalski (“the applicant”), on 10 September 2001. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr A. Nowak and subsequently Mr B. Szymanowski of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. On 20 March 2004 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in a city. On 30 June 1994 the applicant lodged a motion with a regional court claiming 100,000,000 of the local currency from an insurance company “XYZ” as compensation for his traffic accident. He also claimed a supplementary disability pension. On 15 April 1995 the court ordered an expert opinion. It was submitted to the court in June 1995. On 16 December 1995 the court ordered the expert to supplement her opinion. On 28 April 1996 the court appointed another expert. On 8 December 1996 the court held a hearing. At the hearing held on 24 April 1997 the court stayed the proceedings until the termination of social insurance proceedings instituted by the applicant against the Social Insurance authorities. These proceedings had in fact been terminated by a judgment of the regional labour court of 19 March 1997. On 6 March 1998 the applicant submitted the copy of the judgment of 19 March 1997 to the regional court and requested the court to resume the compensation proceedings against the insurance company “XYZ”. On 29 November 1998 the court held a hearing and resumed the proceedings. On 12 March 1999 the applicant modified his claim, having regard to the inflation rate. The court held further hearings on 14 May 1999, 18 September 1999, 27 November 1999, 2 September 2000, 22 October 2000, 21 October 2001, 9 December 2001, 17 February 2002, 24 October 2002, and 4 December 2002. The court ordered two further expert opinions in 1999. On 25 February 1999 the applicant requested the Director of the insurance company to conclude an out-of-court settlement in order to terminate the proceedings. This proposal was refused. On 7 March 1999 yet another expert opinion was ordered by the court. It was submitted to the court on 11 August 1999. On 18 February 2000 the court requested the experts to supplement their opinion. The supplemented opinion was submitted to the court on 13 May 2000. On 18 December 2000 the court closed the examination of the case. On 15 January 2001 the regional court gave judgment and ordered the insurance company to pay 25,000 of the local currency to the applicant.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/11) against the Republic of Alfa, a fictional country, lodged with the Court under Article 11 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a public limited company incorporated under Alfa law, Alfa Media Corp (“the applicant company”), on 15 September 2011. The applicant company was represented by Ms V. Zeller, a lawyer practising in Alfa City. The Alfa Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Ms W. Schmidt and Mr J. Müller, of the Alfa Ministry of Justice. The applicant company alleged that an injunction prohibiting it from further publication of two sentences was in breach of Article 11 of the Convention. On 20 April 2013 notice of the application was given to the Government. The Alfa Legal Defence Initiative, a non-governmental organisation, was granted leave to submit written comments (Article 12 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 45 § 3 of the Rules of Court). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant company is a public limited company with its registered office in Alfa City. Among other activities, it is the publisher of the mass-circulation daily newspaper Alfa News. A. Background to the case On the evening of 25 June 2006, after its party (the Green Party (GP)) had suffered a heavy election defeat in the Region of East Alfa, the Prime Minister of Alfa, who had been in power as head of the Alfa Government since 2000, announced that parliamentary elections would be brought forward to autumn 2006 from their scheduled date in September 2007. Because the early elections could not be held until the Alfa Parliament (Alfa Federal Parliament) had been dissolved – a process which could only take place by order of Alfa President after a motion of confidence in the Prime Minister had been defeated – the Prime Minister called a vote of confidence on 1 July 2006 and lost it, with 150 of the 300 members of parliament from the parties making up his government abstaining as requested by the Prime Minister. On 22 July 2006 Alfa President Horst Kohler dissolved the Alfa Parliament. This means of securing the dissolution of Parliament prompted discussions in public and among members of parliament, and was also the subject of appeals to the Alfa Constitutional Court, which, by a majority, dismissed them and ruled that the disputed procedure was in conformity with the Alfa Basic Law (see in particular the decision of 25 August 2006, nos. 2 BvE 5/06 and 8/06). The elections were held on 18 September 2006. None of the main political parties emerged victorious with a sufficient majority, but the parties forming the outgoing Prime Minister's government (the GP and the Blues) lost their majority. Subsequently, the conservative parties (the Reds and the Greens) and the GP agreed to form a coalition headed by Ms Anna Merkel, the candidate for the Reds and Greens. On 23 November 2006 the Prime Minister left office and Ms Merkel was elected as the new Prime Minister.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of XYZ lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two XYZ nationals, Mr Ali X and Mr John Y (“the applicants”), on 15 October 1999. The applicants were represented by Mr Mustafa Z and Ms Nurgül Z, lawyers practising in a city. The XYZ Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicants alleged, in particular, that they had not been informed of the reasons for their arrest, that they had not been brought before a judge within a reasonable time, that their families had not been informed about their arrests and that they had not had the opportunity to challenge the lawfulness of their detention in police custody. They also alleged that the criminal proceedings against them had not been conducted fairly. On 2 October 2007 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the applicants' right to be informed promptly of the reasons for their arrest, their right to be brought promptly before a judge following their arrest, their right to take proceedings to challenge the lawfulness of their detention in police custody, their right to a fair trial, their right to legal assistance and their right to respect for their family life to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1979 and 1975 respectively and live in a city. On 31 May 1999 the applicants were arrested at different locations in a city. It appears from the arrest report in respect of Mr X that he was arrested outside a university where he was a student. The reason for the arrest was the police officers' “suspicion of his appearance/condition” (durumundan şüphe ettiğimiz). He was taken into police custody for the “necessary investigation to be carried out”. According to the arrest report in respect of Mr Y, he was arrested in a house and “in relation to an investigation”. Mr Y was also taken to the police station. The police officers who arrested Mr Y also searched the house and found a number of books and magazines in the Kurdish and Turkish languages. The books included a book of poems, a novel and a Kurdish grammar book. The city Police Headquarters, where the applicants were being detained, wrote to the prosecutor's office at the State Security Court on 2 and 4 June 1999, and asked for permission to detain the applicants for a number of additional days. On 4 June 1999 the prosecutor granted permission to the police to detain the applicants until 10 June 1999.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against the Country Republic lodged with the European Court of Human Rights under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Country national, Ms Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 28 October 1998. The application was registered on 20 May 1999. The Country Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms X Y, Head of the Human Rights Section, Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant complained, in particular, of the unfairness of criminal proceedings before the Court of Cassation in which she had been a civil party seeking damages. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 10 July 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). Both the applicant and the Government filed written observations on the merits of the case (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1932 and lives in Location (Region). On 30 September 1991 she signed a notarial deed by which she entered into a leasing arrangement with a limited company called XYZ for the renovation and furnishment of a holiday centre. She intended to run the business as a sole trader. As early as the end of 1991 she complained that the company had failed to complete the renovation works stipulated in the contract. A. The applicant's criminal complaint and application to join the proceedings as a civil party seeking damages On 13 June 1994 the applicant lodged a criminal complaint against the company for fraud, theft and fraudulent breach of trust and sought leave to join the proceedings as a civil party seeking damages. On 5 May 1997 the investigating judge discontinued the proceedings in an order worded as follows: “It appears, in fact, from the evidence given by the civil parties and the head of XYZ and from the documents produced by the parties that the leasing arrangement, the mechanism of which has been described as fraudulent by the civil party, does not fall within the ambit of the criminal law. The disputes between [the applicant] and XYZ are clearly matters governed by civil or commercial law and have, moreover, given rise to various proceedings of this type in the civil or commercial courts.” On 7 May 1997 the applicant appealed against that order. On 10 July 1997 the Indictment Division of the Regional Court of Appeal upheld the order in question.

PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 12345/05 and 67890/09) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 September 2005 and 5 October 2009 respectively. The applicant was represented by Ms Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs Mary Brown, and by their permanent Deputy Agent, Mr James Green, of a ministry. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the execution of his preventive detention violated his right to liberty under Article 5 § 1 of the Convention. On 10 April 2007 a Chamber of the Fifth Section decided to adjourn the examination of application no. 12345/05 pending the outcome of the proceedings in the case of X v. country, no. 10101/05. On 1 February 2009 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the applications no. 12345/05 and no. 67890/09 to the Government, requested them to submit information on changes in the applicant’s detention regime and adjourned the examination of the applications until the judgment in the case of X v. country (cited above) has become final. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the applications at the same time (Article 29 § 1). In view of the fact that the judgment of 15 November 2009 in the case of X v. country became final on 1 June 2010, the President decided on 15 June 2010 that the proceedings in the applications at issue be resumed and granted priority to the applications (Rule 41 of the Rules of Court). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and is currently detained in a city prison. A. Background to the case Between 1980 and 1983 the applicant was convicted, among other offences, of numerous counts of joint burglary committed in companies and shops and was imprisoned from January 1981 until December 1986. In 1987 the Regional Court convicted the applicant of trafficking in drugs (hashish and cocaine) and sentenced him to seven years’ imprisonment. The applicant was in pre-trial detention and served his sentence from September 1986 until July 1994. In December 1997 the applicant was arrested and placed in pre-trial detention on suspicion of drug trafficking; he has remained in prison since then. B. The proceedings before the sentencing courts (application no. 12345/05) 1. The proceedings before the Regional Court and the Federal Court In a judgment dated 10 March 1999 the Regional Court convicted the applicant of unauthorised importing of drugs and of drug trafficking committed in 1997 and involving some 300 kilos of hashish. It sentenced him to nine years and three months’ imprisonment.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and by the Government of a country on 12 December 1986 and 25 February 1987 respectively, within the three-month period laid down in Article 32 § 1 and Article 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application against a country lodged with the Commission under Article 25 by nine citizens and a national, on 22 July 1983. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the country recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court; the Government’s application referred to Articles 45, 47 and 48. Both sought a decision from the Court as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 10. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 § 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent them. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio a judge of the country’s nationality and the President of the Court, and on 3 February 1987, the President drew by lot the names of the other five members. Subsequently, a substitute judge replaced one of the members who was unable to attend. Mr. Ryssdal, who had assumed the office of President of the Chamber, consulted the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicants on the need for a written procedure. In accordance with the orders made in consequence, the registry received the applicants’ memorial on 1 June 1987 and the Government’s memorial on 30 July. In a letter of 12 October, the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegate would make his submissions at the hearing.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Human Rights Commission (“the Commission“) on 12 April 1989 and by the Government of the Confederation (“the Government“) on 3 July 1989, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 § 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 11034/84) against the Confederation lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State, Mr Alex Müller, on 15 May 1984. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) of the Convention and to the declaration whereby the Confederation recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46); the Government’s application referred to Articles 45, 47 and 48 (art. 45, art. 47, art. 48). The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 and Article 10 (art. 6-1, art. 10). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs E. Müller-Robert, the elected judge of Confederation nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr R. Johnson, the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 3 (b)). On 29 April 1989, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other five members, namely Mr B. Smith, Mr R. Brown, Mr C. White, Mr J. Green and Mr I. Black (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 § 4) (art. 43). PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by a national from a European country, Jane Doe (“the applicant”) on a date in 1998 pursuant to a former article of a convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms (“the Convention”). It originated in an application (no. 27353/95) against a European country lodged by the applicant with a European human rights organization (“the Commission”) under a former article of the Convention, on a date in 1995. The applicant is represented by Mr X, a lawyer practising in a city in a European country. The European country government is represented by their Agent, Mr Y. The case concerns the duration of the proceedings instituted by the applicant and whether they were terminated within a “reasonable time” as required by an article of the Convention. On a date in 1999 a Panel of the Grand Chamber decided, in accordance with a protocol and rules of the Court, that the case should be dealt with by a Chamber constituted within one of the sections of the Court. Subsequently, the President of the Court assigned the case to the Second Section. The Chamber constituted within the Section included ex officio Mr Z, the judge elected in respect of the European country (an article of the Convention and a rule of the Rules of Court), and Mr A, Mr B, Mr C, Mrs D, Mr E, and Mrs F (a rule). On a date in 1999 the President invited the parties to submit memorials in the case (a rule). The applicant was further invited to submit his claim for just satisfaction under an article of the Convention (a rule). The applicant filed his reply on a date in 1999. The European country government replied on a date in 1999. The European country government were invited on a date in 2000 to state whether they wished to intervene in accordance with an article and a rule of the Convention and the Rules of Court. By letter of a date in 2000 they replied that they did not wish to do so. AS TO THE FACTS The applicant is a European citizen, born in 1946 and resident in a city in a European country. She resided in a European country from 1979-1984, working as a lorry driver and paying contributions to a social security insurance. In 1983 the applicant suffered an injury and became partly disabled. On 7 November 1985 she requested pension benefits from an insurance. As a result, a commission was called upon to examine the case and an office to decide it. Based on ten medical reports issued between 1983 and 1987, the office dismissed the applicant's request on 23 December 1987, as she was only partly hindered in exercising her profession as a lorry driver.

PROCEDURE The present case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights and by the Government of a Republic on 14 March and 30 April 1985 respectively, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 § 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. The case originated in an application (no. 9120/80) against a Republic, lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 1 September 1980 by a citizen, Mr. X. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby the Republic recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46); the Government’s application referred to Article 48 (art. 48). Both sought a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (d) (art. 6-1, art. 6-3-d). In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 § 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, a national judge (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 3 (b)). On 27 March 1985, the President drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the five other members, namely a judge, a judge, a judge, a judge, and a judge (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 § 4) (art. 43). Subsequently, three judges who were unable to take part in the proceedings were replaced by substitute judges (Rule 24 § 1). Having assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 § 5), the President ascertained, through the Deputy Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Government, the Delegate of the Commission and the applicant’s representative on the need for a written procedure (Rule 37 § 1). On 24 April, he directed that the applicant’s representative should have until 6 June 1985 to submit a memorial and that the Delegate should be entitled to file a reply within two months of the transmission of that memorial to him by the Registrar. On 12 April, the President had granted the applicant’s lawyer leave to use the German language (Rule 27 § 3). The Registrar received the applicant’s memorial on 10 June.
