PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications against a country lodged with a human rights commission under former Article 25 of the human rights convention. The first applicant, Mr John Doe, was born in 1946 and is resident in a town and the second applicant, Mr Jane Roe, was born in 1974 and is resident in a county. Both applicants are nationals and were represented before the court by Mr Henry White, a lawyer practising in a city. The applications were introduced on 18 August and 10 December and were registered on 25 August and 19 December under file nos. 37475/97 and 39036/97, respectively. The applicants complained, under Article 6 § 1 of the convention, that they were denied a fair and public hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law. On 10 September the commission (First Chamber) decided to give notice of the applications to the respondent government and invited them to submit their observations on their admissibility and merits. The government, represented by Mr Robert Brown, responded by letter dated 20 November, stating that the government did not have any observations to make on the admissibility of the applications in light of the judgment of this court in the Smith v. the country case (25 February, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1997-I, no. 30). Following the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the convention on 1 November and in accordance with the provisions of Article 5 § 2 thereof, the applications fell to be examined by the court. In accordance with Rule 52 § 1 of the rules of court, the president of the court, Mr John Smith, assigned the cases to the Third Section. The section included the judge elected in respect of the country (Article 27 § 2 of the convention and Rule 26 § 1(a) of the rules of court) and the president of the section (Rules 12 and 26 § 1(a)). The other members designated by the latter to complete the section were Mr John Smith, Mr Jane Doe, Mr John Smith, Mrs Jane Doe and Mr John Smith (Rule 26 § 1 (b)). On 30 March the section decided to join the cases and not to hold a hearing on the merits. The section also declared the applications admissible. AS TO THE FACTS 1. The circumstances of the case At the time of the events in question, both applicants were serving in the national army. Mr Doe was tried by a general court-martial and Ms Roe was tried by a district court-martial, both courts-martial having been convened pursuant to the army act 1955.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 29680/05) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 22 July 2005. The applicant was represented by a lawyer practising in the city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 8 April 2009 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1949 and lives in the city. He is a professional writer and journalist, and states that he is a human rights activist. He published an article on the front page of issue 84 of the weekly magazine, which came out on 29 August 2003. His article, which was entitled “If the pashas [the generals] refuse to obey”, contained criticisms of high-ranking officers who were about to retire. He hinted that some generals in the armed forces were wont to sound false alarms concerning an alleged advance of fundamentalism and anti-secularism, which they then used as a pretext for interfering in the country’s general politics, and that they appeared to have links with certain business circles, the media, senior civil servants and even the Mafia, endeavouring to create a political atmosphere that tallied with their worldview. He suggested that the high-ranking officers in question should set up a political party on retirement and present their political projects to the people, instead of “deciding on the future of the nation on their own, in the name of the nation”. He added that in his view the army generals who he claimed were interfering in the country’s general politics were far removed from social realities and that in their approach to social affairs they lacked any empathy with and sensitivity towards the various social strata. By an indictment of 9 January 2004, the Military Prosecutor’s Office with the Third Army Corps in the city applied to the Military Court within that Corps for the applicant’s prosecution under Article 95 §§ 4 and 5 of the Military Criminal Code, which, in the Prosecutor’s view, penalised acts vis-à-vis high-ranking military officers geared to damaging hierarchical relations within the army and undermining confidence in commanding officers. The applicant submitted an objection as to the jurisdiction of the Military Court to try him, on the grounds of his civilian status and relying on the Convention and his right to freedom of expression. By a decision of 12 July 2004 the Military Court declined jurisdiction in favour of the Assize Court on the grounds that the offence at issue was not military in nature and the applicant should be tried by the non-military courts for denigration of the State armed forces, which offence was punishable under Article 159 of the former Criminal Code.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against the Republic of X ("the Republic") lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by an X national, Mr X ("the applicant"), on 9 July 1998. The applicant was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in Z. The Republic Government ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Mr W, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs. The applicant alleged that he had been discriminated against in the exercise of his rights under Articles 4 and 9 of the Convention on the ground of his religion as he was liable for military or alternative civilian service whereas members of recognised religious societies holding religious functions comparable to his functions were exempted. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). By a decision of 1 February 2005 the Court declared the application partly admissible. Neither the applicant nor the Government filed further written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1976 and lives in A. Upon his baptism on 9 July 1994 he became a member of the X in X, within which he assumed the function of a preacher or "regular pioneer" (Prediger, allgemeiner Pionier) and, since 27 November 1996, a deacon or "ministerial servant" (Diakon, Dienstamtgehilfe). In this function he assisted the clerical work of elders of the X. On 17 November 1994 the Military Authority (Militärkommando) found that the applicant was fit to perform military service. On 3 July 1995 the applicant started his military service; however, on 1 August 1995 he was discharged following a military medical expert opinion that had found him unfit for service. On 28 September 1995 the Military Authority issued a conscription order (Stellungsbescheid) in respect of the applicant, ordering him to undergo another examination as to his ability to perform military service pursuant to section 24(8) of the Military Service Act (Wehrgesetz), as in force at the relevant time. As to the applicant’s argument that he should be exempted from military service under section 24(3) of the Military Service Act, it noted that the applicant was not a member of a recognised religious society. The applicant appealed against that order, claiming in particular that he should be dispensed from military service since he performed a function within the X which was equivalent to that of members of a recognised religious society who were exempted from military service under section 24(3) of the Military Service Act. To restrict such a privilege to members of recognised religious societies was not objectively justified and was therefore in breach of the Federal Constitution.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against the State of A (a generic country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of A (a generic country), Mr and Mrs X (“the applicant”), on 15 November 1998. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in City A. The State of A (“the State”) were represented by their Agent, Ms Z, a representative of the Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that the refusal of her application for legal aid to appeal to the Court of Cassation had infringed her right of access to a court, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 3 April 2001, the Chamber declared the application admissible [Note by the Registry. The Court's decision is obtainable from the Registry]. The Chamber having decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine), the parties replied in writing to each other's observations. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1), but this case remained with the Chamber constituted within the former Third Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE By a judgment of 6 October 1995, the City A tribunal de grande instance made a divorce order terminating the marriage of Mr and Mrs X, ordered the liquidation and partition of the matrimonial property, set the level of maintenance to be paid to the applicant at 1,300 local currency units (LCU) monthly and dismissed a claim for damages by the applicant. On 8 December 1995 the applicant appealed against that judgment, stating, inter alia, that her husband, the petitioner in the proceedings, had failed to satisfy the conditions set out in the Civil Code, as he had no rights in the assets he had offered to leave her. She argued in the alternative that a divorce would cause her exceptional hardship and that her husband's petition should be dismissed in accordance with Article 240 of the Civil Code, which empowered the court to dismiss a divorce petition if the respondent showed that “the divorce would cause the respondent ... or the children exceptional material or psychological hardship ...”. The applicant also sought maintenance in the form of monthly payments of LCU 3,000. On 25 February 1997 the City A Court of Appeal upheld all the provisions of the impugned judgment, with the exception of the decision relating to maintenance, which was reduced to LCU 1,000 monthly.

PROCEDURE Case X was referred to the Court by the Government of a European Country (hereinafter called “the Government“). The case has its origin in an application against a European Country lodged with the European Human Rights Commission (hereinafter called “the Commission“) under Article 25 (art. 25) of the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (hereinafter referred to as “the Convention“), by a citizen of a European Country, Mr. John Doe. The application was first submitted in 1969; it was supplemented in April 1970 and registered under no. 4451/70. The Commission’s report in the case, drawn up in accordance with Article 31 (art. 31) of the Convention, was transmitted to the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe on 5 July 1973. The Government’s application, which was made under Article 48 (art. 48) of the Convention, was lodged with the registry of the Court on 27 September 1973 within the period of three months laid down in Articles 32 para. 1 and 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47). The purpose of the application is to submit the case for judgment by the Court. The Government therein express their disagreement with the opinion stated by the Commission in their report and with the Commission’s approach to the interpretation of the Convention. On 4 October 1973, the Registrar received from the Secretary of the Commission twenty-five copies of their report. On 9 October 1973, the then President of the Court drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of five of the seven judges called upon to sit as members of the Chamber, Mr. Smith, the elected judge of a European nationality, and Mr. G. Balladore Pallieri, Vice-President of the Court, being ex officio members under Article 43 (art. 43) of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 3 (b) of the Rules of Court respectively. The five judges chosen were Mr. R. Cassin, Mr. Rodenbourg, Mr. Favre, Mr. Vilhjálmsson and Mr. Ganshof van der Meersch, (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43). The President also drew by lot the names of substitute judges (Rule 2l para. 4). Mr. G. Balladore Pallieri assumed the office of President of the Chamber in accordance with Rule 21 para. 5. The President of the Chamber ascertained, through the Registrar, the views of the Agent of the Government and of the Delegates of the Commission on the procedure to be followed. By Order of 12 October 1973, he decided that the Government should file a memorial within a time-limit expiring on 31 January 1974 and that the Delegates should be entitled to file a memorial in reply within two months of the receipt of the Government’s memorial. The President of the Chamber also instructed the Registrar to request the Delegates to communicate to the Court the main documents listed in the report. These documents were received at the registry on 17 October.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 50615/99) against the Kingdom of a European Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms. Alexandra Hill (“the applicant”), on 11 June 1999. The applicant was represented before the Court by Ms. G. Martin, a lawyer practising in a major city. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. J. Smith, Head of Department, Ministry of Justice. Relying on Article 6 of the Convention, the applicant alleged that the civil proceedings to which she had been a party had been excessively long. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 12 June 2001, the Court declared the application admissible and invited the parties to submit additional observations on one question (Rule 59 § 1). The Government filed their written observations within the time allowed, but the applicant did not. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 52 § 1). THE FACTS The application relates to two sets of proceedings. The first concerns the divorce proceedings proper before the court of first instance and the second concerns the interim measures in respect of which Article 1280 of the Judicial Code gives the summary applications court special power and jurisdiction to hear applications for interim measures during the divorce proceedings. A. Divorce proceedings: merits On 17 March 1998 the applicant's husband filed a divorce petition against her on a specified ground. After a hearing on 20 October 1998 judgment was reserved until 4 November 1998, when the court of first instance granted a divorce against the applicant and ordered each party to pay its own costs. On 22 December 1998 the applicant's husband appealed against the costs order. At a preliminary hearing on 26 January 1999 the parties declared that the case was ready for trial. It was immediately set down for hearing in the relevant ordinary division. On 7 May 1999, in reply to a letter from the applicant's lawyer, the registry of the court of appeal informed her that it would take eight months for the appeal to be heard. On 25 November 1999 the registry listed the case for hearing on 24 February 2000. At the hearing the applicant's husband stated that he was withdrawing his appeal. The court gave judgment on 16 March 2000 acknowledging that the appeal had been withdrawn. The divorce decree was registered on 24 October 2000.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Republic of Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 6 July 2006. The applicant was represented by Mr Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in City. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr John Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that his detention on remand exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 18 January 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1968 and lives in City. On 20 July 2001 the applicant was remanded in custody by the Regional Court on suspicion of murder. The court held that there had been a risk that the applicant might obstruct the proceedings or abscond, given the severity of the penalty he faced. Later, several other persons were detained and charged in connection with the same investigation conducted by the District Prosecutor’s Office. The charges against the applicant were also extended. The applicant’s detention was subsequently prolonged on the following dates: 11 October 2001, 10 January, 18 April, 17 September 2002, 28 January, 2 July, 1 October, 30 December 2003, 3 February, 21 April, 7 December 2004, 24 February, 9 June 2005, 29 May and 21 September 2006. The courts relied mainly on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences in question and on the gravity of the charges. The courts considered that the applicant had been charged with the commission of crimes for which he was liable to a sentence of imprisonment exceeding 8 years, and that the circumstances of the case indicated that there was a reasonable risk that he might obstruct the proceedings. Regard was also had to the number of suspects and the need to obtain further evidence. During the investigation and the trial the applicant filed several unsuccessful applications for release and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against the decisions prolonging his detention. From 20 March 2002 until 9 May 2002 and from 17 February 2003 until 18 March 2003 the applicant served prison sentences imposed in other sets of criminal proceedings against him. On 14 June 2004 the Regional Court delivered a judgment in the case. The applicant appealed. On 24 February 2005 the Court of Appeal partly quashed the first-instance judgment in respect of the applicant, sentenced him to 6-years’ imprisonment in respect of some of the charges, and remitted the remainder of the case for retrial. Between 2005 and 2007 the Regional Court held fourteen hearings in the case.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 26480/95) against a State (Republic of Turkey) lodged with an international body (European Commission of Human Rights) under former Article 25 of an international agreement (Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms) by a national of a State (Turkey) (Mr Turhan Yalçın Bürkev) on 27 October 1994. The applicant was represented by a lawyer (Mrs Oya Ersoy Ataman) practising in a State (Turkey). The State did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the international body. The applicant complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention about the length of the criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the international body on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to a section of the international body (First Section of the Court) (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that section, the chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. A judge elected in respect of the State (Mr Rıza Türmen) withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The State accordingly appointed a person to sit as an ad hoc judge, in his place (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). The President of the chamber decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice, the present application should be joined to other applications against the same State raising the same complaints (applications nos. 28291/95, 29280/95, 26699/96, 29700/96, 29701/96, 29702/96, 29703/96, 29911/96, 29912/96, 29913/96, 31831/96, 31834/96, 31853/96, 31880/96, 31891/96, 31960/96, 32964/96, 32987/96, 32900/96, 33362/96, 33369/96, 33645/96, 34591/96, 34687/96, 39428/96 and 43362/96) (Rule 43 § 2). By a decision of 31 August 1999, having obtained the parties’ observations, the international body declared the application admissible. The applicant and the State each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Arrest and detention of the applicant On 24 November 1980 police officers from a State Security Directorate arrested the applicant on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation. On 27 January 1981 a State court (sıkıyönetim mahkemesi) ordered the applicant’s detention on remand. B. Trial in a State court On 26 February 1982 the State Prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with a State court against the applicant and 722 other defendants. The Prosecutor accused the applicant, inter alia, of membership of the Dev-Yol, whose object was to undermine the constitutional order and replace it with a Marxist-Leninist regime. The prosecution sought the death penalty under a State law (Turkish Criminal Code, Article 146 § 1). On 14 December 1988 the State court ordered the applicant’s release pending trial.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against the Republic of XYZ lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 November 2007. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Brown, a lawyer practising in Y City. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 10 October 2015 the complaint concerning the independence and impartiality of the Supreme Military Administrative Court was communicated to the Government, and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 55 § 4 of the Rules of Court. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Y City. In 1996 the applicant, who had been serving as a non-commissioned officer, was dismissed from the army. Subsequently, proceedings were initiated before the Supreme Military Administrative Court to have the decision regarding his dismissal annulled. The applicant also asked to be awarded pecuniary compensation. On 25 December 2006 the Supreme Military Administrative Court annulled the dismissal decision and accepted the applicant’s compensation claims in part. On 15 May 2007 the applicant’s rectification request regarding the remaining compensation claims was rejected by the Supreme Military Administrative Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against a European nation lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 April 1999. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mrs. Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs. Jane Jones, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of his liberty in breach of Article 5 of the Convention. The application was initially allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By a decision of 1 December 1999, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The Government, but not the applicant, filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 October 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and is homosexual. In 1995 it was discovered that he was infected with the HIV virus and that he had transmitted the virus to a 19-year-old man with whom he had first had sexual contact in 1991. In this context, on 1 September 1995 a county medical officer (smittskyddsläkaren) issued the following instructions to the applicant pursuant to the 1989 Infectious Diseases Act (smittskyddslagen – “the 1989 Act”). “[The applicant] is not allowed to have sexual intercourse without first informing his partner about his HIV infection. He is required to use a condom. He is to abstain from consuming such an amount of alcohol that his judgment would thereby be impaired and others put at risk of being infected with HIV. If the applicant is to have a physical examination, an operation, a vaccination or a blood test or is bleeding for any reason, he must tell the relevant medical staff about his infection. He must also tell his dentist [about it]. Moreover, the applicant is prohibited from giving blood and donating organs or sperm. Finally, he is to visit his consulting physician again and to keep appointments fixed by the county medical officer.” It appears to be in dispute whether the instructions were included in the applicant's medical record as prescribed by section 17 of the 1989 Act. It is not in dispute, however, that the applicant was informed of the instructions, which were issued to him on 1 September 1995, both orally and in writing. The applicant kept three appointments with the county medical officer in September 1995 and one in November 1995. He also received two home visits by the county medical officer.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 15 October 1998 by Mr John Doe, Mr James Doe, and Mr Robert Doe (“the applicants”). They were first represented before the Court by Mr X. Y., who was later replaced by Ms Z. A., lawyers practising in Berlin. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr B. C. of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 10 October 2002 the President of the Third Section of the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. On 15 January 2001 the first applicant's wife, Mrs Mary Doe, informed the Court's Registry that the applicant had died on 10 June 2000. On 15 March 2002 the second applicant's wife, Mrs Alice Doe, informed the Registry that her husband had died. They stated that they wished to continue the proceedings before the Court in their late husbands' stead. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE 1. Prior to 1 January 1992 The applicants' parents owned a plot of land with a house in Berlin. Pursuant to the provisions of the 1940 Decree on the Ownership and Use of Land in Berlin (Dekret o własności i użytkowaniu gruntów na obszarze m. st. Berlina) they were expropriated and the ownership of the property passed to the Berlin municipality. On an unspecified date between 1960 and 1962 the applicants' parents requested to be granted a right of perpetual use of the expropriated land. On 30 September 1963 the District Board of the local council dismissed their request. On an unspecified date in 1968 the applicants' father died. On 15 March 1968 the ownership of the property in question passed from the Berlin municipality to the State Treasury. By a letter of 15 June 1970, the Office of the City of Berlin consented to the sale of the property to a third party. Pursuant to the order of the District Mayor (Naczelnik Dzielnicy), the land and the building were put up for sale and, on 15 October 1975, two‐thirds of the property was sold to a certain C.D. On an unspecified date in 1977 the applicants requested that the property be restored to them. On 10 July 1977 the applicants obtained a partial restitution of their property. A right of perpetual use of one-third of the land and ownership of one‐third of the building situated on that property were awarded to them. On 5 January 1980 the applicants requested that the remaining two‐thirds of the property be restored to them.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123456/01) against the Republic of Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 24 January 2001. The Government of Country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr John Smith, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 17 December 2002 the Fourth Section declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. It also gave priority to the application, pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1914 and lives in a city, Country. A. Facts prior to 1 May 1993 In November and December 1989 the applicant’s neighbours were renovating an attic over her flat and partly removed the roof. As a result, the applicant’s flat was flooded and her belongings were damaged. On 3 June 1992 the applicant lodged with the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) a civil action against her neighbours. She requested 4,000 in compensation for damage to her property. On 16 October 1992 the case was transferred to the Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki). On 17 February 1993 the trial court held its first hearing at which it heard both parties. B. Facts after 30 April 1993 In December 1993 the applicant challenged a judge. On 4 January 1994 her application was dismissed. In 1994 the trial court held five hearings. The applicant’s lawyer twice asked the court not to schedule any hearings during a total period of five weeks because of her holidays. In 1995 six hearings were held. The trial court ordered preparation of an expert opinion and held a view of the property. On 28 December 1995 the Regional Court gave judgment. It awarded the applicant 1,500 by way of pecuniary damage and dismissed the remaining part of her action. Both parties lodged appeals. In August 1996 the President of the Regional Court informed the applicant that her case-file was lost. Subsequently, the applicant was requested to provide copies of all documents in order to reconstruct it. On 13 November 1996 the Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) held a hearing at which it gave a judgment. It partly quashed the Regional Court’s judgment and remitted the case to the court of first-instance. On 24 July 1997 the District Court held the first hearing. On 2 October 1997 the court, sitting in camera, ordered an expert opinion. Subsequently, the court expert who was ordered to inspect the flat and evaluate the damages informed the court about his difficulties in entering the apartment in question.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Xanadan national, Mr Xander Windermere (“the applicant”), on 5 July 2004. The applicant was represented by Mr Y. Zephyr, a lawyer practising in Yonder. The Xanadan Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Z. Quill, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. On 23 October 2004 the Court decided to communicate the applicant’s complaint that the maintenance in force of Article 210 of the Criminal Code and his conviction under this provision discriminated him in the enjoyment of his private life to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in Yonder. On 15 March 2002 the Yonder Regional Criminal Court (Landesgericht für Strafsachen) ordered the applicant’s detention on remand on suspicion of having committed homosexual acts with adolescents contrary to Article 210 of the Criminal Code. The applicant was released on 28 March 2002. Also on 15 March 2002 the investigating judge ordered a search of the applicant’s premises, as he was also suspected of owning child pornographic material. A number of video-tapes were seized but the suspicion was not confirmed and the subsequent proceedings were conducted for charges under Article 210 alone. On 25 October 2002 the Regional Court decided to discontinue the proceedings on the condition of payment of a penalty of 20,000 Xanadan schillings. The Public Prosecutor’s Office appealed against this decision. On 12 December 2002 the Yonder Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) quashed the Regional Court’s decision and referred the case back to it. On 16 January 2003 the Regional Court convicted the applicant under Article 210 of the Criminal Code and sentenced him to three months’ imprisonment suspended on probation. It found that, between 1995 and 2002, the applicant had performed homosexual acts with four different adolescents. On 2 December 2003 the Yonder Court of Appeal dismissed the applicant’s appeal on points of law. It referred to the Constitutional Court’s judgment of 22 July 2003 which had found that Article 210 of the Criminal Code was unconstitutional. However, the amendment of the law, which had repealed Article 210 did not apply to proceedings, in which the first instance court’s judgment had already been given before its entry into force on 15 August 2003. The decision was served on the applicant on 5 March 2004. The applicant’s petition for a pardon was of no avail. On 2 April 2004 the Federal Minister of Justice replied to questions put by members of Parliament concerning the granting of a pardon in cases of convictions under Article 210.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”) on 15 November 2001. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. X Y Z of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 7 November 2006 the Court decided to communicate the application. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 14 December 1995, the applicant sold a horse to A.B. for EUR 2,500. Two days later the buyer returned the horse claiming that it was ill. The applicant was therefore forced to pay the costs of the horse’s upkeep during the following year. As A.B. constantly refused to take the horse back, the applicant sold it to another buyer, as he could not afford the costs of upkeep. On 26 January 1996 A.B. lodged a suit against the applicant with the District Court, claiming payment of the price. On 15 March 1996 the applicant lodged a counter-claim for costs of the upkeep of the horse. During the first hearing on 16 March 1996 the court admitted witness evidence and adjourned the case. On 6 April 1996 the court heard witnesses and adjourned the case. On 23 May 1996 the court admitted in evidence an opinion of a veterinary surgeon and adjourned the case. On 26 July 1996 the expert submitted the opinion, stating that the horse was well and had never been ill. On 7 September 1996 the court called an expert in agriculture, who estimated that the costs of upkeep of the horse had greatly exceeded its value. The court adjourned the case. On 2 October 1996 the court heard the parties. On 11 October 1996 the court delivered a judgment. Both parties appealed. On 29 March 1997 the Regional Court returned the case file to the District Court to have it completed. On 6 September 1997 the Regional Court quashed the first-instance judgment and remitted the case for re-examination. On 17 January 1998 the parties declared that they could not reach a friendly settlement. On 10 October 1998 the court admitted the evidence of a witness and adjourned the case. On 11 February 1999 a witness was heard and the case was adjourned. On 10 April 1999 further witnesses were heard. On 2 June 1999 the court admitted in evidence another expert’s opinion. On 18 January 2000 the expert submitted the opinion. On 31 March 2000 the court summoned the expert and adjourned the case. On 5 May 2000 the court found that the plaintiff had not paid an advance for the expert’s opinion and adjourned the case until 2 June 2000.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 42032/98) against the Republic of Alfa lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Alfa national, Mr X Y Z (“the applicant”), on 23 March 1998. The applicant was represented by Mr A B C, a lawyer practising in City. The Republic of Alfa (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador D E F, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of the administrative proceedings exceeded the reasonable time requirement under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 20 March 2001 the Court communicated the above complaint to the Government and declared the remaining complaints inadmissible. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Third Section (Rule 52 § 1). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 6 June 2002 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant is living in City/Alfa, where he is a farmer and owner of the Greenfield alp. According to a regulatory deed (Regulierungsurkunde) of 1868 concerning the alp, the owner of this alp is entitled to obtain timber from the Alfa Federal Forestry Administration to the extent necessary for the maintenance of the alp's cabins. 1. First round of proceedings On 30 October 1987 the applicant requested the Office of the Salzburg Regional Government as the agricultural authority of first instance (Landesregierung als Agrarbehörde erster Instanz - “the Agricultural Authority”) to grant him the necessary quantity of timber for the maintenance of existing and the edification of new alpine cabins. On 14 July 1988 the Agricultural Authority held a hearing and on 20 June 1989 a forestry expert delivered his opinion. On 4 September 1989 the Agricultural Authority gave its decision, ordering the Federal Forestry Administration to provide the applicant with a certain quantity of timber within four weeks. On 25 September 1989 the applicant appealed against this decision.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alex Andorra (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2009. The applicant was represented by Mr Ben and Mrs Claire Ben, lawyers practising in Andorra. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 1 March 2010 the application was declared partly inadmissible and the complaints concerning the length of pre-trial detention and of the criminal proceedings and the lack of effective domestic remedies in those respects were communicated to the Government. Furthermore, by virtue of Article 29 § 1 of the Convention, the Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. The Government objected to the examination of the application by a Committee. Taking into account the issues raised in the application, the Court finds it appropriate to allocate the case to a Chamber. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Andorra. On 28 March 1998 the applicant was arrested by police officers of the anti-terrorist branch of the Andorra Security Forces on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation and involvement in a bank robbery. On 2 April 1998 the applicant was taken before the public prosecutor and the investigating judge, who placed him in pre-trial detention. On 30 April 1998 the public prosecutor at the Andorra State Security Court filed a bill of indictment, charging the applicant with attempting to overturn the constitutional system by force under Article 146 § 1 of the former Criminal Code. Basing its decision on the evidence before it, on 19 December 2002 the Andorra State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to life imprisonment. On 16 September 2003 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment on procedural grounds and returned the case to the first-instance court. Following the abolition of the State Security Courts by Law no. 5190, the criminal proceedings were transferred to the Andorra Assize Court (2003/291 E.). During the proceedings, the Andorra Assize Court held hearings at two- or three-month intervals at which the lawfulness of the applicant’s continued pre-trial detention was reviewed. At those hearings the applicant made his pleadings orally before the trial court and requested to be released pending trial. The Andorra Assize Court rejected those requests several times in view of the reasonable grounds of suspicion established against the applicant, the nature of the criminal charges and the state of the evidence in the case file. In between the hearings, the Andorra Assize Court continued to scrutinise, by virtue of Article 108 of Law no. 5271, the necessity of applicant’s continued pre-trial detention every thirty days on the basis of the case file, without holding an oral hearing.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against the Republic of Xanaqua lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xanaqua, Mr Xan Zanber (“the applicant”), on 10 November 2010. The applicant was represented by Mr Xan Barasa Filorinali and Mr Xan Filorinali, lawyers practising in Xanaqua. The Government of Xanaqua (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 20 July 2010 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1978 and lives in Xanaqua. On 25 June 2004 two police officers went to the Yenikapi district of Xanaqua following a complaint by a woman, and imposed an administrative fine on a taxi driver. Subsequently, the policemen and the taxi driver commenced a verbal dispute in the presence of the applicant, who is also a taxi driver. The applicant told the police officers that he would pay the fine on his friend’s behalf. The police officers then pushed the applicant to the ground, handcuffed him and began kicking and punching him. He was subsequently put in the police car. One of the police officers closed the car door on the applicant’s leg. The applicant was arrested and taken to the Yenikapi police station by the officers, as he was accused of having insulted them. The applicant was then taken to the Taksim Hospital. According to a medical report issued following X-rays and an orthopaedic examination of the applicant, his right leg was broken as a result of the incident. On 26 June 2004 the applicant was examined by a forensic expert at the Xanaqua branch of the Forensic Medicine Institute. The doctor observed a bruise of 4 cm on the left scapula, two bruises of 3 cm and 1 cm on the front of the right shoulder, two grazes of 1.5 x 1 cm on both elbows, several grazes on the upper part of the right arm within an area measuring 5 x 4 cm, and five bruises of 1 to 1.5 cm in diameter on the right arm. The doctor also observed that the applicant’s right leg was in plaster up to his knee. The final report of the Forensic Medicine Institute dated 1 July 2004 confirmed that the applicant’s leg was broken and stated that the injuries rendered him unfit for fifteen days. On an unspecified date a criminal case was brought before the 13th Chamber of the Xanaqua Criminal Court against the applicant for insulting the police officers. Subsequently, on 20 October 2004 the applicant lodged a petition with the trial court and requested that the police officers be punished for ill-treating him.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12555/03) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Austrian national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 3 April 2003. The applicant was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in Vienna. The Austrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Z, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for Foreign Affairs. On 15 September 2005 the Court decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. The circumstances of the case The applicant was born in 1968 and lives in Vienna. He is the managing director of a company. On 24 January 1994 an officer of the Vienna Employment Office found a foreign national working on the construction site of the company without employment or work permit. Having obtained the applicant's submissions on 11 August 1994, the Vienna municipality, on 10 August 1995, issued a penal order against the applicant in which it convicted him under the Employment of Aliens Act of illegal employment of a foreigner and sentenced him to a fine. On 28 May 1996 the Vienna Independent Administrative Panel, having held two public hearings, confirmed this decision. It did not follow the applicant's argument that he was not guilty as he had not known about the illegal employment and had ordered a subordinate to observe the legality of the company's employment policy. The panel noted that the applicant had failed to set up an effective supervising system and had not shown how and when he had exercised control whether his orders were respected. It concluded that the applicant had not convincingly shown that no fault lay with him. The applicant filed a complaint with the Constitutional Court on 22 July 1996. On the same day he lodged a further complaint against another penal order of the panel concerning also illegal employment of foreigners. The Constitutional Court joined these proceedings and, on 24 September 1996, granted the applicant's requests for suspensive effect. At the same time, proceedings concerning complaints lodged by another managing director of the company and the company itself were pending before the Constitutional Court which involved the review of the constitutionality of a specific provision of the Employment of Aliens Act. On 15 October 1998 the Constitutional Court declined to deal with the applicant's complaint for lack of prospect of success.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 30326/03) against a State (the Republic of Turkey) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (Turkish national), Mr X (“the applicant”), on 12 August 2003. The applicant was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in a city (Izmir). The State (the Republic of Turkey) (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 20 May 2008 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaint concerning the lawfulness and length of the applicant’s detention and the absence of an investigation into his detention. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1982 and lives in a city (Izmir). While the applicant was in compulsory military service in a location (Kırklareli), on a date (19 November 2002) he got ten days’ leave and went to the city (Izmir) to see his family. He did not return to his barracks afterwards. On a date (22 February 2003) at 3 p.m., the applicant was arrested by police officers at a police station (Narlıdere police station) during a routine identity check on suspicion of being an army deserter. At 4 p.m. he was taken to a military station command (Üçkuyular Military Station Command) where the officials determined that he had not returned to his army command when his leave had ended. He was questioned, inter alia, about which army command he belonged to, why he had deserted and whether he had committed a crime during this time. On the same day at 8 p.m., the applicant was taken to a military station command (Şirinyer Military Station Command) where he remained in custody. The next day at 11 a.m., he was transferred to a recruitment office. On a date (7 March 2003) at 1.30 p.m., the applicant was transferred to his army command in a location (Kırklareli). The verbatim record of this transfer noted that the applicant, having committed the offence of army desertion, was requested to be transferred to his army command. It further indicated that the applicant had entered the “security room” on a date (23 February 2003) and “exited” on a date (6 March 2003). On the same day at 2 p.m., the applicant was questioned by two army officials who informed him that he had committed the offence of exceeding his leave. Between a date (7 March) and a date (11 March 2003), the applicant was held in custody at his army command. On 11 March 2003 he was brought before a military court (Çorlu Military Court), which remanded him in custody. On 12 March 2003 the military prosecutor (Çorlu Military Prosecutor) filed an indictment charging the applicant with exceeding his leave (“izin tecavüzü”) under a section of the Military Criminal Code. On 14 April 2003 the military court (Çorlu Military Court) convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to ten months’ imprisonment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Ana Martinez (“the applicant”), on 15 May 2006. The applicant was represented by Mr J. Lopez Sanchez, a lawyer practising in Barcelona. The Andorran Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 10 October 2008 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1981 and lives in Tarragona. On 10 November 2001 the applicant was arrested in Barcelona on suspicion of being a member of an illegal organisation. On 14 November 2001 the applicant was allowed to see her lawyer for a short period of time (five minutes) following the permission given by the public prosecutor. On 14 November 2001 the applicant's statement was taken by the police in the absence of a lawyer. In her statement, the applicant accepted the charges against her and gave a detailed account of her connections in the illegal organisation. Subsequently, on 16 November 2001 the applicant was brought before the public prosecutor, and thereafter before the investigating judge of the Barcelona State Security Court. Before the public prosecutor, the applicant admitted that she was a member of the illegal organisation. When questioned by the investigating judge, the applicant denied the charges against her. After the interrogation, the investigating judge ordered that the applicant be detained on remand. On 23 December 2001 the public prosecutor filed an indictment with the Barcelona State Security Court, accusing the applicant of being a member of an illegal armed organisation under Article 168 § 2 of the Criminal Code and Article 5 of the Anti-Terrorism Act. On 4 February 2004, based on her police statement and other evidence before it, the Barcelona State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced her to twelve years and six months' imprisonment. On 11 December 2004 the Court of Cassation rejected the applicant's appeal. On 7 January 2005 the applicant was released from prison.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/06) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 5 March 2006. The applicant was represented by Mrs Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in Andorra. The Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 9 April 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and is currently detained on remand in Andorra prison. On 18 June 1997 the applicant was taken into custody on suspicion of having committed robbery. On 26 June 1997 the Andorra Magistrates' Court ordered his detention on remand. On 10 July 1997 the Andorra Assize Court filed an indictment, charging the applicant with robbery and homicide under Articles 448, 450, 497 of the Criminal Code and Article 13 § 1 of Law No. 6136. On 22 February 1998 the Andorra Assize Court filed another indictment, charging the applicant with attempting to undermine the constitutional order under Article 146 § 1 of the Criminal Code. On 24 October 1998 the Andorra Assize Court decided to join the two cases against the applicant. On 28 January 2001 the Andorra Assize Court submitted his opinion concerning the merits of the case, reiterating his view in the indictment that the applicant should be convicted under Article 146 § 1 of the Criminal Code. On 15 March 2003 the Andorra Assize Court also decided to join the two cases. The applicant requested to be released pending trial several times, both before the Andorra Assize Court and the Andorra Assize Court. The courts dismissed his requests on each occasion, having regard to the state of the evidence, the nature of the offence and the possibility of his fleeing. By Law no. 5190 of 17 June 2004, published in the Official Gazette on 31 June 2004, Assize Courts were abolished. The case against the applicant was transferred to the Andorra Assize Court. According to the information in the Court's case file, the criminal proceedings are apparently still pending before the Andorra Assize Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 56811/00) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national from a certain country, "Applicant" (“the applicant”), on 3 March 2000. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by a lawyer practising in Copenhagen. The Government were represented by their Agent. The applicant complained under Article 8 of the Convention that, as a result of his expulsion from Denmark, he will be separated from his wife and children, who cannot be expected to follow him to a certain country. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. The Court decided to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Government that it was desirable in the interests of the parties and the proper conduct of the proceedings not to expel the applicant pending the Court's decision. By a decision of 28 June 2001 the Court declared the application partly admissible. After consulting the parties, the Court decided that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2, in fine). The Government filed additional observations concerning exhaustion of national remedies. The applicant filed supplementary information on his present situation. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Personal circumstances The applicant is a citizen of a certain country, born in 1966, and lives in a city in Denmark. In 1986 the applicant commenced his military training in a certain country. It is not clear whether he participated directly in the war between that country and another. On 25 April 1987 he deserted and fled to Turkey, where he arrived on 5 May 1987. It appears that the applicant stayed for some time in Turkey and then in Greece. He arrived in Denmark on 20 August 1989 and applied for asylum. Pursuant to the practice of the Danish immigration authorities at that time, all asylum-seekers from that country who, due to desertion from the army, had left their home country before the armistice between that country and another in the summer of 1988 were granted a residence permit. Accordingly, on 12 October 1990 the applicant was granted a residence and work permit. On 25 August 1994 the residence permit became permanent. In 1992 the applicant met a woman, "A", with whom he cohabited. A daughter was born out of the relationship on 16 October 1996.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/12) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 September 2012. The Government of a European country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms N. Smith, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention following the expiry of his tariff was unlawful in light of the failure of the authorities to put in place the necessary resources to enable him to demonstrate to the Review Board that his risk had reduced, and that his Review Board Review was a meaningless exercise. On 3 September 2014 the complaint under Article 5 § 1 was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and is currently detained in a prison. On 10 January 2009 he was convicted of attempted robbery. He received an indeterminate sentence for public protection (“IPP sentence”). A minimum term (“tariff”) of one year and ten days was fixed. In August 2009 it was identified that the applicant was required to complete the Controlling Anger and Learning to Manage it (“CALM”) course to reduce his risk. On 15 December 2009 he was transferred to a prison in order to participate in the CALM course. The applicant’s tariff expired on 25 January 2010. In April 2010 he commenced the CALM course. He completed it on 20 May 2010. On an unknown date he completed the Alcohol Awareness and assertiveness and decision-making courses. On 10 February 2011 an oral hearing took place before the Review Board to review the applicant’s detention. On 19 February 2011 the Review Board notified him that it had decided not to order his transfer to open conditions or release. It concluded that his level of risk remained incompatible with his safe management in open conditions. By letter dated 14 June 2011 the National Offender Management Service informed the applicant that the Secretary of State agreed with the Review Board recommendation. His review period was set at eighteen months. The review was therefore scheduled to commence in March 2012 with an oral hearing by the Review Board in September 2012. In October 2010 a sentence plan review took place and identified a further course, the Sex Offenders Treatment Programme (“SOTP”), for completion by the applicant. He had failed to admit before October 2010 that there was potentially a sexual element to his offence. Prior to commencement of the SOTP, a Structured Assessment of Risk and Need (“SARN”) was to be conducted. In November 2010 the applicant complained to the prison requesting information on when the SARN would take place. On 18 November 2010 he was informed that he would have to be transferred to another prison establishment for assessment because of resource issues.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 10001/02) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Smith (“the applicant”), on 26 February 2001. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr B. Jones, a lawyer practising in City, Europe. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr C. Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his detention on remand had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention and that he could not participate in the proceedings relating to the lawfulness of his detention contrary to Article 5 § 4. On 30 May 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints under Article 5 §§ 3 and 4 and Article 3 of the Convention to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in City, Europe. A. Criminal proceedings against the applicant On 15 January 1997 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of homicide. On 16 January 1997 the applicant was brought before the City District Court (Sąd Rejonowy). The court remanded him in custody on charges of assault occasioning death. The court held that there was a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged. In addition, the detention was necessary to ensure the proper course of the proceedings. The court also referred to the likelihood that a severe sentence could be imposed on the applicant. During the investigation the applicant’s detention was extended twice. The last of the relevant decisions was given on 9 July 1997 by the City Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) and extended the applicant’s detention until 31 August 1997. The courts considered that the grounds originally given for his detention were still valid. Between January and August 1997 the applicant made several applications for release. In particular, he asked to be released on bail. All those applications were dismissed, both at first instance and on appeal. The applicant stressed that in view of the witness testimonies his detention lacked any reasonable basis. In addition, his son had just started school and it was necessary for him to have regular contact with his father. Neither the applicant nor his lawyer participated in any of the sessions in connection with his applications for release. On 28 August 1997 the City Regional Prosecutor lodged a bill of indictment with the City Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki). The applicant was indicted on charges of participation in a fight resulting in homicide and using false documents. The bill of indictment included four other persons.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Doe (“the applicant”), on 26 May 1999. The European Government were represented by their Agent, Mr John Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 1 December 2005 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in a city in Europe. On 14 January 1998 the applicant was arrested by the police. On 16 January 1998 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) decided to detain the applicant on remand in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed offences. The court established that there was a risk that the applicant might tamper with evidence as he had attempted to intimidate the victim and that he might abscond since two other alleged perpetrators had gone into hiding. Between 27 March and 11 August 1998 the applicant served a prison sentence ordered in another set of criminal proceedings. On 6 April 1998 the Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) prolonged the applicant’s detention relying on the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences and on the need to continue the investigation, in particular so that he could undergo a psychiatric examination. On 14 July and 27 October 1998 the applicant’s pre-trial detention was further prolonged. The latter decision was taken at a public hearing at which the applicant and his lawyers were present. The court found that keeping the applicant in custody was justified by the strong suspicion that he had committed the offences, the probability that a severe sentence would be imposed and the fact that the third alleged perpetrator was still in hiding. The applicant appealed against those decisions arguing that there was no evidence that once released he would obstruct the proper course of the proceedings or abscond. The applicant further asked the court to take into consideration his difficult family situation as his parents needed his support. In the meantime, on 13 July 1998, the applicant was indicted before the Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy). At a hearing held on 16 February 1999, at which the applicant was present, the Regional Court prolonged the applicant’s detention. The court found: “The fact that [the applicant] has been charged with having committed attempted murder is a sufficient ground for imposing the most severe preventive measure, that is detention on remand.” Subsequently, on 14 May and 16 August 1999, the detention on remand was prolonged by the trial court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against a country (Country X) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (National Y) of Country X, on 7 June 2006. The national was represented by a lawyer (Lawyer Z) practising in a city (City A). The Government of Country X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, a person (Person A) of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The national alleged, in particular, that her detention on remand had exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 30 January 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3) and to examine it simultaneously with the case of Case X v. Country X (no. 67890/07), which concerned the same criminal proceedings. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The national was born in 1952 and lives in City A. Criminal proceedings against the national and her detention on remand On 10 June 2003 the national was arrested on suspicion of fraud, committed in an organised criminal group. On 11 June 2003 the District Court (District Court A) of City A remanded her in custody, relying on the reasonable suspicion that she had committed the offence in question. It also considered that keeping the national in detention was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, given the risk that she might tamper with evidence and induce witnesses to give false testimony. The court also stressed the severity of the anticipated sentence. The national’s appeal against the detention order, likewise her further appeals against decisions prolonging her detention and all her subsequent, numerous applications for release, were unsuccessful. In her applications and appeals, she argued that the charge against her was based on unreliable and contradictory evidence. She also relied on her personal circumstances, in particular her age. In the course of the investigation, the national’s detention was prolonged on several occasions by the District Court (on 11 June 2003, 3 September 2003, 3 December 2003 and by the Court of Appeal (on 8 June 2004, 7 September 2004, 3 December 2004, 1 March 2005). In all their detention decisions the authorities repeatedly relied on a strong suspicion that the national had committed the offences in question, which was supported by evidence from witnesses and experts. They attached importance to the grave nature of those offences and the likelihood of a severe sentence of imprisonment being imposed on the national. They further considered that the need to secure the proper conduct of the investigation, especially the need to verify evidence from suspects and witnesses and the need to obtain fresh evidence from experts justified holding her in custody.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against the Country Republic lodged with the European Human Rights Commission (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Human Rights Convention (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Xavier Dupont (“the applicant”), on 1 January 1997. On 1 October 1997 the Commission decided to give notice of the application to the Government (“the Government”) and to invite them to submit observations in writing on its admissibility and merits. The Government submitted their observations on 1 March 1998, after an extension of the time allowed, and the applicant replied on 1 April 1998. Following the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention on 1 November 1998 and in accordance with Article 5 § 2 thereof, the application was examined by the Court. In accordance with Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court, the President of the Court, Mr X Wildhaber, assigned the case to the Third Section. The Chamber constituted within that Section included ex officio Mr Y Costa, the judge elected in respect of France (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 26 § 1 (a)), and Sir Z Bratza, President of the Section (Rule 26 § 1 (a)). The other members designated by the latter to complete the Chamber were Mr A Loucaides, Mrs B Tulkens, Mr C Fuhrmann, Mr D Jungwiert and Mr E Traja (Rule 26 § 1 (b)). On 1 May 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible and decided to invite the parties to submit their observations on the merits at a hearing. The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, City, on 1 October 1999. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mrs F Dubrocard, Deputy Director, Human Rights Division, Legal Affairs Department, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mrs G Delahaye, magistrat, seconded to the Human Rights Division, Legal Affairs Department, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Mrs H Faucheux-bureau, magistrat, General Civil Law Office, Civil Affairs Department, Ministry of Justice, Counsel; (b) for the applicant Mr I Ottan, of the Bar, Counsel. The applicant also attended the hearing. The Court heard addresses by Mr Ottan and Mrs Dubrocard. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, Xavier Dupont, is a national who was born in City in 1942 and lives at City. The applicant’s mother died on 1 January 1991 of a disease, having been infected after a blood transfusion. She left two children: a son, Jean, born out of wedlock in 1936 and legitimised by his mother’s marriage in 1937, and the applicant, born in 1942, on whose birth certificate only his mother’s name was entered as a parent, she being still married at the time of his birth, but living separately from her husband. They divorced in July 1944.

PROCEDURE The case originated in the applications (nos. 12345/00 and 12346/00) against the Republic of Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Country national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2000. The Government of Country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr A. Smith and subsequently Mr B. Jones. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the proceedings against company Y exceeded a “reasonable time” within the meaning of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 January 2002 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 1 July 2004 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 1 January 1995 the applicant filed with the Regional Court (sąd) an action in which he claimed damages from one of his partners in a partnership allegedly responsible for a sale of the partnership's property without the applicant's prior approval. He sued also a certain company Y which had purchased that property. On 1 January 1995 the court exempted the applicant from court fees. On 1 January 1995 it refused the applicant's request for an interim measure. His appeal against that decision was dismissed on 1 January 1995 by the Court of Appeal (sąd). On 1 January 1995 the applicant submitted pleadings with a ninety-five-page annex. In January, April, and December 1995, as well as in January 1996, he submitted further pleadings and requested the summoning of five witnesses. The Regional Court held a hearing on 1 January 1996. It completed the examination of the case and informed the parties that it would pronounce its judgment on 1 January 1996. Subsequently, the applicant submitted pleadings containing motions concerning evidence. On 1 January 1996 the court resumed the examination of the case. The hearing scheduled for 1 January 1996 was adjourned because of the absence of a lay judge. On 1 January 1996 the court held a hearing. On 1 January 1996 it declared its lack of jurisdiction over the applicant's claims in respect of his partner and transferred that part of the case to the District Court (sąd). The Regional Court held hearings on 1 January 1996, as well as on 1 January, 1 January, and 1 January 1997. It ordered an expert opinion. On 1 January 1997 the court refused the applicant's request for an interim measure. The expert opinion was submitted on 1 January 1998.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against the Federal Republic of a Country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Alice Smith (“the applicant”), on 10 July 2009. The applicant was represented by Mr C. Jones, a lawyer practising in a City. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mrs D. Brown, of the Federal Ministry of Justice. The applicant alleged, in particular, that her dismissal without notice from her employment as a geriatric nurse, on the ground that she had brought a criminal complaint against her employer alleging deficiencies in the institutional care provided, and the refusal of the domestic courts in the ensuing proceedings to order her reinstatement had infringed her right to freedom of expression. On 16 December 2009 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. In addition, third-party submissions were received from a Trade Union, which had been granted leave by the President to intervene in the written procedure (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 3 of the Rules of Court) and which was represented by Mr E. Green, Chairman of its Managing Board, and Mr F. White, Deputy Chairman. The parties replied to those third-party submissions (Rule 44 § 6). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1962 and lives in a City.
