She had been working as a geriatric nurse for a Health Care Company from 15 September 2000 until 10 February 2005, when she was dismissed. A. The events leading to the applicant’s dismissal Since January 2002 the applicant had been working in a geriatric nursing home operated by the Health Care Company, where the patients were partly bedridden, disorientated, and generally dependent on special assistance. In 2002 the Medical Review Board of the Health Insurance Fund established serious shortcomings in the daily care provided there, caused by a shortage of staff. Between 25 January 2003 and 20 October 2004 the applicant and her colleagues regularly indicated to the management that they were overburdened on account of staff shortages and therefore had difficulties carrying out their duties. They specified the deficiencies in the care provided and also mentioned that services were not properly documented.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 July 2006. The applicant was represented by Mr and Ms Jane Smith, lawyers practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 15 September 2009 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in a town. On 10 July 1997 the applicant was arrested in a city during a bank robbery. On 25 July 1997 he was brought before the investigating judge at the State Security Court, who remanded him in custody. On 6 August 1997 the public prosecutor at the State Security Court filed an indictment against the applicant. Invoking a law, he accused the applicant of membership of an illegal armed organisation and of involvement in activities which undermined the constitutional order of the State. The trial commenced before the State Security Court. In the subsequent hearings, the court refused to release the applicant on account of the nature of the alleged offence and the state of the evidence. On 12 December 1997 the State Security Court pronounced its judgment. It convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to life imprisonment. On 4 December 1998 the Court of Cassation quashed this judgment. The case was accordingly remitted to the State Security Court. On 6 January 1999 the State Security Court resumed the trial. During the subsequent hearings, the court rejected the applicant’s requests for release, having regard to the state of the evidence. On 20 December 2002 the State Security Court once again convicted the applicant as charged and, pursuant to a law, sentenced him to life imprisonment. On 17 September 2003 the Court of Cassation once again quashed the judgment of the first instance court. The proceedings continued before the State Security Court. On 8 May 2004 the State Security Courts were abolished following a constitutional amendment, and the applicant’s case was transferred to the Assize Court. According to the information in the case file, the proceedings are still pending and the applicant is still remanded in custody.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Ana Silva (“the applicant”), on 15 July 2002. The applicant was represented by Mr J. Doe, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant alleged, in particular, that she had been denied a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal. On 7 November 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Andria. On 12 March 1998 the applicant was arrested and taken into police custody on suspicion of her involvement in the activities of an illegal organisation, namely the XYZ. The police officers drew up an arrest protocol in which they noted that they had found a false identity card on the applicant and seized it for the investigation. Following the Andria public prosecutor's order, the applicant's detention period was extended. On 17 March 1998 police officers took statements from the applicant. She confessed to being a member of the XYZ and stated that she had been involved in armed clashes with the security forces. On 18 March 1998 the applicant's statements were taken by the Andria public prosecutor to whom she again confessed to being a member of the XYZ and stated that she had been involved in political education and propaganda activities for the organisation. On the same day she was brought before a single judge at the Andria Magistrates' Court who took her statement and ordered her detention on remand. On 3 April 1998 the principal public prosecutor at the Andria State Security Court filed a bill of indictment, charging the applicant under Articles 125 and 40 of the Criminal Code with carrying out activities for the purpose of bringing about the secession of part of the national territory and aiding and abetting an illegal organisation. Between 4 April 1998 and 19 March 2001, the Andria State Security Court held twenty hearings and heard a number of witnesses. During these hearings, the applicant renounced her statements taken during her detention in police custody. Witnesses heard by the court stated that the applicant was an active member of the XYZ and that she had been involved in armed clashes with the security forces. On 19 March 2001 the Andria State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced her to death under Article 125 of the Criminal Code.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”), on 10 June 2002. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. Richard Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 25 November 2008 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in Warsaw. 1. First set of criminal proceedings against the applicant The applicant was charged with handling stolen property and, on an unspecified later date, he was detained on remand. On 15 November 1994 the Warsaw District Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to 2 years’ imprisonment. The applicant appealed. On 10 April 1995 the Warsaw Regional Court upheld the first-instance judgment. 2. Second set of criminal proceedings against the applicant The applicant was charged with handling stolen property, forgery of documents and unlawful possession of a firearm and, on an unspecified later date, he was detained on remand. On 1 March 1996 the Warsaw Regional Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to 3 years and 6 months’ imprisonment. Both the applicant and the prosecutor appealed. On 15 October 1996 the Warsaw Court of Appeal amended the first-instance judgment and increased the sentence to 5 years’ imprisonment. On 15 December 1996 the Warsaw Regional Court gave a cumulative judgment (wyrok łączny) and sentenced the applicant to 5 years’ imprisonment as cumulative penalties for the former conviction given in the first set of criminal proceedings (see paragraph 7 above) and the latter conviction given on 15 October 1996. 3. Third set of criminal proceedings against the applicant On an unspecified later date the applicant was charged with handling stolen property. On 15 February 1998 the Warsaw Regional Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to 2 years and 6 months’ imprisonment. The applicant appealed. On 15 June 1998 the Warsaw Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance judgment. A cassation appeal was available. On 15 June 2003 the applicant requested to have the criminal proceedings against him re-opened. On 25 July 2003 the Supreme Court dismissed his request. 4. Censorship of the applicant’s correspondence On 15 March 2003 the Court received the applicant’s letter of 25 February 2003. The envelope bore the following stamp: “Censored on 28 February 2003” (Ocenzurowano dnia 28.02.2003) and an illegible signature.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of A against the Republic of B lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of B, Ms A B. On 15 April 2000. The applicant was represented by Ms C D, a lawyer practising in C. In the instant case, the Government of B (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 29 May 2002 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. On 1 December 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). On 30 December 2004 the Chamber decided to apply the accelerated procedure under Article 29 § 3 of the Convention and examine the admissibility and merits at the same time. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1961 and lives in D. On 16 December 1997 the applicant was arrested by the Anti-Terrorist Branch of the E Police Headquarters on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, the F Union and placed in custody. In her statement of 19 December 1997 the applicant declared that she aided and abetted the members of the F Union and that she provided information to the F Union members who were held in prison. On 20 December 1997 the applicant was brought before the Public Prosecutor at the F Court and then before the judge, where she denied all the charges against her. She declared that her statement in police custody was taken under duress and that she had been given electric shocks. The judge ordered the applicant’s detention pending trial. On 24 December 1997 the Public Prosecutor at the F Court filed an indictment accusing the applicant of membership of an illegal terrorist organisation, aiding and abetting the organisation, providing information to its members who were imprisoned and participating in the demonstrations organised by the organisation. On 5 June 1998 the F Court convicted the applicant under Article 170 of the Criminal Code and sentenced her to three years and nine months’ imprisonment. On 24 June 1998 the applicant appealed against this decision to the G Court. On 21 September 1999 the G Court upheld the decision of the F Court. On 15 October 2000 the G Court’s decision was deposited with the registry of the F Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Alphaville lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Alphavillian national, Ms. Eliza Green (“the applicant”), on 30 August 2002. The applicant was represented by Ms. N. Brown, a lawyer practising in Alphaville. The Alphavian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. J. Smith, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, a violation of her right to freedom of assembly. The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 22 April 2006, the Court declared the application admissible. The parties did not submit further observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in Alphaville. On 29 October 1999 the applicant, who is a member of parliament for the Green Party, notified the Salzburg Federal Police Authority (Bundespolizeidirektion) under section 2 of the Assembly Act (Versammlungsgesetz) that on All Saints' Day, 1 November 1999, from 9 a.m. until 1 p.m., she would be holding a meeting at the Salzburg municipal cemetery in front of the war memorial. She noted that the meeting would coincide with the gathering of Comradeship IV (Kameradschaft IV), which she considered to be unlawful. The purpose of the meeting was to be to commemorate the Salzburg Jews killed by the SS during the Second World War. The applicant expected about six participants, who would carry commemorative messages in their hands and attached to their clothes. The applicant stated that no other means of expression (such as chanting or banners) which might offend piety or undermine public order would be used. On 30 October 1999 the Salzburg Federal Police Authority, relying on section 6 of the Assembly Act and on Article 11 of the Convention, prohibited the meeting on the ground that it would endanger public order and security. The authority noted that F.E., also a member of parliament for the Green Party, had informed the Salzburg Federal Police Authority of the allegedly illegal assembly of Comradeship IV in memory of the SS soldiers killed in the Second World War which was to be held at the same time and place, but had refused to give an undertaking that the proposed meeting in memory of the murdered Salzburg Jews would not disrupt that gathering. The Salzburg Federal Police Authority noted that Comradeship IV was a registered association. Like a number of other organisations, it traditionally held a commemoration ceremony at the Salzburg municipal cemetery on All Saints' Day.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2005. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr A Smith, of a foreign office. On 10 November 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in a region. He grew raspberries there and had a lucrative contract with a shop, but lost it in 1995 when the local environmental health officer let it be known to the shop that the applicant was packing raspberries in his kitchen. The applicant and his wife sued a government department for mis-statement and were awarded over GBP 16,000 in damages by a regional court on 1 March 1996. The applicant did not consider that this was enough, and, wishing to appeal, instructed a new (regional) advocate, a Mr Brown, then a partner in a firm of advocates called Brown Jones Smith ('BJS'). Mr Brown advised that there was merit in an appeal, and applied for legal aid on his client's behalf in March 1996: this application was rejected on 20 April 1996. The applicant's Petition of Appeal from the first instance judgment was rejected the next day because it had been filed two days late. Mr Brown advised (via letter and at a meeting) that it would not be unduly difficult to apply for an extension of time in which to lodge the appeal, but that, in the circumstances, the best course of action was for the applicant to cut his losses and to accept an offer put forward by the government department. The applicant accepted this advice and, on 15 May 1996, the government department's offer of GBP 20,000. BJS issued proceedings against the applicant for payment of their fees on 5 December 1996. An advocate instructed by the applicant to defend the claim failed to file a Defence in the prescribed period, and judgment was entered for BJS on 3 January 1997. After taxation of BJS's costs, judgment was issued on 1 March 1998 for a total of GBP 929.80. Mr Brown then applied for execution of the judgment and on 10 October 1998, the applicant's property was placed under arrest by the coroner. The applicant appealed on 20 October 1998 and on 25 October 1998 Mr Brown wrote to the coroner and the applicant requesting that no further steps be taken in respect of the enforcement of the execution against the applicant until specifically instructed. It appears that the execution remained suspended until the judgment of 25 October 2004 detailed below.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Government ("the Government") on 7 August 1995, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 of the Convention (art. 32-1, art. 47). It originated in an application (no. 20368/92) against the Republic lodged with the Commission ("the Commission") under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national, Mr X Y, on 18 November 1991. The Government’s application referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48). The object of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 of the Convention (art. 6-1). In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr Z A, the elected judge of national origin (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr B C, the Vice-President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 4 (b)). On 5 September 1995, in the presence of the Registrar, the President of the Court, Mr D, drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr E F, Mr G H, Mrs I J, Mr K L, Mr M N, Mr O P, Mr Q R and Mr S T (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 5) (art. 43). As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 6), Mr C, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the applicant’s memorial on 11 March 1996 and the Government’s memorial on 29 March 1996. On 30 April 1996 the Secretary to the Commission informed the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. On 7 May 1996 the Commission produced the file on the proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar on the President’s instructions. In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Region, on 24 June 1996. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. There appeared before the Court: for the Government Mr U V, Deputy Director of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Agent; Mr W X, on secondment to the Legal Affairs Department, Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Mr Y Z, Counsel; for the Commission Mr A B, Delegate; for the applicant Mr C D, Counsel.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Xanadan nationals, Mr Xanadu and Mr Xanadu (“the applicants”), on 15 September 2006. The applicants were represented by Mr Xanadu, a lawyer practising in Yonder. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicants alleged that they had been subjected to torture during their detention in the custody of security forces and that the national authorities had failed to establish the criminal and administrative responsibilities of the accused police officers. This had consequently allowed the police officers to enjoy impunity. The applicants relied on Articles 3, 5, 6 and 13 of the Convention. On 10 June 2008 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1970 and 1972 and live in Zephyria and Zephyria respectively. On 22 June 1998, at about midnight, the applicants were taken into police custody at the Myntra Security Headquarters for car theft. They were allegedly ill-treated by police officers, who stripped them naked, beat them and subjected them to electric shocks. On 24 June 1998, at about 10.00 a.m., the applicants were brought before a forensic doctor (Xanadu) who reported that there were no traces of ill‐treatment on their bodies. The applicants were released the same day (24 June), following which they lodged a complaint with the public prosecutor against the police officers (Xanadu and Xanadu) who had interrogated them and against the doctor (Xanadu) who had drawn up their medical report. The public prosecutor referred the applicants to a forensic doctor who reported the same day (24 June) that the first applicant had red marks of various sizes on both the scapula and the thorax, a 2‐cm‐wide bruise on the lower right lip and an 0.5‐cm‐wide ecchymosis on his right eye. Moreover, it was noted that the second applicant had a red 1 x 1 cm skin wound on his groin. The report stated that the marks and bruises on their bodies did not render the applicants unfit for work. By an indictment filed on 28 November 1998, the public prosecutor instituted criminal proceedings against Xanadu and Xanadu for having insulted and tortured the applicants, and against Xanadu for professional misconduct. On 14 December 1999 the Myntra Assize Court delivered its judgment. Referring to the second medical report, which noted the presence of marks on the applicants’ bodies, the court found Xanadu and Xanadu guilty of ill-treatment during the performance of their duties under Article 245 of the former Criminal Code, and sentenced them to imprisonment, which was converted to a fine.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 19583/05) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 12 May 2005 by Mr P. Ryckie (“the applicant”). The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Ms R. Orlikowska-Wrońska, a lawyer practising in Sopot. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr J. Wołąsiewicz of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 10 October 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1972 and lives in a city. On 24 May 1999 the applicant was detained on remand on suspicion of having committed numerous offences, inter alia kidnapping and aggravated robbery. The court based its detention order on a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences and on the severity of the likely penalty, which gave rise to a fear that the applicant would obstruct the proceedings. His pre-trial detention was extended by decisions of various dates. In all the above-mentioned decisions the courts relied on the same grounds for detention as those given in the first detention order. In some the courts also referred to the complexity of the case, the need to conduct further investigations, the probability of collusion between the applicant and the co-accused and exertion of unlawful pressure on witnesses by the applicant and the fear that the applicant would go into hiding. On many occasions the applicant requested release or that a more lenient preventive measure be applied. Each time his requests were dismissed. The applicant appealed against the decisions extending his detention on several occasions. Only one of his appeals was allowed to the effect that the period of extension of his detention was reduced by two months. On 24 January 2000 the prosecution service filed with the court a bill of indictment. The applicant was charged with twelve offences, including aggravated robbery, kidnapping and illegal possession of a weapon. The first hearing planned for 10 April 2000 was adjourned. Subsequent hearings were held on various dates.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/11) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 11 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Janusz Kowalski (“the applicant”), on 29 June 2011. The applicant was represented by Mr T. Novak, a lawyer practising in Vienna. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms K. Nowak, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that his right to freedom of expression was breached in violation of Article 11 of the Convention. On 14 April 2014 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Kraków. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. The applicant is a film director, historian, and author of press articles often commenting on current issues. The Government contested that the applicant could be considered a journalist. On 20 March 2008 the applicant participated in a debate on a regional radio station, Polskie Radio Kraków. During the debate he stated as follows: “... among the informers (informator) of the [communist-era] secret political police is Professor [J.M.] – this information confirms the theory that among those who speak out the most against lustration are people who have good reasons for doing so.” On the same day the applicant called Mr J.M. an “informant” (konfident) on television. The matter was widely commented on in the media. On 17 April 2008 a special commission set up at Kraków University to examine the problem of covert surveillance of academics issued a statement in the case of Mr J.M. The statement included a list of documents concerning Mr J.M., which had been found in the archives. The commission concluded that those documents had not led it to the unequivocal conclusion that Mr J.M. had been a collaborator with the secret police. On 24 April 2008 Mr J.M. brought a civil action for protection of his personal rights against the applicant. On 3 June 2009 the Warsaw Regional Court allowed the action. It ordered the applicant to pay 20,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) to a charity and to reimburse the claimant PLN 5,800 for the costs of the proceedings. The applicant was also ordered to publish an apology for having damaged the claimant’s good name in six national and regional newspapers, on three national TV channels and on Radio Kraków. The court considered that the applicant had clearly used several expressions indicating that the claimant had been a secret collaborator with the communist-era secret services. The main question to be considered was whether such statements could be considered true. The court noted that Mr J.M. was a distinguished linguist and well‐known person in Europe. He was a member of the European Language Council and for many years had been presenting a programme on television.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/11) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Norwegian national, Mr Andersson (“the applicant”), on 15 April 2011. The applicant was represented by Mr Brown and Mr Green, lawyers practising in Oslo. The Norwegian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Jensen, Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that he had been deprived of effective access to court and that the State had failed to provide him with sufficient protection against allegations that violated his right to privacy. On 3 April 2013 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Oslo. He is self-employed and runs a business. On 25 May 2005 the Norwegian commercial television channel Channel X broadcast an episode of a television show entitled “Investigation”, in which it was claimed that “suspicious transactions and suspicious characters” were revealed. The show was broadcast live with a few recorded features. In the show, the applicant, who was unknown to the broader public, appeared in pictures and was mentioned by name. He was singled out as the central figure of organized crime within media and advertising and as being guilty of several counts of fraud and other economic offences. The programme was re-broadcast on 28 May and 15 October 2005. At this time, no criminal investigation had been initiated against the applicant. The television programme was produced in Norway by the Norwegian company MediaWorks AB. It was sent by satellite link from Norway to the London-based company BroadcastUK Ltd and from there sent unaltered to a satellite which transmitted the programme to the Norwegian audience. The encoded programme was viewable via a satellite receiver or a cable connection in Norway a fraction of a second after it had been sent by satellite link. Even if it was viewable in the United Kingdom, which is doubtful, it would have been watched there by a small audience. It was presented in the Norwegian language for a Norwegian-speaking audience, and was sponsored by companies competing in the Norwegian market. The anchorman of the show, Y, a Norwegian national, was a celebrity and a well-known television personality in Norway; he was also the Chief Executive Officer of MediaWorks AB. The show had a long run and was watched by many viewers. In December 2007 the applicant brought a private prosecution against Y for gross defamation, claiming damages in the amount of 300,000 Norwegian kroner (NOK; approximately 33,000 euros). He maintained that he had been unreservedly pointed out as the central figure of organized crime within media and advertising and as being directly or indirectly responsible for a large number of serious crimes.

PROCEDURE The cases originated in two applications (nos. 12345/08 and 67890/08) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals, Mr A and Mr B (“the applicants”), on 29 May and 15 August 2008, respectively. The first applicant, Mr A, was represented by Mr C, a lawyer practising in a city. The second applicant, Mr B, was represented by Mr D, a lawyer practising in another city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 13 May 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASES The applicants were born in 1973 and 1965, respectively, and live in a city and another city. A. Application no. 12345/08 On 17 October 2001 the applicant was discharged from his civil service post following his previous criminal conviction by a martial law court. The conviction had been finalised by the Military Court of Cassation's decision of 11 November 1997. On 4 January 2002 the applicant brought an action before the administrative court to annul the discharge order. On 5 June 2002 the administrative court rejected the applicant's request. On 7 February 2005 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the judgment of the administrative court. The written opinions of the public prosecutor and of the judge rapporteur concerning his appeal request were not communicated to the applicant. On 31 December 2007 the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's request for rectification of its previous decision. B. Application no. 67890/08 On 11 January 2002 the applicant was discharged from his civil service post after a disciplinary decision. Criminal proceedings were also commenced against the applicant on the same grounds as those which had led to his discharge. On 15 March 2002 the applicant brought an action before the administrative court to annul the discharge order. On 25 June 2002 the Assize Court acquitted the applicant of the offences with which he had been charged. On 22 March 2004 the Court of Cassation upheld the applicant's acquittal. In the meantime, on 31 March 2003 the administrative court refused the applicant's request to annul the discharge order. Relying on a section of the Civil Servants Law, the administrative court held that the applicant's acquittal of the criminal charges did not absolve him from the disciplinary sanction. On 26 April 2005 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the judgment of the administrative court. The written opinions of the public prosecutor and of the judge rapporteur concerning his appeal request were not communicated to the applicant. On 23 January 2008 the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's rectification request.

PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 12345/08 and 12346/08) against the Republic of Xlodaria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Xlodarian nationals, Mr Xander Smith and Mr Yara Jones (“the applicants”), on 15 October 2008. The Xlodarian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 25 December 2008 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASES The applicants were born in 1975 and 1971 respectively and are currently detained in Xlodaria. On 20 February 2001 the applicants were taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of the Xorganization, an illegal organisation. On 3 March 2001 a single judge at the Third Chamber of the X State Security Court ordered the applicants' pre-trial detention. On 2 June 2001 the public prosecutor at the X State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicants, charging them under Article 146 §1 of the former Criminal Code with attempting to undermine the constitutional order. On 10 August 2001 the first hearing was held before the Fourth Chamber of the X State Security Court. By Law no. 5200 of 17 June 2004, published in the Official Gazette on 30 June 2004, State Security Courts were abolished. The case against the applicants was transferred to the Seventh Chamber of the X Assize Court. At the end of each hearing, the X State Security Court, and subsequently the X Assize Court, considered the applicants' detention either of their own motion or at the applicants' request. Each time, they ordered the applicants' continued detention pending trial, having regard to the nature of the offence with which they were charged, the existence of a strong suspicion that they had committed the offence and the state of evidence. According to the information in the case file, the proceedings are still pending before the Seventh Chamber of the X Assize Court and the applicants are still remanded in custody.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 20087/06) against a State (Republic of Austria) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (Austrian national), Mr Michael Stechauner (“the applicant”), on 3 May 2006. The applicant was represented by a lawyer (Mr M. Lechner) practising in a location (Lochau). The State (Republic of Austria) was represented by their Agent, Ambassador F. Trauttmansdorff, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs. The applicant alleged that the proceedings concerning his doctor’s fees had not been dealt with within a reasonable time and that the body which dealt with his case had not been impartial or independent. On 2 May 2008 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the State. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant lives in a location (Großau). The applicant is a practitioner of general medicine. He has an individual contract with a health insurance board. The applicant has also obtained special diplomas in certain areas and performs these types of examination on his patients. One part of the individual contract between the applicant and the health insurance board is the Remuneration Regulation which states that certain types of examinations will only be reimbursed if they are performed by a specialist doctor. The health insurance board refused to reimburse certain examinations as the applicant was not a specialist doctor but a general practitioner. On 2 February 1998 the applicant claimed payment for certain services before a committee; on 23 April 1998 he submitted another claim for payment; at an unknown date this claim was increased. On 6 July 1998 the applicant submitted a claim for payment of a certain amount for the first quarter of 1998. The committee held hearings on certain dates. As the committee did not reach a decision because of a tie, the applicant filed an application for transfer to a commission on 2 July 1998 and 7 October 1998, respectively. Meanwhile, on 6 October 1998 the applicant had claimed payment for certain services amounting to a certain amount for the second quarter of 1998. At a later date this claim was reduced. On 25 November 1998 the commission refused to grant the applicant’s claims concerning certain quarters.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of A (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of A (a fictional country), Mr Ali Yılmaz (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2003. The applicant was represented by Mr T. Öztürk, a lawyer practising in Ankara. The Republic of A (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention that he was not tried by an independent and impartial tribunal and that the disciplinary penalty which was imposed on him by the Military Disciplinary Courts contravened Article 5 § 1. On 30 November 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1979 and lives in A (a fictional city). At the time of the events, the applicant was a corporal in the A (a fictional brigade) of the A (a fictional forces). On 30 January 2003 the colonel (yağasıncı) filed an indictment against the applicant with the A Military Disciplinary Court which was attached to the A Brigade. He accused the applicant of insulting his subordinates, of deliberately hiding the truth from his superiors and of giving abusive commands to his subordinates which did not concern military service. In particular, the applicant was accused of forcing his subordinates to make his bed, or do his personal shopping and laundry. On 7 February 2003, the A Military Disciplinary Court, which was composed of a lieutenant colonel (altıbaşı), a captain (yüzbaşı) and a sergeant major (başçavuş), found the applicant guilty as charged and sentenced him to “room arrest” for 110 days. On 20 February 2003 the applicant appealed. On 6 March 2003 the A Supreme Disciplinary Court attached to the General Command of the Gendarmerie gave a decision of non-jurisdiction regarding the first charge and sent the case file to the Military Court attached to the General Command of the Gendarmerie for reconsideration. It acquitted the applicant of the second charge. It therefore upheld the decision of 7 February 2003 in respect of the third charge. As a result, the applicant was ordered to serve 40 days' “room arrest”. On 17 April 2003 the applicant petitioned the Minister of Defence for a referral of his case to the office of the public prosecutor at the Military Court of Cassation, by means of an appeal against the decision of the A Supreme Disciplinary Court. He complained, in particular, of a breach of Articles 5 § 1 and 6 §1 of the Convention.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xanadu, Mr Ali Xanadu (“the applicant”), on 29 April 2003. The applicant was represented by Mr Y Zanadu and Mrs Y Zanadu, lawyers practising in Yonder. The Government of Xanadu (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 11 September 2007 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate to the Government the complaints concerning the applicant’s right to release pending trial, to take proceedings to challenge the lawfulness of his detention and to a fair hearing within a reasonable time. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1972 and lives in Zazaland. On 1 April 1996 the applicant was arrested by gendarmerie officers while he was leaving Zazaland. He was then transferred to the Anti-Terrorist Branch of the Zazaland Police Headquarters on suspicion of involvement in the activities of the Yonderland Workers’ Party, an illegal organisation. On 18 April 1996 the applicant was brought before the Zazaland public prosecutor and the judge at the Zazaland Magistrates’ Court. The judge remanded the applicant in custody. On an unspecified day the Zazaland public prosecutor issued a decision of non-jurisdiction and sent the case file to the public prosecutor’s office at the Yonderland State Security Court. On 22 May 1996 the public prosecutor filed a bill of indictment against the applicant, along with other persons, charging him with membership of the Yonderland Workers’ Party under Article 168 § 2 of the former Criminal Code. On 30 July 1996 the Yonderland State Security Court held the first hearing on the merits of the case. On 25 December 2001 the Fourth Chamber of the Yonderland State Security Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment. Throughout the proceedings, the applicant and his representative requested several times that the applicant be released pending trial. At the end of each hearing the State Security Court rejected the applicant’s requests, having regard to the nature of the offence, the state of the evidence and the content of the case file. On 9 October 2002 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first-instance court. The case was subsequently remitted to the Yonderland State Security Court. On 13 May 2003 the Yonderland State Security Court ordered the applicant’s release pending trial. On 23 March 2004 the State Security Court once again convicted the applicant under Article 168 § 2 of the former Criminal Code and sentenced him to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment. On 19 October 2004 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 23 March 2004. Pursuant to Law no.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of Xana lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xana, Mr Ali Xana (“the applicant”), on 28 July 2001. The applicant was represented by Mr S. Xana, a lawyer practising in Yzmir. The Government of Xana (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 24 April 2003 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section (Rule 52 § 1). In a letter of 1 March 2005, the Court informed the parties that in accordance with Article 29 §§ 1 and 3 of the Convention it would decide on both the admissibility and merits of the application. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1953 and was serving a sentence in Zzz prison at the time of lodging his application. On 5 January and 30 June 1994, and on 11 July 1995, the public prosecutor at the Yzmir State Security Court issued arrest warrants in respect of the applicant on suspicion of his involvement with the PKK0. On 23 May 2001 the applicant was arrested and taken into custody by police officers at the Diyarbakir Security Directorate. According to the arrest protocol, signed by a police officer and the applicant, the latter was arrested at 18.00 p.m. and was told of his rights, in particular, the right to object to the prolongation of his arrest and detention to a judge. On an unspecified date, the applicant’s wife filed a petition with the Diyarbakir public prosecutor’s office and requested information as to where her husband was being held and when he would be brought before the public prosecutor. She submitted that her husband was arrested on 23 May 2001 at around 15.00 p.m. On 24 May 2001 the public prosecutor informed the applicant’s wife that her husband was held in custody on account of his involvement with the PKK. The Government submitted that the applicant was taken for a medical examination at Diyarbakir State Hospital on the day of his arrest and on 24 and 25 May 2001. They maintained that on 24 May 2001 the Yzmir Security Directorate requested the transfer of the applicant from Diyarbakir to Yzmir and that the applicant arrived, accompanied by a police officer from the Diyarbakir State Security Directorate, by plane, in Yzmir on 25 May 2001 at 14.30 p.m. On 25 May 2001 the applicant was handed over to the police officers at the Yzmir Security Directorate.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against the Republic of A against the Republic of B lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms X. The applicant was represented by Ms Y, a lawyer practising in City A. The Government of B (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 15 September 2004 the Court (Fourth Section) declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the length of the applicant's police custody, her right to an effective remedy by which she could challenge the lawfulness of her detention, and to receive compensation for the excessive length of the custody period to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1985. She is imprisoned in Prison A. On 15 October 2001 the applicant was at a bus stop in Village A in City B when she was arrested by plain-clothes police officers on suspicion of being a member of the Organization X. She was taken to the Anti-Terrorism Branch of the State Security Directorate in City B. On the same day, the police officers drafted an arrest protocol stating that the applicant had been arrested on account of her involvement in Organization X-related activities. The applicant signed this protocol. The applicant's lawyer challenged the arrest before the investigating judge of the State Security Court and requested that the applicant be released from detention. Her request was dismissed. On 16 October 2001 the public prosecutor at the State Security Court extended the detention period until 19 October 2001. On 19 October 2001 the applicant could see her lawyer for a short period of time following the permission of the public prosecutor. On 20 October 2001 police officers from the Anti-Terrorism Branch requested that the applicant's custody period be extended for three more days. The single judge of the State Security Court granted the request and extended the custody period until 22 October 2001 pursuant to Article 130 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The applicant's lawyer challenged this decision before a panel of three judges of the State Security Court and requested that the applicant be brought before a judge. Her request was dismissed. On 21 October 2001 the applicant was brought before the public prosecutor, and thereafter before the investigating judge of the State Security Court. Subsequently the judge ordered that the applicant be detained on remand.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123456/98) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms. Anna Novak (“the applicant”), on 15 July 1998. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr. M. Smith and subsequently Mr. N. Jones of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 22 December 2002 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Warsaw, Europe. She is a historian by profession and used to work as a curator in the Warsaw City Museum. On 15 October 1995 the applicant brought a private prosecution on charges of libel against T.M. the director of the Warsaw City Museum to the Warsaw District Court (Sąd Rejonowy). On 25 June 1996 the court held a conciliatory hearing. The applicant requested that T.M. retract in the press her defamatory statements. The defendant refused. The trial began on 28 July 1996 but the applicant failed to appear. The court discontinued the proceedings on the ground that the applicant had been duly summoned. The court considered that the applicant had been notified about the service of the summons but failed to collect it from the post office. On 18 July 1996 the applicant appealed against this decision. On 2 October 1996 the Warsaw Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) quashed that decision and ordered that the District Court proceed with the case. On 15 May 1997 the applicant filed a complaint with the District Court submitting that the length of the proceedings in her case had exceeded any reasonable time limit. On 20 June 1997 the president of the Criminal Division of the District Court informed her that the delay in the proceedings was caused by the presiding judge's illness. On 15 August 1998 the president of the Criminal Division of the District Court ordered that the case be transferred to another judge. The next hearing was held on 10 February 1999. On that date upon the court's order, the applicant specified the charges against T.M. Consequently, the court adjourned the hearing to consider discontinuation of the proceedings. On 15 March 1999 the Warsaw District Court discontinued the proceedings, as the offence was time-barred. The court held that the applicant submitted her private prosecution after the time-limit of 3 months from the date on which she had become aware of the identity of the defendant.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court on 15 February 1994 by the International Commission of Rights ("the Commission") and on 18 February 1994 by the Government of a European Country ("the Government"), within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 12345/90) against the country lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) on 10 May 1990 by a national, Mr John Doe. The Commission's request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby the country recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46); the Government's application referred to Article 48 (art. 48). The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 5 and 6 (art. 5, art. 6) of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Sir Richard Green, the elected judge of national origin (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr Peter Brown, the Vice-President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 4 (b)). On 10 March 1994, in the presence of the Registrar, the President of the Court, Mr Charles White, drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr Jane Black, Mr Chris White, Mr David Green, Mr Frank Brown, Mr Tom White, Mr Steve Green, and Mr John Black (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 5) (art. 43). The President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 6), Mr Brown, through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant's lawyer and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the Government's memorial on 25 May 1994 and the applicant's memorial on 5 June 1994. In accordance with the President's decision, the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, a European city, on 15 August 1994. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr James Smith, Deputy Legal Adviser, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr David Jones QC, Mr Peter Brown, Counsel, Mr Michael White, Lord Chancellor's Department, Adviser; (b) for the Commission Mrs Jane Black, Delegate; (c) for the applicant Mr John Doe Professor Jane White, Counsel, Mr Chris Black Adviser. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 32869/96) against a country ("the Republic of Austria") lodged with an international organization ("the European Commission of Human Rights") under former Article 25 of a document ("the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms") by a national of that country ("the applicant"), on 10 May 1996. The applicant was represented by a lawyer practicing in the country (Austria). The country's government ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, a diplomat, Head of the International Law Department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings against him lasted unreasonably long. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when a protocol to the Convention came into force. The application was allocated to a section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 12 October 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible and requested the parties to submit further observations. Thereupon the applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant is a certified accountant and tax consultant, residing in a city (Salzburg). On 29 June 1989 a court (Salzburg Regional Court) started preliminary investigations against the applicant and several others on suspicion of large-scale fraud and breach of trust in the context of investments in a real estate fund. They were suspected of having sold so called “partial house ownership certificates” to several thousand investors with the assurance that their value was secured by real property, but in fact they had sold the real property in 1986 and misappropriated the proceeds of the sale. On 31 January 1990 the Review Chamber (Ratskammer) of the Salzburg Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal against the opening of preliminary proceedings. On 14 March 1990 the Court of Appeal (Oberlandesgericht) rejected the applicant’s further appeal. As of the beginning of 1990 the investigating judge was relieved of all other business and two junior judges completing their training period were assigned to assist him. In May 1990 one of them took over as the new investigating judge. During the preliminary investigations, which concerned a network of more than 300 firms, about 1,800 bank accounts were examined and about 8,000 volumes of documents were seized and studied. A special computer programme was designed in order to cope with the large volume of data. Most of the time was consumed by the preparation of an expert opinion, whereby the team of accounting experts first had to clear the balance sheets of the companies, most of which were intertwined.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/06) against the Republic of A (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of A (a fictional country), Mr John Doe (a fictional person) (“the applicant”), on 8 February 2005. The applicant was represented by Ms Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in A (a fictional city). The Government of A (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant complained in particular that the refusal to lift his parliamentary immunity had hindered criminal proceedings against him, thereby depriving him of his right of access to a court under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. In a decision of 15 January 2008, following a hearing on admissibility and the merits (Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court), the Chamber declared the application admissible. A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 15 January 2008 (Rule 59 § 3). There appeared before the Court: – for the Government Mr Alex Brown, Co-Agent, Ms Claire Green, Ms Fiona White, Ms Yasmin Black, Ms Emma Red, Ms Zoe Blue, Mr Ian Smith, Mr Adam White, Mr Liam Brown, Advisers; – for the applicant Ms Jane Smith, Counsel, Mr John Doe, Applicant. The Court heard statements by Ms Smith and Mr Brown. On 1 February 2008 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1), but this case remained with the Chamber constituted within the former Second Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in A (a fictional city). In the parliamentary elections of 3 November 2002, as a member of the People's Democratic Party (a fictional organization), he was elected MP for the K (a fictional city) constituency to the Grand National Assembly of A (a fictional country) (“the National Assembly”). Prior to his election he practised as a lawyer in K (a fictional city), and, in the course of his professional activities, two sets of criminal proceedings were brought against him, one for insulting a lawyer and the other for insulting a public official. As an MP he enjoyed parliamentary immunity. On 23 December 2002 the Karapınar public prosecutor applied to the General Directorate of the Ministry of Justice to have the applicant's parliamentary immunity lifted for the purposes of the criminal proceedings against him for insulting a lawyer. On 17 January 2003 the General Directorate of the Ministry of Justice transmitted the request to the Prime Minister's Office. On 11 April 2003 the K (a fictional city) Assize Court (“the Assize Court”) adopted a decision suspending the criminal proceedings against the applicant for insulting a public official, by virtue of Article 83 of the Constitution (on parliamentary immunity) and Article 253 § 4 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. On 4 December 2003 the Assize Court transmitted the case file to the Ministry of Justice with a view to having the applicant's parliamentary immunity lifted.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (nos. 12345/03) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 November 2001. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr James Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 30 December 2006 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1935 and lives in Zegrze. A. Judicial proceedings 1. Facts before 1 May 1993 In 1988 the applicant’s spouse filed a petition for divorce. The divorce was granted shortly afterwards. On 25 November 1988 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) gave a decision and divided the property. On an unspecified date the applicant appealed. On 8 November 1989 the Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) remitted the case. 2. Facts after 1 May 1993 On 11 March 1999 the District Court again gave a decision. On unspecified dates both parties appealed. On 12 September 1999 the Regional Court dismissed both appeals. On 24 October 1999 the applicant lodged a cassation appeal with the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy). On 15 May 2001 the Supreme Court refused to hear the applicant’s cassation appeal. The applicant submitted that as a consequence of the prolonged proceedings in his case he had been deprived of his property and had to live in a Welfare Home (Dom Pomocy Społecznej). B. Enforcement proceedings On an unspecified date the applicant instituted enforcement proceedings against his spouse who apparently had failed to comply with the final decision on the division of their property. On 7 May 1999 the District Court informed the applicant that the enforcement had proved ineffective. On 10 May 1999 the applicant lodged a complaint with the District Court against the actions taken by the bailiff (skarga na czynności komornika). He submitted that those actions had been incorrect, because the money obtained from the debtor had been distributed wrongly. He also complained about the ineffectiveness of the enforcement. On 22 July 1999 the District Court dismissed his complaint. It held that the order of distribution had been in accordance with the Code of Civil Procedure. As regards the ineffectiveness of the enforcement, the court held that no valuable objects had been found in the debtor’s house which could be sold and used to satisfy the debt. On an unspecified date the applicant appealed. On 22 July 1999 the Regional Court dismissed his appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123456/02) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xanadu, Mr Xanadu Man (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2002. The applicant was represented by Mr Y. Zane, a lawyer practising in Yonder. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 25 September 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in Yonder. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. 1. Destruction of the applicant's property and the determination of damage On 12 March 1995 the applicant's stores and goods were burned and destroyed in the course of an armed clash between members of the State Security Forces and militants from the PKK (the Workers' Party of Kurdistan, an illegal organisation), in the Silopi district of the province of Yonder. On 15 March 1995 the applicant filed a declaratory action before the Silopi Magistrates' Court for an assessment of the damage he had suffered as a result of the clash and the fire. On the same day the Silopi Magistrates' Court appointed an expert to determine the damage. On 17 March 1995 the expert submitted a damage assessment report to the court. The expert noted in his report that his conclusions were based on the applicant's claims since the receipts for some of the goods had been burned as a result of the fire. 2. Compensation proceedings before the Administrative Court a) First set of proceedings 10. On 28 November 1995 the applicant filed an action with the Yonder Administrative Court against the Ministry of Interior and requested compensation for the damage he had suffered. 11. On 30 November 1995 the Yonder Administrative Court dismissed the action on the ground that the applicant had failed to apply to the Ministry of the Interior with his claim. The court reasoned that, under Article 13 of Law no. 2577, an action of this kind could be filed only after the administrative authorities had refused the litigant's request. b) Second set of proceedings 12. On 1 February 1996 the Ministry of the Interior received the case file from the Yonder Administrative Court. The Ministry did not respond to the applicant's request for compensation within the 60-day period prescribed by Law no. 2577. 13. On 3 April 1996 the applicant filed an action with the Yonder Administrative Court and requested compensation for the damage suffered as a result of the destruction of his stores. 14.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Human Rights Organization on 15 November 1995, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 § 1 and Article 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 12345/93) against the State of Europe lodged with the Organization under Article 25 by a European national, Mr John Doe, on 10 July 1993. The Organization’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby Europe recognized the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 § 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant designated the lawyers who would represent him (Rule 30). The lawyers were given leave by the President to use the European language in the written procedure (Rule 27 § 3). Zeller, the elected judge of European nationality (Article 43 of the Convention), and Mr W. Voss, the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 4 (b)). As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 § 6), Mr Voss, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the State of Europe (“the Government”), the applicant’s lawyers and the Delegate of the Organization on the organization of the proceedings (Rules 37 § 1 and 38). In accordance with the decision of the President, who had also given the Government’s representative leave to address the Court in European (Rule 27 § 2), the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Europe, on 22 September 1996. Smith, Head of the Legal Department for the European Commission and European Court of Human Rights, Ministry of Justice, Agent; (b) for the Organization Mr S.T. Wilson, Delegate; (c) for the applicant Mr U.V. Wright, professor at the University of Europe, Mr W.X. Young, of the Europe Bar, Counsel. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 633/03) against the Republic of Poland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 26 November 2002. The Polish Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Y, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 19 April 2005 the President of the Fourth Section Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1959 and lives in a city in Germany. On 25 July 2001 the applicant was arrested by the police. On 26 July 2001 the District Court ordered that the applicant be remanded in custody in view of the reasonable suspicion that, acting in an organised gang, he had been involved in the traffic of human beings and narcotics, had committed robberies and had derived profits from prostitution. The court considered that, given the fact that the applicant had been living in Germany, there was a real risk that he might go into hiding. In addition, it found that the case was complex as it concerned an organised criminal group and that, once released, the applicant might tamper with evidence or otherwise obstruct the proceedings. The applicant appealed against the detention order. However, on 22 August 2001 the Regional Court dismissed the appeal. On 18 October 2001 and 16 January 2002 the Regional Court prolonged the applicant’s detention. The court repeated grounds given previously: the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences, the severity of the anticipated sentence, the complexity of the case and the risk that the applicant might go into hiding as he had no permanent residence in Poland. His appeals against both decisions were dismissed. On 18 February 2002 the applicant and his accomplices were indicted before the Regional Court. On 16 April 2002, the Regional Court again prolonged the applicant’s detention until 31 October 2002. It reiterated the grounds that had been stated in the previous decisions. On 3 and 24 June 2002 the Regional Court dismissed his applications for release reiterating the previously given grounds for detention. On 18 August 2002 the Regional Court held the first hearing. Subsequently, several hearings were held, and the court fined the witnesses who failed to appear. The applicant and his lawyer were present at those hearings. Subsequently, the applicant’s detention on remand was prolonged and his applications for release dismissed. On 18 June 2003 the Court of Appeal, on the application of the Regional Court, further prolonged the applicant’s detention. The court repeated the grounds originally given and stressed the fact that the case concerned an organised criminal gang.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Maria Novak (“the applicant”), on 15 March 1999. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agents, Mr A. Smith and subsequently Mr. B. Jones of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 22 March 2003 the Court decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1925 and lives in Praszka. On 29 March 1991 the applicant lodged a motion with the Oleśno District Court, claiming a division of inheritance and dissolution of co-ownership of a certain property. The court held hearings on: 16 May 1991, 29 August 1991, 30 January 1992, 11 April 1992, 19 May 1992, 26 August 1992, 30 September 1992, 24 February 1993, 8 June 1993 and 29 March 1994. Having regard to the lack of progress in the proceedings, and apparently aiming at obtaining possession of the property by other legal means, on 14 April 1993 the applicant lodged a motion with the Oleśno District Court, claiming acquisitive prescription of half of the property in question. By a decision of 12 May 1994 the Oleśno District Court dismissed her motion. By a decision of 28 September 1994 the Częstochowa Regional Court dismissed her further appeal and upheld the contested decision. Further hearings in the dissolution case were held on 4 June 1998, 30 December 1999, 29 March 2000 and 24 May 2000. The court ordered a number of expert opinions. They were submitted to the court on: 21 December 1991, 6 July 1992, 10 September 1997, 15 May 1998, 17 June 1998, 10 December 1998, 10 February 1999, 18 April 1999, 14 May 1999, 7 October 1999 and 26 November 2000. By a decision of 11 January 2001 the Oleśno District Court stayed the proceedings due to the fact that one of the parties to the proceedings had died. By virtue of the same decision the court resumed the proceedings, having regard to his heirs' request that the proceedings be resumed. On 4 June 2003 the Oleśno District Court gave a judgment on the merits. On 18 December 2003 the Opole Regional Court dismissed the applicant's appeal. By a decision of 30 June 2004 the Supreme Court declined to examine the cassation appeal, considering that it had not been shown that arguable public interest grounds existed which would justify the examination of the appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1001/05) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xanadu, Mr Xanadu Xanadu (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2008. The applicant was represented by Ms Xanadu Xanadu, a lawyer practising in Xanadu. The Government of Xanadu (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 30 August 2010 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, Mr Xanadu Xanadu, is a national of Xanadu who was born in 1975 and is currently serving a prison service in Xanadu. On 10 October 1997 the applicant was taken into police custody during an operation carried out against Zephyr, an illegal organisation. On an unspecified date the applicant was questioned in the absence of a lawyer by police officers, who asked him about his affiliation to Zephyr and events in which he was alleged to have taken part. On 15 October 1997 the applicant was brought before the Y City Public Prosecutor. He confirmed the content of his police statements before the prosecutor in the absence of a lawyer. On the same day, an investigating judge at the Y City Magistrate’s Court ordered the applicant’s pre-trial detention, again in the absence of a lawyer. He accepted the allegations against him and confirmed the statements he had made before the police and the public prosecutor. According to two reports in the case file, dated 12 and 15 October 1997 respectively, the applicant was medically examined by a doctor who noted that there were no signs of physical violence on the applicant’s body. By way of an application dated 31 December 1997, the applicant retracted his statements made before the police and the public prosecutor and requested his release from the X City Public Prosecutor’s office. He maintained that he had been tortured in police custody and that he had been threatened whilst being taken to the public prosecutor. On 28 October 1997 the X City Public Prosecutor lodged an indictment before the X City State Security Court, charging the applicant under Section 146 of the former Xanadu Criminal Code with attempting to undermine the constitutional order of the State. On 30 December 1998 at the first court hearing in the applicant’s case, the applicant retracted his statements made to the police, the public prosecutor and the investigating judge, alleging that they had been made under duress. State Security Courts were abolished on 15 June 2005 by Law no. 5200. The case was accordingly transferred to the X City Assize Court. Throughout the proceedings, the applicant denied all the accusations against him. On 31 May 2006 the first-instance court convicted the applicant as charged. On 10 November 2007 the X City Assize Court once again convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to life imprisonment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of that country, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 April 2001. The government of that country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Richard Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Capital City. The applicant alleges that the criminal proceedings brought against him exceeded a reasonable time, invoking Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 51 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 26 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 25 § 1. On 7 March 2002, the Chamber invited the respondent government to make observations on the applicant's complaints about the length of proceedings and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. By a decision of 5 December 2003, the Court declared the remainder of the application admissible. The applicant and the government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 58 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 58 § 3 in fine). THE FACTS The applicant was born in October 1940 and is resident in Hillside, County X.
