The Government of the country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr John Smith, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant complains, principally, under Articles 8 and 13 of the Convention that the interception of her pager messages by the police and subsequent reference to them at her trial amounted to an unjustified interference with her private life and correspondence which was not “in accordance with the law” and in respect of which there was no remedy under the country’s law. The application was originally allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. On 27 June 2000 the Court declared the applicant’s complaint under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention inadmissible. On 29 May 2001 it declared her complaints under Articles 8 and 13 admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, to dispense with a hearing (Rule 59 § 2 in fine). The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. Between August 1995 and the applicant’s arrest on 21 January 1996, she was the target of surveillance by the police. Using a “clone” of the applicant’s pager, the police were able to intercept messages sent to her. The pager system used by the applicant and intercepted by the police operated as follows: The sender, whether in the country or overseas, would telephone the pager bureau in the country via the public telephone network. The pager operator would key the message into a computer and read it back to the sender to confirm its accuracy. The computer message was transmitted via the public telephone system to the pager terminal, from where it was relayed by radio to one of four regional base stations and thence, again by radio, simultaneously to the applicant’s and the police’s clone pagers, which displayed the message in text. The applicant was arrested and charged with conspiracy to supply a controlled drug.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 10001/01) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2001. The applicant was represented by Ms Q. Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr A. Brown of a government department, a city. By a partial decision of 15 October 2002 the Court decided to adjourn the applicant’s complaint and to declare inadmissible the remainder of the application. Subsequently, under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, the Chamber to which the case had been allocated decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1951 and lives in a county. His wife died on 1 January 1996. On 5 May 1996 the applicant made a claim for a benefit to a government department. On 23 November 2001 he was informed that his claim could not be accepted because there was no basis in the country’s law allowing widowers to claim this benefit. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such benefit was payable to widowers under the country’s law.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against a country in Europe (hereinafter referred to as "the country") lodged with an international human rights organization (hereinafter referred to as "the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by Mr John Doe ("the applicant") on 1 October 2000. The applicant was represented before the Court by Ms A. Smith, a solicitor practising in a city in Europe. The country Government ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Jones of a foreign ministry. The applicant complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that, because he was a man, he was denied social security benefits equivalent to those received by widows. On 10 June 2000 the Court decided to communicate this application. On 6 February 2001, after obtaining the parties' observations, the Court declared this application admissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in a region in Europe. His wife died in February 2000, leaving two children born in 1985 and 1989. His claim for widows' benefits was made on 12 February 2000 and was rejected on 17 August 2000 on the ground that he was not entitled to widows' benefits because he was not a woman. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no security benefits were payable to widowers under country law. COMPLAINTS The applicant complained that social security legislation in the country discriminated against him on grounds of sex, in breach of Article 14 of the Convention taken in conjunction with both Article 8 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court within the three-month period by a regional human rights organization and a national government, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 21928/93) against a national state lodged with the organization under Article 25 (art. 25) on a date in March 1993 by a national, Mr X. Y. The organization’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby the national state recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46); the government’s application referred to Article 48 (art. 48). The object of the request and of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent state of its obligations under Article 5 para. 4 (art. 5-4) of the Convention. The organization further sought a decision as to whether there had been a breach of Article 14 (art. 14) of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the case of X v. the national state (no. 56/1994/503/585) should be heard by the same Chamber (Rule 21 para. 6) and that a joint hearing should be held. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr Z, the elected judge of national nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr A, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On a date in January 1995, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr B, Mr C, Mr D, Mr E, Mrs F, Mr G and Mr H (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43). As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5), Mr A, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the government, the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the organization on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the government’s memorial on a date in April 1995 and the applicant’s memorial on a date in April. The Secretary to the organization informed the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in a human rights building, a city, on a date in September 1995. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 21831/03) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by fourteen Turkish nationals, Mr. A. B., Mr. C. D., Mr. E. F., Mr. G. H., Mr. I. J., Mr. K. L., Mr. M. N., Ms. O. P., Ms. Q. R., Ms. S. T., Ms. U. V., Ms. W. X., Ms. Y. Z., and Mr. A. B. (“the applicants”), on 19 June 2003. The applicants were represented by Ms. C. D., Mr. E. F., and Mr. G. H., lawyers practising in a city. The Turkish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicants complained of an unjustified interference with their right to freedom of assembly and unfairness of the criminal proceedings against them in violation of Articles 6, 9, 10, and 11 of the Convention. On 16 April 2007 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1975, 1964, 1982, 1976, 1983, 1978, 1961, 1947, 1955, 1975, 1979, 1953, 1952, and 1976 respectively and live in a city. On 31 July 2000 the applicants, together with several other persons, gathered in a public park in a city in protest against F-type prisons and the events which had occurred in a prison (violent clashes had taken place between the detainees and security forces on 27 July 2000). The participants wanted to read out a press statement in order to express their concerns about F-type prisons and the events in the prison. Police officers warned the crowd over a megaphone that the demonstration was illegal under Law no. 2911 on Meetings and Demonstration Marches. The group ignored the police warning. The police officers then arrested twenty-four persons, including the applicants, and took them into custody. It appears from the newspaper articles submitted by the applicants that the police officers used force in order to disperse the protesters. As a result, some of the protestors were injured and a number of them were arrested by the police officers. According to the arrest report, drawn up and signed by the police officers, the applicants were demonstrating with protest banners in their hands. After having warned them to desist, the police arrested the protesters who continued demonstrating. It was also noted in the arrest report that three police officers, who had been injured during the clash with the demonstrators at the time of the arrest, had had to be taken to hospital. The medical reports stated that the police officers were unfit for work for two days.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 10001/07) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Andria (“the applicant”), on 15 January 2008. The applicant was represented by Mr X.Y. Zan, a lawyer practising in Andria. On 12 June 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1942 and lives in Andria. In 2004 the General Directorate of Highways seized a plot of land belonging to the applicant without any formal expropriation, for the construction of a highway. The applicant brought an action before the Civil Court to obtain compensation for the de facto expropriation of his property. He requested 5,000 local currency units (LCU) as compensation from the court and reserved his right to increase this claim in due course. On 15 June 2006 the Civil Court awarded the applicant 5,000 LCU as compensation for the de facto expropriation of his land, as requested, plus interest. The applicant initiated execution proceedings before the Execution Office to obtain that amount (file no. 2009/1234). On 13 March 2007 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court. The applicant subsequently brought an additional action before the Civil Court to obtain further compensation for his land in the light of the expert report obtained during the previous proceedings, which had valued the land at a rate higher than that initially requested by him. On 24 May 2007 the Civil Court awarded the applicant 60,000 LCU, plus interest. The applicant initiated another set of execution proceedings before the Execution Office to obtain the amount awarded (file no. 2007/5678). On 23 October 2007 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the Civil Court. On 24 March and 13 November 2009 the administration paid 8,000 LCU and 90,000 LCU respectively in respect of the debt arising from the actions before the Execution Office. According to the information provided by the applicant, there has been no outstanding debt in the execution files.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 November 2006. The applicant was represented by Mr Y. Smith, a lawyer practising in Luxembourg. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Z. Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 30 June 2008 the President of the Fifth Section of the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in Gdynia. A. Criminal proceedings against the applicant and his detention on remand On 5 November 2002 the applicant was arrested in Barcelona, Spain, under an international search and arrest warrant on suspicion of having committed several offences of fraud, forgery, perjury, uttering threats, robbery and kidnapping, while acting in an organised criminal group. On 15 January 2003 the Central Investigating Court in Madrid no. 4 (Juzgado Central de Instrucción) granted a request for the applicant’s extradition. On 30 June 2003 the applicant was brought to Europe. On 1 July 2003 the Warsaw District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) remanded him in custody until 30 September 2003. It relied on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged. It further referred to the likelihood of a severe sentence of imprisonment being imposed on the applicant and to the risk that he might go into hiding. As regards the latter, the court stressed that this had happened before and had given rise to the issue of the international search and arrest warrant and to the extradition proceedings. On 22 December 2003 the Warsaw District Court extended the applicant’s detention until 31 December 2003. It relied on the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences in question, the severity of the anticipated sentence, the fear that he might tamper with evidence and the complexity of the case. The applicant appealed. On 31 December 2003 the Warsaw Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) dismissed an appeal lodged by the applicant. It repeated the grounds previously given for his detention. The applicant maintains that when he was detained between 30 June 2003 and 1 April 2004 he was forced to testify, subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment and that the conditions of his detention were poor. Moreover, he maintains that he was deprived of contact with his family. On 20 March 2004 the applicant was indicted before the Warsaw District Court. The bill of indictment listed several charges of fraud, forgery, perjury, robbery and kidnapping brought against thirteen accused, committed in the context of an organised criminal group.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court on a date in 1992 by a body ("the body") and on a date in 1993 by a government of a country ("the government"), within the three-month period laid down in Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. The body’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby the country recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The object of the request and of the government’s application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent state of its obligations under Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mrs A B C, the elected judge of a nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr D E F, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On a date in 1993 the Vice-President, Mr G H I, drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the other seven members, namely Mr J K L, Mr M N O, Mr P Q R, Mr S T U, Mr V W X, Mr Y Z A and Mr B C D (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43). As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5), Mr E F G, through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the government, the applicant’s lawyer and the Delegate of the body on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the government’s memorial on a date in 1993 and the applicant’s memorial on a date in 1993. On various dates between a date in 1993 and a date in 1993 the body filed a number of documents which the Registrar had requested from it on the President’s instructions. On a date in 1993 the Secretary to the body had informed the Registrar that the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in a building, in a city, on a date in 1993. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. There appeared before the Court: for the government Mr X Y Z, Assistant Under-Secretary for Legal Affairs, Ministry for Foreign Affairs, Agent, Mr A B C, Under-Secretary, Ministry of Justice, Adviser; for the body Mr D E F, Delegate; for the applicant Mr G H I, advokat, Counsel, Ms J K L, Assistant.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xanadu, Mr Xanadu X (“the applicant”), on 1 October 1995. The applicant was represented by Mr Y and Mrs Z, lawyers practising in Xanadu. The government of Xanadu (“the government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant complained that he had been subjected to ill-treatment while in police custody. He further alleged that he had been deprived of his right to legal assistance during questioning by the police, the public prosecutor and the judge who ordered his detention on remand. The applicant invoked Articles 3 and 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 7 October 2003, the Court declared the complaint under Article 3 of the Convention admissible. The applicant and the government each filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1). On 1 November 2004 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). On 10 October 2006 the Court decided to examine the merits of the complaint under Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) of the Convention at the same time as its admissibility under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Xanadu. A. The alleged ill-treatment of the applicant in police custody On 12 December 1994 the applicant and five other persons were arrested by police officers from the anti-terror branch of the Xanadu Security Directorate in the house of one of the arrestees, M.O., in the course of a police operation carried out against the PKK. Between 12 and 27 December 1994 the applicant was detained in the Xanadu Security Directorate. The applicant alleges that, while there, he was blindfolded and forced to listen to the cries of other detainees being tortured. He was threatened with torture and forced to admit that he was a member of the PKK.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against a country in Europe lodged with an international organization under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms by a national, Mr John Doe ("the applicant"), on 10 July 1996. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Brown, a lawyer at Brown Consulting, solicitors practising in a town in a region. The Government of a country in Europe ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Green, of the Foreign Ministry. The applicant, a discretionary life prisoner who had been released on licence and recalled to prison, made two complaints under Article 5 § 4 of the Convention. He complained, firstly, that he had been denied a fair hearing before the Parole Board on 8 November 1996 and, secondly, that he had not had his detention reviewed until just over two years later. On 22 October 1998 the organization decided to give notice of the application to the Government and invited them to submit their observations on its admissibility and merits. The Government submitted their observations on 19 March 1999, after an extension of the time-limit fixed for that purpose, to which the applicant replied on 4 May 1999. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 7 March 2000 the Court declared the complaint concerning the fairness of the Parole Board hearing inadmissible. It declared admissible the complaint concerning the delay between reviews [ Note by the Registry. The Court's decision is obtainable from the Registry.]. The Registrar received the applicant's and the Government's further comments on 19 May 2000 and 7 June 2000 respectively. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE In April 1970 the applicant, then aged 21, was convicted of manslaughter, qualified as such on the grounds of diminished responsibility, and sentenced to life imprisonment. Medical evidence adduced at the trial showed that the applicant suffered from a mental abnormality induced by alcohol. On 27 July 1993 the applicant was released on life licence for the third time subject to the condition, amongst others, that he should comply with any reasonable requirement imposed by his probation officer for the treatment of his alcohol problem. He had been recalled to prison twice previously and had since been transferred to open prison conditions in 1989. On 1 July 1996 the police were called to the home of the applicant's partner, M., who is a deaf mute. She was taken to hospital where she received treatment for injuries to her face and back. On 2 July 1996 the Secretary of State revoked the applicant's licence and recalled him to prison.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Anonym (“the applicant”), on 15 May 2000. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr John Doe of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 10 June 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate ex officio the issue of the possible monitoring of the applicant's correspondence to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1972 and lives in Warsaw, Europe. A. The criminal proceedings against the applicant The applicant was the owner of a company in Berlin (Innovative Business Development). On 10 May 1999 he was arrested on suspicion of fraud. On 12 May 1999 the Berlin District Court (Local Court) ordered his detention on remand. On 22 June 1999 the applicant began serving a 4 years and 11 months' prison sentence, which resulted from another conviction. On 10 January 2000 the Berlin District Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to 4 years and 7 months' imprisonment. On 19 October 2001 the Berlin Regional Court upheld the applicant's conviction. On 10 May 2002 the applicant was again arrested on suspicion of fraud. On 11 May 2002 the Osnabrück District Court ordered his detention on remand. On 17 September 2002 the Osnabrück District Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to 4 years' imprisonment. Upon the applicant's appeal, the Osnabrück Regional Court amended the first‐instance judgment on 31 January 2003. The applicant filed a cassation appeal. On 2 March 2004 the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant's cassation appeal as manifestly ill‐founded. B. The monitoring of the applicant's correspondence At the time of lodging his application with the Court the applicant had been detained on remand in the course of criminal proceedings against him. At the same time, as of 22 June 1999 he was serving a prison sentence imposed in the course of another set of criminal proceedings against him. On 7 June 2000, the Registry of the Court received the applicant's letter dated 13 April 2000. Both the letter and the envelope bear a stamp “Censored on... judge” and no signature (Cenzurowano dn... sędzia.). The envelope had been opened and then sealed with adhesive tape. On 14 February 2001, the Registry of the Court received another letter from the applicant (dated 30 December 2000). It was delivered in an envelope bearing a stamp “Censored on ... judge” and no signature (Cenzurowano dn... sędzia.). It also bears a red stamp “Remand Centre in Berlin” (Areszt Śledczy w Berlinie).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/11) against the Kingdom of Norway lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr Ivan Petrovic and Mrs Maria Petrovic, a married couple, and their sons Daniel and Marko, Ivan Petrovic and (“the applicants”), on 20 April 2011. The applicants were represented by Mr T. Andersson, a lawyer practising in Oslo. The Norwegian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms E. Jensen, of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicants complained that deportation of the first, second and fourth applicants to Albania or Macedonia would be in violation of Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention. On 28 April 2011 the President of the Third Section decided to apply Rule 39 of the Rules of Court, indicating to the Government that it was desirable in the interests of the parties and the proper conduct of the proceedings not to deport the first, second and fourth applicants until further notice. On 15 November 2011 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). On 1 March 2012 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1 of the rules of Court) and the above application was assigned to the newly composed Sixth Section. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The first applicant is Mr Ivan Petrovic born in 1970, the second applicant is Mrs Maria Petrovic born in 1972, and the third and fourth applicants are their sons, born in 1992 and 1995. They are currently in Norway. A. Background and proceedings before the national authorities The applicants are of Roma descent and lived in the village of Albania Polje. Following the outbreak of war in 2000, the first applicant refused to participate in the fighting and hid from the armed forces. Due to this, the other applicants were subjected to threats and beatings by Macedonian military. Finally, they were driven out of their home by Albanian militia. They fled by train to Suva Do, another village in Albania. On their way, they lost a bag containing their passports and identification papers. They hid at a friend’s home, where they remained completely isolated from the world until they travelled to Norway in 2007. They had felt harassed in Albania because of their being Roma, but they had not been subjected to any persecution, allegedly due to their isolation. They applied for asylum and permanent residence permits on arrival. On 15 March 2009 the Migration Board (Migrationsverket) rejected their applications. First, the Board found that the applicants had not proved their identity. By submitting an UNMIK certificate on their residency in Albania Polje, they had made it plausible that they were from Albania or Macedonia.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 26268/08) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms X (“the applicant”), on 16 May 2008. The applicant was represented by Ms Y, lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the refusal by the domestic courts to allow her to bear only her maiden name unjustifiably interfered with her right to respect for her private life under Article 8 of the Convention. She claimed that the fact that the law allowed married men but not married women to bear their own surname after marriage constituted discrimination on grounds of sex and was incompatible with Article 14 of the Convention. On 22 October 2010 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in a city. On 30 March 2005 the applicant, who is a lawyer, got married and took her husband’s surname pursuant to a law. She, however, kept her maiden name in front of her husband’s surname as provided for by the same law. On 9 May 2007 the applicant brought proceedings before a court for permission to use only her maiden name, “X”. On 18 July 2007 the court dismissed the applicant’s request on the ground that, under the law, married women had to bear their husband’s name throughout their marriage and were not entitled to use their maiden name alone. The applicant appealed. On 22 November 2007 the highest court upheld the judgment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against the Republic of X (the "Republic") lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a Turkish national, Ms X ("the applicant"), on 25 April 1996. The applicant was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in Z, Mr A and Ms B of the Human Rights Organization in W, as well as by Mr C, Mr D and Ms E, lawyers practising in W. The Republic did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant complained that she was detained for 11 days and was not brought before a judge within a reasonable time. She invoked Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. Mr X, the judge elected in respect of the Republic, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 28). The Republic accordingly appointed Mr Y to sit as an ad hoc judge (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 29 § 1). By a decision of 30 April 2002 the Court declared the application partly admissible, retaining the applicant’s complaint under Article 5 § 3 of the Convention. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The applicant and the Republic each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1951 and lives in X. On 10 November 1995 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of PKK membership and brought to the Intelligence and Anti-Terrorism Headquarters in Y. On 21 November 1995 the applicant was brought before the prosecutor at the State Security Court in Y who ordered her detention on remand. She was taken to the High Security Prison in Y. The applicant was released on bail at the first hearing before the State Security Court in Y on 15 February 1996.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”) on 15 July 2004. The applicant was represented by Ms. Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in Berlin. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. Michael Brown of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that he had been deprived of his right of access to a court, contrary to Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. On 12 August 2008 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). The President also gave priority to the application, pursuant to Rule 41 of the Rules of the Court. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1935 and lives in Berlin. In 1998 the applicant instituted civil proceedings in which he asked for the division of his late parents’ marital property. The applicant’s mother died in the 1960s and he was her heir. The applicant’s father died in 1993 and his second wife inherited after him according to his last will. The applicant claimed that his parents’ marital property included a collection of 200 valuable paintings worth approximately 350,000 euros (EUR). The applicant’s father’s second wife contested the fact that the paintings belonged to the estate in question and submitted that they were her own assets. On 24 December 1998 the applicant was exempted from court fees. In 2002 the other party to the proceedings, the second wife of the applicant’s late father, died and her daughter joined the proceedings as her heir. On 18 July 2004 the Berlin District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) decided of its own motion to order the preparation of an expert opinion regarding the value and origin of the paintings allegedly acquired during the applicant’s parents’ marriage. The court found that the applicant described many of the paintings, some of which had been in the possession of the other party and whose existence and ownership had been contested, as belonging to his parents. The assessment of his submissions required special knowledge concerning the authors of the paintings, their description and authenticity. It had thus been impossible to assess those issues without the assistance of an expert. The court considered that since the applicant had initiated the proceedings he should bear the costs of the opinion and ordered him to pay EUR 4,000 (approximately 1,000 euros (EUR)) as an advance on the costs of the expert opinion. On 22 August 2004 the applicant applied for an exemption from court fees. He submitted that he was a pensioner and was receiving an old‐age pension of EUR 500.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/08) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Andrian nationals, Ms Xena Andria and Mr Yon Andria (“the applicants”), on 12 May 2007. The applicants were represented by Ms Zeta Andria, a lawyer practising in Andria. The second applicant was granted legal aid. The Andrian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 12 June 2009 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1978 and 1981 and live in Andria and Andria respectively. On 1 May 2006 a demonstration was held in Andria to celebrate Labour Day. The applicants, who were participants in this demonstration, claimed that they were attacked by police officers from the Rapid Response Force (Çevik Kuvvet) during the demonstration. According to the applicants, the police officers initially targeted the first applicant. When she fell to the ground, the second applicant tried to shield her, at which point he was also attacked, sprayed with pepper gas, kicked and beaten with truncheons. They submitted a photograph in which the second applicant is covering a person on the ground a couple of metres behind a group of police officers holding truncheons, and an officer is bending down towards them. The photograph was published on 2 May 2006 in a local newspaper. The applicants were not arrested. On the same day, after the demonstration, the applicants applied to the Human Rights Centre at the Andria Bar Association with a view to requesting legal aid in order to lodge their complaints against the police. At the Andria Bar Association, photographs showing their injuries were taken. On 2 May 2006 the applicants lodged a complaint with the Andria public prosecutor against the police officers involved in the incidents. They complained that they had been subjected to ill-treatment by the police and requested to be referred to the Forensic Medicine Institute and to a hospital. In their complaint they noted that their representative had been appointed by the Andria Bar Association to act on their behalf. In support of their complaint the applicants submitted to the public prosecutor’s office the aforementioned photograph published on 2 May 2006. On the same day the Andria public prosecutor took statements from the applicants regarding their complaints. The first applicant stated that she had attended the demonstration with the trade unions and had been attacked by police officers who wanted to disperse certain demonstrators. She further stated that the second applicant had also been beaten while he was attempting to shield her from the police attacks. The second applicant made a statement along the same lines.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Ali Anadol (“the applicant”), on 15 September 1999. The applicant was represented by Mr N. Yilmaz, a lawyer practising in Konya. The Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 31 May 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1955 and was detained in the Konya prison, in Konya at the time of the application. On 11 October 1998 following receipt of information that the applicant was in possession of narcotic substances, police officers from the Konya Security Directorate arrested the applicant, his son and one of the applicant's employees, X.Y., in the applicant's house. During the search of the applicant's house and farm, a certain amount of cannabis was found. On 12 October 1998 the suspects were brought before the Konya Magistrates' Court who ordered their detention on remand. On 14 October 1998, the Konya Magistrates' Court sent the case file to the public prosecutor's office at the Diyarbakır State Security Court holding that the case concerned the prosecution of organised drug trafficking. On 24 October 1998 the public prosecutor at the Diyarbakır State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicant and the two other suspects. The public prosecutor charged them under Article 403 § 5 of the Criminal Code of being in possession of hashish with the aim of trafficking. X.Y. was also charged with the consummation of hashish. On 26 May 1999 the Diyarbakır State Security Court convicted the applicant and X.Y. The applicant was sentenced to three years and four months' imprisonment. On 5 October 1999 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first-instance court. On 24 November 1999 the Diyarbakır State Security Court once again convicted the applicant and his co-accused and sentenced them to six years and three months' imprisonment. On 15 April 2000 the Court of Cassation again quashed the first-instance court's judgment, holding that the applicant's and his co-accused's defence rights had not been respected as they had not been informed about the date of the hearing. On 15 June 1999 the Diyarbakır State Security Court convicted the applicant and his co-accused and sentenced them to six years and three months' imprisonment. It also ordered their release from detention having regard to the time that they had spent in prison. On 20 April 2000 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of the first-instance court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alex Anderson (“the applicant”), on 15 March 2006. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/09) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 27 December 2007. The applicant was represented by Mr X Y, a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their then Agent, Mr Z W of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He further complained about the length of criminal proceedings against him. On 17 November 2010 the application was communicated to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1957 and lives in a city. A. First set of criminal proceedings. On an unknown date in 1991 the applicant was charged with aggravated robbery. In 1993 the Regional Prosecutor stayed the investigation as the applicant’s whereabouts were not known. In July 1993 the applicant was arrested and began serving a prison sentence which had been imposed in 1982. On 14 March 1994 a bill of indictment was lodged with the Regional Court. The applicant was charged with robbery. The proceedings were stayed on 6 March 1996 in view of the applicant’s health. In December 1996 he underwent spinal surgery. The trial was resumed on 28 September 1997. The applicant failed to appear at some hearings in 2003, however the trial court found that this was because he had been serving a prison sentence imposed in another set of criminal proceedings. On 5 April 2004 the charges against the applicant and several co-accused were severed and dealt with in a separate set of proceedings. The applicant failed to appear at a hearing held on 30 June 2005. On the same date the Regional Court issued a wanted notice in respect of the applicant and ordered that he be arrested and remanded in custody. On 18 July 2005 the court severed the charges against the applicant, to be dealt with in a separate set of the proceedings, and on the same date stayed the proceedings as the applicant was in hiding. The applicant was arrested on 18 May 2007. He was placed in a detention centre on 21 May 2007. On 11 June 2007 the Regional Court resumed the proceedings against the applicant. In the course of the proceedings, the applicant’s detention was extended on 13 August and 17 December 2007 and 26 March, 21 April, 21 July and 26 September 2008. In their decisions on the matter the authorities relied on the original grounds given for holding him in custody.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 3 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 September 2005. The applicant was represented by Legal Firm, solicitors practising in a city. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr A. B. of the Foreign Ministry, a city. The applicant alleged that there had been no adequate investigation into allegations of collusion and/or involvement by security forces in his being seriously injured, nor any effective remedy for the same. He invoked Articles 2 and 13 of the Convention. By a decision of 1 March 2007 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1), to which they each responded with further written comments (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1925 and lives in Greenfield, a county. A. The attack on the applicant and the initial investigation At about 10.30 p.m., shortly after closing time, on 7 June 1977, a police officer in the National Security Force (“NSF”) drove a car, stolen by NSF Reserve Constable Laurence Smith, up to the Oak Bar, a public house. The applicant was leaving the bar at that time. He was shot twice in the stomach by Smith, who then placed a 10lb gelignite bomb against the door of the pub. The detonator exploded but the bomb failed to explode. At the later trial a reserve police constable, William Jones, stated that shots were fired by his companions at the injured man on the ground and then he fired a number of shots through the window of the bar. Bullet strike marks were later found around the dart board inside the bar, where there had been seventeen people. No-one else was physically injured. The applicant was taken to hospital in an ambulance and police attended the scene, sealing off the area while an army technical officer examined the explosive device and ensured that it was in a safe condition. A Scene of Crime Officer examined the scene, took possession of material associated with the bomb and a gun recovered from a burnt out car found approximately one mile away, which police linked to the attack. Photographs of the bar were taken and maps prepared. B. The investigations concerning Jones and Weir The investigation did not close and became active again in 1979, when a priest Father James Brown was abducted by paramilitaries intending to use him as a hostage vis-à-vis the IRA.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Novak (“the applicant”), on 15 March 2000. The applicant was represented by Mr B. Smith, a lawyer practising in Berlin, Europe. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Charles Brown, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that his right to a “hearing within a reasonable time” had not been respected. The application was allocated to the Fifth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2002 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fifth Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 15 October 2003 the Court declared the application admissible. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in Berlin, Europe. The applicant was a manager of the Berlin health resort. On 15 May 2000 he filed an action with the Berlin Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki), in which he requested that a certain C.Q. (“the defendant”) be ordered to stop spreading information damaging to the good name of the applicant and to retract in the press his defamatory statements. Subsequently, the court held hearings on 20 July and 5 September 2000. On 3 October 2000 the court held a hearing. It heard a witness and decided to stay the proceedings until the completion of proceedings concerning the applicant’s dismissal from the position of manager. On 27 December 2001 the dismissal proceedings were terminated. On 30 January 2002 the applicant requested the court to resume the defamation proceedings. On 7 December 2002 the trial court resumed the proceedings. On 5 March 2003 the court adjourned a hearing, because of the lack of the defendant’s pleadings in the case file. On 11 August 2003 the applicant extended his claim. On 21 October 2004 the court held a hearing. On 6 December 2005 the court adjourned a hearing at the defendant’s request. On 24 January 2006 the court closed the examination of the case and announced that the judgment would be delivered on 7 February 2006. On 6 February 2006 the court reopened the examination of the case and decided that the defendant would be heard in Berlin. On 19 February 2006 the court heard the defendant. On 28 February 2006 the Berlin Regional Court gave judgment. It ordered the defendant to retract his statements concerning the applicant in certain newspapers at his own expense. On 8 August 2006 the applicant received a copy of the judgment. Subsequently, the defendant lodged an appeal against that judgment.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Smith (“the applicant”), on 15 July 2004. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr John Doe of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 7 October 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant's detention to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Berlin. He is currently serving a prison sentence in Munich Prison. On 29 June 2002 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of several counts of fraud. On 30 June 2002 the Berlin District Court remanded him in custody, relying on the reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offence in question. It also considered that keeping the applicant in detention was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings, given the risk that he might go into hiding (since he did not have any permanent place of residence). The court also stressed the severity of the anticipated sentence (up to ten years of imprisonment) and the fact that the applicant had a criminal record. Later, several members of an organised crime group were detained and charged in connection with the investigation against the applicant. Certain witnesses were granted special status. The prosecutor called, inter alia, two State's witnesses and several anonymous witnesses. Several confrontations between the suspects and witnesses took place. Several expert opinions were ordered, namely an expert opinion on ballistics, an expert opinion as to the identification number of a vehicle, and several psychiatric opinions regarding some of the suspects. The applicant's appeal against the detention order, his subsequent appeals against decisions prolonging his detention and all his numerous applications for release and appeals against refusals to release him were all unsuccessful. On 1 August 2002 the Berlin District Court decided that the applicant should be detained in connection with another set of criminal proceedings instituted against him by the District Prosecutor in Berlin (case no. X 1K 856/03). On 14 November 2002 the Berlin Regional Prosecutor decided to amend the charges against the applicant. He was suspected of several counts of fraud committed while acting in an organised criminal gang. On 19 September 2002 the applicant's detention was extended until 28 December 2002. The court relied on a strong suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences in question, which was supported by evidence from witnesses and experts. Further, the court attached importance to the grave nature of those offences.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/96) against the Republic of X (a fictional country) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of X, Mr Ali Yılmaz (“the applicant”), on 21 November 1995. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X Y Z (“the applicant”), on 15 August 2005. On an unspecified date the Land Registry Commission attached to the General Directorate of Land Registration conducted a land registry survey of plots of land in Belen village in the Ereğli district of Zonguldak. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Andorran nationals, Mr Alvaro Verde and Mr Mariano Verde (“the applicants”), on 10 May 2003. The applicants were represented by Mr Carlos Marín, a lawyer practising in Andorra. The Andorran Government (“the Government”) are represented by their agent. On 5 October 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to notify the Government of the applicants’ complaint concerning the non-communication to them of the submissions of the Principal Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1980 and 1985 respectively and live in Andorra. On 29 May 2001 the applicants were taken into police custody. On 1 June 2001 the applicants were brought before the investigating judge, who ordered their detention on remand. On 4 June 2001 the Andorran State Security Court public prosecutor filed an indictment against the applicants. He accused the first applicant of aiding and abetting an illegal organisation, and the second applicant of being a member of an illegal organisation. On 14 October 2001 the Andorran State Security Court found the applicants guilty as charged and sentenced each of them to ten months’ imprisonment and a fine. On 7 December 2001 the Principal Public Prosecutor at the Court of Cassation submitted his written opinion on the merits of the appeal. He advised that the appeal be rejected and that the first-instance judgment be upheld. On 25 January 2002 the Court of Cassation quashed the first-instance court’s judgment on the ground that the applicants should have been sanctioned under Article 169 of the Criminal Code for aiding and abetting an illegal armed organisation. On 17 May 2002 the Andorran State Security Court adhered to the reasoning of the Court of Cassation and convicted the applicants pursuant to Article 169 of the Criminal Code. On 13 November 2002 the Principal Public Prosecutor submitted his written opinion on the merits of the case and stated that the Court of Cassation should uphold the judgment of the State Security Court. On 28 November 2002, the Court of Cassation, in conformity with the opinion of the Principal Public Prosecutor, upheld the first instance judgment.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Human Rights Commission (“the Commission“) on 19 April 1991, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 10533/83) against the State in question lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by Mr X Y Z, a national of a European country, on 27 November 1978. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby the State in question recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Articles 3, 5 (paras. 1, 3 and 4), 8, 10 and 13 (art. 3, art. 5-1, art. 5-3, art. 5-4, art. 8, art. 10, art. 13). In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him (Rule 30). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr A B C, the elected judge of a European nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr D E F, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On 23 April 1991, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr G H I, Mr J K L, Mr M N O, Mr P Q R, Mr S T U, Mr V W X and Mr Y Z A (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43). Mr B C D and Mr E F G, substitute judges, subsequently replaced Mr L K J and Mr R M C, who were unable to take part in the further consideration of the case (Rules 22 para. 1 and 24 para. 1). Mr R E F assumed the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5) and, through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the State in question (“the State“), the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant on the organisation of the procedure (Rule 37 para. 1 and Rule 38). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the applicant’s memorial, which incorporated his claims for just satisfaction (Article 50 of the Convention) (art. 50), on 16 October and 20 December. On 20 June the State in question informed him that they would not be submitting a memorial. On 22 October 1991 Mr R E F gave the applicant leave to use the German language (Rule 27 para. 3). In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 21 April 1992. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against the Republic of Xana in an application (no. 12345/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Xana Yezilur (“the applicant”), on 28 May 2006. The applicant was represented by Mr Zana Talay, a lawyer practising in Yezir. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 11 October 2008 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1979 and lives in Batam. On 13 November 1996 the applicant was taken into custody by police officers from the anti-terror branch of Istanbul Security Directorate on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation. On 26 November 1996 she was brought before the investigating judge at the Istanbul State Security Court, who ordered her detention on remand. On 30 December 1996 the Istanbul State Security Court Public Prosecutor declared a lack of jurisdiction and transferred the case file to the Yezir State Security Court. On 31 January 1997 the Public Prosecutor at the Yezir State Security Court filed an indictment with that court accusing her, inter alia, of membership of an illegal armed organisation and of involvement in activities that undermined the constitutional order of the State. The prosecution requested that the applicant be sentenced pursuant to Article 125 of the Criminal Code. The trial commenced before the Yezir State Security Court. In the subsequent hearings, the court refused to release the applicant on account of the nature of the alleged offence and the state of evidence. On 13 July 2002 the applicant submitted a petition to the Yezir State Security Court, alleging that she had been ill-treated during police custody. The case against the applicant continued before the Yezir State Security Court until 8 April 2005 when, following a constitutional amendment, State Security Courts were abolished. Thereafter, the applicant's case was transferred to the Yezir Assize Court. On 2 November 2004 the applicant was released pending trial. On 27 March 2005 the Yezir Assize Court declared its lack of jurisdiction and transferred the applicant's case to the Yezir Juvenile Court, holding that the applicant had been a minor at the time of the events. On an unspecified date, the Yezir Juvenile Court also declared its non-jurisdiction and the case file was then transferred to the Batam Assize Court. 10 May 2005 the Batam Assize Court declared a lack of jurisdiction and transmitted the case file to the Court of Appeals to resolve the jurisdictional conflict. On 18 September 2006 the Court of Appeals decided that the case should be heard by the Batam Assize Court. On 5 November 2007 the Batam Assize Court acquitted the applicant of the charges against her.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alexan Derian (“the applicant”), on 15 April 2010. The applicant was represented by Mr J. Smith, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Republic of Andria (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his right of access to court was breached by the domestic court’s refusal of his legal aid request. On 30 June 2011 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1988 and lives in Andria. In 2009, during his military service, the applicant was discharged from the army as he was diagnosed with a psychotic illness by the Andria Military Hospital. Subsequently, on 8 November 2009 he initiated compensation proceedings, claiming that he had become ill during his military service as a result of the degrading treatment he had been subjected to in the army. He claimed that he had been healthy before and that the Ministry of Defence had failed to provide medical treatment for his condition. The applicant requested a total of 160,000 local currency units (LCUs) (approximately 90,000 euros (EUR) at the time) in both pecuniary and non-pecuniary damages, submitting the medical records from the Andria Military Hospital in support of his claims. He also requested legal aid for the court fees, presenting a certificate from the office of the headman (muhtar) attesting to his poverty. On 29 November 2009 the Supreme Military Administrative Court rejected the applicant’s legal aid request, after having stated that pursuant to the Code on Civil Procedure, a legal aid request must be supported by proof that the case is well-founded and that the plaintiff does not have the means to pay the required court fees. The court concluded that the requirements were not met in the applicant’s case. On 3 December 2009 the court informed the applicant that he was to pay a total of 2,500 local currency units (approximately 1,400 euros) in court fees within thirty days for the proceedings to be continued. On 5 March 2010 the Supreme Military Administrative Court decided to discontinue the compensation proceedings because the applicant had not paid the necessary court fees.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 September 1999. The applicant was represented by Ms Q. Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr R. Brown of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, a city. By a partial decision of 15 October 1999 the Court decided to adjourn the applicant’s complaint in relation to his claims for Widow’s Benefits and Widows’ Bereavement Allowance and to declare the remainder of the application inadmissible. Subsequently, under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, the Chamber to which the case had been allocated, decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1946 and lives in a region. His wife died on 27 February 1999 having no children. On around 4 April 1999 the applicant applied for benefits equivalent to those to which a widow, whose husband had died in similar circumstances to those of his wife, would have been entitled, namely a Widow’s Payment and a Widow’s Pension, payable under the Social Security and Benefits Act 1992 (“the 1992 Act”). He was informed on 25 April 1999 that the Benefits Agency was unable to accept his application as a valid claim because there was at that time no legislation providing an equivalent of the widows’ benefits concerned to widowers. He was told that he had no right of appeal since his claim had not been considered by a decision-maker. In or around September 1999 the applicant made a claim for Widow’s Bereavement Tax Allowance (“WBA”) to the Inland Revenue for the years 1999-2000. On 5 October 1999 he was informed that his claim could not be accepted because there was no basis in domestic law allowing widowers to claim this benefit. On 24 November 1999 the applicant re-applied for WBA and on 28 November 1999 the Inland Revenue replied confirming its decision and asking the applicant if he wished to appeal. On 30 November 1999 the applicant made a further claim for WBA which was rejected on 25 December 1999. On 3 January 2000 the applicant wrote to the Inland Revenue asking for his appeal claim to be left open pending a domestic decision on the matter. The applicant received incapacity benefit in the sum of GBP 240.80 per month.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/11) against the Republic of X (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Y (a fictional country), on 15 January 2011. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr A. B., a lawyer practising in Z (a fictional city). The Government of X (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms C. D., of the Ministry of Justice. By a letter dated 30 January 2014 the applicant’s lawyer informed the Court that the applicant had changed his place of residence from X to Y where he was now living under a different name. The Court advised the parties on 16 February 2014 that it would continue processing the application under the name Schatschaschwili v. X, which was the applicant’s name as referred to in the domestic proceedings at issue as well as in his application lodged with the Court. The applicant alleged, in particular, that neither he nor counsel had been granted an opportunity at any stage of the criminal proceedings instituted against him to examine the only direct witnesses and victims of the crime allegedly committed by him in G (a fictional city) in February 2008 and on whose testimonies the applicant’s related conviction relied in breach of Article 6 § 3 (d) of the Convention. On 17 February 2013 the application was communicated to the Government. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the admissibility and merits of the application. The Y Government, who had been informed of their right to intervene under Article 36 of the Convention, did not make use of this right. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1980. When lodging his application he was detained in A prison, B (a fictional state). By a judgment of 26 March 2009 (file no. 74 Js 1123/08) the Göttingen Regional Court convicted the applicant of two counts of aggravated robbery in conjunction with aggravated extortion by means of coercion, committed jointly with further perpetrators (gemeinschaftlicher schwerer Raub in Tateinheit mit schwerer räuberischer Erpressung), and imposed an accumulated prison sentence (Gesamtfreiheitsstrafe) of nine years and six months. The crimes were committed in C on 15 November 2005 and in Göttingen on 4 January 2008 respectively. A. The facts established by the Göttingen Regional Court 1. The events in C The Regional Court found it established that in the evening of 15 November 2005 the applicant, acting jointly with an unidentified accomplice and according to a previously agreed plan, entered by force into an apartment in C and robbed its occupants. The men were aware that the apartment was used for prostitution and expected its two female occupants to keep valuables and cash in there. They had passed by the apartment in the early evening in order to make sure that no clients were present.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 4236/03) against a State (Republic of Turkey) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a national (Turkish national), Mr Ramazan Balaban ("the applicant"), on 8 November 2002. The applicant was represented by a lawyer (Mrs N. Bener) practising in a city (Bursa). The State (Republic of Turkey) ("the Government") were represented by their Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 5 June 2007 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the criminal proceedings brought against the applicant, the non-communication of the principal public prosecutor’s observations before the Court of Cassation, the lack of a public hearing in the determination of his compensation claim and the alleged damage he suffered as a result of the domestic court’s failure to order payment of interest to the State (Republic of Turkey). Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in a city (Bursa). A. The criminal proceedings against the applicant On 17 October 1996 the applicant was taken into police custody on suspicion of complicity in an armed robbery and homicide in a city (Bursa). On 27 October 1996 he was detained on remand. On 4 November 1996 the public prosecutor filed a bill of indictment with the Assize Court, charging the applicant and three others with the murder of a person (M.T.) and armed robbery. On 21 November 1996 the Assize Court acquitted the applicant and two of his co-accused. The fourth accused was convicted. The first-instance court ordered the applicant’s release from prison. The public prosecutor (M.T.’s father), who had joined the proceedings before the Assize Court, and the fourth accused appealed. On an unspecified date the principal public prosecutor at the Court of Cassation submitted his written opinion on the merits of the appeal. This opinion was not served on the applicant. On 28 April 1997 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 21 November 1996, holding that the first-instance court had failed to collect certain relevant evidence. The case was remitted to the Assize Court. On 29 June 1999 the Assize Court once again acquitted the applicant and two of his co-accused after gathering the evidence mentioned in the Court of Cassation’s decision. In its judgment, it held that there was insufficient evidence to conclude that the applicant had committed the offences in question. The public prosecutor, M.T.’s father and the fourth accused again appealed. On an unspecified date the principal public prosecutor at the Court of Cassation submitted his written opinion on the merits of the appeal. This opinion was not served on the applicant. On 19 March 2000 the Court of Cassation upheld the judgment of 29 June 1999.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by three Andrian nationals, Mr Andrian, Mr Andrian, and Mr Andrian (“the applicants”), on 15 March 2001. The applicants were represented by Mr Andrian, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Republic of Andria (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 20 May 2008 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1984, 1945 and 1935 respectively. The first and the third applicant live in Andria and the second applicant resides in Andria. The application concerns the wounding of the first applicant, who was twelve years old at the time, and the death of the second and third applicants' sons, Andrian and Andrian, who were fourteen and thirteen years old respectively, as a result of the explosion of an RPG-7 (anti-tank grenade launcher) grenade outside the applicants' village, Andria, in Andria. The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties and as they appear from the documents submitted by them, may be summarised as follows. A. The incident On 20 April 1993 Andrian, Andrian and Andrian took their animals out to graze. When the animals returned to the village without the children, the villagers launched a search party and informed the military nearby; the Andria Armoured Brigade Barracks. A search was also unsuccessfully conducted within the military confines. The next day, the dead bodies of Andrian and Andrian were found in a wheat field between the army barracks and Andria Mountain. The first applicant, who had injuries to his eyes and legs, was found a few hundred metres away. He was immediately taken to Andria State Hospital for treatment. As a result of the explosion, the first applicant suffered partial loss of the sight of one eye and the total loss of sight in the other. According to the first applicant's testimony, given to a prosecutor on 15 June 1993, the children were grazing their sheep in the field when they found an object with an iron head which looked like a bullet. The first applicant left the other two children to find water while they were trying to hit the iron head with pieces of metal. At that moment the bullet exploded. B. The criminal investigation On 21 April 1993 the Andria public prosecutor instigated an investigation into the incident. The prosecutor noted that there were numerous trenches around the area for tank and gun practice. The remains of the ammunition at the scene were secured.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/09) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by five Andorran nationals, Mr Alex Andorra, Mr Abdul Andorra, Mr Abdulcelleb Andorra, Mr Sal Andorra and Mr Derg Andorra (“the applicants”), on 23 June 2008. The applicants were represented by Ms Z. Andorra and Ms E. Andorra, lawyers practising in Andorra. The Andorran Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 16 March 2010 the application was declared partially inadmissible and the complaint concerning the applicants’ right to have effective review proceedings, by which they could challenge the lawfulness of their continued detention, was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants were born in 1947, 1976, 1973, 1983 and 1987 respectively. At the time of the application they were being held in detention in Andorra F-Type prison in Andorra. On 23 July 2007 the Andorra Assize Court decided to restrict access to the investigation file, under Article 153 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (the “CCP”), Law no. 5271. On 24 July 2007 the applicants were arrested and taken into custody on suspicion of being members of a criminal organisation. On 27 July 2007 the applicants were questioned by the investigating judge, in the presence of their lawyer.
