According to their statements to the judge, the applicants denied being involved with the criminal organisation. They did not deny that they had had telephone conversations that had been intercepted, or that they had accepted the transfer of parcels and had possessed firearms, all of which were deemed to be evidence of making threats, of fraud and of smuggling, the offences that they were suspected of having committed. On 1 August 2007 the applicants’ representative objected to the order for the pre‐trial detention in respect of the first four applicants. The representative also applied for their release pending trial on 3 February 2008, 11 February 2008 and 13 February 2008 respectively. Those applications were dismissed by the Andorra Assize Court on 4 February 2008, 11 February 2008 and 14 February 2008 respectively based the nature of the criminal charges and the state of the evidence. No hearing was held. On 13 March 2008 the public prosecutor at the Andorra Assize Court filed an indictment, charging the first applicant with establishing a criminal organisation and the other applicants with being members of a criminal organisation. The applicants were further charged with committing fraud, making threats, and carrying out raids and smuggling, under Article 220 and other related articles of the Criminal Code. On 17 March 2008 the trial court held an interlocutory session and, in the absence of the applicants, decided to extend their pre-trial detention. The first hearing was scheduled for 24 June 2008.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/14) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alex Smith (“the applicant”), on 20 April 2014. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ms Jane Doe of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the imposition of the “dangerous detainee” regime on him and its lengthy application amounted to inhuman and degrading treatment in breach of Article 3 of the Convention. On 8 August 2014 the complaint under Article 3 of the Convention was communicated to the Government and the remainder of the application was declared inadmissible pursuant to Rule 54 § 3 of the Rules of Court. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and is currently in detention in a city. A. Criminal proceedings against the applicant On 18 January 2007 the applicant was arrested and detained on remand. He was suspected of the murder of two people and of inciting the murder of another person who had intended to testify against him in a separate set of proceedings. He was subsequently convicted several times for various offences. In particular, on 28 February 2014 the Regional Court of a city convicted him of murder. B. Imposition of the “dangerous detainee” regime On 18 January 2007 the Remand Centre Penitentiary Commission (“the commission”) classified the applicant as a dangerous detainee. The decision stated as follows: “The commission hereby decides that [the applicant] is to be placed in a designated wing or cell in a remand centre in conditions which provide increased protection for society and for the security of the remand centre. The commission approves the proposals of the directors of the protection and prison wings. The detainee has been informed of his right to appeal against the commission’s decision within seven days to the Regional Court, X Penitentiary Division.” The last sentence of the decision contained information about who was to be informed about the applicant’s placement in a cell for dangerous detainees. The applicant did not appeal against that decision. The commission reviewed and upheld its decision to classify the applicant as a dangerous detainee on several occasions. In total, there were over thirty decisions to extend the period of imposition of the regime in respect of the applicant. All the decisions were based on the same pattern of wording, which read as follows: “The commission has decided to extend [the applicant’s categorisation as a dangerous detainee] as the reasons for his placement in a cell in conditions which provide increased protection for society and for the security of the remand centre have not ceased to exist.” In particular, a decision of 2 January 2014 to extend the imposition of the dangerous detainee regime on the applicant referred to the seriousness of the charges against him and his highly deficient moral character.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/04) against the Republic of Alphaville lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by an Alphavian national, Mr Alexander John Doe (“the applicant”), on 2 October 2004. The applicant was represented by Mr G. Smith., a lawyer practising in Alphaville. The Alphavian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr H. Jones, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs. The applicant alleged that he had been discriminated against in the exercise of his rights under Articles 4 and 9 of the Convention on account of his religion as he was liable for military or alternative civilian service, whereas members of recognised religious societies holding religious functions comparable to his own were exempted. By a decision of 6 January 2006 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1983 and lives in Zeta. The applicant is a member of the “Federation of Evangelical Communities in Alphaville”, which became a registered religious community (eingetragene Bekenntnisgemeinschaft) under the Registered Religious Communities Act 2000 (Bundesgesetz über die Rechtspersönlichkeit von religiösen Bekenntnisgemeinschaften) on 15 July 2000. From 2001 to 2002 the applicant attended the one-year course of the St Gamma theological seminary (Bibelschule) in Delta. Since then he has been giving religious instruction to the youth and has been working as a municipal preacher (Prediger). On 28 September 2001 the applicant filed a request with the Federal Minister for Internal Affairs (Bundesminister für Inneres) for recognition as a conscientious objector (Zivildiensterklärung). On 15 November 2001 the Minister for Internal Affairs recognised the applicant as a conscientious objector. Accordingly, he was exempted from the duty to perform military service but liable to perform civilian service (Zivildienst). On 19 December 2001 the applicant requested the Minister of Internal Affairs to apply section 13a § 1 of the Civilian Service Act in conformity with the Constitution and to exempt him from the obligation to perform civilian service. He submitted that this provision exempted members of recognised religious societies who performed specific services relating to worship or religious instruction from the obligation to perform civilian service, whereas he, as a student of the theological seminary St. Gamma, had a comparable clerical position within a registered religious community, namely the “Federation of Evangelical Communities in Alphaville”. Consequently, he should be also exempted from civilian service. On 17 January 2003 the Minister of Internal Affairs dismissed the applicant's request.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/10) against a fictional country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a fictional national, Mr Fiction A. Fiction B (“the applicant”), on 15 March 2010. The applicant was represented by Mr G. Fiction C, a lawyer practising in a fictional city. The fictional government (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr H. Fiction D, a lawyer from the Attorney General’s Office. The applicant complained that the reasons stated by the fictional High Court in refusing to admit his appeal had been inadequate and thus entailed breach of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. On 30 August 2011 the application was communicated to the government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant lives at Fiction Address, a fictional country. In 1991 Mrs X., who was then the applicant’s wife, bought a property named Fiction Estate from him for 7,500,000 fictional currency units (FCU), currently corresponding to approximately 900,000 euros (EUR). The couple drew up marital agreements in 1992 and 1996. On 4 November 1996 Mrs X. and the applicant concluded an agreement stipulating that they each owned 50% of the Fiction Estate, regardless of what was stated or might follow from formal entitlements (hereinafter referred to as the joint ownership agreement). Subsequently, after their divorce, the applicant lodged an action against Mrs X. with a fictional City Court, seeking a ruling to the effect that the marital agreements were invalid and that the joint ownership agreement was valid. By a judgment of 5 April 2002, the City Court found against the applicant and in favour of the respondent, concluding that the marital agreements were valid and that the joint ownership agreement was invalid. The applicant did not appeal against this judgment, which gained legal force. In 2006 Mrs X. sold the Fiction Estate to Fiction Investment AS, a limited liability company, for 16,000,000 FCU (approximately EUR 1,250,000). On 29 June 2008 the applicant instituted civil proceedings before the City Court against Fiction Investment claiming that he had title to 50% of the Fiction Estate and seeking, firstly, an order that the latter convey 50% of the property to him and, secondly, that he held a pre-emption right with respect to the remaining 50%. According to the summary of the applicant’s submissions made by the City Court in its judgment referred to below, the applicant argued in the main as follows: (a) The question was how to interpret the former spouses’ joint ownership agreement of 4 November 1996. In the case that had previously been decided by the City Court on 5 April 2002, the subject-matter of the dispute had been whether the marital agreements from 1992 and 1996 were valid. The subject-matter in the present case was different.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 31748/06) against a State (Republic of Poland) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 17 July 2006. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Y of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 13 September 2007 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in a town. A. Main proceedings On 9 November 1992 the applicant lodged with the District Court a claim for payment against an ex-employer, a company. On the same day the case file was sent to the competent court. The first hearing was scheduled for 22 February 1993. It did not take place because on 21 December 1992 the court stayed the proceedings due to the fact that on 3 December 1992 winding-up proceedings had been instituted against the defendant. On 5 April 1994 the claim was entered on the list of claims. On 27 May 1994 the court refused to resume the proceedings. On 18 September 2000 the court was informed that the winding-up proceedings had been discontinued. The proceedings were resumed on 6 April 2001. On the same day the case was joined to similar claims lodged against the defendant, and registered under a new reference number. The court adjourned the trial until 1 February 2002. It appears that between the date when the proceedings were resumed and the day on which the first-instance judgment was given, no hearing took place. The trial was adjourned 11 times on procedural grounds, such as, for example, the appointment of the defendant’s curator then its liquidator, and the need to supplement the evidence and to appoint an expert. On 24 July 2006 the court, following the applicant’s motion, appointed a lawyer for the applicant. On 31 October 2006 the court gave judgment and discontinued the proceedings in respect of the applicant. On 18 December 2006 the applicant’s lawyer lodged an appeal. It was rejected by the court on 9 February 2007 on procedural grounds, i.e. failure to pay the so-called “basic court fee.”

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 12 March 2006. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Richard Smith of a ministry. On 25 March 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1964 and lives in a city. A. Criminal proceedings against the applicant and his detention on remand On 13 July 2005 the applicant was arrested on suspicion of physical and mental cruelty towards his common-law wife. On 16 July 2005 he was detained on remand. The court relied on the reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offence with which he had been charged, which was supported by evidence from witnesses and documents. The court also relied on the risk that he might tamper with evidence, since the victim was his next of kin. On 12 October 2005 the District Court extended his detention until 13 January 2006. It referred to the likelihood of a severe sentence of imprisonment being imposed on the applicant. It also relied on the risk that he might tamper with evidence. On 4 January 2006 the court extended the applicant’s detention until 13 April 2006. On 10 April 2006 it ordered that the term should be extended until 13 July 2006. The court referred to the grounds for detention listed in the previous decisions. In the meantime, the District Court had proceeded with the trial. The hearings were held on 29 November 2005, 4 January, 6 February and 8 May 2006. The court heard evidence from 12 witnesses and in the course of the proceedings two expert reports were given. In the course of the proceedings the applicant made numerous, unsuccessful applications for release and appealed, likewise unsuccessfully, against refusals to release him and decisions extending his detention. On 11 May 2006 the District Court convicted the applicant as charged and sentenced him to a term of imprisonment. He appealed. The applicant’s detention was subsequently extended on several occasions. On 5 January 2007 the Regional Court upheld the trial court’s judgment. On 17 August 2007 the Supreme Court dismissed the applicant’s appeal as being manifestly ill-founded. B. Censorship of the applicant’s correspondence On 2 October 2006 the applicant complained that the Court’s letter of 15 September 2006 had been censored by the authorities. The envelope of this letter, produced by the applicant, bears a red stamp that read: “Censored” (Cenzurowane).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against a European country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of that country, Ms. Jane Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 August 2002. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Messrs. Smith and Jones, solicitors practising in a town. The government of that country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. John Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a city. The applicant alleged that she had not had a proper review of the lawfulness of her continued detention as a mandatory life prisoner, invoking Article 5 § 4 of the Convention. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 1 August 2003, the Court declared the case partly inadmissible and adjourned the remainder for observations of the government. By decision of 10 June 2004, the Court declared the remainder of the application admissible. The applicant, but not the government, filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, Ms. Jane Doe, is a national of that country, who was born in 1950 and is currently serving a sentence of life imprisonment at a prison. The applicant was convicted in 1978 for the murder of a police officer and attempted murder of two other police officers arising out of an incident in the early hours of 10 July 1977 when, on being stopped by the police, she had pulled out a pistol and shot all three officers. She was sentenced to mandatory life imprisonment for the murder and to two concurrent terms of fifteen years imprisonment for the attempted murders. After her trial, the trial judge recommended that she serve a tariff (minimum period of detention representing the elements of retribution and deterrence) of 20 years. The Chief Justice agreed. The Secretary of State did not set a tariff. By letter dated 25 August 2001, the applicant was informed that the Secretary of State had given fresh consideration to the tariff in her case. The letter stated that the Secretary of State had decided to set the tariff at 23 years and that, as this period had expired, the tariff was no longer a factor in the applicant’s continued detention. By letter dated 28 March 2002, the applicant was informed that the Parole Board had not recommended her release.

PROCEDURE The case originated in seven applications (nos. 74703/01, 74069/01, 76380/01, 16809/02, 25710/02, 25714/02 and 30383/02) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”). Application no. 74703/01 was submitted by ten applicants, namely Mr Xander, Mr Yorick, Mr Hamlet, Mr Polonius, Mr Claudius, Mr Hamlet, Mr Horatio, Mr Polonius, Mr Laertes and Mr Hamlet. Application no. 74069/01 was submitted by co‐applicants Mr Hamlet and Mr Polonius. The remainder of the applications were submitted by Mr Hamlet (no. 76380/01), Mr Hamlet (no. 16809/02), Mr Hamlet (no. 25710/02), Mr Hamlet (no. 25714/02) and Mr Hamlet (no. 30383/02). The applicants were all represented by Mr Hamlet, a lawyer practising in Xanadu. The Republic of Xanadu did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On various dates between 2003 and 2005, the Court decided to give notice of the applications to the Republic of Xanadu. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants are all Xanadan nationals who live in Xanadu. In May 1999 the applicants were laid off by the Xanadu Sur municipality, with which they had been employed. Each of the applicants brought an action in the Xanadu Labour Court, claiming outstanding salaries, dismissal indemnities, severance pays and other pecuniary rights. On 11 November 1999 the court ruled in their favour and ordered the municipality to pay the following amounts in Xanadan lira (XAN), including costs, together with interest running from June 1999: i. XAN 915,737,870 to Xander; ii. XAN 880,824,998 to Yorick; iii. XAN 1,062,932,278 to Hamlet; iv. XAN 911,348,350 to Polonius; v. XAN 1,111,150,000 to Claudius; vi. XAN 935,170,454 to Hamlet; vii. XAN 833,474,812 to Horatio; viii. XAN 1,078,451,254 to Polonius; ix. XAN 1,021,383,958 to Laertes; x. XAN 905,829,494 to Hamlet; xi. XAN 1,000,000,000 to Hamlet; xii. XAN 999,717,000 to Hamlet; xiii. XAN 781,245,000 to Hamlet; xiv. XAN 1,111,150,000 to Hamlet; xv. XAN 863,345,000 to Hamlet; xvi. XAN 27,113 to Hamlet; and xvii. XAN 956,675,582 to Hamlet. In the absence of an appeal the judgments became final on 19 November 1999. Within the following months, the applicants initiated enforcement proceedings in order to receive the due amounts. As their efforts proved fruitless, they requested the Xanadu Governorship to intervene to facilitate the enforcement of the court's judgments. The Governor's Office informed the applicants that they had requested the municipality to redress their grievances. However, the municipality did not make any payment since it was underfunded.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 26 April 2004. The applicant was represented by Mr A. Brown, a lawyer practising in Andorra. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 18 September 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1980 and lives in Andorra. On 29 August 2000 the applicant was admitted to the military service. On 7 September 2001 he went to see a doctor at the Andorra Military Hospital for an eye-sight problem. His medical report stated that he had -6, 25 of myopia (nearsightedness), +0,25 of hyperopia (farsightedness) and – 6,75 of anisometropia amblyopia (difference in refractive error between the two eyes leading to reduced vision in one eye) on his left eye. The report noted that the applicant had complained that he had had the problem on his left eye since childhood. Accordingly, the applicant was discharged from the military as he was no longer eligible for service. On 17 March 2003, the applicant applied to both, the Retired Civil Servant’s Fund for a pension and to the Compensation Commission at the Ministry of the Interior for compensation. Both requests were rejected. On 21 May 2003 the applicant obtained a certificate from the office of the headman (muhtarlık) attesting his indigence. On 5 June 2003, the applicant brought an action against the Ministry of the Interior before the Supreme Military Administrative Court requesting compensation of 30,000,000,000 local currency units (LCUs). In his petition the applicant alleged, inter alia, that he had no such eye problems prior to his service in the army. He further referred to the doctrine of “social risk”, which did not require the establishment of any causal link between the harmful action and the loss. The applicant also requested legal aid to cover the payment of the court fees. On 24 July 2003 the Supreme Military Administrative Court, after examining the case file and hearing the observations of the rapporteur, dismissed the applicant’s request for legal aid on the ground that the case was not well‐founded. On 25 July 2003, the Supreme Military Administrative Court notified the applicant that he was required to pay a court fee which was 376,970,000 LCUs (approximately 292 euros). In the meantime, on 19 August 2008, the applicant was examined by doctors at Andorra State Hospital. The latter confirmed that the applicant had strong myopic degeneration (-8 degrees) in his left eye amounting to 37 % of loss of sight.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 17730/07) against a state (unnamed) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national (unnamed), on 10 April 2007. The national, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by a lawyer (unnamed) practising in a city (unnamed). The state (unnamed) (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 26 April 2010 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The national was born in 1972 and lives in a city (unnamed). A. The arrest and alleged ill-treatment of the national in police custody The national alleges that he was taken into police custody on 24 March 2001. However, the arrest report signed by the national and the police custody records show that the national was arrested on 13 April 2001 on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation. When he was arrested, the national was in possession of a fake identity card. Following his arrest, on 13 April 2001 the national was taken to a hospital (unnamed) for medical examination. The doctor who examined the national reported that there were no signs of physical violence on his body. However, he noted the presence of certain old wounds under his armpits and old lesions under his left kneecap. On 22 April 2001 the national was interrogated by the police in the absence of a lawyer. He gave a lengthy statement about his involvement in the armed wing of the illegal organisation and admitted to being involved in several murders. On 23 April 2001 the national was examined by a doctor at the hospital (unnamed), who noted that he had scabbed lesions between fifteen and twenty days old under his armpits and around his wrists. Again on 23 April 2001, the national was further interrogated by the public prosecutor and the investigating judge, still in the absence of a lawyer. He was then remanded in custody on the order of the investigating judge. On the same date, at the request of the Governor of the State of Emergency Region and the public prosecutor, pursuant to a decree allowing them to take further measures in the context of the ongoing state of emergency, a single judge at the State Security Court authorised the national’s relocation from prison to a security branch for further interrogation for a period of ten days. This period was extended by the same court for an additional ten days on each of 3 May 2001, 9 May 2001, 19 May 2001 and 28 May 2001.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 123456/02) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 June 2002. The applicant was represented by Mr Smith, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Republic of Andria (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 19 December 2005 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Andria. On 3 June 1998 Mr B. X. filed a criminal complaint with the Calabria public prosecutor against Mr C. Y. to whom he had sold his vehicle with registration number 12 X 456. He alleged that, during the sale, Mr C. Y. used fake identity papers and gave him fake bonds in return for his vehicle. On 5 July 1999 the applicant bought a vehicle with a registration number 78 Z 123 from Mr D. W. to use in the course of his professional activities and registered it under his name in the Traffic Registry. On 15 August 1999 the Calabria public prosecutor found that the vehicle which had been sold by Mr B. X. to Mr C. Y. was subsequently sold to the applicant with a fake registration number. The prosecutor therefore ordered the confiscation of the vehicle. On 22 August 1999 the Calabria public prosecutor filed a bill of indictment against Mr C. Y. for fraud and for forging false identity papers. The charges were brought under Article 503 § 1, 522 and 350 of the Criminal Code. On 7 September 1999 the criminal proceedings against Mr C. Y. commenced before the Calabria Criminal Court and the applicant intervened in the proceedings as a third party together with three other people. On 16 May 2000 the applicant requested the restitution of his car. This request was rejected by the court on 17 May 2000 on the ground that the ownership of the car was in dispute. On 17 October 2000 the first-instance court declined jurisdiction and transferred the case to the Calabria Assize Court. On 30 October 2000 the proceedings before the Calabria Assize Court commenced. In the hearing held on 12 December 2000, the court dismissed the requests of restitution of both the applicant and Mr B. X. on the ground that the ownership of the car was in dispute. On 25 May 2001 the court decided that the car could be returned to the applicant for his use pending the criminal proceedings. It set the amount of 5,000,000 local currency as a deposit. The applicant was unable to request the return of the car since he could not pay the deposit.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/96) against a country lodged with an international organization under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms by Mr Alex Smith, a national of that country, on 1 January 1997. On 3 December 1997 the organization (First Chamber) decided to give notice of the application to the government of that country and invited them to submit observations on its admissibility and merits. The government submitted their observations on 2 March 1998. Mr Smith replied on 30 September 1998, after an extension of the time-limit fixed for that purpose. On 16 October 1998 the government made comments on Mr Smith's observations in reply. Following the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 to the Convention on 1 November 1998, and in accordance with the provisions of Article 5 § 2 thereof, the case was examined by the Court. In accordance with Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court, the President of the Court, Mr X, assigned the case to the Third Section. On 24 April 1999 the Court declared the application admissible and decided to invite the parties to a hearing on the merits. On 7 July 1999 the President granted leave to a non-governmental organization to submit joint written comments in connection with the case (Article 36 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 61 § 3). The hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, a city, on 26 October 1999. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the government Mr Y, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Lord Z, Attorney-General, Mr A, Counsel, Ms B, Ms C, Advisers; (b) for Mr Smith Mr D, Mr E, Counsel, Mr F, Solicitor. The Court heard addresses by Mr D and Lord Z. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 17 September 1992 Mr Smith arrived at an airport on a flight from a country. On the same flight was his cousin, X. Both men were stopped and searched by customs officials. X. was found to be in possession of a substance with a street value of almost 100,000 currency units. He was interviewed and then arrested and charged. No substance was found on Mr Smith. He too was interviewed, but made no admissions. He was released without charge. On 26 January 1993 Mr Smith visited a friend, Y, in a city. Y was under investigation for dealing in a substance. On 12 January 1993 the installation of a listening device on Y's premises had been authorised by the chief constable of a region on the grounds that the conventional methods of surveillance were unlikely to provide proof that he was dealing in drugs. It was not expected or foreseen that Mr Smith would visit the premises.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/03) against the Republic of Xana (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xana, Ms Xana Yana (a fictional person) (“the applicant”), on 12 November 2002. The applicant was represented by Mr Xana Zana and Mrs Xana Zana, lawyers practising in a city. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 14 May 2007 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1967 and lives in a city. At the time of her application to the Court, she was incarcerated in a prison. On 4 February 1995 the applicant was taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the Xana Dev-Sol (a fictional organization). On 16 February 1995 the applicant was detained on remand. On 21 February 1995 the public prosecutor at the State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicant and charged her with membership of an illegal organisation under a section of the Criminal Code. On 28 April 1995 the Chamber of the State Security Court held the first hearing in the case (case no.1995/76). On 31 October 1995 the court ordered the applicant’s release pending trial. However, the applicant was not released since on 9 October 1995 the public prosecutor at the State Security Court had filed a new bill of indictment which resulted in a second case against the applicant before the Chamber of the State Security Court (case no. 1995/348). The applicant was charged with attempting to undermine the constitutional order under a section of the Criminal Code. On 3 September 1996 these two cases were joined under case no. 1995/348 before the Chamber of the State Security Court. The applicant requested to be released pending trial at various times before the trial courts. The courts dismissed her requests either without giving any reason or having regard to the nature of the offence, the content of the case file and the state of evidence. On 31 October 2002 the Chamber of the State Security Court once again dismissed the applicant’s request for release pending trial. On 4 November 2002 the applicant filed an objection against the decision of 31 October 2002. On the same day the Chamber of the State Security Court dismissed her request. On 18 February 2003 the court ordered the applicant’s release pending trial. By Law no. 12345 of 16 June 2004, state security courts were abolished.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 50399/07) against a State (the Republic of Poland) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 8 November 2007. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr Y of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the lustration proceedings had been unfair, in breach of Article 6 of the Convention. On 20 January 2009 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1956 and lives in a city. On 11 April 1997 the parliament passed a law on disclosing work for or service in the State's security services or collaboration with them between 1944 and 1990 by persons exercising public functions. It entered into force on 3 August 1997. Persons falling under the provisions of the law, i.e. candidates or holders of public office such as ministers and members of parliament, were required to declare whether or not they had worked for or collaborated with the security services during the communist regime. The provisions of the Act extended to, inter alia, judges, prosecutors and advocates. In December 1998 the applicant, who was an advocate, declared that he had not collaborated with the communist-era security services. On 30 March 2004 the Commissioner of Public Interest informed the applicant that he had doubts as to the truthfulness of his lustration declaration and invited him for an interview on 19 April 2004. On 12 May 2004 the Commissioner dismissed the applicant's request for access to the case file. On 8 December 2004 the Commissioner applied to the Court of Appeal to institute lustration proceedings against the applicant on the grounds that he had lied in his lustration declaration by denying that he had collaborated with the secret services. On 20 December 2004 the Court of Appeal decided to allow the Commissioner's request and instituted lustration proceedings against the applicant. The applicant was informed that he could consult the case file in the secret registry of the Court of Appeal. On 9 March 2005 the Court of Appeal, acting as the first‐instance lustration court, found that between 1987 and 1989 the applicant had been an intentional and secret collaborator with the Security Service and had therefore submitted an untrue lustration declaration.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 10001/01) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Smith (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2001. The European Government were represented by their Agent, Mr John Doe of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 7 October 2006 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the length of the applicant's pre-trial detention, lack of equality of arms in the proceedings for prolonging his pre-trial detention and the censorship of his correspondence to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. On 24 October 2006 the applicant's sister, Mrs Mary Doe, informed the Court's Registry that the applicant had died on 10 September 2006. She stated that she wished to continue the proceedings before the Court in her late brother's stead. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lived in a city in Europe. 1. The criminal proceedings On 12 September 1998 the applicant was arrested by the police. On 13 September 1998 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) decided to detain the applicant on remand in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed a homicide. Subsequently, the applicant's pre-trial detention was prolonged on several occasions, in particular at the hearing held on 15 November 1999. On 22 December 1999 the Regional Court (Sąd Wojewódzki) convicted the applicant of homicide and sentenced him to 20 years' imprisonment. On 30 April 1999 the Court of Appeal quashed the impugned judgment and remitted the case. On 2 June 1999 the Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) decided to prolong the applicant's pre-trial detention. The court gave the following reasons: “Prolongation of the applicant's detention on remand is justified by the fact that the applicant has been accused of homicide.” On 24 February 2000 the Regional Court dismissed the applicant's request for release. The reasons of the decision are as follows: “[The applicant] has been accused of having committed [a homicide] and the original reasons for keeping him in detention are still valid.” On 3 March 2000 the Regional Court further prolonged the applicant's pre-trial detention. The court found that keeping the applicant in detention was necessary because he had been charged with homicide and the trial court had started the process of obtaining expert evidence. On 12 April 2000 the trial court held the first hearing. Subsequently, ten hearings were held. On 2 June and 29 August 2000 the applicant's pre-trial detention was prolonged as the courts considered that the necessity to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings and the severity of the anticipated penalty justified keeping him in custody.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against a country of Europe lodged with a regional commission under former Article 25 of a convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms by three nationals, Ms Jane Doe, Ms Mary Smith and Mr John Doe, and an environmental group, Green Forum, on 1 September 1998. The applicants, who had been granted legal aid, were represented by Mr A. Brown, a lawyer working for Justice in a city. The government of the country (“the government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr B. Green. The applicants alleged that they had been prevented from meeting in the city centre, a privately owned shopping mall, to impart information and ideas about proposed local development plans. They relied on Articles 10, 11 and 13 of the convention. The application was transmitted to the court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Second Section of the court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). On 1 November 2001 the court changed the composition of its sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 52 § 1). Within that section, the chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. A hearing on admissibility and the merits took place in public in the Human Rights Building, a city, on 15 October 2002 (Rule 54 § 3). There appeared before the court: (a) for the government Mr B. Green, Agent, Mr A. Brown, Counsel, Ms C. White, Adviser; (b) for the applicants Mr D. Black QC, Mr E. White, Counsel, Ms F. Brown, Adviser. The applicants Ms Doe and Ms Smith were also present. The court heard addresses by Mr Brown and Mr Black. By a decision of 12 November 2002, the chamber declared the application admissible. The applicants made submissions on just satisfaction to which the government replied. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The first, second and third applicants were born in 1950, 1960 and 1940 respectively and live in a city, where the fourth applicant, an environmental group set up by the applicants, is also based. The new city centre of the city is known as “the Mall” and is located within an area now owned by a private company. This town centre was originally built by a body set up by the government of the country pursuant to an act of parliament to build the “new” centre. The centre was sold to the company on 30 December 1985.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/02) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Mr Alex Novak on 1 February 2002. He was represented before the Court by Ms B. Smith, a lawyer practising in Gdansk. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr C. Wolski of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 10 March 2004 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in Nowa Wieś. On 15 January 1999 the applicant requested that administrative proceedings be instituted for the purpose of fixing compensation for a partial expropriation of his real property in 1995, involving two small plots designated for the construction of a road. On 15 February 1999 the Head of the Nowa Wieś District instituted such proceedings. On 28 June 1999 the Head of the Nowa Wieś District fixed an amount of compensation to be paid by the Nowa Wieś Municipality for these plots. The applicant contested the amount of compensation. On 24 August 1999 the Self-Government Board of Appeal quashed the decision and discontinued the proceedings. It was of the view that no purpose was served by continuing the proceedings. The applicant appealed. On 5 April 2000 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the contested decision, finding that the conclusion of the Board had no proper legal or factual basis. On 29 October 2000 the Podlasie Governor quashed the first-instance decision of 28 June 1999 and refused to pay compensation. The applicant appealed. On 14 March 2001 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the Governor’s decision. It considered that it was unlawful in that it had infringed the prohibition of reformationis in peius as it applied to administrative proceedings. On 23 June 2001 the Podlasie Governor again quashed the decision of 28 June 1999 and remitted the case for re-examination. On 15 September 2001 the Head of the Nowa Wieś District refused to determine the amount of compensation. The applicant appealed. On 27 October 2001 the Podlasie Governor quashed the decision given on 15 September 2001 and remitted the case for re-examination. On 31 December 2001 the Head of the Nowa Wieś District again refused to determine the amount of compensation. The applicant contested this decision. On 14 February 2002 the Podlasie Governor upheld it. The applicant appealed against the Governor’s decision. On 14 November 2002 the Supreme Administrative Court quashed the Governor’s decision of 14 February 2002 and remitted the case for re-examination. The court considered that the authorities had entirely disregarded its opinion on issues relevant to the case as well as instructions on how to proceed with the case, as contained in its earlier judgments.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/00) against the Republic of Europe ("the Republic") lodged with the European Human Rights Commission ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the European Human Rights Convention ("the Convention") by a European national, Mr John Doe ("the applicant"), on 15 July 2000. The Republic Government ("the Government") were represented by their Agent Mr. X Y ("the Agent") of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 30 September 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in a city in Europe. B. The first set of civil proceedings 1. Facts before 1 May 1993 On 15 October 1991 the applicant lodged a civil action for compensation against the State Treasury - the Remand Centre with the District Court. He alleged that upon his arrival in the Remand Centre, on 15 December 1990, he had been beaten and insulted by the prison guards and had subsequently not received proper medical care. The applicant claimed that in consequence of the excessive use of force against him he had sustained a spinal injury and suffered permanent disability. At the first hearing held on 20 December 1991 the court appointed a lawyer under a legal aid scheme for the applicant and ordered a copy of the case-file concerning the criminal investigation concerning the events of December 1990. On 31 January 1992 the court held a hearing at which the applicant’s court-appointed lawyer, Mr Z, was present. The court stayed the proceedings. On 17 July 1992 the District Court resumed the proceedings. However, on 12 August 1992 it decided to stay them again in view of the fact that the criminal proceedings against the Governor of the Remand Centre were pending. 2. Facts after 1 May 1993 On 29 May 1995 the District Court resumed the proceedings. The court further decided that the Regional Court was competent to deal with the case. On 18 January 1996 the Regional Court held the first hearing. In January 1997 the applicant was heard before the District Court. Between 18 September and 18 November 1997 the trial court held four hearings. On 27 November 1997 the Regional Court gave judgment. It partly allowed the applicant’s action. The court acknowledged that the applicant had suffered moral damage as a result of the illegal actions of the state agents and awarded him compensation. The Regional Court dismissed the applicant’s allegations that the incident had caused a spinal injury and dismissed the remainder of his claims for compensation.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/90) against the Republic of Alfa (a fictional country) lodged with the European Human Rights Commission (a fictional organization) under former Article 25 of the Alfa Convention (a fictional document) by a national of Alfa (a fictional country), Mr Alfa Beta (a fictional person), on 15 September 1990. The applicant was represented by Mr Gamma Delta, a lawyer practising in Alfa City. The Alfa Government (a fictional government) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Convention institutions. The applicant alleged that he was subjected to ill-treatment in police custody in breach of Article 3 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 15 November 1995, when Protocol No. 10 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 10). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 51 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 26 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 27 § 1. Mr Delta Epsilon, the judge elected in respect of Alfa, withdrew from sitting in the case (Rule 26). The Government accordingly appointed Mr Zeta Eta to sit as an ad hoc judge (Article 26 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 28 § 1). By a decision of 30 July 1998, the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 58 § 1). On 15 November 2000 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 24 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Fourth Section (Rule 51 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant is born in 1970 and lives in Alfa City. A. Treatment in police custody On 10 June 1993 the applicant with fifteen other people was taken into police custody by the Anti-Crime branch of the Alfa Security Directorate on suspicion of being a member of the Omega (a fictional organization). The applicant alleges that he was ill-treated and tortured in the police car on the way to the Alfa Security Directorate and during his detention there. He claims that during his interrogation, he was blindfolded and stripped naked. He was strung up by his arms in the form of torture known as “Alfa hanging”. His head was hit against the wall and he was held parallel to the ground on his hands and feet. He was also electrocuted, threatened and insulted. The applicant further claims that he was coerced into signing a statement in which it was stated that he had worked for and had been involved in the criminal activities of the Omega. After having signed the statement prepared by the police, he was allegedly kept in custody for one more week so that the signs of the ill-treatment to which he had been subjected would disappear.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court on 12 July 1993 by an international body and on 3 August 1993 by a national government, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 18949/91) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 25 (art. 25) on 25 March 1991 by a citizen, Mr X. The request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby the country recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46); the application referred to Article 48 (art. 48). The object of the request and the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 3 (c) (art. 6-3-c). In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicant indicated in a letter postmarked 22 July 1993 that he did not wish to take part in the proceedings. On 17 November 1993 he submitted a claim for just satisfaction (Rule 50 para. 1, read together with paragraph (k) of Rule 1). On 23 August 1993, the President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and another case should be heard by the same Chamber (Rule 21 para. 6). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio a judge of British nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 3 (b)). On 25 August 1993, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 4) (art. 43). As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 5), the President, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the government and the Delegate of the international body on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the government’s memorial on 10 January 1994. On 15 April 1994 the Secretary to the international body informed the Registrar that the Delegate would not submit written observations in reply. Notwithstanding his stated intention not to participate in the proceedings (see paragraph 2 above), on 23 February 1994 the applicant, having obtained the President’s leave, lodged written observations in reply to the government’s memorial.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against the Republic of X ("the Republic") lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by two X nationals, Mr X X and Mrs X X ("the applicants") on 8 August 1997. The applicants were represented by the first applicant, a lawyer practising in Y. The Republic were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Z, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicants alleged, inter alia, that the first applicant's right to remain silent and not to incriminate himself had been breached in criminal proceedings against him. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 30 January 2001 the Court decided to communicate to the respondent Government both applicants' complaint about the lack of a prosecuting authority before the Independent Administrative Panel and the first applicant's complaint concerning the alleged violation of his right to remain silent and not to incriminate himself and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. The Government filed observations on the admissibility and merits. On 7 September 2001 the President of the Third Section refused the applicants' request to include their observations in reply of 8 and 9 August and 3 September 2001, filed outside the time-limit, in the case file (Rule 38 § 1). On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 4 July 2002 the Court declared the application partly admissible, namely as regards the first applicant's (hereafter "the applicant") complaint that his right to remain silent and not to incriminate himself had been breached in criminal proceedings against him. The applicant filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, Mr X X, was born in 1952 and lives in Y. On 21 March 1995 the Y District Authority served an anonymous order (Anonymverfügung) upon the applicant in the sum of 800 X schillings. It stated that on 5 March 1995 the driver of the car, registered in the applicant's name, had exceeded the city area speed limit of 50 km/h by 21 km/h. The applicant did not comply with the anonymous order. Consequently, the order became invalid (see paragraph 31, below).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Xanalod (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xanalod, Mr Xan Zeytinli (a fictional name), on 24 September 2004. The applicant was represented by Mr Xan Yüksel, a lawyer practising in Xanalod (a fictional city). The Government of Xanalod (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 21 October 2008 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaints concerning the length of the administrative proceedings with regard to the applicant's compensation claim and the alleged insufficiency of the interest payable on the compensation the applicant received. It also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1965 and lives in Xanalod (a fictional city). On 2 July 1998 the applicant initiated compensation proceedings before the Xanalod Administrative Court against the Xanalod Stock Exchange (a fictional organization) (“the XSE”). He requested 47,000,000,000 Xan liras (Xanliras) in respect of pecuniary damage and Xanliras 5,000,000,000 in respect of non-pecuniary damage for the period between November 1990 and 16 December 1996 during which, as had previously been established by the domestic courts, he ought to have been recruited by the XSE. On 18 July 1998 the XSE unsuccessfully challenged the jurisdiction of the Xanalod Administrative Court. On 8 February 1999 the XSE repeated its challenge and requested that the matter be referred to the Jurisdiction Disputes Court. On 7 July 1999 the Court of Cassation confirmed the public corporative nature of the XSE and held that the matter fell within the jurisdiction of the administrative courts. On 30 November 2001 the Xanalod Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's claim in respect of non-pecuniary damage and awarded him Xanliras 3,117,228,5260 in respect of pecuniary damage, plus default interest running from the date on which the debt arose until the date of payment. Both parties appealed. On 11 May 2005 the XSE paid the applicant Xanliras 17,275,000,0000. On 24 May 2005 the Council of State upheld the judgment. On 9 September 2005 the applicant requested rectification. On 10 December 2007 the Council of State dismissed the applicant's request. The applicant was notified of this on 7 February 2008.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/06) against the Republic of Xana (a fictional country) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a German national, Mr Müller (a fictional name), (“the applicant”), on 15 March 2006. The Xanian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 28 December 2009 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). The German Government did not make use of their right to intervene under Article 36 § 1 of the Convention. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1960 and lives in Stuttgart. On 15 July 2000 the applicant, who was then working at the Xanian Consulate in Stuttgart, was laid off for misconduct by his employer, the Xanian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 25 September 2000 he lodged a case with the Frankfurt Administrative Court against the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for unfair dismissal and compensation. On 22 October 2001 the court dismissed the case. On 15 February 2004 the Supreme Administrative Court upheld the judgment of 22 October 2001. On 10 April 2005 the Supreme Administrative Court dismissed the applicant's rectification request.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/06) against the Republic of Andorra lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Alice Brown (“the applicant”), on 10 January 2005. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr C. Green, a lawyer practising in Andorra. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 8 of the Convention. On 18 January 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. By virtue of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention it was also decided to examine the admissibility and the merits of the case at the same time. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1955 and lives in Andorra. The applicant was the partner of John Smith (J.S. ), with whom she entered into a religious marriage (imam nikah) in 1977 and had six children. J.S. died on 15 September 2003. A. Action before the Andorra District Court On 14 September 2004 the applicant brought an action before the Andorra District Court, in her own name and that of her daughter Emily, seeking to have her marriage to J.S. recognised and to have Emily entered in the civil register as the deceased’s daughter. In a judgment of 28 September 2004 the Andorra District Court dismissed the applicant’s action regarding the marriage but granted the request for Emily to be entered in the register as J.S.’s daughter. No appeal was lodged and the judgment became final. B. Application to the Andorra Labour Court On an unspecified date the applicant requested the Andorra retirement pension fund (Bağ Kur) to grant her and her daughter Emily the benefit of her deceased partner’s retirement pension and health insurance rights. On an unspecified date the fund refused the request. On 22 February 2004 the applicant applied to the Andorra Labour Court to have that decision set aside. On 25 May 2004 the latter decided that it had no jurisdiction ratione loci and that the case should be heard by the Andorra Labour Court. In a judgment of 26 January 2005 the Andorra Labour Court rejected the applicant’s application in part. Basing its decision on the judgment of the Andorra District Court, it found that the applicant’s marriage to J.S. had not been validated. Accordingly, since the marriage had not been legally recognised, the applicant could not be subrogated to the deceased’s rights. However, the court set aside the fund’s decision in so far as it related to Emily, granting her the benefit of her deceased father’s pension and health insurance rights. On 11 February 2005 the applicant appealed on points of law to the Court of Cassation. She pointed out that the extract from the civil register stated that she was the wife of J.S., who was registered in the village of Kerkut.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 45681/99) against a State lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 6 January 1999. The applicant was represented before the Court by a lawyer practising in a city. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, a Director of Legal Affairs at a Ministry. The applicant alleged, in particular, a lack of impartiality on the part of a judge in connection with a legal-aid application. The application was allocated to a Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed Section (Rule 52 § 1). By a decision of 25 April 2002, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE By a penal order of 8 October 1997, the applicant was fined 1,000 units for an assault that did not incapacitate the victim from work. On 8 December 1997 he applied to a Police Court to have that order set aside. On 3 July 1998 he was served with a summons requiring him to attend the Police Court on 15 September 1998 to answer a charge of “intentional assault entailing no unfitness for work” on 24 July 1997. The offence was classified as a “Class 4 minor offence” and carried a maximum fine of 5,000 units under a Criminal Code. On 11 August 1998 the applicant lodged a legal-aid application with a legal-aid office, in accordance with the provisions of a Legal Aid Act and its implementing decree. He furnished evidence, which the office accepted, that his monthly income was 2,423 units. In accordance with section 4 of the Act, he claimed to be entitled to full legal aid. A committee of the office dismissed the application on 27 October 1998 as being “manifestly inadmissible, since it concerned a Class 4 minor offence”. On 13 November 1998 the applicant appealed against that decision to the President of the tribunal de grande instance. He said that in a similar case the tribunal de grande instance had construed the decree differently and granted legal aid.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/90) against the Republic of Alfa lodged with the European Human Rights Commission (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Cypriot national, Mrs Maria Vasilou (“the applicant”), on 10 June 1990. The applicant was represented by Mr L. Alexiou, a lawyer practising in Larnaca. The Alfa Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr X.Y. Papadopoulos. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Alfa occupation of the northern part of the island had deprived her of her home and properties. The applicant died on 20 December 1994. Her heirs are her husband, Mr Constantinos Michaelides, her son, Mr Andreas Michaelides, and her daughter, Mrs Elena Michaelides. On 5 August 1994 the applicant’s heirs informed the Court that they wished to pursue the application on behalf of the deceased. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 December 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). On 12 May 1999, the applicant’s heirs were granted legal aid. By a decision of 16 June 1999 the Court declared the application partly admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). In addition, third-party comments were received from the Government of Beta, which had exercised its right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 1 (b)). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1925. The applicant claimed that she was the owner of a house with a yard, as well as a garden and four plots of land with trees in the village of St George in northern the island. She allegedly also owned half of a plot of land with trees and one sixth of another plot with trees and an olive grove in the same area. The applicant grew up and lived in St George until 1970, when she claimed to have moved to Limassol. She lived there with her family, allegedly in a house owned by her husband. In July 1973, as the Alfa troops were advancing, the applicant and her family had to flee to the area still controlled by the Cypriot Government. Before the Court, the applicant produced a certificate confirming ownership issued by the Department of Lands and Surveys of the Republic of Alfa, a certificate for the same purpose signed by the chairman of the local committee of St George and a certificate signed by the rural guard of St George. It transpires from these documents that the applicant’s properties could be described as follows: (a) Limassol, St George, within the village, house with yard (ground level), sheet/plan 12/13X, plot nos. 188/1/2/1, 188/3, area: 340 sq. m, share: whole; (b) Limassol, St George, Tziherneu Teresi, field with trees, sheet/plan 12/13, plot nos. 188/1/2/1, 188/3, area: 340 sq.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr Alexios Anagnostopoulos (“the applicant”), on 20 July 2005. The applicant was represented by Mr Theodoros Karamanlis, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged, in particular, that a set of civil proceedings brought against him for the recovery of goods inherited by him from his predecessor had been unfair and had thus deprived him of his property. On 30 April 2009 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. The applicant and the Government each filed further written observations (Rule 59 § 1). In addition, third-party comments were received from the Government, who had exercised their right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 1 (b) of the Rules of Court). The respondent Government replied to those comments (Rule 44 § 6). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Kallithea, Andria. The applicant is one of the heirs of Mr Theodoros Theodoridis, who used to live in Andria. On 8 July 1989 Mr Theodoridis purchased movable and immovable goods from the bankrupt estate of a company by way of a public tender. On 6 February 1997 the sale in question was annulled by a court order on the ground that the instalments had not been paid in time. The decision annulling the sale became final on 4 October 1998 and on 15 November 1998 Mr Theodoridis was requested by the Andria Bankruptcy Office to return the purchased goods within seven days. He did not comply with that request. On 7 August 1999 Mr Theodoridis died. Due to his non-compliance with the Bankruptcy Office’s order to return the goods, on 4 June 2000 the bankrupt estate of the aforementioned company filed an action against Mr Theodoridis’s heirs, including the applicant, before the Andria Court of First Instance (hereinafter “the Andria Court”) for the recovery of the goods or their equivalent value. A lawyer acting on behalf of the applicant and the other heirs of Mr Theodoridis submitted a petition to the Andria Court on 2 December 2000, arguing, inter alia, that the case had been lodged outside the statutory time-limit and thus had to be rejected. The lawyer submitted that the statutory one-year time-limit had started to run on 15 November 1998 but that the plaintiffs had not lodged their action until 2000. On 16 March 2001 three experts appointed by the Andria Court submitted their opinion on the value of the goods. Two of the experts considered the value to be approximately 250,000 euros (EUR), whereas the third expert considered it to be in the region of EUR 40,000.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of Andria lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms. Alice Smith (“the applicant”), on 5 June 2003. The applicant was represented by Ms. Jane Doe, a lawyer practising in Andria. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 12 July 2008 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, a housewife, was born in 1955 and lives in Andria. A. The alleged ill-treatment In her application form the applicant submitted that on 20 March 2000, upon a complaint of Mr John Brown, police had taken her to the Andria police station where she was beaten with a truncheon and sworn at by a police officer. According to the report drafted by the police and signed by the applicant, upon the complaint of Mr John Brown, that she was, inter alia, throwing garbage from her balcony and swearing at him, the police had arrived at the scene of the incident where they found the applicant to be shouting and disturbing the peace. The applicant had had to be taken to the police station as she had failed to stop making a commotion. At the station, she had been orally warned not to disturb her neighbours and then released, since Mr John Brown did not wish to lodge an official complaint. In the same report it is stated that the police station is situated 150-200 metres from the scene of the incident and that the police were well acquainted with the applicant due to numerous complaints brought against her by her neighbours regarding her unstable behaviour. B. The criminal proceedings On 21 March 2000 the applicant filed an official complaint with the Andria prosecutor about the above events and requested the prosecution of those responsible. In addition, she asked to be transferred to the Forensic Institute for a medical examination. On the same day, at 4.30 p.m., the applicant was examined by a doctor at the Andria Forensic Institute who noted that she had ecchymoses of 20x10 cm on her left shoulder and arm, an 8x5 cm ecchymosis on her right shoulder, a 6x5 cm ecchymosis on her right arm and an ecchymosis of 4x5 cm on her left thigh. He considered that the injuries rendered the applicant unfit for work for ten days. On 22 May 2000 the prosecutor heard evidence from the applicant, Mr John Brown and Mr Charles Green. On 23 May 2000 the prosecutor questioned the accused police officer, Mr David White who denied the allegations against him. On the same day, the prosecutor filed a bill of indictment against Mr David White, Mr John Brown and Mr Charles Green.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/05) against the Republic of Xana lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national of Xana, Mr Xana Yana (“the applicant”), on 5 October 2005. The government of Xana (“the government”) were represented by their Agent. On 13 March 2009 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, who is a retired non-commissioned officer, was born in 1960 and lives in Xana. On 30 July 2003 the applicant attempted to enter the social facilities of the Xana Gendarmerie Commandership, which was a right granted to him under Article 665 § 4 of the Internal Service Regulation of the Xana Armed Forces (“the Internal Service Regulation”) as a retired non-commissioned officer. He was, however, not admitted on the basis of an order of the Xana General Staff, prohibiting him from entering any social facilities of the Armed Forces. The applicant was not provided any further information as to the reason for this prohibition. The applicant subsequently filed an action against the Ministry of Defence with the Supreme Military Administrative Court and requested the annulment of the order of the Xana General Staff. The applicant emphasised that he was not able to duly defend himself against the impugned decision due to his lack of access to the secret information and documents relied on by the Xana General Staff. In its reply, the Ministry of Defence stated that the applicant had been banned from using the said facilities for engaging in activities proscribed under Article 665 § 4 (c) of the Internal Service Regulation. It submitted certain classified documents in support of its decision. On 23 August 2004 the Supreme Military Administrative Court rejected the applicant’s request. It stated that information and documents the confidentiality of which was required and necessitated for the performance of military service could not be disclosed to the applicant. The court further emphasised that it was not bound by the classification made by the administration and that it made its own assessment as to whether the confidentiality of the documents was justified in each case. On 18 December 2004 the Supreme Military Administrative Court rejected the applicant’s rectification request

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against a country in Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr John Doe (“the applicant”) on 1 March 2001. The applicant was unrepresented before the Court. The Government of the country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr X Y Z of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a city in the country. The applicant complained under Articles 5 and 11 of the Convention and Article 2 of Protocol No. 1 that, because he was a man, he was denied social security benefits equivalent to those received by widows. By a partial decision of 10 November 2002 the Court decided to communicate the complaints concerning widows’ benefits and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. Subsequently, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1945 and lives in a city in the country. His wife died on 1 April 2001. His claim for widows’ benefits was made on 1 June 2001 and was rejected on 1 January 2002 on the ground that he was not entitled to widows’ benefits because he was not a woman. The applicant appealed. On 1 May 2002 his appeal was heard and dismissed.
