On 15 March 2007 the judgment was served on the applicant's representative.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 31246/02) against a State ("the Republic of Poland") lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a national ("a national"), on 29 July 2002. The Government ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 18 October 2005 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the excessive length of the detainee's detention on remand to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The detainee was born in 1976 and lives in a city, . On 10 March 1999 the detainee was arrested on suspicion of robbery and extortion. The detainee was also suspected of being a member of an organised criminal group. On 12 March 1999 the court ordered that the detainee be detained until 9 June 1999. The court found that there was a reasonable suspicion that the detainee had committed the offences in question. On 1 June 1999 the court prolonged the detainee’s detention. It referred to the interests of the pending investigation, such as the need to obtain additional evidence. The court also considered that the detainee, if released, could induce witnesses to give false testimony. The detainee’s detention was subsequently prolonged several times by the court for the same reasons as before. On 27 August 1999 the prosecutor lodged with the court a bill of indictment against the detainee and others. They were indicted of several counts of robbery, extortion, and membership of an organised criminal group. The detainee’s detention was subsequently extended by the court on 6 March, 26 June, 28 September and 30 November 2001. The court considered that keeping the detainee in custody was justified by the existence of strong evidence against him and the gravity of the charges. It was also necessary as the detainee could obstruct the proper course of the proceedings or induce witnesses to give false testimony. The detainee’s appeals against those decisions were dismissed. On 16 January 2002 the court convicted the detainee of several counts of robbery and extortion committed in an organised criminal group. The detainee was sentenced to 9 years’ imprisonment. The court upheld the first-instance judgment on 6 February 2003. On 28 October 2003 the court dismissed the detainee’s appeal.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/96) against the Republic of X ("the Republic") lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a national of X, Mr John Doe ("the applicant"), on 2 October 1995. The applicant was granted leave by the President to represent himself in the proceedings before the Court (Rule 36 § 3 of the Rules of Court). The President refused the applicant’s request for anonymity (Rule 47 § 3). The respondent Government ("the Government") did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings. The applicant complained under Article 6 of the Convention about the unreasonable length of time taken by his employer to reinstate him following a decision in his favour by a domestic court. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 21 March 2000 the Chamber declared the application admissible. After consulting the parties, the Chamber decided that it was not necessary to hold a hearing. Neither the applicant nor the Government submitted observations on the merits in the post-admissibility procedure. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant worked on the basis of a two-year contract, beginning on 9 December 1985, as an assistant Professor in the Faculty of Medicine of the University of X. Under X law he had the status of a civil servant. In an administrative decision dated 21 December 1987 the Office of the University President concluded that the applicant’s contract would not be renewed on the grounds of his professional incompetence. The applicant maintained that he was not informed of this decision until he went to the bank to draw out his monthly salary. On 4 March 1988 the applicant challenged the decision before the Administrative Court. In a judgment dated 6 December 1989 (Judgment no. 1) the court ruled in the applicant’s favour finding that the administration failed to substantiate its view that he was not competent for the post. The court annulled the administrative decision. On 29 January 1990 the court’s judgment was served on the Office of the University President, which failed to comply with it within the 60-day period prescribed by domestic law. The Office of the University President appealed and the file was sent to the Supreme Court on 22 May 1990. On 13 June 1990 the 5th Chamber of the Supreme Court quashed the judgment of the Administrative Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 26803/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 15 March 2002. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. On 19 September 2006 the Court decided to give notice of the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1969 and lives in a city. On 8 September 1999 at 5.15 a.m. the applicant was arrested by police officers from the anti-terror branch of the Security Directorate on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation. According to the arrest protocol, the police officers had to use force to apprehend the applicant since he resisted the arrest. The applicant refrained from signing this document. The applicant alleged that, contrary to what was indicated in the arrest protocol, he had been arrested on 5 September 1999. Following his arrest, the applicant was blindfolded, put in a car and threats were uttered against him. After being driven around for some time, still blindfolded, he was taken to the anti-terror branch of the Security Directorate. There, the applicant was allegedly punched, kicked, beaten on the head and the back with a truncheon and threatened with death. He also alleged that his testicles were squeezed. On 8 September 1999 at 7.10 a.m. the applicant was examined by a doctor in a hospital who noted an ecchymosis of 9 x 3 cm on the left of the lower part of his abdominal region. The doctor concluded that there were marks of physical violence on the applicant's body and considered that he should be examined by an urologist. On the same day at 7.25 a.m. the applicant was examined by an urologist who found, by using the technique of palpation, that the applicant's testicles were painful and sensitive. On 9 September 1999 the applicant was again examined by a general practitioner in the hospital who considered that the applicant should be taken to an internist. According to the report drawn up by the doctor, the applicant was brought to him as he was on a hunger strike in police custody. The applicant was then taken back to the Security Directorate. On 11 September 1999 the applicant was again examined by a general practitioner in the hospital who noted that the applicant was brought before him because of hunger strike. The doctor considered that the applicant should be examined by an internist.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against a European country lodged with an international human rights organization ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the European Convention on Human Rights ("the Convention") by a national, John Doe ("the applicant"), on 10 September 1997. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr. Q. Brown, a lawyer practising in a city. The government of the country ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Mr. R. Green, a foreign affairs office. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the prison authorities had interfered with a letter from him to a state minister. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 December 1999, when a protocol to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of the protocol). It was originally allocated to a section of the Court, which declared it partly admissible on 15 September 2002. On 1 December 2002 the Court changed the composition of its sections (Rule 26 § 1). The application was allocated to a new section of the Court. Within that section, the chamber that would consider the case (Article 28 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 27 § 1 of the rules of court. The chamber decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 60 § 2 in fine). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant, who was born in 1950, was released from detention in March 2000. Prior to that he was detained at a prison, on temporary transfer from a state prison while serving a five year sentence for a crime. On 1 August 1997 a sealed letter sent by him to a state minister was returned to him by the prison authorities. Following the Court’s admissibility decision, the Government informed the Court that the prison service was unable to explain why the letter had not been sent, since there was nothing untoward in its content.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against a European country lodged with an international human rights organization (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the European Convention on Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 June 1998. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by his counsel. The government of the country (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged principally that he had not been arrested on a reasonable suspicion that he had committed an offence, that he had not been brought promptly before a judge or other judicial officer and that he did not have an enforceable right to compensation in respect of these matters. He relied on Article 5 §§ 1, 3 and 5 of the Convention. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 12 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 12). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 53 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 28 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 27 § 1. By a decision of 15 March 2001, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible [Note by the Registry. The Court’s decision is obtainable from the Registry]. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 60 § 1). A hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 12 July 2002 (Rule 60 § 2). There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Mr A. Smith, Foreign and Commonwealth Office, Agent, Mr B. Jones, Counsel, Mr C. Brown, Mr D. Green, Mrs E. White, Advisers; (b) for the applicant Mr F. Black, Counsel, Mr G. Red, of the London Bar, Solicitor. The Court heard addresses by Mr Black and Mr Jones. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was, and still is, a prominent member of a political organization. He has been arrested by the police on a number of occasions and has issued proceedings relating to his allegations, inter alia, of arbitrary arrest, assault and ill-treatment arising out of six incidents. In proceedings lodged for incidents in 1989 and on 20 March 1994, he received an award of damages (amount unspecified). In or about February 1995 he was awarded damages of 3,000 euros (EUR) for an incident in a square on 20 March 1994 when the judge found that he had been wrongfully arrested by police officers who had purported to arrest the applicant for obstruction in failing to give his name when in fact they were fully aware of his identity. This case concerns his arrest in 1986 in relation to the murder of Mr Peter Smith.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/06) against a country of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two nationals, Ms X.Y. and Ms Z.A. Burden (“the applicants”), on 29 March 2005. The applicants were represented by Ms A.B. of Law Firm, solicitors practising in a town. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr C.D., Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The applicants complained under Article 14 taken in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that, when the first of them died, the survivor would be required to pay inheritance tax on the deceased's share of the family home, whereas the survivor of a married couple or a homosexual relationship registered under the Civil Partnership Act 2004, would be exempt from paying inheritance tax in these circumstances. The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. On 30 June 2005 the President decided to give the case priority treatment under Rule 41 of the Rules of Court and that the admissibility and merits should be examined jointly, in accordance with Article 29 § 3 of the Convention and Rule 54A. The applicants and the Government each filed written observations (Rule 59 § 1). On 11 April 2006 the Chamber decided, after consulting the parties, to hold a hearing on the admissibility and merits (Rule 59 § 3 in fine). The hearing on admissibility and merits took place in public in the Human Rights Building, Strasbourg, on 12 September 2006. There appeared before the Court: (a) for the Government Ms E.F., Agent, Mr G.H. Counsel, Mr I.J., Adviser, Ms K.L., Adviser, Mr M.N., Adviser, (b) for the applicant Mr O.P., Counsel, Ms Q.R. Solicitor, The Court heard addresses by Mr H. and Mr P., as well as their answers to questions put by Judge S.T. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows. The applicants are unmarried sisters, born on 26 May 1918 and 2 December 1925 respectively. They have lived together all their lives; for the last 30 years in a house built on land inherited from their parents in a county. The house is owned by the applicants in their joint names. According to an expert valuation dated 12 January 2006, the property was worth GBP 425,000, or GBP 550,000 if sold together with the adjoining land. The sisters also jointly own two other properties, worth GBP 325,000 in total. In addition, each sister owns in her sole name shares and other investments worth approximately GBP 150,000.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 21768/02) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr X (“the applicant”), on 27 May 2002. The applicant was represented by a lawyer practising in a city. The Government did not designate an Agent for the purpose of the proceedings before the Court. On 8 November 2004 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1985 and lives in a city. On 27 December 2001 the applicant, who was sixteen years old at the time, was arrested by police officers from a police station in connection with an ongoing investigation concerning a robbery that had taken place in a school. In his police statement, the applicant confessed that he had been involved in a robbery on 26 November 2001 together with two of his friends. He explained that he had helped his friends in carrying a computer from the school. The same day he was brought before the public prosecutor, and the investigating judge at a magistrate’s court, where he repeated his statement to the police. Having regard to the evidence in the file and considering that there was a risk of absconding, the investigating judge ordered that the applicant be detained on remand in a prison together with adults. The applicant’s representative challenged this decision before a criminal court and maintained that the evidence in the file did not suffice to keep her client in detention. Invoking Articles 5 and 6 of the Convention, she requested that the applicant be released. On 10 January 2002 the public prosecutor instituted criminal proceedings against the applicant in the criminal court. He charged him with robbery. On 14 January 2002 the criminal court commenced the trial against the applicant. Taking into account the seriousness of the offence and the evidence in the case-file, it ordered that the applicant’s detention on remand be continued. On 16 January 2002 the applicant’s representative challenged this decision. She invoked Articles 5 and 6 of the Convention and alleged that there was not sufficient evidence in the file to keep her client in detention. She further maintained that pursuant to a criminal procedure code, a person could only be held in detention on remand if there were a risk of absconding and/or of tampering with evidence. She stated that the authorities knew where the applicant lived and there were no sufficient grounds to believe that the applicant would try to flee.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1001/03) against the Republic of Aland against the Republic of Aland lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Alandan nationals, Mr Alper Anadolu and Mr Talat Kuru (“the applicants”), on 15 November 2003. The applicants were represented by Mrs N. Yilmaz, a lawyer practising in Aland. The Alandan Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 7 September 2008 the President of the Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (former Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 23 January 1993 the applicants were taken into police custody in Aland on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation. On 10 February 1993 the applicants were brought before the investigating judge at the Aland State Security Court, who ordered their detention pending trial. On 22 May 1993, the public prosecutor at the Aland State Security Court filed a bill of indictment against the applicants, charging them under Article 124 of the former Criminal Code with carrying out activities with the aim of bringing about the secession of part of the national territory. On 4 April 1998 the Aland State Security Court convicted the first applicant as charged and sentenced him to death. As regards the second applicant, the court decided that his case should be disjoined from the file as his defence had not been submitted to the court. On 28 February 2000 the Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of 4 April 1998. The case was remitted to the Aland State Security Court for further examination. On 4 February 2001 the second applicant's case was joined to the file again. On 20 June 2004 the applicants were released pending trial. By Law no. 5180 of 15 June 2004, published in the Official Gazette on 29 June 2004, State Security Courts were abolished. The case against the applicants was subsequently resumed before the Aland Assize Court. According to the information submitted to the case file on 2 February 2010 the proceedings are currently pending before the Aland Assize Court.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/07) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr. John Doe (“the applicant”), on 15 October 2007. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr. Alex Smith of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that his right to respect for his family life had been infringed. On 1 October 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1975 and lives in a city. On 15 October 2004 the city court ordered the applicant's pre-trial detention for a period of fourteen days. The court referred to the reasonable suspicion that the applicant was guilty of fraud while acting in an organised group. On 15 June 2006 the applicant was arrested. On 20 June 2006 the city court ordered his detention for a period of three months. The court held that there was a reasonable suspicion that the applicant had committed the offences with which he had been charged (including establishing and leading an organised criminal group). Furthermore, he had confessed to the charges. The court also stressed that the detention was necessary in order to ensure the proper course of the proceedings, in particular as the applicant had been in hiding. In July his detention was extended until 15 November 2006. The court repeated the reasons previously given. On 15 June and 3 July 2006 the applicant's wife, Ms. Jane Smith, asked for permission to visit her husband in prison. On 20 June and 5 July 2006 respectively, the city prosecutor refused her requests. The prosecutor made handwritten notes on Ms. Smith's applications – “no permission” and “permission refused” respectively. On 25 July 2006 the applicant was again refused permission to be visited by his wife and children by a district court. The prosecutor made a handwritten note on the applicant's motion “permission refused”. On 25 September 2006 the applicant was visited by his daughter. On 27 October 2006 the city court extended the applicant's detention until 15 May 2007. The court held that the original reasons for his detention were still valid. The court also referred to the likelihood of a heavy sentence and the fact that the applicant had acted in a criminal group. The court further refused the applicant's request for release. On 22 February 2007 the city court refused the applicant's application for release and the replacement of detention by more lenient preventive measures. The court referred to the grounds given in previous decisions.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/04) against the Republic of Aalandia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms Alice Smith (“the applicant”), on 5 February 2004. The applicant was represented by Mr Bob Jones, a lawyer practising in City. The Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged, in particular, that she had been subjected to ill-treatment in a gendarmerie station and that the criminal proceedings subsequently brought against her had not been fair. On 30 December 2008 the President of the Court's Third Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1980 and lives in City. On 7 April 2001 the applicant was arrested by the gendarmerie in the border city of City on her return from Country. She was detained in a gendarmerie station. According to an arrest report prepared by the gendarmerie the same day, the applicant was informed of her right to be represented by a lawyer and to inform her family about her arrest. Nevertheless, it was also stated in the same document that, if the offence in respect of which she was arrested fell within the jurisdiction of State Security Courts, she could consult a lawyer only if her detention period was extended by a judge or if a judge ordered her detention in a prison. The applicant signed the report and wrote on it that she had “no requests”. The applicant was interrogated during her detention at the gendarmerie station, and an eight-page statement was taken from her between 8 and 10 April 2001. In her statement the applicant admitted to having engaged in activities on behalf of the Organization0. On 10 April 2001 the applicant was examined by a doctor at the City branch of the Forensic Medicine Directorate. According to the medical report drawn up the same day, there were “no injuries or signs of ill-treatment on her body”. The same day she was brought before the prosecutor and then before the City Magistrates' Court, which ordered her pre-trial detention in prison. In two statements made during meetings with the prosecutor and the judge the applicant admitted to being a member of the Organization. According to the three statements referred to above, the applicant did not want to be represented by a lawyer during the questioning. On 4 May 2001 the prosecutor at the City State Security Court filed an indictment against the applicant with that court for the offence of membership of an illegal organization, namely the Organization.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/97) against a country lodged with an international organization ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of a convention ("the Convention") by a national, Mr John Doe ("the applicant"), on 17 September 1997. The applicant was represented by Mr C. Smith, a solicitor practising in a city. The government ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Mr G. Brown. The applicant alleged that the delay of two years between his original sentence which was non-custodial and his subsequent custodial sentence, following the Attorney General’s reference of his case to the Court of Appeal for a review of his sentence, amounted to a breach of the "reasonable time requirement" under Article 6 of the Convention and a breach of Article 3. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Fourth Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 14 September 1999 the Chamber declared the application admissible. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant is a national, born in 1945. On 17 March 1993 the applicant was interviewed by officers of an organization in connection with allegations of market rigging, theft and false accounting, alleged to have taken place in the course of the takeover of one company by the company in which the applicant, a chartered accountant, was involved. The alleged offences took place during the period 1990 to 1991. The applicant was further interviewed on 27 April 1993 and 21 June 1993, and was formally charged on 30 July 1993. The applicant’s trial began in October 1994 and on 10 February 1995, after a trial lasting 63 days, the applicant was convicted of conspiracy to defraud and four counts of theft. The proceedings were adjourned for pre-sentence reports, and on 10 March 1995 the applicant was ordered to perform 220 hours community service. He was also ordered to pay compensation of GBP 151,042.36 within two years, with 12 months' imprisonment in default, and was further ordered to pay GBP 20,000.00 towards prosecution costs. The applicant lodged a notice of appeal against conviction on 11 March 1995, and on 5 April 1995, the Attorney General made a reference to the Court of Appeal for a review of the applicant’s sentence under Section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988. In May 1995, the applicant was refused legal aid on financial grounds. On 20 September 1995 the applicant, privately represented, submitted perfected grounds of appeal and his response to the Attorney General’s reference.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 20 March 2002. The applicant was represented by Mr Jane Smith, a lawyer practising in a city. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr Alex Brown of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the length of several sets of proceedings in which he was involved exceeded a reasonable time, as provided for in Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. On 10 September 2007 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of one set of civil and one set of criminal proceedings to the Government. Applying Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of these complaints at the same time. I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE A. Civil proceedings for payment On 15 June 1993 the applicant lodged a claim for payment against a certain company with a district court. On 10 May 1994 the district court granted the claim and made an order for payment. On an unspecified date the defendant appealed. On 20 June 1995 the court stayed the proceedings. Following a request by the applicant, on 22 January 1996 the court resumed the proceedings. Subsequently the case lay dormant until 31 September 2001. On 31 September 2001 the applicant requested the court to reconstruct the case file. He had become aware in the course of another set of proceedings against the member of the management board of the defendant company that the case file was incomplete. On 24 May 2003, after the proceedings for reconstruction, the district court held that it was not possible to reconstruct the file and decided to continue the main proceedings for payment on the basis of the case file as it stood. On 20 November 2004 the district court dismissed the defendant's appeal lodged against the order for payment. This decision became final on 5 January 2005. B. The applicant's complaint under the 2003 Act in relation to the above proceedings On 20 November 2004 the applicant lodged a complaint with a regional court under the Law of 17 June 2003 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time (Ustawa o skardze na naruszenie prawa strony do rozpoznania sprawy w postępowaniu sądowym bez nieuzasadnionej zwłoki – “the 2003 Act”). He sought both a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings before the district court had been excessive and just satisfaction. On 25 January 2005 the regional court gave a decision in which it acknowledged that the length of the proceedings had been excessive.

PROCEDURE The case originated in two applications (nos. 12345/07 and 67890/07) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Xanadan nationals, Mr X Y and Mr Z A (“the applicants”), on 1 August 2006. The applicants were represented by Mr B C and Mr D E, lawyers practising in Yonder. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. On 16 September 2009 the President of the Second Section decided to give notice of the applications to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it was also decided to examine the merits of the applications at the same time as their admissibility. THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASES The applicants were born in 1956 and 1946 respectively and live in Zville, Yonder. 1. The first set of proceedings Each of the applicants, who were employees of Zville Municipality, brought proceedings before the Yonder Civil Court of First Instance acting as a labour court, claiming unpaid wages and other pecuniary rights on 10 October 2001 and 21 November 2001, respectively. On 21 May 2004 and 23 May 2003, respectively, the Yonder Civil Court of First Instance granted the applicants’ requests partially and ordered the payment of 14,288 Xanadan Liras (XLY) to the first applicant and XLY 18,514 to the second applicant, together with interest. These judgments became final as no appeal was filed against them. The first applicant further initiated execution proceedings before the Yonder Execution Office to obtain the amount ordered by the Yonder Civil Court of First Instance (file no. 2005/8415). At the date of introduction of the applications, the aforementioned judgment debts were still outstanding. 2. The second set of proceedings On 14 November 2002 and 14 September 2002, respectively, the applicants retired from their jobs at the Zville Municipality. The town council calculated the applicants’ severance benefits accordingly. On 18 March 2003, not having been paid the amounts awarded, the applicants brought proceedings before the Yonder Civil Court of First Instance acting as a labour court, claiming severance benefits and other pecuniary rights. On 15 July 2004 the labour court ordered the Municipality to pay XLY 11,918 to the first applicant and XLY 12,119 to the second applicant, together with interest. These judgments became final as no appeal was filed against them. The applicants further initiated execution proceedings before the Yonder Execution Office to obtain those amounts ordered by the Yonder Civil Court of First Instance (file nos. 2004/351 and 2004/352). At the date of introduction of the applications, the aforementioned judgment debts were still outstanding.

The FACTS . The applicant church is a fictional church institution. On a date in March 1985, the government of a fictional region issued an expropriation order in respect of certain plots of land belonging to the applicant church. The latter was awarded 114,790,590 fictional currency in compensation. The land, which was earmarked for urban development projects that were scheduled for completion by a date in 1987, was only partially used. On a date in February 1987, the applicant church applied to the government seeking to recover possession of the unused land. On a date in October 1987, the government refused the application on the ground that the land in question could still be used in the interests of the community. 1. Proceedings in the civil courts On a date in November 1988, relying on a section of a law, the applicant church brought an action before the first-instance civil judge to recover possession. The first hearing, which was set for a date in January 1989, could not be held on that date as the government had not been notified. The government joined the proceedings on a date in May 1989. At a hearing on a date in September 1989, the government requested that a particular witness be heard. That request was granted on a date in January 1990. On the date in question, namely a date in April 1990, the witness failed to attend the hearing. On a date in September 1990, the government waived its right to have the witness heard. The parties submitted their written pleadings on a date in May 1991. Preparation of the case was concluded on a date in November 1991. By a judgment of a date in January 1992, deposited at the registry on the same date, the court dismissed the applicant church’s request on the grounds that, firstly, the expropriation order of a date in October 1987 was an administrative act and thus fell outside the civil court’s jurisdiction and, secondly, that the applicant church could not bring an action to recover possession, since the disputed land had been lawfully expropriated and had not been obtained by the State without title. On a date in March 1992, the applicant church brought an action before the judge of civil appeals to establish title to land, seeking to obtain restitution of the land in question in accordance with a section of a law. It also alleged that the authorities’ conduct had breached Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. The first hearing was held on a date in April 1992. On a date in May 1992, the applicant church filed a number of documents. On a date in May 1992, the proceedings were adjourned on the ground that an attempt to reach a friendly settlement was in progress. On a date in December 1992, noting that the negotiations had failed, the official responsible for preparing appeal cases ordered that the proceedings be resumed.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court, as established under former Article 19 of the Convention, by the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 16 March 1998, within the three-month period laid down by former Articles 32 § 1 and 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 26083/94) against a State lodged with the Commission under former Article 25 by two nationals, Mr X and Mr Y, on 24 November 1994. The Commission’s request referred to former Articles 44 and 48 and to the declaration whereby the State recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (former Article 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyers who would represent them (Rule 31 of former Rules of Court B0). The Government of a State, having been informed by the Registrar of their right to intervene (former Article 48 (b) of the Convention and former Rule 35 § 3 (b)), indicated that they did not intend to do so. As President of the Chamber which had originally been constituted (former Article 43 of the Convention and former Rule 21) in order to deal, in particular, with procedural matters that might arise before the entry into force of Protocol No. 11, Mr Z, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicants’ lawyers and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the written procedure. Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the applicants’ and the Government’s memorials on 30 July and 31 July 1998 respectively. On 22 October 1998 the President of the Chamber decided, under former Rule 28 § 3, to give the applicants’ lawyers leave to use the language at the hearing before the Court. The Agent of the Government was also given leave to address the Court in the language, under former Rule 28 § 2. After the entry into force of Protocol No. 11 on 1 November 1998 and in accordance with the provisions of Article 5 § 5 thereof, the case was referred to the Grand Chamber of the Court. The Grand Chamber included ex officio Mr A, the judge elected in respect of the State (Article 27 § 2 of the Convention and Rule 24 § 4 of the Rules of Court), Mr B, the President of the Court, Mrs C, Vice-President of the Court, and Mr D and Mr E, Vice-Presidents of Sections (Article 27 § 3 of the Convention and Rule 24 §§ 3 and 5 (a)).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/08) against the Republic of Alphaville lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by two Alphavillians, Mr Alphabert and Mrs Alphine (“the applicants”), on 15 November 2008. The applicants were represented by Mr Gamma, a lawyer practising in Betaville. The Alphavillian Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Delta, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry for European and International Affairs. On 11 February 2009 the President of the First Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicants are the joint owners of a house in Betaville which they had acquired in 1997. In spring 1998 they discovered that the distance between an annex to their house and the neighbouring plot of land did not correspond to the minimum distance required by the building permit. On 24 November 1998 the applicants applied to the Betaville Municipal Authority for a retrospective building permit including, among other points, the authorisation to go below the minimum distance between the annex to their house and the neighbouring plot. The Betaville Municipal Authority fixed a date for a hearing on the property in question, but cancelled that date on the applicants’ request. Subsequently, the applicants and their neighbours filed comprehensive submissions and the applicants submitted substitute plans which were then examined by a court-appointed expert, E. A hearing on the applicants’ property was held on 4 November 1999. On the applicants’ request the time-limit for commenting on the results of the hearing was extended from 4 to 31 December 1999. Having announced to submit a private expert opinion by the end of January 2000 the applicants did so on 2 June 2000. On 1 August 2000 the applicant’s neighbours filed comments. The Betaville Municipal Authority granted the applicants’ request on 7 December 2000. On 23 December 2000 the applicants’ neighbours appealed against the authorisation to reduce the minimum distance between their property and the applicants’ house. Until August 2001 the Appeals Commission tried to achieve a settlement between the applicants and their neighbours. As these efforts failed, it took further evidence, asking expert E. to supplement his opinion. The parties were asked to comment by 21 February 2002. That time-limit was extended several times on the applicants’ request until 30 March 2002. The Appeals Commission held an on-site hearing on 6 July 2002. On 17 October 2002, after a further attempt to achieve a friendly settlement had failed, the Appeals Commission requested the applicants for further comments by 6 November. On their request the time-limit was extended until 28 November 2002.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court within a three-month period by a regional human rights body and by the Government of a European country, within the timeframe laid down in the Convention. It originated in an application against the country lodged with the body under the Convention on 9 April 1991. The body's request referred to the relevant articles and to the declaration whereby the country recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court. The object of the request and of the Government's application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under the Convention. In response to the enquiry, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent him. The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio a national judge and the President of the Court. On the date the President drew by lot, in the presence of the Registrar, the names of the other members, namely national judges and the President. As President of the Chamber, the President, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the Government, the applicant's lawyer and the Delegate of the body on the organisation of the proceedings. Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the applicant's memorial and on a date a letter from the Government enclosing their written observations to the body dated a date. On a date the Delegate would submit his observations at the hearing. On dates the body and the Government produced various documents, as requested by the Registrar. On the latter date the applicant submitted additional details on his claims. In accordance with the President’s decision, the hearing took place in public in a European city on a date. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand. There appeared before the Court: for the Government a representative.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/01) against the Republic of Xlodavia lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr Janusz Nowak (“the applicant”), on 15 December 2001. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr A. Zawisza of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 5 June 2004 the Court declared the application partly inadmissible and decided to communicate the complaint concerning the length of the applicant’s pre-trial detention to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Nowa Wieś. On 25 March 2000 the applicant was arrested by the police. On 26 March 2000 the Warsaw District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) ordered that he be detained on remand in view of the reasonable suspicion that he had committed two burglaries. On 30 May 2000 the Warsaw Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) prolonged the applicant’s detention until 10 August 2000. It held that there was a strong suspicion that he had committed the offences with which he had been charged and that keeping him in custody was necessary to secure the proper conduct of the proceedings. The Warsaw Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) upheld that decision on 15 June 2000. It found, invoking Article 258 § 2 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, that the applicant had been charged with two burglaries committed as a recidivist offender and thus he was liable to a statutory maximum sentence of at least 8 years’ imprisonment. On 2 July 2000 the Regional Court extended the applicant’s detention until 18 August 2000. In addition to the grounds previously invoked, it also relied on the severity of the anticipated penalty. That decision was upheld on appeal on 18 July 2000. On 19 August 2000 the Court of Appeal prolonged his detention until 9 September 2000 pending the outcome of the investigation on the grounds that there was a reasonable suspicion that he had committed the offences in question and that he was potentially liable to a severe penalty, which justified the fear that he would obstruct the proper conduct of the proceedings. The court also held that due to the close links between the suspects there was a risk that, if released, they might interfere with the course of the investigation. Thus it was justified to keep them in custody pending the termination of the investigation. That decision was upheld on appeal by the Supreme Court (Sąd Najwyższy) on 20 August 2000. The investigation was terminated on 21 September 2000. On 22 September 2000 the prosecution filed a bill of indictment with the Warsaw Regional Court. The applicant was charged with 2 burglaries.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/03) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Polish national, Mr Zephyr Wind (“the applicant”), on 27 December 2002. The Polish Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr X. Yonder of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant mainly complained under Articles 3 and 5 § 3 of the Convention of the inadequate conditions and the unreasonable length of his pre-trial detention. On 20080930 the President of the Fifth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCE OF THE CASE A. The circumstances of the case The applicant, Mr Zephyr Wind, is a Polish national who was born in 1964 and lives in Xanadu. 1. The applicant’s pre-trial detention and criminal proceedings against him On 9 September 2001 the District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) detained the applicant on remand on suspicion of having committed theft and forgery and of leadership of an organised criminal gang. Subsequently, the applicant’s pre-trial detention was extended on several occasions. In successive decisions, given on 1 December 2001, 15 March and 7 November 2002, 23 May and 2 July 2003, the court repeatedly relied on the strong probability that the applicant had committed the offences and that there was a real risk that he would receive a severe sentence. This – together with the fact that he had acted in a gang and that there were several co-accused in the case –gave rise to a presumption that he would obstruct the proper conduct of the proceedings. In the meantime, on 10 March 2002 a bill of indictment was issued, charging the applicant with multiple theft, forgery, possession of a firearm without a licence and leadership of an organised criminal gang. The first court’s hearing took place on 7 June 2002. Subsequently, ten sessions were scheduled in 2002; eighteen in 2003; sixteen in 2004; and eleven in 2005. In 2002 the trial court heard testimonies of thirty witnesses; in 2003 - of forty; in 2004 – of five; and in 2005 of four. The court also examined other voluminous evidence and considered various procedural motions filed by the applicant and other co-defendants. As the length of the applicant’s detention had reached the statutory 2-year time-limit laid down in Article 263 § 3 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) applied to the Court of Appeal (Sąd Apelacyjny) asking for the applicant’s detention to be extended beyond that period.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/99) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a Xanadan national, Mr Xanadu (“the applicant”), on 1 January 1999. The applicant, who had been granted legal aid, was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in Y City. The Republic of Xanadu (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant alleged that he had been denied a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal due to the presence of a military judge on the bench of the Y City State Security Court which tried and convicted him. He maintained under Articles 9 and 10 of the Convention that he had been convicted on account of his political opinions. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1999, when Protocol No. 12 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 12). The application was allocated to the First Section of the Court (Rule 53 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 28 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 27 § 1. On 1 November 2002 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 26 § 1). This case was assigned to the newly composed First Section (Rule 53 § 1). By a decision of 8 July 2004, the Court declared the application partly admissible. It retained the applicant’s complaint concerning the alleged lack of independence and impartiality of the Y City State Security Court which tried and convicted him and declared inadmissible the remainder of his complaints. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 60 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1970 and lives in Y City. On 15 October 1994 the applicant was arrested by police officers from the Y City Security Directorate following a search conducted in his house. On 20 November 1994 the public prosecutor attached to the Y City State Security Court laid charges against the applicant and six other persons for having formed an illegal organisation (“Partiye Rizgariye Kurdistan”: hereinafter “PRK”) whose aim was to undermine the territorial integrity of the State by illegal means. The applicant and his co-accused were also charged with distributing illegal leaflets and carrying identification cards and driving licences belonging to third parties. The public prosecutor requested the court to convict the applicant and his co-accused under Article 126 of the Criminal Code with reference to Articles 172 § 1, 351 § 2 and 537 §§ 2 and 3 of the same Code as well as Article 6 of the Prevention of Terrorism Act (Law no. 3723 of 15 April 1992).

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Government ("the Government") on 15 January 1998, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 § 1 and Article 47 of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 24271/94) against the Republic ("the State") lodged with the Commission ("the Commission") under Article 25 by a national, Mr John Doe, on 10 June 1993. The Government’s application referred to Article 48 of the Convention. The object of the application was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention. In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 § 3 (d) of the Rules of Court A, the applicant stated that he wished to take part in the proceedings and sought leave to present his own case. The President of the Chamber refused leave and requested the applicant to appoint to represent him an advocate authorised to practise in any of the Contracting States and resident in the territory of one of them (Rule 30 § 1). As the applicant did not designate a representative within the time allowed him by the President, the Court assumed that he did not wish to take part in the proceedings. On 25 January 1998 the President of the Court, Mr X. Yssdal, decided, under Rule 21 § 7 and in the interests of the proper administration of justice, that a single Chamber should be constituted to consider both the instant case and the case of Smith v. State. The Chamber to be constituted for that purpose included ex officio Mr Z. Pettiti, the elected judge of national origin (Article 43 of the Convention), and Mr R. Bernhardt, the Vice-President of the Court (Rule 21 § 4 (b)). On the same day, in the presence of the Registrar, the President of the Court drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr A. Gölcüklü, Mr B. Matscher, Mr C. Spielmann, Mr D. PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/03) against the Republic of Xanadu lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by Mr X Y Z (“the applicant”) on 15 March 2003. The applicant was represented by Mr A B C, a lawyer practising in Yonder (Xanadu). The Xanadu Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Mr D E F, Head of the International Law Department at the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Administrative Court had failed to hold an oral hearing and had thus breached Article 6. On 20 August 2004 the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the Convention, it decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1940 and lives in Zephyr. On 15 April 1995 the applicant requested the mayor of Zephyr to issue a demolition order for his neighbour's wicker fence. He submitted, in particular, that the fence had not been constructed in accordance with the provisions of the Building Act relating to fire-protection measures. Further, the fence hindered him in the exercise of his right to carry out maintenance works on a wooden fence he had erected on his own land. As the mayor had not taken a decision within the statutory time-limit, the applicant lodged a request for transfer of jurisdiction with the Zephyr municipal council on 25 July 2002. On 3 August 2002 the applicant repeated his request of 15 April 2004 for the removal of the neighbour's fence. The mayor notified the applicant on 24 July 2002 that, according to his neighbours' statements, the applicant would be allowed to enter their property provided that they were given seven days' notice. The issuing of an administrative decision (Bescheid) would therefore be superfluous. The applicant filed a further request on 26 July 2002, insisting on a decision by the mayor. By notification of 28 July 2002 the mayor informed the applicant that, according to his neighbours, the fence had already been removed. He asked the applicant if he still wanted the municipal council to decide on his request for transfer of jurisdiction. On 30 July 2002 the applicant wrote to the municipal council saying that he was still waiting for a decision. On 15 August 2002 the Zephyr municipal council, informed the applicant that it did not find it necessary to take a formal decision on the case, as the fence had been removed. On 5 September 2002 the applicant lodged an appeal (Vorstellung) with the Lower Xanadu Regional Government stating that even though the fence itself had been removed, there were still four iron fence posts standing along the common border.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 37715/11) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Ms X (“the applicant”), on 17 December 2010. The applicant was represented by Mr Y, a lawyer practising in Z. The government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the national authorities had failed to carry out an effective investigation into the disappearance of her husband, in breach of Article 2 of the Convention. On 23 October 2012 the application was communicated to the Government. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1966 and lives in Z. The facts of the case as submitted by the parties and as they appear from the documents submitted by them, may be summarised as follows. A. The investigation carried out between 2005 and 2006 On 4 March 2005 the applicant’s mother-in-law, Mrs A, submitted a petition to Suruç prosecutor B, and informed him that on 3 June 1994 her son C, the applicant’s husband, had been travelling home on his motorbike when he was stopped and apprehended by soldiers who had set up a temporary base in a public building near D village. She described the motorbike as “Russian-made, red and with a basket”. She told the prosecutor that nothing had been heard from her son since that date and that the complaint she had made to the authorities some six days after the disappearance had not elucidated any response. She gave the prosecutor the names of two villagers who, she claimed, had witnessed her son being apprehended, and asked the prosecutor to make enquiries in order to find her son. The same day the Suruç prosecutor B questioned Mrs A in relation to her above-mentioned petition. Mrs A confirmed the contents of her petition detailed above and added that the family had been informed about the incident some two days afterwards by villagers who had witnessed the incident. Her elder son, D, had then gone to the military base near D village where he was informed that his younger brother had been transferred to the gendarmerie station in Suruç. When D had gone to the gendarmerie station in Suruç, he was told that his brother’s questioning was continuing and that it would probably continue for another three days. When C was not released, D had gone to the Suruç prosecutor’s office and informed the prosecutor of the detention of his younger brother. When the prosecutor had contacted the military authorities he was told that C had never been detained by the military. The family’s subsequent attempts to find C had not yielded any results. A detailed investigation was carried out by Suruç prosecutor B into the allegations made by Mrs A.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 1234/08) against the Republic of Europe lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a European national, Ms Maria Anna Novakova (“the applicant”), on 1 January 2008. The European Government (“the Government”) were represented by their Agent, Mr A. Zawadowski of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. On 5 July 2008 the President of the Fourth Section decided to give notice of the application to the Government. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 3). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1950 and lives in Warsaw. A. Main proceedings On 10 June 1994 the applicant lodged with the Warsaw District Court (Sąd Rejonowy) an application for division of matrimonial property. She paid the relevant court fees on 10 November 1994. Between 10 June 1994 and 22 February 2004, the District Court scheduled 30 hearings, 7 of which were adjourned due to the failure of the applicant’s husband to appear; only two hearings were scheduled in 1996, no hearing was scheduled between 9 December 1997 and 16 June 1999 and two hearings were scheduled in 2000. On 6 March 2004 the Warsaw District Court delivered a partial decision (postanowienie częściowe) on the parties’ respective shares in the matrimonial property. Between 5 August 2005 and 17 April 2009, the District Court scheduled 15 hearings, 4 of which were adjourned. No hearing was held in 2006. On 24 June 2009 the Warsaw District Court gave a decision. The applicant appealed. The proceedings are pending before the second-instance court. B. Proceedings under the 2005 Act On 2 June 2007 the applicant lodged with the Warsaw Regional Court (Sąd Okręgowy) a complaint under section 5 of the Law on 17 June 2004 on complaints about a breach of the right to a trial within a reasonable time (Ustawa o skardze na naruszenie prawa strony do rozpoznania sprawy w postępowaniu sądowym bez nieuzasadnionej zwłoki) (“the 2004 Act”) which entered into force on 17 September 2004. She sought a ruling declaring that the length of the proceedings before the Warsaw District Court had been excessive and an award of just satisfaction in the amount of 10,000 Polish zlotys (PLN) (approx. 2,500 euros (EUR)). On 5 August 2006 the Warsaw Regional Court gave a decision. The court held that the 2004 Act did not have retroactive effect and, consequently, examined the applicant’s claim only in respect of the period between the entry into force of the 2004 Act on 17 September 2004 and the date on which the complaint had been lodged. The court found that, during that part of the proceedings, there had been some periods of inactivity for which the District Court had been responsible. The court awarded the applicant PLN 2,000 (approx. EUR 526 euros) in just satisfaction.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 32381/96) against a country (Country X) lodged with an organization (Organization Y) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (the Convention) by a national (National X) (Applicant) on 29 May 1996. The applicant was represented before the Court by Mr. Lawyer, a lawyer practicing in a city (City X) (Country X). The government (Government) of Country X were represented by their Agent, Ambassador Y, Head of the International Law Department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The applicant alleged that in criminal proceedings against him relating to an administrative offense no oral hearing has been held. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. By a decision of 16 January 2001 the Court declared the application admissible. As from 1 November 2001 the application was reallocated to the First Section of the Court. Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27 § 1 of the Convention) was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1 of the Rules of Court. Neither the applicant nor the Government filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE On 9 November 1994 a district administrative authority (Authority) convicted the applicant twice under the Motor Vehicles Act (Act) for failure to comply with the instructions of the Authority to inform them who had used his car on specific days (Lenkerauskunft), and sentenced him, on each offence, to a fine of 4,000 currency units or six days’ imprisonment in default. The Authority noted that the applicant had given information but found it to be incorrect. On 29 November 1994 the applicant filed an appeal against this decision with an administrative panel (Panel). He complained that the district administrative authority had incorrectly applied the law and failed to sufficiently assess the evidence before it or clarify why the information he had given was untrue. The applicant did not request a hearing, nor did he expressly waive this right. No oral hearing was held. On 2 January 1995 the panel dismissed the appeal on the merits but reduced the sentence. On 28 February 1995 the applicant filed a complaint with the constitutional court (Court). He complained under Article 6 § 1 of the Convention that the administrative panel had failed to hold a hearing. Such a hearing would have been necessary because his appeal was not limited to points of law.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Human Rights Commission (“the Commission“) within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 of the Convention (art. 32-1, art. 47). It originated in an application (no. 22500/93) against the Republic of X, lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by two X nationals, Mrs X X, née X, and Mr X X on 28 March 1987. The Commission's request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby X recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 8 of the Convention (art. 8). In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 para. 3 (d) of Rules of Court A, the applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings. The President gave the applicants leave, as lawyers, to present their own case to the Court (Rule 30 para. 1). The Chamber to be constituted included ex officio Mr X Pettiti, the elected judge of X nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr X Ryssdal, the President of the Court (Rule 21 para. 4 (b)). On 8 June 1995, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other seven members, namely Mr X Macdonald, Mr X Spielmann, Mr X De Meyer, Mr X Pekkanen, Mr X Morenilla, Mr X Bigi and Mr X Jambrek (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 para. 5) (art. 43). Subsequently, Mr X Baka, substitute judge, replaced Mr Bigi, who was unable to take part in the further consideration of the case (Rule 22 para. 1). As President of the Chamber (Rule 21 para. 6), Mr Ryssdal, acting through the Registrar, consulted the Agent of the X Government (“the Government“), the applicants and the Delegate of the Commission on the organisation of the proceedings (Rules 37 para. 1 and 38). Pursuant to the order made in consequence, the Registrar received the Government's memorial on 27 November 1995. On 30 January 1996, the Secretary to the Commission indicated that the Delegate did not intend to reply in writing. On 7 February 1996 the Registrar received a letter from the applicants requesting that their daughter be heard by the Court. On 21 February 1996 the Chamber decided not to grant this request (Rule 41 para. 1). On 17 August 1995 the Commission had produced the documents of the proceedings before it, as requested by the Registrar on the President's instructions. In accordance with the President's decision, the hearing took place in public in the Human Rights Building, X, on 23 April 1996. The Court had held a preparatory meeting beforehand.

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/02) against a country lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a national, Mr John Doe (“the applicant”), on 1 March 2001. The applicant was represented by a law firm in a city. The Government were represented by their Agent, Mr X Y Z of a government office in the city. The applicant complained under Articles 8 and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 that, because he was a man, he was denied social security benefits equivalent to those received by widows. On 12 November 2002 the Court decided to communicate the complaints concerning widows’ benefits relating to the period after the date on which the applicant lodged his relevant claim and declared the remainder of the application inadmissible. Subsequently, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. THE FACTS I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE The applicant was born in 1949 and lives in a region. His wife died on 11 May 1994 leaving dependent children. His second claim for widows’ benefits was made in July 2000 and was rejected on 11 July 2000 on the ground that he was not entitled to widows’ benefits because he was not a woman. On 2 October 2000 the applicant applied for reconsideration and on 1 November 2000 he was requested to complete another claim form. The applicant did so and his claim was rejected on 20 November 2000. The applicant did not appeal further as he considered or was advised that such a remedy would be bound to fail since no such social security benefits were payable to widowers under the country’s law. At the time of his claim the applicant was in receipt of child benefit.

PROCEDURE The case was referred to the Court by the Human Rights Commission (“the Commission“) on 15 February 1985, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 § 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Human Rights Convention (“the Convention“). It originated in an application (no. 10300/83) against the State in question lodged with the Commission under Article 25 (art. 25) by a national of that State, Ms. Jane Doe, on 7 February 1983. The Commission’s request referred to Articles 44 and 48 (art. 44, art. 48) and to the declaration whereby the State in question recognised the compulsory jurisdiction of the Court (Article 46) (art. 46). The purpose of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether or not the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 § 2 (art. 6-2). In response to the enquiry made in accordance with Rule 33 § 3 (d) of the Rules of Court, Ms. Doe stated that she wished to take part in the proceedings pending before the Court and designated the lawyer who would represent her (Rule 30). On 15 February 1985, the President of the Court decided that in the interests of the proper administration of justice this case and the Lutz and Englert cases should be considered by the same Chamber (Rule 21 § 6). The Chamber of seven judges to be constituted included, as ex officio members, Mr. A. Smith, the elected judge of State nationality (Article 43 of the Convention) (art. 43), and Mr. B. Johnson, the President of the Court (Rule 21 § 3 (b)). On 15 March 1985, in the presence of the Registrar, the President drew by lot the names of the other five members, namely Mr. C. Brown, Mr. D. Green, Mr. E. White, Ms. F. Black and Mr. G. Brown (Article 43 in fine of the Convention and Rule 21 § 4) (art. 43). After assuming the office of President of the Chamber (Rule 21 § 5), Mr. Johnson consulted, through the Deputy Registrar, the Agent of the State Government (“the Government“), the Delegate of the Commission and the lawyer for the applicant on the need for a written procedure. On 15 April, he directed that the Agent and the applicant’s lawyer should have until 1 July 1985 to file memorials and that the Delegate should be entitled to reply in writing within two months (Rule 37 § 1). The President twice extended the first of these time-limits - on 15 July until 31 October, and on 15 November until 21 November 1985. The applicant’s memorial - drafted in the State’s language, with the President’s leave (Rule 27 § 3) - was lodged with the registry on 15 July 1985 and the Government’s on 15 November. On 15 November, the Chamber decided to relinquish jurisdiction forthwith in favour of the plenary Court (Rule 50).

PROCEDURE The case originated in an application (no. 12345/98) against the Republic of X ("the Republic") lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights ("the Commission") under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms ("the Convention") by a Y national, Mr Alex Smith ("the applicant"), on 27 March 1998. The applicant was represented by Mr John Doe, a lawyer practising in City. The Republic ("the Government") were represented by their Agent, Mr John Smith. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the occupation of the northern part of Y had prevented him from having access to his home and properties. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 § 2 of Protocol No. 11). By a decision of 1 February 2000 the Court declared the application admissible. The applicant and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). In addition, third-party comments were received from the Government of Z, which had exercised its right to intervene (Article 36 § 1 of the Convention and Rule 44 § 1 (b)). THE FACTS The applicant was born in 1942 and lives in the United Kingdom. The applicant claimed that until 14 August 1974 he and his family used to live in City (Y) in a detached house with a yard (area: 229 sq. m). This property was registered in the name of the applicant's wife under plot no. 315, sheet/plan 19/32.5.2. On 14 August 1974, as the forces were advancing, the applicant and his family fled their home leaving behind all its contents, including precious personal belongings. The applicant also claimed that he was the owner of the following plots of land in northern Y: (a) City/Z, plot no. 576, sheet/plan 19/16, field, area: 5,017 sq. m; (b) City/W, plot no. 39/1, sheet/plan 5/62W1, field, area: 112,149 sq. m; (c) City/W, plot no. 14, sheet/plan 5/62W2, field, area: 171,549 sq. m; (d) City/W, plot no. 34, sheet/plan 5/63W1, field, area: 22,074 sq. m; (e) City/W, plot no. 45, sheet/plan 5/63W1, field, area: 11,582 sq. m. In support of his claim of ownership the applicant produced the relevant certificates of registration and affirmations of ownership issued by the Republic of Y. The applicant alleged that from 14 August 1974 onwards he had not been able to return to his house and had been continuously prevented from exercising his property rights and enjoying his properties.
